1. The Nature of Guarantor Liability: Section 128 of the Contract Act 1872

In Bangladeshi legal jurisprudence, the relationship between a creditor, a principal debtor, and a surety is fundamentally governed by Chapter VIII of the Contract Act 1872. Section 126 defines a contract of guarantee as a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of their default.

The foundational principle governing enforcement is found in Section 128 of the Contract Act, which establishes that the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract. This means that as soon as the borrower defaults, the creditor bank has the theoretical legal right to demand payment from the guarantor without necessarily exhausting every civil remedy against the primary borrower first.

However, commercial banks operating in Bangladesh do not operate solely under general common law. They are bound by the specialized procedural constraints of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 and the regulatory circulars issued by Bangladesh Bank. These specialized enactments heavily condition how co-extensive liability can be executed in practice.

2. Statutory Mandates: Sections 6 and 12 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003

The Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 is a special law designed for the expeditious recovery of defaulted loans by scheduled commercial banks and non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs). When initiating a recovery lawsuit, banks must adhere strictly to statutory procedural prerequisites concerning guarantors.

Under Section 6(1) of the 2003 Act, the financial institution is legally obligated to implead the principal debtor, all third-party mortgagors, and personal guarantors together in the single original suit. A bank cannot split its claims or file separate piecemeal suits against the guarantor at a later date if they were omitted from the primary plaint.

More critically, Section 12 of the Act establishes a mandatory order of enforcement. Under Section 12(1), if the loan is secured by any immovable mortgaged property or movable hypothecated assets, the financial institution must put those mortgaged properties to public auction before or immediately upon filing the suit. The Supreme Court Appellate Division has firmly ruled that banks cannot bypass primary mortgaged securities and directly seize the unencumbered residential homes or bank accounts of third-party guarantors without first establishing that the mortgaged securities were genuinely auctioned and found insufficient to satisfy the debt.

3. CIB Blacklisting: Impact on Personal Credit, Directors & Travel

One of the most devastating weapons deployed by commercial banks against personal guarantors is negative reporting to the Credit Information Bureau (CIB) of Bangladesh Bank. Under central bank guidelines, once a credit facility is classified as Bad/Loss (BL), the bank reports both the borrower entity and all individual personal guarantors as defaulters.

CIB blacklisting paralyzes a guarantor's commercial life. The individual is barred from obtaining any personal home loans, auto loans, or credit cards from any bank in Bangladesh. If the guarantor is a director or managing partner in other completely healthy, profitable corporate enterprises, the CIB classification can infect those unrelated companies, triggering credit line cancellations, letter of credit (LC) opening blocks, and disqualification from participating in public tenders.

Are you a personal loan guarantor facing Artha Rin suits, bank notices, or CIB blacklisting in Bangladesh? Immediate intervention by specialized banking litigators is vital to protect your assets and credit standing. Message our chamber on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for strategic advice.

Furthermore, under recent banking regulations, individuals classified as habitual loan defaulters face severe administrative restrictions, including prohibitions on directorships and potential restrictions on international travel. However, where a bank reports a guarantor to the CIB prematurely—without serving statutory demand notices or while an Artha Rin suit is actively contested—the affected party has constitutional recourse to challenge the reporting.

4. Civil Imprisonment Risks: Section 34 Rules and 6-Month Hard Cap

A major source of anxiety for personal guarantors is the threat of arrest and imprisonment for another person's defaulted loan. Under Section 34 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003, the Money Loan Court does possess statutory authority in execution proceedings (Artha Jari Mamla) to order the civil detention of a judgment-debtor who fails to satisfy a money decree.

However, Section 34 is subject to strict judicial safeguards that protect against arbitrary incarceration:

  • Maximum 6-Month Hard Cap: Under Section 34(1), the maximum period of civil detention for any judgment-debtor or guarantor is strictly limited to six (6) months. Once a person completes six months of civil detention, they can never be detained again for that specific loan decree.
  • Prior Property Seizure Required: Under Section 34(2), the executing court cannot issue a warrant of arrest unless it is satisfied that the decree cannot be executed through the attachment and sale of the judgment-debtor's movable or immovable properties.
  • Exemption for Women and Infirm Persons: The court exercises strong equitable discretion under the CPC to exempt elderly, critically ill, or female guarantors who did not directly benefit from the disbursed loan proceeds.
  • Civil Jail, Not Criminal Conviction: Civil detention under Section 34 is not a criminal punishment and does not result in a criminal record; it is purely a coercive execution mechanism.

5. Legal Grounds for Discharge of Guarantor under the Contract Act

When defended by seasoned banking litigators, personal guarantors possess powerful statutory shields under the Contract Act 1872 that can completely discharge them from financial liability. If the bank or borrower took actions behind the guarantor's back, the guarantee may be legally extinguished.

The primary grounds for legal discharge of a surety include:

  1. Variance in Terms Without Consent (Section 133): Any variance made without the surety's consent in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and creditor discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance. If the bank rescheduled the loan, increased the interest rate, or extended fresh tenure without the guarantor's signature, liability ceases.
  2. Release of Principal Debtor (Section 134): The surety is discharged by any contract between the creditor and debtor by which the principal debtor is released, or by any act or omission of the creditor resulting in the debtor's discharge.
  3. Compounding or Giving Time (Section 135): A contract between the creditor and principal debtor by which the creditor makes a composition with, or promises to give time to, or not to sue, the principal debtor, discharges the surety unless the surety assents to such contract.
  4. Impairment of Surety's Remedy (Section 139): If the creditor does any act inconsistent with the rights of the surety, or omits to do any act which his duty requires, and the eventual remedy of the surety against the principal debtor is impaired, the surety is discharged. For instance, if the bank negligently failed to register a mortgage over borrower land, allowing the borrower to sell it off, the personal guarantor is discharged to the extent of that lost security.

6. Summary Matrix: Principal Debtor vs. Third-Party Guarantor Rights

To assess exposure and formulate defense tactics, understand how the law treats the primary borrower compared to an independent guarantor. The following comparative matrix outlines key distinctions under Bangladeshi banking law:

Legal Dimension Principal Borrower Third-Party Personal Guarantor
Receipt of Loan Proceeds Direct beneficiary of disbursed funds Usually receives zero direct financial disbursement
Enforcement Sequence Directly liable; primary mortgaged assets auctioned first Protected by Section 12 until primary collateral is exhausted
Right to Indemnity Must indemnify surety for all lawful payments made Entitled to step into bank's shoes under Section 140 Contract Act
Discharge by Alteration Remains liable despite rescheduling or restructuring Discharged under Section 133 if terms altered without consent
Civil Detention Risk Subject to Section 34 (max 6 months) Subject to Section 34 only after all borrower assets fail

7. High Court Writ Remedies (Article 102) Against Arbitrary Bank Action

When scheduled banks act in flagrant violation of statutory mandates—such as blacklisting a guarantor on CIB without issuing prior mandatory 12-day demand notices, or freezing the guarantor's personal operating accounts without a court attachment order—the High Court Division offers swift equitable protection under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh.

Through a Writ of Mandamus or Certiorari, an aggrieved guarantor can challenge the arbitrary reporting to the Credit Information Bureau. The High Court Division frequently grants interim orders directing Bangladesh Bank to stay the negative CIB status of the guarantor, or permitting the guarantor to continue operating unrelated business bank accounts and renew trade licenses pending final adjudication of the Artha Rin suit.

Similarly, where the Artha Rin Adalat issues a warrant of arrest under Section 34 without first verifying whether the bank complied with Section 12 mortgage auction requirements, the High Court Division will intervene to stay the arrest warrant and direct the executing court to follow the mandatory statutory sequence of property realization. For detailed insights on corporate debt litigation, review our guide on Artha Rin Adalat bank loan default defense.

8. Illustrative Scenario: Protecting a Managing Director's Personal Estate

To understand how guarantor defense operates in the Money Loan Court, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A textile entrepreneur in Dhaka served as a minority director in a manufacturing enterprise that secured a 40 Crore BDT project loan from a private commercial bank in 2017. As part of the standard loan sanction letter, the bank required all directors to sign personal guarantee forms, while the company pledged 15 bighas of factory land and imported machinery as primary collateral. Following global supply disruptions, the company defaulted.

Rather than auctioning the factory land and machinery under Section 12 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, the bank filed an Artha Rin suit, immediately reported the director to CIB, and applied for the attachment of his personal residential apartment in Dhanmondi. The director retained a Supreme Court advocate to mount an aggressive legal defense.

The defense team demonstrated before the Artha Rin Adalat that the primary mortgaged factory assets had an independent market valuation exceeding 55 Crore BDT, which the bank had arbitrarily refused to auction. Simultaneously, the advocate filed a Writ Petition before the High Court Division challenging the premature CIB blacklisting. The High Court stayed the CIB classification, while the Artha Rin Court dismissed the bank's petition to attach the director's personal apartment, ordering the bank to first auction the mortgaged factory land. The dispute was subsequently resolved through a negotiated one-time settlement (OTS).

9. Essential Risk Mitigation Checklist for Prospective & Existing Guarantors

Before signing a personal guarantee or when navigating an existing bank loan dispute in Bangladesh, follow these critical legal safeguards:

  • Insist on a Limited-Amount Guarantee: Never sign a standard 'unlimited and continuing guarantee.' Ensure the guarantee deed contains a strict financial cap and an expiration date tied to specific project milestones.
  • Verify Collateral Adequacy: Confirm that the borrower provides robust first-charge immovable property mortgages that comfortably cover the principal debt and projected interest.
  • Monitor Facility Restructuring: Never verbally consent to loan reschedulings. If the bank and borrower restructure the loan facility without your formal written consent, assert your immediate statutory discharge under Section 133 of the Contract Act.
  • Respond Immediately to Bank Demand Notices: When an advocate notice or bank default letter arrives, issue a formal written reply through an advocate denying liability, putting the bank on notice to exhaust Section 12 mortgaged securities first.
  • Retain Specialized Artha Rin Counsel: Do not ignore summons from the Artha Rin Adalat. File an immediate written statement (Jabab) asserting all defenses under the Contract Act 1872 and Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003.

For strategic representation in commercial banking litigation, explore our dedicated company and corporate legal counsel and Supreme Court litigation services.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a Banking & Corporate Advocate in Dhaka: To defend against Artha Rin execution warrants, challenge premature CIB blacklisting before the High Court Division under Article 102, or negotiate a structured guarantor release, reach out via WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call our chamber at +880 1712-655546. Confidential consultations for corporate directors and expatriates are available.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a bank sue a loan guarantor without suing the main borrower in Bangladesh?

No. Under Section 6(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003, the financial institution is legally mandated to implead the principal borrower, mortgagors, and all third-party personal guarantors together in the single original lawsuit.

Can a bank directly seize a guarantor's personal house or property?

Not immediately. Under Section 12 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003, the bank is statutorily required to put all primary mortgaged and hypothecated securities of the borrower to public auction before pursuing unencumbered personal assets of guarantors.

Can a guarantor be sent to civil jail for another person's defaulted loan?

Under Section 34 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, the court can order civil detention during execution proceedings, but it is strictly capped at a maximum of six (6) months, and only after the court is satisfied that the decree cannot be satisfied through property sales.

What happens if a bank reports a guarantor to Bangladesh Bank's CIB?

Negative CIB reporting blocks the guarantor from securing personal loans, auto credit, or business credit lines. However, if the reporting was done arbitrarily or without required statutory notice, the guarantor can challenge and stay the CIB status via a High Court writ.

Does loan rescheduling without the guarantor's consent release the guarantor?

Yes. Under Section 133 of the Contract Act 1872, any variance made in the terms of the credit contract between the creditor bank and borrower without the surety's consent legally discharges the surety from liability for subsequent transactions.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi guarantor be arrested at Dhaka airport for an Artha Rin case?

If the Artha Rin Adalat issues a warrant of civil arrest under Section 34 in execution proceedings and law enforcement is notified, an individual could be stopped. Retaining counsel to obtain a stay order from the High Court Division protects against airport interception.

What is Section 140 of the Contract Act (Subrogation) for guarantors?

Under Section 140 of the Contract Act 1872, once a guarantor pays the debt to the bank, they step into the shoes of the bank and acquire all rights of the creditor to sue the principal debtor and seize the borrower's properties for complete reimbursement.

Can a guarantor resign or revoke a personal guarantee in Bangladesh?

Under Section 130 of the Contract Act 1872, a continuing guarantee may at any time be revoked by the surety as to future transactions by issuing formal written notice to the creditor bank, subject to the specific terms of the signed guarantee deed.

BIDA Work Permit in Bangladesh: Expatriate Visa, Security Clearance & NBR Tax Rules

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-08 · 19 minutes

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

With expanding foreign direct investment, infrastructure mega-projects, and multinational corporate presence in Bangladesh, employing expatriate managers, specialized engineers, and technical consultants is common practice. However, foreign nationals cannot lawfully work or receive local compensation in Bangladesh on a tourist, business, or visitor visa. Working without a formal statutory work permit constitutes a severe breach of immigration and foreign exchange laws, exposing both the expatriate employee and the employer company to heavy financial penalties, deportation, and immigration blacklisting. For industrial and commercial sectors, work permits are primarily granted by the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA) under the Prime Minister's Office, alongside the Bangladesh Export Processing Zones Authority (BEPZA) for EPZ units. This legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate and corporate practitioner in Uttara and Dhaka, outlines the end-to-end statutory procedure for securing BIDA work permits, E-visas, security clearances, and NBR tax compliance.

1. Statutory Framework: BIDA, BEPZA & Immigration Laws

In Bangladesh, foreign nationals cannot engage in gainful employment without prior official authorization from the Government. The regulatory framework is anchored in the Foreigners Act 1946 (Act No. XXXI of 1946), the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority Act 2016 (Act No. XXXVI of 2016), and statutory guidelines formulated by the Security Services Division of the Ministry of Home Affairs.

Different statutory bodies issue work permits based on the industrial location and corporate structure of the sponsoring enterprise:

  • BIDA (Bangladesh Investment Development Authority): Regulates private limited companies, foreign branch offices, liaison offices, and commercial establishments operating outside export processing zones across Bangladesh.
  • BEPZA (Bangladesh Export Processing Zones Authority): Governs foreign nationals employed within designated Export Processing Zones (EPZs) under the Bangladesh Export Processing Zones Authority Act 1980.
  • BHTPA (Bangladesh Hi-Tech Park Authority): Regulates expatriate technology personnel employed in government-notified software technology parks and hi-tech zones.
  • NGO Affairs Bureau (NGOAB): Governs foreign consultants and executives working with registered non-governmental organizations funded by foreign donations.

Engaging expatriates without statutory permission exposes companies to penal sanctions, corporate tax penalty assessments from the National Board of Revenue, and cancellation of foreign remittance permissions. For company incorporation guidance, examine our guide on registering a 100% foreign-owned company in Bangladesh.

2. Step 1: Securing the E-Visa Recommendation via BIDA OSS

A common error made by international corporations is sending foreign executives to Dhaka on a Business Visa (B-Visa) or Tourist Visa (T-Visa) with the expectation of converting it locally. Bangladeshi immigration laws strictly bar local visa status conversion. An expatriate destined for employment must arrive with an official Employment Visa ('E' Visa) stamped in their passport prior to departure.

The procedural workflow to secure an E-Visa is as follows:

  1. BIDA Company Registration: The employer entity in Bangladesh must be registered with BIDA and possess an active profile on the BIDA One-Stop Service (OSS) digital portal.
  2. Board Resolution & Appointment Letter: The company board passes a formal resolution approving the employment, detailing designation, salary structure, and necessity of specialized overseas skills.
  3. Submission of E-Visa Recommendation Application: The company submits an online application on the BIDA OSS platform, attaching the expatriate's academic credentials, resume, passport copy, company memorandum, and appointment contract.
  4. Issuance of BIDA Recommendation Letter: Upon scrutiny, BIDA issues a formal Visa Recommendation Letter addressed to the relevant Bangladesh Embassy, High Commission, or Consulate abroad.
  5. Consular Visa Stamping: The expatriate presents the BIDA recommendation letter along with their passport to the designated Bangladesh mission abroad, which stamps the initial 3-month Employment ('E') Visa.

3. Step 2: Work Permit Filing & 15-Day Post-Arrival Rule

Upon touchdown at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (HSIA) or another international port of entry on a valid E-Visa, a strict statutory deadline begins. Under BIDA regulatory guidelines, the sponsoring employer must submit the formal online application for a Work Permit within fifteen (15) calendar days of the expatriate's physical arrival in Bangladesh.

The application packet submitted via the BIDA OSS platform must incorporate:

  • Copy of the stamped E-Visa and immigration entry seal showing the exact arrival date.
  • Certified copies of the employer company's BIDA Registration Certificate, RJSC Certificate of Incorporation, Memorandum and Articles of Association, and current Trade License.
  • Detailed curriculum vitae, professional certificates, and university degrees of the expatriate (authenticated by relevant authorities if requested).
  • Copy of employment advertisement published in at least two widely circulated Bangladeshi national daily newspapers, demonstrating that qualified local candidates were unavailable.
  • Complete list of all local and foreign personnel currently employed by the enterprise, verifying adherence to statutory staffing ratios.

Submitting the work permit application after the 15-day window incurs daily administrative delay fines and can lead to immediate rejection by the BIDA Scrutiny Committee.

4. The 1:5 and 1:20 Local Employment Ratio Rules

Need legal assistance with BIDA work permits or expatriate visas? Contact our corporate immigration desk on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007. We provide complete document vetting and government liaison.

To preserve domestic employment opportunities, the Government of Bangladesh enforces mandatory staffing ratios that companies must satisfy before work permits are sanctioned:

  • Commercial & Service Sector Companies (1:5 Ratio): For commercial offices, software firms, consulting agencies, branch offices, and liaison offices, the company must employ at least five (5) full-time Bangladeshi personnel for every one (1) expatriate employee.
  • Industrial & Manufacturing Enterprises (1:20 Ratio): For manufacturing plants, factories, and industrial facilities, the sponsoring entity must maintain an employment ratio of at least twenty (20) Bangladeshi workers for every one (1) foreign national.

The sponsoring enterprise must substantiate these ratios by submitting payroll sheets, bank salary transfer records, and employee e-TIN certificates. Top corporate executive appointments (such as Managing Director or Chief Executive Officer of a 100% foreign-owned subsidiary) may qualify for specialized consideration, but overall ratio thresholds remain strictly enforced during subsequent permit renewals.

6. Security Clearance: Home Ministry & Special Branch (SB) Vetting

Issuance of the physical BIDA work permit is conditional upon obtaining formal security clearance from the Government of Bangladesh. Upon granting provisional approval, BIDA automatically transmits the file to the Security Services Division of the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The security verification process unfolds through two intelligence channels:

  1. Special Branch (SB) Verification: Officers from the Special Branch of Police visit the employer's registered commercial premises to verify physical operations, examine company books, interview local directors, and verify the foreign national's physical residence and passport credentials.
  2. National Security Intelligence (NSI) Review: State intelligence agencies review international background databases, travel histories, and INTERPOL records to ensure the individual poses no security, financial, or political risks.

Security clearance is typically concluded within 45 to 60 days. If an adverse report is rendered due to administrative errors or mistaken identity, the sponsoring enterprise must promptly submit a formal review petition accompanied by verified credentials. In arbitrary rejection cases, remedies lie before the High Court Division under Article 102. See our guide on travel bans and airport offloading in Bangladesh.

7. Expatriate Income Tax Compliance Under Income Tax Act 2023

A critical statutory obligation accompanying any work permit in Bangladesh is personal income taxation administered by the National Board of Revenue (NBR) under the Income Tax Act 2023 (Act No. XII of 2023).

Key statutory tax mandates include:

  • Mandatory e-TIN Registration: Within thirty (30) days of receiving the work permit, the expatriate employee must register for a 12-digit electronic Tax Identification Number (e-TIN) through the NBR digital portal.
  • Taxation Rates: Foreign nationals qualifying as non-residents are taxed at a flat rate of 30% on total Bangladeshi-sourced income without the personal basic exemption thresholds available to domestic taxpayers, unless beneficial double tax avoidance treaties (DTAA) apply.
  • Monthly Source Tax Deduction (TDS): Under Section 86 of the Income Tax Act 2023, the employer company must deduct tax at source on a monthly payroll basis and deposit it into the government exchequer via treasury e-chalans.
  • Tax Clearance Certificate for Final Departure: Under Section 166 of the Income Tax Act 2023, an expatriate cannot lawfully leave Bangladesh permanently upon completion of employment without obtaining a formal Tax Clearance Certificate from the competent Deputy Commissioner of Taxes (DCT). Immigration authorities at international airports can prevent departure if tax clearances are unverified.

8. Renewal, Extension & Final Cancellation Procedures

Work permits are initially granted for a term of one to two years and require structured legal maintenance:

  1. Timely Renewal Application: The employer must file the work permit extension application through BIDA OSS at least thirty (30) to sixty (60) days prior to the expiration date of the current permit. Late applications trigger administrative penalties and risk visa lapses.
  2. Documentation for Extension: Submissions must include updated tax payment chalans, personal income tax returns, audited company accounts, proof of local training succession planning, and current staff ratio certifications.
  3. Maximum Cumulative Tenure: Under national policy, an expatriate employee is generally permitted to work in Bangladesh for a maximum cumulative period of five (5) years. Extensions beyond five years require exceptional justification demonstrating that specialized technical expertise remains unavailable in the domestic labor force.
  4. Final Cancellation & Surrender: When the employment contract concludes, the company must submit a formal Work Permit Cancellation Application to BIDA, surrender the permit, obtain NBR tax clearance under Section 166, and apply to the Department of Immigration & Passports (DIP) for an exit permit.

9. Illustrative Scenario: Regularizing an Expatriate Technical Director

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): A European industrial manufacturing joint venture based in the Gazipur industrial belt appointed a German national as Chief Technical Officer to oversee high-precision automation installation. The executive entered Dhaka on a short-term 90-day business visa, but the enterprise failed to file for an employment visa recommendation prior to arrival. As the 90-day visa neared expiry, commercial operations faced severe disruption, and the local company faced penalties from the Directorate of Registration and BIDA.

The company engaged Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber to structure a lawful resolution:

  1. Audited the corporate structure and verified that the joint venture maintained a compliant 1:22 local-to-foreign staffing ratio.
  2. Advised the executive to complete a scheduled business trip to Singapore, during which our chamber filed an emergency E-Visa Recommendation Application on the BIDA OSS portal with supporting board resolutions and engineering credentials.
  3. Coordinated with BIDA and secured the official E-Visa Recommendation Letter within five working days, transmitting it to the Bangladesh High Commission in Singapore, which stamped the official Employment ('E') Visa.
  4. Upon the executive's return to Dhaka, filed the formal BIDA Work Permit Application within eight days, facilitating physical Special Branch premises verification.
  5. Assisted the executive in obtaining an e-TIN, structuring monthly payroll tax deductions under the Income Tax Act 2023, and successfully securing the final 2-year BIDA work permit without disruption to the industrial plant.

10. Talk to an Advocate: Corporate Immigration & BIDA Vetting

Navigating BIDA work permits, E-visas, Special Branch security verification, and NBR expatriate tax compliance requires proactive legal guidance. Advocate Md. Shah Alam and his dedicated corporate immigration team assist foreign corporations, joint ventures, and expatriates with complete statutory compliance in Bangladesh.

Need an advocate for this matter in Bangladesh? Send your documents on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: a first document review can be done remotely.

Our principal chamber is located in Uttara, Dhaka, minutes from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, alongside our daily litigation chamber at the Supreme Court Bar Association and Dhaka Judge Court.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a foreign national work in Bangladesh on a Business or Tourist visa?

No. Working or receiving compensation on a Tourist (T) or Business (B) visa is strictly illegal under the Foreigners Act 1946. Expatriates must enter on an Employment (E) visa recommended by BIDA or BEPZA.

What is the minimum local-to-foreign employee ratio required by BIDA?

BIDA mandates a minimum ratio of 1 foreign employee for every 5 Bangladeshi employees (1:5) in commercial and consulting firms, and 1 foreign employee for every 20 local employees (1:20) in industrial manufacturing enterprises.

How long does it take to obtain a BIDA work permit in Bangladesh?

The initial BIDA work permit approval typically takes 2 to 4 weeks following application. Full security clearance from the Home Ministry and Special Branch (SB) generally takes an additional 45 to 60 days.

What happens if a work permit application is not filed within 15 days of arrival?

Failing to submit the application within 15 days of entering on an E-visa violates BIDA guidelines, incurring administrative delay fines and jeopardizing visa extension before the Department of Immigration & Passports.

What is the personal income tax rate for foreign expatriates in Bangladesh?

Non-resident foreign employees are subject to a flat income tax rate of 30% on total Bangladeshi-sourced compensation under the Income Tax Act 2023, subject to applicable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAA).

Can an expatriate transfer employment to another company in Bangladesh?

Yes, but the expatriate must first obtain a formal No Objection Certificate (NOC) and tax clearance from the original employer, cancel the existing work permit, and secure a fresh work permit sponsored by the new entity.

What is a Section 166 Tax Clearance Certificate for departing expatriates?

Under Section 166 of the Income Tax Act 2023, an expatriate permanently departing Bangladesh must obtain an official certificate from the NBR confirming all taxes have been fully satisfied before airport immigration permits exit.

What is the maximum cumulative period an expatriate can work in Bangladesh?

The standard maximum cumulative term is five (5) years. Extensions beyond five years are granted only under exceptional circumstances where specialized technical skills remain demonstrably unavailable in the local labor market.

Common Errors

  • Spelling mistakes in the name.
  • Wrong date of birth or place.
  • Wrong parents' names or NID numbers.
  • Mismatch between the Bangla and English versions.
  • Name changed after marriage or conversion not reflected.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Online Correction Process

  1. Open the official birth and death registration portal (BDRIS) and find your registration number.
  2. Fill in the correction application and select the field to be corrected.
  3. Upload supporting documents: old certificate, NID/passport, school certificates, parents' ID, hospital record.
  4. Pay the correction fee online.
  5. The Registrar reviews the application, may call for a hearing, and issues the corrected certificate.

NRBs can apply online and let a relative or attorney attend if a hearing is needed.

Documents That Strengthen Your Application

  • Oldest school certificate (SSC or primary) showing the correct date of birth.
  • Vaccination card or hospital discharge certificate.
  • Parents' NID and marriage certificate.
  • Passport and NID of the applicant.
  • Affidavit sworn before a Magistrate or Notary stating the correct details.

When the Registrar Refuses

If the Registrar rejects the application, you can appeal to the authority specified in the Act (generally the Deputy Commissioner or the Director General of the registration authority) within the time limit given in the rejection order. For serious disputes, such as changing the date of birth by a large margin or parentage, a civil suit for declaration may be needed. An advocate can advise on the best route.

Death Certificates and Inheritance

Death certificates are needed for heirship certificates, mutation and bank claims. Errors in the deceased's name or date can delay inheritance. Correct them using the same online process, and make sure the deceased's name matches the land records (see inheritance guide).

Tips for NRBs

  1. Fix errors before applying for visas or citizenship abroad.
  2. Keep the name consistent across passport, NID and certificates.
  3. Use certified English translations for foreign authorities and attest them (see attestation guide).
  4. Do not use touts; use official portals and receipts.
  5. Ask your advocate for an affidavit if documents conflict.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I correct a birth certificate from abroad?

Yes, through the online BDRIS system, with a relative or advocate attending any hearing.

Can I change my date of birth in Bangladesh?

Small corrections with strong evidence can be made administratively; large changes may require a court order.

What documents are needed for correction?

Old certificate, school records, NID/passport, parents' documents and an affidavit if needed.

How long does correction take?

It varies by office, from a few weeks to months, depending on the case.

Can I correct a death certificate?

Yes, with the same process; supporting documents of the deceased are needed.

Breach of Contract Law in Bangladesh: Legal Remedies, Monetary Damages & Specific Performance

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-02 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In Bangladesh's booming economic landscape—spanning real estate developments in Dhaka, export manufacturing supply chains, IT outsourcing contracts, and cross-border procurement agreements—commercial disputes arising from broken promises are frequent. When a vendor fails to deliver machinery, a real estate developer refuses to register an apartment deed after receiving advance payments, or a corporate partner reneges on a supply agreement, the aggrieved party must navigate the intricate framework of Bangladeshi contract law. Governed by the **Contract Act 1872** and the **Specific Relief Act 1877**, plaintiffs have two primary legal avenues: suing for **Monetary Damages** under Sections 73 and 74 to recover actual financial loss, or petitioning the civil court for **Specific Performance of Contract** under Section 12 to legally compel the defaulting party to execute the agreement. This exhaustive legal guide breaks down the evidentiary standards, statutory limitation periods, ad valorem court fee caps, and strategic litigation workflows necessary to enforce contractual rights in Bangladesh.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

📋 In This Article

  2. 2. Monetary Damages: Section 73 (Actual Loss) vs. Section 74 (Liquidated Penalties)
  3. 3. Specific Performance of Contract: Enforcing Land & Apartment Agreements
  4. 4. Rescission, Injunctions & Restraining Orders (Sections 52-57)
  5. 5. Pre-Suit Protocol: Drafting the Strategic 15-to-30 Day Legal Notice
  6. 6. Comparative Matrix: Specific Performance vs. Damages vs. Criminal Action
  7. 7. Court Fees, Valuation Caps & Strict Limitation Deadlines
  8. 8. Cross-Border & Corporate Contracts: Foreign Choice of Law & Arbitration
  9. 9. NRB Property Disputes: Handling Defaulting Real Estate Developers in Dhaka
  10. 10. Real-Life Case Study: Enforcing a 3.5-Crore Commercial Land Contract
  11. 11. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1. Statutory Basis: Contract Act 1872 & Specific Relief Act 1877

In Bangladesh, contract enforcement is anchored upon two foundational pieces of legislation enacted under the common law tradition:

  • The Contract Act 1872: Defines valid contracts, reciprocal promises, anticipatory repudiation, and the statutory principles governing financial compensation when an agreement is broken. Sections 73 and 74 set the boundaries of financial liability.
  • The Specific Relief Act 1877: Provides equitable and judicial remedies when mere money cannot repair the harm done. It governs the discretionary power of civil courts to order Specific Performance—compelling a promisor to physically perform their exact obligation (e.g., executing a registered sale deed for land).
  • Civil Court Hierarchy: Contract disputes are adjudicated in the civil judiciary governed by the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC). Commercial suits exceeding 25 Lakh BDT fall within the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court of the Joint District Judge.

2. Monetary Damages: Section 73 (Actual Loss) vs. Section 74 (Liquidated Penalties)

When an innocent party seeks monetary recovery, Bangladeshi law imposes strict boundaries on what damages can be granted:

  • Section 73 (General Damages for Actual Loss): The injured party is entitled to receive compensation for any loss or damage caused to them which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach. Critically, Section 73 explicitly bars compensation for remote or indirect loss or damage.
  • Section 74 (Liquidated Damages vs. Penalties): If the contract stipulates a specific sum to be paid in case of breach (e.g., forfeiture of earnest money or agreed penalty of 50 Lakh BDT), Bangladeshi courts do not automatically enforce that exact number. Section 74 mandates that the court will only grant reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named. The plaintiff must still provide foundational evidence of actual harm suffered.
  • Duty to Mitigate Loss: The explanation to Section 73 imposes an affirmative legal duty on the plaintiff to take all reasonable steps to mitigate the loss resulting from the breach. An aggrieved party who sits idly and allows losses to escalate will have their damages proportionally reduced by the court.

3. Specific Performance of Contract: Enforcing Land & Apartment Agreements

In real estate transactions, monetary compensation is rarely acceptable to a purchaser when land prices in Dhaka or Chattogram appreciate rapidly. Under Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act 1877, specific performance may be granted:

  • Statutory Presumption for Immovable Property: The Explanation to Section 12 establishes a conclusive legal presumption: 'Unless and until the contrary is proved, the Court shall presume that the breach of a contract to transfer immovable property cannot be adequately relieved by compensation in money.'
  • Mandatory Registration of Bainanama (Section 17A Registration Act): Under the 2004 amendments to the Registration Act 1908, a contract for the sale of immovable property (Bainanama deed) must be in writing and registered within 30 days of execution. An unregistered Bainanama cannot be enforced through a suit for specific performance in a Bangladeshi civil court.
  • Readiness and Willingness: The plaintiff must prove before the court that they have always been, and remain, ready, willing, and financially capable of paying the balance consideration and accepting execution of the deed.

4. Rescission, Injunctions & Restraining Orders (Sections 52-57)

Preserving the subject matter of the contract while litigation proceeds is paramount to prevent the defaulting party from selling the property to a third-party bona fide purchaser:

  • Temporary Injunction (Order XXXIX CPC): Alongside filing a plaint for specific performance, the plaintiff's advocate immediately files an application for a Temporary Injunction under Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2 of the CPC, restraining the defendant from alienating, encumbering, or changing the physical nature of the land or asset.
  • Perpetual Injunction (Section 54, Specific Relief Act): Granted at the final decree stage to perpetually prevent the breach of an obligation existing in favor of the plaintiff.
  • Rescission of Voidable Contracts (Section 35): Where a contract was induced by fraud, misrepresentation, or undue influence, an aggrieved party can petition the court to judicially rescind the agreement and restore the parties to their pre-contractual status.

5. Pre-Suit Protocol: Drafting the Strategic 15-to-30 Day Legal Notice

A lawsuit for breach of contract cannot be instituted abruptly without laying an unshakeable evidentiary foundation. Serving a comprehensive Legal Notice is an indispensable requirement:

  • Contents of the Notice: (1) Detailed recitation of the contract, date of execution, and total consideration; (2) Specific proof of advance payments made via banking channels (cheques, pay orders, wire transfers); (3) Explicit documentation of the defendant's failure or refusal to perform; (4) Formal tender of the remaining balance consideration; and (5) A strict 15 or 30-day ultimatum to perform, failing which civil litigation will be commenced at the defendant's sole cost and peril.
  • Service via Registered Post with A/D: Must be served via Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due (A/D) to the defendant's official registered office and permanent residential address, accompanied by courier delivery and email notice.
  • Establishing the Date of Refusal: The legal notice crystallizes the exact 'Date of Refusal', which starts the clock running for statutory limitation.

6. Comparative Matrix: Specific Performance vs. Damages vs. Criminal Action

Choosing the correct procedural vehicle determines whether your dispute is resolved swiftly or trapped in procedural dead-ends. The table below delineates the statutory options:

RemedyPrimary StatuteCompetent ForumStatutory LimitationPrimary Outcome
Specific PerformanceSpecific Relief Act 1877, Sec 12Joint District Judge Court1 Year from date of refusal / breachCourt executes registered deed in place of defaulting seller
Money Suit for DamagesContract Act 1872, Sec 73-74Civil Court (Joint District Judge)3 Years from date of contract breachMonetary compensation decree for actual financial loss
Temporary InjunctionCPC 1908, Order XXXIXTrial Court hearing the main suitFiled contemporaneously with plaintImmediate freeze on sale, transfer, or construction
Criminal Cheating CasePenal Code 1860, Sec 420/406Metropolitan / Judicial MagistratePromptly following fraud discoveryCriminal arrest warrant (only if dishonest intent existed ab initio)

7. Court Fees, Valuation Caps & Strict Limitation Deadlines

Filing a commercial breach suit requires careful accounting of court costs and statutory deadlines:

  • Limitation Deadlines (Limitation Act 1908): Under Article 113 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act 1908, a suit for Specific Performance of a contract must be instituted within one (1) year from the date fixed for performance, or if no date is fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused. For general damages under contract, Article 115 provides a three (3) year limitation window. Filing even one day late results in absolute dismissal.
  • Ad Valorem Court Fees: In civil money suits and specific performance suits, court fees are calculated based on the valuation of the suit property or claimed damages under the Court-Fees Act 1870. The fee is subject to a statutory maximum cap (typically capped at 50,000 to 60,000 BDT), preventing exorbitant litigation costs for high-value multi-crore transactions.

8. Cross-Border & Corporate Contracts: Foreign Choice of Law & Arbitration

When international entities enter commercial contracts with Bangladeshi corporations, domestic court litigation can be bypassed through structured dispute resolution clauses:

  • Arbitration Act 2001: If the contract incorporates an arbitration clause, civil courts in Bangladesh are legally mandated under Section 7 of the Arbitration Act 2001 to stay judicial proceedings and refer the dispute to arbitration upon application by either party.
  • Enforcing Foreign Arbitral Awards: Bangladesh is a signatory to the 1958 New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards. An award obtained from SIAC (Singapore), ICC (Paris), or LCIA (London) can be directly executed in Bangladesh through the Court of the District Judge under Section 45 of the Arbitration Act.
  • Foreign Choice of Law: While parties can agree that foreign substantive law governs their commercial relationship, procedural and land-transfer matters located inside Bangladesh must strictly comply with mandatory Bangladeshi public policy and property registration statutes.

9. NRB Property Disputes: Handling Defaulting Real Estate Developers in Dhaka

Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) in the United States, UK, Canada, and Australia represent the largest demographic of victims facing contract breaches by Dhaka real estate developers. Developers routinely accept 70% to 100% advance bookings for apartments in Uttara, Mirpur, Bashundhara, or Dhanmondi, and then delay project delivery by 5 to 10 years or demand unlawful price escalations.

Under the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 (REDMA), buyers enjoy specialized statutory protections:

  • Section 24 of REDMA mandates that if a developer fails to hand over possession within the contractual deadline, they must pay agreed monthly financial compensation to the buyer.
  • If the developer defaults completely, the buyer is entitled to a full refund of all deposited funds along with commercial interest within statutory deadlines.
  • Disputes under REDMA can be submitted to arbitration or prosecuted before the Special Criminal Magistrate Courts established under the Act, creating immediate personal criminal liability for developer directors.

10. Real-Life Case Study: Enforcing a 3.5-Crore Commercial Land Contract

A London-based Bangladeshi entrepreneur entered into a registered Bainanama agreement to purchase a prime commercial plot in Uttara Sector 11, Dhaka, for 3.5 Crore BDT, paying an advance of 1 Crore BDT with a 6-month completion window. During those 6 months, real estate values in the area surged, prompting the local seller to evade phone calls, refuse to accept the remaining 2.5 Crore BDT, and attempt to sell the plot to a rival commercial builder.

Engaging our legal chamber from London, our team initiated an assertive strategic litigation campaign:

  1. Executed a Special Power of Attorney in London, authenticated by the Bangladesh High Commission, London, and stamped by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and DC Treasury Dhaka.
  2. Drafted and served an urgent 15-day Legal Notice formally tendering the balance 2.5 Crore BDT via Bank Pay Order and demanding execution of the registered sale deed.
  3. Upon the seller's failure to comply, filed Title Suit (Specific Performance) No. 42/2023 before the 1st Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka, within the strict 1-year limitation period.
  4. Moved an emergency application under Order XXXIX Rules 1-2 CPC on Day 1, securing an immediate Ad-Interim Temporary Injunction restraining the seller from transferring, mortgaging, or creating third-party rights over the commercial plot.
  5. Confronted with an unassailable registered Bainanama and a locked property injunction, the seller capitulated before trial, accepted the remaining consideration deposited in court, and executed the registered sale deed before the Sub-Registrar.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the limitation period for filing a Specific Performance lawsuit in Bangladesh?

Under Article 113 of the Limitation Act 1908, a suit for Specific Performance of a contract must be instituted within one (1) year from the date fixed for performance, or if no date is fixed, within one year from the date when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.

Can an unregistered Bainanama (land sale contract) be enforced in court?

No. Following the 2004 amendments to the Registration Act 1908 (Section 17A), a contract for the sale of immovable property must be in writing and registered. An unregistered Bainanama cannot be enforced through a suit for specific performance in a Bangladeshi civil court.

Can a plaintiff claim both specific performance and financial damages in the same suit?

Yes. Under Section 19 of the Specific Relief Act 1877, any person suing for specific performance may also ask for compensation for the breach, either in addition to or in substitution for such performance, giving the civil court wide discretion.

Does a contract penalty clause mean the court will award the entire penalty amount?

No. Under Section 74 of the Contract Act 1872, the court will only grant 'reasonable compensation' not exceeding the penalty amount stipulated in the contract. The court does not blindly enforce arbitrary or punitive penalty clauses.

Can an overseas NRB file a breach of contract lawsuit without visiting Bangladesh?

Yes. An overseas buyer or investor can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, empowering a Supreme Court advocate or representative in Bangladesh to institute and manage the lawsuit.

What court has jurisdiction over high-value commercial breach of contract suits?

Commercial breach of contract suits claiming damages or specific performance exceeding 25 Lakh BDT are instituted before the Court of the Joint District Judge having territorial jurisdiction over the subject property or place of contract execution.

What should a buyer do if a real estate developer delays flat handover in Dhaka?

Under the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 (REDMA), the buyer can serve a formal legal notice demanding contractual monthly delay compensation or a full refund with commercial interest, followed by filing an arbitration claim or criminal case under the Act.

Can a temporary injunction be obtained to stop the seller from selling the land to someone else?

Yes. Under Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, the court can issue an immediate temporary injunction restraining the defaulting seller from alienating, transferring, or mortgaging the disputed property while the suit is pending.

Bribery & Corruption Cases Bangladesh – Law, Penalties, ACC & Your Rights

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-08 · 9 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Corruption and bribery cases in Bangladesh are investigated and prosecuted by the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) — one of the most powerful enforcement bodies in the country. Whether you are a government official accused of taking a bribe, a businessperson accused of paying one, or a whistleblower seeking to report corruption, understanding the law is essential.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

📋 In This Article
  1. Anti-Corruption Laws in Bangladesh
  2. The Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) – Powers and Jurisdiction
  3. What Constitutes Bribery Under Bangladesh Law?
  4. Penalties for Corruption and Bribery
  5. Who Can Be Prosecuted for Corruption?
  6. ACC Investigation Process
  7. Your Rights If Accused by the ACC
  8. Key Defence Strategies in Corruption Cases
  9. Reporting Corruption in Bangladesh
  10. Asset Recovery and Corruption Proceeds

Anti-Corruption Laws in Bangladesh

Bangladesh's anti-corruption legal framework is primarily built around the following statutes:

  • Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2004: Establishes the ACC and defines its powers, functions, and investigation jurisdiction.
  • Prevention of Corruption Act 1947 (as amended): Still the primary substantive law defining corruption offences — bribery, misuse of public office, and related offences. Bangladesh courts regularly apply this Act alongside the ACC Act 2004.
  • Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012: Corruption proceeds (unexplained wealth, bribe money) are also treated as proceeds of money laundering — attracting separate money laundering charges.
  • Penal Code 1860: Sections 161–171 address bribery and related offences, including offering bribes to public servants.
  • Public Interest Disclosure Act (Whistleblower Protection Act): Provides protection for persons who disclose information about corruption in good faith.

The ACC is constitutionally independent and has broad powers to investigate any person — including government ministers, judges, military officers, and private sector individuals — for corruption-related offences.

The Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) – Powers and Jurisdiction

The Anti-Corruption Commission (Durniti Daman Commission) established under the ACC Act 2004 is Bangladesh's primary corruption-fighting body. Its powers include:

  • Investigation: The ACC has the power to investigate all persons, regardless of rank or position, for corruption offences. No prior government permission is needed to investigate a public servant.
  • Arrest: ACC officers can arrest persons suspected of corruption offences without a warrant from the Magistrate in certain circumstances.
  • Search and seizure: The ACC can search premises, seize documents, freeze bank accounts, and attach property suspected to be the proceeds of corruption.
  • Summons: The ACC can summon any person to appear before it for questioning — and failure to comply with an ACC summons is an offence.
  • Asset declaration review: Government officials are required to file annual asset declarations — the ACC reviews these and investigates unexplained wealth.
  • Prosecution: The ACC, once investigation is complete, can file a charge sheet before the Special Anti-Corruption Tribunal, which has exclusive jurisdiction over ACC cases.

The ACC cannot be directed by the government to stop an investigation — this constitutional independence makes it a powerful body. However, critics have raised concerns about selective enforcement and politically motivated prosecutions.

What Constitutes Bribery Under Bangladesh Law?

Bribery encompasses several specific offences under Bangladesh law:

  • Taking a bribe (gratification by a public servant): A public servant who accepts, obtains, or agrees to accept any gratification (money, property, advantage) beyond their legal remuneration, as a motive or reward for doing or omitting to do an official act, commits an offence under Section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947.
  • Giving a bribe: A person who gives, promises, or offers a bribe to a public servant commits an offence under Section 161 of the Penal Code 1860.
  • Criminal misconduct: A public servant who misappropriates government property, obtains property through corrupt means, or abuses their position to gain advantage for themselves or others commits criminal misconduct under Section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
  • Unexplained wealth: A public servant who possesses or has enjoyed assets disproportionate to their known sources of income commits an offence — the disproportionate assets are presumed to be corruption proceeds.
  • Private sector corruption: Bribery is not limited to public officials — private sector corruption (e.g., bribing a bank employee to approve a loan) is also prosecutable under various provisions.

Penalties for Corruption and Bribery

The penalties for corruption and bribery offences in Bangladesh are severe:

  • Section 5, Prevention of Corruption Act 1947 (criminal misconduct by public servant): Rigorous imprisonment from 1–7 years, fine, and forfeiture of corruption proceeds.
  • Section 161, Penal Code (taking bribe): Imprisonment up to 3 years, fine, or both.
  • Section 165A, Penal Code (abetting bribery): Same punishment as the principal offence — the person who offers or arranges a bribe faces the same penalty as the public servant who takes it.
  • Money laundering charges (Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012): Where corruption proceeds are laundered — imprisonment of 4–12 years and fine not less than the laundered amount.
  • Forfeiture of assets: In addition to imprisonment, courts routinely order forfeiture of all assets acquired through corruption — even assets held in family members' names if acquired with corruption proceeds.

In practice, ACC-convicted persons often face several concurrent sentences — the corruption conviction, the money laundering conviction, and asset forfeiture — resulting in decades of imprisonment and total loss of assets.

Who Can Be Prosecuted for Corruption?

A common misconception is that only government officials can be prosecuted for corruption. In fact, the ACC's jurisdiction extends to:

  • All government officials: Civil servants, police, military, judiciary, and elected representatives.
  • Statutory corporation and state-owned enterprise employees: Officials of government banks, SOEs, autonomous bodies, and public universities.
  • Local government officials: City Corporation mayors, Union Parishad Chairmen, and their employees.
  • Private individuals who bribe or facilitate corruption: Business owners who pay bribes, intermediaries who arrange bribes, and persons who receive corruption proceeds knowingly.
  • Family members: Family members who hold assets on behalf of a corrupt official may face prosecution for money laundering or being "benami" (proxy) holders of corruption proceeds.

The ACC's approach of prosecuting not just the corrupt official but also the family members who benefited from corruption proceeds has made it one of the most feared enforcement agencies in Bangladesh.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

ACC Investigation Process

The ACC investigation process for corruption cases typically proceeds as follows:

  1. Complaint or suo motu initiation: The ACC may begin an investigation based on a complaint from any person, media reports, or on its own initiative based on asset declarations or surveillance.
  2. Preliminary inquiry: ACC officers conduct an initial review to determine whether there is sufficient basis for a formal investigation.
  3. Formal investigation: If the preliminary inquiry discloses potential corruption, a formal investigation is opened. ACC officers have powers to search, seize documents, freeze accounts, and question witnesses.
  4. ACC summons: The suspect and witnesses are summoned to appear before the ACC for recorded statements.
  5. Asset investigation: The ACC examines bank records, land records, and other financial data to trace unexplained wealth or corruption proceeds.
  6. Arrest: If sufficient evidence is gathered, the ACC may arrest the suspect and produce them before the Special Anti-Corruption Tribunal.
  7. Charge sheet: After completing investigation, the ACC files a formal charge sheet before the Tribunal specifying the offences and the accused.

If you receive an ACC summons, do not appear without a lawyer. An ACC summons to appear for questioning is not the same as being charged — but what you say during questioning can be used as evidence in any later prosecution. Contact Adv. Shah Alam immediately if you receive an ACC summons.

Your Rights If Accused by the ACC

Even in ACC cases, the accused retains fundamental constitutional rights:

  • Right to remain silent: You cannot be compelled to make a statement incriminating yourself. You have the right to refuse to answer questions that may incriminate you.
  • Right to legal representation: You have the right to be represented by a lawyer of your choice at all stages — from the initial ACC questioning to the trial at the Special Tribunal.
  • Right to know the charges: Before or at the time of arrest, you must be informed of the specific charges against you.
  • Right to bail: Corruption charges are generally non-bailable. However, the Special Anti-Corruption Tribunal and the High Court Division have bail jurisdiction. Bail is available in exceptional cases — serious illness, long pre-trial detention, or weak evidence.
  • Right to a fair trial: The Constitutional guarantee of a fair trial applies fully in ACC cases — including the right to cross-examine prosecution witnesses and present a defence.
  • Right to challenge unlawful ACC actions: If the ACC acts outside its jurisdiction, violates your constitutional rights, or conducts an unlawful search/arrest, these can be challenged by writ petition before the High Court Division.

Key Defence Strategies in Corruption Cases

Corruption cases are complex and require expert legal strategy. Key defence approaches include:

  • Challenge the ACC's jurisdiction: The ACC can only investigate matters within its statutory jurisdiction. If the accusation relates to a matter outside the ACC's remit, challenge jurisdiction at the outset.
  • Explain the assets: In unexplained wealth cases, the central defence is producing credible evidence of legitimate sources of income — salary certificates, bank statements, business income records, inherited property documents, loans, and gifts.
  • Challenge the bribe amount: If the allegation is that money was paid/received as a bribe, challenge whether the transaction was truly gratuitous — whether it had a legitimate contractual basis instead.
  • Attack witness credibility: ACC cases often rely on witnesses who themselves have motivations for making the accusation — competitors, dismissed employees, or politically opposed parties.
  • Challenge procedural irregularities: ACC investigations that violate the accused's rights — unlawful arrest, coerced statements, evidence obtained by unlawful search — can be challenged in court.
  • Distinguish corruption from administrative error: Government officials sometimes make administrative decisions that benefit third parties without any corrupt intent. Showing the decision was bona fide and within official discretion is a complete defence.

An experienced criminal lawyer in Bangladesh with specific experience in ACC cases is essential. ACC prosecutions are prepared by specialist lawyers — matching their expertise requires a specialist defender.

Reporting Corruption in Bangladesh

If you wish to report corruption in Bangladesh, you have several channels:

  • ACC Complaint Cell: File a complaint directly with the Anti-Corruption Commission at its head office in Dhaka or any district ACC office. Complaints can also be submitted online at the ACC website (acc.org.bd).
  • ACC Hotline: The ACC operates a dedicated corruption reporting hotline.
  • Primary Court Complaint: Any person can file a direct complaint before a Magistrate's Court even for corruption offences — though the Magistrate will typically refer it to the ACC for investigation.
  • Newspapers and media: Investigative journalism has historically played a major role in exposing corruption in Bangladesh — though journalists must be cautious about defamation risks when reporting allegations without verification.

Whistleblower protections exist in Bangladesh law — persons who report corruption in good faith are entitled to legal protection from retaliation. However, practical enforcement of these protections remains a challenge. Consult a lawyer before reporting corruption in a situation where you may face personal risk.

Asset Recovery and Corruption Proceeds

Bangladesh law provides comprehensive asset recovery powers for corruption proceeds:

  • Attachment before judgment: The ACC can apply to the court to attach (freeze) assets suspected to be corruption proceeds even before a conviction — preventing the accused from dissipating assets during the trial.
  • Forfeiture upon conviction: Upon conviction, the court orders forfeiture of all assets that are proved to be corruption proceeds — including property held in the names of family members.
  • International asset recovery: Bangladesh has mutual legal assistance treaty (MLAT) arrangements with several countries that allow recovery of corruption proceeds hidden abroad — though this process is slow and complex in practice.
  • Benami (nominee) property: Assets held in the names of family members or trusted persons (benami holders) on behalf of the corrupt official are subject to forfeiture under the Benami Property Act and the Money Laundering Prevention Act.

If you believe you are at risk of asset attachment by the ACC — even before any charge is formally made — contact Adv. Shah Alam immediately to protect your legitimate assets and ensure any attachment order is lawfully made and challengeable.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a private citizen (non-government employee) be prosecuted for bribery in Bangladesh?

Yes. While many corruption offences specifically target public servants, private individuals who offer or give bribes to public servants can be prosecuted under Section 161 (and related provisions) of the Penal Code 1860. Additionally, private sector corruption — bribing a bank employee, a private doctor, etc. — may also attract prosecution.

What should I do if I receive an ACC summons?

Do not ignore an ACC summons — failure to comply is an offence. Equally, do not appear without a lawyer. Contact an experienced criminal lawyer immediately who can advise you on your rights, what not to say during ACC questioning, and how to prepare for the summons appearance.

Can the ACC freeze my bank account without a court order?

The ACC has the power to request Bangladesh Bank to freeze bank accounts as part of an investigation. In practice, this is often done through a court order from the Special Anti-Corruption Tribunal. If your account has been frozen, challenge the order immediately through your lawyer.

Is it a crime to give a bribe even if the official demanded it?

Yes. Under Bangladesh law, both giving and receiving a bribe are criminal offences. However, courts may take into account the circumstances — for example, where a person was extorted and had no realistic option but to pay — as a mitigating factor. This does not provide a complete defence but may affect sentencing.

How long does an ACC trial take in Bangladesh?

ACC cases are heard by Special Anti-Corruption Tribunals, which have procedural rules designed for faster disposal than ordinary courts. In practice, contested ACC cases often take 2–5 years at the Tribunal level, with appeals to the High Court and Appellate Division adding further years.

How to Buy Land in Bangladesh from Abroad: Complete Legal Checklist for NRBs

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-04 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Thousands of Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) invest in land and flats back home every year, and thousands also lose money to fake deeds, double sales and dishonest brokers. The risk is highest when the buyer is thousands of miles away and relies on relatives or agents. This guide is written by <a href="/advocate-md-shah-alam" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">Advocate Md. Shah Alam</a>, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, for Bangladeshis living in the UK, USA, UAE, Canada and elsewhere. For case-specific help you can call the chamber on <a href="tel:01712655546" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">01712655546</a> or WhatsApp the same number.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order
Official Portalssupremecourt.gov.bd, judiciary.gov.bd, pcc.police.gov.bd & land.gov.bd
Supreme Court ChamberAdvocate Md. Shah Alam — Uttara & Dhaka Judge Court (+880 1712-655546)
📋 In This Article
  1. Who Can Buy Land in Bangladesh from Abroad?
  2. Step 1: Decide the Type of Property and Appoint a Lawyer
  3. Step 2: Verify the Chain of Title
  4. Step 3: Physical Verification and Possession
  5. Step 4: Agreement, Payment and Deed Drafting
  6. Step 5: Registration, With or Without Travelling
  7. Step 6: Mutation (Namjari) and Land Tax
  8. Common Frauds Targeting NRBs
  9. Estimated Costs and Timeline
  10. Final NRB Checklist

Who Can Buy Land in Bangladesh from Abroad?

Under the Transfer of Property Act 1882 and the Registration Act 1908, a Bangladeshi citizen has the right to buy and own immovable property regardless of where he or she lives. Holding a UK, US, Canadian or Gulf residence does not by itself remove that right. Many NRBs also hold a second nationality; Bangladesh recognises dual citizenship for citizens of certain countries and issues a "No Visa Required" (NVR) endorsement on the foreign passport. Confirm your own status with the relevant Bangladesh Mission.

Purely foreign nationals face restrictions and usually need government permission, and restrictions on agricultural land are stricter. If you or your spouse are not a Bangladeshi citizen, get legal advice before signing anything.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Step 1: Decide the Type of Property and Appoint a Lawyer

Land, a flat in a developer project and a plot in a private housing society carry different risks. Before looking at price, appoint an independent advocate who works only for you, not for the seller or the broker. The advocate will:

  • Collect and read every document, not just the deed.
  • Run searches in the Sub-Registrar office and the AC (Land) office.
  • Draft or review the agreement and sale deed.
  • Act on your behalf under a Power of Attorney if you cannot travel.

Do not rely on the seller's lawyer. Their duty is to the seller.

Step 2: Verify the Chain of Title

Title is proved through a continuous chain of valid transfers from the original recorded owner to the present seller. Ask for and check the following:

  • Khatian / Record of Rights: CS (Cadastral Survey), SA (State Acquisition), RS and BS (Revisional / Bangladesh Survey) and, in cities, City Jarip. Each should show the seller or his predecessor.
  • Mother deed (Mul Dolil) and all earlier deeds, with registered copies obtained from the Sub-Registrar office (not just photocopies).
  • Mutation (Namjari) record and Dakhila in the seller's name, with paid land development tax (khajna) receipts. These can often be checked online through the government land portals (e-Porcha / e-Namjari).
  • Inheritance papers (heirship certificate) if the seller inherited the land; all heirs must sign.
  • Court records: check whether any civil suit, injunction or lis pendens exists over the land, and whether it is mortgaged, vested, or acquired by the government.

Ask your lawyer to obtain a certified "deed search" for at least 30 years from the Sub-Registrar to rule out double sales.

Step 3: Physical Verification and Possession

Papers can be perfect and the land still not exist where the seller says it does. Have a trusted person (ideally a surveyor with your advocate) visit the site and check the plot against the Khatian map. Confirm that:

  • The boundary and area on the ground match the deed.
  • Nobody else is in possession or claims a share.
  • There is road access and no pending acquisition.
  • The land is not low land / water body / agricultural land that cannot be built on. Check land classification.

Take dated photos and video and speak to neighbours. A local witness statement can save years of litigation later.

Step 4: Agreement, Payment and Deed Drafting

Before the deed, you normally sign an agreement for sale with a part payment (earnest money). Keep it simple and in writing:

  • Name, NID, address and photo of each seller; all co-owners must sign.
  • Exact land description by dag number, khatian number, mouza and area.
  • Price, payment schedule and deadline, and what happens on default.
  • Seller's declaration that the land is free from encumbrances.

Pay by bank transfer or banker's cheque only, to the seller's own account, and keep the receipts. For NRBs, inward remittance through a bank also gives an official trail of the source of funds. Avoid cash.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Step 5: Registration, With or Without Travelling

A sale of immovable property above Tk 100 must be registered under Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908. The deed is registered at the Sub-Registrar office of the area, where the registration fee and stamp duty (plus applicable taxes such as source tax) are paid.

If you cannot travel, you can appoint an attorney under a Power of Attorney executed abroad (see our complete Power of Attorney guide). The attorney appears on your behalf before the Sub-Registrar. Alternatively, you can plan a short trip to sign in person, which removes most PoA-related risks.

  1. Draft the deed (stamp paper of the right value).
  2. Pay the registration fee and applicable taxes.
  3. Appear with biometrics/identification at the Sub-Registrar office.
  4. Receive the registered deed copy; keep the original safely.

Step 6: Mutation (Namjari) and Land Tax

Registration alone does not update the government land record. After the deed is registered, apply for mutation (Namjari) at the Assistant Commissioner (Land) office, where your name is recorded in the Khatian, and you receive a Dakhila (rent receipt) after paying land development tax. Keep paying the tax every year; the receipt is your evidence of possession.

Failure to mutate is one of the most common reasons NRBs later face disputes and double sales. Complete it quickly.

Common Frauds Targeting NRBs

  • Double sale: the seller sells the same plot to two buyers. Prevent with registered deed search and immediate registration + mutation.
  • Fake or forged deed / Khatian: prevent by obtaining certified copies directly from government offices.
  • Seller without full title: one heir sells everyone's share. Check all heirs and the heirship certificate.
  • Fraudulent Power of Attorney: a forged PoA is used to sell your own land. Keep your PoA limited and revocable and register revocations.
  • Broker's "advance" scam: never pay a broker; pay the owner only.
  • Developer projects without approval: check RAJUK / city corporation approval and the developer's licence before booking a flat.

Estimated Costs and Timeline

Costs vary by location and value, but budget for the following in addition to the price: stamp duty and registration fee, source tax/transfer taxes, advocate and drafting fees, mutation fees and travel/attestation costs. In total these can add several percent of the property value, so ask your advocate for a written estimate before you commit.

A clean purchase from title search to mutation commonly takes about 2 to 4 months. Cases with inheritance, missing records or disputes can take much longer.

Final NRB Checklist

  1. Hire your own advocate and give him a limited, written brief.
  2. Verify 30 years of title and all Khatians.
  3. Check court cases, mortgages and acquisition status.
  4. Inspect the site physically; match the map.
  5. Pay by traceable bank channel to the owner only.
  6. Register the deed; collect the registered copy.
  7. Apply for mutation and keep paying land tax.
  8. Store scans of all documents in cloud storage and with your advocate.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can an NRB buy land in Bangladesh without visiting?

Yes, by appointing an attorney under a properly executed and attested Power of Attorney. However, a personal visit to sign the deed is safer if you can manage it.

Can I buy land in Bangladesh if I have UK, US or Canadian citizenship?

Bangladeshi citizens who also hold another nationality can generally own property in Bangladesh. Pure foreign nationals face restrictions. Check your status with the Bangladesh Mission and a lawyer.

What documents should I check before buying land?

The mother deed and all earlier deeds, CS/SA/RS/BS Khatians, mutation record and land development tax receipts, heirship papers, and a search for court cases or mortgages.

Is registration enough to become owner?

Registration transfers legal title, but you should also apply for mutation (Namjari) so the government records show your name, and pay land development tax every year.

How can NRBs avoid land grabbing?

Keep your mutation and tax records up to date, put a boundary wall and signboard, appoint a trusted caretaker, and consult a lawyer promptly if anyone challenges possession.
