Buying Land Dhaka Bangladesh – Complete Legal Guide Property Buyers

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-08 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Buying land or property in Dhaka is one of the biggest financial decisions most people make in their lifetime. It is also one of the riskiest — without proper legal due diligence, you can lose everything to title disputes, forged deeds, encumbrances, and regulatory violations. This comprehensive guide walks you through every legal step of a safe property purchase in Bangladesh.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)

📋 In This Article
  1. Overview: Property Purchase Process in Bangladesh
  2. Step 1: Find the Property and Negotiate the Price
  3. Step 2: Engage a Property Lawyer for Due Diligence
  4. Step 3: Verify Land Records and Title Chain
  5. Step 4: Check for Encumbrances and Court Cases
  6. Step 5: Sign the Bai-Baina (Agreement to Sell)
  7. Step 6: Calculate Registration Costs
  8. Step 7: Execute and Register the Sale Deed
  9. Step 8: Mutation (Namjari) After Purchase
  10. Step 9: Pay Land Development Tax
  11. Common Mistakes to Avoid When Buying Land in Bangladesh

Overview: Property Purchase Process in Bangladesh

Land and property transactions in Bangladesh involve multiple steps across different government offices — the Sub-Registrar's office, AC Land office, and (in urban areas) RAJUK or other development authority. The process is governed primarily by:

  • Registration Act 1908: Governs the registration of property deeds
  • Transfer of Property Act 1882: Governs how ownership of property passes from seller to buyer
  • Stamp Act 1899: Governs stamp duty on property transactions
  • State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950: Governs land tenure and mutation
  • Town Improvement Act 1953 and RAJUK Ordinance 1987: Governs development control in Dhaka

The typical property purchase in Bangladesh from start to finish involves approximately 8–12 weeks if all parties are cooperative and documents are in order. A property lawyer in Dhaka is essential at every stage to identify problems before they become expensive emergencies.

Step 1: Find the Property and Negotiate the Price

The first step is identifying the property you wish to buy and negotiating a purchase price with the seller. At this initial stage:

  • Inspect the physical property personally — check boundaries, access, neighbours, and any visible encroachments or structures.
  • Get a rough idea of market prices for comparable properties in the area through local real estate agents or recent registration records (accessible through the Sub-Registrar's deed index).
  • Do not pay any money — not even a token advance — before engaging a property lawyer and completing at least a preliminary title check.
  • Be cautious of sellers who present only photocopies of documents or who are in an unusual rush to complete the transaction.

Many property buyers in Bangladesh pay "booking money" or an advance before any legal check — this is a serious mistake. The small amount paid as advance can lock you into a problematic transaction that costs far more to exit than to avoid.

Step 2: Engage a Property Lawyer for Due Diligence

Before any agreement is signed or money paid, engage a property lawyer in Dhaka to conduct due diligence. A comprehensive property due diligence includes:

  • Title chain examination: Review of the full chain of ownership from (ideally) the original government khatian through every transfer to the current seller. Each link in the chain must be a registered deed.
  • Land records verification: Cross-referencing the deed chain with the government's land survey records (CS, SA, RS, BS khatians) and current mutation records at the AC Land office.
  • RAJUK/Development authority check: In Dhaka, checking whether the land is within a development control zone, whether it has any development plan restrictions, and whether any government acquisition notices have been issued.
  • Court search: Searching the district courts for any pending title suits, partition suits, injunction orders, or criminal cases involving the property or the seller.
  • Physical boundary verification: Comparing the deed description (khatian plot number, area, boundary description) with the physical land on the ground.
  • Mortgage/encumbrance check: Verifying through the Sub-Registrar's records whether any mortgage, charge, or lien has been registered against the property.

This due diligence typically takes 2–3 weeks and produces a written title opinion that either confirms the property is safe to buy or identifies specific problems to address before purchase.

Step 3: Verify Land Records and Title Chain

The land records verification is the most critical part of due diligence in Bangladesh. Here is what to check:

  • CS Khatian (Colonial Survey Records): The earliest government land record — established during British colonial surveys. Shows original recorded ownership.
  • SA Khatian (State Acquisition Survey): Records established during the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 implementation. Shows ownership after the zamindari system was abolished.
  • RS Khatian (Revisional Survey): The most commonly referenced survey record in Bangladesh — conducted in different periods for different districts. Most land disputes involve RS record discrepancies.
  • BS/City Survey Khatian: The most recent and accurate survey records in areas where BS survey has been completed.
  • Current Mutation Record (Namjari): The AC Land office's current record of who is recorded as the occupant/tenant for land development tax purposes. Must match the deed chain.

Your lawyer will obtain certified copies of all relevant khatians and trace whether the current seller's name appears in the current mutation record — and whether the mutations follow logically from the deed chain.

Step 4: Check for Encumbrances and Court Cases

A property that looks clean in the deed chain can still have hidden problems:

  • Mortgage registration: Banks and financial institutions register mortgages against properties as security for loans. A registered mortgage must be discharged before the property can be freely sold. Check the Sub-Registrar's encumbrance register.
  • Court injunctions: An injunction order from a court can prohibit sale or transfer of the property. Search the relevant courts' cause lists and writ orders.
  • Lis pendens (pending suits): A pending title suit automatically makes the property subject to any order the court may eventually make — affecting the buyer even if they bought without knowledge of the suit.
  • Government acquisition: Check whether any land acquisition notification has been issued under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982.
  • WASA, DESCO, TITAS: Check whether the land is subject to any utility corridor restrictions or service line easements that might limit development.
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Step 5: Sign the Bai-Baina (Agreement to Sell)

Once due diligence is satisfactory, the parties typically enter into a Bai-Baina — an agreement to sell (executory contract). This is an important and legally binding document:

  • It specifies the agreed price, payment schedule, and date for execution of the final sale deed
  • It confirms the seller's representations about title, freedom from encumbrances, and possession
  • An advance payment (typically 10–25% of the price) is made upon signing
  • A time limit for completion of the sale is specified

Important caution: The Bai-Baina is binding on both parties. If the seller backs out, the buyer can sue for specific performance (compelling the sale) or return of the advance plus damages. If the buyer backs out, they may lose the advance.

Have your property lawyer draft or review the Bai-Baina before signing. Poorly drafted agreements often lead to expensive disputes at the final sale stage.

Step 6: Calculate Registration Costs

The registration of a land deed in Bangladesh involves several government charges that the buyer must budget for:

  • Stamp duty: 1.5% of the deed value (government valuation, not necessarily market price) for agricultural land; higher rates for urban property. Calculated on the mauza rate (government assessed value) or actual consideration, whichever is higher.
  • Registration fee: 1% of the deed value
  • Local government surcharge: Additional percentage for city corporations or municipalities
  • E-TIN fee: Applicable if the property value exceeds certain thresholds
  • Gain tax (capital gains): The seller may be required to pay advance income tax on capital gains from the property sale

Important: Undervaluing property in deed registration to save stamp duty is an offence under the Stamp Act and can result in rejection of the deed or penalties. The government uses district-specific mauza rate schedules as minimum valuation benchmarks.

Your property lawyer will calculate the exact registration costs based on the specific property, its location, and the agreed price.

Step 7: Execute and Register the Sale Deed

The final sale deed execution and registration is the crucial step that legally transfers ownership:

  1. Deed preparation: Your property lawyer prepares the sale deed — a formal document describing the property, the parties, the price, and the warranties given by the seller.
  2. Stamp paper: Non-judicial stamp paper of the correct value (based on stamp duty calculated) is purchased.
  3. Attendance at Sub-Registrar's office: Both buyer and seller (or authorised representatives) attend the Sub-Registrar's office on the agreed date with all original documents.
  4. Identity verification: The Sub-Registrar verifies the identities of both parties (NID cards) and the property documents.
  5. Fee payment: Registration fee, stamp duty, and other charges are paid.
  6. Deed execution: The deed is signed by the seller (and buyer where required) in the presence of the Sub-Registrar.
  7. Registration: The deed is officially registered and entered in the Sub-Registrar's deed register. A registration number and date is endorsed on the original deed. The original registered deed is returned to the buyer after a few days.

Step 8: Mutation (Namjari) After Purchase

Registration of the sale deed gives you legal ownership — but the government's land records (khatian) still shows the previous owner's name until mutation is completed. Mutation (namjari) is the process of updating the AC Land office's records to show the new owner's name.

Why mutation is essential:

  • Without mutation, you cannot pay land development tax in your own name — and unpaid tax creates government debt against the property
  • Government notices and any future acquisition compensation go to the name in the mutation record
  • In any future sale, banks and lawyers check the mutation record as part of due diligence — an unmutated property is harder to sell and may create financing problems

Mutation process: File an application with the AC Land office of the upazila where the land is located, attaching the registered sale deed, copy of khatian, and mutation fee payment. The AC Land office investigates, hears any objections, and if satisfied, issues a mutation order (namjari) updating the khatian to show the new owner.

Common Mistakes to Avoid When Buying Land in Bangladesh

Based on common legal problems seen by property lawyers in Bangladesh, these are the mistakes to absolutely avoid:

  • Buying without a lawyer: The single most common and costly mistake. A small legal fee is nothing compared to the potential loss of the entire property.
  • Trusting photocopies: Always insist on reviewing original documents. Fraudsters often present high-quality photocopies of forged documents.
  • Paying full price before registration: Never pay the full purchase price before the deed is registered. A standard arrangement is: advance on Bai-Baina, balance on the day of registration at the Sub-Registrar's office.
  • Ignoring court cases: Do not buy property with pending court cases — even if the seller assures you it is a minor matter. A pending suit can result in a court order that defeats your title.
  • Skipping mutation: Not completing mutation after purchase causes compounding problems. Do it within 3–6 months of registration.
  • Buying without RAJUK clearance in Dhaka: Urban properties in Dhaka must comply with RAJUK's development plan. Properties in restricted zones or without proper approvals may be uninsurable and unsaleable.

Contact Adv. Shah Alam before signing any property agreement in Bangladesh. Prevention is always less expensive than litigation.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does it cost to register land in Bangladesh?

The main costs are stamp duty (approximately 1.5–4% of the deed value depending on property type and location), registration fee (1% of deed value), and local government surcharges. For example, for a BDT 50 lakh property in Dhaka, total registration costs are typically BDT 3–5 lakh, plus your property lawyer's professional fee.

Can a foreigner buy land in Bangladesh?

Foreigners generally cannot own agricultural or rural land in Bangladesh. Foreign nationals can own urban commercial and residential property subject to Bangladesh Bank and government permissions. Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) with dual citizenship have specific rules — consult a property lawyer for NRB-specific property purchase guidance.

What is the difference between a Bai-Baina and a sale deed?

A Bai-Baina is a preliminary agreement to sell — it binds the parties to complete the sale but does not itself transfer ownership. A sale deed is the final registered document that legally transfers ownership from seller to buyer. Both documents are important in a Bangladesh property transaction.

How long does land registration take in Bangladesh?

The actual registration at the Sub-Registrar's office typically takes 1–2 days. However, the overall process from due diligence to completed registration usually takes 4–8 weeks, depending on the complexity of the title chain and whether all documents are readily available.

Is it safe to buy land through a real estate agent in Bangladesh?

Agents can help find properties but do not provide title verification or legal protection. Always engage your own independent property lawyer regardless of what the agent tells you about the property. The agent represents the seller's interest — not yours.

Can a Father Disinherit a Child in Bangladesh? Property Rights & Muslim Law Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-09 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

A common question among Bangladeshi families and non-resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) is whether a father can legally disinherit a biological son or daughter from his ancestral or self-acquired estate. Emotional disputes, second marriages, or sibling rivalries frequently lead an aging parent to declare that a particular child has been 'disowned' through a newspaper notice or notary public affidavit. Under the codified principles of Islamic jurisprudence applied through the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937, such unilateral declarations carry zero legal force. Bangladeshi law strictly regulates testamentary succession, making it impossible to disinherit a legal heir from their Quranic inheritance share by mere declaration or last will.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

1. Legal Status of 'Disowning' Affidavits and Newspaper Notices

In Bangladesh, family disagreements sometimes culminate in an elderly father publishing a notice in a local daily newspaper or executing an affidavit before a Notary Public declaring that he has 'disowned' (tejjoputro or tejjokonna) a son or daughter. Many parents and siblings mistakenly believe that such an affidavit permanently strips the child of any right to inherit land, apartments, or bank deposits upon the father's demise.

From a legal standpoint, the concept of 'disowning' a child is non-existent under Bangladeshi law. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly affirmed that succession among Muslim citizens is governed strictly by religious personal law as recognized under the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937. A parent cannot alter the statutory order of devolution prescribed by Islamic law through a personal contract, affidavit, or press statement.

An affidavit executed before a first-class magistrate or notary public asserting that a child has been severed from the family line is purely an emotional expression without judicial weight. When the father passes away, the surviving children automatically inherit their respective legal shares under the rules of inheritance, completely unaffected by any prior declarations of disinheritance.

2. Muslim Inheritance Framework: Fixed Quranic Heirs and Residuaries

The overwhelming majority of Bangladeshi Muslims follow the Hanafi school of Sunni jurisprudence. Under this system, inheritance opens immediately upon the death of the property owner. The law divides eligible relatives into specific classes, starting with Sharers (Zawil-Furud), followed by Residuaries (Asaba), and Distant Kindred (Zawil-Arham).

Biological children hold an unassailable position in this hierarchy. A son is a primary residuary who can never be completely excluded from succession by any other relative. A daughter is a primary sharer if there is no son, receiving one-half of the net estate if single, or two-thirds shared equally if there are multiple daughters. When a son and daughter survive together, they inherit jointly as residuaries, with the son receiving twice the share of the daughter.

Because these shares are fixed by religious law and enforced by the civil courts, no parent possesses the statutory power to modify the percentages or substitute one heir for another in respect of property remaining in the father's name at the moment of death. If you need clarity on how ancestral estates are demarcated, review our comprehensive analysis of property inheritance in Bangladesh for NRBs.

3. Limits on Testamentary Succession: The One-Third Wasiyat Rule

Under secular western jurisdictions, testators enjoy broad freedom of testation and can generally draft a last will and testament leaving their entire estate to a preferred beneficiary or charity. In Bangladesh, Muslim inheritance law strictly curtails testamentary freedom to prevent the arbitrary disinheritance of family members.

Under Hanafi law, a Muslim may execute a Will (Wasiyat) in respect of no more than one-third of their net estate after the settlement of funeral expenses and valid debts. The remaining two-thirds must devolve upon the legal heirs in accordance with statutory Quranic proportions. Any testamentary bequest attempting to dispose of more than one-third is ultra vires and invalid unless all surviving heirs give their voluntary consent following the testator's death.

Crucially, a bequest cannot be made in favor of an existing legal heir even within the one-third limit. The fundamental legal maxim provides that there is no bequest to an heir unless consented to by all other heirs. Consequently, if a father executes a will attempting to bequeath his entire house or land exclusively to one son or a favorite relative, that will is null and void unless the excluded children willingly consent after the father's death. For deeper insight into probate and wills, consult our guide on probate and wasiyat inheritance in Bangladesh.

4. Lifetime Transfers: Can a Father Gift (Heba) Everything to One Child?

While a father cannot disinherit a child through testamentary means (wills or affidavits), the legal position is different during his lifetime. As an absolute owner of self-acquired or partitioned ancestral property, a mentally competent adult possesses full authority under the Transfer of Property Act 1882 and Muslim personal law to dispose of his property while alive.

A father may sell, transfer, or gift his property to anyone during his lifetime. Under Bangladeshi law, a gift among specified close blood relatives—including father to son or daughter—can be accomplished through a registered Heba deed (Hebanama) under Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908 for a nominal fixed registration fee. If a father knowingly, voluntarily, and competently executes a registered Heba deed transferring his land to one child and genuinely delivers physical possession, that transfer is legally binding upon completion.

However, when a father attempts to transfer all assets to one child shortly before his passing, questions frequently arise regarding undue influence, mental incapacity, fraud, or lack of actual physical possession. In many cases, elderly parents suffering from dementia or chronic illness are misled into signing registered deeds by one manipulative sibling without realizing they are completely stripping their other children of their future inheritance.

5. Legal Grounds to Challenge Coerced or Sham Lifetime Deeds

When an excluded son or daughter discovers that a sibling has secretly registered a Heba deed or sale deed transferring the family estate, civil law provides specific avenues of judicial relief. A lifetime gift under Muslim law requires three essential elements: a clear declaration of gift by the donor, acceptance by the donee, and actual delivery of physical possession (Qabda).

If physical possession was never transferred and the father continued to reside on the land, collect rents, and manage the property until his death, the gift remains incomplete under classic Hanafi jurisprudence. Furthermore, if the father was advanced in age, bedridden, blind, or suffering from cognitive impairment, the transaction may be challenged under the doctrine of Marz-ul-Maut (death-bed illness). Under this doctrine, a gift made during an illness that induces an apprehension of death is treated as a Wasiyat, subject to the strict one-third limit and requiring co-heir consent.

Similarly, where fraud, misrepresentation, or coercion is established, the deed can be impeached. For instance, if an elderly parent was told they were signing an authorization for a utility connection or power of attorney, but a registered Heba deed was executed instead, the transaction constitutes fraud on the donor and can be struck down by the civil court.

6. Summary Matrix: Testamentary vs. Lifetime Transfers in Bangladesh

Understanding the distinction between attempted disinheritance methods is essential for heirs seeking to protect their rights. The following matrix illustrates the legal validity and remedies associated with common property transfer mechanisms in Bangladesh:

Transfer Mechanism Legal Validity under Bangladeshi Law Impact on Excluded Children Recommended Judicial Remedy
Newspaper Notice / Affidavit 'Disowning' Child Completely Void No impact; child inherits statutory share automatically upon death. File Partition Suit (Batwara) in Joint District Judge Court if resisted.
Will (Wasiyat) of entire estate to one child Void without consent of all other heirs Bequest to an heir is nullified; normal Quranic inheritance applies. Object during probate/succession or file declaratory title suit.
Registered Heba executed under duress / fraud Voidable upon proof of fraud, coercion, or lack of possession Deprives heirs unless challenged and declared void by civil court. Suit for cancellation of deed under Section 39 Specific Relief Act.
Bona fide voluntary lifetime Heba with possession Valid and binding Property ceases to belong to father; does not enter inheritance pool. Verify true voluntariness, mutation status, and mental capacity.

7. Court Remedies: Cancellation Suits and Partition Proceedings

When an excluded heir is confronted with a disputed property transfer or denial of their inheritance rights, two primary civil remedies must be considered in the relevant Assistant Judge or Joint District Judge Court having territorial jurisdiction.

First, if a fraudulent deed exists, the excluded heir must file a suit for declaration and cancellation of the deed under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act 1877. The plaintiff must plead the specific facts demonstrating fraud, lack of consideration, absence of physical possession, or the donor's mental incapacity. Under Article 91 or 95 of the Limitation Act 1908, the statutory limitation period is generally three years from the date the fraud or deed became known to the plaintiff.

Second, where the father died intestate without any valid lifetime transfer, but dominant siblings refuse to distribute the land or grant access to rental income, the appropriate remedy is a Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla). In this proceeding, the civil court determines the respective fractional shares of each co-sharer, appoints an Advocate Commissioner to physically inspect and demarcate the plots, and issues a final decree partitioning the estate. If you are facing an unlawful land grab by relatives, consult our detailed walkthrough on partition suit procedures and commissioner decrees in Bangladesh.

8. Illustrative Scenario: Excluded Daughter Overturning a Secret Transfer

To understand how Bangladeshi civil courts approach these disputes in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A businessman residing in Uttara, Dhaka, passed away leaving behind substantial residential land, a commercial building, and three children: an elder son managing the local businesses and two daughters settled in London and Toronto. While the daughters were overseas, the elder son produced an affidavit signed by the late father ten months before his death asserting that both daughters had been 'disowned' for marrying without his consent, followed by a registered Heba deed gifting the entire commercial complex exclusively to the son.

Upon learning of their exclusion, the daughters engaged a Supreme Court advocate in Dhaka to conduct a thorough search of the Sub-Registry Office records and municipal mutation files. The investigation revealed that the father was bedridden in an intensive care facility on the date of the alleged deed execution, and the hospital records confirmed severe cognitive impairment. The daughters filed a suit in the Joint District Judge Court under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act 1877 to cancel the Heba deed on grounds of fraud and Marz-ul-Maut, combined with a Partition Suit.

The civil court evaluated the medical evidentiary trail, found that the father lacked disposing capacity, and held that the disowning affidavit possessed no legal standing. The court cancelled the fraudulent deed, declared the daughters rightful Quranic co-sharers, and issued a preliminary partition decree guaranteeing their lawful shares in the estate.

9. Practical Steps for Non-Resident Bangladeshis Facing Property Exclusion

Non-resident Bangladeshis are particularly vulnerable to inheritance exclusion due to geographical distance and prolonged absence from Dhaka or ancestral village jurisdictions. Relatives on the ground frequently exploit this absence by fabricating death certificates, altering land records, or creating sham deeds.

If you are living abroad and suspect that family members are attempting to exclude you from your late father's estate, take the following proactive legal steps immediately:

  • Procure Certified Land Records: Obtain certified copies of the CS, SA, RS, and City/BS Khatians, together with the latest Namjari (mutation) Porcha from the relevant Assistant Commissioner (Land) office.
  • Conduct Sub-Registry Searches: Commission a formal inspection of the Balam Boi (volume books) at the Sub-Registry Office to uncover any registered Heba, sale, or power of attorney deeds executed prior to death.
  • Obtain Warishan Sanad (Succession Certificate): Secure an authentic Heirship Certificate from the City Corporation Councillor or Union Parishad Chairman listing all biological heirs without omission.
  • Execute a Specific Power of Attorney: If you cannot travel to Dhaka, execute a Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission in your host country, appointing a trusted representative or advocate to file protective civil suits.
  • Seek Temporary Injunction: File an application under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) to restrain siblings from selling, developing, or altering the nature of the property pending final decree.

For additional strategies on safeguarding real estate from overseas, explore our dedicated resource on land dispute advocacy in Bangladesh and remote legal support for non-resident Bangladeshis.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to an Advocate in Dhaka: To examine family deeds, challenge fraudulent Heba transfers, or file a partition suit in Dhaka or district courts, send your documents via WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007 or call our chamber at +880 1712-655546. Non-resident Bangladeshis can conduct initial reviews remotely.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a father disown a child through a newspaper advertisement in Bangladesh?

No. A newspaper advertisement or public declaration disowning a child has zero legal effect under Bangladeshi law. Muslim inheritance rights are statutory and cannot be overridden by unilateral public notices.

Is a notary public affidavit disinheriting a son or daughter valid in court?

No. Notary public affidavits or magistrate declarations purporting to disinherit an heir are legally void. They do not alter the devolution of property under the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937.

Can a Muslim father leave his entire estate to one child in a Will (Wasiyat)?

No. Under Hanafi Sunni law, a testator cannot bequeath more than one-third of the estate, and any bequest to an existing legal heir is completely void unless all other heirs give their voluntary consent after the testator's death.

Can a father gift all his property to one child while alive through a Heba deed?

A father may execute a registered Heba deed during his lifetime if he is of sound mind and voluntarily delivers physical possession. However, if the deed was executed under fraud, duress, or during a fatal illness (Marz-ul-Maut), it can be challenged and cancelled in civil court.

What is Marz-ul-Maut and how does it affect lifetime property transfers in Bangladesh?

Marz-ul-Maut refers to a death-bed illness that creates an apprehension of death. A gift executed by an individual during such an illness is legally treated as a Wasiyat, meaning it cannot exceed one-third of the estate and cannot favor an heir without co-heir consent.

What is the time limit to challenge a fraudulent gift deed in Bangladesh?

Under Articles 91 and 95 of the Limitation Act 1908, a suit to cancel a fraudulent deed under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act must generally be filed within three years from the date the plaintiff discovered the fraud or existence of the deed.

Can an overseas daughter claim her inheritance share if her brothers occupy the property?

Yes. An overseas daughter is an absolute Quranic sharer. If brothers refuse to deliver her rightful share, she can execute an embassy-attested Power of Attorney and file a Partition Suit in the Joint District Judge Court in Bangladesh to demarcate and recover her share.

What court has jurisdiction over inheritance and property partition suits in Dhaka?

Depending on the total pecuniary valuation of the property, inheritance partition suits and deed cancellation cases are adjudicated by the Assistant Judge, Senior Assistant Judge, or Joint District Judge Court having territorial jurisdiction over where the property is situated.

Can a Foreigner or Dual Citizen Own Property in Bangladesh? Rules for NRBs and Foreign Spouses

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-04 · 10 min read

Your passport colour changes how Bangladeshi law sees you. A Bangladeshi dual citizen, a Bangladeshi-born person who gave up citizenship, and a pure foreigner are treated very differently when they want to buy, inherit or sell property. Three Categories of People

  • Bangladeshi citizen living abroad: keeps full property rights.
  • Bangladeshi dual citizen: holds Bangladeshi and another nationality (permitted for citizens of certain countries); rights continue if citizenship is retained with the proper endorsement.
  • Foreign national, including former Bangladeshis who renounced citizenship: treated as a foreigner for most purposes.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Dual Citizens and the NVR Endorsement

The Citizenship Act 1951 and Bangladeshi policy allow dual citizenship for citizens of specified countries. Bangladesh Missions and the Immigration authority issue a "No Visa Required" (NVR) endorsement on the foreign passport to prove citizenship at the border. Having a valid NVR makes buying, selling and mutation easier because it connects your foreign passport to your Bangladeshi identity. If you lack it, see our guide on dual citizenship and NVR.

Foreign Nationals Buying Property

For a pure foreign national, ownership of land is restricted. Typical routes are:

  • Government permission or a BIDA-approved project for business premises or factories.
  • Long-term lease for commercial use instead of freehold.
  • Investment through a Bangladesh company with the required approvals.
  • Flats under certain developer schemes, where allowed.

Rules change often and differ by area and land type, so do not rely on a broker's assurance. Get written advice from an advocate first.

Agricultural Land

Agricultural land is subject to special limits on who may own and how much one may hold. Many purchases by non-farmers or foreigners require permission, and conversion to non-agricultural use also needs approval. NRBs who are citizens should still check the land classification in the Khatian (see record checking guide).

Foreign Spouse and Children

A foreign spouse does not automatically gain ownership of the Bangladeshi spouse's property, but may inherit as an heir under the applicable personal law, subject to the foreigner restrictions. Put estate planning in place: a will, registered gift deeds, or properly documented joint ownership, all drafted by an advocate.

Practical Checklist

  1. Confirm your citizenship status with the Bangladesh Mission.
  2. Get the NVR endorsement if you are a dual citizen.
  3. Ask an advocate whether your purchase needs permission.
  4. Check land classification and mutation record.
  5. Document your funds through bank channels.
  6. Consider a will to avoid disputes after death (see inheritance guide).

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can an NRB with a UK/US/Canadian passport buy land in Bangladesh?

If you remain a Bangladeshi citizen (with dual citizenship where allowed), you can generally buy land. If you renounced Bangladeshi citizenship, you are treated as a foreigner.

Can a foreigner buy a flat in Bangladesh?

In some cases, yes, under approvals and specific schemes, but freehold land purchase is restricted. Get legal advice.

Can my foreign wife inherit my Bangladeshi property?

She can inherit as an heir under the personal law, but foreign ownership restrictions and procedures may apply.

What is NVR?

The No Visa Required endorsement placed on a dual citizen's foreign passport to prove Bangladeshi citizenship.

Can I buy agricultural land as an NRB?

It is more restricted than other land; check the current limits and approval requirements with your advocate.

Can You Sue for Unpaid Money on an Oral Agreement in Bangladesh? Money Suit Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-12 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In Bangladesh's vibrant commercial ecosystem, millions of taka change hands daily on the strength of a handshake, personal trust, or verbal promises between business associates, friends, or relatives. Goods are delivered, contractor services rendered, or personal loans extended without executing a formal stamp agreement. When the debtor suddenly defaults, cuts off communication, and brazenly challenges the creditor by saying, 'Show me where I signed,' creditors assume all hope is lost. Fortunately, under the Contract Act 1872, the Evidence Act 1872, and the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, oral contracts are fully valid and enforceable in Bangladesh. Here is the comprehensive legal roadmap to successfully proving an oral agreement, recovering your debt through a Money Suit, and securing court decrees.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

The Reality of Unwritten Commercial Agreements in Bangladesh

Across the wholesale hubs of Khatunganj in Chattogram, Chawkbazar and Islampur in Old Dhaka, and suburban industrial zones, traditional commerce still relies heavily on verbal trust. Suppliers ship consignments of raw materials worth tens of lakhs of taka on oral phone orders; contractors begin construction based on informal promises; and friends or relatives advance substantial sums during family emergencies without requesting formal promissory notes.

However, when personal relationships sour, business ventures fail, or debtors turn dishonest, the lack of a stamped written agreement becomes an acute crisis. The defaulting party often counts on the common myth that 'without a signature on non-judicial stamp paper, no case can stand in court.' Creditors frequently feel paralyzed by this misconception, delaying legal consultation until statutory limitation periods expire. Knowing how statutory civil law treats unwritten promises transforms what seems like a hopeless situation into an actionable, winnable judicial recovery.

Contract Act 1872: The Statutory Validity of Oral Contracts

The foundational statute governing all contractual relationships in Bangladesh is the Contract Act 1872. Section 10 of the Act sets out what agreements are contracts: 'All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.'

Crucially, Section 10 does not state that a contract must be written. It specifically adds: 'Nothing herein contained shall affect any law in force in Bangladesh, by which any contract is required to be made in writing or in the presence of witnesses, or any law relating to the registration of documents.' While specific laws explicitly mandate written, registered deeds for transactions like land transfers (Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908) or trusts, commercial debts, loans, supply agreements, and service contracts do not require written deeds. Under settled principles upheld by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, an oral contract containing a clear offer, unequivocal acceptance, and lawful consideration is 100% legally binding and enforceable.

Evidence Act 1872: Proving Verbal Agreements in Court

While establishing an oral agreement is legally permissible, the primary battleground in court is evidentiary proof. Under Section 59 of the Evidence Act 1872, all facts, except the contents of documents, may be proved by oral evidence. However, Section 60 mandates that oral evidence must in all cases whatever be direct—meaning that if it refers to a fact which could be heard, it must be the evidence of a witness who says he heard it.

When an oral debt is contested, the plaintiff cannot rely solely on their own uncorroborated oral statement. The court demands a coherent narrative supported by credible third-party witnesses who were physically present when the money was handed over, when the terms were negotiated, or when the debtor subsequently acknowledged the debt and promised repayment. Depositions from business partners, shop managers, or shared associates who witnessed the transaction form the oral foundation of your plaint.

Crucial Evidence: Bank Statements, SMS, and Chat Logs

In modern commercial litigation, contemporaneous electronic and financial records provide the definitive corroboration that elevates an oral contract into an unassailable court claim. Key evidentiary categories include:

  • Banking Audit Trails: Cheque counterfoils, bank account debit advice, RTGS/BEFTN transfer slips, and deposit receipts showing funds moving directly from your account to the debtor's account. This disproves any claim that no money ever changed hands.
  • Mobile Financial Services (MFS): Verified transaction statements from bKash, Nagad, or Rocket detailing transaction IDs, sender/receiver wallet numbers, and timestamps.
  • Electronic Messages & WhatsApp Chats: WhatsApp conversations, SMS messages, and emails where the debtor discusses the transaction, acknowledges the debt, requests more time to pay, or apologizes for default. Under Section 65B of the Evidence Act, printouts of electronic records accompanied by certificate of authenticity are admissible.
  • Chalan and Delivery Slips: Signed goods delivery challans, gate passes, store ledger entries, or transport receipts proving physical handover of merchandise.

When these paper and digital trails corroborate witness testimony, civil judges readily find in favor of the plaintiff.

Need legal guidance or representation for your case in Bangladesh? Send your documents and dispute details on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007. Overseas clients and local litigants can arrange an immediate confidential document review.

Mandatory Limitation Deadlines: Article 115 Limitation Act

The single most dangerous trap for creditors seeking to recover an oral debt is the law of limitation. Under the Limitation Act 1908, the state will not aid a creditor who sleeps on their legal rights. Unlike debts backed by registered mortgage deeds (which enjoy longer limitation windows), oral contracts are subject to strict, abbreviated deadlines.

Under Article 115 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act 1908, for compensation for the breach of any contract, express or implied, not in writing registered and not specifically provided for, the limitation period is exactly three (3) years. The three-year countdown begins from the date when the contract is broken—meaning the date on which the debtor failed to repay the money as promised, or the date of the last partial payment or written acknowledgment of liability under Section 19 of the Limitation Act. If you file your Money Suit three years and one day after the cause of action arose, the civil court is statutorily mandated to dismiss your suit under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, regardless of how genuine your claim is.

Drafting and Serving the Advocate Legal Notice

Before approaching the civil court to institute a formal Money Suit, serving a formal Advocate Legal Notice is a mandatory strategic prerequisite. The legal notice achieves several decisive objectives:

  1. Establishes Formal Demand: It places on record the exact dates, amounts, bank transaction references, and verbal terms agreed upon, demanding full settlement within a specified deadline (usually 15 to 30 days).
  2. Fixes the Cause of Action: It formally establishes the date of default, crystallizing the cause of action for the subsequent Money Suit.
  3. Opportunity for Acknowledgment: If the debtor replies to the legal notice through their advocate, even a partial admission or evasive reply serves as written evidence that an underlying transaction existed, destroying their defense that they never knew you.

The legal notice must be dispatched via Registered Post with Acknowledgment Due (AD) to the debtor's residential and business addresses, and postal receipts and signed AD cards must be preserved as primary suit exhibits.

Money Suit Procedure in the Joint District Judge Court

If the legal notice period expires without payment, your advocate files a Money Suit under the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. In Bangladesh, pecuniary jurisdiction determines the forum: suits involving substantial commercial sums (typically exceeding BDT 25,00,000) are instituted in the Court of the Joint District Judge having territorial jurisdiction where the debtor resides or where the cause of action arose.

The litigation progresses through defined stages: filing of the plaint with ad-valorem court fees; service of summons on the defendant; filing of the Written Statement (WS) by the debtor; framing of issues by the court; alternative dispute resolution (ADR) mediation under Section 89A CPC; and the trial stage where the plaintiff and supporting witnesses take the stand for examination-in-chief and cross-examination. Upon reviewing the oral testimonies and electronic exhibits, the court delivers a Money Decree specifying the principal sum plus statutory interest from the date of default.

Order 38 CPC: Attachment of Debtor Assets Before Judgment

A major concern in commercial debt recovery is that while the Money Suit is pending, the debtor will sell off their properties, withdraw bank balances, or transfer assets to relatives, rendering an ultimate decree a hollow victory. To prevent this, the law provides an aggressive interlocutory remedy under Order 38, Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC): Attachment Before Judgment.

Under Order 38 Rule 5, where the court is satisfied that the defendant, with intent to obstruct or delay the execution of any decree that may be passed against him, is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property or remove it from local jurisdiction, the court may direct the defendant to furnish security, and failing that, order the interim attachment of their immovable properties, commercial inventories, or bank accounts. Securing an Order 38 attachment freezes the debtor's financial mobility, often compelling them to negotiate an immediate out-of-court settlement.

Comparison Table: Written vs. Oral Contract Money Suits

The table below highlights the comparative procedural aspects of recovering debts based on written versus oral contracts in Bangladesh:

Legal ParameterWritten Registered ContractOral Agreement (Unwritten)
Legal Enforceability100% enforceable under Contract Act §10100% enforceable under Contract Act §10
Burden of ProofDocument proves itself under Evidence ActRequires direct witness & electronic proof
Limitation PeriodUp to 6 years (if registered deed)Strict 3-year deadline under Article 115
Interim Asset FreezeAvailable via Order 38 CPCAvailable via Order 38 CPC with proof
Admissibility of ChatsSupplementary evidencePrimary corroborative evidence

While an oral agreement demands more meticulous evidentiary assembly, the ultimate judicial remedies and debt execution powers of the court are identical.

Illustrative Scenario: Recovering BDT 18 Lakh on an Oral Deal

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) demonstrates how a structured Money Suit recovered substantial funds without a written deed in Dhaka:

A garment accessories manufacturer in Tongi supplied zipper and button consignments valued at BDT 18,50,000 to a buying house in Uttara based entirely on verbal telephone orders and WhatsApp requests. The supplier delivered the goods across four consignments with signed delivery receipts. However, the buyer delayed payment for eight months, offering verbal excuses. Eventually, the buyer blocked the supplier's calls and informed third parties that because there was no stamped contract, the supplier could never recover the money.

The manufacturer retained an experienced civil litigation advocate. Within one week, the advocate served a comprehensive Legal Notice via registered post, detailing the four delivery dates, attaching the signed delivery challans, and quoting verbatim WhatsApp messages where the buyer acknowledged receipt and promised payment by 'next month.' When the buyer ignored the notice, the advocate filed a Money Suit in the Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka, within the three-year limitation period. Simultaneously, they moved an application under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC for interim attachment of the buyer's corporate bank account, proving that the buyer was preparing to close the firm.

Faced with a frozen bank account and confronted with unassailable electronic and delivery records, the debtor's counsel approached the court during pre-trial mediation under Section 89A CPC. The parties executed a court-sanctioned Solenama (compromise decree): the debtor paid BDT 10,00,000 upfront via bank pay order and the remaining BDT 8,50,000 in two post-dated cheques backed by personal guarantees, achieving 100% debt recovery without enduring a full multi-year trial.

Talk to an Advocate

Navigating complex litigation in Bangladesh requires meticulous evidentiary preparation, prompt statutory filings, and strategic courtroom advocacy. Whether you are dealing with business debts, family property partitions, corporate oppression, employee theft, or administrative overreach, attempting to resolve disputes without seasoned legal counsel frequently causes irreversible procedural defaults. A qualified advocate protects your rights, secures urgent injunctions or stay orders, and ensures complete statutory compliance across civil, criminal, and constitutional forums.

Need an advocate for this legal matter in Bangladesh? Send your case documents on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: remote consultation and court representation available.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is an oral contract legally binding in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under Section 10 of the Contract Act 1872, an agreement does not need to be in writing to be legally enforceable, provided it contains mutual consent, competent parties, lawful consideration, and a lawful object. Oral contracts are valid unless a specific statute explicitly mandates written registration.

How long do I have to file a lawsuit for an unpaid oral debt?

Under Article 115 of the Limitation Act 1908, the statutory limitation period to file a Money Suit for breach of an unwritten contract is strictly three (3) years from the date of default or from the date of the last partial repayment or written acknowledgment.

Can I use WhatsApp messages and SMS to prove an oral agreement in court?

Yes. Under modern evidentiary practice and Section 65B of the Evidence Act, digital communications such as WhatsApp chats, text messages, and emails acknowledging the debt or discussing delivery terms are fully admissible as electronic corroboration.

What court do I file a Money Suit in for recovering business debts?

Money Suits are filed in the Civil Court based on pecuniary jurisdiction. Modest claims are heard by Senior Assistant Judges, while substantial commercial claims (typically above BDT 25,00,000) are filed in the Court of the Joint District Judge.

What is an Order 38 Rule 5 CPC attachment before judgment?

It is an emergency civil court order that temporarily freezes the debtor's bank accounts, real estate, or commercial inventories while the lawsuit is ongoing, preventing them from hiding or selling assets before the decree is passed.

Do I have to pay court fees to file a Money Suit in Bangladesh?

Yes. Money Suits require an ad-valorem court fee calculated as a percentage of the claimed debt amount under the Court-fees Act 1870, subject to a statutory maximum cap. If you win the suit, the court typically decrees that the debtor must reimburse your court fees and legal costs.

Can an oral debt be converted into a criminal case under Section 420 Penal Code?

If the debtor had fraudulent intentions from the very inception (such as providing fake identities or non-existent company names), a criminal case for cheating under Section 420 and criminal breach of trust under Section 406 can be filed alongside or prior to civil recovery.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi (NRB) sue for unpaid business money from abroad?

Yes. An NRB creditor can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the local Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, appointing a representative or advocate in Bangladesh to institute and prosecute the Money Suit on their behalf.

entries.body:
How to Challenge a Court Order Bangladesh: Revision, Review, and Appeal

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-04-12 · 14 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Receiving an adverse court order is not the end of your legal road in Bangladesh. The law provides several mechanisms to challenge court orders — revision, review, and appeal — each with distinct criteria, time limits, and courts. Choosing the right mechanism at the right time is critical to protecting your legal rights.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order
Official Portalssupremecourt.gov.bd, judiciary.gov.bd, pcc.police.gov.bd & land.gov.bd
Supreme Court ChamberAdvocate Md. Shah Alam — Uttara & Dhaka Judge Court (+880 1712-655546)
📋 In This Article
  1. The Three Routes to Challenge a Court Order
  2. What is an Appeal in Bangladesh?
  3. What is a Revision Petition?
  4. What is a Review Petition?
  5. Comparison: Appeal vs. Revision vs. Review
  6. Time Limits for Filing
  7. Comparison: Appeal vs Revision vs Review
  8. Filing at the High Court: Step-by-Step Process
  9. Writ Petition: The Constitutional Route

The Three Routes to Challenge a Court Order

In Bangladesh, court orders can be challenged through three main mechanisms:

  • Appeal: A superior court rehears the case on merit — both facts and law.
  • Revision: A superior court examines only whether the lower court had jurisdiction and whether it followed proper legal procedure — not a rehearing on facts.
  • Review: The same court that passed the order is asked to reconsider it based on specific grounds.

Selecting the correct route depends on the nature of the order, the court that passed it, and the grounds of challenge. A Supreme Court lawyer in Dhaka is essential for High Court and Appellate Division challenges.

What is an Appeal in Bangladesh?

An appeal is the most comprehensive challenge — the superior court effectively re-examines the case, both the factual findings and the application of law. Key features:

  • Available as a right in most cases (statutory right of appeal).
  • Goes to a higher court: District Court appeal from Magistrate Court, High Court appeal from District Court, Appellate Division from High Court.
  • Can challenge findings of fact, evaluation of evidence, and legal errors.
  • For criminal cases: the State can also appeal against acquittals.

What is a Revision Petition?

A revision petition under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) or Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) allows the High Court to examine whether a subordinate court:

  • Acted without jurisdiction or exceeded its jurisdiction.
  • Failed to exercise jurisdiction it should have exercised.
  • Acted with material irregularity or illegality in the exercise of jurisdiction.

Important: Revision is not a second appeal. The High Court in revision does not re-examine factual findings — it only examines jurisdictional and procedural errors. A revision cannot be used merely because you disagree with the decision on facts.

What is a Review Petition?

A review petition (Order 47 CPC) asks the same court that passed the order to reconsider it. Grounds for review are limited:

  • Discovery of new and important evidence not previously available.
  • A mistake or error apparent on the face of the record.
  • Any other sufficient reason.

Review is the narrowest remedy — courts rarely grant review unless there is a clear error on the face of the judgment. It is not a mechanism to relitigate the case or introduce new arguments that could have been raised originally.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Time Limits for Filing

Time limits under the Limitation Act 1908 are strict — missing the deadline usually ends your right to challenge:

  • Civil appeal to District Court: 30 days from the decree.
  • Civil appeal to High Court: 90 days.
  • Criminal appeal: 60 days from the date of conviction or sentence.
  • Revision (civil): 90 days from the order.
  • Revision (criminal): No strict limitation but delay must be explained.
  • Review: 30 days from the date of decree/order.

Limitation can be condoned (extended) if you show sufficient cause for the delay — but courts are strict and delays must be genuinely explained. Act immediately after an adverse order.

Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam in Uttara immediately upon receiving an adverse court order — delay costs legal rights.

Comparison: Appeal vs Revision vs Review

The three remedies for challenging a court order in Bangladesh — appeal, revision, and review — are frequently confused. This comparison clarifies when each applies and what outcomes are possible:

Criterion Appeal Revision Review
CourtSuperior court (next level up)High Court DivisionSame court that passed the order
GroundsFacts and/or lawJurisdiction and procedural errors onlyNew evidence, face-of-record error
Right vs. discretionUsually a statutory rightDiscretionary (court decides whether to interfere)Discretionary (rarely granted)
Re-examination of evidence?Yes — full re-examinationNo — jurisdictional review onlyLimited — only specific new evidence
Typical timeframe1–5 years6 months – 3 years3–12 months

The most important practical distinction: if you believe the lower court reached the wrong factual conclusion on the evidence, an appeal is your remedy. If the lower court had no power to make the order it made (jurisdictional error), a revision is appropriate. If there is an obvious clerical or mathematical error in the judgment itself, a review may be available. A Supreme Court lawyer in Dhaka can immediately identify the correct remedy for your specific situation.

Filing at the High Court: Step-by-Step Process

Whether you are filing a criminal appeal, civil revision, or constitutional writ petition at the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, the procedural steps are broadly similar. Understanding the process reduces delays and prevents technical rejections.

Step 1: Obtain the Lower Court Record

Secure certified copies of: the judgment/order being challenged; all pleadings, evidence, and documents filed in the lower court; the charge sheet or plaint (as applicable). These are obtainable from the lower court's record room upon payment of prescribed copy fees. Your lawyer will know exactly which documents are needed.

Step 2: Prepare the Petition or Memo of Appeal

Your lawyer prepares the formal petition. For an appeal: a Memo of Appeal specifying the grounds on which the lower court judgment is wrong. For a revision: a Revision Petition under Section 115 CPC or Section 439 CrPC setting out the jurisdictional error. For a writ: a Writ Petition under Article 102 of the Constitution. The petition must be precise — the High Court only considers grounds specifically pleaded.

Step 3: File at the High Court Registry

The petition, supporting affidavit, certified copies of lower court documents, court fees (through judicial stamps), and a vakalatnama (authority letter from the client to the advocate) are filed at the Supreme Court registry. The case receives a cause list number and is allocated to a bench.

Step 4: Apply for Stay/Interim Order

Simultaneously with filing, your lawyer will apply for a stay of the lower court order pending hearing — preventing enforcement of the judgment while the appeal/revision is pending. Courts grant conditional stays in most genuine cases.

Step 5: Hearing and Judgment

The case is listed for hearing before a High Court bench. After arguments, the court issues its ruling — either confirming, modifying, or reversing the lower court order. For expert representation at the Bangladesh High Court and Appellate Division, contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam — Supreme Court lawyer in Dhaka.

Writ Petition: The Constitutional Route

Beyond the ordinary appeals and revisions, Bangladesh law provides a powerful constitutional remedy — the writ petition under Article 102 of the Bangladesh Constitution. A writ petition is filed directly in the High Court Division and is available when ordinary legal remedies are inadequate or where a fundamental constitutional right is at stake.

Types of Writs Available

  • Writ of Certiorari: Quashing an illegal order of a lower court, tribunal, or public authority — used when the order is made without jurisdiction or through procedural abuse. Very commonly used to quash FIRs and lower court criminal orders in Bangladesh.
  • Writ of Mandamus: Compelling a public authority to perform a duty it is legally required to perform but is refusing — e.g., compelling a government office to process your application or compelling police to register an FIR.
  • Writ of Prohibition: Preventing a lower court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction in an ongoing proceeding.
  • Writ of Habeas Corpus: Challenging unlawful detention — requiring the detaining authority to produce the detainee before the court and justify the detention. One of the most powerful remedies for illegal arrest or imprisonment in Bangladesh.

When to Use a Writ Instead of Appeal or Revision

  • When ordinary appeals/revisions would take too long and immediate relief is needed
  • When a government authority (not just a court) has acted illegally against you
  • When an FIR is clearly false, vexatious, and should be quashed before trial begins
  • When someone is being held in detention without lawful authority (habeas corpus)
  • When a lower court or tribunal is acting entirely outside its jurisdiction

The High Court has broad power under Article 102 and regularly uses it to correct injustices that ordinary appeal channels would address too slowly. For urgent constitutional matters, the High Court can hear writ applications on the same day they are filed in genuine emergencies. Contact a High Court writ lawyer in Dhaka immediately if you believe a constitutional remedy is needed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I file both a review and a revision on the same order?

Generally no — you should use the appropriate remedy. Filing a review and then a revision (or vice versa) can complicate your case. Choose the right mechanism based on the nature of the error with guidance from a lawyer.

What is a writ petition and is it different from revision?

Yes. A writ petition before the High Court under Articles 102 of Bangladesh Constitution challenges the constitutional validity of actions or laws, or enforces fundamental rights. Revision challenges ordinary procedural or jurisdictional errors in lower court orders. Both are different tools for different situations.

Can I get a stay of the lower court order while filing revision?

Yes. When filing a revision or appeal, you can simultaneously apply for a stay of the lower court order (execution of the decree). Courts often grant a conditional stay pending hearing of the revision or appeal.

How to Check Land Ownership in Bangladesh Online: Complete Khatian, Mutation & Porcha Verification Guide 2026

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-04 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

With the full digitalization of land records under the Ministry of Land and the Directorate of Land Records and Surveys (DLRS), verifying property ownership in Bangladesh no longer requires visiting tehsils blindly. Buyers, institutional investors, and Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) can now inspect historical Khatians, mutation orders, and land tax receipts from anywhere in the world. However, digital portals do not detect un-registered mortgages, forged title deeds, or undisclosed heirs. This comprehensive 2026 verification guide by <strong>Advocate Md. Shah Alam</strong> (Advocate, Supreme Court of Bangladesh) explains how to verify property records online and what offline checks remain indispensable.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Official Government Portalsland.gov.bd, mutation.land.gov.bd, dlrms.land.gov.bd & eporcha.gov.bd
Total Official E-Namjari FeeBDT 1,170 (Court fee 20 + Notice 50 + Record fee 1,000 + Khatian 100)
Standard Processing Time28 Working Days (9–12 working days for NRB / expatriate applicants)
National Land Helpline16122 (24/7 Ministry of Land Call Center)
📋 In This Article

  2. Understanding the Survey Chain: CS, SA, RS, and BS/City Khatians
  3. Step-by-Step: How to Search Khatian (Porcha) Online on eporcha.gov.bd
  4. Checking Mutation (Namjari) & DCR Authenticity on mutation.land.gov.bd
  5. Verifying Land Development Tax (LD Tax / Khajna) Online
  6. Critical Limitations: What Online Portals Cannot Reveal
  7. The Lawyer's Offline Title Search: Balaam Boi & Non-Encumbrance (NEC)
  8. Document Checklist Before Paying Earnest Money (Baina)
  9. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Why Online Land Verification is Mandatory Before Any Property Purchase

Purchasing real estate in Bangladesh without rigorous due diligence carries substantial risk of fraud, double sales, and inheritance disputes. The Ministry of Land's digital infrastructure allows buyers to review records of rights instantly, preventing obvious impersonation and forged surveys.

However, digital records represent fiscal survey entries (presumption of possession) rather than indisputable evidence of legal title. A verified property must possess an unbroken chain of ownership connecting the oldest cadastral survey down to the present vendor.

Understanding the Survey Chain: CS, SA, RS, and BS/City Khatians

To establish clean title, your legal counsel will inspect each successive land survey conducted across Bangladesh:

  • CS (Cadastral Survey - 1888–1940): The baseline colonial survey establishing historical root title.
  • SA (State Acquisition Survey - 1956–1962): Created after the abolition of the zamindari system to record tenant-farmers.
  • RS (Revisional Survey - 1966–1990s): Updated survey rectifying SA discrepancies and reflecting partitioned plots.
  • BS / City Survey (Bangladesh Survey - 1998–Present): The latest survey in Dhaka, Chittagong, and major municipalities. Mutation must match the BS Khatian.

Step-by-Step: How to Search Khatian (Porcha) Online on eporcha.gov.bd

Follow these official steps to inspect or download records on eporcha.gov.bd:

  1. Navigate to the Survey Khatian (জরিপ খতিয়ান) module on the homepage.
  2. Select the Division (বিভাগ), District (জেলা), Upazila/Thana (উপজেলা), and exact Mouza with JL Number.
  3. Choose the survey type: CS, SA, RS, or BS.
  4. Enter the Khatian Number or Dag (Plot) Number, or search by the recorded owner’s name.
  5. View the online preview showing plot shares, boundaries, and recorded owners.
  6. For legal proceedings or registration, apply online for a certified certified copy (সার্টিফাইড কপি) by paying the statutory fee (৳100).

Checking Mutation (Namjari) & DCR Authenticity on mutation.land.gov.bd

Whenever land changes hands through purchase, gift (Heba), or inheritance, the buyer must mutate their name under Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. To verify a mutation:

  • Log onto mutation.land.gov.bd and enter the Application ID or Khatian Number.
  • Inspect the AC Land Order Sheet to verify whether due process, newspaper notices, and hearing of all co-sharers occurred.
  • Confirm the Duplicate Carbon Receipt (DCR) showing payment of the ৳1,170 government mutation fee.
  • Scan the QR code on the computerized Mutation Certificate to ensure it matches the database of the Ministry of Land.
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Verifying Land Development Tax (LD Tax / Khajna) Online

Since 2023, manual land tax collection in Bangladesh has ceased. All taxes must be cleared via ldtax.gov.bd.

Request the vendor’s Holding Number and NID-linked profile. The digital Dakhila (tax receipt) must reflect cleared arrears up to the current fiscal year (১৪৩২-১৪৩৩ বঙ্গাব্দ / 2026). Incomplete tax records obstruct smooth deed registration.

Critical Limitations: What Online Portals Cannot Reveal

Online government portals are administrative databases; they do NOT certify clean legal title. Major vulnerabilities that online portals miss include:

  • Unregistered Encumbrances: Equitable mortgages with financial institutions where original deeds are deposited without mutation alteration.
  • Pending Civil Suits: Lis pendens suits in Civil Courts for partition (বণ্টন), cancellation of deed (দলিল বাতিল), or pre-emption (অগ্রক্রয়).
  • Disinherited Heirs: Missing heirs under Muslim or Hindu succession laws whose shares were fraudulently omitted in vendor's mutation.
  • Physical Possession Deficits: Adverse possession or land-grabbing by local encroachers.

The Lawyer's Offline Title Search: Balaam Boi & Non-Encumbrance (NEC)

To eliminate purchase risks, a Supreme Court property lawyer performs manual offline vetting:

  1. Balaam Boi Search (বালাম বই তল্লাশি): Physical inspection of the volume record index at the concerned Sub-Registry Office to ensure the vendor's deed was genuine and not cancelled.
  2. Non-Encumbrance Certificate (NEC / ১২ ধারা তল্লাশি): Applying for an official 12-to-30-year search certificate certifying that the property has not been encumbered, mortgaged, or transferred to third parties.
  3. Chain of Title Report: Drafting a formal Title Vetting Opinion analyzing the legal coherence of all predecessor deeds.

Document Checklist Before Paying Earnest Money (Baina)

Ensure you have certified copies of the following documents in hand before signing any Baina Agreement:

  • Original Title Deed (মূল দলিল) and all Bia Deeds (বায়া দলিল) for 25–30 years.
  • Certified CS, SA, RS, and City/BS Survey Khatians.
  • Registered Mutation Khatian, AC Land Order Sheet, and DCR.
  • Up-to-date online Land Development Tax (Khajna) Dakhila.
  • Sub-Registry 12-year Non-Encumbrance Search Receipt.
  • Approved building plan and clearance letters (for residential plots/apartments).

⚖️ Urgent Case Evaluation & Legal Consultation

Facing property litigation, criminal arrest risk, commercial dispute or constitutional infringement? Consult directly with Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Advocate, Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

💬 WhatsApp Chambers (+8801712655546) 📞 Direct Call (01712655546) Chamber Address & Booking →

📍 Chamber 1: House 46, Road 6/B, Sector 12, Uttara, Dhaka-1230 | Chamber 2: Supreme Court Bar Association Annex, Dhaka.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can an online Khatian prove 100% legal ownership?

No. A Khatian creates a legal presumption of possession, but true ownership depends on valid registered deeds, unbroken title chain, and actual peaceful physical possession.

How much does a certified copy of Khatian cost online?

The government fee is ৳100 for an online certified copy delivered via post or downloadable directly from eporcha.gov.bd.

What is the difference between Khatian and Mutation?

A Khatian is an official survey record prepared periodically by the government. Mutation (Namjari) is the intermediate process by which a new owner's name replaces the seller's name in official records after purchase or inheritance.

Why is a 12-year Non-Encumbrance Certificate (NEC) necessary?

An NEC issued by the Sub-Registrar proves that no other registered deeds, mortgages, or transfers have occurred on the specified property within the searched duration.

entries.body:
Defending a Cheque Bounce Case Bangladesh: What the Law Requires and How to Win

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-04-16 · 9 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

⚡ Quick Answer: If you received a legal notice for cheque dishonour under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, you have 30 days to pay or respond before a criminal case is filed. Even after a case is filed, strong defences exist — and conviction is not automatic. The complainant must prove four strict elements, and failure to prove any one of them means the case fails. — This guide tells you exactly how to defend yourself.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order
Official Portalssupremecourt.gov.bd, judiciary.gov.bd, pcc.police.gov.bd & land.gov.bd

📋 In This Article
  1. What Must the Complainant Prove?
  2. The 30-Day Window – Act Now
  3. Common Defences That Work
  4. Defence 1: Security Cheque
  5. Defence 2: Legal Notice Not Properly Served
  6. Defence 3: Underlying Debt Disputed
  7. Defence 4: Post-Dated Cheque Presented Early
  8. Timeline of a Section 138 Case
  9. Penalties If Convicted
  10. Settlement – When to Consider It

What Must the Complainant Prove?

Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, the complainant must prove all four of these elements to obtain a conviction:

  1. The cheque was issued by the accused (not forged or issued under duress)
  2. The cheque was presented within six months of the date it was issued
  3. The bank dishonoured it due to insufficient funds (not a bank error or technical issue)
  4. The accused received the legal demand notice and failed to pay the amount within 30 days of receipt

If any one element is missing, the case fails entirely. This is why an experienced criminal lawyer in Dhaka examines the complaint carefully before even fielding a plea — many cases have defects that can be identified and exploited immediately.

The 30-Day Window – Act Now

The most important action you can take after receiving a legal notice is to act within 30 days of receipt:

  • If the cheque amount is genuinely owed and you can pay, pay it within 30 days — this completely prevents the case from being filed
  • If you dispute the debt or the notice, immediately consult a lawyer — your response strategy must be prepared now
  • Do NOT ignore the notice. Ignoring it is treated as a refusal to pay, and the case will be filed against you within one month of the 30-day deadline

Once a case is filed in Magistrate Court and summons are issued, your options become more limited. The 30-day window is your best opportunity.

Common Defences That Work

The following defences have been successfully argued in Bangladesh courts under Section 138:

  • Cheque was a security cheque — issued as a guarantee, not to pay an existing debt
  • Legal notice not properly served — sent to wrong address, or not actually received
  • Underlying debt is disputed — the alleged loan never existed or was a gift
  • Cheque was post-dated and presented before the due date
  • Cheque was stolen or forged — you did not issue it
  • Limitation period expired — the complaint was filed more than one month after the 30-day notice period

The right defence depends entirely on the specific facts of your case. A criminal lawyer in Uttara will identify which ground applies and build the strongest argument around it.

Defence 1: Security Cheque

If the cheque was issued as security — as a guarantee for a future obligation that has not yet been fulfilled or has been cancelled — the debt or liability did not exist at the time of dishonour. Section 138 requires that the cheque was issued 'in discharge of a debt or other liability.' A security cheque with no crystallised debt does not meet this element.

Evidence to gather: any written agreement stating the cheque was security, WhatsApp messages between parties discussing the arrangement, bank transfer records showing the underlying transaction never happened, and witness statements.

Defence 2: Legal Notice Not Properly Served

The 30-day payment window under Section 138(b) only starts running from the actual receipt of the legal demand notice by the accused. If the notice:

  • Was sent to the wrong address
  • Was returned unclaimed without the accused actually receiving it
  • Was sent by ordinary post with no proof of delivery
  • Was sent to an old address the accused no longer lives at

...then the notice requirement may not be properly satisfied, and the entire case can fail at the threshold. Courts have dismissed cases on this ground alone. Carefully check the address on the notice and compare it to your registered address on NID.
