  7. Visitation Rights for the Non-Custodial Parent
  8. Key Supreme Court Decisions on Muslim Law Custody Bangladesh

Hizanat: The Islamic Law of Maternal Custody

Hizanat is the Arabic term for the right and duty of a mother (or female relative) to have physical custody of a young child for the purposes of nurturing, care, and upbringing. Under Islamic jurisprudence as applied in Bangladesh, this right belongs first and foremost to the natural mother.

The rationale for maternal custody of young children is rooted in the child's need for maternal care during the formative years. Classical Islamic scholars — both Hanafi (followed by Sunni Muslims in Bangladesh) and Shafi'i — recognised that young children, especially infants and toddlers, require the physical and emotional care of a mother in ways that fathers are typically unable to replicate.

Under the Hanafi school (the predominant school in Bangladesh), the age limits for hizanat are:

  • For boys: Until the age of 7 years, the mother has the primary right of custody.
  • For girls: Until the onset of puberty (which courts generally treat as approximately 9–15 years depending on individual development), the mother has the primary right of custody.

After these ages, the father (as legal guardian) becomes entitled to custody — though as discussed below, Bangladesh courts apply the welfare principle flexibly rather than rigidly adhering to these age limits.

If the biological mother is unavailable or unfit, hizanat passes to other female relatives in the following order of priority: maternal grandmother, paternal grandmother, full sisters, uterine sisters (daughters of the same mother but different father), consanguine sisters (same father, different mother), maternal aunts, and finally paternal aunts. Courts follow this order of preference while always keeping the child's welfare central.

When Does the Mother's Right of Hizanat End?

The mother's right of hizanat can be forfeited before the age limit in specific circumstances recognised under both Islamic law and Bangladesh court practice:

  1. Remarriage to a Stranger: If the mother remarries a person who is not a mahram of the child (i.e., not a relative within the forbidden degrees of marriage to the child), she automatically forfeits her right of hizanat under classical Hanafi law. Courts in Bangladesh apply this rule but also consider whether the new stepfather has a good relationship with the child.
  2. Gross Immorality or Misconduct: If the mother is found guilty of immoral conduct — such as living in an adulterous relationship, chronic substance abuse, or prostitution — the court will terminate her custody rights.
  3. Neglect or Ill-Treatment: Proven neglect of the child's basic needs — food, clothing, healthcare, education — can lead to forfeiture.
  4. Apostasy: Under classical Islamic law, a mother who leaves Islam loses her right of hizanat over Muslim children, though this ground has rarely been applied by Bangladesh courts in modern practice.
  5. Separation by Distance: If the mother relocates to a place so far away that the father would be deprived of his right to see and supervise the child, the court may transfer custody to the father.
  6. General Unfitness: Any circumstance that renders the mother unsuitable to raise the child — including serious mental or physical illness — can be grounds for forfeiture.

Importantly, Bangladesh courts have repeatedly held that poverty alone is not a ground for depriving a mother of hizanat. The father's maintenance obligation continues even when the mother has custody, and financial inability of the mother does not per se make her unfit.

Wilayat: The Father's Guardianship Rights

While the mother has hizanat (physical custody), the father holds wilayat — the legal guardianship and authority over the child's person and property. These rights exist independently of the custody arrangement and continue throughout the child's minority (until age 18 under Bangladesh law).

The father's rights as wali (guardian) include:

  • Religious upbringing: The father determines the child's religion. Children of a Muslim father must be raised as Muslims.
  • Education decisions: School selection, subject choices, and educational planning fall within the father's guardianship.
  • Property management: The father manages any property owned by or inherited by the minor child until the child reaches majority.
  • Travel and documentation: Passports, visas, and travel consent for the child require the father's approval as guardian.
  • Medical decisions: Major medical decisions about the child's health fall within the father's purview, though in practice the custodial mother handles day-to-day healthcare.
  • Marriage guardianship (ijbar): For daughters, the father (or grandfather) acts as wali nikah (marriage guardian) in arranging marriage.

Even when the mother has physical custody, the father's role as legal guardian remains intact. Courts frequently make orders specifying how guardianship duties are to be exercised so that both parents can fulfil their respective roles. If you have questions about your guardianship rights, a family lawyer in Bangladesh can advise you.

Role of Other Relatives in Custody (Agnates and Cognates)

When neither the mother nor the father is able or willing to assume custody, Islamic law provides a detailed scheme of alternative custodians from among the child's relatives. Courts in Bangladesh have occasionally needed to apply these rules in cases of parental death, incapacity, or disappearance.

The priority order among female relatives (for the right of hizanat) after the biological mother is:

  1. Maternal grandmother (nani), ascending in order;
  2. Paternal grandmother (dadi), ascending in order;
  3. Full sisters;
  4. Uterine (half) sisters (same mother, different father);
  5. Consanguine (half) sisters (same father, different mother);
  6. Full maternal aunts;
  7. Paternal aunts.

Among male relatives (for guardianship/wilayat when the father is unavailable), the order of priority is:

  1. Paternal grandfather;
  2. Full brother;
  3. Half-brother (consanguine);
  4. Full paternal uncle;
  5. Half paternal uncle.

Courts have the power under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 to appoint any suitable person as guardian — whether a relative or not — if it is for the welfare of the child. The personal law priority list is a guide, not an absolute rule.

How Courts Balance Islamic Law with the Welfare Principle

The single most important principle in Bangladesh's approach to child custody is the welfare of the child. While Islamic personal law provides the framework, courts have consistently held that the child's welfare is the paramount — and overriding — consideration.

This means that:

  • If giving custody to the father (even after the hizanat age expires) would better serve the child's welfare, the mother may retain custody beyond the prescribed age limits.
  • If the mother is unfit but the next-in-line Islamic relative is also unfit, the court can appoint an entirely different guardian who is not in the Islamic list of priorities.
  • Courts can impose conditions on custody — such as requiring the custodial parent to live in a particular city, maintain the child's existing school enrollment, or facilitate regular contact with the other parent.
  • The welfare principle allows courts to adapt the personal law rules to 21st-century family structures, including cases involving joint parenting, working mothers, and fathers who are the primary caregivers.

The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has in multiple decisions emphasised that the welfare of the child supersedes the technical rules of personal law when the two conflict. This progressive judicial approach provides both parents with a fair opportunity to argue their case on its merits.

Filing a Custody Case Under Muslim Law in Bangladesh

Whether you are a mother seeking to retain or enforce your hizanat rights, or a father seeking custody or enhanced visitation, the procedural steps are the same:

  1. Consult a Specialist Lawyer: Engage a family law specialist who is familiar with both Islamic personal law and the Family Courts Ordinance 1985.
  2. File at the Family Court: The Family Court at the district level (Senior Assistant Judge's Court) has jurisdiction over custody and guardianship matters.
  3. Draft the Petition: The petition should cite the relevant provisions of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 and the Family Courts Ordinance 1985, and set out the factual basis for the claim.
  4. Seek Interim Relief: If the child has been wrongfully withheld, apply for an interim custody order at the first hearing.
  5. Attend Hearings: Both parents must attend hearings and present evidence — character witnesses, school records, home visit reports, and any relevant documents.
  6. Final Order: The court passes a decree on custody, visitation schedule, and maintenance.
  7. Enforcement: If the other party refuses to comply with the order, file a contempt application before the same court.

Visitation Rights for the Non-Custodial Parent

Even when one parent is granted custody, the non-custodial parent retains the right to regular, meaningful contact with the child. Bangladesh courts recognise mulaqat (visitation) as an enforceable right under both Islamic law and general family law.

Courts typically specify the visitation schedule in the custody decree, including:

  • Regular weekly or bi-weekly visits (e.g., every weekend from Friday to Saturday);
  • Extended stays during school holidays and Eid vacations;
  • Special occasions such as birthdays and religious festivals;
  • Telephone and video call access if the parents live in different cities.

Denial of court-ordered visitation is treated as contempt of court and can result in fine or imprisonment of the defaulting parent. Courts may also vary the custody arrangement in favour of the aggrieved parent if visitation is persistently denied.

If you are being denied contact with your child, immediately consult a family lawyer to file an enforcement or contempt application before the Family Court.

Key Supreme Court Decisions on Muslim Law Custody Bangladesh

Several landmark decisions from the Supreme Court of Bangladesh have shaped the modern application of Muslim law custody rules. These include:

  • Welfare as the Paramount Test: The Appellate Division has repeatedly held that in all custody matters, the welfare of the child is the paramount and overriding consideration, which can override even clear rules of Muslim personal law (see various cases under the Guardians and Wards Act).
  • Mother's Right Beyond Age Limits: High Court Division benches have upheld the mother's right to retain custody beyond the technical hizanat age when the child's welfare so requires, particularly where the child has a strong emotional bond with the mother and the father is shown to be unfit.
  • Poverty Is No Ground: Courts have consistently held that the mother's poverty alone cannot deprive her of hizanat — the father's maintenance obligation must be enforced instead.
  • Habeas Corpus for Child Recovery: The High Court Division has used its habeas corpus jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution to order the return of children wrongfully withheld by one parent in defiance of a custody order.

For advice on how these principles apply to your specific situation, contact a qualified Supreme Court lawyer in Bangladesh who can provide guidance based on current judicial trends.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a Muslim father automatically get custody when his son turns 7 in Bangladesh?

Not automatically. While Islamic law provides that the mother's hizanat for sons ends at age 7, Bangladesh courts apply the welfare of the child as the paramount principle. If the child's welfare is better served by remaining with the mother, the court can allow her to retain custody beyond age 7. The father must apply to court and demonstrate that custody should be transferred.

Can a Muslim mother remarry and still keep custody of her children?

Under classical Hanafi law, remarriage to a stranger (someone not a close relative of the child) results in forfeiture of hizanat. However, Bangladesh courts have softened this rule by also examining the child's welfare — if the new stepfather treats the child well and the child is thriving, some courts have been reluctant to transfer custody automatically. Each case is assessed on its individual facts.

Can grandparents apply for custody of grandchildren in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, any person with a sufficient interest in the child's welfare — including grandparents — can apply to be appointed as guardian. Grandparents are also recognised within the Islamic priority list for hizanat when the parents are unavailable or unfit.

What maintenance is the father obliged to pay during the mother's custody period?

Under Muslim law, the father is obliged to pay maintenance (nafaqa) for the children regardless of which parent has custody. This includes food, clothing, shelter, healthcare, and education costs. The mother is also entitled to a fee (ajr al-hadana) for her services as custodian if she demands it. Courts fix the maintenance amount based on the father's income and the child's needs.

What happens if the custodial parent takes the child abroad without permission?

Taking a child abroad without the other parent's consent or a court order can amount to contempt of court and child abduction. The aggrieved parent should immediately apply to the High Court for a habeas corpus order and seek a port alert to prevent the child's removal from Bangladesh. Consult an experienced family lawyer immediately in such situations.

Who gets custody, who can take the child abroad, and what happens if one parent refuses to return the child? Custody vs Guardianship

Custody (hizanat) means physical care of the child. Guardianship means legal authority over the child's person and property. Under Muslim law, the father is the natural guardian, but the mother usually has custody of young children: boys generally until about seven years and girls until puberty, although courts treat these ages as guidelines, not rigid limits. The welfare of the child can override them.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Which Court Decides?

The Family Court in the district where the child ordinarily lives has jurisdiction. Applications are made under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, read with the Family Courts Ordinance 1985. The court first tries mediation and reconciliation, then hears evidence from both sides and may order a social inquiry or interview the child.

Factors Courts Consider

  • The child's age, health and emotional bond with each parent.
  • Stability of home, education and schooling.
  • Each parent's income, conduct and ability to provide care.
  • Wishes of an older child.
  • Whether a parent is in a position to maintain regular contact if the child is moved.

When One Parent Lives Abroad

A parent abroad can:

  • File or defend the case through an advocate with a notarised and attested Power of Attorney (see PoA guide).
  • Give evidence by video if the court permits.
  • Apply for interim visitation or video call access.
  • Seek an order for maintenance of the child.

If the parent abroad wants custody, the court will ask how the child's schooling, residence and contact with the other parent will be arranged. A realistic plan matters.

Visitation and Relocation

Courts can order structured visitation: weekend contact, holiday stays, or video calls. If one parent wants to relocate the child abroad, the court's permission is usually needed when there is a dispute. A parent who removes a child abroad without consent risks a custody order against him or her, and possible criminal action. Bangladesh is not a party to the Hague Convention on child abduction, which makes cross-border enforcement harder, so negotiate and document arrangements early.

Maintenance and Practical Steps

  1. Gather the child's birth certificate, school records and proof of residence.
  2. Keep a record of financial support and communication.
  3. Seek interim orders for custody, visitation and maintenance at the start.
  4. Consider mediation or a written parenting agreement approved by the court.
  5. Obtain a mirror order or recognition abroad if the child will live there.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who gets custody of a child in Bangladesh?

The Family Court decides on the child's welfare; mothers commonly keep young children, but this is not an absolute rule.

Can the father take the child abroad without the mother's consent?

If there is a dispute, doing so can lead to court orders and legal action. Get the court's permission or the other parent's written consent.

Can I fight a custody case from abroad?

Yes, through an advocate and Power of Attorney, and by giving evidence by video if allowed.

Does a foreign custody order apply in Bangladesh?

It is not automatically enforced. A Bangladesh court considers the child's welfare, so you may need to apply there as well.

Is child maintenance compulsory?

Yes. The father has a duty to maintain his children, and the court can order it.

Child Custody Law in Bangladesh (2026) – Complete Guide: Who Gets Custody & How

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-04-07 ·

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

After a divorce or separation, the most painful question parents face is: who will the children live with? In Bangladesh, custody law is complex — it depends on the child's religion, age, and gender. Many parents make critical mistakes by assuming custody will be automatic. This guide explains exactly how child custody works in Bangladesh and what you must do to protect your relationship with your child.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

What Is Child Custody Under Bangladesh Law?

Child custody law in Bangladesh is primarily governed by two frameworks:

  • Muslim Personal Law (Hizanat): For Muslim families, Islamic principle of Hizanat determines who has the right to physical custody of young children.
  • Guardian and Wards Act 1890: Governs legal guardianship and is used by courts of all religions when appointing a legal guardian for children.

There is an important distinction: Physical custody (Hizanat) — who the child lives with day-to-day; and Legal guardianship — who has the legal authority to make decisions about the child's property, education, and well-being. Both may be held by different parties.

Who Has the Legal Right to Child Custody?

Under Muslim law in Bangladesh, the general rule is:

  • Mother has the primary right of physical custody (Hizanat) for young children — sons until age 7, daughters until puberty (approximately 15).
  • Father is the natural legal guardian of the child's person and property.
  • After the custody ages above, the father typically assumes physical custody, but courts always consider the child's welfare above rigid age rules.

The mother loses her right to Hizanat if she: remarries (a non-relative), is found unfit (substance abuse, neglect), or voluntarily relinquishes custody. A custody lawyer in Dhaka can assess your specific situation.

Age and Gender Rules in Muslim Custody Law

The classical age rules under Hizanat in Bangladesh are:

  • Sons: Mother has custody until age 7. After 7, custody passes to the father unless the court determines the child's welfare requires otherwise.
  • Daughters: Mother has custody until puberty (typically 15). After that, custody may pass to the father.

Important: Bangladesh courts increasingly apply a welfare of the child standard that can override these traditional age rules. If a court finds the father's home environment is better for the child's welfare — even for a 5-year-old son — the father may be awarded custody. The child's welfare is always paramount.

Factors Courts Consider in Custody Decisions

When the Family Court decides a custody dispute, it weighs all of these factors:

  • The child's age and maturity
  • The child's own wishes (if old enough to express a preference)
  • Each parent's moral character and fitness
  • Each parent's financial capacity to maintain the child
  • The child's educational and religious requirements
  • Physical and mental health of each parent
  • Continuity — which parent has been the primary caregiver
  • Proximity to the child's school and support network

The court will never award custody to a parent who is found to be abusive, habitually intoxicated, or otherwise unfit, regardless of the age-based rules.

How to Apply for Child Custody in Bangladesh

To apply for child custody through the courts:

  1. Consult an experienced family lawyer to assess your case and determine the grounds for custody.
  2. Your lawyer files a custody petition under the Guardian and Wards Act 1890 at the Family Court in your district.
  3. The court issues notice to the other parent.
  4. Both parents attend hearings; the court may appoint a welfare officer to interview the child.
  5. The court issues a custody order based on the child's best interests.
  6. If custody needs to be transferred, the court enforces the order through a bailiff if necessary.

Pro tip: File the custody petition simultaneously with or immediately after filing for divorce. Custody applications filed early demonstrate commitment and prevent the other parent from taking the child abroad or to another location.

Required Documents for Custody Application

  • Birth certificate of the child
  • Parents' National Identity Cards (NID)
  • Marriage certificate (Kabinnama) or divorce certificate
  • School records and medical records of the child
  • Proof of income and financial stability of the applying parent
  • Evidence of the child's current living arrangement
  • Any previous court orders relating to custody
  • Character references (if available)

Visitation Rights for the Non-Custodial Parent

The parent who does not have physical custody retains the right to visitation (access) with the child. Bangladesh courts typically set out a visitation schedule in the custody order, specifying:

  • Regular weekly or bi-weekly visitation days and times
  • Holiday and Eid visitation arrangements
  • School holiday arrangements
  • Conditions under which visitation may be supervised

Denying visitation without a court order is contempt of court and can result in sanctions against the custodial parent. Similarly, the non-custodial parent cannot take the child outside the country without both parents' consent or a court order.

Can Custody Orders Be Changed?

Yes. Custody orders are not permanent. A parent can apply to the Family Court to modify a custody order if there has been a material change in circumstances, such as:

  • The custodial parent remarries
  • The custodial parent is relocating abroad
  • Evidence of abuse, neglect, or the parent becoming unfit
  • The child's wishes change as they grow older
  • Significant change in either parent's financial or living situation

Courts take modification applications seriously. You will need to demonstrate that the change is in the child's best interests, not merely in your own convenience.

Common Mistakes in Child Custody Cases

  • ❌ Assuming custody is automatic — There is no automatic custody arrangement. If both parents cannot agree in writing, you must apply to the court.
  • ❌ Taking the child abroad without consent — This is child abduction under Bangladesh law and can result in criminal charges.
  • ❌ Using the child as leverage in divorce proceedings — Courts strongly disapprove; it can damage your custody case.
  • ❌ Not filing simultaneously with divorce — Delay allows the other parent to establish a status quo that can be hard to change.
  • ❌ Verbal custody agreements — Only written, court-endorsed agreements are enforceable.
  • ❌ Ignoring child's wishes — For older children, their expressed preference carries significant weight in court.

Cost and Time for Custody Court Cases

Here is what to expect in Bangladesh:

  • Court filing fees: ৳500–৳2,000
  • Lawyer fees: ৳20,000–৳80,000 for an uncontested custody case; ৳80,000–৳2,00,000+ for contested proceedings.
  • Timeline: Uncontested custody — 2–6 months. Contested custody — 1–5 years depending on complexity.

Many families resolve custody through a written parenting agreement drafted by a lawyer — this is faster and cheaper and avoids prolonged court battles that are traumatic for children.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who gets custody of children in Bangladesh after divorce?

Under Muslim law, the mother typically has physical custody (Hizanat) — sons until age 7, daughters until puberty. After those ages, the father may assume custody. However, courts can override these rules based on the child's best interests.

Can a father get custody of children in Bangladesh?

Yes. The father is the natural legal guardian of the child. He can obtain physical custody when children exceed the Hizanat ages, or earlier if the court finds it is in the child's best interests.

How do I apply for child custody in Bangladesh?

File a custody petition under the Guardian and Wards Act 1890 at the Family Court in your district. A family lawyer can prepare the petition and represent you throughout the proceedings.

Can the mother lose custody in Bangladesh?

Yes. A mother loses her right to Hizanat (physical custody) if she remarries a non-relative, is found unfit (neglect, abuse, substance abuse), or voluntarily relinquishes custody.

Can a custody order be changed in Bangladesh?

Yes. Either parent can apply to the Family Court to modify a custody order if there is a material change in circumstances — such as the custodial parent relocating abroad, remarrying, or becoming unfit.

What happens if my spouse takes my child abroad without permission?

This is child abduction under Bangladesh law. Contact the police immediately and file a habeas corpus petition before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court for return of the child.

Does the child's preference matter in custody decisions in Bangladesh?

Yes. For older children who can express a clear preference, courts give significant weight to the child's wishes. The older and more mature the child, the more influential their preference becomes.

  6. Custody Disputes: Filing a Petition
  7. Visitation Rights for the Non-Custodial Parent
  8. International Child Custody Issues

Legal Framework for Child Custody in Bangladesh

Child custody in Bangladesh is primarily governed by:

  • The Guardians and Wards Act 1890: The main statute for appointing guardians and settling custody disputes, applicable to all religions.
  • Muslim Personal Law (Shariat Application Act 1937): Governs custody rights (hizanat) for Muslims based on Islamic jurisprudence.
  • Family Courts Ordinance 1985: Family Courts have exclusive jurisdiction over custody, guardianship, and related matrimonial matters.

The ultimate guiding principle in all custody decisions in Bangladesh is the welfare of the child, regardless of what the religious personal law provides. Contact a family law expert in Uttara for advice specific to your situation.

What Is Hizanat (Maternal Custody)?

Under Islamic law as applied in Bangladesh, hizanat refers to the primary right of the mother to have physical custody of young children. The age limits under classical Islamic jurisprudence (as applied traditionally) are:

  • Sons: Till approximately 7 years of age
  • Daughters: Till puberty

However, Bangladesh courts do not apply these age rules rigidly. If the mother has remarried, is morally unfit, or cannot adequately care for the child, the court may reduce or override hizanat. The father retains guardianship throughout — he is legally responsible for the child's upbringing, education, and maintenance even if the mother has physical custody.

Father's Rights and Responsibilities

Under both Islamic law and the Guardians and Wards Act, the father is the natural guardian of the child in Bangladesh. This means:

  • The father has the right and duty to make decisions about the child's education, religion, and major life events.
  • Financial maintenance of the child is exclusively the father's obligation.
  • Once boys reach approximately 7 years and girls reach puberty, custody may move to the father if the mother's hizanat period ends — but courts still apply the welfare test.

A father who is denied access to his children can apply for visitation rights or custody in the Family Court regardless of the mother's hizanat rights.

How Family Courts Decide Custody

The Family Court weighs all relevant facts including:

  • Age and gender of the child
  • Physical and mental health of both parents
  • Financial ability of each parent to provide for the child
  • The child's own wishes (if old enough to express them clearly)
  • Which parent has been the primary caregiver historically
  • Any history of domestic violence, substance abuse, or neglect
  • Educational stability and continuity for the child

Courts in Bangladesh increasingly prioritise joint parental involvement rather than complete exclusion of one parent.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

The Best Interest of the Child Principle

The welfare or best interest of the child is the paramount consideration in all custody decisions. Bangladesh courts have consistently held that no religious rule or parental preference can override what is truly best for the child's physical, emotional, and moral development.

This principle was firmly established in landmark High Court Division decisions that override rigid application of age-old hizanat rules when circumstances demand it. Courts have granted mothers custody of older boys and fathers custody of young daughters when the facts warranted it.

Custody Disputes: Filing a Petition

To initiate a custody dispute, the parent must file a Guardianship Petition or a suit in the Family Court. The main steps are:

  1. Instruct a family lawyer in Dhaka/Uttara to draft a petition.
  2. File in the Family Court of the area where the child ordinarily resides.
  3. The court issues notice to the other parent.
  4. An interim custody or visitation order may be requested pending the full hearing.
  5. Both parents present their case; welfare reports may be ordered.
  6. The court delivers a custody order.

Custody proceedings can be emotionally taxing but a skilled advocate can help navigate the process calmly and effectively.

Visitation Rights for the Non-Custodial Parent

A parent who does not have primary custody is entitled to reasonable visitation rights unless the court finds compelling reasons to deny access. Courts typically set specific visitation schedules — weekends, holidays, and vacation periods — to ensure the child maintains a relationship with both parents.

If a custodial parent wilfully denies court-ordered visitation, this is contempt of court and can lead to sanctions including modification of custody in favour of the other parent.

International Child Custody Issues

Cases where one parent takes a child out of Bangladesh without the other parent's consent or a court order are complex. Bangladesh is not a Hague Convention signatory on child abduction, which means international recovery mechanisms are limited.

However, the High Court Division has jurisdiction to issue orders preventing removal of children from Bangladesh, ordering return of children wrongfully taken abroad, and directing immigration authorities to place children on the watch list. Act immediately if you believe your child may be taken out of the country. Consult a Supreme Court lawyer in Bangladesh for urgent relief.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who gets custody of children after divorce in Bangladesh?

It depends on the child's age, welfare, and circumstances. Mothers typically retain custody of young children (hizanat) but courts always apply the best interest principle.

Can a father get custody of a young child in Bangladesh?

Yes. If the mother is found unfit or if the child's welfare requires it, the court can grant custody to the father regardless of traditional hizanat rules.

At what age can a child choose which parent to live with?

There is no fixed age in law, but Bangladesh courts give weight to a mature child's preferences, particularly children aged 10 and above.

Can a non-Muslim ask a Family Court for child custody in Bangladesh?

Yes. The Guardians and Wards Act applies to all religions. Family Courts have jurisdiction over all custody matters in Bangladesh.

Can I take my child abroad without the other parent's permission?

Without a court order or written consent from the other parent, taking a child abroad can be viewed as wrongful removal and may lead to court action.

What happens if the other parent refuses to follow a custody order?

You can file a contempt of court application. The court can enforce the order, impose sanctions, or modify custody in your favour.

Does remarriage affect a mother's custody rights in Bangladesh?

Under classical hizanat rules, a mother's remarriage can end her hizanat rights. However, courts may still grant her custody if it is in the child's best interest.

Is child support separate from custody in Bangladesh?

Yes. Maintenance (child support) is the father's obligation regardless of who has custody. It can be determined by the Family Court separately from custody proceedings.

Child Marriage Law Bangladesh – Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 Complete Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-06 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Bangladesh has one of the highest rates of child marriage in the world, with millions of girls married before reaching adulthood. The Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 — which replaced the colonial-era 1929 Act — represents the most significant legal overhaul of child marriage law in nearly a century. This guide explains the new legal minimum ages, the controversial special provision allowing underage marriage in limited circumstances, penalties for offenders, and how communities can fight back against this persistent violation of children rights.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

  6. Offences and Penalties Under the 2017 Act

  8. How to File a Complaint Against Child Marriage
  9. The National Action Plan and UNICEF Data

Understanding Child Marriage in Bangladesh – The Scale of the Problem

Child marriage — defined as a formal or informal union where at least one party is under 18 years of age — remains a deeply entrenched social practice in Bangladesh, particularly in rural areas. Despite significant legal and social progress, Bangladesh currently ranks among the countries with the highest absolute numbers of child brides in the world.

According to UNICEF data, approximately 59% of women aged 20–24 in Bangladesh were married before age 18, and around 22% were married before age 15. While these figures have improved substantially over the past two decades — driven by girls education, social protection programmes, and legal reforms — child marriage remains a critical development challenge.

The consequences of child marriage for girls are severe:

  • Early pregnancy and associated maternal and infant mortality
  • Interruption or permanent end of formal education
  • Increased vulnerability to domestic violence, including dowry-related abuse
  • Lifetime economic dependence and poverty
  • Severe psychological harm from premature adult responsibilities

For boys, early marriage also results in economic and educational disruption, though the harm is generally less severe due to gender dynamics in Bangladesh society. The law currently applies to both genders, setting different minimum ages reflecting biological and social factors.

The Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 – Overview

The Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 (Act No. VI of 2017) — known in Bangla as the বাল্যবিবাহ নিরোধ আইন ২০১৭ — replaced the Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929 and came into force upon presidential assent in March 2017. The 2017 Act brought significant changes to both the substantive law and the enforcement mechanisms for child marriage prohibition.

Key features of the 2017 Act include:

  • Updated minimum marriage ages consistent with international norms (with a controversial exception discussed below)
  • Stronger penalties for those who contract, conduct, or facilitate child marriages
  • New enforcement officers designated specifically for child marriage prevention
  • Criminal liability extended to parents, guardians, and officiating persons (e.g., qazis, priests) who participate in child marriages
  • A controversial special provision (Section 19) allowing underage marriage in unspecified special circumstances with court approval — which has drawn sharp criticism from child rights advocates and international organisations

The Act applies to all citizens of Bangladesh regardless of religion, though it works alongside personal law (Muslim, Hindu, Christian) rather than completely displacing it. This creates some complexity in application.

Legal Minimum Age of Marriage in Bangladesh

The Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 sets the following minimum ages of marriage currently in force:

  • Girls: Minimum age of 18 years
  • Boys: Minimum age of 21 years

Any marriage involving a person below these ages is a child marriage (বাল্যবিবাহ) under the 2017 Act, regardless of parental consent, custom, or religious practice. A marriage contracted in violation of these ages is not automatically void under the Act — it remains valid but the parties involved in arranging or solemnising it become criminally liable.

This is an important distinction: the validity of the marriage itself is not affected by the 2017 Act. Child marriages, once contracted, are legally recognised under personal law. However, the adults responsible for arranging the marriage face criminal prosecution. This approach has been criticised for not adequately deterring child marriage, since the marriage remains valid even after prosecution of the responsible adults.

Proof of age for marriage purposes is established through:

  • Birth certificate issued by the local government
  • School certificate (SSC/JSC results showing date of birth)
  • National Identity Card (for those aged 18+)
  • Medical certificate in cases where documentary evidence is unavailable

Comparison: 1929 Act vs 2017 Act

The following table compares the key differences between the repealed Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929 and the currently applicable Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017:

FeatureChild Marriage Restraint Act 1929Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017
Minimum age – Girls18 years18 years (unchanged)
Minimum age – Boys21 years21 years (unchanged)
Special provision for underage marriageNoneYes – Section 19 allows court-approved exceptions
Penalty for contracting child marriageUp to 1 month imprisonment or Tk. 1,000 fineUp to 2 years imprisonment and/or Tk. 1,00,000 fine
Penalty for parent/guardian facilitating child marriageUp to 1 month imprisonment or Tk. 1,000 fineUp to 2 years imprisonment and/or Tk. 1,00,000 fine
Child Marriage Prevention OfficerNot designatedDesignated under Section 13
Cognizability of offenceNon-cognizable (police needed warrant)Cognizable – police can act without warrant
Offender – the adult being marriedLiable if over 18/21Liable if over 18/21, exempt if also a child

The Controversial Special Provision for Underage Marriage

Section 19 of the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 is the most contested provision in the legislation. It reads (in substance):

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, in case of a marriage of a son or daughter in the best interest of the minor, considering special circumstances, a marriage may be solemnised under the direction of the court.

The provision does not define what constitutes special circumstances, leaving the determination entirely to judicial discretion. This vagueness has attracted intense criticism for several reasons:

  • Backdoor legalisation: Critics, including UNICEF, the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, and numerous Bangladeshi civil society organisations, argue that Section 19 effectively creates a legal loophole that can be used to legalise child marriages under the guise of special circumstances — including pregnancy resulting from rape, honour concerns, or poverty.
  • Contradiction of international law: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (ratified by Bangladesh) and CEDAW (Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women) both call for a firm minimum marriage age of 18 with no exceptions.
  • Risk of abuse: Families can pressure local courts to grant permissions by claiming the marriage is in the best interest of the child, when in reality economic pressure, social stigma, or coercion drives the decision.

In defence of Section 19, the government has argued that it addresses genuine edge cases — such as cases of pregnancy outside marriage that might expose a girl to social harm — and that court oversight provides a safeguard. However, child rights advocates maintain that the provision should be removed and that the correct response to such situations is protection, not an underage marriage permit.

As of the current date, Section 19 remains in force and continues to generate debate. Courts applying this provision are expected to rigorously scrutinise any application and consider the full range of options to protect the child interest beyond marriage.

Offences and Penalties Under the 2017 Act

The Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 creates criminal liability for multiple categories of persons involved in child marriage:

Section 7 – Contracting a Child Marriage

A male adult (18+ for marriage purposes) who marries a child (below 18 if female, below 21 if male) is guilty of an offence. Penalty: up to 2 years rigorous imprisonment and/or a fine of up to Taka 1,00,000. The child party to the marriage is not prosecuted.

Section 8 – Solemnising a Child Marriage

Any person (e.g., a qazi, priest, or marriage registrar) who performs or registers a child marriage is guilty of an offence. Penalty: up to 2 years rigorous imprisonment and/or a fine of up to Taka 1,00,000.

Section 9 – Facilitating a Child Marriage

Parents, guardians, or other adults who direct, permit, promote, or in any way facilitate a child marriage commit an offence. This is a critical provision targeting the adults (typically parents) who arrange child marriages. Penalty: up to 2 years rigorous imprisonment and/or a fine of up to Taka 1,00,000.

Section 10 – Injunction Against Child Marriage

Courts have power to issue injunctions prohibiting a child marriage that is about to be contracted. Any violation of such an injunction constitutes contempt of court and carries additional penalties.

All offences under the 2017 Act are cognizable (police can arrest without warrant) and non-bailable (bail is not automatic). They are tried by the Judicial Magistrate First Class.

Role of the Child Marriage Prevention Officer

One of the most significant innovations of the 2017 Act is the creation of designated Child Marriage Prevention Officers (CMPOs) under Section 13 of the Act. These officers play a frontline role in preventing child marriages before they occur.

Currently designated CMPOs in Bangladesh include:

  • District Level: Deputy Commissioner (DC) or a designated Additional DC
  • Upazila Level: Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO)
  • Union Level: Chairman of the Union Parishad
  • City Corporation/Paurashava Level: Ward Commissioners

The powers and duties of a CMPO include:

  • Receiving complaints about child marriages from any person
  • Preventing child marriages by visiting locations where child marriages are reported to be imminent
  • Seeking injunctions from the Magistrate to stop imminent child marriages
  • Filing cases under the 2017 Act against persons responsible for child marriages
  • Raising awareness about child marriage laws and consequences in their jurisdiction

In practice, the effectiveness of CMPOs varies considerably. In areas with engaged and proactive UNOs and DC offices, child marriage prevention has improved noticeably. In areas where the culture of early marriage remains dominant, enforcement remains weak. NGOs and civil society organisations play a crucial supplementary role in reporting and prevention.

How to File a Complaint Against Child Marriage

Any person who has knowledge of a child marriage that has occurred or is about to occur can take legal action. The process is as follows:

  1. Contact the Child Marriage Prevention Officer (CMPO): The most immediate step for an imminent child marriage is to contact the UNO (at Upazila level) or the Union Parishad Chairman directly. They have power to intervene and stop the marriage before it occurs.
  2. File a Case at the Police Station: Since offences under the 2017 Act are cognizable, a complainant can file an FIR at the nearest police station. Police are obligated to register the case and investigate.
  3. File a Petition before the Magistrate: A petition can be filed directly before the Judicial Magistrate First Class seeking an injunction to stop an imminent child marriage or initiate prosecution after the fact.
  4. Contact NGOs: Organisations such as BRAC, Plan International Bangladesh, Save the Children, and Girls Not Brides partner NGOs in Bangladesh operate hotlines and local response teams for child marriage cases. They can provide immediate support and facilitate legal action.
  5. National Child Helpline 1098: Bangladesh operates a National Child Helpline (call 1098) that can receive reports of child marriage and other child protection violations and coordinate with local authorities for an emergency response.

Complainants are protected from retaliation under the Act. Filing a complaint in good faith about a child marriage does not expose the complainant to legal liability, even if the complaint ultimately proves unfounded.

The National Action Plan and UNICEF Data

Bangladesh has committed at the international level to ending child marriage. The government has adopted the National Plan of Action to End Child Marriage (2018–2030), aligned with the global commitment under Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 5.3 to eliminate child marriage by 2030.

Key targets under the National Action Plan include:

  • Reducing child marriage rate among girls under 15 to less than 10% by 2021 (partially achieved)
  • Reducing overall child marriage rate to less than 40% by 2025
  • Completely eliminating child marriage under 15 by 2021 and child marriage of all girls by 2041

Current UNICEF data highlights both progress and continuing challenges:

  • The proportion of women aged 20–24 married before age 18 has declined significantly over the past decade, but remains among the highest globally.
  • Child marriage is most prevalent in rural areas, in certain districts (particularly in the north and south of the country), and among the poorest quintile of the population.
  • Girls who complete secondary education are dramatically less likely to be child brides — making girls education the single most effective intervention against child marriage.
  • The COVID-19 pandemic is estimated to have reversed some of the progress made, as school closures and economic hardship pushed families toward early marriage as a financial coping strategy.

Effective enforcement of the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, combined with sustained investment in girls education, economic empowerment, and social norm change, remains the path to eliminating child marriage in Bangladesh.

Rights of the Child and International Law Obligations

Bangladesh is a signatory to several key international human rights instruments that bear on child marriage:

  • UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), ratified 1990: Requires Bangladesh to take all appropriate measures to protect children from practices harmful to their welfare. The Committee on the Rights of the Child has repeatedly called on Bangladesh to set a firm minimum marriage age of 18 with no exceptions and remove Section 19 of the 2017 Act.
  • Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), ratified 1984: Requires states to ensure the full and free consent of both parties to a marriage and to specify a minimum marriage age. The CEDAW Committee has recommended that Bangladesh set the minimum age at 18 for both boys and girls.
  • Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): SDG 5.3 specifically targets the elimination of child marriage globally by 2030. Bangladesh has formally committed to this target.

Under international law, children under 18 are considered incapable of giving fully informed, free, and meaningful consent to marriage. Child marriage is accordingly classified as a human rights violation regardless of cultural or religious traditions. Bangladesh domestic law under the 2017 Act is substantially (though not fully) consistent with these obligations.

Get Legal Help Today

Child marriage cases often intersect with family law, criminal law, and child protection law — requiring coordinated legal and social responses. Whether you are a family member trying to protect a child from early marriage, a survivor of child marriage seeking divorce or other relief, or a community worker navigating the legal enforcement system, expert legal guidance is essential.

Advocate Md. Shah Alam, operating from his Uttara, Dhaka chamber, has extensive experience in family law matters including child marriage cases, Muslim and civil divorce proceedings, custody disputes, and child protection petitions before both family courts and the High Court Division. His team can advise on both the criminal and civil dimensions of child marriage cases and represent clients at all court levels.

If you are facing an urgent situation involving an imminent child marriage, do not delay. Contact our family and divorce lawyer today for an immediate confidential consultation. Early legal intervention can stop a child marriage before it happens.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the legal minimum age of marriage in Bangladesh?

Under the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, the legal minimum age of marriage is 18 years for girls and 21 years for boys. Any marriage below these ages is a child marriage and makes the responsible adults criminally liable, even though the marriage itself remains legally valid under personal law.

What is the penalty for arranging a child marriage in Bangladesh?

Under Sections 7, 8, and 9 of the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, any adult who contracts, solemnises, or facilitates a child marriage is liable to up to 2 years rigorous imprisonment and/or a fine of up to Taka 1,00,000 (one lakh). Parents or guardians who arrange child marriages are equally liable.

What is the special provision under Section 19 of the 2017 Act?

Section 19 of the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 is a controversial provision that allows a court to approve a marriage involving a minor in unspecified special circumstances, if it considers the marriage to be in the minor best interest. Critics argue this creates a dangerous loophole that can be misused to legalise child marriages under pressure. UNICEF and other international bodies have called for its removal.

Can a child marriage be annulled or voided in Bangladesh?

The Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 does not automatically void child marriages. Once contracted, a child marriage is legally recognised under personal law (Muslim, Hindu, or Christian, as applicable). However, a girl who has been married as a child can seek divorce or judicial separation through the appropriate family court. Legal aid is available for such cases.

How can I report a child marriage in Bangladesh?

You can report a child marriage by: (1) contacting the Child Marriage Prevention Officer (UNO or Union Parishad Chairman); (2) filing an FIR at the nearest police station; (3) filing a petition before the Judicial Magistrate First Class; (4) calling the National Child Helpline at 1098; or (5) contacting a child rights NGO such as BRAC or Save the Children Bangladesh.

Does the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 apply to all religions in Bangladesh?

Yes, the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 applies to all citizens of Bangladesh regardless of religion. Muslim, Hindu, and Christian marriages are all subject to the minimum age requirements of 18 for girls and 21 for boys. The Act works alongside (rather than replacing) personal law, meaning that marriages contracted in violation of the Act may still be valid under personal law but will expose responsible adults to criminal liability.

Child Passport After Divorce in Bangladesh: Custody & Law Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-10 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Following marital breakdown or divorce in Bangladesh, one of the most stressful bureaucratic battles single mothers encounter is securing a national machine-readable or e-passport for their minor children. Regional passport offices under the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP) routinely insist upon the physical presence or a written No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the biological father. When an estranged father maliciously withholds consent, is untraceable, or resides overseas, the child's fundamental right to travel, undergo medical treatment, or pursue education abroad is paralyzed. Under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 and established Supreme Court writ precedents, mothers holding physical custody (Hizanat) possess clear legal remedies to compel passport issuance without paternal obstruction.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

📋 In This Article

  2. 2. Legal Framework: Custody (Hizanat) vs. Guardianship (Wilayat) in Bangladesh
  3. 3. The Paramount Doctrine: Welfare of the Minor in Travel & Education
  4. 4. Procuring a Guardianship Certificate from the Family Court (Act VIII of 1890)
  5. 5. High Court Division Writ Petitions (Article 102) for Urgent Passport Issuance
  6. 6. Summary Matrix: Administrative Obstacles, Legal Options & Timelines
  7. 7. Taking the Child Abroad: Preventing Airport Offloading and Travel Injunctions
  8. 8. Illustrative Scenario: Mother Overcoming Father's Malicious Passport Block
  9. 9. Practical Document Checklist for Divorced Mothers Applying for Passports
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate

1. The Bureaucratic Barrier: Why Passport Offices Demand Father's Consent

Under the standard application protocols established by the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP) in Bangladesh, any passport application submitted on behalf of a minor under 18 years of age requires parental verification. Frontline passport enrolment officers at regional offices (such as Agargaon, Uttara, Jatrabari, or district branches) routinely demand the national identification cards (NID) of both parents alongside an explicit No Objection Certificate (NOC) signed by the father.

When parents have undergone a divorce or separation, this administrative requirement frequently becomes an instrument of harassment. An estranged father may deliberately refuse to sign the NOC, demand that the mother forfeit her pending dower (Denmohar) or past child maintenance in exchange for his signature, or simply vanish and become untraceable.

Because desk officers fear accusations of facilitating child abduction or cross-border custody violations, they often summarily reject the mother's solo application. However, departmental circulars and administrative guidelines are subordinate to statutory law and constitutional protections. A passport is an essential identity document belonging to the citizen child, not a personal asset of the father.

2. Legal Framework: Custody (Hizanat) vs. Guardianship (Wilayat) in Bangladesh

To effectively challenge passport denials, one must understand the crucial legal distinction between custody and legal guardianship under Bangladeshi family jurisprudence. In Muslim personal law, physical custody of a child is known as Hizanat, while legal guardianship over the person and property is termed Wilayat.

Under Hanafi law, the mother is entitled to the custody (Hizanat) of her male child until he completes the age of seven years, and of her female child until puberty. Even after these ages, the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has established in a series of landmark judgments that custody does not automatically shift to the father; the primary inquiry remains whether the child's overall welfare is best preserved in the mother's care.

While classical personal law recognizes the father as the natural legal guardian (Wilayat), this status is not absolute. When a father fails in his parental duties, refuses maintenance, or abandons the child, the civil courts have statutory authority under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 to appoint the mother as the sole legal guardian for personal and administrative affairs, including obtaining government identity documents. For broader perspectives on custody principles, consult our guide on child custody laws in Bangladesh.

3. The Paramount Doctrine: Welfare of the Minor in Travel & Education

The cornerstone of Bangladeshi family law regarding children is Section 17 of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, which mandates that in appointing or declaring a guardian, the court shall be guided by what appears to be for the welfare of the minor. This statutory principle overrides traditional rigid dogmas.

The Appellate Division and High Court Division have consistently ruled that administrative barriers cannot be used to deprive a child of their welfare, which includes the freedom of movement under Article 36 of the Constitution, access to advanced medical treatment in foreign hospitals, and the pursuit of international schooling or higher education.

Facing passport denial or father NOC disputes for your minor child in Bangladesh? Speak directly with an experienced family and writ advocate. Message our legal team on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for confidential case review.

When an estranged father uses his refusal to sign a passport application purely as spite or extortion, the courts view this conduct as detrimental to the child's best interests. In such circumstances, judicial authority promptly steps in to override the father's passive veto and ensure that the child's identity documents are promptly released.

4. Procuring a Guardianship Certificate from the Family Court (Act VIII of 1890)

The most permanent and robust civil mechanism for a single mother seeking independent legal authority over her child's documentation is filing a guardianship petition before the Family Court. Under the Family Courts Act 2023, the Family Court (presided over by an Assistant Judge or Senior Assistant Judge) has exclusive original jurisdiction over custody and guardianship matters.

The mother files an application under Section 10 of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, naming the biological father as the opposite party. The petition must set out the facts of the divorce, the father's abandonment or refusal to cooperate, and the specific necessity of obtaining an official guardianship decree to facilitate the minor's e-passport application, schooling, and healthcare.

The court issues summons to the father. If the father appears and contests, the court evaluates the evidence focusing strictly on the child's welfare. If the father fails to appear after service of summons, the court proceeds ex parte. Upon being satisfied that the child resides permanently with the mother and that the father has neglected his obligations, the Family Court passes a decree appointing the mother as the legal guardian of the person of the minor, explicitly empowering her to apply for and collect the child's passport.

5. High Court Division Writ Petitions (Article 102) for Urgent Passport Issuance

While a Family Court guardianship proceeding provides a complete adjudication, it can take six to twelve months to conclude. In situations of urgent necessity—such as where the child requires immediate medical surgery abroad, has received a time-sensitive foreign visa or university admission, or the mother must relocate for employment—the High Court Division offers swift constitutional relief.

Under Article 102(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution of Bangladesh, the mother can file a Writ Petition seeking a Writ of Mandamus against the Director General of the Department of Immigration and Passports, the Ministry of Home Affairs, and the regional passport officer. The petition asserts that the arbitrary refusal to issue an e-passport violates the child's fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 27 (equality before law), Article 31 (protection of law), and Article 36 (freedom of movement).

Upon hearing preliminary submissions from counsel, the High Court Division bench routinely issues a Rule Nisi accompanied by an interim mandatory direction instructing the passport authorities to accept the mother's application without the father's NOC and deliver the e-passport within a specified period (typically 7 to 15 days). This constitutional mechanism has empowered hundreds of single mothers to secure emergency travel papers without submitting to paternal coercion. For specialized insights, review our practice overview on Supreme Court writ litigation.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

6. Summary Matrix: Administrative Obstacles, Legal Options & Timelines

Single mothers evaluating their options can compare the procedural routes, required documentation, and expected timelines in the following comparative matrix:

Procedural Pathway Primary Authority / Forum Key Prerequisites Estimated Resolution Time
Mutual Consent / Father's NOC Regional Passport Office (DIP) Signed standard NOC, father's NID copy, joint presence if requested Standard delivery (7 to 21 days)
Family Court Guardianship Suit Family Court (Assistant Judge) Divorce proof, birth certificate, evidence of father's refusal/neglect 4 to 9 months (permanent decree)
High Court Writ of Mandamus High Court Division (Article 102) Proof of application submission, proof of urgency, refusal receipt 2 to 4 weeks (urgent interim order)
Administrative Appeal to DIP DG Director General, Passports (Agargaon) Formal legal notice, divorce papers, police verification report 1 to 2 months (discretionary)

7. Taking the Child Abroad: Preventing Airport Offloading and Travel Injunctions

Procuring the physical e-passport is only the first hurdle; single mothers planning to take their child abroad for permanent relocation, schooling, or holidays must also protect against potential border interception. In bitter matrimonial disputes, fathers frequently file applications before the Family Court seeking an order of temporary injunction restraining the mother from removing the child from Bangladesh.

Alternatively, some fathers lodge police General Diaries or file false abduction petitions under Section 363 of the Penal Code 1860, resulting in the child's name being placed on the immigration watchlist at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (HSIA). To prevent traumatic offloading at the departure gate, mothers should obtain a clear declaration from the Family Court permitting foreign travel.

When the Family Court or High Court authorizes international travel, it may require the mother to submit an undertaking or provide reasonable visitation access through digital video conferencing during overseas stays. Carrying certified copies of the court judgment, guardianship order, and birth certificate during international transit provides ironclad legal immunity at immigration counters. For broader guidance on travel bans, see our analysis on travel bans and airport offload challenges in Bangladesh.

8. Illustrative Scenario: Mother Overcoming Father's Malicious Passport Block

To understand how this dual judicial remedy operates in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A divorced mother residing in Uttara, Dhaka, had custody of her eight-year-old daughter following a finalized divorce in 2023. The mother secured a prestigious academic fellowship in Canada and prepared to relocate with her daughter. When she visited the regional passport office to renew her daughter's expiring passport, the assistant director refused to process the biometrics, stating that under departmental directives, a divorced mother could not renew a minor's passport without the father's in-person signature or a notarized NOC.

The biological father, who had contributed zero maintenance for three years, explicitly refused to sign the NOC unless the mother relinquished her pending 15 Lakh BDT dower claim. Faced with an impending visa deadline, the mother retained a Supreme Court advocate.

The advocate filed a Writ Petition under Article 102 before the High Court Division, demonstrating that the child's fundamental right to education and travel was being held hostage for private financial extortion. The High Court issued an immediate interim directive commanding the Director General of Immigration and Passports to enroll the child's biometrics and issue the e-passport within ten working days based solely on the mother's guardianship. Concurrently, the Family Court finalized her legal guardianship decree, enabling the mother and child to travel abroad without impediment.

9. Practical Document Checklist for Divorced Mothers Applying for Passports

Single mothers preparing to navigate passport applications or judicial proceedings should compile a meticulous evidentiary dossier before approaching authorities:

  • Child's Official Birth Registration: Secure an online-verified, 17-digit digital Birth Registration Certificate (BRC) from the local City Corporation or Union Parishad.
  • Proof of Finalized Divorce: Procure the certified Talaqnama and the final Failure of Reconciliation Certificate issued by the City Corporation or Union Parishad Chairman under Section 7 MFLO.
  • Custody & Maintenance Records: Compile any Family Court orders, compromise deeds (Solenama), or bank records demonstrating that the mother is the primary custodian and financial provider.
  • Proof of Father's Refusal or Absence: Maintain copies of registered legal notices sent to the father requesting cooperation, WhatsApp or email refusals, or police GDs confirming that his whereabouts are unknown.
  • Evidence of Travel Necessity: Keep school admission letters, medical diagnosis reports, foreign visa appointment confirmations, or employment relocation contracts.

For strategic representation in family dispute resolution, consult our dedicated divorce and custody lawyers and remote NRB legal advisors.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a Family & Writ Advocate in Dhaka: To obtain Family Court guardianship certificates, challenge arbitrary passport office refusals before the High Court Division under Article 102, or secure legal custody decrees, reach out via WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call our chamber at +880 1712-655546. Remote legal consultations are available for non-resident mothers and fathers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a mother get a passport for her child without the father's consent in Bangladesh?

Yes. Although passport offices routinely ask for the father's NOC, a divorced mother can obtain the child's passport by securing a guardianship decree from the Family Court under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, or by obtaining an interim direction from the High Court Division via a writ petition.

Why do Bangladeshi passport offices refuse passport applications without the father's NOC?

Regional passport offices adhere to internal administrative operating rules designed to prevent cross-border parental child abduction. However, these departmental guidelines cannot override statutory family court decrees or constitutional rights.

What is the difference between custody (Hizanat) and guardianship (Wilayat)?

Custody (Hizanat) refers to the day-to-day physical care and living arrangement of the child, which typically resides with the mother. Guardianship (Wilayat) relates to legal authority over the child's person and property, which the Family Court can grant to the mother.

How long does it take to obtain a Family Court guardianship decree for a child passport?

A standard guardianship case under Section 10 of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 generally takes four to nine months, depending on court schedules and whether the biological father contests the proceedings.

What is the fastest way to get a child passport if the mother has an urgent travel deadline?

The fastest mechanism is filing a Writ of Mandamus before the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. Upon proof of urgency (such as foreign medical treatment or visa deadlines), the bench can issue an interim order within two to four weeks.

Can a father stop a divorced mother from taking their child out of Bangladesh?

A father can file an application for an injunction in the Family Court to restrict international travel. However, courts will only grant a restriction if travel is shown to be harmful to the child's welfare; courts routinely allow travel for education and healthcare.

What happens if the biological father cannot be traced or lives abroad without contact?

If the father's whereabouts are unknown, the mother can file a police GD and initiate a Family Court guardianship case where summons will be served via national newspaper publication, leading to an ex parte decree appointing her legal guardian.

Does having physical custody automatically allow a mother to renew a minor's e-passport?

Physical custody alone is often disputed by passport desk officers. Having a formalized Family Court guardianship decree or High Court writ direction provides an indisputable legal instrument that compels passport officers to issue or renew the document.

Evicting Commercial Tenants & Rent Recovery in Bangladesh: Premises Rent Control Act Guide for NRB Landlords (2026)

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-02 · 19 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Commercial real estate across Dhaka (Gulshan, Banani, Motijheel, Uttara, Dhanmondi) and regional commercial centers like Chattogram and Sylhet represents a premier investment vehicle for Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs). Expatriate investors lease out high-value shopping complexes, corporate office floors, diagnostic centers, and retail showrooms expecting steady monthly rental yields. However, absent overseas landlords frequently encounter a devastating legal quagmire: commercial tenants who abruptly stop paying rent, refuse to vacate upon lease expiry, sublet premises without consent, or drag landlords into decade-long civil court stalemates under manufactured tenancy disputes. Navigating tenant eviction in Bangladesh requires mastering the dual interplay between the **Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 (বাড়ি ভাড়া নিয়ন্ত্রণ আইন, ১৯৯১)** and the **Transfer of Property Act, 1882**. By serving airtight statutory notices under Section 106, instituting Ejectment Suits before the Rent Controller or Civil Courts, and securing orders for arrears recovery and mesne profits (ওয়াসিলাত), expatriate owners can successfully dislodge delinquent commercial occupants and reclaim their prime properties.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka
