  2. 2. Distinguishing Civil Contempt from Criminal Contempt
  3. 3. Injunction Violations in Subordinate Courts: Order 39 Rule 2A CPC
  4. 4. The Pre-Litigation Contempt Demand Notice Protocol
  5. 5. Procedural Matrix: Injunction Breach to High Court Rule
  6. 6. High Court Division Procedure: Moving Contempt Petitions
  7. 7. Penalties: Imprisonment, Fines & Property Attachment
  8. 8. Substantive Defenses & Purging Contempt via Unconditional Apology
  9. 9. Illustrative Scenario: Enforcing a High Court Stay Against Illegal Demolition
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate: Contempt of Court Litigation

1. Constitutional Mandate: Article 108 & Act No. XXIV of 2013

In Bangladesh, the rule of law collapses if executive officers or private citizens can ignore judicial decrees with impunity. The judicial power to enforce obedience is grounded in Article 108 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, which designates the Supreme Court as a Court of Record with all the powers of such a court, including the power to make an order for the investigation of or punishment for any contempt of itself.

Subordinate civil and criminal courts derive their contempt referral powers through the Contempt of Courts Act 2013 (Act No. XXIV of 2013), which repealed the archaic Contempt of Courts Act 1926. While Parliament introduced certain provisions attempting to immunize civil servants in 2013, the High Court Division subsequently declared Sections 11 and 13(2) unconstitutional, affirming that no bureaucrat, minister, or police officer is above the contempt jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

Contempt proceedings are quasi-criminal in character. While the objective is coercive (compelling obedience to the court's decree), the proceedings can culminate in penal incarceration, making strict procedural compliance essential for both petitioners and respondents.

2. Distinguishing Civil Contempt from Criminal Contempt

The law draws an essential boundary between two distinct forms of contempt:

  • Civil Contempt: Defined as the wilful disobedience to any judgment, decree, direction, order, writ, or other process of a court, or a wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court. Typical examples include a municipal authority demolishing a building in defiance of a status quo order, a police officer refusing to execute a court bail directive, or an employer refusing to reinstate an employee after a High Court writ judgment.
  • Criminal Contempt: Defined as the publication (whether by words, spoken or written, or by signs or visible representations) of any matter or the doing of any other act whatsoever which: (i) scandalizes or tends to scandalize, or lowers or tends to lower the authority of any court; (ii) prejudices, or interferes or tends to interfere with, the due course of any judicial proceeding; or (iii) interferes or tends to interfere with, or obstructs or tends to obstruct, the administration of justice.

While Civil Contempt is instituted by private aggrieved litigants to enforce private remedies, Criminal Contempt can be initiated on the motion of the Attorney General, the court itself, or by private citizens with court leave.

3. Injunction Violations in Subordinate Courts: Order 39 Rule 2A CPC

In subordinate civil courts (such as Assistant Judge or Joint District Judge Courts), disobedience of temporary injunction orders is governed by a specialized statutory remedy: Order 39 Rule 2A of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC) (inserted by civil procedure amendments).

Under Order 39 Rule 2A, in case of disobedience to any injunction granted under Rule 1 or Rule 2, or breach of any of the terms on which the injunction was granted, the court may:

  1. Order Attachment of Property: The court may order the movable or immovable property of the guilty party to be attached. Such attachment remains in force for up to one year, after which, if disobedience continues, the property may be sold and compensation awarded to the injured party.
  2. Civil Imprisonment: The court may order the guilty person to be detained in civil prison for a term not exceeding six (6) months, unless in the meantime the court directs their release upon purging the contempt.

Filing an application under Order 39 Rule 2A directly before the trial judge who issued the injunction provides immediate localized pressure without having to move the High Court Division.

4. The Pre-Litigation Contempt Demand Notice Protocol

Is an authority or adversary violating a binding court order in Bangladesh? Contact our Supreme Court contempt litigation team on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007. We serve immediate contempt notices and move the High Court.

A fundamental prerequisite established by Supreme Court practice before filing a Contempt Petition is the service of a formal Advocate's Contempt Demand Notice. Because contempt requires proof of wilful and deliberate disobedience, establishing that the contemnor possessed unequivocal, verified knowledge of the court order is vital.

The service protocol involves three essential steps:

  • Service of Certified Order Copy: The advocate prepares a formal notice attaching a certified copy of the injunction, stay order, or writ judgment.
  • Explicit Recital of Violative Acts: The notice details the precise violative actions committed by the respondent, cites the operative parts of the judicial order, and demands immediate cessation and compliance within seven (7) to fifteen (15) days.
  • Verified Delivery Tracking: The notice must be served via registered post with acknowledgment due (AD), hand delivery with an official receipt seal, or courier, ensuring that postal tracking receipts are preserved as primary evidence for the contempt petition.

5. Procedural Matrix: Injunction Breach to High Court Rule

The procedural trajectory of contempt of court litigation in Bangladesh:

Procedural StageLegal BasisKey Actions & Thresholds
1. Violation OccursFactual breach of orderDocumenting breach via photographs, video, GD, and witness affidavits
2. Advocate's Contempt NoticeSupreme Court Practice RulesServed via Registered Post AD; 7 to 15 days compliance window
3. Filing Contempt PetitionArticle 108 / Act XXIV of 2013Petition moved before the specific High Court Bench that passed the order
4. Contempt Rule NisiContempt of Court RulesCourt issues Rule directing contemnor to explain or appear in person
5. Physical Personal AppearanceHigh Court DirectivesContemnor must stand before the judges in open court dock
6. Adjudication & SentencingSection 5, Act XXIV of 2013Imprisonment up to 6 months, fine, or acceptance of unconditional apology
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

6. High Court Division Procedure: Moving Contempt Petitions

When a writ order, ad-interim direction, or judgment passed by the High Court Division under Article 102 is flouted by a government department or private individual, the petition is styled as a Contempt Petition (Civil Contempt).

Key procedural dimensions of High Court contempt include:

  • Bench Jurisdiction: Under Supreme Court internal assignment rules, a Contempt Petition must generally be moved before the exact Division Bench that passed the original order, or its successor bench assigned by the Chief Justice of Bangladesh.
  • Issuance of Contempt Rule: Upon hearing the advocate and reviewing evidence of deliberate violation, the bench issues a Contempt Rule calling upon the named contemnors (e.g. Deputy Commissioner, SP, City Corporation Chief Engineer, or private adversary) to show cause why they should not be penalized.
  • Direction for Personal Appearance: In aggravated instances of defiance, the High Court issues a peremptory order directing the contemnor to appear physically in person before the bench on a designated date to stand in the court dock. The humiliation of being summoned to the Supreme Court dock frequently compels administrative agencies to comply overnight.

7. Penalties: Imprisonment, Fines & Property Attachment

Under Section 5 of the Contempt of Courts Act 2013, the statutory punishments for contempt of court are clearly delineated:

  1. Simple Imprisonment: A person found guilty of contempt of court may be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six (6) months.
  2. Monetary Fine: The court may impose a fine extending up to two thousand (2,000) BDT, or both imprisonment and fine.
  3. Civil Attachment and Custody: In civil contempt cases under Order 39 Rule 2A CPC, property attachment remains valid for up to one year, coupled with detention in civil prison.
  4. Mandatory Invalidation of Violative Acts: Crucially, the Supreme Court has ruled that any act done in violation of a court order is void ab initio. If a building is constructed in breach of an injunction, the court can direct police to demolish the structure; if property is sold in violation of a status quo, the sale deed is null and void.

8. Substantive Defenses & Purging Contempt via Unconditional Apology

When defending an individual or official accused of contempt, an advocate can raise established legal defenses under the Act:

  • Lack of Notice or Ambiguous Order: Demonstrating that the court order was never legally served, was worded ambiguously, or admitted of two reasonable interpretations where the respondent acted in good faith.
  • Impossibility of Performance: Demonstrating that physical compliance was objectively impossible due to supervening events or statutory legal bars beyond the respondent's control.
  • Fair Criticism of Judicial Acts: Under Section 6 of Act No. XXIV of 2013, fair comments on the merits of any decided case or administrative acts of judges do not constitute criminal contempt.
  • Purging Contempt via Unconditional Apology: Under the proviso to Section 5, the accused contemnor may be discharged or the punishment remitted on an unconditional apology being tendered to the satisfaction of the court. The apology must be submitted at the earliest opportunity, demonstrate genuine remorse, and be accompanied by complete rectification of the violative act. An insincere, conditional, or belated apology will be rejected by the judges.

9. Illustrative Scenario: Enforcing a High Court Stay Against Illegal Demolition

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): A commercial building owner in Uttara, Dhaka, obtained an Ad-Interim Stay Order from the High Court Division restraining a municipal development corporation from demolishing a licensed commercial annex. Two weeks later, a zonal executive officer accompanied by demolition bulldozers arrived on site, claiming verbal orders from superiors, and began breaking boundary walls.

The property owner contacted Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber. Our litigation team acted swiftly:

  1. Served an emergency Hand-Delivery Contempt Notice with the certified High Court stay order directly on the site magistrate and police officer, documenting the delivery via video recording.
  2. Drafted and filed an emergency Contempt Petition under Article 108 of the Constitution before the Division Bench of the High Court Division the following morning, producing photographic evidence of the bulldozers operating in defiance of the stay.
  3. The High Court Division took immediate judicial notice, issuing a Contempt Rule Nisi and passing a peremptory direction ordering the Zonal Executive Magistrate and Officer-in-Charge to appear physically before the bench within 48 hours.
  4. Appearing in the Supreme Court dock, the contemnors faced imminent imprisonment. The officials submitted an unconditional written apology, undertook to reconstruct the damaged boundary walls at state expense, and withdrew all demolition machinery immediately.
  5. The High Court accepted the apology on condition of full restitution, successfully preserving the client's commercial property permanently.

10. Talk to an Advocate: Contempt of Court Litigation

Enforcing court orders against recalcitrant government authorities or defending against contempt allegations in Bangladesh requires decisive advocacy before subordinate courts and the Supreme Court. Advocate Md. Shah Alam and his dedicated team of Supreme Court advocates provide prompt representation before trial courts, the High Court Division, and Appellate Division.

Need an advocate for this matter in Bangladesh? Send your documents on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: a first document review can be done remotely.

Our principal chamber is located in Uttara, Dhaka, minutes from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, alongside our daily litigation chamber at the Supreme Court Bar Association and Dhaka Judge Court.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the constitutional source of contempt of court in Bangladesh?

The constitutional authority resides in Article 108 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, which designates the Supreme Court as a Court of Record with all inherent powers to punish for contempt of itself.

What is the difference between civil contempt and criminal contempt?

Civil contempt involves wilful disobedience of court judgments, orders, writs, or undertakings. Criminal contempt involves acts or publications that scandalize the court, lower judicial authority, or obstruct justice.

What is the maximum penalty for contempt of court in Bangladesh?

Under Section 5 of the Contempt of Courts Act 2013, the court can impose simple imprisonment for up to six (6) months, a monetary fine up to 2,000 BDT, or both.

What is an Advocate's Contempt Notice?

An Advocate's Contempt Notice is a formal legal demand served on the violator attaching certified court orders and demanding compliance within 7 to 15 days, providing essential proof of wilful disobedience.

Can an unconditional apology save a person from going to prison for contempt?

Yes. Under Section 5 proviso of the Act, if the court is satisfied that the contemnor has tendered a sincere, bona fide unconditional apology at the earliest stage and rectified the violation, it may remit the punishment.

How are injunction violations handled in subordinate civil courts?

Under Order 39 Rule 2A CPC, subordinate civil courts can order the attachment of the violator's property for up to one year and sentence the person to civil imprisonment for up to six months.

Can government officials or police officers be punished for contempt?

Yes. Under Supreme Court rulings declaring civil servant exemptions unconstitutional, all public officials, police officers, and bureaucrats are fully amenable to contempt prosecution and imprisonment.

Can an overseas client file a Contempt Petition in the High Court from abroad?

Yes. An overseas litigant whose court order is being violated in Bangladesh can instruct a Supreme Court advocate through a local attorney or relative to file and move a Contempt Petition in Dhaka.

How to Take Legal Action Contract Breach Bangladesh

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-03-24 · 7 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Contract breaches are common in business — unpaid invoices, undelivered goods, broken construction contracts, and service agreement violations. Bangladesh contract law provides clear remedies, but enforcing them requires the right legal steps taken promptly.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

What Constitutes a Breach of Contract in Bangladesh?

Bangladesh contract law is governed by the Contract Act 1872. A breach occurs when a party without lawful excuse:

  • Fails to perform an obligation when due (non-performance)
  • Performs defectively or partially
  • Anticipatorily repudiates the contract (indicates they will not perform before the due date)

To pursue a remedy, the non-breaching party must show: (1) a valid contract existed; (2) the other party breached; (3) loss was caused by the breach.

Legal Remedies Available

Under the Contract Act and Specific Relief Act 1877, you can pursue:

  • Compensatory damages: Money to put you in the position you would have been in had the contract been performed.
  • Special/consequential damages: If the breaching party knew of special circumstances at the time of contracting.
  • Specific performance: Court orders the breaching party to perform. Available only when damages are an inadequate remedy (e.g., unique property, irreplaceable goods).
  • Injunction: Prevents the breaching party from violating a contract term or doing an act contrary to the contract.
  • Quantum meruit: Reasonable compensation for work done before the breach.

How to File a Contract Dispute Case

  1. Send a legal notice through a lawyer — gives the other party a chance to remedy the breach and is often required before filing suit.
  2. File a money suit or civil suit in the appropriate civil court (value determines court jurisdiction).
  3. The trial court will hear evidence and witnesses.
  4. Obtain a decree — a court order for payment of damages or specific performance.
  5. Enforce the decree through execution proceedings (attachment of assets, bank accounts).

A civil litigation lawyer in Dhaka can assess the strength of your claim and take prompt action.

How to Strengthen Your Contract Before Disputes Arise

Prevention is better than litigation:

  • Always use a written, signed contract — verbal agreements are enforceable but hard to prove.
  • Include specific performance obligations, timelines, and payment terms.
  • Add a dispute resolution clause: arbitration or mediation before court.
  • Specify liquidated damages (pre-agreed compensation for breach) to avoid arguments over quantum.
  • Have contracts drafted or reviewed by a lawyer before signing.

Advocate Md. Shah Alam in Uttara handles commercial contract disputes and can draft agreements that protect your interests.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the limitation period for a contract breach case in Bangladesh?

Under the Limitation Act 1908, the limitation period for a contract breach suit is 3 years from the date the breach occurred or the right to sue accrued. Do not delay.

Can I get an injunction to stop a breach from happening?

Yes. If a breach is threatened or ongoing, apply for an urgent injunction in civil court to prevent it. This is particularly useful for exclusive contracts or property-related agreements.

Is arbitration faster than court litigation in Bangladesh?

Generally yes. Arbitration under the Arbitration Act 2001 can resolve disputes in months rather than years, is private, and the award is enforceable like a court decree.

What if the breaching party has no assets?

If the breaching party is insolvent, recovering a money decree becomes difficult. This is why financial due diligence before entering contracts with new parties is important.

Contract Breach and Specific Performance Suit in Bangladesh: A Complete Legal Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-12 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

When a party to a contract fails to fulfil their obligations, the innocent party has a range of legal remedies available under Bangladesh law. The most powerful of these is the suit for specific performance — a court order compelling the breaching party to perform their contractual obligations. Understanding when specific performance is available, how to file a civil suit, and what defences can be raised is essential for anyone dealing with a broken contract in Bangladesh.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)

📋 In This Article
  1. What Is Breach of Contract Under Bangladesh Law?
  2. Legal Remedies for Breach of Contract in Bangladesh
  3. Specific Performance: The Specific Relief Act 1877
  4. When Courts Will and Won't Grant Specific Performance
  5. How to File a Suit for Specific Performance in Bangladesh
  6. Defences Against a Specific Performance Suit
  7. Damages vs. Specific Performance: Which Is Better for You?
  8. Practical Tips for Land and Property Contract Disputes

What Is Breach of Contract Under Bangladesh Law?

A contract is a legally binding agreement between two or more parties. Under the Contract Act, 1872 — which applies in Bangladesh — a contract is enforceable if it is made by competent parties, for lawful consideration, with free consent, and for a lawful object.

A breach of contract occurs when one party fails to perform their obligations under the contract without legal justification. Breaches may be:

  • Actual breach: The party fails to perform when performance is due (e.g., a seller fails to hand over possession of land after receiving the sale price).
  • Anticipatory breach: A party clearly indicates, before the performance date, that they will not perform (e.g., a developer tells a buyer they are cancelling the flat purchase agreement).
  • Partial breach: A party performs only part of their obligations (e.g., supplying only half the agreed goods).
  • Fundamental breach: A breach so serious that it goes to the root of the contract and justifies the innocent party treating the contract as terminated.

In Bangladesh, the most common contract disputes involve:

  • Sale agreements for land (baina deed disputes);
  • Construction contracts between developers and buyers;
  • Commercial supply and service agreements;
  • Employment contracts;
  • Franchise and joint venture agreements.

Legal Remedies for Breach of Contract in Bangladesh

When a contract is breached, the innocent party has several legal remedies under Bangladesh law:

  1. Specific Performance: A court order compelling the breaching party to perform the contract as agreed. This is the most direct remedy and is particularly valuable where money damages cannot adequately compensate the loss (e.g., a unique piece of land).
  2. Damages: Monetary compensation for the loss suffered as a result of the breach. Damages can be ordinary (flowing naturally from the breach), special (arising from special circumstances known to both parties), or nominal (where a breach occurred but no actual loss is proved).
  3. Injunction: A court order restraining the breaching party from doing something that would violate the contract — for example, preventing a seller from selling the land to a third party while the specific performance suit is pending.
  4. Rescission: Cancellation of the contract, releasing both parties from further obligations. If the innocent party suffers a loss from rescission, they can also claim restitution.
  5. Quantum Meruit: Recovery of the reasonable value of work done or services rendered under a partially performed contract.

The choice of remedy depends on the nature of the contract, the circumstances of the breach, and what the innocent party most needs. An experienced civil and corporate lawyer can advise on the optimal strategy for your case.

Specific Performance: The Specific Relief Act 1877

The primary statute governing specific performance in Bangladesh is the Specific Relief Act, 1877. This Act provides the legal framework for obtaining court orders compelling a party to perform their contractual obligations rather than merely paying damages.

Key provisions of the Specific Relief Act relevant to Bangladesh litigation:

  • Section 9: Courts can enforce specific performance of a contract where standard money compensation is inadequate.
  • Section 10: Contracts for the transfer of immovable property (land, apartments, buildings) are presumed to be cases where money compensation is inadequate — making specific performance the appropriate remedy in most property cases.
  • Section 11: Specific performance of contracts connected with trusts and other fiduciary relationships can be ordered.
  • Section 12: Part performance — where the court can order performance of the part of the contract that can be performed, along with compensation for the remainder if full performance is impossible.
  • Section 14: Lists the types of contracts that cannot be specifically enforced (see the next section).
  • Section 21: Provides for the court to award damages in addition to, or instead of, specific performance in appropriate cases.

For land disputes, the Specific Relief Act is the most important legal tool. If you have paid an advance (baina) for land and the seller is refusing to execute the registered deed, a specific performance suit under the Specific Relief Act is the correct legal remedy. Contact a land lawyer in Bangladesh immediately to protect your rights.

When Courts Will and Won't Grant Specific Performance

Specific performance is a discretionary remedy — even if you have a strong legal case, the court may decline to grant it in certain circumstances. Understanding when courts grant and refuse specific performance helps in assessing your case realistically.

Courts WILL typically grant specific performance when:

  • The contract is for the sale of immovable property (land, flat, building);
  • Money damages would be an inadequate remedy (e.g., the property is unique or sentimental);
  • The plaintiff has been ready, willing, and able to perform their own obligations;
  • The plaintiff files the suit within the limitation period (3 years from date of breach for most contract suits).

Courts WON'T grant specific performance when:

  • The contract involves personal services (courts will not compel a person to work for another);
  • The contract terms are uncertain or ambiguous;
  • Performance would be impossible due to changed circumstances;
  • The plaintiff is in breach of their own obligations;
  • Third parties have acquired bona fide rights in the property without notice of the prior contract (e.g., an innocent purchaser);
  • The plaintiff delayed unreasonably in filing suit (laches);
  • Performance would be inequitable or oppressive given the circumstances.

Courts balance the equities of both parties. Preparing a strong factual record of your readiness and willingness to perform is critical to success. Consult a land and civil lawyer to evaluate whether your case qualifies for specific performance.

How to File a Suit for Specific Performance in Bangladesh

Filing a specific performance suit in Bangladesh follows the civil court procedure under the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), 1908. The steps are:

  1. Engage a Civil Lawyer: Retain an experienced civil and land lawyer to draft the plaint and conduct the suit.
  2. Draft the Plaint: The plaint must contain: the parties' details, the contract and its terms, the breach, the plaintiff's readiness and willingness to perform, and the prayers (relief sought — specifically performance plus any supplementary relief).
  3. Attach Documents: Include the original contract/baina deed, proof of payment of advance, any correspondence showing the defendant's refusal to perform, and evidence of the plaintiff's readiness to perform (e.g., bank statement showing funds available).
  4. File at the Correct Court: For immovable property, file at the Civil Court (Sub-Judge's Court or District Judge's Court) where the property is situated. For other contracts, file where the contract was to be performed.
  5. Pay Court Fees: Court fees are payable based on the value of the subject matter (usually the contract price).
  6. Injunction Application: Simultaneously file an application for a temporary injunction (TI) to restrain the defendant from selling or transferring the property to anyone else pending the hearing of the suit.
  7. Summons and Written Statement: The court serves summons on the defendant, who files a written statement (defence).
  8. Evidence: Both parties file affidavit evidence and cross-examine witnesses.
  9. Judgment and Decree: The court passes a decree for specific performance, directing the defendant to execute and register the sale deed. If they refuse, the court can execute the deed itself or through a court official.

Defences Against a Specific Performance Suit

A defendant facing a specific performance suit can raise several valid defences:

  • No Valid Contract: Argue that the alleged contract was never concluded — for example, there was no consensus on essential terms, the contract lacked consideration, or it was void for illegality.
  • Plaintiff in Breach: If the plaintiff (buyer) failed to pay the full purchase price or failed to perform their own obligations under the contract, the defendant can resist specific performance.
  • Limitation: A specific performance suit must be filed within the limitation period (generally 3 years from the date of the breach or refusal to perform). A suit filed after this period is barred by limitation.
  • Laches: Even within the limitation period, unreasonable delay by the plaintiff that prejudices the defendant may lead the court to refuse specific performance in equity.
  • Impossibility: If performing the contract has become impossible (e.g., the property has been acquired by the government, or destroyed), specific performance cannot be ordered.
  • Bona Fide Purchaser: If the defendant sold the property to a third-party buyer who purchased without knowledge of the plaintiff's prior contract, the third party's rights may prevail — especially if they registered their title before the plaintiff's suit.
  • Fraud or Misrepresentation: If the plaintiff induced the contract through fraud or material misrepresentation, the contract is voidable and specific performance should be refused.

Damages vs. Specific Performance: Which Is Better for You?

Choosing between claiming damages and seeking specific performance requires careful legal and practical analysis. Here is a comparative overview to help you decide:

  • Specific Performance is better when: The subject matter is unique (e.g., a particular plot of land, an ancestral property, or a rare asset); when money cannot adequately compensate your loss; when you genuinely want the contract performed rather than money; or when the property's value has increased significantly since the contract was signed.
  • Damages are better when: The subject matter is easily replaceable in the market; when you have already mitigated your loss by finding an alternative; when the specific performance suit would take many years while you have urgent cash flow needs; or when the defendant is insolvent and a money decree can be enforced against assets.
  • Both together: Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act allows the court to award damages in addition to specific performance where the defendant's delay caused loss even before the decree was passed. Claiming both gives you maximum protection.

A practical note: specific performance suits in Bangladesh can take 3–7 years at the trial court level, with further appeals. An experienced civil lawyer in Dhaka will help you weigh the timeline against your commercial interests before deciding on your litigation strategy.

Practical Tips for Land and Property Contract Disputes

Land contract disputes are by far the most common setting for specific performance suits in Bangladesh. Here are practical tips to protect yourself:

  • Always Use a Registered Agreement: A baina (advance payment) agreement for land purchase should be registered before the Sub-Registrar to give it legal validity and to create a public record of your rights.
  • Retain All Payment Records: Keep bank transfer receipts, demand drafts, pay orders, or cash payment acknowledgements for every payment made to the seller.
  • File an Injunction Early: As soon as the seller shows signs of backing out, apply for an injunction to prevent them from registering the deed in favour of a third party. Once a bona fide purchaser registers their title, your specific performance suit becomes much harder to succeed.
  • Check the Property's Title Before Buying: Always conduct a thorough title search through a land lawyer before signing any agreement. Prior encumbrances, court orders, or disputed ownership can defeat your claim even if your contract is valid.
  • Act Promptly: The 3-year limitation period runs from the date of breach. Do not wait — seek legal advice immediately when the seller signals non-performance.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the limitation period for filing a specific performance suit in Bangladesh?

Under the Limitation Act, 1908, a suit for specific performance of a contract must generally be filed within 3 years from the date fixed for the performance, or if no date is fixed, from the date the plaintiff first heard that the defendant refused to perform. Missing this deadline means your suit will be barred by limitation and dismissed.

Can I get an injunction to stop the seller from selling the land while my case is pending?

Yes. You can file an application for a temporary injunction (TI) simultaneously with your specific performance suit. The court can grant an interim injunction (ex parte or after hearing both parties) restraining the defendant from selling, mortgaging, or otherwise encumbering the property pending the final decision of the suit.

What if the seller registers the land to a third party before I file my case?

If the third-party purchaser had actual or constructive notice of your prior contract (e.g., through your registered baina deed), your specific performance suit can still succeed against both the seller and the third party. However, if the third party was a bona fide purchaser without notice, your rights may be defeated. This is why filing early and registering your baina agreement is critical.

How long does a specific performance suit take in Bangladesh?

A specific performance suit at the trial court level typically takes 3 to 7 years in Bangladesh, depending on the complexity, the number of witnesses, and court workload. Appeals to the High Court and Appellate Division can add further years. Interim injunctions provide protection during this period.

Can I claim both specific performance and damages in the same suit?

Yes. Under Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act 1877, the court can award damages in addition to specific performance where the breach caused loss before the decree was passed. Many plaintiffs claim specific performance as the primary relief and damages as an alternative or supplementary relief in the same plaint.

Court Marriage in Bangladesh (2026) – Complete Guide: Process, Cost & Legal Requirements

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-04-07 ·

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Court marriage in Bangladesh — though not as common as traditional nikah — offers a legally recognized path to marriage outside conventional religious ceremonies. Whether you're from different religions, seeking civil registration without a ceremony, or need a legally documented marriage for visa or property purposes, court marriage can be the right option. This guide explains exactly how it works, who can use it, and what it costs.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

What Is Court Marriage in Bangladesh?

Court marriage in Bangladesh refers to a marriage registered through a legally prescribed civil process — typically without a religious ceremony, or independent of one. It is governed by the Special Marriage Act 1872 and provides a formal legal record of the marriage that is recognized under Bangladesh law.

The term 'court marriage' is commonly used in Bangladesh to mean registration of a marriage, sometimes done alongside a religious ceremony (for legal documentation purposes) or completely separately as a civil marriage. It is particularly relevant for:

  • Couples from different religions (interfaith marriages)
  • Couples who want a marriage registered under civil law rather than personal religious law
  • Those needing an internationally recognized marriage certificate (for visa, property, immigration purposes)

Who Can Get a Court Marriage in Bangladesh?

Under the Special Marriage Act 1872, court marriage is available to:

  • Any two adults — regardless of religion — as long as they both consent freely
  • The minimum age is 18 for women and 21 for men
  • Neither party should have a living spouse from an existing valid marriage
  • The parties should not be within the prohibited degrees of relationship (close blood relatives)

Court marriage is particularly relevant for interfaith couples (Hindu-Muslim, Muslim-Christian, etc.) for whom a traditional religious nikah may not be available or may not provide the full legal recognition they need.

Legal Framework: The Special Marriage Act 1872

The Special Marriage Act 1872 — a colonial-era law still in force in Bangladesh — provides the legal framework for civil marriages. Key features:

  • Marriages under this Act are registered with a Marriage Registrar appointed by the government
  • A marriage certificate is issued which is legally equivalent to any other marriage registration certificate
  • The Act requires a 30-day advance notice to the Marriage Registrar before the ceremony
  • Any person can lodge an objection within 30 days of the notice — the Registrar must investigate before proceeding
  • The marriage is solemnized in the presence of three witnesses

Note: Many people in Bangladesh informally call any officially registered marriage a 'court marriage' — including nikah registration at a Kazi's office. The Special Marriage Act 1872 is specifically for non-religious civil registration.

Step-by-Step Court Marriage Procedure in Bangladesh

The formal court marriage procedure under the Special Marriage Act 1872:

  1. Give Notice: Both parties jointly give written notice to the Marriage Registrar in the district where at least one of them has lived for at least 30 days. The notice includes personal details, address, and a declaration of intent to marry.
  2. 30-Day Waiting Period: The notice is displayed publicly for 30 days. Anyone may object during this period. If no valid objection is lodged, the marriage proceeds.
  3. Sign the Declaration: Both parties appear before the Marriage Registrar, sign a declaration in the prescribed form, and three witnesses also sign.
  4. Marriage Solemnized: The Marriage Registrar signs and seals the register. The marriage is now formally solemnized.
  5. Marriage Certificate Issued: A marriage certificate is issued immediately — this is your legal proof of marriage.

Many couples engage a lawyer to handle the notice drafting, documentation, and coordination with the Registrar's office to ensure everything is procedurally correct. Contact a family lawyer in Dhaka for assistance.

Required Documents for Court Marriage

Documents typically required for court marriage under the Special Marriage Act 1872:

  • National Identity Cards (NID) of both parties
  • Birth certificates of both parties
  • Proof of residence (utility bill or rent agreement) — at least one party must have lived in the district for 30+ days
  • Passport-size photographs of both parties
  • Divorce certificate (if previously married)
  • Death certificate of previous spouse (if widowed)
  • NIDs of three witnesses
  • Affidavit declaring no existing legal spouse

Requirements may vary slightly by district. Your lawyer will advise on the exact documents required by the specific Marriage Registrar's office.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Cost of Court Marriage in Bangladesh

The costs involved in a court marriage in Bangladesh:

  • Government registration fees: ৳500–৳2,000 (approximately, varies by district)
  • Stamp duty and documentary charges: ৳500–৳1,500
  • Lawyer fee (if engaged): ৳5,000–৳20,000 for handling all paperwork, notice drafting, and coordination
  • Certification and notarization: ৳500–৳2,000

Total cost for a straightforward court marriage in Bangladesh (with a lawyer): approximately ৳8,000–৳25,000 depending on location and complexity.

How Long Does Court Marriage Take?

The critical factor is the mandatory 30-day notice period:

  • 30-day notice period: This is legally fixed and cannot be shortened, even if both parties are in a hurry.
  • Document preparation: 1–5 working days (with a lawyer's assistance)
  • Actual solemnization: Takes 1–2 hours on the appointment day
  • Marriage certificate issuance: Same day as solemnization

Total minimum time: approximately 35–40 days from starting the process to receiving your certificate.

Is Court Marriage Valid Under Bangladesh Law?

Yes. A court marriage performed under the Special Marriage Act 1872 is fully legally valid in Bangladesh. The marriage certificate issued is:

  • Recognized by all government agencies in Bangladesh
  • Accepted for visa applications, passport, NID updates
  • Valid proof of marriage for property and inheritance purposes
  • Internationally recognized (though some countries may require apostille / legalization)

However, court marriage under the Special Marriage Act does NOT give the parties the same personal law rights as a nikah in terms of mahr, talaq, and inheritance — since those are governed by Muslim personal law. Couples should understand which regime applies to their rights after marriage.

Difference Between Court Marriage and Nikah

Many people confuse these two terms. Here is the key distinction:

  • Nikah is an Islamic marriage contract performed under Muslim personal law. It is registered by a licensed Kazi (Nikah Registrar) and produces a Kabinnama. Rights like mahr, talaq, and Islamic inheritance apply.
  • Court Marriage (Special Marriage Act 1872) is a purely civil marriage registration. It is secular — no religious ceremony is required. It applies when both parties want civil law to govern their marriage, or for interfaith couples.

In practice, many Bangladeshis do BOTH — perform a nikah for religious validity AND register under civil law for documentary purposes. A family lawyer can advise which approach best protects your interests.

Common Reasons People Choose Court Marriage

  • Interfaith couples: The most common reason — Muslim-Hindu, Muslim-Christian couples who cannot register under either party's personal religious law alone.
  • Legal documentation for overseas: Visa applications (UK, US, Canada, Europe) often require officially registered marriage certificates.
  • Marriages opposed by family: Couples who are legally adults and consent freely can marry under court marriage regardless of family opposition.
  • Property and banking purposes: Joint property ownership, joint bank accounts, insurance nominations — all require documented proof of marriage.
  • Second marriage documentation: In some circumstances, parties seek formal civil documentation for second marriages.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is court marriage legal in Bangladesh?

Yes. Court marriage under the Special Marriage Act 1872 is fully legally valid in Bangladesh. The marriage certificate is recognized by all government agencies, banks, and for visa and property purposes.

How long does court marriage take in Bangladesh?

A minimum of 35–40 days due to the mandatory 30-day notice period under the Special Marriage Act 1872. Document preparation takes 1–5 days; the actual marriage solemnization takes 1–2 hours.

What documents do I need for court marriage in Bangladesh?

NID and birth certificates of both parties, proof of residence, photographs, affidavit of no existing marriage, NIDs of 3 witnesses, and divorce/death certificate if previously married.

Can a Muslim and Hindu get married through court marriage in Bangladesh?

Yes. Interfaith couples (Muslim-Hindu, Muslim-Christian etc.) can register their marriage under the Special Marriage Act 1872, which applies regardless of religious affiliation.

How much does court marriage cost in Bangladesh?

Government fees: ৳500–৳2,000. With a lawyer's assistance for paperwork: ৳8,000–৳25,000 total, depending on location and complexity.

Do we need a lawyer for court marriage in Bangladesh?

Legally no, but practically yes for most people. The notice drafting, document verification, and coordination with the Marriage Registrar's office have procedural requirements where errors cause delays. A lawyer ensures everything is done correctly the first time.

Can families oppose a court marriage in Bangladesh?

Any person can lodge an objection within the 30-day notice period. The Registrar must investigate valid objections. However, if both parties are legally adults (18/21+) and consent freely, family opposition alone is not a legitimate legal ground for refusal.

Court Marriage Bangladesh – Process, Documents, Cost & Legal Rights

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-28 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Court marriage — often called registry marriage — in Bangladesh refers to the formal legal registration of a marriage, giving it full force and recognition under the law. Whether you are registering a Muslim nikah at a Kazi office, solemnizing an inter-religious marriage under the Special Marriage Act 1872, or formalising a marriage through an affidavit-based process, this comprehensive 2026 guide covers every step, required document, cost, and legal right you need to know.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

  2. Muslim Marriage Registration – Nikah and Kabinnama
  3. How to Register a Muslim Marriage at the Kazi Office

  5. Affidavit-Based Court Marriage Procedure
  6. Documents Required for Court Marriage

What Is Court Marriage in Bangladesh?

The term "court marriage" in Bangladesh is commonly used to describe the legal registration of a marriage, rather than a marriage ceremony performed in a courtroom. In practice, it refers to one of three mechanisms:

  1. Muslim Nikah Registration: Registering a Muslim marriage (nikah) with a licensed Kazi (marriage registrar) under the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974. This produces the Kabinnama (Nikah Certificate).
  2. Special Marriage Act 1872 Marriage: Solemnizing a civil or inter-religious marriage before a Marriage Registrar under the Special Marriage Act 1872.
  3. Affidavit-Based Marriage: Executing sworn affidavits before a Notary Public or First Class Magistrate, declaring the marriage, typically used by couples who have already married informally or want a quick documented record.

All three methods produce a legally recognized marriage under Bangladeshi law. However, they differ in procedure, cost, eligibility, and the courts that have jurisdiction over related disputes.

Muslim Marriage Registration – Nikah and Kabinnama

For Muslim citizens, the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974 governs the registration of nikah. Under this law, every Muslim marriage in Bangladesh must be registered. Failure to register is an offence under Section 5 of the Act, punishable with simple imprisonment up to 2 years or a fine of Tk. 3,000, or both — though in practice enforcement varies.

The Kabinnama (also called Nikah Nama) is the official marriage contract document. It records:

  • Full names and addresses of bride and groom
  • National ID numbers of both parties
  • Names and NID numbers of witnesses (minimum 2 per side)
  • Mahr (dower) amount — prompt (moajjal) and deferred (muwajjal)
  • Any special conditions agreed upon by the parties
  • Signature of the Kazi (registrar) and witnesses

The Kabinnama is the most important document in any subsequent family law proceeding — divorce, mahr claim, inheritance, child custody — and should be kept safely. Certified copies can be obtained from the Kazi office at any time.

How to Register a Muslim Marriage at the Kazi Office

The Kazi office process is the standard route for Muslim court marriage in Bangladesh. Here is the step-by-step procedure:

  1. Locate the Registered Kazi: Find a Kazi (Nikah Registrar) licensed by the government for your Union Parishad / Ward area. Marriages must generally be registered in the area where the bride resides.
  2. Submit Documents: Submit all required documents to the Kazi (see the documents table below). Both parties must be present, along with their witnesses (at least 2 per party).
  3. Nikah Ceremony: The Kazi performs or records the nikah. Both parties must give their free and voluntary consent (ijab and qabul). The mahr amount is agreed and recorded.
  4. Kabinnama Executed: The Kazi fills in the Kabinnama form (in duplicate), which is signed by both parties, witnesses, and the Kazi. Both parties receive a copy.
  5. Entry in Register: The Kazi enters the marriage in the official marriage register maintained at the Kazi office.
  6. Certified Copy: A certified copy of the Kabinnama can be obtained from the Kazi office at any time for a nominal fee.

Age Requirements: Under the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, the minimum marriage age in Bangladesh is 18 years for females and 21 years for males. The Kazi must verify age through National ID or birth certificate before registering the marriage.

Prior Marriage Check: If either party has been married before, the previous marriage must have been legally dissolved (divorce certificate or death certificate of previous spouse must be produced).

Special Marriage Act 1872 – Inter-Religious and Civil Marriages

The Special Marriage Act 1872 provides a legal framework for marriages between persons of different religions, or for those who do not wish to marry under their personal religious law. This is the closest equivalent to a truly civil or secular court marriage in Bangladesh.

Key Features of a Special Marriage Act 1872 Marriage:

  • Applicable to all persons in Bangladesh regardless of religion
  • Solemnized before a Marriage Registrar (typically a government-designated official)
  • Requires a 30-day notice period published publicly, during which objections can be filed
  • Both parties must appear in person before the Registrar with their witnesses
  • A Marriage Certificate is issued under Section 12 of the Act
  • Minimum age: 18 years for the bride, 21 years for the groom
  • Either party must not have a living spouse at the time of the marriage

Step-by-Step Process Under the Special Marriage Act 1872:

  1. Both parties submit a Notice of Intended Marriage to the Marriage Registrar of the district where at least one party has resided for at least 30 days.
  2. The notice is entered in the Marriage Notice Book and a copy affixed to a conspicuous place at the Registrar's office.
  3. After the 30-day objection period with no valid objection, the Registrar solemnizes the marriage in the presence of 3 witnesses.
  4. Both parties and witnesses sign the Marriage Register and a Certificate of Marriage is issued.

This type of marriage is particularly relevant for inter-faith couples (e.g., Muslim–Christian, Hindu–Christian) and Bangladeshis marrying foreign nationals.

Affidavit-Based Court Marriage Procedure

An affidavit-based court marriage is a practical option when a couple has already married informally (e.g., in a family ceremony without official registration) and now needs documentary proof of their marriage for legal, administrative, or visa purposes. It is also used by couples who want to establish a legal record quickly.

Steps for an Affidavit-Based Marriage Declaration:

  1. Draft the Affidavit: A lawyer drafts a sworn affidavit in which both parties declare that they are lawfully married to each other, specifying the date, place, and witnesses of the marriage.
  2. Execute Before Notary or Magistrate: The affidavit is sworn before a Notary Public or a First Class Magistrate. Both parties must appear in person.
  3. Notarisation: The Notary Public seals and signs the affidavit, giving it legal evidentiary value.
  4. Gazette or Newspaper Publication (Optional): Some couples additionally publish a marriage notice in a national newspaper or the Bangladesh Gazette for added documentary proof.
  5. File with Registrar: In some cases, the affidavit is filed in the relevant court for additional recognition.

Important Note: An affidavit alone does not substitute for a registered Kabinnama or a Special Marriage Act certificate for all legal purposes. For matters such as passport applications, inheritance proceedings, or overseas visa applications, a properly registered marriage document (Kabinnama or Special Marriage Certificate) is strongly preferred. An affidavit is best used as a supplementary document.

Documents Required for Court Marriage

The required documents vary by the type of court marriage. Use the checklist table below to ensure you are fully prepared:

Document Kazi (Muslim Nikah) Special Marriage Act Affidavit Marriage

Birth Certificate Recommended Required Recommended
Passport-size photographs (4 each) Required Required Required
Witnesses (at least 2 per party) Required Required (3 total) Required (2)
Divorce Certificate or Death Certificate (if previously married) Required Required Required
Wali's (guardian's) consent (bride under 21) Recommended Not required Optional
Notice of Intended Marriage (30-day) Not required Required Not required
Sworn Affidavit Not required Not required Required
Religion conversion certificate (if applicable) If applicable Not required If applicable

Cost Breakdown – Government Fees and Lawyer Fees

The cost of court marriage in Bangladesh is generally affordable. Below is a comprehensive breakdown for 2026:

Item Kazi (Muslim) Special Marriage Act Affidavit
Government Registration Fee Tk. 200 – 500 Tk. 500 – 1,500 N/A
Kazi / Registrar Fee Tk. 1,000 – 5,000 Tk. 2,000 – 5,000 N/A
Stamp Duty (affidavit/deed) Tk. 300 Tk. 300 – 500 Tk. 300 – 600
Notary / Magistrate Fee (affidavit) Optional Not applicable Tk. 500 – 1,500
Lawyer Fee (document preparation) Tk. 2,000 – 8,000 Tk. 5,000 – 15,000 Tk. 2,000 – 6,000
Certified Copy of Certificate Tk. 100 – 300 Tk. 200 – 500 Tk. 100 – 300
Approximate Total Tk. 4,000 – 15,000 Tk. 8,000 – 25,000 Tk. 3,000 – 10,000

These figures are estimates for Dhaka in 2026. Kazi fees are negotiable and can vary significantly between registrars. Lawyers with more experience may charge higher fees but provide more comprehensive assistance.

Timeline for Court Marriage Registration

The time required to complete a court marriage depends on the type chosen:

  • Muslim Nikah at Kazi Office: Can be completed in a single day if all documents are in order and all parties (including witnesses) are present. The Kazi generally issues the Kabinnama on the same day.
  • Special Marriage Act 1872: Requires a mandatory 30-day notice period before the marriage can be solemnized. Total timeline: approximately 35–45 days from the date of notice submission.
  • Affidavit-Based Marriage: Can typically be completed within 1–3 days once documents are prepared. The Notary Public can execute the affidavit the same day in most cases.

If any party's NID or birth certificate needs to be obtained first, or if a previous marriage dissolution needs to be documented, additional time will be required before commencing the marriage registration process.

Legal Validity and Rights After Court Marriage

A court marriage in Bangladesh confers full legal rights on both spouses. The key legal consequences include:

  • Proof of Marriage: The Kabinnama or Special Marriage Certificate is the primary legal proof of marriage accepted by courts, government offices, banks, embassies, and employers.
  • Mahr Rights: The wife's mahr as recorded in the Kabinnama is legally enforceable. She can sue for recovery of unpaid mahr in the Family Court.
  • Inheritance Rights: A registered marriage entitles the surviving spouse to inherit from the deceased spouse under the applicable personal law (Muslim law of inheritance for Muslims).
  • Maintenance Rights: The wife is entitled to maintenance (nafaqa) from the husband under Muslim personal law. The registered marriage is evidence of the marital relationship in any maintenance suit.
  • Divorce Proceedings: All divorce procedures (talaq, khul, court divorce) begin with verification of the registered marriage — the Kabinnama or marriage certificate.
  • Child Legitimacy: Children born of a registered marriage are legally legitimate and entitled to full rights of inheritance, custody, and maintenance.
  • Passport and Visa: Government passport offices and foreign embassies require a registered marriage certificate for spouse visa applications, family reunion visas, and passport dependent endorsements.

Common Problems and Solutions

Couples seeking to register a court marriage in Bangladesh often face practical hurdles. Here are the most common issues and their solutions:

Problem Solution
Family opposition to marriage Adult parties (18+ bride, 21+ groom) can legally marry without parental consent in Bangladesh. A lawyer can advise on safe registration options.
Lost or missing Kabinnama Apply for a certified copy at the Kazi office where the marriage was registered. If the Kazi is unavailable, the Union Parishad Chairman may have records.
One party is a foreign national The foreign national must produce a valid passport and, if required, a No Objection Certificate (NOC) or certificate of single status from their home country's embassy. The Special Marriage Act 1872 is typically used.
Previous marriage not dissolved The previous marriage must be legally dissolved first. For a widow or widower, a death certificate of the former spouse is required. For divorcees, the divorce certificate from the Union Parishad Chairman is required.
Kazi refuses to register the marriage A Kazi cannot arbitrarily refuse registration. Consult a lawyer who can escalate the matter or identify an alternative licensed Kazi in the area.
Under-age party Under the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, the marriage cannot be legally registered until the minimum age is reached. A Kazi who registers a child marriage faces criminal liability.

How Advocate Md. Shah Alam Can Help

Advocate Md. Shah Alam, based at his Uttara chamber in Dhaka, provides comprehensive legal assistance for all types of court marriage registration in Bangladesh. Whether you are a Muslim couple registering your nikah, an inter-faith couple seeking a Special Marriage Act 1872 ceremony, or a couple needing to formalise an existing marriage through affidavit, the chamber offers tailored support.

Services provided include:

  • Identifying and coordinating with the appropriate Kazi or Marriage Registrar
  • Preparing all required legal documents including affidavits, nikah deeds, and applications
  • Advising on mahr amounts and drafting favourable Kabinnama terms
  • Assisting foreign nationals or NRBs with court marriage requirements
  • Handling subsequent matters — mahr enforcement, divorce, child custody — arising from registered marriages
  • Obtaining certified copies of lost or damaged Kabinnama

The Uttara chamber is conveniently located for clients from Uttara, Turag, Dakshinkhan, Airport area, Tongi, and Gazipur. To book a consultation, contact the office here or visit the Family Law service page.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is court marriage legal in Bangladesh without a religious ceremony?

Yes. Under the Special Marriage Act 1872, a marriage can be legally solemnized before a Marriage Registrar without any religious ceremony. This applies to all persons regardless of religion. The resulting Marriage Certificate is fully valid under Bangladeshi law.

Can I do a court marriage in Bangladesh without my parents' knowledge?

Adult parties — a bride aged 18 or above and a groom aged 21 or above — can legally register a marriage without parental consent or knowledge under Bangladeshi law. The Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 only requires parental involvement for under-age marriages. An experienced lawyer can advise on how to proceed discreetly and safely.

What is a Kabinnama and is it the same as a marriage certificate?

The Kabinnama (also called Nikah Nama) is the official Muslim marriage registration document issued by the licensed Kazi registrar under the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974. It serves as the primary proof of a Muslim marriage in Bangladesh and is equivalent to a marriage certificate for all legal purposes including passport applications, divorce proceedings, and inheritance claims.

How long does it take to register a court marriage in Bangladesh?

A Muslim nikah at the Kazi office can be completed and the Kabinnama issued on the same day, provided all documents and witnesses are present. A Special Marriage Act 1872 marriage requires a mandatory 30-day notice period, making the total process about 35–45 days. An affidavit-based marriage declaration can be done within 1–3 days.

Can a Muslim man marry a non-Muslim woman in Bangladesh through court marriage?

Under classical Islamic law, a Muslim man may marry a Christian or Jewish woman (People of the Book). Such a marriage can be registered with a Kazi in Bangladesh. For a Muslim woman marrying a non-Muslim man, the Special Marriage Act 1872 may be used, though this is legally complex and legal advice should be sought. Conversion to Islam by the non-Muslim party simplifies the process.

What happens if my Kabinnama is lost or damaged?

You can obtain a certified copy of your Kabinnama from the Kazi office where the marriage was originally registered. The Kazi maintains an official register. If the Kazi is no longer available, the relevant Union Parishad or Ward Commissioner office may have records. A lawyer can assist in the retrieval process and obtain a certified copy for use in legal proceedings.

A notary public affidavit does not constitute a valid marriage under Bangladesh family laws; without formal registration before an authorized Muslim Marriage Registrar (Kazi) or Special Marriage Registrar, the union remains invalid, jeopardizing the wife's statutory dower (Mahr), alimony, and inheritance rights. 1. The Legal Reality of Court Marriage in Bangladesh

Strictly speaking, the phrase 'Court Marriage' does not exist as a statutory concept in Bangladesh legislation. Instead, it refers to a two-step legal procedure combining:

  1. A formal Affidavit of Declaration and Mutual Consent sworn before a 1st Class Judicial Magistrate or Notary Public; and
  2. Solemnization and registration under personal status laws (such as the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974 or the Special Marriage Act 1872).

Both elements are necessary to achieve complete legal security and religious validity.

2. Notary Affidavit vs Kazi Registration: The Common Fatal Mistake

A widespread legal pitfall in Bangladesh is the belief that an affidavit stamped by a Notary Public constitutes a complete marriage. In landmark judgments, the High Court Division has repeatedly affirmed that a notary public holds no power to solemnize a marriage.

The affidavit serves merely as evidentiary proof of the parties' majority, mental sanity, and uncoerced consent. The substantive validity of the marriage springs solely from the statutory registration recorded in the official marriage register (Nikahnama).

3. Mandatory Eligibility Criteria and Required Documents

Before initiating the court marriage process, couples must ensure the following documentation is intact:

  • Proof of Majority: National ID Cards (Smart NID) or digital online birth certificates. The groom must be at least 21 years old and the bride at least 18 years old under the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017.
  • Passport Photographs: 3 to 4 passport-size photographs of both parties.
  • Adult Witnesses: Two adult male witnesses (or one male and two females) holding valid National IDs.

4. Official Government Fees and Realistic Court Expenses in 2026

Statutory government fees are prescribed by the Ministry of Law and Judicial Affairs:

  • Non-Judicial Stamp Paper: BDT 300 government stamp for the affidavit.
  • Notary Public Attestation: Standard fee between BDT 500 and BDT 1,000.
  • Government Kazi Registry Fee: BDT 14 per thousand up to the first BDT 4,00,000 of Mahr (maximum BDT 5,600). For Mahr amounts above BDT 4,00,000, the fee is BDT 100 per additional BDT 1,00,000.
  • Certified Nikahnama Extract: BDT 100 to BDT 300 for obtaining official certified copies.

5. Step-by-Step Procedure for Completing Court Marriage

The lawful execution follows three consecutive stages:

  1. Drafting the Affidavit: A lawyer drafts the declaration of marriage on non-judicial stamp paper affirming free consent and sound mental state.
  2. Execution before Magistrate / Notary: Both parties appear in person, verify identity through biometric NID checks, and swear the oath.
  3. Nikah Registry Execution: The couple proceeds to an authorized Muslim Marriage Registrar, completes the 25-column Nikahnama, ensures Column 18 (delegated divorce rights) is executed, and receives the marriage certificate.

6. Interfaith Unions under the Special Marriage Act 1872

When bride and groom belong to different religious faiths (such as Hindu-Muslim or Muslim-Christian) and neither wishes to renounce their religion or undergo conversion, they can marry under the Special Marriage Act, 1872.

This requires a 14-day statutory notice period before the Special Marriage Registrar. The marriage creates full civil legality, and children born of such unions have full inheritance rights under civil property statutes.

7. Defending Against False Abduction and Kidnapping Charges

A common hazard following court marriage is that aggrieved relatives file a First Information Report (FIR) alleging abduction under Sections 7 or 8 of the Prevention of Women and Children Repression Act 2000 (Nari O Shishu Nirjaton Daman Ain).

Protective Legal Strategy:

  • Promptly record a General Diary (GD) enclosing certified copies of the Nikahnama and Notary Affidavit at the local police station.
  • If an FIR is initiated, the bride should appear voluntarily before the Cognizance Magistrate under Section 22 / 164 CrPC to record her voluntary statement confirming her lawful marriage and majority.

Can a court marriage take place without parental consent in Bangladesh?

Yes. If both parties have attained legal adulthood (male 21, female 18), they possess the absolute constitutional right to marry without parental permission.

How long does a court marriage take in Dhaka?

If documents and adult witnesses are ready, the entire process—including affidavit execution and Nikah registration—is typically completed within 2 to 4 hours.

Is an interfaith marriage valid without religious conversion in Bangladesh?

Yes, under the Special Marriage Act 1872, individuals of different faiths can lawfully marry without religious conversion.

  1. A formal Affidavit of Declaration and Mutual Consent sworn before a 1st Class Judicial Magistrate or Notary Public; and
  2. Solemnization and registration under personal status laws (such as the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974 or the Special Marriage Act 1872).

Both elements are necessary to achieve complete legal security and religious validity.

2. Notary Affidavit vs Kazi Registration: The Common Fatal Mistake

A widespread legal pitfall in Bangladesh is the belief that an affidavit stamped by a Notary Public constitutes a complete marriage. In landmark judgments, the High Court Division has repeatedly affirmed that a notary public holds no power to solemnize a marriage.

The affidavit serves merely as evidentiary proof of the parties' majority, mental sanity, and uncoerced consent. The substantive validity of the marriage springs solely from the statutory registration recorded in the official marriage register (Nikahnama).

3. Mandatory Eligibility Criteria and Required Documents

Before initiating the court marriage process, couples must ensure the following documentation is intact:

  • Proof of Majority: National ID Cards (Smart NID) or digital online birth certificates. The groom must be at least 21 years old and the bride at least 18 years old under the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017.
  • Passport Photographs: 3 to 4 passport-size photographs of both parties.
  • Adult Witnesses: Two adult male witnesses (or one male and two females) holding valid National IDs.

4. Official Government Fees and Realistic Court Expenses in 2026

Statutory government fees are prescribed by the Ministry of Law and Judicial Affairs:

  • Non-Judicial Stamp Paper: BDT 300 government stamp for the affidavit.
  • Notary Public Attestation: Standard fee between BDT 500 and BDT 1,000.
  • Government Kazi Registry Fee: BDT 14 per thousand up to the first BDT 4,00,000 of Mahr (maximum BDT 5,600). For Mahr amounts above BDT 4,00,000, the fee is BDT 100 per additional BDT 1,00,000.
  • Certified Nikahnama Extract: BDT 100 to BDT 300 for obtaining official certified copies.

5. Step-by-Step Procedure for Completing Court Marriage

The lawful execution follows three consecutive stages:

  1. Drafting the Affidavit: A lawyer drafts the declaration of marriage on non-judicial stamp paper affirming free consent and sound mental state.
  2. Execution before Magistrate / Notary: Both parties appear in person, verify identity through biometric NID checks, and swear the oath.
  3. Nikah Registry Execution: The couple proceeds to an authorized Muslim Marriage Registrar, completes the 25-column Nikahnama, ensures Column 18 (delegated divorce rights) is executed, and receives the marriage certificate.

6. Interfaith Unions under the Special Marriage Act 1872

When bride and groom belong to different religious faiths (such as Hindu-Muslim or Muslim-Christian) and neither wishes to renounce their religion or undergo conversion, they can marry under the Special Marriage Act, 1872.

This requires a 14-day statutory notice period before the Special Marriage Registrar. The marriage creates full civil legality, and children born of such unions have full inheritance rights under civil property statutes.

7. Defending Against False Abduction and Kidnapping Charges

A common hazard following court marriage is that aggrieved relatives file a First Information Report (FIR) alleging abduction under Sections 7 or 8 of the Prevention of Women and Children Repression Act 2000 (Nari O Shishu Nirjaton Daman Ain).

Protective Legal Strategy:

  • Promptly record a General Diary (GD) enclosing certified copies of the Nikahnama and Notary Affidavit at the local police station.
  • If an FIR is initiated, the bride should appear voluntarily before the Cognizance Magistrate under Section 22 / 164 CrPC to record her voluntary statement confirming her lawful marriage and majority.

8. Chambers Legal Consultation and Representation

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a court marriage take place without parental consent in Bangladesh?

Yes. If both parties have attained legal adulthood (male 21, female 18), they possess the absolute constitutional right to marry without parental permission.

How long does a court marriage take in Dhaka?

If documents and adult witnesses are ready, the entire process—including affidavit execution and Nikah registration—is typically completed within 2 to 4 hours.

Is an interfaith marriage valid without religious conversion in Bangladesh?

Yes, under the Special Marriage Act 1872, individuals of different faiths can lawfully marry without religious conversion.

In Bangladesh, while traditional marriages are solemnized under personal religious laws (Muslim, Hindu, Christian, Buddhist), couples of different faiths who do not wish to convert to another religion can legally marry under the <strong>Special Marriage Act 1872</strong>. Known commonly as 'Special Court Marriage', this statutory framework allows interfaith couples, atheists, or civil partners to register a legally binding marriage before an appointed Marriage Registrar. For confidential legal guidance and affidavit drafting, consult Supreme Court Advocate <a href="/advocate-md-shah-alam" style="color:var(--accent);font-weight:600;">Advocate Md. Shah Alam</a>.

What Is the Special Marriage Act 1872 in Bangladesh?

The Special Marriage Act 1872 (Act III of 1872) is a civil marriage statute in Bangladesh designed for individuals who profess different religions (e.g., Hindu-Muslim, Christian-Hindu, Buddhist-Muslim) or who declare they do not profess any specific religion.

Unlike Muslim Nikahnama or Hindu Shastric rites, Special Marriage is a purely civil contract administered by a government-appointed Special Marriage Registrar.

Consult an experienced Family Lawyer in Dhaka to ensure all statutory steps are executed smoothly.

Statutory Pre-requisites (Age, Consent, Single Status)

To qualify for marriage under the Special Marriage Act 1872, the parties must fulfill these legal requirements:

  • Age Requirement: The groom must be at least 21 years of age; the bride must be at least 18 years of age.
  • Marital Status: Neither party must have a living spouse at the time of marriage (monogamy requirement).
  • Mental Capacity: Both parties must be capable of giving valid free consent.
  • Prohibited Degrees of Consanguinity: The parties must not be related within prohibited degrees of relationship.

Step 1: The Mandatory 14-Day Public Notice to Marriage Registrar

Under Section 4 & 6 of the Special Marriage Act 1872, one of the parties must reside in the district of the Special Marriage Registrar for at least 14 days before submitting notice.

Process:

  1. Submit written Notice of Intended Marriage (ফরম-ক) to the Special Marriage Registrar.
  2. The Registrar files the notice in the Marriage Notice Book and displays a copy at their office for 14 consecutive days.
  3. If no valid legal objection is received within 14 days, the marriage can be solemnized anytime within 3 months.

Step 2: Declaration Affidavit before First Class Magistrate / Notary

Along with registrar notice, the couple must execute a sworn joint Declaration Affidavit (হলফনামা) before a First Class Magistrate or Notary Public in Dhaka:

  • Stating free voluntary consent without any coercion, threat, or kidnapping.
  • Affirming age proof (NID / Passport / SSC Certificate).
  • Affirming single status (unmarried/divorced/widowed).
  • Declaring intent to marry under Special Marriage Act III of 1872.

Step 3: Solemnization Ceremony & Special Marriage Register Entry

After the 14-day notice period expires:

  • The couple appears before the Special Marriage Registrar along with 3 adult witnesses.
  • Both parties sign the statutory declaration in the presence of the Registrar and witnesses.
  • The Registrar enters details into the official Special Marriage Register and issues the government Marriage Certificate.

Is Religious Conversion Mandatory for Interfaith Marriage?

No! This is the most crucial aspect of the Special Marriage Act 1872. Neither partner is legally required to change their name or convert to another religion. Both partners retain their original religious identity or non-religious status.

However, under Section 2 to 4, parties sign a declaration stating they do not profess specific religious personal laws for the purpose of this civil marriage contract.

Inheritance Rights of Children Born to Special Marriage Partners

Under Section 22 to 25 of the Special Marriage Act 1872:

  • Severance from Joint Family: Marriage under this Act operates as a severance from any joint Hindu or religious family system.
  • Inheritance Law: Succession to property of persons married under this Act, and the property of their issue (children), is governed exclusively by the Indian Succession Act 1925 (civil inheritance) rather than personal religious laws.
  • Children born to special marriage partners are 100% legitimate under Bangladesh law and hold full legal inheritance rights.

Why You Need a Qualified Family Advocate in Dhaka

Interfaith couples often face family opposition or police harassment threats. Having a senior advocate ensures your court marriage affidavit and registrar filings are legally bulletproof.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a court marriage affidavit on 200 Taka stamp alone a valid marriage in Bangladesh?

No! A notary affidavit alone is NOT a legal marriage. It is merely a declaration of intent. A valid marriage requires registration before an official Nikah Registrar (for Muslims) or Special Marriage Registrar (for interfaith under Special Marriage Act 1872).

Is a Special Marriage certificate recognized for foreign spouse visas (US, UK, Canada)?

Yes. Foreign embassies and immigration authorities fully recognize Marriage Certificates issued by the Special Marriage Registrar under the Special Marriage Act 1872.

Can parents stop an adult couple from doing court marriage in Bangladesh?

No. Any male aged 21+ and female aged 18+ is a legal adult. If both freely consent, parents cannot legally stop or invalidate the marriage. Attempts to file false abduction cases can be quashed in court.

Can a Muslim man and a Hindu woman marry without conversion?

Yes. They can legally marry under the Special Marriage Act 1872 without either party converting.

Court Marriage Bangladesh – Procedure, Documents, Cost & Legal Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-03-02 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Court marriage in Bangladesh is a legally registered marriage performed and documented by authorized officials. Whether you are a Muslim, Hindu, or Christian couple, understanding the procedure, required documents, and costs will help you complete the process quickly and correctly in 2026.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
