A single mistake in the deed draft, an error in stamp duty calculation, or failure to detect an encumbrance can cost you your entire investment.

Advocate Md. Shah Alam, practising from his chamber in Uttara, Dhaka, offers comprehensive legal services for all types of property deed registration in Bangladesh. With extensive experience in property law, Advocate Shah Alam can:

  • Draft sale deeds, gift deeds, power of attorney, mortgage deeds, and partition deeds with precision
  • Conduct thorough title searches and encumbrance checks
  • Calculate correct stamp duty and registration fees based on current circle rates
  • Accompany clients to the Sub-Registrar's office and manage the entire registration process
  • Resolve disputes arising from defective registrations, pre-emption claims, and title disputes
  • Handle mutation applications and khatian corrections after purchase

Do not risk one of the biggest financial decisions of your life without proper legal guidance. Contact our office today for a consultation on your property transaction.

Consult Our Expert Property Lawyer in Dhaka

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the total cost to register a sale deed in Dhaka currently?

For a sale deed in Dhaka (a City Corporation area), the total cost is currently approximately 7.5-8% of the deed value, comprising: stamp duty (3%), registration fee (1.5%), local government tax (2%), e-fee/stamp vendor fee (0.5-1%), plus deed writer/lawyer fees and any applicable advance income tax. For a Tk 50 lakh property, total registration costs (excluding capital gains tax) would be approximately Tk 3.75-4 lakh.

Can a deed be registered without the seller being physically present?

Yes, if the seller has granted a duly registered General or Special Power of Attorney to an attorney, that attorney can represent the seller at the Sub-Registrar's office. The Power of Attorney must itself be registered and must specifically authorise the attorney to execute and register the sale deed. Without a registered POA, the seller must appear personally.

How long does deed registration take in Bangladesh?

On the day of execution, the actual registration process at the Sub-Registrar's office typically takes 2-4 hours if all documents are in order. The certified registered copy is usually returned within 1-3 working days in most offices, though Dhaka offices may take longer due to workload. You can track registration status online at eporcha.gov.bd.

What is the difference between a baina deed and a sale deed?

A baina deed (বায়না দলিল) is an agreement to sell — a promise to execute the final sale deed in future, usually after payment of an advance amount. It does not transfer ownership. A sale deed (বিক্রয় দলিল) is the final document that actually transfers ownership from the seller to the buyer upon payment of the full consideration. Both should be registered, but only the registered sale deed creates legal title in the buyer.

Is stamp duty the same for gift deeds between family members?

No. Gift deeds (হেবা দলিল) between blood relatives attract a highly concessional fixed stamp duty of Tk 200 (as opposed to 3% for urban sale deeds). However, the registration fee (1.5%) is still calculated on the market value of the property, and local government tax and other fees also apply based on market value. The gift must be genuine — disguised sales dressed as gifts to save stamp duty can be challenged by the tax authorities.

What happens if a co-owner sells their share without telling other co-owners?

Under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, co-sharers of agricultural land have a statutory right of pre-emption. A co-owner can go to court within 4 months of learning of the sale and acquire the sold share by paying the same price the outside buyer paid. For non-agricultural jointly owned property, there is no statutory pre-emption right, but co-owners may have contractual rights depending on any joint ownership agreement.

Defamation Law in Bangladesh: Civil Compensation Suits, Libel, Slander & Criminal Prosecution

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-02 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In an era of hyper-connected digital media, viral Facebook posts, unverified online YouTube portals, and bitter commercial rivalries, reputation is both a person's most valuable asset and their most vulnerable target. In Bangladesh, Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs), corporate executives, physicians, politicians, and business owners frequently face orchestrated smear campaigns, character assassination, and fabricated accusations designed to extort money or destroy professional credibility. Bangladeshi jurisprudence provides a dual legal remedy: filing a **Civil Suit for Damages** under the law of torts to recover monetary compensation for reputational harm, or initiating **Criminal Prosecution** under Sections 499 and 500 of the Penal Code 1860 and cyber legislation to jail the offender. This comprehensive guide outlines the evidentiary standards for libel and slander, how to draft and serve a mandatory 15-day Legal Notice, court fees in civil damage claims, criminal complaint procedures in the Magistrate Court, and constitutional free speech defenses.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

📋 In This Article

  2. 2. Civil Action for Tortious Damages: The Joint District Judge Forum
  3. 3. Criminal Defamation Under Sections 499 & 500 of the Penal Code
  4. 4. Social Media & Online Defamation: Facebook, YouTube & Cyber Tribunals
  5. 5. The Ten Statutory Exceptions & Defenses to Defamation
  6. 6. Drafting the 15-Day Legal Notice: Mandatory Evidentiary Steps
  7. 7. Comparative Matrix: Civil Money Suit vs. Criminal Defamation vs. Cyber Complaint
  8. 8. Court Fees, Quantum of Damages & Valuation Caps
  9. 9. Protecting Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) Against Smear Campaigns Abroad
  10. 10. Real-Life Case Study: Recovering 1-Crore Damages for Business Defamation
  11. 11. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1. Legal Definition: Libel vs. Slander Under Bangladeshi Law

In Bangladeshi legal jurisprudence, defamation is both a civil wrong (tort) actionable without proof of special damage in written form, and a criminal offence codified in statute. The law draws a classic common-law distinction:

  • Libel: A defamatory statement expressed in some permanent, visible, or recorded form—such as printed newspaper articles, published books, cartoons, television broadcasts, website blog posts, or digital social media statuses (Facebook posts, tweets, YouTube videos). Libel is actionable per se, meaning the law presumes general damage to reputation without the plaintiff having to prove specific monetary financial loss.
  • Slander: A defamatory imputation conveyed through transitory spoken words, gestures, or audible sounds in a public gathering, business meeting, or press conference. Under civil tort law, slander generally requires establishing that the spoken words caused actual special harm or directly imputed a criminal offence, contagious disease, or professional incompetence.

2. Civil Action for Tortious Damages: The Joint District Judge Forum

When a defamatory campaign inflicts catastrophic commercial loss, cancelled contracts, or severe mental agony, a civil lawsuit for monetary damages is the ultimate judicial remedy. Governed by the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC), the civil mechanism operates as follows:

  • Filing Forum: Civil compensation suits for substantial amounts (exceeding 25 Lakh BDT) must be instituted before the Court of the Joint District Judge having territorial jurisdiction over the area where the defamatory publication occurred or where the defendant resides.
  • Establishing the Tortious Elements: To succeed, the plaintiff's advocate must prove three foundational elements: (1) The words were defamatory; (2) The words explicitly referred to the plaintiff (or were reasonably understood by the public to refer to the plaintiff); and (3) The words were published—communicated to at least one third party other than the plaintiff.
  • Injunction Against Further Defamation: Under Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2 of the CPC, the plaintiff can simultaneously file an application for a Temporary Injunction restraining the defendant, media house, or online platform from further publishing, broadcasting, or circulating the defamatory material pending trial.

3. Criminal Defamation Under Sections 499 & 500 of the Penal Code

For victims seeking swift punitive justice and criminal records against malicious agitators, the Penal Code 1860 provides criminal remedies:

  • Section 499 (The Definition): 'Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said... to defame that person.'
  • Section 500 (Punishment): Mandates that whoever defames another shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two (2) years, or with fine, or with both.
  • Section 501 & 502 (Printers and Publishers): Imposes identical 2-year criminal penalties upon anyone who prints, engraves, or sells defamatory materials knowing them to contain character assassinations.
  • Procedure (C.R. Case): A formal petition of complaint is filed directly before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM). The magistrate examines the complainant on solemn affirmation under Section 200 CrPC and issues summons or an arrest warrant against the accused.

4. Social Media & Online Defamation: Facebook, YouTube & Cyber Tribunals

The explosion of online viral misinformation has made social media the primary battleground for reputation warfare in Bangladesh. Digital defamation involves specialized evidentiary and jurisdictional procedures:

  • Evidentiary Preservation: Merely taking a screenshot is insufficient in court because digital evidence can be fabricated. Evidence must be certified under the Information and Communication Technology Act 2006 and the Evidence Act 1872 (as amended in 2022). It is essential to preserve full URL links, video file downloads, IP header logs, server metadata, and execute a formal Notarial Affidavit of Web Preservation before the perpetrator deletes the post.
  • Cyber Tribunal Jurisdiction: If the online defamation involves fake obscene images, morphed videos, deepfakes, or threats to national security or public order, complaints can be lodged directly before the Divisional Cyber Tribunal or the Police Cyber Support for Women / CID Cyber Crime Investigation Division.
  • Takedown Requests: A formal legal notice can be served upon local representatives or parent entities of Meta, Google/YouTube, or local ISPs to remove defamatory URLs under intermediary liability doctrines.

5. The Ten Statutory Exceptions & Defenses to Defamation

Defamation law in Bangladesh balances personal dignity against the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 39 of the Constitution. Section 499 of the Penal Code contains Ten Statutory Exceptions which operate as complete legal defenses:

  1. Imputation of Truth for Public Good: It is not defamation to state true facts concerning any person if the publication is genuinely for the public welfare.
  2. Public Conduct of Public Servants: Expressing good-faith opinions regarding the official discharge of duties by public servants.
  3. Conduct of Any Person Touching Any Public Question: Good-faith opinions respecting the conduct of individuals participating in public affairs.
  4. Publication of Reports of Court Proceedings: Substantially true and accurate reports of proceedings in courts of justice.
  5. Merits of Case Decided in Court: Fair comments on the conduct of witnesses, parties, or judicial decisions after trial conclusion.
  6. Merits of Public Performance: Good-faith critiques of published books, films, theatrical performances, or architecture submitted to the judgment of the public.
  7. Censure by Person Having Lawful Authority: Good-faith disciplinary censure passed by a parent, schoolmaster, employer, or judge over a subordinate.
  8. Accusation Preferred in Good Faith to Authorized Person: Lodging a complaint of crime to a police officer or magistrate in good faith.
  9. Imputation Made in Good Faith for Protection of Interests: Statements made to protect one's own legal rights or commercial property.
  10. Caution Intended for Good of Person or Public: Conveying private warnings in good faith regarding an individual's financial creditworthiness or character.

6. Drafting the 15-Day Legal Notice: Mandatory Evidentiary Steps

Before rushing into a civil courtroom, delivering a devastating, airtight Legal Notice is an indispensable strategic step:

  • Service via Registered Post with A/D: The notice must be drafted by an enrolled advocate and served upon the perpetrator via Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due (A/D) and courier service, creating an indisputable record of delivery.
  • Core Demands: The notice must set forth: (a) The exact defamatory statements quoted verbatim with date and publication medium; (b) The falsity and malice behind the statements; (c) A strict demand for an unconditional written apology published in the identical prominent medium within fifteen (15) days; and (d) A specified liquidated financial sum demanded as damages for reputational devastation.
  • Evidentiary Role in Trial: If the defendant fails to reply or issues an arrogant, evasive response, that refusal is exhibited in court as prima facie evidence of continuous malice, vastly strengthening the plaintiff's claim for exemplary punitive damages.

7. Comparative Matrix: Civil Money Suit vs. Criminal Defamation vs. Cyber Complaint

Choosing the correct legal path depends on whether your ultimate goal is financial compensation, criminal imprisonment, or instant digital content removal. The table below delineates the statutory options:

Legal RemedyStatutory BasisFiling ForumPrimary ObjectiveStatutory Penalty / Relief
Civil Money Suit for DamagesLaw of Torts & CPC 1908Joint District Judge CourtMonetary compensation for business & reputational lossMonetary money decree & perpetual injunction
Criminal Defamation CasePenal Code 1860, Sec 499/500Metropolitan / Judicial Magistrate CourtCriminal conviction and public accountabilityUp to 2 years imprisonment + judicial fine
Cyber Defamation ComplaintCyber Security Legislation / ICT ActCyber Tribunal / CID Cyber PoliceEmergency digital takedown & cyber arrestImprisonment, fines & mandatory URL blocking
Temporary InjunctionOrder XXXIX, Rules 1-2 CPCCivil Court where suit is pendingImmediate gag order preventing continuous publicationCourt restraining order; civil jail for breach

8. Court Fees, Quantum of Damages & Valuation Caps

A critical consideration in instituting a civil money suit for defamation is calculating the mandatory ad valorem court fee under the Court-Fees Act 1870:

  • Statutory Maximum Court Fee Cap: Unlike jurisdictions where plaintiffs can claim 100 Crore BDT without paying fees, Bangladeshi law prevents frivolous claims by requiring an ad valorem fee of approximately 2% on the claimed amount. However, the law provides a statutory maximum cap (presently capped at approximately 50,000 to 60,000 BDT depending on statutory amendments) for civil plaints.
  • Assessment of Quantum: In awarding damages, civil courts examine: (1) The social, professional, and commercial standing of the plaintiff; (2) The gravity and venom of the false accusation (e.g., alleging embezzlement, moral turpitude, or treason); (3) The extent of circulation (local gossip vs. nationwide prime-time television broadcast); (4) Provable commercial loss, cancelled deals, or lost contracts; and (5) The subsequent conduct of the defendant.

9. Protecting Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) Against Smear Campaigns Abroad

Expatriates living in North America, Europe, and the Middle East are favorite targets of blackmail syndicates and predatory relatives in Bangladesh. Rogue elements often circulate fabricated videos, forge false matrimonial complaints, or spread rumors in village communities to force NRBs to forfeit ancestral land or yield to extortionate demands.

Under Bangladeshi procedural law, an NRB defamed while living abroad does not need to abandon their career and travel to Bangladesh to initiate legal action. By executing a Special Power of Attorney attested by the nearest Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission, an overseas citizen can empower a Supreme Court advocate or trusted representative in Dhaka to:

  • Serve legal notices demanding retractions and apologies.
  • Institute a formal Criminal Defamation Complaint (C.R. Case) before the Magistrate Court.
  • File a Civil Money Suit for Damages with an immediate application for a Gag Order / Injunction.
  • File an emergency report with the CID Cyber Crime Division to block overseas access and remove malicious Facebook posts.

10. Real-Life Case Study: Recovering 1-Crore Damages for Business Defamation

The managing director of an ISO-certified pharmaceutical export company in Tejgaon, Dhaka, became the target of a vicious smear campaign orchestrated by a terminated procurement officer. The ex-employee launched multiple anonymous Facebook pages, circulated doctored letters alleging that the company's exported medicines were contaminated, and emailed foreign importers in the UK and Australia.

The company engaged our legal chamber to dismantle the malicious campaign. Our multidisciplinary legal strategy was executed as follows:

  1. Secured forensic digital evidence via a Notarial Certificate of Web Preservation, documenting IP connections, email headers, and timestamps before pages could be wiped.
  2. Issued an emergency 15-day Legal Notice to the perpetrator's permanent address and served formal takedown notifications to Meta Platforms Inc.
  3. Instituted a Criminal Case under Section 500 of the Penal Code before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court, Dhaka. The Magistrate took cognizance, recorded depositions, and issued an immediate arrest warrant.
  4. Concurrently filed a Civil Suit for Damages (Money Suit No. 19/2023) before the 1st Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka, claiming 1 Crore BDT in commercial damages, alongside an application under Order XXXIX CPC.
  5. The Joint District Judge granted an immediate temporary injunction restraining the defendant and his agents from uttering or publishing any statements concerning the plaintiff.
  6. Facing imminent criminal arrest by DB Police and escalating civil liability, the perpetrator surrendered in court, submitted an unconditional judicial apology published in two national dailies, and executed a formal settlement deed paying substantial monetary compensation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the legal difference between libel and slander in Bangladesh?

Libel is defamation in permanent or written form (such as newspaper reports, printed letters, books, website posts, or Facebook statuses) and is actionable without proof of actual financial damage. Slander is defamation in temporary, spoken words or gestures and generally requires proving actual harm or severe personal imputations.

What is the maximum criminal punishment for defamation in Bangladesh?

Under Section 500 of the Penal Code 1860, criminal defamation is punishable with simple imprisonment for up to two (2) years, or with a judicial fine, or with both.

Is it mandatory to send a Legal Notice before filing a defamation lawsuit?

While not strictly mandatory for criminal complaints, serving a 15-day Legal Notice through an advocate is practically indispensable before filing a Civil Suit for Damages. It establishes prior notice, proves persistent malice, and affords the defendant an opportunity to issue an apology.

Can I sue someone for defaming me on Facebook or YouTube in Bangladesh?

Yes. Online defamation can be prosecuted criminally before the Magistrate Court under Section 500 Penal Code or before the Cyber Tribunal under cyber security legislation, as well as pursued for monetary damages in the Civil Court.

What court has jurisdiction over civil defamation suits for money damages?

Civil suits claiming significant monetary compensation for reputational damages are instituted before the Court of the Joint District Judge having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the defamatory material was published or where the defendant resides.

Is stating the truth considered a complete defense against defamation?

Under the First Exception to Section 499 of the Penal Code, stating the truth is a complete defense only if it is published for the public good. Simply proving that a statement is factually true may not suffice if it was published purely out of private malice without any public interest.

Can an NRB living in the US or UK sue someone in Bangladesh for defamation?

Yes. An overseas Bangladeshi can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, authorizing a Supreme Court advocate or representative in Bangladesh to institute civil suits and criminal complaints.

Can a civil court issue a gag order stopping someone from continuing defamatory posts?

Yes. Under Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a plaintiff can apply for a Temporary Injunction restraining the defendant from publishing or uttering further defamatory material while the suit is pending.

Defamation Law Bangladesh – Civil and Criminal Remedies

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-03-09 · 8 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

A false accusation posted online. A malicious rumour spread in your community. A rival's statement to your employer that destroys your career. Defamation in Bangladesh carries both criminal and civil consequences — and with social media, the scale of reputational damage can be instant and devastating. Knowing your remedies is the first step to protection.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

📋 In This Article

  2. Criminal Defamation: Sections 499–502 of the Penal Code
  3. Exceptions to Criminal Defamation
  4. Civil Defamation: Suing for Damages
  5. Online Defamation and the Cyber Security Act 2023
  6. How to File a Defamation Complaint in Bangladesh
  7. Defences Available to the Accused
  8. Real-Life Scenario: Defamation via WhatsApp Group

What Is Defamation Under Bangladesh Law?

Defamation is the act of making a false statement of fact that damages the reputation of another person. In Bangladesh, defamation has two legal dimensions:

  • Criminal defamation: Governed by Sections 499–502 of the Bangladesh Penal Code 1860 (BPC). A criminal offence punishable by imprisonment and/or a fine. The complaint is filed with the Magistrate's court.
  • Civil defamation (tort of defamation): A civil wrong for which the victim can claim monetary compensation (damages) in a civil court.

Additionally, online defamation is addressed under the Cyber Security Act 2023 (CSA), which carries its own distinct remedies and penalties. Both tracks can be pursued simultaneously in appropriate cases.

Criminal Defamation: Sections 499–502 of the Penal Code

Section 499 of the BPC defines defamation as making or publishing any imputation that harms the reputation of a person, by words (spoken or written), signs, or visible representations, intending to harm or knowing it will harm that person's reputation.

Key elements that must be proven:

  • The statement was made: spoken, written, or communicated in any form.
  • The statement referred to the complainant: it must be about the specific person claiming to be defamed.
  • The statement was published or communicated to at least one third party.
  • The statement harmed the reputation of the complainant.
  • The accused had the intention or knowledge that the statement would cause harm.

Punishment (Section 500 BPC): Simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both.

Section 501: Printing or engraving defamatory matter — same punishment.

Section 502: Sale of printed defamatory material — same punishment.

Exceptions to Criminal Defamation

Section 499 provides 10 exceptions — statements that cannot constitute criminal defamation even if reputationally damaging. The most commonly invoked are:

  • Truth for public good: The statement is true and its publication is for the public benefit.
  • Fair comment on public figures: Opinion on the conduct of a public servant in their public functions is not defamation.
  • Court reports: Fair reporting of court proceedings.
  • Literary criticism: Fair criticism of published books, works of art, or public performances.
  • Caution given in good faith: A warning given in good faith to a person about one's own interests or society's interest.

These exceptions are only valid if the statement is genuinely within their scope. A defendant claiming "fair comment" who actually acted maliciously will not succeed. Courts examine the intent carefully.

Civil Defamation: Suing for Damages

A civil defamation suit is different from a criminal complaint and pursues monetary compensation rather than punishment. In a civil suit:

  • The standard of proof is on the balance of probabilities (lower than the criminal standard of beyond reasonable doubt).
  • The plaintiff proves that the defendant made a defamatory statement, it was published to a third party, and it caused reputational damage.
  • The court may award general damages (presumed harm to reputation), special damages (provable financial loss), and in serious cases, aggravated damages.
  • An injunction can be sought to prevent repeated publication of the defamatory statement.

Civil defamation suits in Bangladesh are filed before the Civil Courts. The limitation period for filing a civil defamation suit is generally one year from the date of publication. Act promptly — delay weakens your case and may bar your claim. Consult a civil litigation lawyer in Dhaka without delay.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Online Defamation and the Cyber Security Act 2023

The Cyber Security Act 2023 (which replaced the much-criticised Digital Security Act 2018) addresses online defamation under Section 29. This provision makes it an offence to publish, broadcast, or transmit material on the internet that is defamatory within the meaning of the Penal Code.

Key features of Section 29 CSA:

  • Offence: Publishing defamatory content online (social media, websites, messaging apps).
  • Punishment: Imprisonment up to 2 years, fine up to Tk. 5 lakh, or both.
  • Non-bailable in serious cases involving wider public harm.
  • Investigation: By the Cyber Security Authority or designated police units with digital forensics capability.

This section is particularly relevant for defamatory Facebook posts, WhatsApp messages sent to groups, YouTube videos, and online news articles. Screenshots of the defamatory content must be preserved immediately — content is often deleted once a complaint is filed. Also consider filing a civil suit alongside the criminal complaint.

How to File a Defamation Complaint in Bangladesh

Depending on the type of defamation:

For criminal defamation (Penal Code):

  1. Gather evidence: Screenshots, witness statements, copies of publications, recordings.
  2. File a complaint (Naraji) before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) of the relevant area.
  3. The Magistrate examines the complaint and may direct police investigation or issue process against the accused directly.
  4. A case is registered and the accused is summoned.

For online defamation (Cyber Security Act):

  1. Preserve all digital evidence (screenshots, URLs, timestamps).
  2. File a complaint with the Cyber Security Authority or the Cyber Unit of the police.
  3. Alternatively, file a complaint before the Cyber Tribunal established under the CSA.

For civil defamation:

  1. File a plaint in the Civil Court claiming damages.
  2. Simultaneously apply for an injunction to stop further publication.

An experienced defamation lawyer in Dhaka will advise on the optimal combination of remedies for your specific situation.

Defences Available to the Accused

If you are accused of defamation, the following defences are available in Bangladesh:

  • Truth: In criminal defamation, truth is a defence if the statement was made for public good. In civil defamation, truth (justification) is an absolute defence.
  • Fair comment: A genuine opinion on a matter of public interest, based on true facts, made without malice.
  • Privilege: Statements made in Parliament, court proceedings, or official government reports enjoy absolute privilege. Statements made in good faith in certain other contexts (e.g., a reference letter) may enjoy qualified privilege.
  • Consent: If the complainant consented to the publication, there is no defamation.
  • Absence of publication: If the statement was never communicated to a third party, there is no actionable defamation.

Each defence must be supported by evidence and argued specifically. Generic claims of "I was just telling the truth" without corroborating evidence rarely succeed in court.

Real-Life Scenario: Defamation via WhatsApp Group

A business competitor of Rahim sends messages to a WhatsApp group of 50 business contacts, falsely claiming that Rahim's company has defrauded clients and defaulted on contracts. The message includes fabricated screenshots of bank transactions. Rahim's business suffers immediate losses as clients cancel meetings.

Rahim takes the following steps with his lawyer:

  1. Screenshots of the WhatsApp messages (with timestamps and group member list) are preserved immediately.
  2. Affidavits are collected from two group members confirming they received the messages.
  3. A complaint is filed before the Cyber Tribunal under Section 29 CSA for online defamation.
  4. Simultaneously, a civil suit is filed in the Civil Court claiming damages of Tk. 50 lakh based on provable loss of business (supported by cancelled contracts and client correspondence).
  5. The civil court grants an interim injunction directing the defendant not to publish any further statements about Rahim's business.

The cyber complaint results in the defendant being summoned and eventually entering into a settlement that includes a public retraction, damages, and a private apology. Acting quickly and with a two-track legal strategy made all the difference.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is defamation a criminal offence in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under Sections 499–502 of the Bangladesh Penal Code, criminal defamation is punishable by up to 2 years simple imprisonment, a fine, or both.

Can I sue someone for defamation on social media in Bangladesh?

Yes. Online defamation is addressed under Section 29 of the Cyber Security Act 2023 and can also be prosecuted under the Penal Code. A civil suit for damages can be filed simultaneously.

Is truth a defence to defamation in Bangladesh?

In criminal defamation, truth is a defence only if the statement was made for public good. In civil defamation, truth (justification) is an absolute defence regardless of motive.

What is the time limit for filing a defamation case in Bangladesh?

For civil defamation, the limitation period is generally one year from publication. For criminal defamation, consult a lawyer immediately — delay affects both the legal and practical strength of your case.

Can I claim both criminal punishment and civil damages for the same defamatory statement?

Yes. Criminal and civil defamation actions are independent. You can pursue both tracks simultaneously — criminal for punishment and civil for monetary compensation.

Developer Delayed Flat Handover in Bangladesh? Legal Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-10 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Purchasing a residential apartment in Dhaka, Chittagong, or other urban centers represents a lifetime investment for local buyers and non-resident Bangladeshis (NRBs). However, one of the most widespread grievances in the housing sector is project delay. Real estate developers routinely promise completion within thirty-six to forty-eight months, but buyers frequently find their projects stalled for five to ten years while builders divert funds to subsequent commercial ventures. Under the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 (রিয়েল এস্টেট উন্নয়ন ও ব্যবস্থাপনা আইন, ২০১০), developers do not enjoy unlimited discretion. The law establishes strict statutory compensation requirements for every month of delay under Section 15, alongside criminal prosecution and imprisonment under Section 24 for fraudulent builders.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order
Official Portalssupremecourt.gov.bd, judiciary.gov.bd, pcc.police.gov.bd & land.gov.bd
Supreme Court ChamberAdvocate Md. Shah Alam — Uttara & Dhaka Judge Court (+880 1712-655546)
📋 In This Article
  1. 1. The Statutory Framework: Developer Obligations under the 2010 Act
  2. 2. Section 15 Delay Compensation: Monthly Rent Payments & Interest Calculations
  3. 3. Contract Cancellation & Full Refund with Statutory Interest (Section 15(2))
  4. 4. Building Plan Deviations: Section 14 Violations and Structural Alterations
  5. 5. Criminal Penalties: Jailing Fraudulent Builders under Sections 24, 27 & 28
  6. 6. Summary Matrix: Builder Breaches, Buyer Rights & Judicial Fora
  7. 7. Mandatory Arbitration Protocols under Section 36 of the 2010 Act
  8. 8. Illustrative Scenario: Expatriate Flat Buyer Forcing Handover and 18 Lakh BDT Compensation
  9. 9. Essential Contract Vetting Checklist for Prospective Apartment Buyers
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate

1. The Statutory Framework: Developer Obligations under the 2010 Act

For years, real estate builders in Bangladesh operated in an unregulated environment, exploiting one-sided, boilerplate buyer agreements. In 2010, the government enacted the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 (Act No. XLVIII of 2010) to protect flat buyers, establish building safety, and eliminate rogue real estate entities.

Under Section 5 of the Act, no developer can launch, market, or advertise a real estate project without obtaining formal registration from the government (RAJUK, CDA, KDA, RDA, or the National Housing Authority). Under Section 13, all terms of sale must be documented in a registered bilateral contract that clearly specifies the apartment unit, floor layout, parking allotment, total purchase price, installment breakdown, and the exact handover date.

Crucially, Section 13(2) prohibits developers from including arbitrary clauses that unilaterally relieve the builder of liability for delays. The statutory protections established in the 2010 enactment are mandatory; they cannot be overridden by fine-print contractual waivers.

2. Section 15 Delay Compensation: Monthly Rent Payments & Interest Calculations

The core economic protection for apartment purchasers is established in Section 15 of the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 ('Handover of Real Estate'). Under Section 15(1), the developer is legally bound to complete construction and hand over possession of the real estate, along with all promised common utilities, within the timeline specified in the contract.

If the developer fails to hand over the apartment within the contractual timeframe due to reasons within their control, Section 15(1) establishes that the developer must pay the purchaser compensation at the rate agreed upon in the contract for every month of delay. If the contract fails to stipulate a specific penalty rate, the developer must pay monthly compensation equivalent to the reasonable prevailing market rental value of the apartment.

This monthly compensation continues to accumulate for every single month until actual physical possession is delivered along with the completion certificate. Builders cannot escape this statutory compensation by claiming material price escalation or routine labor delays, as these represent standard commercial risks assumed by the developer.

3. Contract Cancellation & Full Refund with Statutory Interest (Section 15(2))

In numerous stalled projects, construction ceases completely, and the purchaser loses confidence that the developer will ever complete the building. In such circumstances, the buyer is not forced to wait indefinitely.

Under Section 15(2) of the Real Estate Act 2010, if the developer completely fails to complete the real estate or if the purchaser chooses to cancel the agreement due to prolonged, unauthorized delay, the purchaser is entitled to cancel the contract. The developer is statutorily mandated to refund the entire amount of money deposited by the purchaser, alongside interest at the prevailing commercial banking rate, within a maximum of sixty (60) days from the date of cancellation notice.

Is a real estate developer delaying your apartment handover or demanding extra unauthorized money in Dhaka? Immediate legal action enforces your statutory compensation and delivery rights. Message our real estate litigators on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for professional case review.

If the developer fails to disburse the full refund within sixty days, Section 15(3) empowers the purchaser to proceed with immediate legal action, treating the unpaid sum as a statutory debt. For comprehensive property acquisition due diligence, review our guide on flat apartment registration fees and vetting in Bangladesh.

4. Building Plan Deviations: Section 14 Violations and Structural Alterations

A frequent malpractice among developers in Dhaka and Chittagong is deviating from approved architectural and structural plans. Builders often construct unauthorized additional floors, convert mandatory car parking into commercial shops, curtail common stairways, or reduce the net square footage of the purchased apartment.

Under Section 14 of the Real Estate Act 2010, the developer is strictly prohibited from making any structural alteration, layout modification, or utility change without the prior written consent of the purchaser and the formal approval of the planning authority (e.g., RAJUK under the Dhaka Building Construction Rules).

If a developer delivers an apartment with reduced square footage, Section 14(2) mandates that the developer must refund the proportionate value of the missing square footage, calculated at the original purchase rate, plus statutory interest. Constructing beyond approved height limits exposes the building to demolition notices, making plan verification an essential buyer safeguard.

5. Criminal Penalties: Jailing Fraudulent Builders under Sections 24, 27 & 28

The Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 is not merely a civil compensation statute; it contains teeth in the form of severe criminal punishments for defaulting builders.

Key penal provisions applicable against unscrupulous developers include:

  • Section 24 (Unauthorized Alteration / Delayed Handover Failure): Punishes developers who willfully fail to complete construction or alter approved plans without consent with imprisonment up to three (3) years, or a fine up to 20 Lakh BDT, or both.
  • Section 27 (Double Selling / Multiple Allocation): If a developer sells, mortgages, or transfers the same apartment unit to more than one purchaser, such fraudulent act is punishable with imprisonment up to three (3) years, or a fine up to 20 Lakh BDT, or both.
  • Section 28 (Unauthorized Commercial Charges): Imposes criminal penalties on builders who demand illegal extra fees or escalate agreed prices without contractual basis.

Criminal complaints under these sections are filed directly before the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM), resulting in the immediate issuance of summons or arrest warrants against the Managing Director and directors of the developer enterprise.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

6. Summary Matrix: Builder Breaches, Buyer Rights & Judicial Fora

Apartment buyers can assess their legal remedies, statutory penalties, and procedural options in the following comparative matrix:

Developer Violation Governing Provision (2010 Act) Statutory Remedy for Buyer Primary Enforcement Forum
Delayed Flat Handover Section 15(1) Mandatory monthly compensation or market rent until handover Arbitration (Sec 36) / Joint District Judge
Total Project Abandonment Section 15(2) & (3) Full refund of all deposits plus commercial bank interest within 60 days Money Suit (Artha Adalat) / Arbitration
Selling Flat to Another Buyer Section 27 Criminal prosecution; developer faces 3 years jail & 20 Lakh fine Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court (CR Case)
Refusal to Register Saf Kabala Section 16 & Sec 21A Specific Relief Court executes and registers title deed on builder's behalf Specific Performance Suit (Joint District Judge)

7. Mandatory Arbitration Protocols under Section 36 of the 2010 Act

Under Section 36 of the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010, the legislature created an expedited dispute resolution framework: any dispute arising between a developer and a purchaser must initially be referred to amicable settlement and arbitration under the Arbitration Act 2001.

The purchaser serves a formal thirty-day statutory notice detailing the breach (e.g., accumulated handover delay compensation) and nominating an independent arbitrator. If the developer fails to respond, disputes the claim, or refuses to appoint an arbitrator within thirty days, Section 36(3) establishes that the dispute shall be resolved through judicial proceedings.

The buyer can then immediately file a civil suit before the Joint District Judge Court for recovery of the compensation or initiate criminal proceedings under Section 24 and Section 27 before the Magistrate Court. Furthermore, if the developer is an active member of the Real Estate and Housing Association of Bangladesh (REHAB), the buyer can file a formal complaint with the REHAB Mediation Committee to freeze the builder's membership standing.

8. Illustrative Scenario: Expatriate Flat Buyer Forcing Handover and 18 Lakh BDT Compensation

To illustrate how legal remedies unfold against defaulting builders, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

An expatriate physician residing in Manchester, UK, purchased a 2,200 sq. ft. luxury apartment in Gulshan, Dhaka, from a prominent real estate firm in 2019 for 3.5 Crore BDT. The registered agreement stipulated a handover date of December 2022, with an explicit delay penalty clause of 50,000 BDT per month. By mid-2025—thirty months past the deadline—the building remained an unpainted shell, while the developer demanded an additional 25 Lakh BDT citing construction material inflation.

The doctor engaged a Supreme Court property advocate in Dhaka. The advocate served a statutory legal notice under Section 15 and Section 36 of the Real Estate Act 2010, demanding immediate completion, rejecting the unauthorized price escalation, and claiming 15 Lakh BDT in accumulated delay compensation. When the builder ignored the notice, the advocate filed an emergency application for an injunction under Order 39 CPC, coupled with a criminal complaint under Section 24 before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court.

Faced with arrest warrants for its corporate directors and frozen marketing operations on the Gulshan project, the developer immediately negotiated a binding settlement (Solenama). The developer completed the apartment within four months, waived all unauthorized price escalation, and paid 18 Lakh BDT in accrued delay compensation, handing over the registered Saf Kabala deed.

9. Essential Contract Vetting Checklist for Prospective Apartment Buyers

Purchasers can avert years of agonizing litigation by conducting rigorous legal vetting before signing developer agreements in Bangladesh:

  • Verify RAJUK/CDA Project Approval: Never buy based on glossy brochures. Verify the original building approval letter, architectural layout plan, and structural clearance from the planning authority.
  • Inspect Landowner-Developer Joint Venture Deed: If the project is a joint venture (JV), examine the registered power of attorney given by the landowner to the developer to confirm the builder's legal authority to sell that specific apartment unit.
  • Ensure Strict Delayed Handover Penalty Clause: Ensure the agreement contains a specific monthly compensation figure (e.g., 50,000 to 100,000 BDT per month) and avoid ambiguous 'unforeseen delay' exceptions.
  • Avoid Cash Payments: Disburse all installment payments strictly through account-payee cheques, pay orders, or international bank transfers with detailed transaction descriptions.
  • Check REHAB & Ministry Registration: Confirm that the developer is formally registered under the Real Estate Act 2010 and holds active membership with REHAB.

For dedicated representation in real estate transactions and builder litigation, explore our specialized land dispute lawyer services and NRB legal services in Bangladesh.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a Real Estate Advocate in Dhaka: To draft statutory developer breach notices, initiate arbitration under Section 36 of the Real Estate Act 2010, or file criminal cases before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate for handover refusal, reach out on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call our chamber at +880 1712-655546. NRB flat buyers can instruct counsel remotely via embassy-attested power of attorney.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010?

The Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 (Act No. XLVIII of 2010) is the primary statute in Bangladesh regulating real estate builders, protecting flat buyers, mandating handover timelines, and imposing criminal penalties for construction fraud.

Can I get compensation if a developer delays handing over my flat in Dhaka?

Yes. Under Section 15(1) of the Real Estate Act 2010, the developer is legally obligated to pay agreed monthly compensation or the prevailing market rental value for every month of delay beyond the contractual handover date.

Can I cancel my apartment contract and get a full refund if the project is stalled?

Yes. Under Section 15(2), if the developer fails to complete the building, the purchaser has the statutory right to cancel the agreement and demand a full refund of all deposited money plus bank interest within 60 days.

Can a real estate developer be jailed for delaying flat handover?

Under Section 24 of the Real Estate Act 2010, developers who willfully fail to complete construction or deliver property without valid cause face criminal imprisonment for up to three years, or a fine up to 20 Lakh BDT, or both.

What should I do if a developer sells my booked flat to someone else?

Double-selling an apartment is a grave criminal offence under Section 27 of the 2010 Act, punishable with up to three years imprisonment. You can file an immediate criminal CR case before the Magistrate and obtain an injunction.

Can a builder demand extra money above the agreed contract price?

No. Under Section 13 and Section 28 of the Act, a developer cannot unilaterally escalate the purchase price unless explicitly provided for in a registered contract approved by the purchaser.

What is the role of REHAB in resolving developer-buyer disputes?

If the developer is a member of REHAB, buyers can lodge formal mediation complaints. However, REHAB mediation is voluntary and does not prevent you from pursuing civil and criminal court remedies.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi buyer sue a developer without traveling to Dhaka?

Yes. An overseas buyer can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission, empowering an advocate in Dhaka to issue legal notices, initiate arbitration, and conduct court trials.

entries.body:
Digital Security Act Bangladesh: Your Legal Rights and Defences Explained

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-12 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

The Digital Security Act 2018 (DSA) and its successor the Cyber Security Act 2023 (CSA) have been used to prosecute thousands of people in Bangladesh — journalists, activists, students, business owners, and ordinary citizens — for online speech and conduct. Whether you are facing charges yourself or want to understand your rights, this guide explains the legal protections available to you under Bangladesh law and how an experienced lawyer can help you navigate these proceedings.

: · Cyber Crime & Criminal Defense Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing LawCyber Security Act, 2023 & Penal Code, 1860 (Bangladesh)
First Step at Police StationFile an Online or In-Person General Diary (GD) at gd.police.gov.bd / local Thana
Police Cyber Support for Women (PCSW)Helpline: 01320-000888 | Email: cybersupport.women@police.gov.bd
CID / CTTC Cyber Crime Unit24/7 Emergency: 999 | Police Headquarters & Cyber Tribunal Dhaka
Required Digital EvidenceFull URLs, unedited screenshots, transaction IDs (bKash/Nagad), and call logs
📋 In This Article
  1. Understanding the DSA and CSA in Bangladesh
  2. Your Constitutional Rights When Facing a Cyber Case
  3. Rights at the Time of Arrest Under the CSA
  4. Bail Rights Under the Digital Security/Cyber Security Act
  5. Challenging Digital Evidence in Court
  6. Constitutional Defences: Free Speech and Article 39
  7. Role of Your Lawyer in a DSA/CSA Case
  8. How to File a Complaint If You Are a Victim of Misuse

Understanding the DSA and CSA in Bangladesh

The Digital Security Act, 2018 (DSA) was enacted in Bangladesh on 8 October 2018, replacing Section 57 of the ICT Act 2006. It was widely criticised by press freedom organisations and human rights bodies for its broad scope, vague definitions, and use to silence journalists and critics.

On 18 August 2023, the DSA was repealed and replaced by the Cyber Security Act, 2023 (CSA). While the government presented the CSA as a more balanced framework, many civil society groups noted that the core problematic provisions were retained with only minor modifications.

Key continuities between the DSA and CSA:

  • Both criminalise online publication of 'false', 'offensive', or 'defamatory' content — with vague definitions that courts interpret broadly.
  • Both establish a dedicated Cyber Tribunal for trial of offences.
  • Both provide police with significant powers to search, seize, and arrest.
  • Both allow for long periods of remand and investigation.

Key changes under the CSA compared to the DSA:

  • Some non-bailable offences under the DSA became bailable under the CSA.
  • Maximum penalties for some offences were reduced.
  • Definitions of some offences were slightly narrowed.

Despite these changes, the fundamental concerns about the law's potential for misuse remain. Knowing your rights is the first line of defence if you are charged. Consult a criminal lawyer in Bangladesh with cyber law experience immediately.

Your Constitutional Rights When Facing a Cyber Case

The Constitution of Bangladesh provides fundamental rights that apply to all criminal proceedings, including those under the DSA/CSA. These cannot be waived or overridden even by a special law like the CSA:

  • Article 27 – Equality before law: All citizens are equal before the law. You cannot be discriminated against in the application of criminal law.
  • Article 31 – Right to protection of law: No action detrimental to your life, liberty, or property can be taken without lawful authority.
  • Article 32 – Right to personal liberty: No person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except in accordance with law. Unlawful detention is a violation of this fundamental right.
  • Article 33 – Protection on arrest: Every arrested person must be informed of the grounds for arrest as soon as possible, and must be allowed to consult and be defended by a lawyer of their choice.
  • Article 35(3) – Right to a fair trial: Every person accused of a criminal offence is entitled to a fair and public trial.
  • Article 35(4) – Protection against self-incrimination: No person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against themselves.
  • Article 39 – Freedom of thought, conscience and speech: The right to freedom of speech and expression is guaranteed, subject to reasonable restrictions — a constitutional ground for challenging overbroad cybercrime prosecutions.
  • Article 102 – Enforcement of rights by High Court: The High Court Division has jurisdiction to issue directions, orders, or writs to enforce fundamental rights — a powerful tool for those unlawfully detained under the CSA.

Rights at the Time of Arrest Under the CSA

Understanding your rights at the moment of arrest is critical to protecting yourself. The following rights apply under the Constitution and the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC):

  1. Right to Know the Grounds of Arrest: The arresting officer must inform you of the specific offence you are being arrested for. Demand this information immediately — an arrest without clear grounds is unlawful.
  2. Right to Remain Silent: You are not obliged to answer any police questions beyond confirming your identity. Exercise your right to remain silent until your lawyer is present. Anything you say can be used against you in court.
  3. Right to a Lawyer: You must be allowed to contact and consult a lawyer immediately after arrest. Police cannot legally deny this right. Insist on it firmly and calmly.
  4. Right to Inform Family: You must be allowed to inform your family or a trusted person of your arrest and location of custody.
  5. Right to be Produced Before a Magistrate: Under Section 61 CrPC, an arrested person must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest (excluding journey time). Extended detention beyond 24 hours without production is unlawful.
  6. Right Against Torture: Torture or ill-treatment during custody is prohibited under Article 35(5) of the Constitution and Bangladesh's international treaty obligations. If you are mistreated, document it and report it to your lawyer immediately.

If any of these rights are violated, your bail lawyer can raise these violations before the Magistrate or the High Court Division to challenge the legality of your detention.

Bail Rights Under the Digital Security/Cyber Security Act

One of the most important immediate steps after arrest is securing bail. The bail position under the CSA depends on the specific section you are charged under:

  • Bailable Offences: For bailable CSA offences, bail is a right. You or your lawyer can apply for bail at the police station or before the Magistrate. The police/Magistrate must grant bail if the offence is bailable.
  • Non-Bailable Offences: For non-bailable offences, bail is discretionary. Apply to the Cyber Tribunal (or the Sessions Judge acting as Tribunal Judge). Factors considered include the nature of the offence, the accused's background, and the risk of flight or tampering with evidence.
  • High Court Bail: If the Tribunal refuses bail, the accused can approach the High Court Division under Section 498 CrPC for bail. The High Court has broad discretion and has granted bail in many CSA cases where the Tribunal was reluctant.
  • Anticipatory Bail: If you apprehend arrest under the CSA before being arrested, you can apply for anticipatory bail before the Sessions Court or High Court Division — see our High Court anticipatory bail guide.

Given the complexity of bail proceedings in cyber cases, engaging an experienced bail lawyer in Bangladesh immediately upon arrest is the most important step you can take.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Challenging Digital Evidence in Court

In cybercrime cases, the prosecution's case largely depends on digital evidence — screenshots, social media posts, device data, server logs, and forensic reports. Your lawyer can challenge this evidence in several important ways:

  • Authenticity: The prosecution must prove that the digital evidence is authentic — that it has not been altered, edited, or fabricated. Screenshots alone, without corroborating metadata, can be challenged for authenticity.
  • Chain of Custody: Digital evidence must be collected, preserved, and presented in accordance with proper forensic procedures. If the chain of custody is broken — for example, if unauthorised persons handled the device — the evidence may be inadmissible or given reduced weight.
  • Procedural Compliance: Evidence collected through an illegal search (without a warrant where required) can be challenged as improperly obtained.
  • Attribution: Proving that the accused was the actual author of an online post requires more than just identifying the account. Accounts can be hacked, accessed by multiple people, or the device may have been used by another person. Challenge the prosecution's evidence of attribution.
  • Context and Meaning: Posts, comments, or messages may have a different meaning in context. Defence counsel can present evidence of the context in which the statement was made to show it was not criminal in nature.

Challenging digital evidence requires technical expertise alongside legal skill. Your criminal lawyer should work with digital forensic experts where necessary to effectively contest the prosecution's evidence.

Constitutional Defences: Free Speech and Article 39

One of the most powerful defences available in DSA/CSA cases — particularly those involving online speech — is the constitutional right to freedom of expression under Article 39 of the Constitution of Bangladesh.

Article 39 guarantees freedom of thought and conscience, and the right to freedom of speech and expression. This right can be restricted by law only in the interests of:

  • The security of the state;
  • Friendly relations with foreign states;
  • Public order;
  • Decency or morality;
  • Defamation or incitement to an offence.

The constitutional defence works as follows:

  • Proportionality: Even where a restriction on speech is permissible, it must be proportionate to the harm sought to be prevented. A criminal prosecution for a mild criticism of a public official is arguably disproportionate.
  • Vagueness: Laws that restrict speech using vague and overbroad terms (like 'offensive' or 'tending to disturb public order') may be challenged as unconstitutional for violating the standard of legal certainty required by the Constitution.
  • Public Interest Defence: Statements made in the genuine public interest — reporting on corruption, holding officials accountable, exposing public health risks — are protected expression even if they are critical or uncomfortable for the subjects.

These constitutional defences are best raised before the High Court Division through a writ petition or during the trial before the Cyber Tribunal. A Supreme Court lawyer with constitutional law expertise is best placed to argue these defences.

Role of Your Lawyer in a DSA/CSA Case

Having an experienced lawyer is not just advisable in a DSA/CSA case — it is indispensable. Here is what your lawyer can do for you:

  • Immediate Bail Application: Your lawyer will file a bail application at the earliest possible stage — before the police, Magistrate, Tribunal, or High Court as appropriate.
  • Challenging the FIR/Complaint: Your lawyer will examine the complaint to identify procedural irregularities, lack of jurisdiction, or substantive weaknesses that can be exploited to have the case dismissed or weakened.
  • Quashing the Case: In appropriate cases, your lawyer can file a writ petition before the High Court Division to quash the criminal proceedings entirely — for example, if the complaint is clearly an abuse of process or the allegations do not disclose any offence.
  • Cross-Examination Strategy: At trial, your lawyer will cross-examine prosecution witnesses — including digital forensic experts — to expose gaps and inconsistencies in the evidence.
  • Constitutional Arguments: Your lawyer can raise fundamental rights violations before the Tribunal and higher courts, including challenges to the constitutionality of the specific CSA provision applied to your case.
  • Negotiated Resolution: In cases where the complainant is a private party (rather than the state), your lawyer may be able to negotiate a settlement and withdrawal of the case.
  • Appeals: If convicted, your lawyer will file and conduct an appeal before the High Court Division with expertise in cyber law appeals.

How to File a Complaint If You Are a Victim of Misuse

If you believe the DSA or CSA has been used against you maliciously or in bad faith — for example, by a business rival, an estranged spouse, or a political opponent — you have remedies:

  • Quashing Petition: File a writ petition before the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution seeking quashing of the FIR or criminal proceedings on the grounds that they are an abuse of process or maliciously motivated.
  • Anticipatory Bail: If you anticipate arrest in connection with a malicious complaint, apply for anticipatory bail immediately before the Sessions Court or High Court Division.
  • Complaint to the Digital Security Agency: The Digital Security Agency (DSA) — the regulatory body established under the CSA — can receive complaints about misuse of the Act.
  • Human Rights Commission: The National Human Rights Commission of Bangladesh can be approached if you believe your fundamental rights have been violated through malicious prosecution.
  • Civil Suit for Malicious Prosecution: Once the criminal proceedings are terminated in your favour, you can file a civil suit against the complainant for damages arising from malicious prosecution.

The combination of these remedies — pursued strategically by an experienced criminal lawyer in Bangladesh — can effectively counter malicious DSA/CSA complaints.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a DSA or CSA case be quashed by the High Court in Bangladesh?

Yes. The High Court Division has the power to quash criminal proceedings under its inherent jurisdiction and under Article 102 of the Constitution if it finds that the case is an abuse of process, that no offence is disclosed, or that the proceedings are maliciously initiated. Filing a quashing petition is a powerful legal strategy in DSA/CSA cases.

What is the maximum period of remand (police custody) in a CSA case?

Under the CrPC, police can seek remand of an accused for investigation purposes. The Magistrate has discretion to grant remand for a period not exceeding 15 days in total (in the first instance). Your lawyer should contest excessive or unnecessary remand applications and seek bail or transfer to judicial custody as soon as possible.

Can someone file a DSA/CSA case against me for criticising them on social media?

Yes, technically any person can file a complaint. However, whether the complaint constitutes a genuine offence under the CSA depends on the content. Criticism of public figures or posting opinions — even strongly worded ones — does not automatically constitute a cybercrime. Your lawyer can argue that the content is protected expression under Article 39 of the Constitution.

If I delete the social media post, does the cybercrime case go away?

No. Deleting the post after it has been seen, documented, and complained about does not erase the offence. Prosecution authorities and complainants typically take screenshots before filing a case. However, the deletion may affect the availability of evidence and could be relevant to the sentencing or compounding of the case.

Is there a limitation period for filing a DSA/CSA case against me?

The CSA does not expressly provide a specific limitation period for all offences. For cognisable offences (where police can act without a warrant), the general CrPC rules on investigation timelines apply. For cases filed before the Tribunal directly, the court's discretion and principles of justice apply. Delays in filing may weaken the prosecution's case.

entries.body:
DSA Rights and Defences in Bangladesh Courts: A Practical Legal Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-12 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Thousands of people in Bangladesh have been charged under the Digital Security Act 2018 (DSA) and the Cyber Security Act 2023 (CSA) — often for online speech that in many democratic countries would be entirely lawful. If you are facing a case under these laws, you need to know the specific defences available in Bangladesh courts, the procedural strategies that experienced lawyers use, and the rights that the Constitution guarantees you even in the face of a cybercrime charge.

: · Cyber Crime & Criminal Defense Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing LawCyber Security Act, 2023 & Penal Code, 1860 (Bangladesh)
First Step at Police StationFile an Online or In-Person General Diary (GD) at gd.police.gov.bd / local Thana
Police Cyber Support for Women (PCSW)Helpline: 01320-000888 | Email: cybersupport.women@police.gov.bd
CID / CTTC Cyber Crime Unit24/7 Emergency: 999 | Police Headquarters & Cyber Tribunal Dhaka
Required Digital EvidenceFull URLs, unedited screenshots, transaction IDs (bKash/Nagad), and call logs
📋 In This Article
  1. Key Procedural Defences in DSA/CSA Cases
  2. Substantive Legal Defences: When Your Conduct Is Not a Crime
  3. The Quashing Remedy: Stopping the Case Before Trial
  4. Challenging the Cyber Tribunal's Jurisdiction
  5. Bail Strategy in DSA/CSA Cases
  6. Using Article 39 (Free Speech) as a Constitutional Defence
  7. Practical Steps on Day One of a DSA/CSA Arrest
  8. Long-Term Strategy: From Arrest to Acquittal

Key Procedural Defences in DSA/CSA Cases

Procedural defences attack the form rather than the substance of the prosecution's case. They are often the most powerful tool available at early stages of proceedings because a successful procedural challenge can end the case without requiring a full trial. Key procedural defences include:

  • Defect in the FIR/Complaint: If the complaint does not specifically identify the offending online content, the date, the URL, or the precise section of the CSA alleged to have been violated, it may be challenged as vague and insufficient to disclose a cognisable offence.
  • Wrong Forum: Cases under the CSA must be tried before the Cyber Tribunal. If the case is initiated or tried before the wrong court, jurisdiction can be challenged.
  • Failure to Follow Prescribed Procedure: The CSA and CrPC prescribe specific procedures for arrest, search, and seizure. Non-compliance with these procedures can make the arrest unlawful and the evidence inadmissible.
  • Limitation: If the complaint is filed long after the alleged offence and no satisfactory explanation is given for the delay, the court can take this into account in assessing the credibility and legitimacy of the prosecution.
  • Lack of Territorial Jurisdiction: If the online content was published or accessed outside the jurisdiction of the specific Cyber Tribunal, jurisdiction can be challenged — though the CSA's extraterritorial provisions make this a complex argument.
  • Non-Compliance with Arrest Procedure: If the arresting officer failed to provide grounds of arrest, denied access to a lawyer, or held the accused beyond 24 hours without producing them before a Magistrate, these procedural violations are grounds for challenging the validity of the detention.

Substantive Legal Defences: When Your Conduct Is Not a Crime

Substantive defences challenge the prosecution's evidence and legal theory — arguing that even if the facts are as alleged, no crime was committed. Key substantive defences in DSA/CSA cases:

  • The Statement Was True: Truth is a complete defence to defamation-based cyber charges. If the online statement complained of is factually accurate, it cannot constitute criminal defamation. The defence requires presentation of evidence proving the truth of the statement.
  • Public Interest and Good Faith: Statements made in good faith and in the genuine public interest — such as reporting on government corruption, documenting human rights violations, or whistleblowing — are protected. Courts recognise that holding power to account serves a legitimate democratic function.
  • Satire and Parody: Satirical content is protected expression in Bangladesh courts, provided it is clearly identifiable as satire and not as a false statement of fact. Contextual evidence of the satirical nature of the content must be presented.
  • No Offensive Intent: If the content alleged to be offensive was not intended to offend and a reasonable person would not find it offensive in context, this weakens the prosecution's case that an offence was committed.
  • No Attribution: The prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused was the author of the offending content. If the account was hacked, used by another person, or if the evidence of authorship is weak, this is a critical defence.
  • Consent: In cases involving sharing of images or information, consent of the person depicted or described is a complete defence.

The Quashing Remedy: Stopping the Case Before Trial

One of the most powerful legal tools available to an accused in a DSA/CSA case is the quashing petition before the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution and the inherent jurisdiction of the High Court.

Quashing is appropriate when:

  • The complaint is clearly malicious, frivolous, or vexatious — designed to harass rather than vindicate any genuine legal grievance;
  • The allegations, even if taken at face value, do not disclose any offence under the CSA;
  • Continuing the criminal proceedings would be an abuse of the court's process;
  • The evidence on which the complaint is based has been fabricated or obtained illegally;
  • The prosecution is barred by limitation or by an earlier judgment on the same facts (res judicata / double jeopardy).

The quashing petition is filed as a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution (Rule Nisi). The High Court may issue an interim stay of all proceedings before the Cyber Tribunal pending the hearing of the writ — effectively stopping the case in its tracks while the High Court considers whether to quash it.

The quashing remedy is one of the most effective tools in a DSA/CSA defence arsenal, but it requires careful drafting and powerful arguments. Engage a Supreme Court lawyer experienced in constitutional and cyber law to assess whether quashing is appropriate in your case.

Challenging the Cyber Tribunal's Jurisdiction

The Cyber Tribunal established under the CSA has jurisdiction over CSA offences. However, challenges to jurisdiction can succeed in several scenarios:

  • Territorial Jurisdiction: The CSA provides that the Tribunal shall have jurisdiction over offences committed within Bangladesh and by Bangladeshi nationals abroad. If the alleged offence does not have a sufficient nexus to Bangladesh, jurisdiction can be challenged.
  • Personal Jurisdiction: If the accused is not a Bangladeshi national and the offence was committed entirely outside Bangladesh, jurisdiction arguments can be raised.
  • Subject Matter Jurisdiction: If the conduct charged does not actually constitute an offence under the CSA (e.g., it was classified under the wrong section), the Tribunal's jurisdiction over the specific charge can be challenged.
  • Double Jeopardy: If the accused has already been tried and acquitted or convicted for the same act in another court, a second prosecution is barred by Article 35(2) of the Constitution (protection against double jeopardy).

Jurisdictional challenges should be raised at the earliest possible stage — ideally as a preliminary objection before the Tribunal begins trial on the merits. Delay in raising jurisdictional points can sometimes result in the court treating them as waived.
