Why Bangladeshi Americans Need a Separate Guide

Most online explainers on Bangladesh dual citizenship are written for a general audience of Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs). If you are a United States citizen of Bangladeshi origin, your position has its own features. You became a US citizen by naturalisation, by birth in the US to Bangladeshi parents, or through a parent. Each route raises a slightly different question when you deal with Bangladeshi offices: are you still a Bangladeshi citizen, a foreign national of Bangladeshi origin, or both?

That question is not academic. It decides whether you can enter Bangladesh without a visa, whether a sub-registrar or land office treats you as a citizen when you buy or inherit property, whether you can hold certain accounts, and what you can lawfully do about voting, an NID card or an e-passport. It also decides which documents you must carry, because a Bangladeshi official will usually want to see proof in the form of a stamp, an endorsement or an old passport rather than an oral explanation.

This guide explains the legal framework in plain language and then turns to the practical steps for US-based applicants. For the shorter general overview, see our Bangladesh dual citizenship and NVR explainer. For the property side, see whether a foreigner or dual citizen can own property in Bangladesh. Nothing here replaces advice on your own papers, because small differences in dates and documents can change the answer.

US Naturalisation vs the Bangladesh Citizenship Act 1951

Two separate legal systems apply to you, and neither automatically cancels the other.

The United States side. US law allows a person to hold more than one nationality. The US government does not require you to give up your Bangladeshi nationality when you naturalise, although the naturalisation oath contains language about renouncing allegiance to foreign states. In practice, US authorities have long treated this as not requiring formal renunciation of another nationality. As a US citizen you must use your US passport to enter and leave the United States, and when abroad you remain subject to US law, including tax law. If you have a specific worry about the oath or about your US status, ask a US immigration attorney.

The Bangladesh side. Bangladesh nationality law is built on the Citizenship Act 1951 as adapted after independence, together with later orders, amendments and government policy. Whether a person was a citizen at birth, or became one later, depends on the legal rules that applied at the relevant time. Under the older approach, voluntarily acquiring another nationality could end Bangladeshi citizenship. Bangladesh later adopted a policy of permitting dual citizenship for citizens who acquire the nationality of specified countries. That policy is the reason many Bangladeshi Americans remain recognised as Bangladeshi citizens after naturalisation.

The practical consequence is this: Bangladesh decides who is its citizen, and the US decides who is its citizen. Each country will usually accept proof issued by its own authorities. A US passport proves US nationality. It does not by itself prove to a Bangladeshi land office that you still hold Bangladeshi citizenship. That proof comes from the Bangladeshi endorsement process described below.

Dual Citizenship Policy: What Bangladesh Allows

As a general position, Bangladesh permits its citizens to hold the nationality of certain listed countries without losing Bangladeshi citizenship, and the United States is commonly understood to be among those countries. The exact list of countries, the conditions and the formalities are fixed by government notification and policy, which can be revised. Do not rely on an old blog post, an agent or a relative. Confirm the current position with the Embassy of Bangladesh in Washington DC or the consulate that serves your area.

A few points follow from the general policy:

  • Origin matters. The policy is designed for people who held or were entitled to Bangladeshi citizenship, and for certain descendants. Your own proof of Bangladeshi origin is the foundation of any application.
  • Recognition is documentary. Dual status becomes usable in practice only when it is recorded by the competent authority, normally as an endorsement in a passport.
  • Renunciation is different. If you formally renounced Bangladeshi citizenship, or surrendered your Bangladeshi passport in a way that was recorded as renunciation, you are generally treated as a foreigner and the dual citizenship route may not be open to you. Look at the paperwork you signed before assuming anything.
  • Children are a separate question. Whether a US-born child can be recognised depends on the parents' status at the child's birth and on the rules then in force. Ask the Mission to confirm eligibility before you prepare an application.

If any of the above is unclear for your family, a short written consultation before applying is usually cheaper than correcting a wrong filing later.

NVR Stamp vs Dual Citizenship Endorsement

People use the words NVR and dual citizenship as if they were the same thing. They are related but they are not identical, and the difference matters when a Bangladeshi office asks for your papers.

NVR (No Visa Required). This is an endorsement placed in a foreign passport for a person of Bangladeshi origin. It works as a visa-free entry permission and shows the immigration authority that you have a recognised link with Bangladesh. It is tied to the foreign passport in which it is placed. If that passport expires or is replaced, the endorsement does not move on its own.

Dual citizenship endorsement. This is the recognition that you remain a Bangladeshi citizen while holding another nationality. Depending on current practice, it may be recorded in a Bangladeshi passport or in the foreign passport. It speaks to your status as a citizen, not merely your permission to enter.

Why this matters for property and documents: an NVR stamp answers the question "can this person enter Bangladesh without a visa?". A dual citizenship endorsement answers the question "is this person still a citizen of Bangladesh?". A bank, land office or registration office may ask for one, the other, or both, depending on the transaction. Ask the receiving office exactly which document it will accept before you travel, and carry both along with your old Bangladeshi passport, birth certificate and NID, if you have them.

Do not assume that having NVR means you have been recognised as a dual citizen, or the reverse. Read what is actually written in your passport and keep a clear scan of that page.

How to Apply Through the Embassy in Washington DC or a Consulate

Applications from the United States are normally made through the Embassy of Bangladesh in Washington DC or a Bangladeshi consular office in the US, depending on where you live. The Mission websites publish the current forms, the list of required documents, the appointment or mail-in method, the processing approach and the fee. We do not quote any fee or processing time here because both change and we would rather you read the current official notice than rely on a figure that may be out of date.

What the process usually involves:

  • Finding the right office. Check which Mission or consulate covers your US state. Some offices accept mail-in applications, others require an appointment or in-person visit.
  • Proving Bangladeshi origin. This is usually done through an old Bangladeshi passport, a birth certificate, an NID, or parents' documents.
  • Proving your US status. A copy of your valid US passport and, for naturalised citizens, often the naturalisation certificate.
  • Verification. The Mission may verify your papers and, in some cases, consult authorities in Dhaka before approving. Delays here are common, so plan travel dates with a margin.
  • Endorsement. If approved, the endorsement is placed in your passport or issued as the Mission directs.

Use only the official Mission channels and the fee instructions published there. Be cautious of anyone who offers to arrange the endorsement for a private payment without going through the Mission, because forged stamps are a real risk and a forged endorsement can create criminal exposure for you.

Step-by-Step Checklist for US-Based Applicants

Use this as a working checklist. Tick each step before you submit anything.

  1. Confirm eligibility. Read the Mission's current guidance. Confirm that your situation, including any past renunciation, qualifies.
  2. Gather proof of Bangladeshi origin. Old Bangladeshi passport, birth certificate, NID, school or marriage certificates, parents' passports or NIDs.
  3. Gather proof of US status. Valid US passport, plus the naturalisation certificate if relevant. Make clear scans.
  4. Check name consistency. Compare spelling and dates of birth across every document. If they differ, plan a correction through an affidavit or the appropriate authority before applying.
  5. Download the current form. Use the form on the Mission website, not a copy from a third party.
  6. Prepare photographs and any required translations or attestations. Follow the Mission's specifications exactly.
  7. Pay the fee in the way the Mission specifies. Keep the receipt.
  8. Submit and record the date. Keep a copy of everything you sent, and note any tracking or reference number.
  9. Follow up politely and in writing. Keep a record of who you spoke to.
  10. On receipt, check the endorsement. Confirm spelling, passport number and validity, and photograph the page.
  11. Plan for passport renewal. Ask the Mission how to carry the endorsement forward when your US passport is renewed, and always keep the old passport.

US Passport + NVR vs Bangladeshi Passport vs Bangladesh Visa

The table below compares the three common ways a Bangladeshi American may enter and deal with Bangladeshi authorities. It is a general comparison; check current rules before relying on it.

FeatureUS passport + NVRBangladeshi passport (for recognised dual citizens)US passport + Bangladesh visa
Status in BangladeshForeign passport holder of Bangladeshi origin with a recognised linkCitizen travelling on a national passportForeign national
EntryVisa-free entry as endorsedEntry as a citizenNeeds a valid visa for each purpose and period
Proof for land and bank officesOften accepted as proof of origin; some offices also ask for a dual citizenship endorsementStrongest document of citizenship, if available to youWeakest; foreign status can restrict some property transactions
Use at US borderUS passport must be used to enter and leave the USNot used for entering or leaving the USUS passport must be used
Dependency on passport validityEndorsement is tied to the passport in which it is placedTied to the Bangladeshi passport and its validityVisa is tied to the visa period and purpose
Typical riskExpired or replaced passport without the endorsement carried forwardMisusing a national passport in a way that conflicts with US rulesOverstay and treatment as a foreigner for land rules

The point of the table is not that one route is always best. It shows that the same person can be treated differently by different offices depending on the document placed on the counter.

Property, Bank Accounts and Inheritance Rights

Property. A recognised Bangladeshi citizen is generally in a stronger position to hold and transfer land than a foreign national, because several property rules distinguish between citizens and non-citizens. A US citizen without recognised Bangladeshi status may face restrictions on certain categories of land and on transfers. Do not assume; check the category of land and your status before paying anything. Our guide on buying land in Bangladesh from abroad covers the verification steps.

Bank accounts. Banks in Bangladesh usually open NRB-type accounts on production of a passport, proof of foreign residence and, where relevant, proof of Bangladeshi origin. The product available to you (NRB account, foreign currency account or a resident account) depends on your documented status and on the bank's own policy and central bank rules. Ask the bank in writing which documents it needs, and keep the answer.

Inheritance. In Bangladesh, succession is governed by the personal law of the deceased: Muslim law for Muslims, and the relevant Hindu or Christian rules for others. Becoming a US citizen does not change the family share you are entitled to under that law. What may change is the paperwork you need, because you will often have to prove your identity and relationship, appoint a representative if you cannot be present, and satisfy the office that you are entitled to receive the property. For the full picture, see property inheritance in Bangladesh for NRBs.

Whatever the transaction, keep every document that shows your link to Bangladesh in one folder: the old passport, the endorsement page, the birth certificate and any family certificates.

Land Purchase and Mutation (Namjari): How Your Status Affects It

Land transactions in Bangladesh follow a sequence: due diligence on title, a deed, registration, and then mutation (namjari) of the record in your name at the land office. Your status as a citizen or a foreign national can affect several of those stages.

  • Due diligence. Verify the khatian, the chain of title, any pending suits and any mortgage. Citizenship status does not remove the need for this.
  • Deed and registration. The registering office may ask for identity documents. A passport with an endorsement, along with an NID or old passport where available, is the document set that normally helps.
  • Power of attorney. If you cannot be present, you may need a power of attorney signed in the US and authenticated according to the current rules. Read our guide on power of attorney registration before signing a general document.
  • Mutation. The land office may look at your status again when you apply for mutation. Inconsistent names or a missing endorsement are a common reason for delay.
  • Foreign status risk. If your status as a Bangladeshi citizen cannot be shown, the transaction may be challenged later by someone who benefits from the title being unsettled.

The safest practice is to settle your documentary status before you sign a deed rather than after.

Voting, NID and e-Passport for Dual Citizens

Voting and public office. Voting rights in Bangladesh depend on being a citizen, being of voting age and being enrolled on the electoral roll. Rules on postal or overseas voting, if any, are set by the Election Commission and change over time. For elected office, the Constitution and electoral laws contain disqualifications related to acquiring citizenship of, or owing allegiance to, a foreign state. If you are considering political activity or a public appointment in Bangladesh, take specific advice before acting; do not assume that dual status leaves that path open.

National ID (NID). The NID is issued to citizens. Overseas Bangladeshis can in some circumstances register through Missions or the Election Commission, but eligibility for a dual citizen and the documents required are matters to confirm directly. Keep the NID details consistent with the passport and birth certificate, because mismatches cause problems with banks, land offices and mutation.

e-Passport. Bangladesh issues machine-readable e-passports, including through Missions abroad. A dual citizen who wishes to hold a Bangladeshi passport must satisfy the issuing authority that Bangladeshi citizenship has been retained and recognised. Ask the Mission whether a dual citizenship endorsement is required first, and which documents they need.

Keep in mind that a Bangladeshi passport is for travel to and from Bangladesh. You must still use your US passport to enter and leave the United States.

US Tax Duties: FBAR, FATCA and Why You Need a US Tax Professional

US citizens are generally taxed on worldwide income, wherever they live. Owning land, a bank account or rental income in Bangladesh does not remove your US filing duties. This is general information and not US tax advice; speak to a US tax professional who understands foreign assets.

  • FBAR. A US person with financial interests in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts above the reporting threshold in a year generally must file a Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FinCEN Form 114). Check the current threshold and the due date.
  • FATCA. Under the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act, certain US taxpayers must report specified foreign financial assets on Form 8938, filed with their tax return, if they exceed thresholds that depend on filing status and residence. Check current thresholds.
  • Foreign gifts and inheritances. Receiving a large gift or inheritance from a foreign person can trigger a separate US information return, even where no US tax is due. Ask your adviser before you receive property or money by inheritance.
  • Rental income and sale of property. Rent from, or gain on sale of, Bangladeshi property may be reportable in the US and may also be taxable in Bangladesh. Exchange rate and treaty questions should be handled by a professional.
  • Penalties. Late or missing foreign reporting can attract significant penalties. Do not guess.

On the Bangladesh side, income, land holding tax and capital gains rules also apply, and these are separate from the US duties above. Keep receipts, remittance records and bank statements for both systems.

Travel Tips and the Risk of Losing Documentation

Most problems that Bangladeshi Americans face are paperwork problems, not legal ones. A few habits prevent them:

  • Carry the old passport. If your NVR or dual citizenship endorsement is in an expired passport, carry it with your new one. Ask the Mission how to move the endorsement before you renew.
  • Use the right passport at the right border. Use your US passport to enter and leave the US. Follow the Mission's guidance on which passport to present at Bangladesh immigration.
  • Keep digital copies. Scan the endorsement page, the data page and your naturalisation certificate. Store copies in secure cloud storage and with a trusted family member.
  • Report loss quickly. If a passport with an endorsement is lost, report it to local police, apply for a replacement and contact the Mission about restoring the endorsement. A police report is usually the first document asked for.
  • Check validity before booking. Verify the validity of your passport and any endorsement before you buy a ticket.
  • Do not alter documents. Never try to correct a stamp or page yourself. A damaged or altered document can be rejected and may attract questions at immigration.

If something goes wrong while you are in Bangladesh, such as a missing document or an immigration query, contact a lawyer and the nearest US Embassy services if appropriate, and avoid paying any unofficial fee to fix it on the spot.

Common Mistakes Bangladeshi Americans Make

  • Treating NVR and dual citizenship as the same thing. They answer different questions and offices may ask for either.
  • Relying on a broker or relative. Using unofficial channels for the endorsement or for land paperwork creates the risk of forged documents.
  • Name and date-of-birth mismatches. The same person appears with different spellings or birth dates on a passport, NID and birth certificate. This is among the most common causes of delay at registration and mutation.
  • Not carrying forward the endorsement. The endorsement stays with the old passport unless it is renewed or moved according to the Mission's process.
  • Ignoring US tax reporting. Failing to report foreign accounts or foreign property income can cause serious penalties that are unrelated to Bangladeshi law.
  • Signing a broad general power of attorney. A general document that gives wide powers can be abused. Prefer a limited document for the specific transaction.
  • Assuming citizenship is automatic or permanent. Formal renunciation, or losing proof, can change your treatment. Keep your records safe.
  • Skipping legal due diligence because of NVR. Status does not cure a defective title. Verify the land record, any pending case and the seller's title independently.
  • Assuming a short answer from the internet applies to your case. Your birth date, route to US citizenship and family history can change the analysis.

Our NRB legal help hub collects guides on property, inheritance, powers of attorney and documentation for Bangladeshis abroad.

Legal Disclaimer

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Citizenship, immigration, property and tax rules change, and your facts may differ from the examples above. Fees, forms, eligible countries, procedures and processing times are set by the relevant authorities and may be revised without notice. Verify current requirements with the Embassy of Bangladesh in Washington DC or the relevant consular office, and obtain advice from a qualified Bangladeshi advocate, a US immigration attorney and a US tax professional before acting on any part of this guide. Nothing here creates a lawyer-client relationship.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a US citizen also be a Bangladeshi citizen?

Both countries recognise their own citizens under their own laws. US law does not prohibit dual nationality, and Bangladesh has a policy of permitting dual citizenship with certain countries, which is generally understood to include the United States. Your own position depends on how and when you acquired each nationality and on whether you ever formally renounced Bangladeshi citizenship. Confirm the current list and conditions with the Embassy of Bangladesh in Washington DC.

What is the difference between an NVR stamp and a dual citizenship endorsement?

NVR (No Visa Required) is an endorsement that allows a person of Bangladeshi origin to enter Bangladesh on a foreign passport without a visa. A dual citizenship endorsement records that you remain a Bangladeshi citizen while holding another nationality. A bank or land office may ask for one or the other, so ask the receiving office which document it accepts.

Where do I apply for NVR or dual citizenship in the USA?

Applications are normally made through the Embassy of Bangladesh in Washington DC or the Bangladeshi consular office that covers your US state. Use the forms and instructions published on the official Mission website and confirm the current fee and method of payment there, since these change.

Can I buy land in Bangladesh as a US citizen of Bangladeshi origin?

A recognised Bangladeshi citizen is generally in a stronger position than a foreign national, because property rules distinguish between citizens and non-citizens. Your rights depend on your documented status and the category of land, so settle your documents and verify the title before paying. See our guides on buying land from abroad and on property ownership by dual citizens.

Do I have to file US tax forms for my Bangladeshi bank account or land?

US citizens are generally taxed on worldwide income and may have to report foreign accounts and certain foreign assets (FBAR and FATCA), depending on thresholds that change. Rental income, sale proceeds and certain gifts or inheritances may also trigger US reporting. Speak to a US tax professional who understands foreign assets before you receive or transfer money.

What happens to my NVR when my US passport expires?

The endorsement is tied to the passport in which it was placed. When you renew your US passport, ask the Bangladesh Mission how to carry the endorsement forward and keep the old passport with you when you travel to Bangladesh.

Can a dual citizen vote or hold public office in Bangladesh?

Voting requires citizenship, voting age and enrolment on the electoral roll, and rules on overseas voting are set by the Election Commission. The Constitution and electoral laws contain disqualifications for public office relating to foreign citizenship or allegiance. Take specific advice before assuming that you can stand for office or accept a public appointment.

Can my US-born child get NVR or dual citizenship?

It can depend on the parents' status at the time of the child's birth and on the rules then in force. Ask the Mission to confirm eligibility and the documents required before you prepare an application.

E-Namjari Online Check Bangladesh 2026 | Mutation Application Tracking (land.gov.bd)

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-28 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Namjari (mutation) is the essential legal process by which a new landowner's name is officially recorded in government land registers after acquiring property through purchase, inheritance, or gift in Bangladesh. With the launch of the e-Namjari system under the Ministry of Land's digital services platform, Bangladeshis can now apply for and track mutation status entirely online — saving significant time, cost, and the need to visit government offices repeatedly. This comprehensive guide covers everything you need to know about e-Namjari online check and application in 2026.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

What Is Namjari (Mutation) in Bangladesh?

Namjari (also written as Namjari in Bengali: নামজারি) is the official administrative process of updating government land records to reflect a change of ownership. In English, it is referred to as mutation. When a person acquires land — whether by purchase (kabala deed), inheritance (waris), gift (heba), exchange, or court decree — the government land register (Khatian) must be updated to remove the former owner's name and insert the new owner's name. This process is called namjari or mutation.

In Bangladesh, land records are maintained at two levels:

  • The Khatian: The survey record prepared during the CS, SA, RS, or BS survey, which records the original owner's name at the time of the survey.
  • The Mutation Register (Namjari Register): The updated administrative record maintained at the AC Land (Assistant Commissioner Land) office, which reflects all ownership changes since the last survey through successive namjari orders.

Without namjari, even if you hold a registered deed, the land records will continue to show the previous owner's name — creating legal complications for future sales, mortgages, and inheritance. The namjari record also determines who is responsible for paying annual land development tax (khajna).

Why Is Mutation (Namjari) Legally Important?

Many landowners — particularly in rural Bangladesh — underestimate the importance of completing namjari promptly after acquiring property. Here is why namjari is critically important:

  • Establishes recognised possession: A namjari order from the AC Land office officially recognises the new owner as the possessor for government purposes. Without it, government records show the former owner.
  • Required for future transactions: When you subsequently sell or mortgage the land, the buyer or bank will require the Khatian to be in your name — which requires completed namjari.
  • Required for construction permits: Local government bodies (Union Parishad, Pourasabha, City Corporations) and RAJUK require the Khatian to be in the applicant's name before issuing building permits.
  • Land development tax (khajna): Khajna can only be paid in the recorded owner's name. Unpaid khajna can lead to government action including land forfeiture in extreme cases.
  • Prevents title disputes: When the previous owner's name remains in the record, it creates opportunities for fraudulent sales to third parties or false title claims.
  • Inheritance purposes: When property passes to multiple heirs, namjari in all heirs' names establishes the correct fractional ownership before any partition or further sale.

Under the Land Reforms Ordinance 1984, all transfers of agricultural land must be reported to the AC Land office for mutation within a specified period. Failure to mutate can create legal vulnerability in subsequent disputes.

What Is the E-Namjari System in Bangladesh?

The e-Namjari system is the Government of Bangladesh's online platform for submitting, tracking, and managing mutation (namjari) applications digitally. It was developed and launched as part of the Digital Bangladesh initiative under the Ministry of Land, accessible through the Land Management Automation System (LAMS) at land.gov.bd and integrated with the e-Porcha system at eporcha.gov.bd.

Key features of the e-Namjari system in 2026 include:

  • Online application submission: Submit namjari applications from home without visiting the AC Land office
  • Document upload: Upload scanned copies of required documents digitally
  • Online payment: Pay government fees via mobile banking (bKash, Nagad, Rocket) or internet banking
  • Real-time status tracking: Check the current status of your application using your application number or NID
  • SMS notifications: Receive automated SMS updates at each stage of the process
  • Hearing notices online: Field investigation and hearing notices are communicated digitally
  • Digital Khatian issuance: Once approved, the updated Khatian (porcha) can be downloaded from eporcha.gov.bd

The e-Namjari system has significantly reduced the scope for corruption and middlemen (dalal culture) that previously plagued the namjari process, though some applicants still face challenges with document upload quality requirements and rural connectivity limitations.

How to Apply for E-Namjari Online: Step-by-Step

The following is the step-by-step procedure for submitting an e-Namjari application online in Bangladesh as of 2026:

  1. Visit the official portal: Go to land.gov.bd or the e-Namjari section at eporcha.gov.bd. Click on "নামজারি আবেদন" (Namjari Application).
  2. Register or log in: Create an account using your mobile number and NID number, or log in if you have an existing account. OTP verification via mobile SMS is required.
  3. Select location details: Choose your Division, District, Upazila, and Union/Mouza from the dropdown menus.
  4. Enter applicant information: Fill in your name, father's name, mother's name, NID number, mobile number, and address.
  5. Enter land details: Provide the existing Khatian number (RS/BS), Dag number(s), and area of the land you are mutating. The system will auto-fetch the existing owner's name from the e-Porcha database.
  6. Select basis of transfer: Choose the reason for mutation: Purchase (kabala), Inheritance (waris/succession), Gift (heba), Court decree, or Exchange.
  7. Upload required documents: Upload clear, legible scanned copies or photographs of all required documents (see the documents table in the next section).
  8. Pay the application fee: Select your payment method (bKash/Nagad/Rocket/bank transfer) and complete payment of the government fee (BDT 1,000–1,170 typically including all charges).
  9. Submit and note the application number: After submission, you will receive an application number (আবেদন নম্বর) via SMS and on-screen. Keep this number safe — it is needed to track your application status.
  10. Attend hearing if required: The AC Land office may schedule a field investigation (tahqiqat) and hearing. You will be notified via SMS. Attend as scheduled and present original documents if requested.

Pro tip: Ensure all document images are clear, properly oriented, and under the file size limit specified by the portal (usually 2MB per file). Blurry or illegible uploads are a leading cause of application rejection or delay.

Documents Required for Namjari Application

The documents required for a namjari (mutation) application in Bangladesh vary depending on the basis of the transfer. The following table provides a comprehensive overview:

DocumentPurchase (Kabala)Inheritance (Waris)Gift (Heba)Court Decree
Registered sale/kabala deed (certified copy)✓ Required———
Registered gift/heba deed——✓ Required—

Death certificate of previous owner—✓ Required——

NID of applicant✓ Required✓ Required✓ Required✓ Required
NID of seller/transferor✓ Required—✓ Required—
Land development tax (khajna) payment receipt (up-to-date)✓ Required✓ Required✓ Required✓ Required
Mouza map (if dag location is disputed)OptionalOptionalOptionalOptional
No-objection certificate (NOC) from seller (for large tracts)Sometimes required———

For inheritance (waris) namjari, the waris certificate is crucial. This is obtained from the local Union Parishad Chairman or Ward Commissioner and must be attested by a Notary Public or an Oath Commissioner. It lists all legal heirs and their relationship to the deceased.

All documents must be uploaded as clear scans or photos in JPG, PNG, or PDF format as per the portal's requirements. Original documents must be retained for presentation at the hearing before the AC Land office.

Namjari Fees and Processing Timeline

Understanding the fees and expected timeline for namjari in Bangladesh helps applicants plan appropriately and identify if their application is being unreasonably delayed.

Fee / ChargeAmount (Approx.)Payment Method
Government namjari application feeBDT 200Online (bKash/Nagad/Rocket/bank)

Notice publication fee (if applicable)BDT 150–300Online
Total approximate cost (online)BDT 1,000–1,170Various online methods

Processing Timeline:

  • Standard processing time: 45 to 60 working days from submission of complete application
  • Field investigation (tahqiqat): Typically scheduled within 15–20 working days of application submission
  • Hearing (shunani): Scheduled within 30–40 working days after field investigation
  • Final order: Issued within 7–15 days after the hearing if no objections are pending
  • Updated Khatian (porcha) available: Downloadable from eporcha.gov.bd within 7–14 days of the final namjari order

Note: These are standard timelines. In practice, delays of 3–6 months are not uncommon due to administrative backlogs, objections filed by third parties, or incomplete documentation. Engaging a land lawyer to monitor and follow up on your application can significantly reduce processing time.

How to Check Namjari Application Status Online

One of the most valuable features of the e-Namjari system is the ability to track your mutation application status online without visiting the AC Land office. Here is how to check your namjari application status in 2026:

Method 1: Via eporcha.gov.bd

  1. Visit eporcha.gov.bd
  2. Click on "নামজারি আবেদনের অবস্থা" (Namjari Application Status) or "আবেদন ট্র্যাক করুন" (Track Application)
  3. Enter your Application Number (received via SMS at the time of submission) or your NID number
  4. Click Search to view the current status

Method 2: Via land.gov.bd

  1. Visit land.gov.bd
  2. Navigate to the e-Mutation or Namjari section
  3. Log in to your account using your mobile number and password
  4. View your application dashboard showing current stage and pending actions

Application status stages you may see:

  • আবেদন গৃহীত (Application Received): Your application has been submitted and received by the system
  • তহকিকাত চলছে (Field Investigation Ongoing): The Land Officer is verifying facts on the ground
  • শুনানির জন্য নির্ধারিত (Scheduled for Hearing): A hearing date has been fixed; attend with original documents
  • আপত্তি দাখিল হয়েছে (Objection Filed): A third party has filed an objection; you will be notified to respond
  • অনুমোদিত (Approved): Namjari has been granted; download your updated Khatian from eporcha.gov.bd
  • প্রত্যাখ্যাত (Rejected): Application has been rejected; see the reason and consider filing an appeal or correcting and re-applying

You can also receive status updates via SMS to your registered mobile number at each stage of the process.

What to Do If Namjari Is Rejected or Delayed

Not all namjari applications proceed smoothly. Understanding your options when an application is rejected or excessively delayed is crucial.

If Your Application Is Rejected:

  1. Read the rejection reason carefully: The AC Land office is required to state specific grounds for rejection. Common reasons include: incomplete documents, objection by a third party, discrepancy in land records, or failure to attend the hearing.
  2. Appeal to the Additional DC (Revenue): An appeal against a namjari rejection order lies before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) of the district, to be filed within 30 days of the rejection order.
  3. Appeal to the Divisional Commissioner: If the Additional DC's order is also unfavorable, a second appeal lies before the Divisional Commissioner.
  4. Land Appeal Board: Further appeals lie before the Land Appeal Board under the Ministry of Land.
  5. Civil Court: If the rejection is based on a title dispute (i.e., a third party claims superior title), you may need to file a title suit (declaration suit) before the civil court to establish your ownership before re-applying for namjari.

If Your Application Is Excessively Delayed:

  • File a written complaint before the Additional DC (Revenue) requesting expedition of the application
  • File an application under the Right to Information Act 2009 to obtain information about the delay
  • Contact the National Land Helpline 16122 (Ministry of Land's toll-free helpline) to report delays
  • File a writ petition before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court under Article 102 of the Constitution if the delay amounts to unlawful inaction by a public authority

A land lawyer can draft and file appeal petitions, follow up with government offices, and if necessary, initiate writ proceedings to compel the AC Land office to decide on a pending namjari application.

Online vs Offline Namjari Application: Key Differences

While the e-Namjari system is now the government's preferred mode for receiving applications, some applicants — particularly those in rural areas with limited digital access — still use the offline (in-person) process. The following table compares the two approaches:

FeatureOnline (E-Namjari)Offline (In-Person)
Application SubmissionVia eporcha.gov.bd or land.gov.bd from any deviceIn person at the AC Land office
Document SubmissionScanned/photographed digital uploadsPhysical photocopies submitted at the office
Fee PaymentMobile banking (bKash, Nagad, Rocket) or online bankingTreasury challan at bank/post office
Status TrackingReal-time online tracking + SMS updatesManual enquiry at AC Land office
TransparencyHigh – all steps logged digitallyLow – prone to delays and middlemen
Time Required45–60 working days (standard)Often 3–12 months due to manual processing
Cost (Official)BDT 1,000–1,170 (total government fees)BDT 1,000–1,170 (same government fees)
Risk of CorruptionLower – reduced human contactHigher – dalal culture prevalent
Hearing RequirementStill required for field investigation and hearingRequired
AvailabilityAll districts with internet connectivityAll districts regardless of connectivity

The government's policy, reiterated in the Ministry of Land's 2025 circular, is that e-Namjari through the online portal is the preferred and encouraged method. AC Land offices are instructed to prioritise online applications and to process them within the statutory 45-working-day window.

The Land Reforms Ordinance 1984 and Namjari

The Land Reforms Ordinance 1984 (Ordinance No. LV of 1984) is a key piece of legislation that regulates agricultural land ownership and the namjari process in Bangladesh. Key provisions relevant to mutation include:

  • Section 5: Imposes a ceiling on agricultural land ownership at 60 bighas (approximately 20 acres) per family. Any land held in excess of this ceiling must be surrendered to the government. The namjari process triggers a review of whether the applicant's total holdings (after mutation) will exceed the ceiling.
  • Section 6: Requires any transfer of agricultural land to be reported to the AC Land office, and the AC Land office must be satisfied that the transfer does not result in a violation of the land ceiling.
  • Section 7: Prohibits fragmentation of agricultural land below a minimum viable size (5 decimals per plot typically), to prevent uneconomic sub-division of cultivable land.
  • Section 18: Grants agricultural tenants (bargadars/sharecroppers) certain pre-emption rights when the landowner sells agricultural land — meaning a registered sharecropper has the right of first refusal to purchase the land. The namjari office checks for such rights before approving mutation in a purchaser's favour.

The interaction between the Land Reforms Ordinance 1984 and the namjari process means that in agricultural land transactions, compliance with the Ordinance is a mandatory pre-condition for successful mutation. Non-compliance can result in rejection of the namjari application or even cancellation of the sale deed.

In addition, the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (SA&T Act) provides the broader framework within which namjari operates, particularly its provisions on raiyati rights, sub-letting restrictions, and the maximum land ceiling for different categories of land.

How a Land Lawyer Can Help with Namjari

Although the e-Namjari system is designed to be user-friendly, many applicants encounter complications that require professional legal assistance. A qualified land lawyer in Bangladesh can provide the following support for namjari matters:

  • Pre-application title verification: Before applying for namjari, a lawyer verifies the title chain (CS, SA, RS, BS Khatians and deed chain) to ensure the application will succeed
  • Document preparation: Ensuring all documents are in order, correctly attested, and meet the AC Land office requirements
  • Online application filing: Preparing and submitting the e-Namjari application with precision to avoid rejection for technical reasons
  • Hearing representation: Representing the client at field investigation and hearing proceedings before the AC Land office
  • Objection handling: Where a third party files an objection to the namjari application, drafting a legal response and appearing at the hearing
  • Appeal filing: Filing appeals before the Additional DC (Revenue), Divisional Commissioner, or Land Appeal Board against rejection orders
  • Writ petitions: Filing writ petitions before the High Court Division where namjari is unreasonably delayed or wrongfully rejected

Advocate Md. Shah Alam, based at his Uttara chamber in Dhaka, has extensive hands-on experience handling namjari applications, mutation appeals, and land record disputes across multiple districts of Bangladesh. His office assists clients from across the country — in-person and remotely — to navigate the e-Namjari system, respond to objections, and enforce their right to mutation through legal proceedings where necessary.

Whether you are mutating inherited land, freshly purchased property, or court-decreed land, our team ensures a smooth and legally sound namjari process. Contact our office today for a consultation on your namjari matter.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is e-Namjari and how is it different from regular namjari in Bangladesh?

E-Namjari is the online system launched by Bangladesh's Ministry of Land for submitting and tracking mutation (namjari) applications digitally through eporcha.gov.bd or land.gov.bd. The substantive process — field investigation, hearing, and decision — remains the same as the traditional offline process. The key difference is that you can apply, pay fees, upload documents, and track status from home, without visiting the AC Land office for the initial application.

How do I check my namjari application status online in Bangladesh?

Visit eporcha.gov.bd and click on the namjari application status tracking section. Enter your application number (received via SMS at the time of submission) or your NID number to view the current status of your application. You will see the stage your application is at — whether it is under field investigation, scheduled for hearing, approved, or rejected. You can also log in to land.gov.bd to access your full application dashboard.

How long does namjari (mutation) take in Bangladesh?

Under the government's standard timeline, an e-Namjari application should be decided within 45 to 60 working days from the date of complete application submission. In practice, delays of 3 to 6 months are common due to administrative backlogs or objections by third parties. If your application is unreasonably delayed, you can file a complaint before the Additional DC (Revenue) or contact the National Land Helpline at 16122.

What documents are needed for namjari after buying land in Bangladesh?

For a purchase-based namjari, you need: (1) certified copy of the registered kabala (sale) deed, (2) certified copy of the existing RS or BS Khatian showing the seller's name, (3) up-to-date land development tax (khajna) payment receipt, (4) NID copies of both buyer and seller, and (5) any other document specific to the property such as previous mutation orders. All documents must be uploaded in clear digital format for e-Namjari applications.

What happens if someone files an objection to my namjari application?

If a third party files an objection to your namjari application, the AC Land office will serve you notice and schedule a hearing where both sides can present their evidence and arguments. The AC Land officer will then decide whether to grant or reject the namjari based on the merits. If the objection raises a genuine title dispute, the AC Land office may refer the matter for a civil suit. It is strongly advisable to engage a land lawyer immediately upon receiving notice of an objection.

Can namjari be done for inherited land in Bangladesh and what documents are needed?

Yes, namjari for inherited land (waris namjari) is one of the most common types of mutation applications in Bangladesh. Required documents include: the death certificate of the deceased owner, a waris (heirship) certificate obtained from the local Union Parishad Chairman or Ward Commissioner (attested by a Notary Public), the existing Khatian in the deceased's name, NID copies of all heirs applying for mutation, and up-to-date khajna payment receipts. All heirs must be named in the application to properly reflect the inherited shares.

entries.body:
Employee Embezzlement and Fund Theft in Bangladesh: Penal Code Section 408 Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-12 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Every business owner's worst nightmare is discovering that a trusted accountant, store manager, procurement executive, or cashier has systematically siphoned corporate funds for months or years. In Bangladesh, internal financial fraud takes many forms: manipulating ERP accounting software, fabricating fake vendor invoices, skimming customer cash payments, diverting collection cheques into personal accounts, or creating ghost employees. When confronted, dishonest employees often resign abruptly, destroy ledgers, or threaten counter-cases of wrongful termination. The Penal Code 1860 and the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 provide severe, specialized criminal sanctions for white-collar workplace theft. Under Section 408, employee embezzlement is a non-bailable offense carrying up to 7 years rigorous imprisonment. Here is the definitive legal playbook for business owners to preserve forensic evidence, file an unshakeable FIR, and recover stolen corporate capital.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

  6. Police Investigation, Arrest, and Bail Opposition
  7. Asset Tracing and Civil Recovery: Money Suits and Injunctions

  10. Talk to an Advocate

The Growing Epidemic of Workplace Embezzlement in Bangladesh

As businesses expand across Bangladesh's manufacturing, retail, e-commerce, and logistics sectors, corporate owners are forced to delegate financial authority. Managers handle petty cash, accountants manage online banking tokens, and sales executives collect cash on delivery (COD) from retail distribution networks. Unfortunately, weak internal controls and misplaced personal trust create fertile ground for systematic embezzlement.

Employers often discover the fraud accidentally: an unexpected tax audit reveals discrepancies, a supplier issues a legal notice for unpaid invoices that were purportedly cleared months ago, or an accountant fails to report to work, leaving behind a trail of fabricated bank challans. When the scale of theft is uncovered—frequently totaling tens of lakhs or crores of taka—business owners panic. Taking emotional steps, such as physically confining the employee or seizing their family's belongings, exposes the employer to retaliatory extortion and kidnapping allegations. Recovering stolen funds requires disciplined, strategic execution of statutory criminal and civil procedures.

Penal Code Section 408: Criminal Breach of Trust by Clerk or Servant

The core statutory weapon against internal employee theft is Section 408 of the Penal Code 1860. While Section 406 covers general criminal breach of trust (carrying up to 3 years imprisonment), Section 408 recognizes that employees occupy a special position of trust and fiduciary duty, prescribing far harsher penalties:

'Whoever, being a clerk or servant or employed as a clerk or servant, and being in any manner entrusted in such capacity with property, or with any dominion over property, commits criminal breach of trust in respect of that property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.'

To secure a conviction under Section 408, the prosecution must establish three essential legal ingredients: (1) that the accused was an employee (clerk, manager, officer, or servant) of the complainant; (2) that the accused was entrusted with the company's property, cash, or financial dominion; and (3) that the accused dishonestly misappropriated, converted to their own use, or disposed of that property in violation of company rules. Offenses under Section 408 are cognizable, meaning police have statutory authority to arrest the employee without an arrest warrant.

Section 477A: Falsification of Accounts and Ledgers

Embezzlement rarely occurs without documentary concealment. To mask stolen funds, dishonest employees routinely falsify accounting ledgers, forge bank deposit slips, alter invoices, or delete digital sales records. To penalize this administrative deception, prosecutors invoke Section 477A of the Penal Code 1860 (Falsification of Accounts).

Section 477A provides that whoever, being a clerk, officer, or servant, willfully and with intent to defraud, destroys, alters, mutilates, or falsifies any book, paper, writing, valuable security, or account belonging to their employer, or makes false entries therein, shall be punished with imprisonment for up to seven (7) years, or with fine, or with both. Combining Section 408 (theft of money) with Section 477A (cooking the books) and Section 420 (cheating) creates a formidable, multi-layered criminal charge sheet that withstands defense scrutiny in the Magistrate Court.

First 24 Hours: Internal Investigation and Evidence Lockdown

The actions an employer takes within the first 24 hours of uncovering embezzlement determine whether the stolen money will be recovered or lost forever. A disciplined protocol must be executed immediately:

  1. Digital Access Lockdown: Instantly revoke the suspect employee's access to enterprise software (Tally, SAP, Oracle), corporate email accounts, and cloud storage. Freeze any banking tokens, digital signature devices, or mobile financial service (MFS) agent SIMs held by the employee.
  2. Forensic Physical Seizure: Under the supervision of two neutral company witnesses, secure the employee's work desk, desktop computer, hard drives, physical voucher files, and chequebooks. Create a formal seizure inventory list signed by both witnesses.
  3. Emergency Forensic Audit: Retain an independent chartered accountant or certified fraud examiner to review the suspected transaction window, verify bank statements directly from the bank branch, and issue an expedited Audit Discrepancy Report.

Never alert or confront the employee until this documentary evidence is securely backed up off-site.

Need legal guidance or representation for your case in Bangladesh? Send your documents and dispute details on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007. Overseas clients and local litigants can arrange an immediate confidential document review.

Drafting the FIR at the Thana vs. Filing a CR Case

Once the audit report confirms the missing sums, the employer must initiate formal criminal prosecution. The employer has two statutory pathways:

  • First Information Report (FIR) at the Local Thana: The company's authorized representative (backed by a Board Resolution) submits a written complaint to the Officer-in-Charge (OC) of the Thana having territorial jurisdiction over the office. Because Section 408 is a cognizable offense, the police are legally required to register it as an FIR under Section 154 CrPC, initiate an immediate investigation, and apprehend the suspect.
  • Complaint Register (CR) Case Before the Magistrate Court: If the local Thana delays or hesitates to register the FIR due to jurisdictional squabbles, the advocate files a direct petition before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) Court under Section 190 CrPC. The Magistrate examines the complainant under Section 200 CrPC, reviews the audit exhibits, and directs the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) or Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) to conduct a specialized inquiry.
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Police Investigation, Arrest, and Bail Opposition

Following the registration of the case, the investigating officer (IO) executes search and seizure protocols. Under Section 165 CrPC, the IO can search the accused employee's residence, seize passbooks, cash, luxury vehicles purchased with embezzled proceeds, and laptop computers. The IO also issues official requisitions under Section 94 CrPC to commercial banks to freeze the employee's personal and familial bank accounts.

When the accused is arrested and produced before the Magistrate, their defense counsel routinely moves for bail. The employer's advocate must fiercely oppose bail: arguing that Section 408 is a non-bailable offense, that the stolen corporate funds have not yet been recovered, and that the accused possesses access to digital evidence that could be tampered with if released. Sustained detention in custody frequently compels the accused's family to offer restitution of the embezzled sums in exchange for a compromise.

Asset Tracing and Civil Recovery: Money Suits and Injunctions

While criminal prosecution penalizes the dishonest employee with prison time, a criminal court does not automatically write a cheque refunding the company's stolen millions. To achieve complete financial recovery, corporate legal counsel institutes parallel civil proceedings:

  1. Money Suit for Restitution: The company files a formal Money Suit in the Court of the Joint District Judge claiming the exact embezzled sum plus interest, damages, and forensic audit expenses.
  2. Attachment Before Judgment (Order 38 Rule 5 CPC): The advocate immediately petitions the civil court to attach the employee's personal real estate, family residential flats, vehicles, and fixed deposits purchased with stolen proceeds.
  3. Bank Account Injunctions: The civil court issues injunctions restraining commercial banks from permitting the employee or their nominee spouses from withdrawing or transferring funds.

Operating civil asset attachment alongside criminal custody creates unbearable pressure, ensuring that stolen corporate capital is recovered.

Comparison Table: Section 408 Embezzlement vs. General Theft

The table below highlights the crucial distinctions between workplace embezzlement under Section 408 and general theft or cheating under the Penal Code:

ParameterSection 408 (Employee Breach of Trust)Section 379 (General Theft)
Relationship RequiredMust be clerk, manager, servant, or employeeAny stranger or third party
Maximum Prison SentenceUp to 7 years rigorous imprisonment + fineUp to 3 years imprisonment or fine
Bail StatusNon-bailable (Bail is judicial discretion)Generally non-bailable but easily granted
Fiduciary ElementBreach of legal entrustment and dutyUnlawful physical taking without consent
Accompanied ChargesSection 477A (Falsification of Accounts)Section 411 (Receiving Stolen Property)

Utilizing Section 408 ensures that the judicial system treats workplace theft with the severity it warrants.

Illustrative Scenario: Cracking an Accountant's Fraud Ring in Gazipur

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how aggressive corporate prosecution dismantled an embezzlement ring in Gazipur:

A textile spinning mill in Gazipur employed a senior accountant for over five years, entrusting him with preparing monthly utility payments, vendor cheques, and local raw cotton procurement disbursements. Over an eighteen-month period, the accountant conspired with an external supplier to generate inflated cotton procurement invoices, diverting BDT 42,00,000 into a newly opened bank account registered under his wife's maiden name, while altering the company's internal ERP ledger entries to display 'full vendor settlement.'

During an unannounced internal audit, the mill's managing director discovered that vendor balances were still outstanding. Rather than confronting the accountant, the company retained a corporate criminal advocate. Within 48 hours, the advocate oversaw a forensic IT backup of the ERP server, secured original altered cheques from the company's bank branch, and compiled an unshakeable audit dossier. The advocate then drafted an FIR submitted directly to the Gazipur Police, registered under Sections 408, 420, and 477A of the Penal Code.

Police arrested the accountant at his residence, seizing bank passbooks showing BDT 25,00,000 in fixed deposits and documents for a newly purchased residential plot in Gazipur. Concurrently, the advocate filed an emergency petition before the Joint District Judge Court under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC, securing an attachment order against the accountant's newly acquired land and bank accounts. Confronted with sustained criminal detention and total asset freezing, the accountant's family negotiated a complete restitution agreement: the BDT 25,00,000 bank balance was transferred back to the mill, and the residential plot was surrendered to settle the remaining debt, achieving 100% financial recovery for the enterprise.

Talk to an Advocate

Navigating complex litigation in Bangladesh requires meticulous evidentiary preparation, prompt statutory filings, and strategic courtroom advocacy. Whether you are dealing with business debts, family property partitions, corporate oppression, employee theft, or administrative overreach, attempting to resolve disputes without seasoned legal counsel frequently causes irreversible procedural defaults. A qualified advocate protects your rights, secures urgent injunctions or stay orders, and ensures complete statutory compliance across civil, criminal, and constitutional forums.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the punishment for employee embezzlement in Bangladesh?

Under Section 408 of the Penal Code 1860, criminal breach of trust by a clerk or servant is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for up to seven (7) years and a monetary fine. If accompanied by falsification of accounts under Section 477A, an additional sentence of up to 7 years may be imposed.

Is employee embezzlement a bailable offense in Bangladesh?

No. Section 408 of the Penal Code is a non-bailable offense. The police can arrest the employee without a warrant, and obtaining bail from the Magistrate Court is difficult, particularly when substantial sums remain unrecovered.

Can an employer deduct stolen money from an employee's salary or provident fund?

Under the Bangladesh Labour Act 2006, unilateral salary deductions are restricted unless formal disciplinary proceedings and an inquiry committee find the employee guilty of misconduct. To safely recover stolen funds without labor tribunal complications, filing a civil Money Suit with Order 38 attachment is the recommended legal route.

What evidence is needed to prove employee embezzlement?

You need the appointment letter proving employment, proof of entrustment (job description or authorization), original altered receipts or forged vouchers, certified bank statements showing unauthorized transfers, and an independent chartered accountant's audit report.

Can police freeze an employee's personal bank account during investigation?

Yes. Under Section 94 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), the investigating officer has the legal authority to issue formal written orders to commercial banks to freeze the suspect's accounts and provide detailed transaction histories.

What should I do if an embezzling employee resigns and disappears?

Immediately lodge an FIR at the local Thana. The police will track the accused through lawful mobile tower location and NID databases. If the accused absconds, the court will issue arrest warrants and proclamation/attachment orders under Sections 87 and 88 CrPC.

Can an employer file a case against an employee's family member who received stolen money?

Yes. If the employee transferred embezzled corporate funds into their spouse's or relative's personal bank accounts, those individuals can be charged under Section 411 of the Penal Code (dishonestly receiving stolen property) or as conspirators under Section 109.

Can an overseas company operating in Bangladesh prosecute a local employee for fraud?

Yes. A multinational corporation or overseas investor can authorize a local managing director, country manager, or lawyer via a formal Board Resolution or Power of Attorney to institute criminal and civil proceedings against dishonest local personnel.

Enforcing Foreign Arbitral Awards in Bangladesh: Arbitration Act 2001 & Execution Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-08 · 19 minutes

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In international cross-border trade, foreign direct investment, and large-scale infrastructure procurement in Bangladesh, dispute resolution clauses predominantly mandate international commercial arbitration. Whether proceedings are conducted under the rules of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC), London Court of International Arbitration (LCIA), or UNCITRAL, securing a favorable arbitral award abroad is only half the battle. If the defaulting Bangladeshi counterparty or corporate debtor refuses to pay voluntarily, the award creditor must enforce the award against local commercial assets, bank balances, or real estate in Bangladesh. Bangladesh is a signatory to the 1958 New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards, codified into domestic law through the Arbitration Act 2001 (Act No. I of 2001). This authoritative legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate and commercial arbitration practitioner in Dhaka, explains the statutory enforcement framework, execution mechanics, grounds of refusal, and High Court precedents.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

  2. 2. Section 45: Legal Status of Foreign Awards as Court Decrees
  3. 3. Filing Protocol: The Court of the District Judge
  4. 4. Section 46 Grounds: When Can a Bangladeshi Court Refuse Enforcement?
  5. 5. Procedural Matrix: ICC/SIAC Award to Asset Realization
  6. 6. The Public Policy Defense: Supreme Court Judicial Interpretations
  7. 7. Execution Mechanics: Bank Attachment, Garnishee & Asset Auctions
  8. 8. Repatriating Recovered Funds: Bangladesh Bank Guidelines
  9. 9. Illustrative Scenario: Recovering $1.4 Million SIAC Award in Dhaka
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate: International Commercial Arbitration Defense

1. Statutory Architecture: Arbitration Act 2001 & New York Convention

In commercial transactions involving international trade, maritime shipping, petroleum concessions, and foreign joint ventures in Bangladesh, international arbitration provides neutrality and specialized adjudication. Bangladesh acceded to the United Nations Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards 1958 (the New York Convention) with reciprocity reservations.

To modernize domestic arbitration and align with the UNCITRAL Model Law, Parliament enacted the Arbitration Act 2001 (Act No. I of 2001), repealing the colonial Arbitration Act 1940 and the Arbitration (Protocol and Convention) Act 1937. Chapter X of the Act (Sections 45 to 47) establishes an integrated legal regime for recognizing and enforcing foreign arbitral awards.

Under Section 2(k), a 'foreign arbitral award' is defined as an award made in pursuance of an arbitration agreement in the territory of any country other than Bangladesh, which has been declared by the Government by notification in the official Gazette to be a reciprocating territory under the New York Convention. Major commercial trading partners—including Singapore, the United Kingdom, the United States, China, India, Germany, and Switzerland—qualify as recognized reciprocating jurisdictions.

2. Section 45: Legal Status of Foreign Awards as Court Decrees

The core operative provision governing execution is Section 45 of the Arbitration Act 2001. Section 45(1) establishes a mandatory legal presumption: any foreign arbitral award that is enforceable under this Chapter shall be treated as binding for all purposes on the persons as between whom it was made, and may accordingly be relied on by any of those persons by way of defense, set-off, or otherwise in any legal proceedings in Bangladesh.

Under Section 45(2), where a court is satisfied that a foreign arbitral award is enforceable under this Chapter, the award shall be enforced under the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 in the same manner as if it were a decree of the court.

This statutory provision provides immense commercial advantages to international creditors:

  • No Re-Trial on the Merits: The Bangladeshi court does not sit as a court of appeal over the arbitral tribunal. It cannot review the evidence, substitute its own interpretation of contracts, or re-evaluate damages awarded by the foreign tribunal.
  • Direct Execution: The award creditor does not need to institute a de novo lawsuit; they directly file for execution, bypassing years of civil trial stages.
  • Preclusion of Parallel Civil Suits: If a local debtor attempts to file an exploratory civil suit in an Assistant Judge Court to evade an international arbitral award, the court is bound to dismiss or stay the suit under Section 45.

3. Filing Protocol: The Court of the District Judge

Under the Arbitration Act 2001, original jurisdiction to enforce a foreign arbitral award resides exclusively with the Court of the District Judge having territorial jurisdiction over the location where the judgment debtor resides, carries on business, or where movable or immovable assets of the debtor are situated.

Under Section 47 of the Act, the applicant award creditor must file an Execution Application accompanied by authenticated evidentiary documents:

  1. Duly Authenticated Original Award: The original physical arbitral award signed by the tribunal, or a certified copy thereof authenticated in the manner required by the law of the country in which it was made.
  2. Original Arbitration Agreement: The original commercial contract containing the arbitration agreement or submission clause, or a certified copy thereof.
  3. Certified Translation: If the award or agreement is in a language other than English or Bengali, a certified translation produced by an official translator or diplomatic representative.
  4. Schedule of Debtor Assets: A detailed schedule identifying the debtor's commercial bank accounts, factory land, shares, or corporate receivables within the district.

4. Section 46 Grounds: When Can a Bangladeshi Court Refuse Enforcement?

Seeking to enforce or defend against a foreign arbitral award in Bangladesh? Contact our Supreme Court commercial litigation chamber on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007. We represent international award creditors and corporate debtors.

Enforcement of a New York Convention award is mandatory unless the judgment debtor proves one of the narrow, exhaustive grounds specified in Section 46(1) of the Arbitration Act 2001:

  • Incapacity of Parties: A party to the arbitration agreement was under some legal incapacity under the law applicable to them.
  • Invalidity of Agreement: The arbitration agreement is invalid under the governing law chosen by the parties, or failing any indication thereon, under the law of the country where the award was made.
  • Denial of Due Process: The debtor was not given proper notice of the appointment of the arbitrator or of the arbitral proceedings, or was otherwise unable to present their case.
  • Award Exceeding Scope: The award deals with a difference not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission to arbitration, or contains decisions on matters beyond the scope of arbitration.
  • Improper Tribunal Composition: The composition of the arbitral authority or arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties.
  • Award Not Binding or Suspended: The award has not yet become binding on the parties, or has been formally set aside or suspended by a competent court of the country in which it was made.

5. Procedural Matrix: ICC/SIAC Award to Asset Realization

The execution pathway for foreign arbitral awards in Bangladesh:

Procedural StepStatutory ProvisionKey Actions & Timelines

2. Filing Execution PetitionSection 45 & 47, Arbitration ActPetition filed before District Judge; notice issued to debtor
3. Adjudication of ObjectionsSection 46, Arbitration ActDistrict Court examines Section 46 refusal grounds; rejects frivolous delay
4. Enforceability DecreeSection 45(2), Arbitration ActCourt declares award enforceable as a domestic civil decree
5. Attachment & AuctionOrder 21, Code of Civil ProcedureBank accounts attached; debtor properties auctioned; funds realized
6. Fund RepatriationForeign Exchange Regulation Act 1947Authorized dealer bank transmits funds abroad via Bangladesh Bank approval
