WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

6. The Public Policy Defense: Supreme Court Judicial Interpretations

In addition to party-invoked defenses, Section 46(1)(b)(ii) empowers the court on its own motion to refuse enforcement if it finds that the enforcement of the award would be contrary to the public policy of Bangladesh, or if the subject-matter of the dispute is not capable of settlement by arbitration under domestic law.

Local judgment debtors frequently raise the 'public policy' defense as a generic shield. However, the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has adopted a modern, restrictive interpretation of public policy aligned with international commercial standards:

  • Narrow Construction: The High Court Division has repeatedly affirmed that public policy cannot be equated with mere disagreement on legal technicalities. Enforcement violates public policy only if it breaches fundamental principles of Bangladeshi law, involves bribery, fraud, corruption, or violates national sovereignty.
  • Foreign Exchange Regulations: An award directing payment in foreign currency does not violate public policy. Bangladeshi courts routinely enforce foreign currency decrees, directing payment in equivalent Bangladesh Taka (BDT) or through authorized banking channels under central bank oversight.
  • Prohibition on Merits Review: Local courts are barred from reopening the evidentiary merits of the case under the guise of public policy scrutiny.

7. Execution Mechanics: Bank Attachment, Garnishee & Asset Auctions

Once the District Judge determines that the foreign award is enforceable under Section 45, the court proceeds directly to execution proceedings governed by Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC).

Key statutory execution mechanisms available to the award creditor include:

  1. Attachment of Commercial Bank Accounts: The court issues an urgent prohibitory order to the debtor's commercial banks under Order 21 Rule 46, freezing balances and directing bank managers to deposit funds into the court registry.
  2. Garnishee Proceedings: If third-party corporations or government agencies owe receivables or contract payments to the judgment debtor, the court issues garnishee orders directing those third parties to pay receivables directly to the decree holder.
  3. Attachment and Public Auction of Real Estate: Under Order 21 Rule 54 and Rule 66, commercial offices, factories, and lands owned by the debtor are attached, valued by court-appointed commissioners, and sold at public auction to satisfy the decretal debt.
  4. Civil Arrest and Detention: Under Section 51 and Order 21 Rule 37 CPC, if a corporate director or debtor possessing sufficient financial means wilfully refuses to satisfy the decree, the court possesses powers to order civil detention in prison.

8. Repatriating Recovered Funds: Bangladesh Bank Guidelines

For international award creditors, successfully executing an award in Dhaka culminates in the repatriation of recovered funds abroad. Cross-border fund remittances are governed by the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 (Act No. VII of 1947) and the Guidelines for Foreign Exchange Transactions issued by Bangladesh Bank.

The statutory remittance process requires:

  • Certified Copy of Court Execution Order: An authenticated copy of the District Court's final satisfaction order and payment disbursement decree.
  • National Board of Revenue (NBR) Tax Clearance: Proof that any applicable source tax deductions or capital tax assessments have been satisfied or exempted under Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAA).
  • Authorized Dealer Bank Application: The foreign creditor's advocate coordinates with an Authorized Dealer (AD) scheduled commercial bank to compile Form TM and submit a formal outward remittance application to Bangladesh Bank.
  • Central Bank Approval: Bangladesh Bank verifies that the remittance arises from a judicial execution decree under the Arbitration Act 2001 and issues statutory clearance for outward foreign currency wire transfer.

9. Illustrative Scenario: Recovering $1.4 Million SIAC Award in Dhaka

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): A Singaporean commodity trading corporation supplied industrial raw materials to a large conglomerate in Dhaka. The Bangladeshi buyer defaulted on payment, citing foreign exchange fluctuations. The Singaporean corporation initiated arbitration under SIAC rules in Singapore as stipulated in the sales contract. The SIAC sole arbitrator rendered a final award of $1.4 Million USD plus interest in favor of the Singaporean creditor.

When the local debtor refused to honor the award, the Singaporean company retained Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber. Our cross-border litigation team executed a disciplined enforcement strategy:

  1. Obtained certified, apostilled copies of the final SIAC award and original sales agreement and filed an Execution Petition under Section 45 of the Arbitration Act 2001 before the Court of the District Judge, Dhaka.
  2. The debtor filed objections under Section 46, claiming the award violated 'public policy' due to foreign exchange controls and alleging lack of proper notice. Our advocates dismantled these claims, demonstrating that the debtor had fully participated in the Singapore hearings through international counsel.
  3. The District Judge dismissed the debtor's objections, declaring the SIAC award enforceable as a domestic civil decree.
  4. Concurrently filed an emergency application under Order 21 Rule 46 CPC for garnishee attachment of the debtor's export letter of credit receivables across three commercial banks in Motijheel and Gulshan.
  5. Faced with frozen commercial operations and imminent auction of its factory assets, the debtor settled the judgment in full, depositing the BDT equivalent of $1.4 Million into the court registry, which was subsequently repatriated to Singapore via Bangladesh Bank authorization.

10. Talk to an Advocate: International Commercial Arbitration Defense

Enforcing foreign arbitral awards or defending against international arbitration claims in Bangladesh demands specialized knowledge of the Arbitration Act 2001, civil execution procedure, and foreign exchange regulations. Advocate Md. Shah Alam and his corporate arbitration team provide strategic representation before District Courts, the High Court Division, and international tribunals.

Need an advocate for this matter in Bangladesh? Send your documents on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: a first document review can be done remotely.

Our principal chamber is located in Uttara, Dhaka, minutes from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, alongside our daily litigation chamber at the Supreme Court Bar Association and Dhaka Judge Court.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a foreign arbitral award be directly enforced in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under Section 45 of the Arbitration Act 2001, an arbitral award made in a New York Convention signatory state is recognized as binding and executed as if it were a decree of a domestic civil court.

Which court in Bangladesh has jurisdiction to enforce a foreign arbitral award?

Original jurisdiction resides exclusively with the Court of the District Judge having territorial and financial jurisdiction over the location where the debtor resides or where debtor assets are situated.

Can a Bangladeshi court re-examine the merits of a foreign arbitral award?

No. Local courts are strictly prohibited from reviewing the evidentiary merits, contractual interpretations, or financial calculations of the foreign arbitral tribunal. Scrutiny is limited to Section 46 refusal grounds.

What is the time limit for enforcing a foreign arbitral award in Bangladesh?

Under the Limitation Act 1908, execution applications should ideally be filed within three (3) years from the date the award becomes final and binding under its governing foreign law.

Can a foreign award creditor attach commercial bank accounts in Dhaka?

Yes. Under Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, the District Court possesses full statutory powers to attach debtor bank accounts, seize commercial assets, and auction real estate to satisfy the award.

What constitutes a 'public policy' violation under Section 46?

Under Supreme Court precedents, public policy is narrowly construed to include bribery, fraud, corruption, fundamental procedural unfairness, or violations of national sovereignty, rather than routine legal disagreements.

Can recovered funds be repatriated out of Bangladesh in foreign currency?

Yes. Following execution satisfaction in court, an Authorized Dealer commercial bank applies to Bangladesh Bank under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 to obtain clearance for outward foreign remittance.

Can a foreign company instruct a Supreme Court advocate remotely?

Yes. International award creditors can retain a Supreme Court advocate remotely through an embassy-authenticated Power of Attorney to draft, file, and execute award proceedings in Dhaka without traveling.

Ex-Parte Decree Setting Aside in Bangladesh: Complete Legal Guide under Order IX Rule 13 CPC

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-14 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Discovering that a civil court has passed an ex-parte decree against you without your knowledge is one of the most alarming crises in Bangladeshi property litigation. Whether engineered by unscrupulous relatives or predatory land grabbers through forged summons receipts, the Code of Civil Procedure provides robust, enforceable remedies to set aside one-sided judgments and restore your lawful defense.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

  6. Staying the Execution Case: Order XXI and Order XXXIX
  7. Step-by-Step Miscellaneous Case Procedure in Court

The Crisis of Ex-Parte Decrees in Bangladesh

Imagine living abroad as an expatriate wage earner in London, New York, or Riyadh, diligently sending remittances home to build your family homestead, only to receive a panicked telephone call from your ancestral village in Sylhet or Cumilla. A court bailiff has appeared on your land with police personnel, preparing to execute a writ of possession based on an ex-parte civil decree that you had no idea ever existed.

This distressing scenario occurs frequently across the subordinate judiciary of Bangladesh. Dishonest co-sharers, estranged relatives, or predatory land syndicates intentionally file partition suits, title declarations, or specific performance claims while suppressing the defendant's genuine overseas or urban address. By bribing local process servers to submit fictitious service returns or publishing court notices in obscure, uncirculated daily gazettes, plaintiffs secure one-sided judgments behind the defendant's back.

Acknowledge your anxiety, but understand that the judicial system does not allow fraudulent or uninformed decrees to stand unchecked. The Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC) enshrines the fundamental common-law maxim of natural justice: audi alteram partem (no person shall be condemned unheard). With aggressive and prompt legal intervention, an ex-parte decree can be reopened, execution halted, and your rightful defense placed fully before the trial court.

Statutory Framework: Order IX Rule 13 CPC Explained

Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 serves as the principal statutory shield for any defendant subjected to a unilateral civil decree. The rule explicitly provides that in any case where a decree is passed ex-parte against a defendant, that defendant may apply to the court by which the decree was passed for an order to set it aside.

If the applicant satisfies the court of either of two statutory conditions—first, that the summons was not duly served, or second, that they were prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing—the court is statutorily mandated to make an order setting aside the decree as against them. The court may impose such terms as to costs, payment into court, or otherwise as it thinks fit, and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the original suit.

When an ex-parte decree is set aside under Order IX Rule 13, the judicial clock is wound backward. The decree is extinguished, and the original lawsuit is restored to its status prior to the default. The defendant is granted full legal standing to submit a Written Statement (WS), introduce documentary evidence, cross-examine the plaintiff's witnesses, and contest the merits on an equal footing.

Grounds: Summons Not Duly Served vs. Sufficient Cause

To succeed in an application under Order IX Rule 13, the applicant must establish at least one of the two statutory grounds recognized under Bangladeshi civil jurisprudence:

  • Summons Not Duly Served: Under Order V of the CPC, the court must serve summons through personal delivery, registered post with acknowledgment due (A/D), or courier. If the plaintiff provided a deliberately false address, if the process server (Jari-karak) submitted a fraudulent return without visiting the locality, or if substituted service under Order V Rule 20 (hanging on a door or publishing in an obscure newspaper) was granted without genuine efforts to trace the defendant, the summons is legally invalid.
  • Sufficient Cause for Non-Appearance: Even if summons was served, the defendant may have been physically or legally unable to appear on the date of hearing. Bangladeshi courts recognize severe illness certified by government medical boards, sudden bereavement, confinement in foreign jurisdictions, inability to travel due to visa cancellation, or proven gross fraud by engaged legal counsel as sufficient cause.

Judges require credible contemporaneous documentation to substantiate sufficient cause. Mere assertions of busyness or casual ignorance of court dates will be rejected by the bench.

Section 12(2) CPC: Decrees Procured by Fraud or Collusion

While Order IX Rule 13 addresses procedural absence and service irregularities, what happens when an ex-parte decree was manufactured through deep-seated criminal fraud, forged deeds, or impersonation? In such severe instances, Section 12(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure represents the definitive constitutional remedy.

Introduced to prevent endless rounds of independent title suits, Section 12(2) provides that where a person challenges the validity of a decree, judgment, or order on the ground of fraud, misrepresentation, or want of jurisdiction, they must seek their remedy by making an application to the court which passed the final decree, rather than filing a separate lawsuit.

The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly affirmed that fraud vitiates the most solemn judicial acts. If a plaintiff forged the signature of a deceased ancestor, fabricated a power of attorney, or deliberately impersonated the defendant through a hired imposter in court, an application under Section 12(2) enables the trial court to exercise its inherent supervisory jurisdiction, annul the fraudulent decree, and refer the perpetrators for criminal prosecution under Sections 193, 209, and 467 of the Penal Code.

Facing a similar legal dispute in Bangladesh? Don't fight it alone. Contact Advocate MD Shah Alam for expert legal consultation, tactical dispute evaluation, and courtroom representation. WhatsApp: +880 1955-802007 or Call: +880 1712-655546.

Strict Limitation Deadlines: Article 164 Limitation Act

Timing is the most perilous dimension of ex-parte litigation in Bangladesh. Under Article 164 of the Limitation Act 1908, the statutory period to file an application under Order IX Rule 13 to set aside an ex-parte decree is strictly 30 days.

However, the crucial question is when this 30-day countdown begins:

  • Where Summons Was Duly Served: The 30 days run from the exact date of the decree.
  • Where Summons Was Not Duly Served: The 30 days run from the date when the applicant first acquired knowledge of the decree.

If you discover an ex-parte decree months or years after its pronouncement because you were living abroad or unserved, you must document precisely how and when you first learned of the judgment (e.g., when a relative saw strangers inspecting the land, or when mutation was attempted). You must immediately file an accompanying application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act 1908, praying for condonation of delay and explaining every single day between gaining knowledge and filing the petition in court.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Staying the Execution Case: Order XXI and Order XXXIX

Filing an application to set aside an ex-parte decree does not automatically prevent the plaintiff from taking possession of your land. In practice, the victorious plaintiff immediately files a Money Execution Case or Title Execution Case (Jari Mamla) under Order XXI of the CPC to obtain a writ of delivery of possession (Dakhol Parwana) or auction your properties.

Therefore, your legal counsel must file an urgent application for an interim stay of execution proceedings concurrently with your Order IX Rule 13 petition:

  1. Order XXI Rule 26 CPC: Empowers the execution court to stay the execution of a decree for a reasonable time to enable the judgment-debtor to apply to the trial court or appellate court for an order setting aside the decree.
  2. Order XXXIX Rules 1 & 2 CPC: Allows the court hearing the Miscellaneous Case to issue a temporary injunction restraining the opposite party from altering the nature, character, or possession of the suit property during the pendency of the hearing.
  3. Inherent Powers under Section 151 CPC: Invoked where technical procedural gaps exist, empowering the civil judge to pass ad-interim status-quo orders in the interest of justice.

Without securing an interim stay order, the plaintiff may demolish existing structures, fell timber, or convey the land to an alleged innocent third party, creating severe practical complications.

Step-by-Step Miscellaneous Case Procedure in Court

Challenging an ex-parte decree follows a rigorous, multi-stage judicial pathway in the subordinate civil courts of Bangladesh:

  1. Procuring Certified Copies: Apply urgently for certified copies of the ex-parte judgment, decree, order sheet, and crucially, the process server's summons return (Jarikar report) from the court record room.
  2. Drafting the Miscellaneous Application: Your advocate drafts a formal petition under Order IX Rule 13 (and Section 151) CPC, detailing the jurisdictional facts, non-service of summons, and substantial defense on the merits, supported by a verifying affidavit.
  3. Registration as a Misc Case: The civil court admits the petition, registering it as an independent Miscellaneous Case (Misc Case) and assigning it a unique case number.
  4. Notice to the Opposite Party: Summons is issued to the original plaintiff, who is granted time to submit written objections.
  5. Evidentiary Hearing (Hearing on Evidence): Both parties produce oral and documentary evidence. The applicant testifies under oath, and the process server who claimed to have served the summons can be summoned and rigorously cross-examined regarding local identification witnesses.
  6. Final Order and Terms: The civil judge pronounces an order either dismissing the Misc Case or setting aside the ex-parte decree, often imposing moderate court costs (BDT 1,000 to BDT 5,000) payable to the plaintiff.

Comparison Table: Order IX Rule 13 vs. Section 12(2) CPC

Choosing the correct procedural vehicle between Order IX Rule 13 and Section 12(2) CPC determines whether your case survives preliminary judicial scrutiny:

Legal ParameterOrder IX Rule 13 CPCSection 12(2) CPC
Primary GroundNon-service of summons or sufficient cause for absence.Fraud, misrepresentation, or lack of territorial/pecuniary jurisdiction.
ApplicabilityEx-parte decrees only.Any decree, whether ex-parte, contested, or Solenama (compromise).
Statutory LimitationStrictly 30 days under Article 164 Limitation Act (from decree or knowledge).Governed by Article 181 (3 years from discovery of fraud).
Standard of ProofPreponderance of probabilities regarding absence or non-service.High civil standard proving intentional fraudulent deception or forgery.
Immediate ConsequenceRestores the original suit to the trial docket for a fresh hearing.Declares the decree void ab initio, nullifying all execution proceedings.
Right of AppealAppealable under Order XLIII Rule 1(d) CPC to District Judge Court.Civil Revision under Section 115 CPC to District Judge or High Court.

Illustrative Scenario: Overturning a Fraudulent Partition Decree

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): Tariqul, an expatriate software architect working in Birmingham, owned an undivided 12-decimal commercial land parcel along the Sylhet-Sunamganj highway, inherited from his late father. In mid-2025, his paternal uncle filed a Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) in the Joint District Judge Court, intentionally stating Tariqul's address as a defunct village tea stall in Jagannathpur where Tariqul had not lived in thirty years.

The process server allegedly pinned the summons to the vacant shop wall, certifying that the defendant could not be found. Following formal paper publication in a weekly periodical with negligible circulation, the court proceeded ex-parte and decreed the entire roadside commercial frontage to the uncle, relegating Tariqul's share to an unviable waterlogged ditch behind the property.

When Tariqul's maternal cousin noticed boundary fencing being erected in October 2026, Tariqul immediately granted an attested Special Power of Attorney through the Bangladesh High Commission in London to his advocate. His counsel obtained certified copies of the summons return, which bore the forged thumb impression of a fictitious village elder. Within 14 days of knowledge, an Order IX Rule 13 application accompanied by a Section 5 limitation petition and an Order XXI Rule 26 stay application was filed.

During the evidentiary hearing, the process server crumbled under cross-examination, admitting he never verified Tariqul's physical presence. The Joint District Judge set aside the ex-parte partition decree, issued an injunction against construction, and restored the original partition suit, allowing Tariqul to demand an equitable court-appointed Advocate Commissioner survey.

Talk to an Advocate

An ex-parte decree threatens your fundamental constitutional property rights, but it is neither permanent nor unchallengeable when addressed with disciplined, aggressive civil litigation. Allowing days to slip by after discovering an adverse judgment can permanently destroy your right to file under Article 164 of the Limitation Act. A seasoned civil defense advocate ensures that process server returns are scrutinized, immediate stay orders against execution are secured, and your full documentary title is presented to the court.

Need to cancel an ex-parte decree or stop a fraudulent land execution in Bangladesh? Specialized remote legal intake and High Commission power of attorney coordination available for expatriates.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens to the original lawsuit when an ex-parte decree is set aside?

When the trial court sets aside an ex-parte decree under Order IX Rule 13 CPC, the decree is completely nullified and the original lawsuit is restored to the exact procedural stage it was at prior to the defendant being declared absent. The defendant is permitted to file their written statement, submit documents, and contest the case on full merits.

How do I prove that I never received the court summons?

Non-service of summons is proven by examining the certified process server report (Jarikar report). Your advocate will inspect the alleged signatures or thumb impressions of local witnesses, cross-examine the process server in court, and submit documentary proof (such as passport stamps, airline tickets, or employment records) showing you resided elsewhere or abroad when service was allegedly made.

Can an expatriate (NRB) apply to set aside an ex-parte decree from abroad?

Yes. An expatriate living abroad can execute a Special Power of Attorney empowering a trusted relative or their advocate in Bangladesh to file and pursue the Order IX Rule 13 Miscellaneous Case. The power of attorney must be duly signed, verified by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, and stamped by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) in Dhaka.

What is the time limit to file an Order IX Rule 13 application?

Under Article 164 of the Limitation Act 1908, the statutory time limit is strictly 30 days. If summons was duly served, the 30 days run from the date of the decree; if summons was not served, the 30 days run from the date the applicant first gained knowledge of the decree, supported by a Section 5 condonation petition.

What if the plaintiff has already sold the property after obtaining the ex-parte decree?

Under the legal doctrine of Lis Pendens (Section 52 Transfer of Property Act 1882), any third-party purchaser who buys property subject to an ex-parte decree does so at their own peril. When the ex-parte decree is set aside, the subsequent transfer loses its legal foundation, and the property can be recovered through restitution proceedings under Section 144 CPC.

Can the court impose costs or financial conditions when setting aside an ex-parte decree?

Yes. Order IX Rule 13 CPC explicitly empowers the civil judge to set aside the decree 'upon such terms as to costs, payment into court, or otherwise as it thinks fit.' Courts routinely direct the applicant to pay nominal costs (BDT 1,000 to BDT 5,000) to compensate the plaintiff for procedural delays.

What is the difference between Order IX Rule 13 and an appeal under Section 96(2) CPC?

An aggrieved defendant has two concurrent remedies: filing an application under Order IX Rule 13 in the trial court or preferring a regular First Appeal under Section 96(2) CPC before the appellate court. Order IX Rule 13 is vastly preferable because it allows the introduction of fresh evidence regarding non-service of summons, whereas an appeal is confined strictly to the existing trial court paper book.

Can an ex-parte decree in an Artha Rin Adalat or Family Court case be set aside under Order IX Rule 13?

Both Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 and Family Courts Act 2023 have specialized provisions mirroring Order IX Rule 13. However, under Section 19 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003, setting aside an ex-parte money decree requires the judgment-debtor to deposit 10% of the decreed amount in cash or bank guarantee within 30 days of knowledge.

Facebook Defamation Case Bangladesh: Your Legal Options

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-04-01 · 8 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

False posts, doctored images, and malicious content on Facebook can destroy reputations, damage careers, and cause profound emotional harm. Bangladesh law provides real legal remedies — criminal prosecution under the Digital Security Act, civil damages claims, and court orders compelling Facebook to remove harmful content. This guide explains your options.

: · Cyber Crime & Criminal Defense Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing LawCyber Security Act, 2023 & Penal Code, 1860 (Bangladesh)
First Step at Police StationFile an Online or In-Person General Diary (GD) at gd.police.gov.bd / local Thana
Police Cyber Support for Women (PCSW)Helpline: 01320-000888 | Email: cybersupport.women@police.gov.bd
CID / CTTC Cyber Crime Unit24/7 Emergency: 999 | Police Headquarters & Cyber Tribunal Dhaka

📋 In This Article

  2. Facebook Defamation: DSA Section 29 Explained
  3. Defamation Under the Penal Code 1860
  4. Criminal vs. Civil Defamation: Which Route to Take?
  5. How to Get Defamatory Content Removed from Facebook
  6. Evidence You Need to Build a Strong Case
  7. Filing Your Defamation Case: Step-by-Step
  8. Defences the Accused May Raise

What is Online Defamation Under Bangladesh Law?

Defamation is the publication of a false statement that damages another person's reputation. When this happens on Facebook, WhatsApp, or any digital platform in Bangladesh, it becomes online defamation — covered by both the Digital Security Act 2018 and the Penal Code 1860.

Online defamation in Bangladesh includes:

  • False factual posts claiming you committed crimes or unethical acts.
  • Doctored or manipulated photos circulated to harm your reputation.
  • Fake screenshots of conversations or messages.
  • False accusations circulated in Facebook groups or WhatsApp broadcast lists.
  • Malicious reviews or comments on business pages designed to destroy credibility.

Opinion, satire, and truthful statements are generally not defamatory. If you believe you have been defamed, consult a cyber law lawyer in Uttara or Dhaka to assess your case.

Facebook Defamation: DSA Section 29 Explained

Digital Security Act 2018, Section 29 specifically criminalises online defamation. It states that publishing defamatory content about any person through a computer, digital device, or network is a criminal offence punishable by:

  • Up to 3 years' imprisonment, and/or
  • A fine of up to BDT 5 lakh (approximately USD 4,500)

For a repeat offence, the punishment doubles to 6 years and BDT 10 lakh. DSA cases go to the Cyber Tribunal in Dhaka, which has exclusive jurisdiction over digital crimes. The Cyber Tribunal can also issue interim orders to remove defamatory content before the trial concludes.

Criminal vs. Civil Defamation: Which Route to Take?

In Bangladesh, defamation victims can pursue both criminal and civil routes simultaneously:

  • Criminal Route (DSA Section 29 / Penal Code Sections 499–500): The goal is prosecution and punishment of the offender — imprisonment and/or fine. Filed via FIR at the police station or complaint to the Cyber Tribunal.
  • Civil Route (Tort of Defamation): The goal is compensation — monetary damages for harm to your reputation, business losses, and emotional suffering. Filed before a civil court.

Most victims file criminal cases first to get content removed quickly, then pursue civil damages separately. An experienced Dhaka defamation lawyer can manage both tracks simultaneously.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

How to Get Defamatory Content Removed from Facebook

There are two parallel routes to content removal:

  1. Facebook's Internal Reporting: Report the post directly through Facebook's interface. This is free and immediate but often slow and unreliable for serious defamation cases.
  2. Court Order: The Cyber Tribunal can issue an order directing Facebook (through its Bangladesh node) to remove specific content. This is legally binding and faster for cases where Facebook ignores internal reports.

Courts in Bangladesh have issued content removal orders in defamation cases. Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam in Uttara to initiate urgent court proceedings to remove harmful content.

Evidence You Need to Build a Strong Case

Before filing a defamation case in Bangladesh, collect and preserve:

  • Full-page screenshots including the URL, the poster's profile name/photo, date and time of posting.
  • The direct URL of the defamatory post or content.
  • Screenshots of shares, comments, and reactions — to demonstrate spread and harm.
  • Evidence of identity of the poster — if known (their Facebook profile, phone number linked to the account).
  • Proof of harm: screenshots of messages from affected people, business loss records, medical reports for psychological harm.

A lawyer can apply to court to compel Facebook to disclose the account data linked to an anonymous defamer — this is a powerful remedy when the attacker tries to hide behind a fake account.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I file a defamation case if the person used a fake Facebook account?

Yes. The Cyber Tribunal can order Facebook to disclose account registration data, IP addresses, and device information linked to the fake account. The police cyber unit can also trace the real identity through digital forensics.

Is sharing someone else's defamatory Facebook post also a crime?

Potentially yes. A person who knowingly shares defamatory content about another person may also be liable — both criminally under the DSA and civilly for the continued damage caused by the share.

How long does a Facebook defamation case take in Bangladesh?

Getting a content removal order can be achieved within weeks. The full criminal trial at the Cyber Tribunal typically takes 1–3 years. Civil damages cases in regular courts often take longer.

Can I claim compensation for business losses caused by Facebook defamation?

Yes. In a civil defamation suit, you can claim damages for loss of business revenue, loss of contracts, emotional distress, and reputational harm if you can establish these losses were caused by the defamatory content.

False Dowry Case Defense in Bangladesh: Section 5 Punishment Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-10 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In contemporary Bangladeshi marital disputes, allegations of dowry demands are frequently manufactured as retaliatory weapons during divorce negotiations, property disagreements, or emotional estrangement. Disgruntled spouses and their families routinely file criminal complaints dragging not only the husband but also his elderly parents, married sisters, and overseas relatives into protracted criminal proceedings. Recognizing this rampant misuse, parliament enacted the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 (যৌতুক নিরোধ আইন, ২০১৮). While Section 3 punishes genuine dowry demands, Section 5 established an aggressive counter-measure: anyone who files a false, baseless dowry case to harm an innocent person faces up to five years of rigorous imprisonment and criminal fines.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)

📋 In This Article

  2. 2. Statutory Ingredients: Demanding Dowry (Section 3) vs. False Complaints (Section 5)
  3. 3. Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 vs. Nari o Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 2000
  4. 4. Securing Liberty: Regular and Anticipatory Bail Strategies
  5. 5. Evidentiary Tactics: How to Disprove Dowry Claims During Cross-Examination
  6. 6. Summary Matrix: Legitimate Demands, False Charges & Penalties
  7. 7. High Court Quashing (Section 561A CrPC) for Implicated Relatives
  8. 8. Illustrative Scenario: Exonerating a Husband and Prosecuting the Complainant
  9. 9. Step-by-Step Guide to Prosecuting a Malicious Complainant under Section 5
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate

1. The 2018 Legal Transformation: Why Section 5 Was Introduced

For decades, the Dowry Prohibition Act 1980 served as the primary statutory instrument penalizing the giving, taking, or demanding of dowry in Bangladesh. However, over time, the criminal courts observed an overwhelming pattern of weaponization: whenever a marriage broke down due to emotional incompatibility, extra-marital affairs, or differences over domestic living arrangements, complainants routinely added allegations of cash or car dowry demands to force financial settlements.

To curb this widespread abuse of the judicial process, parliament repealed the 1980 enactment and promulgated the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 (Act No. XXXV of 2018). While preserving stringent penalties for genuine dowry demands under Section 3 and Section 4, the legislature introduced a revolutionary deterrent mechanism in Section 5.

Under Section 5 of the 2018 Act, filing a fabricated dowry complaint is recognized as a serious independent criminal offence. The statutory provision specifically aims to protect innocent citizens, their aging parents, and collateral relatives from the indignity of unwarranted arrest, public humiliation, and financial extortion.

2. Statutory Ingredients: Demanding Dowry (Section 3) vs. False Complaints (Section 5)

A successful legal defense requires a precise understanding of the statutory definitions established in the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018. Under Section 2 of the Act, 'dowry' (যৌতুক) is defined as any property, valuable security, or money demanded directly or indirectly as consideration for marriage from one party to the other. Crucially, voluntary wedding gifts, dower (Denmohar), and traditional maintenance are expressly excluded from the definition of dowry.

Section 3 establishes that if any party to a marriage demands any dowry directly or indirectly from the other party, their parents, or guardians, such person shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five (5) years, or a fine up to 50,000 BDT, or both.

In contrast, Section 5 establishes an identical maximum penalty for bad-faith litigants: if any person files or causes to be filed any complaint or case alleging an offence under the Act, knowing that there are no just or lawful grounds for making such charge, with the intent to injure or cause financial or reputational damage to another person, they shall be punished with imprisonment up to five (5) years, or a fine up to 50,000 BDT, or both.

3. Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 vs. Nari o Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 2000

Complainants seeking extreme judicial leverage frequently choose between the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 and the more severe Nari o Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 2000 (Prevention of Repression Against Women and Children Act). Understanding the operational boundaries between these enactments is vital for defense counsel.

Under Section 11(ga) of the Nari o Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 2000, if a husband or his relatives cause simple hurt (physical assault) to a woman for non-payment of dowry, the offence carries imprisonment from one to three years and is tried before the specialized Nari o Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal. In contrast, cases under the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 do not require physical violence; they criminalize the mere demand or agreement for dowry and are adjudicated by the Court of Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate.

Falsely accused of demanding dowry in a police or court complaint in Bangladesh? Immediate defense representation is crucial to protect your freedom and reputational standing. Message our criminal defense advocates on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for a confidential defense assessment.

Complainants frequently attempt to inflate a verbal disagreement into a Section 11(ga) tribunal case by procuring fabricated medical injury certificates. When defense counsel proves that no physical assault occurred and that medical records are manufactured, the tribunal acquits the accused or transfers the case to the regular Magistrate Court, exposing the complainant to counter-prosecution. For trial nuances, review our analysis on stopping false criminal cases in Bangladesh.

4. Securing Liberty: Regular and Anticipatory Bail Strategies

When an accused husband or family member learns that a dowry complaint has been filed—either as an FIR at a police station or as a Complaint Register (CR) case before the Magistrate—safeguarding liberty is the immediate imperative.

Under Section 8 of the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018, offences under Section 3 and Section 4 are classified as cognizable, bailable, and compoundable. Despite being classified as bailable, Magistrate Courts frequently exercise judicial caution during initial surrender, particularly if the complainant appears in person alleging torture or non-payment of dower.

To avoid remand or temporary custody, the defense should prepare a comprehensive bail dossier containing the Nikahnama, proof of employment or business reputation, proof of residence, and documentary evidence of prior marital discord unrelated to dowry. If the complainant has weaponized the case by adding non-bailable penal code sections or approaching the Nari o Shishu Tribunal, the accused should immediately move an anticipatory bail application before the High Court Division under Section 498 CrPC to obtain protective pre-arrest bail. For complete procedural protocols, consult our guide on anticipatory bail in Bangladesh.

5. Evidentiary Tactics: How to Disprove Dowry Claims During Cross-Examination

Winning an acquittal in a false dowry case requires aggressive, forensic cross-examination of the prosecution witnesses (PWs)—namely the complainant, her parents, and local witnesses. Because false dowry claims are almost always concocted after the marriage has broken down, they suffer from inherent chronological and factual contradictions.

Key cross-examination angles utilized by experienced trial advocates include:

  • Timeline Discrepancies: Demonstrating that the alleged dowry demand date coincided with a period when the husband was abroad, at work in another district, or when the parties were happily living together as shown by digital photographs and communications.
  • Financial Implausibility: Showing that the complainant's family lacked the financial capacity to meet the alleged multi-million BDT dowry demand, or that the husband's family possessed superior independent wealth and had no plausible economic motive to demand money.
  • Absence of Prior Complaints: Highlighting that during years of marriage, the complainant never lodged a police GD, never informed the local Ward Councillor, and never mentioned dowry until divorce notices were served under Section 7 MFLO.
  • Independent Witness Contradictions: Discrediting neighborhood or village witnesses who admit under cross-examination that they have no direct personal knowledge of any demand and merely repeated what the complainant's father told them.

6. Summary Matrix: Legitimate Demands, False Charges & Penalties

The following comparative matrix synthesizes the statutory provisions, procedural routes, and legal exposure governing dowry litigation under the 2018 enactment:

Provision Nature of Criminal Act Statutory Punishment Trial Forum & Bail Status
Section 3 (Dowry Demand) Demanding money/property as consideration for marriage Imprisonment up to 5 years, or fine up to 50,000 BDT, or both Judicial Magistrate 1st Class; Bailable & Compoundable
Section 4 (Giving or Taking) Giving, taking, or abetting the transaction of dowry Imprisonment up to 5 years, or fine up to 50,000 BDT, or both Judicial Magistrate 1st Class; Bailable & Compoundable
Section 5 (False Case Filing) Filing a false complaint intending to injure another person Imprisonment up to 5 years, or fine up to 50,000 BDT, or both Judicial Magistrate 1st Class; Trial upon counter-complaint
Section 11(ga) Nari o Shishu Causing simple hurt/violence for dowry demand Imprisonment 1 to 3 years and fine Nari o Shishu Tribunal; Non-Bailable by default

7. High Court Quashing (Section 561A CrPC) for Implicated Relatives

A notorious feature of false dowry litigation in Bangladesh is the indiscriminate naming of the husband's extended family members. Complaints routinely accuse married sisters residing in separate households, elderly bedridden grandparents, and overseas brothers who were not even in Bangladesh on the alleged date of occurrence.

The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly deprecated this practice of 'roping in' innocent family members. Under Section 561A of the CrPC, the High Court Division possesses inherent jurisdiction to prevent abuse of the process of any court and secure the ends of justice.

Defense counsel files a Criminal Miscellaneous petition before the High Court Division on behalf of the implicated relatives. When the petition demonstrates that the complaint contains only vague, omnibus allegations without specifying any overt act, date, or specific role played by the relatives, the High Court regularly issues a Rule Nisi staying all criminal proceedings against the collateral family members and ultimately quashes the proceedings against them. To understand the quashing procedure, explore our guide on quashing criminal cases under Section 561A CrPC.

8. Illustrative Scenario: Exonerating a Husband and Prosecuting the Complainant

To demonstrate how defense and counter-prosecution operate in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A telecommunications engineer residing in Dhanmondi, Dhaka, served his wife with a notice of talaq under Section 7 of the MFLO after discovering prolonged infidelity. In retaliation, the wife immediately filed a Complaint Register (CR) case under Section 3 of the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court. She falsely alleged that the husband, along with his mother and Canada-resident brother, had demanded a 20 Lakh BDT cash dowry and a Toyota sedan, threatening to divorce her if the demand was not satisfied.

The husband engaged a Supreme Court advocate. The defense first obtained anticipatory bail from the High Court Division, followed by a Section 561A petition that quashed all proceedings against the overseas brother and mother due to total lack of specific allegations. During the trial of the husband before the Metropolitan Magistrate, the defense produced flight manifests proving the husband was attending a technical conference in Singapore on the alleged date of the dowry demand, alongside WhatsApp chats confirming the dispute arose solely from infidelity.

The Magistrate passed a comprehensive judgment acquitting the husband with an express finding that the dowry allegations were fabricated for harassment. Following the acquittal, the husband filed a formal counter-complaint under Section 5 of the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018. The court took cognizance, issued a warrant of arrest against the former wife, and placed her on trial for malicious prosecution.

9. Step-by-Step Guide to Prosecuting a Malicious Complainant under Section 5

Securing an acquittal is vindication, but holding the false complainant accountable under Section 5 of the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 establishes lasting legal justice. To initiate a successful counter-prosecution, follow these structured steps:

  • Procure Certified Copy of Acquittal Judgment: Obtain the complete, certified judgment from the trial court containing express judicial observations that the allegations were groundless, unproven, or malicious.
  • Draft a Formal Complaint under Section 5: Prepare a formal complaint detailing the chronological history, the false allegations, the acquittal findings, and the financial, social, and psychological damage inflicted on the accused.
  • File CR Case in Judicial Magistrate Court: File the case before the Chief Judicial Magistrate or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court having territorial jurisdiction over the forum where the original false case was lodged.
  • Combine with Section 211 Penal Code: Plead Section 211 of the Penal Code 1860 (false charge of offence made with intent to injure) alongside Section 5 of the 2018 Act to maximize statutory accountability.
  • Initiate Civil Suit for Damages: File a civil suit in the Joint District Judge Court claiming substantial monetary damages for malicious prosecution and defamation to recover legal fees and compensation.

For specialized trial advocacy in criminal defense, explore our dedicated criminal lawyer services and bail legal counsel.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a Criminal Defense Advocate in Dhaka: To apply for anticipatory bail, contest false dowry trials in the Magistrate Court, or prosecute malicious complainants under Section 5 of the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018, reach out via WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call +880 1712-655546. Dedicated legal defense for non-resident husbands and family members.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Section 5 of the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018?

Section 5 is a landmark provision that penalizes anyone who files a false dowry complaint with intent to injure or harm another person. It prescribes rigorous imprisonment for up to five years, or a fine up to 50,000 BDT, or both.

Is an offence under the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 bailable in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under Section 8 of the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018, offences under Section 3 and Section 4 are classified as bailable and compoundable. The accused can apply for bail as a matter of right before the Magistrate upon surrender.

Can distant relatives and in-laws be prosecuted in a false dowry case?

Complainants often falsely implicate in-laws. However, the High Court Division regularly quashes proceedings against extended family members under Section 561A of the CrPC when allegations are vague and omnibus.

What is the difference between dower (Denmohar) and dowry (Yautuk)?

Dower (Denmohar) is a mandatory statutory right of the Muslim wife payable by the husband under Islamic law. Dowry (Yautuk) is an unlawful property demand made as consideration for marriage, which is strictly criminalized under the 2018 Act.

How can I prove that the dowry allegations against me are fabricated?

You can prove fabrication through timeline evidence, travel records proving absence from the scene, proof of financial status, and correspondence showing the dispute arose over other matrimonial issues without any financial demands.

When can an acquitted husband file a Section 5 case against his former wife?

The husband can file a counter-complaint under Section 5 immediately after obtaining the certified judgment of acquittal from the trial court containing findings that the original dowry allegations were false or malicious.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi husband be arrested for a pending dowry case upon landing in Dhaka?

If a Magistrate Court has issued a warrant of arrest, immigration police may stop the traveler at the airport. Securing anticipatory bail from the High Court Division before arrival provides legal protection against arrest.

Can a false dowry case be settled out of court through compromise?

Yes. Section 8 of the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 expressly classifies offences under Section 3 as compoundable. The parties can execute a compromise deed (Solenama) and have the case dismissed with court approval.

Family Law in Bangladesh: Complete 2026 Guide to Marriage, Divorce, Custody & Inheritance

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-12 · 14 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Family law in Bangladesh governs the most personal aspects of life including marriage, divorce, child custody, maintenance, and inheritance. Governed by a combination of personal laws based on religion and general civil statutes, Bangladesh's family law system can be complex to navigate. This comprehensive 2026 guide covers everything you need to know.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

  2. Marriage Law: Registration and Requirements
  3. Divorce Law in Bangladesh: An Overview
  4. Child Custody and Guardianship

  6. Inheritance and Succession Law
  7. Domestic Violence and Protection Laws
  8. The Family Court System in Bangladesh

Overview of Family Law in Bangladesh

Bangladesh does not have a uniform family code applicable to all citizens. Instead, family law is applied based on the religious personal law of the parties involved. Key statutes include:

  • Muslims: Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939, Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937
  • Hindus: Customary law, Hindu Widows Remarriage Act 1856, Hindu Married Women's Right to Separate Residence and Maintenance Act 1946
  • Christians: Divorce Act 1869, Christian Marriage Act 1872
  • All Communities: Family Courts Ordinance 1985, Guardians and Wards Act 1890, Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017

Understanding which law applies to your situation is the first step. Our family law specialists can assess your case and advise accordingly.

Marriage Law: Registration and Requirements

Muslim Marriage: Muslim marriages in Bangladesh are conducted through a Nikah ceremony and must be registered. The Kabinnama (marriage contract) is drawn up by a licensed Kazi and contains essential details including the dower (mahr) amount. Registration is mandatory under the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974.

Minimum Age: The Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 sets the minimum marriage age at 18 for women and 21 for men.

Hindu Marriage: Hindu marriages are traditionally solemnized by customary rites. There is no comprehensive mandatory registration system for Hindu marriages in Bangladesh, though some districts have administrative registration facilities.

Christian Marriage: Governed by the Christian Marriage Act 1872, Christian marriages require registration with a licensed minister or marriage registrar.

Special Marriage: The Special Marriage Act 1872 allows inter-faith marriages to be registered in a civil ceremony before a Marriage Registrar, without requiring either party to change their religion.

Divorce Law in Bangladesh: An Overview

Divorce law in Bangladesh varies by religion:

Muslim Divorce: Governed by the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961. Options include talaq (husband-initiated), khula (wife-initiated with relinquishment of dower), mubaarat (mutual consent divorce), and judicial divorce (faskh) under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939. All divorces require notice to the Arbitration Council, and a 90-day reconciliation period applies.

Hindu Divorce: Bangladesh lacks a codified Hindu divorce law. Limited judicial divorce is recognized based on customary grounds or conversion. Legal separation and maintenance orders are available.

Christian Divorce: The Divorce Act 1869 governs Christian divorce on grounds including adultery, conversion, cruelty, and desertion.

For a detailed process overview, read our complete divorce process guide for Bangladesh.

Child Custody and Guardianship

Child custody in Bangladesh is governed by the Guardians and Wards Act 1890. The overarching principle is the welfare of the child - courts make custody decisions based on what is in the best interest of the child, not on the rights of the parents.

General Rules for Muslim Families:

  • Mothers have custody (hizanat) of boys until age 7 and girls until puberty, after which fathers may claim custody
  • Courts can depart from these general rules if the child's welfare requires it
  • Fathers are always considered the natural guardian of the person and property of a minor child

Visiting Rights: The non-custodial parent is typically granted visiting and access rights. Courts can order supervised visitation if there are safety concerns.

Modification of Custody: Custody orders can be modified if circumstances change significantly such as a change in the custodial parent's financial situation, remarriage, or relocation abroad.

Consult a family lawyer immediately for urgent custody matters including international child abduction cases.

Maintenance and Alimony Rights

Maintenance During Marriage: Under Muslim personal law, a husband is obligated to maintain (nafaqa) his wife, covering food, clothing, shelter, and medical needs commensurate with his means. Failure to maintain gives the wife grounds for dissolution of marriage.

Post-Divorce Maintenance: A Muslim husband must pay maintenance during the wife's iddat period (approximately 3 months after divorce). Beyond iddat, post-divorce maintenance is not automatic under Muslim personal law but courts often use their equity jurisdiction to award further support.

Child Maintenance: Fathers are obligated to maintain their children regardless of custody arrangements. Courts calculate maintenance based on the father's income, the child's needs, and the standard of living during the marriage.

How to Claim Maintenance: File a petition in the Family Court with jurisdiction. Alternatively, file a complaint under Section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for a faster remedy when urgent maintenance is needed.

Inheritance and Succession Law

Muslim Inheritance: Governed by Islamic personal law (Faraid system). Under the Quran-based inheritance rules applicable in Bangladesh:

  • Sons receive twice the share of daughters
  • Wives receive 1/8 of the estate if there are children, 1/4 if no children
  • Husbands receive 1/4 of the estate if there are children, 1/2 if no children
  • Parents, siblings, and other relatives have defined shares based on Quranic rules

Hindu Inheritance: Governed by customary law and the Hindu Succession rules. Property rights of Hindu women have been strengthened through judicial interpretation.

Christian Inheritance: Governed by the Succession Act 1925. Property passes to the spouse and children, with the spouse receiving one-third if there are children.

Property Registration: All inherited property should be properly transferred and registered. Our property law team can assist with land mutation and inheritance transfer procedures.

Domestic Violence and Protection Laws

The Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act 2010 is Bangladesh's primary law addressing family violence. It provides:

  • Protection orders to prevent abusers from approaching victims
  • Residence orders to ensure victims can remain in the shared home
  • Monetary relief including medical expenses and compensation
  • Emergency custody orders for children

Other relevant laws include the Nari O Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 2000 which provides criminal penalties for rape, acid attacks, kidnapping, and trafficking of women and children, and the Penal Code 1860 provisions on assault and criminal intimidation.

Read our detailed guide on applying for a domestic violence protection order in Bangladesh.

The Family Court System in Bangladesh

The Family Courts Ordinance 1985 establishes dedicated Family Courts in each district of Bangladesh. Key features:

  • Exclusive Jurisdiction: Family Courts have exclusive jurisdiction over dissolution of marriage, dower, maintenance, guardianship, custody, and restitution of conjugal rights
  • Mandatory Conciliation: Before a contested hearing, the Family Court must attempt conciliation between the parties
  • Appeals: Family Court decisions are appealed to the District Court (appellate), then to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court, and potentially to the Appellate Division
  • Location: Dhaka Family Court is located at Bakshi Bazar, Dhaka. Family Courts also operate in all 64 districts of Bangladesh

For complex family disputes involving multiple types of relief, working with an experienced family lawyer who knows the local court system is strongly recommended.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the minimum age for marriage in Bangladesh?

The Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 sets the minimum marriage age at 18 for women and 21 for men. However, the Act contains a provision allowing marriage below these ages in special circumstances with court and parental approval, which human rights groups have criticized.

Can a woman claim maintenance from her husband before divorce in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under Muslim personal law, a wife has the right to maintenance (nafaqa) throughout the marriage. She can file a petition in Family Court or use Section 488 CrPC to claim maintenance if her husband fails to provide adequate support, even without filing for divorce.

How is property divided after divorce in Bangladesh?

Bangladesh does not have a community property system. Upon divorce, each party retains ownership of assets in their individual name. Courts can award the wife her unpaid dower (mahr) and order maintenance. Disputes over jointly-held property are resolved in civil courts.

Can a non-Muslim file a case in the Family Court of Bangladesh?

Yes. The Family Courts Ordinance 1985 applies to all citizens regardless of religion. Non-Muslims file divorce, maintenance, and custody cases in the Family Court, with the applicable personal law governing the substantive rights.

How long does a family court case take in Bangladesh?

Uncontested cases such as mutual divorce or uncontested maintenance may be resolved in 6 to 12 months. Contested family court cases involving custody, property, and divorce simultaneously can take 2 to 5 years in the trial court, with appeals adding additional years.

Partition Suit Family Property Bangladesh – How to Divide Jointly Owned Land

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-08 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Joint family property disputes are among the most emotionally charged and legally complex cases in Bangladesh. When co-heirs or co-owners cannot agree on how to divide jointly owned land, a partition suit in the Civil Court is the legal remedy. This guide explains your rights and the exact process to claim your fair share.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

📋 In This Article

  2. Who Has the Right to File a Partition Suit?
  3. Types of Co-Ownership That Lead to Partition Suits
  4. Preliminary Partition: Can You Divide Property Without Going to Court?
  5. Step-by-Step Partition Suit Process in Bangladesh
  6. Documents Required for Filing a Partition Suit
  7. How the Court Divides Property
  8. Can One Co-Owner Block a Partition?
  9. Timeline for Partition Suits in Bangladesh
  10. Partition of Agricultural vs Urban Property
  11. Costs and Fees for Partition Suits

What Is a Partition Suit in Bangladesh?

A partition suit is a civil lawsuit filed in the District Court (or Artha Rin Adalat for some property matters) seeking the court's intervention to divide jointly owned property among the co-owners, giving each owner their individual exclusive share.

The legal foundation for partition suits in Bangladesh includes:

  • Partition Act 1893: The primary statute governing court-ordered partition of immovable property
  • Code of Civil Procedure 1908: Governs the procedural aspects of filing and conducting the suit
  • State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950: Relevant for agricultural land partition
  • Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937: Governs inheritance shares in Muslim family property division

A partition suit allows a co-owner — even one with a minority share — to compel the division of jointly held property. No co-owner can be permanently forced to remain in a joint ownership arrangement against their will in Bangladesh.

Who Has the Right to File a Partition Suit?

Any co-owner of jointly held immovable property in Bangladesh has the right to file a partition suit. This right arises in many common situations:

  • Inherited property: Multiple heirs who have jointly inherited land or a house from a deceased parent
  • Co-purchased property: Two or more people who purchased land together and now wish to separate their shares
  • Undivided joint family property: Members of a joint family who have never formally divided the ancestral property
  • Co-heirs after intestate succession: When a person dies without a will, their heirs inherit undivided shares in all property

Even if a co-owner holds only a small fractional share — such as 1/8 or 1/16 of the total property — they have the full legal right to file for partition of the entire jointly owned property. The other co-owners cannot block this right.

A property lawyer in Dhaka will first confirm your exact ownership share based on the inheritance records and then calculate your entitlement before filing.

Types of Co-Ownership That Lead to Partition Suits

Partition suits arise from different types of joint ownership:

  • Muslim inheritance: Under Islamic law (applied to Muslims in Bangladesh), when a person dies, all their property vests immediately in their legal heirs in proportionate shares. Sons receive a 2:1 ratio over daughters; wives, parents, and others receive fixed shares under the Faraid rules. Until partition, all heirs are co-owners of the undivided property.
  • Hindu inheritance: Under Hindu law (applicable to Hindus in Bangladesh under the Hindu Succession Act and customary law), property may vest in joint family or be inherited by specific heirs upon a member's death.
  • Voluntary joint purchase: Two or more friends, siblings, or business partners purchase property together and now need to separate.
  • Corporate dissolution: Partners in a business that owned land jointly need to divide the property as part of business wind-up.

Preliminary Partition: Can You Divide Property Without Going to Court?

Yes — and this is almost always preferable to a court suit, which is time-consuming and expensive. A voluntary partition can be achieved through:

  • Partition deed: All co-owners sign a registered partition deed, specifying which portion goes to each owner. The deed must be registered at the Sub-Registrar's office like any other property transaction. After registration, each owner holds their portion exclusively and can apply for separate mutation.
  • Family settlement: A written family settlement agreement (less formal than a registered partition deed) signed by all adult heirs is legally recognised in Bangladesh courts. Courts will generally enforce a genuinely agreed family settlement.
  • Mediation: A neutral mediator — often a respected family elder, religious leader, or professional mediator — can facilitate agreement on division. The mediated settlement is then recorded in a registered deed.

A voluntary partition is faster (days or weeks vs years in court), cheaper (registration fees vs court costs and lawyer fees), and preserves family relationships better than adversarial litigation. Your lawyer can draft and register a partition deed once all parties agree on the division.

Step-by-Step Partition Suit Process in Bangladesh

When voluntary partition is impossible due to one or more co-owners refusing to cooperate, a partition suit before the Civil Court is the legal remedy:

  1. Engage a property lawyer: Instruct an experienced property lawyer in Dhaka who specialises in land partition cases. They will assess your ownership share, identify all co-owners, and evaluate the property's division prospects.
  2. File the plaint: A written plaint (the plaintiff's claim document) is filed in the Civil Court of the district where the property is located. The plaint sets out: the identity of all co-owners, the nature and value of the joint property, the plaintiff's share, and the relief sought (partition and separate possession).
  3. Court notice to all defendants: The court sends formal notices to all other co-owners (defendants), requiring them to appear and submit their response.
  4. Defendants' written statements: Defendants file written statements admitting or disputing the plaintiff's claims about ownership shares and proposing their own division plan if desired.
  5. Evidence stage: Both sides produce documentary evidence (deeds, khatians, mutation records, inheritance documents) and may call witnesses to establish their respective rights.
  6. Commission for division: The court may appoint a Commissioner (usually a survey officer or experienced surveyor) to inspect the property and prepare a plan for partition — dividing it into shares corresponding to each co-owner's legal entitlement.
  7. Preliminary decree: The court first passes a preliminary decree — determining each co-owner's legal share.
  8. Final decree: After the Commissioner's report and any objections are heard, the court passes a final decree specifying exactly which portion each co-owner receives.
  9. Execution of the decree: If the losing party does not voluntarily take possession of their allocated portion, enforcement through execution proceedings is available.

Documents Required for Filing a Partition Suit

To file a partition suit, the following documents are typically needed:

  • Certified copies of all relevant deeds establishing the original ownership and subsequent transfers
  • Certified copies of the property's khatian (CS, SA, RS, BS as applicable)
  • Current mutation records (namjari) from the AC Land office
  • Death certificate(s) of the deceased owner(s) from whom property was inherited
  • Succession/heirship certificate (if obtained)
  • NID cards of all parties
  • Land development tax payment receipts
  • Any prior partition deeds, family settlement agreements, or wills relating to the property
  • Survey maps or site plans (if available)

Obtaining certified copies of khatians and deeds from government offices can take 2–4 weeks. Your lawyer will manage this document collection process on your behalf.

How the Court Divides Property

The court in a partition suit has broad powers to divide jointly owned property. The approach depends on the nature of the property:

  • Divisible property: If the property can be physically divided (typically applicable to larger land parcels, agricultural land, or large properties), the court will order physical division — each co-owner gets their portion as a separate, defined piece of land.
  • Indivisible property: For property that cannot reasonably be divided (a single small plot, an apartment, or a commercial unit), the court may order the property to be sold and the proceeds divided among co-owners in proportion to their shares.
  • Court Commissioner's role: The Commissioner inspects the property, measures it, and prepares a partition plan that divides it as fairly as possible given the physical characteristics of the land — taking into account access roads, water sources, soil quality, and other relevant factors.
  • Equal vs proportional division: Division is not necessarily equal — it reflects each co-owner's legal entitlement, which may be fractional (e.g., a daughter with 1/6 share gets 1/6 of the land by area, or 1/6 of the sale proceeds).

Can One Co-Owner Block a Partition?

No. A co-owner cannot permanently block a partition suit. The right to seek partition is an absolute legal right in Bangladesh — no agreement to the contrary is enforceable in perpetuity.

What a defendant co-owner can do:

  • Dispute the plaintiff's claimed ownership share
  • Challenge the value assessment of the property
  • Propose their own preferred division plan to the court
  • Object to the Commissioner's partition plan if they believe it is unfair

What a defendant co-owner cannot do:

  • Permanently prevent the court from ordering partition
  • Force the plaintiff to remain as a co-owner against their will
  • Unilaterally take or sell the entire jointly owned property without the court's order

However, co-owners who are in physical possession of the jointly owned property may delay matters by continuing to occupy it. The court can order them to vacate their portion upon passing of the final decree — and if they refuse, execution proceedings follow.

Timeline for Partition Suits in Bangladesh

Partition suits in Bangladesh are notoriously time-consuming. Realistic timelines:

  • Uncontested partition (all defendants cooperate): 1–2 years
  • Contested partition (defendants dispute shares): 3–7 years in the District Court
  • If appeal to High Court: Additional 2–4 years

The primary reasons for delay include court backlogs, the time taken by the Commissioner's survey, and strategic delaying tactics by defendants who benefit from the status quo.

This underscores why a voluntary partition agreement — even if it requires some compromise — is almost always preferable to a full partition suit. Your lawyer's first task will be to attempt a negotiated resolution before filing in court.

Costs and Fees for Partition Suits

The costs involved in a partition suit include:

  • Court fees (plaint fee): Calculated as a percentage of the value of the property being partitioned — typically 1–2% of the property's value as assessed by the court. For high-value property, this can be significant.
  • Lawyer's professional fees: Vary based on the complexity of the case, the lawyer's experience, and the court where the case is heard. Partition suits are complex and long-running — fees are typically paid as retainer plus hearing fees.
  • Commissioner's fees: The court-appointed Commissioner charges fees for their survey and report.
  • Expert witness fees: If surveyors or other experts are needed.
  • Registration of the final decree: When the court's partition order is implemented, registration fees apply to formalise the division in the land records.

Contact Adv. Shah Alam for a consultation on your family property partition situation — whether a negotiated solution or court suit is the right approach for your specific circumstances.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a daughter file a partition suit for her share of family property in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under Bangladesh's Muslim inheritance law, daughters have a legal right to their inheritance share (typically half the share of a son). A daughter co-heir can file a partition suit to claim her share — her right to do so is identical to that of any male co-heir.

What if one co-owner has already sold their share of the jointly owned property?

A co-owner can sell their undivided share to a third party — the buyer steps into the seller's position as a co-owner. The remaining original co-owners then have a right of pre-emption to buy the sold share at the same price, within a specified time under the Pre-Emption Act. A property lawyer must be consulted immediately if a co-owner sells their share.

Is partition possible if some heirs are abroad (NRB)?

Yes. Absent heirs can participate through a Power of Attorney given to a local representative. Alternatively, a partition suit can proceed and the absent defendant is served by substituted service. The court will protect the absent heir's rights by appointing a guardian ad litem if necessary.

What happens to a house built on jointly owned land during partition?

If one co-owner has built a structure on the jointly owned land, the court takes this into account when dividing the property — typically allocating the constructed portion to the builder, with corresponding adjustments in the unbuilt land going to other co-owners. If this is not possible, the builder may be directed to pay compensation to other co-owners for the land occupied by the structure.

Can a court force a sale instead of physical partition?

Yes. Under the Partition Act 1893, if the property cannot be conveniently partitioned, the court can order a sale by public auction and divide the proceeds among co-owners. This is common for small urban plots, single-floor buildings, and properties where physical division would be impractical.

Can Children Claim Property While Father Is Alive? Bangladesh Law, Gift Deeds & Senior Protection

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-09-22 · 14 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

A widespread legal dispute across families in Bangladesh arises when adult children attempt to compel an aging, living father to partition or transfer his property. Confronted with family pressure, many elderly parents ask: Can my children legally force me to divide my land while I am still alive? Can a partition suit be filed against a living father? What happens if an aggressive son coerces an elderly parent into executing a gift deed (Hiba) at the Sub-Registry Office? Senior Supreme Court Advocate Md. Shah Alam provides an authoritative judicial roadmap explaining why living parents enjoy absolute ownership under Bangladesh law and how to legally protect family estates from coercion. For immediate chamber counsel, call: <a href="tel:01712655546" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold;">01712655546</a>.

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

📋 In This Article

  2. 2. Can Children File a Partition Suit Against a Living Father?
  3. 3. Lifetime Property Transfers: Rules on Valid Hiba (Gift)
