1. The Doctrine of Spes Successionis in Bangladesh Law

Under Islamic jurisprudence as applied by the civil courts of Bangladesh, inheritance only opens upon the biological death of the property owner. Section 6(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 firmly codifies that the chance of an heir-apparent succeeding to an estate (Spes Successionis) cannot be transferred, claimed, or made the subject of any court litigation.

As long as a father is living and of sound mind, his ownership is absolute. He owes no legal duty to distribute land among his children, nor can any son or daughter demand a demarcation of boundaries or separate mutation. Any family agreement attempting to partition a living parent's land without the parent's voluntary execution is legally null and void.

2. Can Children File a Partition Suit Against a Living Father?

One of the most frequent inquiries brought to our Supreme Court chambers involves sons filing partition suits against their fathers or siblings. The fundamental requirement of a partition lawsuit under the Partition Act, 1883 and the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 is co-ownership (unity of title and possession).

Because children hold zero co-ownership in their living father's property, they lack standing (locus standi). When a father appears in court and submits an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the CPC for rejection of the plaint, civil courts routinely dismiss the lawsuit at the preliminary stage, often imposing exemplary compensatory costs on the litigating children.

3. Lifetime Property Transfers: Rules on Valid Hiba (Gift)

While children cannot demand distribution, a father has full constitutional and statutory discretion to transfer property to any child or third party during his lifetime through a registered Hiba (Gift). For a Hiba to withstand judicial scrutiny in Bangladesh, three essential elements must coalesce:

  • Declaration (Ijab): A voluntary, explicit declaration by the father free from mental distress or coercion.
  • Acceptance (Qabul): Express acceptance by the recipient child.
  • Delivery of Possession (Qabdah): Actual physical or constructive transfer of possession.

Under Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908, oral gifts are no longer recognized in Bangladesh. A formal Hiba deed must be registered at the Sub-Registry Office with statutory stamp duty and registration fees.

4. Challenging Coerced or Fraudulent Deeds Under Section 39 SRA

In real-world practice, elderly fathers in declining health are often subjected to undue influence, isolation, and fraudulent misrepresentation by ambitious children who take them to registry offices under the guise of medical paperwork. Such instruments are legally Voidable.

Under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, an aggrieved father can institute a Title Suit for Cancellation of the Instrument in the competent Assistant Judge Court. Under Section 16 of the Contract Act 1872, where one party holds a dominant position over a frail senior, the legal burden of proof lies upon the child to prove that the deed was executed voluntarily and with independent legal advice.

5. Criminal Protection: The Parents Maintenance Act 2013

To penalize the mistreatment of senior citizens, the Parliament of Bangladesh enacted the Parents Maintenance Act, 2013 (পিতা-মাতার ভরণপোষণ আইন, ২০১৩). Key provisions include:

  • Adult children are statutorily obligated to provide food, lodging, and healthcare to their parents.
  • Children are strictly prohibited from compelling parents to reside in old-age homes against their will.
  • Forcibly occupying a parent's residence or attempting to dispossess them constitutes a cognizable offense punishable by up to 3 months imprisonment or a fine of BDT 1,00,000.

6. Protective Legal Mechanisms for Elderly Property Owners

Senior property owners seeking to safeguard their estates while supporting their children should implement the following courtroom-tested protections:

  1. Conditional Hiba with Life Interest: Draft the registered deed reserving full lifetime usufructuary and possession rights to the father and mother, specifying that full title vests in the child only post-demise.
  2. Refuse Irrevocable Powers of Attorney: Never execute general powers of attorney in favor of children without strict expiration terms.
  3. Emergency Injunctions: If children threaten dispossession, immediately file an injunction petition under Order 39 Rules 1 & 2 of the CPC alongside an executive petition under Section 107/144 CrPC.

7. Supreme Court Chamber Consultation & Litigation Support

Father's Property Distribution Law Bangladesh – Children's Rights & Share

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-09-22 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Understanding your rights to a father's property is one of the most common legal concerns for Bangladeshi families. Whether your father is alive or has passed away, the law in Bangladesh — primarily governed by Muslim Personal Law — sets clear rules about how property must be distributed among children and other heirs. This comprehensive guide explains every aspect of father's property distribution law in Bangladesh for 2026, including the share of sons and daughters, the process of claiming your share, and what to do when disputes arise.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

  5. Who Else Inherits? Other Heirs Under Muslim Law
  6. Types of Property That Can Be Distributed

What Law Governs Father’s Property Distribution in Bangladesh?

In Bangladesh, property distribution after a father’s death is primarily governed by the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 for Muslim families, who constitute over 90% of the population. For Hindu families, the Hindu Succession Act and customary laws apply, while for Christians, the Succession Act, 1925 governs inheritance.

For the majority Muslim population, the rules of inheritance come directly from the Quran and Hadith, codified under Hanafi jurisprudence as applied in Bangladesh courts. The key legislative framework includes:

  • Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 – Makes Shariat law applicable to Muslims for personal matters including inheritance
  • Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 – Regulates family matters and introduces grandchildren’s inheritance rights
  • Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 – Governs how partition suits are filed in courts
  • Partition Act, 1893 – Provides the legal mechanism for dividing jointly held property
  • Registration Act, 1908 – Governs registration of any property transfer after inheritance

It is critically important to understand that under Islamic inheritance law applied in Bangladesh, the shares of each heir are fixed by divine law — no will or agreement can override these shares entirely, though a father may gift property during his lifetime (known as hiba) subject to certain conditions.

Bangladesh courts have consistently upheld Quranic inheritance principles. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh in numerous judgments has affirmed that Muslim heirs cannot be disinherited by a will that violates Quranic shares.

When Father Is Alive: Can Children Claim Property?

This is perhaps the most misunderstood aspect of property law in Bangladesh. While a father is alive, his children have NO legal right to claim his property unless it was specifically gifted or transferred to them. A living father has complete ownership rights over his self-acquired property and can sell, mortgage, or gift it as he wishes.

However, there are important exceptions and nuances:

Ancestral/Joint Family Property

If the property is ancestral property inherited from the father’s own father or grandfather, some legal scholars and courts have held that children may have a pre-existing interest. However, under strict Hanafi Muslim law applied in Bangladesh, even ancestral property is considered the absolute property of the current holder during his lifetime.

Property Gifted During Father’s Lifetime (Hiba)

A father can make a valid gift (hiba) to any child during his lifetime. Under Muslim law, a valid hiba requires:

  • Declaration (Ijab) – The father declares the gift
  • Acceptance (Qabul) – The child accepts the gift
  • Delivery of possession (Qabdah) – The father actually hands over possession

Once a valid hiba is made, that property belongs to the child and is excluded from the inheritance estate. However, a gift made to defraud creditors or deliberately disinherit legal heirs can be challenged in court.

Gift During Death Illness (Marz-ul-Maut)

If a father is terminally ill and attempts to gift away all his property, courts may scrutinize such transfers under the doctrine of marz-ul-maut. Gifts during death illness are limited to one-third of the estate, just like a will, to protect the rights of legal heirs.

When Father Dies: Islamic Inheritance Rules Explained

Upon a father’s death, his property (after paying off debts and funeral expenses) is distributed among legal heirs according to Islamic inheritance law. The process follows this precise order:

  1. Pay funeral and burial expenses from the estate
  2. Pay all outstanding debts of the deceased
  3. Execute any valid will — but only up to one-third (1/3) of the remaining estate. A Muslim cannot will away more than 1/3 of his estate, and cannot make a will in favor of an existing legal heir without other heirs’ consent
  4. Distribute the remaining estate according to Quranic shares among legal heirs

The legal heirs of a deceased father in Bangladeshi Muslim law fall into fixed categories:

HeirRelationshipShare (when applicable)
Wife/WivesSpouse1/8 if children exist; 1/4 if no children
Son(s)Direct childResiduaries — share remainder with daughters at 2:1 ratio
Daughter(s)Direct child1/2 if only one daughter (no son); 2/3 shared if two+ daughters (no son); 1/2 share of each son if son exists
Father’s FatherPaternal grandfather1/6 if children exist
Father’s MotherPaternal grandmother1/6 if children exist
MotherParent1/6 if children exist; 1/3 if no children

The estate that is distributed is called the Tarka and includes all movable and immovable property owned by the deceased at the time of death, including land, buildings, bank accounts, business assets, and vehicles.

Son vs Daughter Share: The 2:1 Ratio Explained

The most frequently asked question about property distribution in Bangladesh is about the difference between sons’ and daughters’ shares. Under Islamic law as applied in Bangladesh: A son receives twice the share of a daughter when they inherit together as residuaries (asaba).

This is derived directly from the Quran (Surah An-Nisa, 4:11): ‘For the male, what is equal to the share of two females.’

Practical Examples of the 2:1 Ratio

ScenarioEstate ValueDistribution
1 Son + 1 Daughter (no wife, no parents)৳30 lakhSon: ৳20 lakh | Daughter: ৳10 lakh
2 Sons + 2 Daughters (no wife, no parents)৳60 lakhEach son: ৳20 lakh | Each daughter: ৳10 lakh
3 Sons + 1 Daughter (no wife, no parents)৳70 lakhEach son: ৳20 lakh | Daughter: ৳10 lakh
Only Daughters (no sons) — 2 daughters৳30 lakhEach daughter: ৳10 lakh (2/3 total) | Remaining ৳10 lakh to agnate male relatives

When Only Daughters Inherit

If a father leaves only daughters (no sons), the daughters receive:

  • 1 daughter alone: Gets exactly 1/2 (one-half) of the estate. The other half goes to the father’s brothers or other agnate relatives.
  • 2 or more daughters: Together they receive 2/3 of the estate, divided equally among them. The remaining 1/3 goes to agnate male relatives.

Can the 2:1 Ratio Be Changed?

Under strict Hanafi Muslim law, inheritance shares are fixed and cannot be altered by a will. However, after inheritance has been established, the heirs themselves can mutually agree to redistribute among themselves — this is legally valid as a family settlement and can be registered as a deed of family arrangement. Many families choose to give daughters equal shares as a voluntary act, which is perfectly lawful as a post-inheritance gift.

Who Else Inherits? Other Heirs Under Muslim Law

Besides children, several other relatives may inherit from a deceased father depending on who is alive at the time of death. Understanding the full picture prevents disputes and ensures property reaches rightful owners.

Spouse (Wife/Wives)

The deceased father’s wife has a Quranic share of 1/8 of the estate if the deceased has children, or 1/4 if there are no children. If the father had multiple wives, they share this portion equally among themselves. The wife’s share is taken first before children’s shares are calculated.

Father’s Parents (Paternal Grandparents)

If the deceased father’s own parents are still alive, each gets 1/6 of the estate when children exist. The father’s mother (grandmother of the heirs) also receives 1/6. Their shares are taken before children inherit the residue.

Siblings (Brothers and Sisters)

Brothers and sisters of the deceased father generally only inherit when there are no children and no parents alive. Full brothers (same father and mother) have priority over half-brothers, who in turn have priority over maternal half-brothers.

Grandchildren Through a Predeceased Child

Under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961, Section 4, if a son or daughter died before their father, their children (the grandchildren of the deceased) are entitled to receive the share their parent would have received. This is a critical legal protection enforced by Bangladesh courts and deviates from classical Hanafi law to prevent grandchildren from being excluded entirely.

Types of Property That Can Be Distributed

Not all property held in a father’s name is necessarily part of his inheritance estate. Understanding what can and cannot be distributed is essential before any partition process begins.

Property That IS Distributed as Inheritance

  • Self-acquired land and buildings — Any property the father purchased, built, or received as a gift
  • Inherited property — Property the father himself inherited from his own parents
  • Agricultural land — Registered in the father’s name under any Khatian (CS/SA/RS/BS)
  • Urban real estate — Flats, commercial spaces, plots in the father’s name
  • Bank accounts and savings — All deposits and investments
  • Business assets — Shares in businesses, shop inventory, equipment
  • Outstanding debts owed TO the deceased — Money others owed to your father

Property That Is NOT Part of the Estate

  • Property already validly gifted during the father’s lifetime (hiba) with delivery of possession
  • Life insurance proceeds — These go directly to the named nominee, not the estate
  • Trust property — If held as trustee, not as personal property
  • Benami property — Held in the father’s name but actually belonging to another person, subject to court determination

Jointly Purchased Property

If property was purchased jointly by the father and another person, then only the father’s proportionate share is part of the estate. The co-owner’s share remains their own property and is not distributed as inheritance.

How to Claim Your Share: Step-by-Step Process

Claiming your rightful share in a father’s property requires following a specific legal process. Here is a complete step-by-step guide for Bangladeshi heirs in 2026:

Step 1: Obtain the Death Certificate

Get the father’s death certificate from the local Union Parishad (rural) or City Corporation/Pourashava (urban) via bdris.gov.bd. This is the foundational document for all inheritance claims.

Step 2: Obtain Legal Heir Certificate

Also known as Varisha Sanad, this document lists all legal heirs and their relationship to the deceased. For bank accounts, a Succession Certificate issued by the civil court under the Succession Act, 1925 is typically required.

Step 3: Conduct a Land Search (Khatian Check)

Identify all land owned by the deceased by checking khatians at the Sub-Registry Office or online at eporcha.gov.bd. Also check at the AC Land office for mutations already recorded in the father’s name.

Step 4: Apply for Namjari (Mutation)

After establishing your right as an heir, apply for Namjari at the Union Land Office (Tahsil Office) to transfer land records to the heirs’ names. Required documents: death certificate, inheritance certificate, original khatians, NID cards of all heirs, application form (available at land.gov.bd).

Step 5: Pay Outstanding Land Development Tax

Ensure all outstanding Khajna (land development tax) is paid. This can be done at ldtax.gov.bd.

Step 6: Execute a Registered Partition Deed (If All Heirs Agree)

If all heirs agree on how to divide the property, execute a registered partition deed at the Sub-Registry Office. This deed must be registered to be legally valid. Stamp duty for partition deeds is lower than for sale deeds.

Step 7: File a Partition Suit (If Heirs Disagree)

If heirs cannot agree, any heir can file a partition suit in the civil court having jurisdiction over the property’s location. The court appoints an Advocate Commissioner to measure and value the property, then passes a preliminary decree followed by a final decree dividing the property.

Filing a Partition Suit in Bangladesh

When family members cannot agree on how to divide inherited property, a partition suit (bintam mamla) is the legal remedy. This is one of the most common civil cases in Bangladeshi courts.

Which Court Has Jurisdiction?

Partition suits are filed in the Civil Court (Assistant Judge Court or Joint District Judge Court) of the district where the property is located.

Documents Required for Partition Suit

  • Death certificate of the father
  • Inheritance/succession certificate listing all heirs
  • All khatians (CS, SA, RS, BS) of the property
  • Deed by which the father originally acquired the property
  • List of all heirs with NID numbers and addresses
  • Recent land survey records
  • Land development tax payment receipts

Court Fees

Court fees in partition suits are calculated based on the value of the plaintiff’s claimed share of the property under the Court Fees Act, 1870. For a property share valued at ৳10 lakh, the court fee would be approximately ৳5,000–10,000. Your lawyer can calculate the exact amount.

Timeline of a Partition Suit

  • Simple cases (amicable): 1–2 years
  • Contested cases: 3–7 years depending on complexity and appeals
  • If appeal goes to High Court: Can extend to 10+ years

Preliminary Decree vs Final Decree

A partition suit results in two decrees: (1) a Preliminary Decree that declares the shares of each co-sharer, and (2) a Final Decree that after the Advocate Commissioner measures and demarcates the land, allocates specific plots to each heir. This final decree is then used to register separate deeds for each heir.

During the pendency of the suit, the court can appoint a Receiver to manage the property and distribute income proportionately, preventing any one heir from exclusively controlling all rental or agricultural income.

Common Disputes and How Courts Resolve Them

Property disputes within families after a father’s death are extremely common in Bangladesh. Here are the most frequent disputes and how they are legally resolved:

1. Elder Son Claims More As ‘Caretaker’

Courts do not recognize caregiving as a basis for additional inheritance under Muslim law. All shares are fixed by Shariat regardless of who cared for the father. The caregiver’s only remedy is if the father had explicitly gifted extra property or made a valid will for up to 1/3 of the estate.

2. Son Claims Daughters Have No Right to Land

This is legally incorrect and unfortunately common. Daughters are Quranic heirs with absolute rights to their share. Courts regularly rule in favor of daughters in such cases. Refusing to give a daughter her share is a violation of her fundamental rights enforceable in civil court.

3. Property Was Secretly Sold or Gifted to One Heir

If a deed was obtained through fraud, undue influence, or when the father lacked mental capacity, it can be declared void by the court. Courts can set aside fraudulent transfers and restore the property to the estate for proper distribution.

4. Disputes About What Property Is Included

Courts examine all documentary evidence — khatians, registered deeds, bank statements, tax receipts — to determine what was owned by the deceased. An advocate commissioner may be appointed to conduct a physical survey and valuation.

5. Grandchildren of Predeceased Son Claiming Share

Under Section 4 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, if a son dies before his father, the son’s children (grandchildren of the deceased) are entitled to receive the share their father would have received. This is an important legal protection that courts enforce consistently.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can a father give all his property to only one child by will?
A: No. Under Muslim law, a will cannot give more than 1/3 of the estate, and it cannot favor an existing legal heir without all other heirs’ consent. Any will exceeding this limit is void to the extent of the excess.

Q: My father died 20 years ago and the property is still in his name. Is it too late to claim?
A: No. There is no absolute statute of limitations preventing heirs from claiming inherited property. However, you should act promptly as long delays can complicate matters, especially if other heirs have adversely possessed the property. You can still file a partition suit and apply for namjari.

Q: Does an adopted child have inheritance rights?
A: Under Muslim law, adoption does not create inheritance rights. An adopted child does not inherit as a natural child does. However, a father can make a valid will of up to 1/3 of the estate in favor of an adopted child.

Q: What if the father left a will giving equal shares to sons and daughters?
A: For the 2/3 of the estate governed by Quranic shares, the will cannot override the fixed ratio. However, for the 1/3 that can be willed freely, the father can give additional amounts to daughters to bring them closer to equality. After death, all heirs can also mutually agree to a different distribution.

Q: Can I sell my inherited share before partition?
A: Yes. Each heir can sell their undivided share. However, other co-sharers have a right of pre-emption (Shuf’a) — they can purchase that share at the same price before an outsider can buy it.

Q: My brother has been collecting rent from our father’s property for years. Can I claim back-rent?
A: Yes. If an heir has been exclusively enjoying the property without accounting to other heirs, you can claim your proportionate share of rents and profits as mesne profits in a partition suit. Courts regularly grant such claims going back several years.

How Adv. Shah Alam Can Help You

Property inheritance disputes are emotionally draining and legally complex. At the Law Chamber of Adv. Md. Shah Alam in Uttara, Dhaka, we have extensive experience handling all aspects of father’s property distribution cases in Bangladesh, including:

  • Legal heir identification: We accurately calculate and document who the legal heirs are and what shares they are entitled to under Islamic inheritance law
  • Namjari (Mutation) assistance: We prepare and file all documents for transferring land records to heirs’ names at the AC Land office
  • Partition deed drafting: If all heirs agree, we draft, verify, and register a legally binding partition deed that protects everyone’s interests
  • Partition suit filing: If heirs are in dispute, we file a partition suit in the appropriate civil court and represent your interests through preliminary and final decrees
  • Fraudulent transfer challenges: We investigate and challenge any fraudulent gifts or sales that may have been made to deprive you of your rightful share
  • Succession certificate: We obtain Succession Certificates from court for releasing bank accounts, insurance claims, and other financial assets of the deceased
  • Pre-emption cases: If your co-sharer’s property has been sold to an outsider, we file pre-emption cases to protect your right of first refusal

Our chamber is located in Uttara, Dhaka, conveniently accessible from all parts of the city. We offer a free initial consultation to understand your situation before you commit to any legal action. We handle cases across all districts of Bangladesh.

Civil Cases: Land, Family, Money

In civil suits, a party can appear by a recognised agent (Order 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908) or by an advocate. You sign a vakalatnama authorising the advocate and, if needed, a Power of Attorney for a family member to sign documents and receive notices (see PoA guide). For evidence, you may later need to testify in person or by video. Ask your advocate early when your testimony is likely.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Family and Property Cases

  • Family Court cases (divorce, dower, maintenance, custody) can be filed and defended through an advocate and PoA.
  • Land suits (title, partition, injunction) usually proceed through the advocate; your presence is needed mainly for evidence.
  • Money recovery and contract suits likewise.

Virtual Hearings and Video Evidence

Since 2020, the law allows courts to hold hearings through video conferencing and to take evidence remotely in suitable cases. In practice, this depends on the court's technical facilities and the judge's discretion. Ask your advocate to apply for a video hearing or to examine you by commission. Prepare a stable internet connection, a quiet room and ID documents when the time comes.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Criminal Cases and Bail

In criminal cases, the accused generally has to appear before the court to apply for bail; a bail petition filed by an advocate for an absent accused is usually not accepted. If there is a warrant or case against you in Bangladesh, speak to an advocate before you travel. You may need to surrender and apply for bail at the right court. Complaints and FIRs can often be fought and quashed in the High Court Division through a writ or criminal miscellaneous case, which an advocate can file without your presence.

Choosing an Advocate

  • Check enrolment and experience in the relevant court.
  • Agree fees and stages in writing, with receipts.
  • Insist on an update after every hearing, with copies of orders.
  • Give limited authority and avoid blank signed papers.
  • Appoint a trusted local contact to attend the court and collect documents.

Practical Checklist

  1. Sign a vakalatnama and, where needed, a Power of Attorney attested at the Bangladesh Mission.
  2. Send scanned copies of all documents to the advocate.
  3. Keep a cause list and a calendar of hearing dates.
  4. Discuss strategy: injunction, mediation or settlement.
  5. Plan your travel only when your presence is truly needed.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I file a case in Bangladesh from abroad?

Yes, in most civil matters through an advocate and Power of Attorney. Criminal cases are more restricted.

Can I attend court by video?

The law allows virtual hearings and video evidence in many courts at the judge's discretion.

Do I have to travel for a criminal case?

Usually the accused must appear for bail and trial, although some quashing proceedings can be filed through an advocate.

What is a vakalatnama?

A signed authority by which a client appoints an advocate to act in a case.

How can I track my case from abroad?

Ask your advocate for hearing updates and copies of orders, and use the court's online case search where available.

  5. Can a False FIR Be Challenged?
  6. How Police Investigation Proceeds After FIR
  7. Charge Sheet and Cognisance by Court
  8. Building Your Defence Early

What Is an FIR and When Is It Filed?

An FIR (First Information Report) is a formal complaint lodged with the police that triggers a criminal investigation. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, a police officer must register an FIR when a cognisable offence (an offence for which police can arrest without warrant) is reported.

An FIR is filed by the complainant (the person who alleges the crime) at the concerned police station. This sets the criminal law machinery in motion — the police are then obligated to investigate. Importantly, an FIR is only the starting point of an investigation; it is not proof of guilt. If an FIR has been filed against you in Dhaka or elsewhere, immediately contact a criminal lawyer in Uttara or Dhaka.

Your Legal Rights After an FIR

Even after an FIR is lodged against you, you retain fundamental constitutional and legal rights:

  • Right to know the charges: You are entitled to know what offence you are accused of.
  • Right to legal representation: You have the right to engage and consult a lawyer at every stage of the process.
  • Right against self-incrimination: You cannot be compelled to be a witness against yourself (Article 35(4), Constitution of Bangladesh).
  • Right to bail: For bailable offences, bail is automatic. For non-bailable offences, you can apply to the court.
  • Right to fair trial: You are presumed innocent until proven guilty by a competent court.

Immediate Steps to Take

If you learn that an FIR has been filed against you, immediately:

  1. Engage a lawyer — this is the single most important step. A criminal lawyer will advise you on your specific situation within hours.
  2. Do not approach the complainant — any contact can be misinterpreted as witness tampering.
  3. Secure your documents: Preserve any evidence that supports your innocence — messages, receipts, CCTV footage, witnesses.
  4. Apply for anticipatory bail if you fear arrest — especially in non-bailable cases.
  5. Do not make public statements about the case on social media.

Acting quickly and calmly is essential. Panicking or making hasty decisions can worsen your situation.

When Should You Seek Bail?

Bail strategy depends on whether the offence in the FIR is bailable or non-bailable:

  • Bailable offence: You are entitled to bail. If arrested, the police must release you on bail. If they do not, apply immediately to the Magistrate Court.
  • Non-bailable offence: Bail is discretionary. Apply to the Magistrate or Sessions Court. If refused, apply to the High Court Division.
  • Anticipatory bail: If you have not yet been arrested, apply to the Sessions Court or High Court for anticipatory bail protection before any arrest occurs.

A bail lawyer in Dhaka can file bail applications with urgency and argue your case effectively before the court.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Can a False FIR Be Challenged?

Yes. If an FIR has been filed falsely or maliciously, there are legal remedies:

  • Anticipatory bail application: Raises the issue of false FIR as a ground before the court.
  • Writ petition (High Court Division): You can petition the High Court to quash (cancel) the FIR if it is frivolous, motivated by malice, or does not disclose a cognisable offence on its face.
  • Counter-complaint: If the FIR is made maliciously, you may have grounds to file a counter-complaint for filing a false report under Section 211 of the Penal Code.

Courts in Bangladesh are vigilant against misuse of criminal process. A well-argued quashing petition can terminate a false case before it reaches trial.

How Police Investigation Proceeds After FIR

After an FIR is registered, the police officer in charge investigates:

  • Visits the scene (if relevant) and collects physical evidence
  • Records statements from the complainant, witnesses, and (voluntarily) the accused
  • May arrest the accused (in a cognisable case) and apply for remand for interrogation
  • Prepares the investigation report

During investigation, you are not required to make any statement to police without your lawyer present. Exercise this right. Anything you say voluntarily to police may be used against you. For remand hearings, an experienced criminal lawyer will oppose unnecessarily long remand periods.

Charge Sheet and Cognisance by Court

Once the investigation is complete (typically within a prescribed period), the Investigating Officer submits either:

  • Charge Sheet (accusation report): Recommends prosecution of the accused. The Magistrate then takes cognisance of the offence and the case proceeds to trial.
  • Final Report (acquittal report): Recommends no action, usually when evidence is insufficient. The case may close, though the complainant can challenge this.

After a charge sheet is filed, the accused must appear before the Magistrate. Your lawyer will handle all court appearances and interlocutory applications (bail renewal, discharge etc.) on your behalf.

Building Your Defence Early

The earlier you start building your defence, the stronger it will be. From the moment you learn of the FIR:

  • Identify and preserve all relevant evidence supporting your innocence
  • Ensure alibi witnesses are available and their accounts are documented
  • Obtain CCTV footage, call records, or digital evidence before it is lost
  • Brief your lawyer fully and frankly — lawyer-client communications are privileged

If the matter may involve the High Court or Supreme Court, engage a lawyer who practices at those levels. An FIR is the start of a process — with the right legal support, many such cases are resolved or dismissed long before reaching trial.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can police arrest me without a warrant after an FIR?

In cognisable offences (serious crimes), yes — police can arrest without a warrant. In non-cognisable offences, they need a Magistrate's warrant.

Do I have to answer police questions after an FIR?

You may be called for questioning but you are not obligated to make any self-incriminating statement. Always have your lawyer present during any questioning.

How do I find out if an FIR has been filed against me?

Your lawyer can check with the concerned police station through official channels. An FIR is a public document once registered.

Can an FIR be cancelled or withdrawn?

The complainant can seek to withdraw the FIR, but police are not bound to stop investigation. A High Court quashing petition is the most reliable route to cancel a false FIR.

What is remand and can I oppose it?

Remand is police custody for investigation. Your lawyer can oppose remand applications before the Magistrate and argue for limiting or refusing remand.

How long can police keep me in custody after FIR arrest?

Police can detain you for up to 24 hours and must produce you before a Magistrate. The Magistrate can then grant judicial custody or remand.

What happens if I am falsely accused?

A lawyer can immediately apply for anticipatory bail, oppose remand, and file a writ petition to quash the FIR. You may also file a counter-complaint for false accusation.

Should I negotiate with the complainant directly?

Never negotiate directly without your lawyer's guidance. Any direct contact risks being portrayed as pressure or inducement, which can weaken your case.

Flat and Apartment Buying Legal Checklist in Bangladesh 2026: Registration Fees, Developer Disputes & Gain Tax

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-20 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Purchasing a flat or apartment in Dhaka—whether in Uttara, Mirpur, Bashundhara, Dhanmondi, or Gulshan—represents one of the largest capital investments an individual or expatriate family will ever make. However, the urban real estate market is fraught with perils: developer delivery delays spanning years, unapproved floor additions violating RAJUK master plans, mortgaged mother land, and staggering hidden registration and tax costs. The <strong>Real Estate Development and Management Act, 2010 (রিয়েল এস্টেট উন্নয়ন ও ব্যবস্থাপনা আইন ২০১০)</strong> grants robust statutory rights to apartment buyers, provided the contractual documents are drafted and vetted with absolute precision. This definitive 2026 guide by <strong>Advocate Md. Shah Alam</strong>, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, provides the ultimate buyer's legal checklist.

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Registration Fee & Stamp Duty1% Registration Fee + 1.5% Stamp Duty on deed value
Local Government Tax & VAT2%–3% Local Govt Tax + 1.5%–4.5% VAT (varies by City/Pourosova/Union)
Source Tax (Gain Tax / TDS)1% to 8% depending on mouza classification under Income Tax Act 2023

📋 In This Article

  2. Phase 1: Mother Land Title & Survey Verification
  3. Phase 2: Verifying RAJUK, CDA & Municipal Approvals
  4. Phase 3: The Developer Agreement & Registered Power of Attorney
  5. Phase 4: Scrutinizing the Deed of Agreement for Sale (Baina Nama)
  6. Apartment Registration Fees & Gain Tax Breakdown (2026 Rates)
  7. Remedies Under Real Estate Act 2010 for Developer Default
  8. Post-Handover Checklist: Mutation, Association & Utility Demarcation
  9. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Why Independent Legal Due Diligence is Vital for Flat Buyers

Never rely on a real estate developer’s in-house panel lawyer. In-house lawyers represent the developer's corporate interests, not the buyer's financial safety. An independent property advocate scrutinizes whether the developer has actual authority to sell the flat, whether the landowner has raised any disputes, and whether the project sits on encumbered or mortgaged soil.

Phase 1: Mother Land Title & Survey Verification

An apartment building stands upon 'Mother Land'. If the mother land's title is flawed, every apartment deed constructed upon it is legally compromised:

  • Chain of Ownership (বায়া দলিল): Verify an unbroken 25-to-30-year chain of title connecting current landowners to historical cadastral records.
  • Survey Khatians: Inspect CS, SA, RS, and BS/City Jarip Khatians to ensure the land classification permits residential construction (not wetland/viti or acquired government property).
  • Sub-Registry Non-Encumbrance Certificate (NEC): Obtain a 12-to-30-year NEC certifying that the landowner has not mortgaged the plot to commercial banks.

Phase 2: Verifying RAJUK, CDA & Municipal Approvals

Unapproved construction is subject to immediate demolition by regulatory authorities:

  • Approved Building Plan (নকশা অনুমোদন): Cross-check the architectural design approved by RAJUK (Dhaka), CDA (Chittagong), or KDA (Khulna).
  • Floor Number Verification: Confirm that the specific flat you are buying is part of the approved floor plan (e.g., buying 8th floor when approval was granted only up to 6 floors is illegal).
  • Fire, Environmental & Civil Aviation NOCs: Ensure high-rise buildings possess valid clearances from the Fire Service and Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB).

Phase 3: The Developer Agreement & Registered Power of Attorney

In joint-venture developments between a private landowner and a developer company:

  1. Examine the Development Agreement (JV Agreement) to see the exact allocation of floors and car parking spaces between landowner and developer.
  2. Verify the Registered Irrevocable General Power of Attorney (IGPA) granted by the landowner to the developer under the Power of Attorney Act 2012, confirming the developer has explicit legal authority to execute sale deeds and accept payments from buyers.
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Phase 4: Scrutinizing the Deed of Agreement for Sale (Baina Nama)

The Baina Nama governs the entire transaction until final registration. Ensure these mandatory clauses are included:

  • Exact Specifications: Clear net square footage, common area allocation percentage, and designated car parking slot number.
  • Strict Handover Date & Grace Period: Exact calendar date of flat delivery and compensation penalties for developer delays.
  • No Alteration Clause: A covenant prohibiting the developer from altering architectural layouts without the buyer's written approval.

Apartment Registration Fees & Gain Tax Breakdown (2026 Rates)

The total government cost for registering an apartment in Bangladesh generally amounts to 7% to 10% of the deed valuation:

Tax / Fee Head Applicable Rate (2026)
Stamp Duty 1.5% of total deed value
Registration Fee 1% of deed value
Local Government Tax 1.5% to 2% (City Corporation / Cantonment)
Advance Income Tax (AIT / Gain Tax) Fixed rate per sq metre (Sec 124 of Income Tax Act 2023)

Remedies Under Real Estate Act 2010 for Developer Default

Under the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010, buyers have robust legal protections:

  • Delay Penalty (Section 15): If the developer fails to deliver the flat within the agreed deadline, they must pay monthly compensation to the buyer at the prescribed statutory rate.
  • Arbitration & Notice: Serving a 30-day statutory legal notice followed by arbitration before the Real Estate Arbitration Board.
  • Criminal Prosecution: Section 27 to 36 impose imprisonment of up to 3 years and heavy fines for developers who defraud buyers, construct unauthorized floors, or pledge allocated apartments to third parties.

Post-Handover Checklist: Mutation, Association & Utility Demarcation

After taking physical possession and executing the final registered sale deed (সাব-কবালা দলিল):

  1. Apply for e-Mutation to record your undivided proportionate land share (অবিভক্ত ও অচিহ্নিত অংশ) in your own name at the local AC Land office.
  2. Transfer DESCO/DPDC electricity meters and Titas Gas connections to your name.
  3. Form the Apartment Owners' Welfare Association to manage common facilities, elevators, and security funds.

⚖️ Urgent Case Evaluation & Legal Consultation

Facing property litigation, criminal arrest risk, commercial dispute or constitutional infringement? Consult directly with Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Advocate, Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a developer sell parking spaces separately?

Under the Real Estate Act 2010, developers cannot sell common areas or open spaces, but designated covered car parking spaces allocated in the approved plan may be allotted to flat buyers.

What is an undivided proportionate land share?

When you buy an apartment, you own both the physical flat space and a proportionate undivided ownership share of the land underneath the building.

What should I do if a developer delays apartment handover?

Serve a formal legal notice through a Supreme Court advocate demanding completion and monthly financial compensation under Section 15 of the Real Estate Act 2010, followed by an arbitration claim or criminal complaint.

Flat Registration Fee in Bangladesh 2026: Stamp Duty, AIT Calculator & Developer Laws

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-08-04 · 18 minutes

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Purchasing an apartment in Dhaka, Chattogram, or other urban hubs represents one of the most substantial financial investments an individual or expatriate family will ever undertake. Beyond agreed builder instalment schedules, prospective buyers must account for mandatory statutory registration expenses, including Stamp Duty, Sub-Registry Fees, Local Government Taxes, Advance Income Tax (AIT), and National Board of Revenue (NBR) developer VAT. Without formal registration under the Registration Act 1908 and the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010, an allotment letter or developer agreement confers no proprietary title. This comprehensive legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate and land law practitioner in Uttara and the Dhaka Judge Court, delivers an authoritative fee calculation matrix, document checklist, and developer dispute remedies.

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Registration Fee & Stamp Duty1% Registration Fee + 1.5% Stamp Duty on deed value
Local Government Tax & VAT2%–3% Local Govt Tax + 1.5%–4.5% VAT (varies by City/Pourosova/Union)
Source Tax (Gain Tax / TDS)1% to 8% depending on mouza classification under Income Tax Act 2023

📋 In This Article

  2. 2. Statutory Fee Schedule: Stamp Duty, Registration & Local Taxes
  3. 3. Advance Income Tax (AIT) & NBR Developer VAT Rules (2026)
  4. 4. Worked Calculation Example: 1,500 Sq Ft Flat in Dhaka vs. Chattogram
  5. 5. Pre-Purchase Legal Checklist: Title Deeds, CS/RS/BS & AC Land Mutation
  6. 6. Building Plan Vetting: RAJUK / CDA Layout Approval & Occupancy Certificate
  7. 7. Step-by-Step Flat Deed Execution & Sub-Registry Procedure
  8. 8. Legal Remedies Against Developer Delay, Fraud, or Non-Registration
  9. 9. Guidelines for NRBs & Expatriates Buying Flats in Bangladesh
  10. 10. Illustrative Scenario: Resolving Delayed Registration and Title Clearance
  11. 11. Talk to an Advocate: Flat Deed Vetting & Registration Support

1. Legal Framework: Registration Act 1908 & Real Estate Act 2010

In Bangladesh, apartment ownership is not merely a commercial handover of keys; it is a formal conveyance of proportionate undivided and indivisible land share coupled with physical apartment space. Under Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908 and Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882, any transfer of immovable property exceeding 100 BDT in value must be effected through a registered instrument. An allotment paper, money receipt, or unregistered builder booking agreement confers zero legal title in the eyes of a civil court.

The relationship between buyers and developers is regulated by the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 (Act No. XX of 2010). This legislation prohibits developers from selling apartments without prior project approval from development authorities (such as RAJUK, CDA, KDA, or RDA), mandates registration of developer power of attorney, and penalizes structural deviations or delivery defaults. When executing the final Saf-Kabala (Sale Deed), both the landowner and the developer holding a registered Power of Attorney must join as executants to ensure valid passage of title.

Understanding statutory expenses prevents unexpected financial strain during the final registration phase. For complex conveyancing, cross-checking chain deeds and vetting developer powers with a land lawyer in Bangladesh protects buyers from protracted title litigation.

2. Statutory Fee Schedule: Stamp Duty, Registration & Local Taxes

Statutory fees are computed either on the declared purchase price in the deed or the official government-notified minimum Mouza value (determined periodically by the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs), whichever amount is higher. Sub-Registrars strictly reject undervalued deed submissions.

The core statutory schedule across various geographic jurisdictions in Bangladesh is summarized below:

Statutory Cost HeadCity Corporation (DNCC, DSCC, CCC)Municipality (Pourashava)Union Parishad / Rural
Registration Fee1.0% of Deed Valuation1.0% of Deed Valuation1.0% of Deed Valuation
Stamp Duty1.5% of Deed Valuation1.5% of Deed Valuation1.5% of Deed Valuation
Local Government Tax3.0% (City Corporation)2.0% (Pourashava)1.0% (Union Parishad)
Affidavit Fee300 BDT Stamp300 BDT Stamp300 BDT Stamp
Sub-Registry N-Fee & E-FeeBDT 240 + Page Copying FeeBDT 240 + Page Copying FeeBDT 240 + Page Copying Fee

All fees are deposited directly into designated treasury accounts at Sonali Bank branches using automated e-Chalan codes. Cash payments directly to Sub-Registry personnel are prohibited under Directorate of Registration anti-corruption circulars.

3. Advance Income Tax (AIT) & NBR Developer VAT Rules (2026)

In addition to standard registration fees, apartment transactions involve direct and indirect taxes administered under the Income Tax Act 2023 and the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act 2012.

Advance Income Tax (AIT / Source Tax): Under Section 125 of the Income Tax Act 2023, source tax must be collected by the registering officer prior to registration. In commercial areas and prime residential sectors of Dhaka (such as Gulshan, Banani, Motijheel, Dhanmondi, Uttara, and Bashundhara), AIT for apartments is levied on a fixed square-meter basis, ranging from 1,000 BDT to 2,000 BDT per square meter. In other residential areas, it is calculated as a percentage (typically 2% to 4%) of deed valuation. By standard legal convention, AIT is the statutory liability of the seller or developer, representing advance tax on business turnover or capital gains.

Developer VAT (NBR Statutory Regulatory Orders): When purchasing directly from a commercial builder or REHAB-affiliated developer, VAT is payable on the building construction value:

  • Apartments up to 1,600 Square Feet: 2.0% VAT on deed valuation.
  • Apartments exceeding 1,600 Square Feet: 4.5% VAT on deed valuation.
  • Commercial Space & Office Suites: 15.0% standard VAT.
  • Private Re-sale Flats (Citizen to Citizen): 0% VAT. Re-sale transactions between individuals do not attract developer VAT because no commercial development service is rendered.

4. Worked Calculation Example: 1,500 Sq Ft Flat in Dhaka vs. Chattogram

To illustrate how these statutory percentages translate into exact expenditure, consider a practical worked example: purchasing a brand-new 1,500 square-foot residential apartment from a developer in Dhaka North City Corporation (e.g. Uttara or Mirpur) with a deed valuation of 10,000,000 BDT (1 Crore BDT), compared with the same flat in Chattogram City Corporation.

Cost ComponentDhaka City Corp (1 Crore BDT)Chattogram City Corp (1 Crore BDT)Statutory Payer
Registration Fee (1.0%)BDT 1,00,000BDT 1,00,000Buyer
Stamp Duty (1.5%)BDT 1,50,000BDT 1,50,000Buyer
Local Govt. Tax (3.0%)BDT 3,00,000BDT 3,00,000Buyer
Developer VAT (2.0% for 1500 sq ft)BDT 2,00,000BDT 2,00,000Buyer (Reimbursed to NBR)
Advance Income Tax (AIT / Source Tax)BDT 2,00,000 (Approx. 2% or sqm)BDT 2,00,000 (Approx. 2% or sqm)Seller / Developer
Affidavit, E-Fee, N-Fee & DraftingBDT 15,000 – 25,000BDT 15,000 – 25,000Buyer
Total Buyer OutlayBDT 7,65,000 – 7,75,000 (~7.7%)BDT 7,65,000 – 7,75,000 (~7.7%)Excluding Developer AIT

If the apartment area exceeded 1,600 square feet (e.g. a 2,000 sq ft luxury flat), the VAT rate rises from 2.0% to 4.5%, adding an additional 2,50,000 BDT in government taxes. Check our guide on land registration fee calculator for comparative plot registration schedules.

5. Pre-Purchase Legal Checklist: Title Deeds, CS/RS/BS & AC Land Mutation

Careful legal due diligence prior to signing any contract or advancing earnest money is vital. A real estate advocate checks a 30-year unbroken chain of title documents before approving an apartment purchase:

  1. Mother Title Deed (Mool Dalil): Verify original ownership deeds of the underlying land. If acquired through inheritance, verify partition deeds (Bonton-nama) or civil court partition decrees.
  2. Record of Rights (Khatian Porcha): Examine Cadastral Survey (CS), State Acquisition (SA), Revisional Survey (RS), and Dhaka City Jarip (BS) records. Ensure the landowner's name matches the latest recorded Khatian.
  3. AC Land E-Namjari Mutation: Confirm that the landowner or developer has completed digital mutation with the relevant Upazila / Circle AC Land office and holds a formal DCR (Duplicate Carbon Receipt) and mutation Khatian.
  4. Land Development Tax (Dakhila): Inspect updated online land development tax receipts for the current Bengali calendar fiscal year.
  5. Non-Encumbrance Certificate (NEC): Conduct an official search at the Sub-Registry Office for the past 12 to 30 years to confirm that the underlying land is free from mortgages, bank hypothecations, or pending civil litigation.

Review our checklist on buying land in Bangladesh from abroad for detailed remote vetting protocols.

6. Building Plan Vetting: RAJUK / CDA Layout Approval & Occupancy Certificate

A registered land title is insufficient if the physical building violates urban planning and structural safety laws. In Dhaka, development is supervised by the Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha (RAJUK); in Chattogram, by the Chattogram Development Authority (CDA); and in other cities by corresponding regional development bodies.

Buyers must verify the following statutory approvals:

  • Special Project Approval & Land Use Clearance: Confirmation that the plot is designated for residential use under the Master Plan.
  • Approved Building Plan (Sthapotik Noksha): Inspect the official architecturally sanctioned plan bearing the official seal and file reference number of RAJUK or CDA. Cross-check approved floor heights, setbacks, car parking allocations, and Far (Floor Area Ratio) limits.
  • Unauthorized Floor Inspection: If the approved plan sanctions 8 stories but the developer has constructed 10 stories, purchasing an apartment on the 9th or 10th floor is illegal. The Sub-Registrar cannot legally register an unauthorized floor, and RAJUK retains powers of demolition.
  • Occupancy Certificate: Under the Bangladesh National Building Code (BNBC) and RAJUK rules, developers must obtain an Occupancy Certificate confirming that construction strictly matches approved plans before utility connections and residential occupancy are lawful.
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

7. Step-by-Step Flat Deed Execution & Sub-Registry Procedure

The legal process of formal conveyance at the Sub-Registry Office follows structured procedural stages:

  1. Drafting the Deed of Sale: The deed must accurately detail the proportionate land share, apartment number, floor level, super built-up area, common facility allocations, and car park demarcations.
  2. Chalan Generation and Fee Payment: Registration fees, stamp duty, local government taxes, and AIT are deposited through treasury chalans at Sonali Bank.
  3. Physical or Biometric Attendance: The buyer and the developer's authorized representative appear before the Sub-Registrar. Both parties submit biometric fingerprint verification matched against the Election Commission NID database.
  4. Execution & Registration Endorsement: The Sub-Registrar examines identity credentials, confirms payment chalans, and signs the registration order.
  5. Issuance of Form-52 Receipt: The buyer receives an official Form-52 token receipt. The original registered volume deed is released upon final volume binding, typically within several months.
  6. Individual Post-Purchase Mutation: Following registration, the buyer must immediately apply for an individual AC Land e-Namjari mutation in their own name and separate holding tax registration with the City Corporation.

8. Legal Remedies Against Developer Delay, Fraud, or Non-Registration

When a developer delays handover, constructs substandard facilities, or refuses to execute registration, buyers possess actionable statutory remedies under Bangladeshi law:

  • Statutory Compensation under Real Estate Act 2010: Under Section 15 of Act No. XX of 2010, if a developer fails to deliver possession within the agreed contractual period, they must pay compensation interest at 15% per annum on the total amount paid by the purchaser for the delay period.
  • Formal Legal Notice: The buyer must dispatch a formal Legal Notice drafted by a Supreme Court advocate demanding completion, registration, and compensation within 30 to 60 days.
  • REHAB Dispute Resolution: If the developer is a registered member of the Real Estate & Housing Association of Bangladesh (REHAB), complaints can be lodged with the REHAB Mediation and Arbitration Cell.
  • Suit for Specific Performance of Contract: Under the Specific Relief Act 1877, the buyer can institute a suit before the Joint District Judge to legally compel the developer and landowner to execute the registered deed. Read our detailed analysis on breach of contract damages and specific performance in Bangladesh.
  • Criminal Complaint for Fraud and Embezzlement: If a developer sells the same flat to multiple buyers or mortgages the property to a bank without authorization, criminal proceedings under Sections 406 and 420 of the Penal Code 1860 can be initiated before a Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court.

9. Guidelines for NRBs & Expatriates Buying Flats in Bangladesh

Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) living in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and the Middle East represent a major segment of apartment buyers in Dhaka. However, managing transactions from abroad creates distinctive legal risks.

NRBs should adhere to these established safeguards:

  • Channel All Funds via Inward Banking Remittance: Always transfer purchase instalments through formal banking channels into a Non-Resident Foreign Currency Deposit (NFCD) or Non-Resident Investor's Taka Account (NITA). Official banking remittance certificates shield the buyer from National Board of Revenue scrutiny and enable legitimate fund repatriation if the property is later liquidated.
  • Execution of Special Power of Attorney: If the expatriate buyer cannot travel to Bangladesh for registration, they can execute a Special Power of Attorney appointing a trusted family member or advocate. The document must be executed and attested before the consular officer at the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission in their host country, authenticated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) in Dhaka, and stamped by the Collector of Stamps under the Power of Attorney Act 2012. Review our guide on power of attorney property transfer in Bangladesh.
  • Independent Chamber Vetting: Never rely on developer-provided lawyers. Retain independent legal counsel to verify title authenticity, RAJUK approvals, and encumbrance records directly at official land registries. Visit our NRB legal help service page for overseas legal representation.

10. Illustrative Scenario: Resolving Delayed Registration and Title Clearance

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): An expatriate physician residing in London purchased a 1,650 square-foot apartment in Uttara Sector 11, Dhaka, paying 90% of the agreed 1.2 Crore BDT price over three years. Although physical handover occurred in late 2024, the developer repeatedly postponed deed registration, citing unresolved disputes with the original landowner over proportionate floor allocations.

Facing escalating uncertainty and unable to obtain an individual utility connection or mortgage, the overseas buyer retained Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber. Our legal intervention unfolded methodically:

  1. Retrieved certified records from the Sub-Registry Office and discovered that while the landowner had granted a registered Power of Attorney, the developer had failed to obtain an amended sanction from RAJUK for minor terrace adjustments.
  2. Issued a statutory 30-day Legal Notice under the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010 to both the developer and the landowner, establishing their joint legal liability to convey title and claiming 15% statutory delay compensation.
  3. Convened a structured tripartite negotiation at our Uttara legal chamber between the developer's managing director and the landowner's legal representative.
  4. Drafted a tripartite Supplementary Conveyance Deed clarifying common space demarcations and ensuring all Sonali Bank treasury e-chalans for Stamp Duty, Local Government Tax, and Developer VAT were correctly apportioned.
  5. Supervised the final registration of the Saf-Kabala deed before the Sub-Registrar through an embassy-authenticated Special Power of Attorney, successfully securing the Form-52 receipt and subsequently completing the buyer's AC Land e-Namjari mutation without litigation.

11. Talk to an Advocate: Flat Deed Vetting & Registration Support

Navigating apartment conveyancing, RAJUK approvals, and complex treasury tax calculations demands experienced legal guidance. Advocate Md. Shah Alam and his team of Supreme Court and Dhaka Court advocates provide end-to-end title vetting, developer agreement drafting, and sub-registry representation.

Need an advocate for this matter in Bangladesh? Send your documents on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: a first document review can be done remotely.

Our principal chamber is conveniently situated in Uttara, Dhaka, within easy access of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, alongside our daily litigation chamber at the Dhaka Judge Court.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the total flat registration cost percentage in Dhaka in 2026?

In Dhaka City Corporation areas (DNCC and DSCC), total registration expenses generally range between 7.5% and 10.5% of deed valuation. This includes 1.0% Registration Fee, 1.5% Stamp Duty, 3.0% Local Government Tax, 2.0% to 4.5% Developer VAT (depending on square footage), and miscellaneous drafting/e-chalan charges.

Who is legally responsible for paying the developer VAT and Advance Income Tax (AIT)?

By law, Advance Income Tax (AIT / Source Tax) is the legal liability of the seller or developer as advance business income tax. Developer VAT is assessed on the consumer by the NBR and is paid by the purchaser to the developer for deposit into the government exchequer. Private re-sale flats between individuals are entirely exempt from developer VAT.

Can a flat be registered without an individual AC Land e-Namjari mutation?

For initial deed registration, the Sub-Registrar requires the parent land mutation (e-Namjari) in the name of the developer or landowner along with updated land tax (Dakhila). Once the flat is registered, the buyer must immediately submit an individual e-Namjari application on land.gov.bd to record their proportionate undivided land share.

What happens if a real estate developer delays handover or deed registration?

Under Section 15 of the Real Estate Development and Management Act 2010, the developer is legally bound to compensate the buyer with 15% annual interest on all monies paid during the delay period. The purchaser can issue a formal Legal Notice and file a suit for Specific Performance of Contract in civil court.

How can overseas expatriates (NRBs) register an apartment without travelling to Dhaka?

An expatriate can execute a Special Power of Attorney appointing a local family member or advocate. The document must be executed before a consular officer at the Bangladesh Embassy abroad, attested by MoFA in Dhaka, and validated by the Collector of Stamps before submission to the Sub-Registry Office.

Is an unregistered allotment letter or sale agreement legally enforceable?

An unregistered allotment letter does not create proprietary title under Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908. It functions solely as evidence of a personal contract. To establish complete ownership enforceable against third parties, a registered Saf-Kabala (Sale Deed) is legally mandatory.

What is the difference between carpet area, super built-up area, and deed measurement?

Carpet area represents actual usable indoor floor space within interior walls. Built-up area includes outer walls and balconies. Super built-up area adds a proportionate share of common spaces such as lobbies, stairs, and generator rooms. The deed specifies both the apartment super built-up area and the proportionate undivided land share.

What legal documents must a buyer collect from the developer after registration?

Following registration, the buyer must collect: (1) Form-52 registration receipt and subsequent original certified registered Saf-Kabala deed; (2) Certified copies of the parent title deed and registered Power of Attorney; (3) Approved RAJUK/CDA architectural plans and Occupancy Certificate; and (4) Updated land development tax Dakhila.

Foreign Company Registration Bangladesh – Branch Office, Liaison & Investment Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-08 · 9 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Bangladesh is one of South Asia's fastest-growing investment destinations, offering 100% foreign ownership in most sectors, competitive labour costs, and significant tax incentives. However, foreign companies entering the Bangladesh market must navigate multiple regulatory layers — BIDA, RJSC, Bangladesh Bank, and sector-specific regulators. This guide explains every option available to foreign investors.

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Registration Fee & Stamp Duty1% Registration Fee + 1.5% Stamp Duty on deed value
Local Government Tax & VAT2%–3% Local Govt Tax + 1.5%–4.5% VAT (varies by City/Pourosova/Union)
Source Tax (Gain Tax / TDS)1% to 8% depending on mouza classification under Income Tax Act 2023
Official Land & Mouza Portalsland.gov.bd, dlrms.land.gov.bd, and eporcha.gov.bd
📋 In This Article

  2. Option 1: Subsidiary Company (Local Incorporation)
  3. Option 2: Branch Office in Bangladesh
  4. Option 3: Liaison/Representative Office
  5. Option 4: Joint Venture Company
  6. BIDA Approval: When Is It Required?
  7. Sectors Restricted to Foreign Investment
  8. Remittance and Profit Repatriation Rules
  9. Work Permit and Visa for Foreign Employees
  10. Tax Benefits for Foreign Companies in Bangladesh
  11. Step-by-Step Setup Process

Foreign Investment Overview in Bangladesh

Bangladesh actively encourages foreign direct investment (FDI) and has among the most open FDI regimes in South Asia. The key legal framework for foreign investment includes:

  • Foreign Private Investment (Promotion and Protection) Act 1980 — the foundational FDI protection statute
  • Companies Act 1994 — governs company formation including foreign-owned companies
  • Bangladesh Investment Development Authority Act 2016 — established BIDA as the one-stop investment facilitation body
  • Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 (FERA) — governs foreign exchange transactions

Key advantages for foreign investors in Bangladesh:

  • 100% foreign equity ownership permitted in most sectors
  • Full repatriation of profits, dividends, and capital
  • No discrimination between foreign and domestic investors
  • Tax holidays in Special Economic Zones (SEZs) and Export Processing Zones (EPZs)
  • Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs) with over 30 countries including the USA, UK, Germany, and China

Option 1: Subsidiary Company (Local Incorporation)

The most common structure for foreign companies entering Bangladesh is to incorporate a private limited company under the Companies Act 1994 — known as a "subsidiary" when the parent company holds a majority of shares.

Key features:

  • The subsidiary is a separate legal entity from the foreign parent — it assumes its own liabilities
  • 100% foreign shareholding is permitted in most sectors
  • No prior government approval required for most sectors — incorporation through RJSC is sufficient
  • Can carry out full commercial operations in Bangladesh
  • Can employ Bangladeshi nationals and obtain work permits for foreign employees

Process:

  1. Name clearance from RJSC
  2. Prepare Memorandum and Articles of Association
  3. File registration documents and pay fees at RJSC
  4. Obtain Certificate of Incorporation
  5. Post-incorporation: Trade Licence, TIN, VAT registration, encashment certificate for inward remittance of capital

A corporate lawyer in Dhaka will handle the complete setup process, including ensuring the MOA/AOA correctly reflects the foreign ownership structure and business objectives.

Option 2: Branch Office in Bangladesh

A foreign company may establish a Branch Office in Bangladesh without incorporating a separate local entity. The branch is an extension of the foreign parent company — not a separate legal person.

Regulatory requirements:

  • Approval from BIDA (Bangladesh Investment Development Authority) is mandatory
  • Registration with the RJSC as a foreign company under Part XII of the Companies Act 1994
  • Bangladesh Bank approval for remittance of branch establishment expenses
  • Minimum inward remittance requirement (typically USD 50,000 or equivalent)

Permitted activities for a Branch Office:

  • Undertaking commercial operations on behalf of the foreign parent
  • Generating revenue from sales of goods/services in Bangladesh
  • Contracting with Bangladesh government or private entities

Restriction: A Branch Office cannot export its own goods from Bangladesh — it operates on behalf of the foreign parent's business only.

Branch offices must file audited accounts with both RJSC and BIDA annually, and remit profits only after obtaining Bangladesh Bank permission for outward remittance.

Option 3: Liaison/Representative Office

A Liaison Office (also called a Representative Office) is a limited-activity presence in Bangladesh. It cannot generate revenue in Bangladesh — it exists solely to promote the foreign parent company's business, collect market information, and facilitate communication.

Permitted activities:

  • Market research and business promotion
  • Facilitating orders and communications between Bangladesh customers and the foreign parent
  • Quality inspection and sourcing liaison (common for garment buyers)

Prohibited activities:

  • Issuing invoices or signing contracts in Bangladesh
  • Generating local revenue or income
  • Engaging in import/export on its own account

Requirements: BIDA approval, RJSC registration, and Bangladesh Bank approval for remittance of operating expenses. The parent company typically remits operating expenses in foreign currency, which the office uses to fund its Bangladesh operations.

A Liaison Office is ideal for foreign companies exploring the Bangladesh market before committing to a full Branch Office or subsidiary.

Option 4: Joint Venture Company

A Joint Venture (JV) is a company incorporated in Bangladesh where a foreign investor co-owns shares with a Bangladeshi partner. This is often preferred:

  • In sectors where local partnership is legally required (e.g., media, certain defence-related industries)
  • When the Bangladeshi partner brings essential local knowledge, licences, or market access
  • To share investment risk while leveraging local networks

A JV company is incorporated like any other private limited company under the Companies Act 1994, but the shareholders include both foreign and Bangladeshi parties. The JV agreement — governing profit sharing, management control, exit mechanisms, and dispute resolution — is a critical document that must be carefully drafted by a corporate lawyer.

Choosing the wrong Bangladeshi partner or having an inadequately drafted JV agreement is one of the most common and costly mistakes foreign investors make in Bangladesh. Engage a corporate lawyer before signing any JV arrangement.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

BIDA Approval: When Is It Required?

BIDA (Bangladesh Investment Development Authority) operates as Bangladesh's primary investment promotion and regulatory body. BIDA approval (now called Investment Registration Certificate / IRC) is required for:

  • Establishing a Branch Office in Bangladesh
  • Establishing a Liaison Office
  • Importing machinery and equipment (for project purposes)
  • Obtaining work permits for foreign employees (BIDA issues work permits)
  • Accessing certain investment incentives and tax holidays

BIDA also facilitates the One-Stop Service (OSS) centre, which allows investors to access up to 152 government services from a single platform — including company registration, work permits, and utility connections.

For subsidiary company incorporation, BIDA registration is not mandatory (though recommended for work permit purposes). For Branch and Liaison Offices, it is essential.

Sectors Restricted to Foreign Investment

Most sectors in Bangladesh are open to 100% foreign ownership. However, a small number of sectors require local partnership or are reserved for Bangladeshi nationals:

  • Reserved sectors (100% Bangladeshi-owned): Small and cottage industries, retail trading (except certain categories), internal waterway transport
  • Sectors requiring local equity: Print and electronic media, certain defence/security-related industries
  • Sectors with additional regulatory approval: Banking (Bangladesh Bank), insurance (IDRA), telecommunications (BTRC), power (BPDB/BERC), pharmaceuticals (DGDA)

Before committing to any Bangladesh investment, a corporate lawyer should conduct a sector-specific regulatory analysis to confirm investment is permitted and identify any additional licences or approvals required.

Tax Benefits for Foreign Companies in Bangladesh

Bangladesh offers significant tax incentives to attract foreign investment:

  • Tax holiday: Companies in designated Special Economic Zones (SEZs) and Export Processing Zones (EPZs) qualify for 10-year tax holidays
  • Reduced corporate tax: Publicly traded companies pay 22.5% vs 27.5% for private companies — encouraging stock market listing
  • Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAAs): Bangladesh has DTAAs with many countries, reducing withholding tax on dividends, interest, and royalties
  • Duty-free machinery import: For new industrial investment, import of capital machinery may be duty-free
  • Accelerated depreciation: Available for certain categories of industrial investment

Tax planning from the outset is essential. Engage a tax lawyer to structure your Bangladesh investment in the most tax-efficient manner.

Step-by-Step Setup Process

For a foreign company setting up a subsidiary (private limited company) in Bangladesh — the most common structure — the process is:

  1. Corporate structure decision: Engage a corporate lawyer to confirm the right structure (subsidiary, branch, liaison, JV) for your business model.
  2. Name clearance: Apply to RJSC for name clearance (1–3 days).
  3. Document preparation: Prepare MOA/AOA, apostilled/notarised parent company documents, board resolution authorising Bangladesh investment, director NID/passports.
  4. RJSC registration: File incorporation documents and pay fees. Certificate of Incorporation issued in 3–7 days.
  5. Post-incorporation: Trade Licence, TIN, VAT (BIN) registration, corporate bank account opening.
  6. Capital remittance: Remit initial equity capital from abroad through banking channels and obtain encashment certificate.
  7. BIDA registration: Apply for Investment Registration Certificate (IRC) from BIDA to facilitate work permits and access to BIDA services.
  8. Work permits: Apply for work permits for foreign employees through BIDA's OSS centre.
  9. Sector-specific licences: Apply for any additional sectoral licences required for your specific business.

Total timeline from engagement to operational readiness: typically 4–8 weeks with proper legal support. Contact Adv. Shah Alam for a customised setup plan for your Bangladesh entry.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a foreign company own 100% of a Bangladesh company?

Yes, in most sectors. Bangladesh permits 100% foreign ownership in the majority of industries. Only a small number of reserved sectors require local equity partnership or are closed to foreign investment. Confirm sector eligibility with a corporate lawyer before proceeding.

What is the minimum investment required to set up a foreign company in Bangladesh?

There is no statutory minimum for a subsidiary (private limited company) incorporated locally. For a Branch Office, BIDA typically requires a minimum inward remittance of USD 50,000. Special Economic Zones may have specific minimum investment thresholds.

Can a foreign company repatriate profits from Bangladesh?

Yes. Bangladesh guarantees full repatriation of dividends, profits, and capital for foreign investors under the Foreign Private Investment Act 1980. Repatriation requires Bangladesh Bank permission for outward remittance, which is routinely granted upon producing audited accounts and tax clearance.

Does a foreign company need a local director?

A private limited company requires a minimum of two directors, but there is no legal requirement for a Bangladeshi director. In practice, banks often prefer at least one director with a Bangladesh address. Foreign directors must provide notarised and apostilled identity documents.

How long does it take to get a work permit for a foreign employee in Bangladesh?

Work permits are issued by BIDA through its One-Stop Service. Processing typically takes 3–8 weeks. Foreign employees should enter Bangladesh on a visa appropriate to their employment status and should not work until the work permit is formally issued.
