entries.body:
GD vs FIR Bangladesh: Key Differences, When to File & Legal Steps

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-05-05 · 9 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Many people in Bangladesh confuse a General Diary (GD) with a First Information Report (FIR) — but they are legally very different. One is simply a record at the police station; the other sets the entire criminal justice system in motion. Filing the wrong one can waste critical time, weaken your legal position, or even expose you to legal risk. This guide explains exactly what each document is, when to file which, and what to do if police refuse to cooperate.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order
Official Portalssupremecourt.gov.bd, judiciary.gov.bd, pcc.police.gov.bd & land.gov.bd
Supreme Court ChamberAdvocate Md. Shah Alam — Uttara & Dhaka Judge Court (+880 1712-655546)
📋 In This Article
  1. What is a General Diary (GD)?
  2. What is an FIR (First Information Report)?
  3. GD vs FIR: Key Differences at a Glance
  4. When Should You File a GD?
  5. When Should You File an FIR?
  6. Can a GD Be Converted Into an FIR?
  7. What If Police Refuse to File Your GD or FIR?
  8. Legal Risks of Filing a False GD or FIR
  9. When to Contact a Criminal Lawyer

What is a General Diary (GD)?

A General Diary (GD) — also called a Daily Diary — is a written entry in the official diary maintained at every police station in Bangladesh. It is not a criminal case. A GD is simply a record of information, events, or complaints that the police station logs for reference.

Key facts about a GD:

  • No investigation is triggered. Police are not legally required to investigate based on a GD alone.
  • Anyone can file a GD — no fee is charged, and no evidence is required at the time of filing.
  • GDs are used for informational purposes: missing persons, lost documents, threats, domestic disputes, or to create an official timestamp of an event.
  • Police are legally obligated to accept and record your GD entry. Refusal is improper.
  • A GD number is issued as proof of filing — always keep this number safe.

A GD is often the first step people take before understanding whether a criminal offence has actually occurred. It creates an official record that can be useful later if the situation escalates.

What is an FIR (First Information Report)?

An FIR (First Information Report) is the formal written document that officially starts a criminal case in Bangladesh. It is governed by Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC).

Key facts about an FIR:

  • An FIR triggers a mandatory police investigation. Once filed, the police must investigate — they cannot ignore it.
  • An FIR can only be filed for cognizable offences — crimes where the police can arrest without a warrant (theft, assault, murder, fraud, robbery, cyber crime, etc.).
  • The person named in the FIR becomes the accused. This has serious legal consequences — including potential arrest.
  • FIRs are numbered, tracked, and become court records.
  • Police must register an FIR when a cognizable offence is reported. Refusing to register is itself an offence.

If you are the victim of a crime, an FIR is the legal mechanism to set the justice system in motion. If you are named in an FIR, you should contact a criminal lawyer in Dhaka immediately — before speaking to the police.

GD vs FIR: Key Differences at a Glance

This comparison table shows the critical differences between a General Diary and a First Information Report in Bangladesh:

Factor General Diary (GD) FIR
Purpose Record information / create timestamp Start a criminal case
Legal effect No case — no investigation required Police must investigate
Who can file Anyone Victim, witness, or their lawyer
Police action Record only Must investigate and submit report to Magistrate
Can lead to arrest? No Yes — for cognizable offences
Court involvement No Yes — charge sheet filed in court
When to use Missing items, threats, minor disputes Theft, assault, fraud, murder, cyber crime

Bottom line: A GD is a record. An FIR is the start of a criminal case. Never accept a GD when you should be filing an FIR — police sometimes pressure victims to accept a GD to avoid workload.

When Should You File a GD?

A GD is appropriate when you want to create an official record but a criminal offence may not have occurred yet — or when you need a timestamp for future reference:

  • Lost documents: National ID card, passport, driving licence, chequebook, or certificates
  • Missing person report: First step before an FIR if the person is simply unreachable
  • Threats or harassment: When someone threatens you verbally but no physical crime has occurred yet — creates a paper trail
  • Domestic or neighbour disputes: Minor altercations where you want an official record
  • Before travelling abroad: Some embassies or authorities require a GD as proof of a reported incident
  • Property boundary arguments: Early disputes before they escalate to criminal damage or assault

Important: If a GD situation escalates into a crime — for example, threats become actual assault — you should immediately upgrade to an FIR. A lawyer can help ensure the transition is handled properly.

When Should You File an FIR?

An FIR is mandatory when a cognizable offence has been committed. Common situations requiring an FIR in Bangladesh:

  • Physical assault or battery — including domestic violence
  • Theft, robbery, or burglary
  • Fraud, cheating, or financial crime — including cheque fraud and business scams
  • Land grabbing or property forgery
  • Cyber crime — hacking, online fraud, blackmail, defamation
  • Threats of violence or extortion
  • Sexual harassment or assault
  • Murder or attempted murder

If you have been the victim of any of these offences, insist on an FIR — not a GD. The FIR is your legal weapon to compel police investigation. If you fear being arrested after someone files an FIR against you, a bail lawyer in Dhaka can file anticipatory bail to protect you before arrest occurs.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Can a GD Be Converted Into an FIR?

Yes — and this happens regularly in Bangladesh. A GD can become an FIR in several ways:

  • Police investigation of the GD reveals a cognizable offence. For example, a missing person GD may uncover evidence of kidnapping — triggering an FIR.
  • You request conversion. If you initially filed a GD but later realise a crime has occurred, return to the police station and request that an FIR be registered based on the same facts.
  • A Magistrate orders it. If police refuse to convert a GD to an FIR, you can file a complaint before the Magistrate who can direct the police to register the FIR.

Having the GD number and date on record strengthens your credibility — it shows you reported the matter promptly, even if you initially underestimated its severity.

What If Police Refuse to File Your GD or FIR?

Police refusal to register a GD or FIR is unfortunately common in Bangladesh. Here is exactly what to do:

If Police Refuse Your GD:

  • Insist firmly — there is no legal basis for refusing a GD entry.
  • Ask for the duty officer's name and badge number.
  • Complain to the Superintendent of Police (SP) of the district.

If Police Refuse Your FIR:

  • Send the FIR by registered post to the Officer in Charge (OC) of the police station. This creates a legal record with timestamp that the police cannot deny receiving.
  • Complaint to the SP: File a written complaint to the Superintendent of Police of the district.
  • Narazi petition: File a complaint directly before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or Chief Judicial Magistrate. The Magistrate can order the police to register the FIR and investigate.
  • Writ petition: In extreme cases of refusal, a Supreme Court lawyer can file a writ petition in the High Court Division directing the police to act.

Do not give up if police refuse. The law provides multiple remedies — all of which an experienced criminal lawyer can pursue on your behalf.

Legal Risks of Filing a False GD or FIR

Filing a false complaint carries serious legal consequences in Bangladesh:

  • False FIR — Section 211 of the Penal Code: Filing a false criminal case with intent to harm someone is punishable by up to 2 years imprisonment and fine.
  • Perjury — Section 193: Making false statements during investigation is punishable by up to 7 years.
  • Counter-FIR: The person falsely accused can file their own FIR against the false complainant.
  • Civil damages: The accused can sue for defamation and claim monetary compensation.

If someone has filed a false criminal case against you, act immediately. Anticipatory bail and FIR quashing are your primary legal defences — contact a criminal lawyer before speaking to police.

When to Contact a Criminal Lawyer

You should seek legal advice before going to the police station in these situations:

  • You are unsure whether to file a GD or FIR — a lawyer can assess whether a cognizable offence has occurred.
  • Police are refusing to register your complaint — a lawyer can compel registration through Magistrate or High Court.
  • Someone has filed an FIR against you — a bail lawyer can file anticipatory bail immediately.
  • You need to convert a GD to an FIR — a lawyer ensures the conversion is done properly.
  • Police are pressuring you to withdraw or settle — do not agree without legal advice.

Advocate Md. Shah Alam is an experienced criminal lawyer in Dhaka handling FIR matters, police complaints, bail applications, and criminal defence. Contact our Uttara chamber for same-day consultation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a GD the same as an FIR in Bangladesh?

No. A GD (General Diary) is an informational record at the police station — it does not start a criminal case. An FIR (First Information Report) is a formal criminal complaint that triggers a mandatory police investigation. They serve completely different purposes.

Can I file a GD online in Bangladesh?

Some metropolitan police forces (Dhaka Metropolitan Police) have introduced limited online GD filing for lost documents. However, for most matters — especially threats, disputes, or criminal incidents — you should file in person at the police station to ensure proper recording.

What happens after an FIR is filed against me?

Police will investigate the complaint. You may be called for questioning, and arrest is possible for cognizable offences. Contact a criminal lawyer immediately — do not make any statement to police without legal advice. An anticipatory bail application can protect you from arrest.

Can a false FIR be quashed in Bangladesh?

Yes. A false or malicious FIR can be challenged through anticipatory bail (to prevent arrest), an application under Section 561A CrPC to quash the case, or a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution. A counter-FIR under Section 211 of the Penal Code can also be filed against the false complainant.

Do I need a lawyer to file a GD or FIR?

Legally, no — anyone can file directly. However, having a lawyer ensures: the complaint is accurately worded with all legally required details, police register it properly without downgrading your FIR to a GD, and you receive your copy immediately. For serious matters, legal guidance from the start protects your case.

entries.body:
Government Pension and Gratuity Withholding in Bangladesh: Administrative Tribunal Remedies and Constitutional Writs

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-14 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

After dedicating thirty or thirty-five years of unblemished service to the republic, a retiring government official expects peace of mind and the timely release of their hard-earned pension, gratuity, and General Provident Fund (GPF). Yet, thousands of retired public servants face bureaucratic harassment, seeing their terminal benefits arbitrarily frozen over frivolous audit objections or stalled departmental inquiries.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)

📋 In This Article

  2. Constitutional and Statutory Nature of Pension Rights
  3. Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974 and Gratuity Rules
  4. The Menace of Audit Objections and Illegal Deductions
  5. Departmental Proceedings After Retirement: Legal Limits
  6. Administrative Tribunal Jurisdiction and Procedure
  7. High Court Division Article 102 Writ of Mandamus
  8. Comparison Table: Administrative Tribunal vs. High Court Writ
  9. Illustrative Scenario: Retiree Recovering Withheld Gratuity
  10. Talk to an Advocate

The Crisis of Pension Withholding for Retired Officials

Imagine retiring as a dedicated government schoolteacher, railway officer, or ministry section officer at the age of 59. You have planned your remaining years around your gratuity lump-sum and monthly pension to pay off housing loans, fund your children's higher education, and secure medical care. Instead, months turn into years as the accounts office cites a vague audit objection from twenty years ago or claims an alleged overpayment of a time-scale increment, refusing to issue your Last Pay Certificate (LPC) or Pension Payment Order (PPO).

This bureaucratic gridlock traps thousands of elderly pensioners across Bangladesh in immense financial and emotional distress. Corrupt administrative staff frequently leverage audit objections as tools of extortion, banking on the retiree's exhaustion and reluctance to pursue legal battles.

You must realize that the law is firmly on your side. The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly ruled that pension is not a charitable dole or a bounty granted at the pleasure of the executive; it is vested constitutional property earned through lifelong service. The government has no legal right to withhold it arbitrarily.

Constitutional and Statutory Nature of Pension Rights

Under the jurisprudence of Bangladesh, pension and gratuity rights enjoy powerful constitutional protection. The Supreme Court has established in landmark precedents (such as the Government of Bangladesh vs. Md. Mofizur Rahman line of authorities) that terminal retirement benefits constitute deferred wages.

Because pension constitutes earned remuneration, it falls squarely within the protection of Article 42 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, which guarantees the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property. Depriving a retired public servant of their pension without explicit statutory authority constitutes a direct violation of their fundamental constitutional rights under Articles 27 (equality before law), 31 (protection of law), and 42.

Furthermore, under the General Provident Fund Rules, GPF savings consist entirely of the employee's personal salary deductions and accrued interest. GPF funds are held in trust by the state; under no circumstances can an administrative authority seize or freeze GPF balances to settle administrative audit queries.

Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974 and Gratuity Rules

The Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974, read with the Civil Service Regulations (CSR) and Ministry of Finance Pension Simplification Orders, outlines strict procedural obligations for disbursing terminal benefits:

  • Mandatory 1-Year Pre-Retirement Timeline: The process of preparing pension papers, verifying service books, and resolving administrative records must commence exactly one year prior to the officer's date of superannuation (PRL - Post Retirement Leave).
  • Immediate Provisional Pension: Under statutory pension simplification rules, if any calculation delay occurs in issuing the final PPO, the appointing authority is legally mandated to disburse Provisional Pension (at least 80% of estimated pension) and provisional gratuity immediately upon retirement.
  • Withholding Only for Pecuniary Loss: Pension can only be reduced or withheld under CSR Rule 351A if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct or having caused pecuniary loss to the government in departmental or judicial proceedings finalized before retirement.

Administrative authorities routinely violate these statutory guidelines by withholding 100% of benefits over trivial, unproven paperwork discrepancies.

The Menace of Audit Objections and Illegal Deductions

The most pervasive pretext used to block pensions is the 'Audit Objection' (Apotti) raised by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audit teams. Decades after a salary increment, promotion, or housing allowance was approved by the ministry, audit inspectors claim the payment was calculated erroneously and demand recovery of lakhs of taka from the retiree's gratuity.

Bangladeshi courts have decisively outlawed this practice. The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed:

  1. Audit Objections Are Not Judicial Decrees: An audit objection is merely an internal accounting observation between government departments; it carries no judicial weight and cannot supersede statutory pension entitlements.
  2. Bar on Recovery of Excess Pay: Where excess salary or allowances were paid to an employee without any fraud or misrepresentation on their part, the government cannot deduct or recover those sums from the employee's post-retirement gratuity or pension.
  3. Time-Barred Demands: Attempting to recover payments made 10, 15, or 20 years earlier without a formal court decree is barred by law and violates natural justice.

Facing a similar legal dispute in Bangladesh? Don't fight it alone. Contact Advocate MD Shah Alam for expert legal consultation, tactical dispute evaluation, and courtroom representation. WhatsApp: +880 1955-802007 or Call: +880 1712-655546.

Departmental Proceedings After Retirement: Legal Limits

Another common weapon used to stall pensions is initiating departmental proceedings under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 2018 on the verge of or immediately following retirement.

The legal framework strictly circumscribes such posthumous inquiries:

  • Termination of Master-Servant Relationship: Once a public servant crosses their age of superannuation and their retirement takes effect, the master-servant relationship between the government and the employee ceases to exist.
  • Bar Against Fresh Inquiries: No fresh disciplinary proceeding under the Discipline and Appeal Rules 2018 can be initiated against an official who has already retired, as disciplinary punishments (such as dismissal, demotion, or suspension) can only be inflicted on serving employees.
  • CSR Rule 351A Conditions: Departmental proceedings can only continue post-retirement under the strict terms of CSR Rule 351A for the sole purpose of determining pension reductions, provided the alleged misconduct occurred within a statutory four-year limitation period and the inquiry was authorized by the President or Ministry.

Inquiries initiated without statutory sanction are ultra vires and can be immediately quashed through judicial intervention.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Administrative Tribunal Jurisdiction and Procedure

Under Article 117 of the Constitution and the Administrative Tribunals Act 1980, specialized Administrative Tribunals hold exclusive primary jurisdiction over service disputes of persons in the service of the republic, including pension and retirement claims.

The procedural roadmap before the Administrative Tribunal operates as follows:

  1. Exhaustion of Departmental Remedies: Before approaching the Tribunal, the aggrieved retiree must submit a formal departmental appeal or review petition to the highest administrative authority (e.g., Senior Secretary of the Ministry) and wait for a decision or the expiry of the statutory 60-day or 90-day waiting period.
  2. Filing the Application (Section 4): The applicant files a comprehensive petition before the Administrative Tribunal having territorial jurisdiction, challenging the illegal withholding order and praying for a mandatory direction to release pension, gratuity, and GPF with interest.
  3. Statutory Limitation (Section 4(2)): The application must be filed within 6 months from the date of the final rejection order or the expiry of the waiting period.
  4. Administrative Appellate Tribunal (Section 6): If the Administrative Tribunal passes an adverse order, an appeal lies to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal (AAT) within 3 months, whose decisions are binding on all executive ministries.

High Court Division Article 102 Writ of Mandamus

While Article 117 vests service matters in the Administrative Tribunal, what happens when an administrative department acts with patent illegality, completely refuses to issue pension papers without any formal order, or when an urgent constitutional property right under Article 42 is violated?

In such compelling circumstances, the High Court Division can be approached directly under Article 102 of the Constitution for a Writ of Mandamus:

  • Undisputed Benefits Withholding: Where the retiree's entitlement to pension is completely undisputed, but local drawing officers simply sit on the file or demand illegal gratification, a Writ of Mandamus lies to compel the performance of their statutory public duty.
  • Quashing Unlawful Recovery Orders: The High Court routinely issues Writs of Certiorari quashing arbitrary audit objection deduction notices issued without show-cause hearings.
  • Direction to Pay Statutory Interest: The High Court Division possesses inherent constitutional authority to direct government ministries to disburse delayed gratuity and pension arrears alongside commercial interest (typically 7% to 9% per annum) to penalize administrative recalcitrance.

Comparison Table: Administrative Tribunal vs. High Court Writ

Choosing between the Administrative Tribunal and the High Court Division depends on the nature of the dispute and whether formal service orders exist:

Judicial ParameterAdministrative TribunalHigh Court Division (Writ Mandamus)
Governing LawAdministrative Tribunals Act 1980 (Art 117 Constitution)Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh
Primary FocusFormal service disputes, disciplinary orders, pension rule interpretations.Enforcing fundamental constitutional rights (Articles 27, 31, 42) & public duty.
Exhaustion of RemediesMandatory departmental appeal required prior to filing.Can be bypassed if alternative remedy is ineffective, delayed, or illusory.
Speed of ReliefFormal trial procedure; typically takes 1 to 3 years.Fast-track emergency hearings; ad-interim stay orders within days/weeks.
Relief ScopeDirects department to comply with service rules and recalculate.Quashes illegal orders, mandates immediate disbursement, awards interest.
Appellate PathwayAppeal to Administrative Appellate Tribunal (AAT), then Leave to Appeal.Direct appeal to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

Illustrative Scenario: Retiree Recovering Withheld Gratuity

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): Khorshed Alam retired as an Executive Engineer from the Roads and Highways Department (RHD) in early 2024. Upon retirement, his drawing and disbursing officer cleared his GPF, but withheld his BDT 42 Lakh gratuity and monthly pension. The Chief Accounts Office cited an audit objection dating back to 2008, claiming that an equipment procurement project headed by Khorshed had exceeded budgetary allocations by BDT 18 Lakh, despite the fact that the Ministry had formally approved the expenditure sixteen years earlier.

For two years, Khorshed shuttled between the accounts office and the ministry, receiving only polite deferrals while his medical conditions worsened and his life savings depleted. His departmental appeals received no formal response.

Khorshed engaged a Supreme Court service law advocate, who served a formal 15-day statutory legal notice upon the Secretary of the Ministry of Road Transport and the Auditor General. Upon their failure to comply, a Writ Petition was filed before the High Court Division under Article 102.

During the hearing, the High Court Division sternly rebuked the department, holding that an unadjudicated 16-year-old audit query cannot be used to confiscate post-retirement property without due process. The High Court issued an absolute Rule and directed the immediate release of the BDT 42 Lakh gratuity and all pension arrears within 30 days, alongside 8% compensatory interest.

Talk to an Advocate

Your post-retirement pension and gratuity represent the fruits of your entire professional life, protected by the Constitution of Bangladesh. Submitting passively to bureaucratic delay or unlawful audit deductions will only result in years of agonizing hardship. A dedicated service law advocate navigates the specialized procedural corridors of the Administrative Tribunal and the High Court Division, forcing recalcitrant ministries to release your rightful terminal benefits promptly.

Is your government pension, gratuity, or GPF unlawfully blocked or delayed in Bangladesh? Send your retirement orders, LPC, and audit objection papers on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call directly at +880 1712-655546. Specialized Administrative Tribunal and High Court Writ representation for retired civil servants.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the government stop my pension if an audit objection was raised years after my retirement?

No. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly ruled that an audit objection is an internal administrative observation, not a judicial decree. Post-retirement pension and gratuity cannot be withheld or reduced based on audit objections raised after retirement without a formal judicial or disciplinary finding under CSR Rule 351A.

How long can a government department legally delay the disbursement of gratuity and GPF?

Under Ministry of Finance Pension Simplification Orders, pension processing must commence one year prior to retirement, and full gratuity and GPF must be disbursed within 30 days of the effective date of retirement. If delays occur, the department is legally required to issue an immediate Provisional Pension.

Is a retired government employee entitled to interest on delayed pension payments?

Yes. In numerous landmark rulings, the High Court Division has held that when retirement benefits are arbitrarily delayed through administrative recalcitrance or negligence, the state is legally liable to pay compensatory commercial interest (typically 7% to 9% per annum) on the withheld arrears.

Can the department initiate a new departmental inquiry against me after I have retired?

No. Fresh departmental proceedings under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 2018 cannot be initiated after retirement because the employment relationship has ended. Proceedings can only be continued under CSR Rule 351A under strict presidential sanction for grave pecuniary loss incurred within four years.

What is the time limit for filing a case before the Administrative Tribunal for pension claims?

Under Section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act 1980, an application must be filed within six months from the date on which the final administrative order was communicated to the employee, or within six months from the expiration of the statutory waiting period following a departmental appeal.

Can family members claim the deceased pensioner's arrears and family pension?

Yes. If a government servant or pensioner passes away, their surviving spouse and dependent minor children have an automatic statutory right to Family Pension and all accumulated gratuity arrears, upon producing a Succession Certificate or Family Member Certificate.

When can a retired public servant bypass the Administrative Tribunal and go directly to the High Court?

A retired employee can approach the High Court Division directly under Article 102 for a Writ of Mandamus when their entitlement to pension is undisputed but authorities completely refuse to act, when an arbitrary deduction violates Article 42 constitutional property rights, or when an administrative order is issued without any jurisdiction.

Can a bank or treasury office deduct money from my pension account without my consent?

No. Under the Pensions Act 1871 and Civil Procedure Code Section 60, pension funds are strictly exempt from attachment, seizure, or unilateral deduction by banks, treasury offices, or creditors, even under court decrees.

Guardianship Law Bangladesh – Guardians and Wards Act Explained

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-05-21 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

When a child loses parental care or when parents are unable to manage a minor's property, the law steps in through the institution of guardianship. In Bangladesh, the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 — supplemented by religious personal laws for Muslims and Hindus — governs who may act as a guardian, how a court appoints one, and what rights and duties flow from that appointment. Whether you are seeking guardianship of a child or wish to protect a minor's property, understanding the legal framework is the first essential step.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

  2. Types of Guardians Under Bangladeshi Law
  3. Muslim Guardianship: Principles and Priority
  4. Hindu Guardianship Rules in Bangladesh
  5. How to Apply for Court-Appointed Guardianship
  6. Rights and Duties of a Legal Guardian
  7. Removal and Termination of Guardianship

Overview of Guardianship Law in Bangladesh

The primary legislation governing guardianship in Bangladesh is the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (Act No. VIII of 1890), a colonial-era statute that remains in force with limited amendments. It provides a secular framework for the appointment and supervision of guardians for minors — defined as persons who have not attained the age of 18 years (or 21 in certain cases involving court-managed property). The Act operates alongside personal laws — the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act and Hindu customary law — which govern natural guardianship within religious communities.

The Act vests jurisdiction in the Family Court (in metropolitan areas) and the Court of the District Judge to appoint and supervise guardians. The overriding principle in all guardianship proceedings is the welfare of the minor — courts are directed by Section 17 of the Act to be guided primarily by what is for the benefit of the minor in matters of health, physical, moral, and psychological well-being, irrespective of technical claims based on religion or family status.

Guardianship in Bangladesh covers two distinct spheres: guardianship of the person (physical care, upbringing, and education of the child) and guardianship of the property (managing the minor's assets, investments, and legal rights). In many cases, these may be held by different individuals — for instance, under Muslim law a mother may have hizanat (custody) of the child while the father retains guardianship of property.

For parents going through divorce or separation who are concerned about their children's welfare and legal protection, consulting an experienced family lawyer in Dhaka is essential to understand how guardianship and custody interact in the Bangladeshi legal system.

Types of Guardians Under Bangladeshi Law

The Guardians and Wards Act 1890 recognises several categories of guardians, each with a different source of authority:

1. Natural Guardian

A natural guardian derives authority from personal law (religious law) rather than a court order. Under Muslim law, the father is the natural guardian of a minor's person and property, with the mother gaining rights of hizanat (physical custody) for young children. Under Hindu law, the father is the natural guardian, followed by the mother. Natural guardianship is automatic and does not require court appointment.

2. Testamentary Guardian

A testamentary guardian is appointed by the will of a deceased parent. Under Section 9 of the Act, a father (or mother in certain circumstances) may appoint a guardian by will who assumes authority after the parent's death. Testamentary guardianship is subject to court oversight if there is a dispute about the will's validity or the appointed person's suitability.

3. Court-Appointed Guardian

When there is no natural or testamentary guardian, or when the existing guardian is found unsuitable, the court may appoint a guardian under Section 7 of the Act. Any person interested in the welfare of the minor — including a relative, family friend, or the minor themselves if over 14 — may apply. The court's decision is governed entirely by the welfare of the minor.

4. De Facto Guardian

A de facto guardian is someone who has taken charge of a minor without legal authority — typically a relative caring for an orphaned child. The Act places restrictions on de facto guardians' ability to deal with a minor's property (Section 11), requiring prior court approval for any significant transaction. This protects minors from exploitation by informal carers.

Muslim Guardianship: Principles and Priority

Bangladesh has a Muslim majority population and the rules of Muslim personal law heavily influence guardianship practice. Islamic jurisprudence (primarily Hanafi school, which is dominant in Bangladesh) distinguishes sharply between wilayat (guardianship of property and legal matters) and hizanat (custody and physical care of the child).

Wilayat (Legal Guardianship)

Under Hanafi law, the order of priority for legal guardianship of a minor's property is:

  1. Father
  2. Paternal grandfather
  3. Executor appointed by the father's will
  4. Executor appointed by the paternal grandfather's will
  5. Court-appointed guardian (in absence of the above)

The mother has no right of legal guardianship over property under classical Hanafi law, though courts in Bangladesh have shown increasing flexibility in this regard when the welfare of the child demands it.

Hizanat (Physical Custody)

The mother enjoys the right of hizanat — the right to physical care and custody — for young children: daughters until puberty and sons until age 7 (with some variations in Hanafi fiqh). This right may be lost if the mother remarries a person unrelated to the child, or if she is found morally unfit. After the hizanat period, the father exercises custody.

Critically, Bangladeshi courts — applying the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 — have repeatedly held that the welfare of the child supersedes strict religious rules on custody and guardianship. The landmark decision in Khurshida Begum v. Salauddin and subsequent High Court cases confirm that courts will deviate from the classical Hanafi priority order when it is not in the child's best interest. If you are involved in a Muslim guardianship dispute, contact a family law specialist who understands both Sharia principles and the court's welfare-oriented jurisprudence.

Hindu Guardianship Rules in Bangladesh

For the Hindu minority community in Bangladesh, guardianship is governed by a combination of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 and customary Hindu law. Bangladesh has not enacted a codified Hindu family code, so courts rely on Smritis, judicial precedents, and the broad welfare principles of the 1890 Act.

Natural Guardianship Under Hindu Law

Under Hindu personal law as applied in Bangladesh:

  • The father is the natural and primary guardian of a minor child's person and property during his lifetime.
  • After the father's death, the mother becomes the natural guardian of the person (and may manage property under court oversight).
  • Where both parents are deceased, a testamentary guardian appointed by the father's will takes precedence, followed by the paternal grandfather, and then other relatives in customary order.

Minor's Property Under Hindu Law

A Hindu minor's property — particularly ancestral joint family property (HUF) — is managed by the karta (senior male member of the joint family). The concept of karta is a unique feature of Hindu law with no equivalent in Muslim or secular law. The karta has broad powers to manage joint family property for the benefit of all members, including minors, but cannot alienate ancestral property without legal necessity (vyavahar) or the court's prior approval.

For Hindu families in Bangladesh, disputes over a minor's inheritance — particularly after the death of a father without a will — can be especially complex. Courts apply the customary rules of Dayabhaga (the school of Hindu law followed in Bengal/Bangladesh), which gives sons and daughters more equal inheritance rights than the Mitakshara school prevalent in India. An experienced family lawyer in Dhaka can help navigate these complex inter-religious property and guardianship matters.

How to Apply for Court-Appointed Guardianship

Applying for court-appointed guardianship under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 follows a formal legal process before the Family Court or District Court. The procedure is as follows:

Step 1: Filing the Petition

The applicant files a Guardianship Petition before the Family Court (in Dhaka, Chittagong, Khulna, Rajshahi, Sylhet) or District Judge's Court (in other districts). The petition must state:

  • The name, age, and religion of the minor
  • The applicant's relationship to the minor
  • The grounds for seeking guardianship (e.g., parents deceased, missing, or incapacitated)
  • A description of the minor's property (if guardianship of property is sought)
  • Details of any existing natural or testamentary guardian

Step 2: Notice and Hearing

The court issues notice to all interested parties — including any existing guardian, near relatives, and in some cases the minor if sufficiently mature. The court then conducts a welfare enquiry, which may involve interviewing the minor, examining the applicant's background, and reviewing financial and social circumstances. The court may also appoint a Court Guardian ad Litem to independently represent the minor's interests during complex proceedings.

Step 3: Order of Appointment

After hearing all parties, the court issues an order either appointing the applicant as guardian, appointing another suitable person, or dismissing the petition. The order specifies the scope of the guardianship — person, property, or both — and may impose conditions such as periodic financial reporting to the court.

Step 4: Ongoing Court Supervision

A court-appointed guardian remains under court supervision. They must typically file annual accounts of the minor's property, seek court permission before selling or mortgaging the minor's assets, and report any material change in the minor's circumstances. Failure to comply can result in removal as guardian.

The entire process from petition to final order typically takes 3–6 months in an uncontested case and longer if opposed. Engaging a skilled family lawyer in Dhaka ensures the petition is properly drafted and the welfare enquiry is handled professionally.

Rights and Duties of a Legal Guardian

Once appointed — whether by operation of law as a natural guardian or by court order — a guardian in Bangladesh carries significant legal rights and corresponding duties toward the minor. These are governed by Sections 24–28 of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 and supplemented by personal law.

Rights of a Guardian

  • Physical possession of the minor: A guardian of the person has the right to physical custody and may apply to the court for an order to recover the minor from anyone unlawfully detaining them (including habeas corpus proceedings).
  • Education and upbringing: The guardian decides the minor's religion, education, and moral training — subject to any court order or the minor's expressed wishes if they are of sufficient maturity.
  • Management of property: A guardian of property may collect rents, manage investments, and conduct routine transactions on the minor's behalf.
  • Legal representation: A guardian may file lawsuits, defend claims, and enter contracts on behalf of the minor. Contracts entered by a guardian bind the minor's property (not personally).

Duties and Restrictions

  • A guardian must act in the minor's best interest at all times and cannot use the minor's property for personal benefit.
  • Sale, mortgage, or gift of immovable property belonging to the minor requires prior court permission under Section 29 of the Act — even for natural guardians. Transactions without court approval are voidable at the minor's election upon reaching majority.
  • A guardian must maintain proper accounts and be ready to present them to the court upon request.
  • A guardian cannot use the minor's funds to speculate, invest in risky ventures, or benefit third parties not connected to the minor's welfare.

Guardians who breach their fiduciary duty may face civil liability, removal by the court, and in cases of deliberate misappropriation, criminal prosecution under the Penal Code. If you believe a guardian is mismanaging a child's interests, contact a lawyer in Dhaka to explore legal remedies including a court application for removal.

Removal and Termination of Guardianship

Guardianship is not a permanent or irrevocable status. The Guardians and Wards Act 1890 provides several mechanisms by which guardianship may end — either automatically or through court intervention.

Automatic Termination

Guardianship terminates automatically in the following circumstances:

  • The minor attains majority (age 18, or 21 if the court had management of the minor's property during minority)
  • In the case of a female minor — her marriage (though this is controversial and increasingly challenged by child rights advocates and the courts)
  • The death of the minor
  • The death of the guardian (a new guardian must then be appointed)

Court-Ordered Removal

The court may remove a guardian at any time if satisfied that removal is in the minor's welfare. Under Section 39 of the Act, grounds for removal include:

  • Abuse, neglect, or ill-treatment of the minor
  • Misappropriation or waste of the minor's property
  • Persistent violation of court directions on guardianship
  • The guardian's own insolvency, mental incapacity, or conviction of a serious offence
  • Change of religion by the guardian that adversely affects the minor's upbringing
  • Any other conduct rendering the guardian unsuitable

Any person with an interest in the minor's welfare — including relatives, social workers, or government authorities — can apply for removal of a guardian. The minor themselves, if 14 or older, may also petition the court to change their guardian. After removing a guardian, the court appoints a substitute, following the same welfare-based enquiry as in the original appointment.

If you are concerned about the welfare of a minor under a negligent or abusive guardian, or if you yourself are a guardian facing unjust removal proceedings, you should consult a qualified family lawyer or reach out to Advocate Md. Shah Alam for professional guidance on your legal options.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the natural guardian of a Muslim child in Bangladesh?

Under Hanafi Muslim personal law applicable in Bangladesh, the father is the natural legal guardian (wali) of a minor's person and property. The mother has the right of hizanat (physical custody) for young children — sons up to age 7 and daughters until puberty — but legal guardianship of property remains with the father or his male relatives in the prescribed order of priority.

How do I get appointed as a court guardian in Bangladesh?

You must file a Guardianship Petition before the Family Court or District Judge's Court in the relevant jurisdiction. The petition must describe the minor's circumstances, your relationship to the minor, and the grounds for guardianship. The court conducts a welfare enquiry, hears all interested parties, and issues an appointment order. The process typically takes 3–6 months in uncontested cases.

Can a guardian sell a minor's property in Bangladesh?

No guardian — not even a natural guardian — can sell, mortgage, or gift a minor's immovable property without prior permission from the court under Section 29 of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890. Any transaction done without court approval is voidable by the minor after reaching adulthood. Court permission requires demonstrating that the sale is in the minor's best interest (e.g., for education, medical needs, or legal necessity).

What happens to guardianship when parents divorce in Bangladesh?

Divorce does not automatically determine guardianship. Courts treat custody (physical care) and guardianship (legal authority) separately. Under Muslim law, the mother retains hizanat for young children even after divorce, while the father retains legal guardianship. For other communities, the court decides based on the welfare of the child. A divorced parent wishing to change guardianship arrangements must apply to the Family Court.

At what age does a guardian's authority end in Bangladesh?

Guardianship automatically ends when the minor attains the age of majority — 18 years under the Majority Act 1875. If the court had jurisdiction over the minor's property during minority, the age of majority is extended to 21 years for those property-related purposes. A guardian's authority also ends upon the minor's death or, for a female minor, upon her marriage (though courts increasingly examine whether marriage genuinely ends the need for protection).

Can a mother be appointed as guardian of her child's property in Bangladesh?

Under classical Muslim personal law, a mother cannot be the legal guardian of property. However, Bangladeshi courts — applying the welfare principle under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 — have appointed mothers as guardians of property when there is no suitable male guardian or when the paternal guardian is unfit. The court's primary concern is always the minor's welfare, not strict adherence to religious hierarchies.

Habeas Corpus Writ in Bangladesh: Illegal Detention, Article 102 & Police Custody Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-08 · 19 minutes

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Personal liberty is the bedrock of constitutional democracy. In Bangladesh, when an individual is unlawfully picked up by law enforcement personnel, detained in plainclothes, held incommunicado past the statutory 24-hour limit, or subjected to unauthorized detention by private parties, the legal system provides an immediate constitutional remedy: the **Writ of Habeas Corpus**. Literally translating to 'produce the body', a Habeas Corpus petition under **Article 102(2)(b)(i) of the Constitution of Bangladesh** empowers the High Court Division to direct the state, police departments, and intelligence agencies to produce the detained person before the court and show lawful authority for their confinement. This essential legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate and constitutional defense practitioner in Uttara and Dhaka, explains your fundamental protections under Articles 31, 32, and 33, the procedural steps to move the High Court Division, and emergency countermeasures against unlawful custody.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

📋 In This Article

  3. 3. The 24-Hour Production Mandate Under Section 61 CrPC

  5. 5. Legal Matrix: Article 102 Habeas Corpus vs. Section 491 CrPC

  8. 8. Habeas Corpus for Private Confinement & Matrimonial Custody
  9. 9. Illustrative Scenario: Securing the Release of an Incommunicado Executive
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate: Emergency Constitutional & Habeas Corpus Defense

1. Constitutional Safeguards: Articles 31, 32 & 33

In Bangladesh, no person can be deprived of life or personal liberty save in accordance with law. This sacrosanct constitutional principle is enshrined in Article 32 and fortified by Article 31, which guarantees that every citizen and resident enjoys the protection of the law and shall be treated only in accordance with law.

When an individual is arrested, Article 33 of the Constitution establishes mandatory safeguards that law enforcement agencies cannot waive or suspend:

  • Right to be Informed of Grounds: Under Article 33(1), no person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest.
  • Right to Legal Counsel: The arrested person has the inviolable constitutional right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of their choice from the moment of apprehension.
  • The Strict 24-Hour Production Rule: Under Article 33(2), every person who is arrested and detained in custody must be produced before the nearest Magistrate within a period of twenty-four (24) hours of such arrest (excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court). No detention beyond 24 hours is lawful without the express authority of a Magistrate.

When state actors detain individuals in secret locations, refuse to acknowledge custody, or hold suspects past 24 hours, the detention is unconstitutional and actionable.

2. High Court Habeas Corpus Jurisdiction Under Article 102(2)(b)(i)

The great constitutional writ that enforces these fundamental safeguards is codified in Article 102(2)(b)(i) of the Constitution of Bangladesh. This provision establishes that the High Court Division may, on the application of any person, make an order directing that a person in custody within the local limits of the court's jurisdiction be brought before it so that it may satisfy itself that they are not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner.

The legal characteristics of a Habeas Corpus petition under Article 102 include:

  1. Relaxed Rules of Locus Standi: The petition does not need to be filed by the victim personally. Any spouse, parent, child, sibling, or advocate acting as 'next friend' can sign the affidavit and move the petition before the High Court.
  2. Priority Cause List Listing: Because life and liberty are at stake, Division Benches of the High Court Division accord the highest priority to Habeas Corpus petitions, often hearing them on the day of filing.
  3. Immediate Judicial Inquiry: If the court finds prima facie merit, it issues a Rule Nisi and directs the Inspector General of Police (IGP) and relevant law enforcement chiefs to produce the person in court on a specific date (often within 24 to 72 hours).

3. The 24-Hour Production Mandate Under Section 61 CrPC

The constitutional protection under Article 33 is directly mirrored in the statutory framework of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC). Under Section 61 of the CrPC, no police officer shall detain in custody a person arrested without a warrant for a longer period than under all the circumstances of the case is reasonable, and such period shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under Section 167, exceed twenty-four (24) hours.

Section 167 of the CrPC governs what must happen when an investigation cannot be completed within 24 hours:

  • Mandatory Production Before Magistrate: The police must physically produce the arrested person before the nearest Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate, accompanied by copies of the case diary (CD).
  • Magistrate's Independent Judicial Discretion: The Magistrate examines whether the arrest was lawful, whether an FIR was recorded, and whether grounds exist for custodial interrogation (remand) or judicial custody.
  • Remand Restrictions: Magistrates cannot grant police remand routinely. If there are allegations of torture or physical coercion, the Magistrate is legally bound to order a medical examination under the Torture and Custodial Death (Prevention) Act 2013.

Detaining an individual in a police station, intelligence cell, or detective branch office for even 25 hours without presenting them to a Magistrate makes the confinement false imprisonment and unconstitutional detention.

4. Guidelines on Plainclothes Arrests: The Landmark Blast Case

Has a family member been detained without warrant or held past 24 hours? Contact our Supreme Court constitutional defense team immediately on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007. We file emergency Habeas Corpus petitions before the High Court.

Unlawful detention frequently begins with plainclothes personnel picking up citizens in unmarked microbuses. This abusive practice was addressed by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the landmark judgment of Bangladesh v. BLAST & Others, reported in 55 DLR (AD) 67 (2003) (commonly known as the Blast Case Guidelines).

The Supreme Court laid down mandatory operational guidelines that all law enforcement agencies (Police, DB, CID, RAB) must follow when making arrests under Section 54 CrPC:

  • Identity Disclosure: Arresting officers must disclose their identity, show official ID cards, and explain the legal grounds of arrest to the detainee and family members present.
  • Immediate Family Notification: The arresting agency must notify a relative of the arrested person within three (3) hours of apprehension, specifying the location where the person is being held.
  • Mandatory General Diary (GD) Entry: The officer must record a formal GD entry at the local police station immediately upon returning with the arrested person.
  • Presence of Legal Counsel: If interrogation is granted by a Magistrate, it must take place in an interrogation room with glass walls visible to defense advocates, and the detainee must be medically examined before and after interrogation.

Citing the Blast Case Guidelines in a Habeas Corpus petition provides powerful judicial leverage before the High Court Division.

5. Legal Matrix: Article 102 Habeas Corpus vs. Section 491 CrPC

A comparative analysis of judicial avenues against unlawful detention in Bangladesh:

ParameterWrit of Habeas Corpus (Article 102)Directions in Nature of Habeas Corpus (Section 491 CrPC)
Constitutional AuthorityArticle 102(2)(b)(i) of the ConstitutionSection 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898
Competent ForumDivision Bench of High Court DivisionHigh Court Division (Criminal Miscellaneous Bench)
Scope of ReliefEnforces fundamental constitutional rights; quashes detention ordersDirects production of illegal custody; sets detainee at liberty
Applicability to Private ActorsYes, directly applicable to state and private custodyYes, frequently used for private confinement and child custody
Speed of Interlocutory ReliefImmediate ex-parte orders to produce within 24–48 hoursSummary orders to police to rescue and produce

6. Step-by-Step Emergency Filing Protocol in the High Court

When a relative is picked up and police deny holding them, executing a structured legal protocol is vital:

  1. Lodge an Immediate General Diary (GD): Visit the local police station having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the abduction or pickup occurred. Demand the recording of a formal General Diary (GD) detailing the time, vehicle license numbers, description of plainclothes personnel, and witnesses. If the OC refuses, dispatch the GD via registered post or email to the Police Commissioner and Superintendent of Police.
  2. Collect Physical Evidence: Secure CCTV footage from nearby buildings, toll gates, or commercial shops capturing the pickup. Collect mobile phone call records and eyewitness statements.
  3. Engage a Supreme Court Advocate: Transmit the GD copy, CCTV stills, and victim details to your advocate in Dhaka. Our chamber drafts the emergency Habeas Corpus petition within hours.
  4. Move the High Court Writ Bench: The advocate files the petition before the designated Division Bench of the High Court Division, seeking an urgent motion hearing.
  5. Securing the Production Order: The High Court issues an ad-interim direction to the state respondents (Home Secretary, IGP, Detective Branch, local police) to produce the person in court on a fixed date.

7. Evidentiary Standards & Court Directives to Produce the Body

When a Habeas Corpus petition is moved, the evidentiary dynamic shifts dramatically. Once the petitioner demonstrates prima facie that the individual was picked up by state agents or was last seen in their custody, the burden of proof shifts to the state to demonstrate:

  • The legal statutory authority under which the person was arrested.
  • The specific FIR or case number registered against the individual.
  • Proof that the individual was physically produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours in compliance with Article 33.

If state law enforcement agencies submit a false affidavit claiming they do not hold the person, while the petitioner produces CCTV footage or eye-witness affidavits proving otherwise, the High Court Division can initiate criminal perjury proceedings and direct the Judicial Magistrate to conduct a formal judicial inquiry. In numerous cases, the mere filing and listing of a Habeas Corpus petition forces agencies to officially 'show' the arrest and produce the detainee before a magistrate rather than maintaining secret detention.

8. Habeas Corpus for Private Confinement & Matrimonial Custody

While Habeas Corpus is predominantly utilized against state detention, it is equally available under Bangladeshi jurisprudence against private unlawful confinement.

Frequent private custody applications include:

  • Forcible Confinement of Adult Spouses: When an adult woman or man is forcibly confined by in-laws, estranged parents, or relatives to prevent them from exercising their personal liberty or marital choice, a Habeas Corpus petition or Section 491 CrPC application directs local police to enter the private premises, rescue the individual, and produce them before the High Court.
  • Cross-Border Child Abduction: When an estranged parent forcibly removes or secretes a minor child away from the lawful custodial parent in violation of court orders or natural custody rights. The High Court exercises parens patriae jurisdiction to ensure the child is produced and their welfare evaluated.
  • Forced Labor or Unlawful Confinement: Individuals held in private detention cells, brick kilns, or unauthorized rehabilitation centers can be liberated through emergency High Court directions.

9. Illustrative Scenario: Securing the Release of an Incommunicado Executive

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): A senior corporate executive at a multinational logistics firm in Uttara, Dhaka, was intercepted by six armed men in plainclothes driving an unmarked microbus while leaving his corporate office. For forty-eight hours, his family received no telephone calls, and local police stations in Uttara claimed they had no record of his arrest or custody.

Facing acute panic and fearing extra-judicial harm, the executive's spouse retained Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber. Our legal team took immediate constitutional action:

  1. Dispatched an emergency formal complaint to the Inspector General of Police (IGP) and Deputy Commissioner of Police (Uttara Division) demanding immediate tracing of the missing executive.
  2. Drafted and filed an emergency Writ of Habeas Corpus under Article 102(2)(b)(i) before a Division Bench of the High Court Division, producing CCTV footage from the office building capturing the plainclothes pickup and vehicle details.
  3. Moved the petition during morning cause list mentions, demonstrating that the detention exceeded 48 hours without production before any magistrate, violating Article 33 and the landmark Blast Case Guidelines (55 DLR (AD) 67).
  4. The High Court Division passed an emergency order directing the Secretary of Home Affairs, the Chief of the Detective Branch (DB), and the local police OC to produce the executive before the High Court by 10:30 AM the following morning.
  5. Faced with the binding High Court order, the law enforcement agency immediately produced the executive before a Metropolitan Magistrate, abandoning secret detention, and allowing our chamber to successfully secure his regular bail.

10. Talk to an Advocate: Emergency Constitutional & Habeas Corpus Defense

When a family member, business executive, or colleague is unlawfully detained, held in secret custody, or denied production before a magistrate in Bangladesh, immediate constitutional litigation before the High Court Division is essential. Advocate Md. Shah Alam and his dedicated team of Supreme Court advocates provide rapid, 24/7 emergency representation before writ benches and magistrate courts.

Need an advocate for this matter in Bangladesh? Send your documents on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: a first document review can be done remotely.

Our principal chamber is located in Uttara, Dhaka, minutes from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, alongside our daily litigation chamber at the Supreme Court Bar Association and Dhaka Judge Court.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a Writ of Habeas Corpus in Bangladesh?

A Writ of Habeas Corpus is a constitutional order issued by the High Court Division under Article 102(2)(b)(i) directing authorities to produce a detained person before the court to determine whether their confinement is lawful.

How long can police legally hold a person before taking them to court?

Under Article 33(2) of the Constitution and Section 61 of the CrPC, police cannot detain an arrested person for more than twenty-four (24) hours without producing them before a competent Judicial Magistrate.

Who can file a Habeas Corpus petition in the High Court?

Because personal liberty is at stake, the rules of standing are relaxed. Any spouse, parent, child, sibling, advocate, or friend can file a Habeas Corpus petition on behalf of the detained person.

Can Habeas Corpus be filed against private individuals who unlawfully confine someone?

Yes. Habeas Corpus under Article 102 and Section 491 CrPC is directly enforceable against private parties who unlawfully confine adult individuals, spouses, or minor children against their will.

What are the Blast Case Guidelines regarding plainclothes arrests?

In 55 DLR (AD) 67, the Supreme Court mandated that arresting officers must display official identity, notify family members within 3 hours, record an immediate GD, and ensure access to legal counsel.

How quickly can the High Court hear a Habeas Corpus petition?

In genuine emergency cases involving missing persons or secret custody, an advocate can mention the matter and obtain a hearing before a High Court Division Bench on the very same day the petition is prepared.

What happens if law enforcement denies having the person in custody?

If authorities deny custody, the High Court can examine CCTV evidence, telephone tracking, and witness affidavits, and order an independent judicial inquiry by a District Judge or Chief Judicial Magistrate.

Can an overseas family member file a Habeas Corpus petition from abroad?

Yes. Overseas relatives in the USA, UK, Canada, or Australia can retain a Supreme Court advocate remotely to draft, swear, and move a Habeas Corpus petition before the High Court Division in Dhaka.

Hacking and Unauthorized Computer Access Under Bangladesh Law

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-04-09 · 7 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Hacking — gaining unauthorized access to a computer system, network, or digital account — is a serious criminal offence in Bangladesh under the Digital Security Act 2018. This guide explains what the law covers, the penalties, how to report a hacking incident, and your legal options as a victim.

: · Cyber Crime & Criminal Defense Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing LawCyber Security Act, 2023 & Penal Code, 1860 (Bangladesh)
First Step at Police StationFile an Online or In-Person General Diary (GD) at gd.police.gov.bd / local Thana
Police Cyber Support for Women (PCSW)Helpline: 01320-000888 | Email: cybersupport.women@police.gov.bd
CID / CTTC Cyber Crime Unit24/7 Emergency: 999 | Police Headquarters & Cyber Tribunal Dhaka

📋 In This Article

  2. DSA Section 19: Unauthorized Computer Access
  3. What Counts as Hacking Under the DSA?
  4. Penalties for Hacking in Bangladesh
  5. Steps to Take If You Are a Hacking Victim
  6. Hacking vs. White Hat Security Testing

What is Hacking Under Bangladesh Law?

Hacking refers to gaining access to a computer, network, server, or digital account without authorization or exceeding the authorization you legitimately have. Bangladesh law covers hacking under:

  • Digital Security Act 2018, Section 19 (Unauthorized Access): Up to 14 years' imprisonment and BDT 1 crore fine.
  • DSA Section 17 (Attacking Critical Infrastructure): Hacking power grids, financial systems, or government networks — up to 14 years.
  • ICT Act 2006, Section 54: Hacking provisions (still applicable for older cases).

If your account, website, or business system has been hacked, contact a cyber law lawyer in Dhaka for guidance on filing a case and securing your systems.

What Counts as Hacking Under the DSA?

DSA Section 19 covers unauthorized access to any computer, computer system, computer network, or any program, information, or data of any person. This includes:

  • Logging into someone's email, social media, or bank account without permission.
  • Installing malware, ransomware, or spyware on another's device.
  • Intercepting communications or data transmissions without authorization.
  • If the access is for committing any other offence (fraud, blackmail, espionage), the punishment escalates significantly.
  • Hacking computer systems containing personal data triggers both DSA and potential data protection liability.
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Steps to Take If You Are a Hacking Victim

If you or your business has been hacked:

  1. Isolate the affected system — disconnect from the network immediately to prevent further damage or data exfiltration.
  2. Do not turn off the device if forensic evidence collection is being considered — a powered system preserves more evidence than one that was shut down.
  3. Preserve logs — server logs, access logs, error messages are critical evidence.
  4. Report to police and file an FIR under DSA Section 19. The Cyber Crime Unit can conduct technical investigations.
  5. Notify affected parties — if customer or employee data was accessed, a data breach notification may be a legal or ethical obligation.
  6. Engage a cyber lawyer to manage the legal response and any civil claims against the hacker.

Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam in Uttara for hacking cases involving business systems or personal data breaches.

Hacking vs. White Hat Security Testing

White hat or ethical hacking — security testing of systems you own or have been explicitly authorised to test — is not a crime. The key legal distinction is:

  • Authorization: Testing with written authorization from the system owner is lawful. Without it, the same acts are criminal hacking regardless of intent.
  • Scope: Even authorized testers can face liability if they exceed their agreed scope.

Companies hiring penetration testers in Bangladesh should obtain a written security testing agreement to clearly define the legal scope of the engagement.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it illegal to access someone's Facebook account even with their shared password?

It depends on the circumstances. If the account owner revokes consent and you continue accessing it, this can constitute unauthorized access. Regular sharing of an account is a grey area — but accessing someone's account to spy on or control them is illegal regardless of how access was obtained.

Can a business sue a former employee for hacking after leaving?

Yes. Former employees who retain or misuse system access after termination can face DSA Section 19 prosecution and civil liability for any damages caused by unauthorized access.

What if the hacker is from a foreign country?

Bangladesh can still prosecute foreign hackers who target Bangladesh-based systems through Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs) for international cooperation, and can pursue local assets of foreign entities operating in Bangladesh.

Heba-bil-Ewaz vs Simple Gift Deed in Bangladesh: Muslim Law, Registration Fees & Cancellation Lawsuits

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-09-22 · 16 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In Bangladesh property transfers governed by Muslim Personal Law, two instruments are widely utilized: 'Simple Hiba' (Gift) and 'Heba-bil-Ewaz' (Gift with Consideration). Despite their common use, many landowners and heirs fail to understand their profound legal divergence. While a simple Hiba is a voluntary transfer of property made purely out of natural love and affection without any exchange, a Heba-bil-Ewaz requires an actual, genuine 'Ewaz' or return gift—such as a prayer mat, a copy of the Holy Quran, or a token monetary sum. Crucially, while simple gifts may be revocable under limited conditions, a Heba-bil-Ewaz operates under the legal fiction of a sale contract and cannot be revoked unilaterally once executed. Senior Supreme Court Advocate Md. Shah Alam breaks down statutory registration fees, the evidentiary requirements of Ewaz, and the exact judicial procedure to annul fraudulent gift deeds in civil court under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act. For tailored chamber advice, call: <a href="tel:01712655546" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold;">01712655546</a>.

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Registration Fee & Stamp Duty1% Registration Fee + 1.5% Stamp Duty on deed value

📋 In This Article

  2. 2. The 4 Fundamental Differences Between Simple Hiba and Heba-bil-Ewaz
  3. 3. Official Sub-Registry Fees Under Section 78B Registration Act
  4. 4. Can a Donor Unilaterally Cancel a Registered Heba Deed?
  5. 5. Protecting Daughters and Sisters Against Fraudulent Gift Transfers
  6. 6. Instituting a Cancellation Lawsuit Under Section 39 Specific Relief Act
  7. 7. Expert Title Verification with Advocate Md. Shah Alam

1. The Juridical Definition of Heba-bil-Ewaz in Bangladesh

Under classical Islamic jurisprudence as recognized by Bangladesh courts, Heba-bil-Ewaz represents a composite transaction: it begins as a gift and ripens into a sale. When a donor presents land to a recipient and the recipient tenders a return consideration (Ewaz), the transaction is legally transformed.

The Supreme Court of Bangladesh in numerous decisions has reiterated that in order for a Heba-bil-Ewaz to be legally valid, the return consideration must be actual, bona fide, and delivered prior to or concurrently with the execution of the instrument. Merely mentioning a symbolic return in the deed text without genuine delivery will render the instrument vulnerable to legal challenge.

2. The 4 Fundamental Differences Between Simple Hiba and Heba-bil-Ewaz

Legal ParameterSimple Hiba (Unconditional Gift)Heba-bil-Ewaz (Gift for Return)
1. Consideration (Ewaz)None. Purely motivated by love, affection, or religious merit.Mandatory delivery of a valuable reciprocal gift.
2. Judicial TreatmentPure gift under Transfer of Property Act.Treated judicially as a contract of sale (Baye).
3. Delivery of PossessionStrict physical delivery (Qabdah) is mandatory to complete title.Possession transfer is formal; reciprocal Ewaz solidifies title.
4. RevocabilityRevocable under narrow conditions prior to delivery or blood bar.Completely irrevocable once consideration and deed coalesce.

3. Official Sub-Registry Fees Under Section 78B Registration Act

The government of Bangladesh provides statutory tax incentives for familial gifts under Section 78B of the Registration Act, 1908:

  • Blood-Relation Gift Deeds (Between spouses, parents, children, full siblings, grandparents, grandchildren): Statutory registration fee is capped at a flat BDT 100, with BDT 300 affidavit stamp and nominal processing fees (totaling roughly BDT 1,200 to 1,500). No local government tax or ad-valorem stamp duty applies.
  • Non-Relative Gifts & External Heba-bil-Ewaz: If transferred outside statutory blood categories, the instrument is assessed as an ordinary conveyance attracting 1.5% Stamp Duty, 1% Registration Fee, 3% Local Government Tax, and source taxes.

4. Can a Donor Unilaterally Cancel a Registered Heba Deed?

A critical misconception among landowners is that a donor who regrets executing a gift deed can simply return to the Sub-Registry Office and execute a 'Cancellation Deed' (দলিল বাতিলকরণ). The Supreme Court has unequivocally ruled that unilateral cancellation deeds are nullities.

Once a registered conveyance transfers title, the registering officer becomes functus officio. The donor cannot divest the grantee of ownership without an adversarial decree from a court of competent civil jurisdiction. Any unilateral revocation deed will be disregarded by Land Offices during mutation hearings.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

5. Protecting Daughters and Sisters Against Fraudulent Gift Transfers

A frequent abusive practice in rural and urban Bangladesh involves male siblings forging a father's thumbprint on a Heba-bil-Ewaz deed shortly before his death to deprive female heirs of their rightful Quranic shares. Aggrieved female heirs must act swiftly:

  1. Obtain Certified Copies: Apply immediately for certified copies (নকল) from the Sub-Registry Office.
  2. Forensic Handwriting Analysis: Apply to the civil court for appointment of a CID Forensic Handwriting Expert under Section 73 of the Evidence Act to inspect the contested signature.
  3. File Mutation Objections: Lodge written caveats with the Assistant Commissioner (Land) to stay separate Khatian mutations based on the questionable deed.

6. Instituting a Cancellation Lawsuit Under Section 39 Specific Relief Act

The sole legitimate forum to invalidate a fraudulent or coerced gift instrument is the Assistant Judge or Senior Assistant Judge Court. The lawsuit is instituted under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Suit for Cancellation of Document).

Statute of Limitations: Under Article 91 of the Limitation Act, 1908, the lawsuit must be filed within 3 (three) years from the date the plaintiff discovers the fraudulent deed. Exceeding this 3-year deadline causes the claim to be barred by limitation. Concurrently, an application for temporary injunction under Order 39 Rules 1 & 2 of the CPC must be pursued to freeze third-party alienation.

7. Expert Title Verification with Advocate Md. Shah Alam

Disputes over gift deeds involve intricate intersections of personal religious law, statutory property codes, and technical civil procedure. Whether you are executing a bona fide family settlement or challenging an illegal deed executed behind your back, consult Supreme Court Advocate Md. Shah Alam at 01712655546.
