Heba (Gift Deed) Law Bangladesh: How to Transfer Property to Family

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-03-15 · 7 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Heba — the Islamic gift of property — is one of the most common methods by which Bangladeshi families transfer land and property to children, spouses, or relatives during the owner's lifetime. But a legally defective Heba can be challenged, cancelled, and become the source of bitter family disputes. Understanding what makes a Heba valid is essential before transferring any property.

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Registration Fee & Stamp Duty1% Registration Fee + 1.5% Stamp Duty on deed value
Local Government Tax & VAT2%–3% Local Govt Tax + 1.5%–4.5% VAT (varies by City/Pourosova/Union)
Source Tax (Gain Tax / TDS)1% to 8% depending on mouza classification under Income Tax Act 2023
Official Land & Mouza Portalsland.gov.bd, dlrms.land.gov.bd, and eporcha.gov.bd
📋 In This Article
  1. What is Heba in Bangladesh Law?
  2. Legal Requirements for a Valid Heba
  3. What Property Can Be Gifted by Heba?
  4. Heba vs. Will (Wasiyyat): Key Differences
  5. Registration of Heba Deed in Bangladesh
  6. When Can a Heba Be Revoked or Challenged?
  7. Heba and Gift Tax Implications
  8. Role of a Property Lawyer in Heba Transfers

What is Heba in Bangladesh Law?

Heba (Arabic: هبة) is an immediate, unconditional gift of property made by one person (the donor, or wahib) to another (the donee, or mawhublahu) during the donor's lifetime, with the intention of permanently transferring ownership. Unlike a Will, Heba takes effect immediately and does not wait for the donor's death.

In Bangladesh, Heba is governed by principles of Muslim personal law (primarily from the Hedaya and Fatawa-e-Alamgiri), as well as the Transfer of Property Act 1882 and Registration Act 1908. For non-Muslims, gifts of immovable property are known simply as "Gift Deeds" governed by the Transfer of Property Act. Before making any gift of property, consult a property lawyer in Dhaka to ensure the transfer is legally secure.

Legal Requirements for a Valid Heba

Under Muslim law in Bangladesh, three elements are required for a valid Heba:

  1. Declaration (Ijab): A clear and unambiguous offer to make the gift by the donor.
  2. Acceptance (Qabul): Clear acceptance of the gift by the donee (or their guardian if a minor).
  3. Delivery of Possession (Qabza): The donor must deliver actual or constructive possession of the property to the donee. Without possession, the Heba is incomplete and can be revoked.

For immovable property (land, flat, building), the Heba must also be:

  • Registered at the Sub-Registrar's office under the Registration Act 1908 — unregistered gifts of immovable property are void against third parties and in court.
  • Made on adequate stamp paper under the Stamp Act 1899.

What Property Can Be Gifted by Heba?

A donor can make Heba of any property that lawfully belongs to them, including:

  • Agricultural land (জমি)
  • Residential plots and buildings
  • Apartments and flats
  • Commercial property
  • Shares in jointly-owned property (with proper documentation of the share)

Limitations: A person cannot make Heba of more than one-third of their estate without the consent of heirs if they are on their deathbed (Maraz ul Maut). Such deathbed gifts are treated partly as a will and are limited to one-third of the estate — similar to the rule for Wasiyyat.

Heba vs. Will (Wasiyyat): Key Differences

Many families confuse Heba with a Will. The key distinctions:

AspectHeba (Gift)Wasiyyat (Will)
When effectiveImmediately during donor's lifetimeOnly after death
Limit on disposalCan gift entire property (during health)Max 1/3 of estate without heir consent
RevocabilityGenerally irrevocable after possession — exceptions applyFreely revocable before death
Registration requiredYes, for immovable propertyRecommended but not mandatory

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Registration of Heba Deed in Bangladesh

The Heba deed must be registered at the Sub-Registrar's office. The process:

  1. Draft the Heba deed on stamp paper of the prescribed value (value calculated on the market value of the property).
  2. Both donor and donee (or their authorized attorneys) must appear before the Sub-Registrar.
  3. Pay registration fees and stamp duty.
  4. Present supporting documents: original title deed, mutation records, NID cards of both parties.
  5. Collect the registered Heba deed — this is the donee's primary evidence of ownership.

After registration, the donee should apply for mutation (Namjari) to update the land records in their name. A property lawyer can handle the entire process seamlessly.

When Can a Heba Be Revoked or Challenged?

Under Muslim law, a donor can revoke Heba in limited circumstances — primarily before the donee takes possession, or with court permission in cases of:

  • Gift to a stranger (non-relative) — revocable before or after possession with court order.
  • Gift to a spouse — revocable if the marriage ends.

A Heba generally cannot be revoked once possession has been delivered if the gift was made to:

  • A direct blood relative (parent, child, sibling)
  • A spouse (during marriage)
  • In consideration of marriage (mehr-related gifts)

Fraudulent or coerced Heba deeds can be challenged in Civil Court. Common grounds include: donor lacked mental capacity, signature forged, donor was under undue influence, or property was gifted twice to different people. If you suspect a fraudulent Heba was registered on your property, contact an Uttara property lawyer immediately.

Role of a Property Lawyer in Heba Transfers

A Dhaka property lawyer plays a critical role in ensuring your Heba is valid, irreversible, and challenge-proof:

  • Verify clean title before the gift — ensure no encumbrance, mortgage, or competing claim exists on the property.
  • Draft the Heba deed precisely — ambiguous deeds are prime targets for litigation.
  • Handle Sub-Registrar registration and collect the registered deed.
  • Apply for mutation (Namjari) to update government land records.
  • Advise on gift tax implications and stamp duty optimization.

Advocate Md. Shah Alam has handled numerous Heba and gift deed registrations across Dhaka and Uttara. Contact our office for a consultation before your property transfer.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a parent gift property to one child through Heba without giving shares to other children?

Yes. A living donor can gift any or all of their property to any person during their lifetime. Unlike inheritance, Heba is not automatically shared among all heirs. However, unfair Heba may cause family disputes and potential legal challenges if made during terminal illness.

Is Heba registration mandatory in Bangladesh?

Yes — for immovable property (land, flat, building). Unregistered Heba is void against third parties and unenforceable in court for immovable property under the Registration Act 1908.

Can a Heba be made without the donee knowing?

No. Valid Heba requires the donee's acceptance (Qabul). A gift without the donee's knowledge and acceptance is not legally complete.

What is Heba-bil-Ewaz?

Heba-bil-Ewaz (gift for consideration) is a transfer that appears to be a gift but involves consideration (payment or exchange). It is treated like a sale for registration and stamp duty purposes.

Can Heba be made of mortgaged property?

Heba of mortgaged property is permitted but the mortgage liability accompanies the property to the donee unless the donor discharges the mortgage first.

1. The Juridical Concept of Heba Under Muslim Personal Law

Under classical Islamic jurisprudence and Bangladeshi civil law, Heba (হেবা) is defined as an immediate, unconditional transfer of property made voluntarily and without consideration (বিনা পণে) by one living person (donor / ওয়াহিব) to another (donee / মৌহুব লাহু) and accepted by or on behalf of the latter.

Unlike a Will (ওয়াসিয়ত / Wasiyat), which only takes effect upon the testator's death and is strictly capped at one-third (1/3rd) of the estate unless other legal heirs consent, a Heba takes effect immediately during the lifetime of the donor. A Muslim landowner of sound mind and legal majority has the absolute, unfettered legal right to gift the entirety (100%) of their self-acquired or ancestral property to any person, even if such gift completely disinherits other natural heirs.

2. The Three Inviolable Legal Essentials of a Valid Heba

Under established Supreme Court jurisprudence (reiterated in 54 DLR 281 and 19 BLC 412), a valid Heba requires three concurrent theological and legal essentials:

  1. Declaration of Gift (ইজাব / Ijab): An explicit, unambiguous statement by the donor manifesting an immediate intention to divest themselves of ownership and vest title in the donee without coercion or undue influence.
  2. Acceptance of Gift (কবুল / Qubul): Express or implied acceptance by the donee. If the donee is a minor child, acceptance must be made on their behalf by the legal guardian (father, paternal grandfather, or court-appointed guardian).
  3. Delivery of Possession (দখল অর্পণ): The donor must completely divest themselves of dominion and control, handing over actual physical possession or constructive possession to the donee.

3. Mandatory Registration Requirement: Section 17 Registration Act 1908

Historically, oral gifts under Islamic law were recognized in Bengal without written documentation. However, widespread fraud and forged inheritance claims prompted a comprehensive legislative overhaul in 2004:

Section 17(1)(aa) of the Registration Act, 1908: Substituted by the Law Reforms Ordinance 2004, it mandates that every instrument of gift of immovable property under Muslim law (Heba) MUST be compulsorily registered. An unregistered or oral Heba has zero legal validity in Bangladesh, cannot be relied upon in civil courts, and cannot be used to mutate names in government land revenue records.

4. The 33 Designated Blood Relations for Fixed BDT 100 Stamp Duty

To encourage family asset consolidation, the government of Bangladesh provides extraordinary fiscal concessions under the Stamp Act 1899 and Finance Act for gifts made among 33 specific degrees of blood relationships:

  • Husband to Wife and Wife to Husband (স্বামী ও স্ত্রী)
  • Father / Mother to Son / Daughter (পিতা-মাতা ও সন্তান)
  • Grandfather / Grandmother to Grandson / Granddaughter (দাদা-দাদী, নানা-নানী ও নাতি-নাতনী)
  • Full Brothers and Sisters (সহোদর ভাই ও বোন)
  • Brother's son/daughter to Paternal Uncle/Aunt (and reciprocal relations defined under statutory rules)

If the gift is made within these 33 degrees, the ad-valorem stamp duty (which is otherwise 1.5% to 3%) is slashed to a nominal fixed fee of just BDT 100.

6. Step-by-Step Procedure to Execute a Heba Deed from USA, UK & Canada

When the expatriate donor or donee resides overseas, follow this exact legal roadmap:

  1. Drafting the Heba Declaration & Special Power of Attorney: Your advocate in Dhaka drafts a Special Power of Attorney for Heba Registration under Form 1 of the 2015 Rules, accompanied by the draft Heba Deed specifying the property schedule and relation.
  2. Consular Attestation Abroad: The donor attends the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission in Washington DC, New York, London, Ottawa, etc., signing the deed before the Consular Officer with photographs affixed.
  3. MOFA & DC Office Endorsement in Dhaka: The original document is couriered to Dhaka, authenticated at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Segunbagicha, and stamped at the Deputy Commissioner's office under Section 18 of the Stamp Act.
  4. Execution at Sub-Registry: The nominated attorney attends the Sub-Registry Office with the donee (or donee's representative). The Sub-Registrar verifies the relationship through birth certificates/NID, collects the nominal BDT 100 fee, and registers the Heba Deed.
  5. Obtaining the Registered Deed: The Sub-Registrar issues an official Receipt (রসিদ / Form 52). The certified copy (নকল) is typically ready within 7 to 15 days.

7. Statutory Government Fees, Taxes & Stamp Duty Breakdown (2026)

For an eligible Heba deed among the 33 designated blood relations, the exact statutory government fee breakdown at the Sub-Registry is remarkably minimal:

  • Stamp Duty (স্ট্যাম্প শুল্ক): Fixed at BDT 100 (paid via Non-Judicial Stamp or Treasury Chalan).
  • Registration Fee (নিবন্ধন ফি): Fixed at BDT 100 under Article A(1) of the Registration Table of Fees.
  • Local Government Tax: Exempted (BDT 0).
  • Advance Source Tax (AIT Section 125): Exempted (BDT 0).
  • E-Fee (নকলনবিশের পারিশ্রমিক): BDT 200–300 depending on page count.
  • N-Fee (কপি বালামের ফি): BDT 240.
  • Total Government Cost: Approximately BDT 2,500 to BDT 5,000, regardless of whether the flat is worth BDT 50 Lakh or BDT 10 Crore!

8. Constructive Delivery of Possession for Overseas Donors & Donees

Because both donor and donee may reside thousands of miles away in New York or London, physical handover of the key or soil is impossible. Under Bangladeshi law, Constructive Delivery of Possession (অনুমানমূলক বা প্রতীকী দখল অর্পণ) is 100% legally recognized:

  • Handing over the original registered title deeds (মূল দলিল) and historical Khatians to the donee.
  • Instructing tenants or commercial caretakers in writing to pay all future rents directly to the donee.
  • Directing the building society or flat owners' association to update their registry with the donee's name.
  • Applying online for e-Namjari mutation in the donee's name.

9. Legal Irrevocability: Can a Registered Heba Be Cancelled Later?

A common dispute arises when a donor later falls out with a child and attempts to unilaterally cancel the gift deed:

Section 126 Transfer of Property Act & Islamic Personal Law: Once a Heba between close blood relations is registered and possession is delivered, it becomes completely and permanently irrevocable. The donor CANNOT unilaterally execute a cancellation deed (বাতিল দলিল) at the Sub-Registry. Any unilateral cancellation deed executed by a Sub-Registrar is illegal and void ab initio (39 DLR 353). A Heba can only be set aside by a formal civil court decree proving fraud, forgery, or coercion under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act 1877.

10. Post-Registration Protocol: e-Namjari Mutation & Online Khajna Update

Registration at the Sub-Registry transfers legal title, but it does NOT automatically update government land revenue records. To seal the transfer:

  1. Access the Ministry of Land mutation portal mutation.land.gov.bd within 28 days of deed issuance.
  2. Submit an application attaching the registered Heba deed, donor's Khatian, and both parties' NID/passports.
  3. The Assistant Commissioner (Land) conducts digital scrutiny, issues a formal Mutation Khatian in the donee's name, and issues a DCR receipt for BDT 1,150.
  4. Pay digital Land Development Tax at ldtax.gov.bd to generate government tax dakhilas in the child's name.

11. Real-Life Case Study: New York Father Gifting a Banani Apartment to His Daughter

Background: Mr. Shawkat Hossain, an expatriate architect residing in Manhattan, New York, wanted to gift a luxury 2,400 sq. ft. residential apartment in Banani, Dhaka (market value BDT 4.2 Crore) to his newly-married daughter living in Toronto, Canada.

Execution Strategy:

  1. If executed as a sale deed, registration taxes would have exceeded BDT 45 Lakh ($38,000 USD).
  2. Our chamber structured the transaction as a simple Heba between Father and Daughter under the 33 blood relations rule.
  3. Mr. Shawkat executed a Special Power of Attorney at the New York Consulate, while his daughter executed a representative power in Toronto.
  4. Both deeds were authenticated at MOFA Segunbagicha and adjudicated at the Dhaka DC office.
  5. Our team attended the Tejgaon Sub-Registry, completed the registered Heba deed for under BDT 5,000 in official fees, and secured the digital e-Namjari Khatian within 21 days. Total savings: over $35,000 USD in avoided transfer taxes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I gift a flat in Dhaka to my daughter living with me in the UK?

Yes. You can execute a Special Power of Attorney at the Bangladesh High Commission in London to register the Heba deed in Dhaka, transferring full title to your daughter with fixed BDT 100 stamp duty.

Do I have to pay capital gains tax on a Heba gift in Bangladesh?

No. Gifting property between eligible close blood relations is completely exempt from capital gains tax and advance source tax under Section 125 of the Income Tax Act 2023.

Can I give a Heba to my cousin, brother-in-law, or daughter-in-law under the BDT 100 rule?

No. Cousins, in-laws, and step-relatives fall outside the designated 33 blood relationships. Gifting to them is treated as a general gift, attracting standard ad-valorem stamp duty (1.5%) and local registration taxes.

Can a father take back property gifted to his son after the Heba deed is registered?

No. Under Muslim personal law and the Registration Act 1908, a registered gift to a direct lineal descendant becomes completely irrevocable upon registration and delivery of possession.

What is the difference between Heba and a Will (Wasiyat) in Bangladesh?

A Heba takes effect immediately during the lifetime of the donor and can cover 100% of assets. A Will takes effect only after death and cannot exceed 1/3rd of the estate without other legal heirs' consent.

Can a Hindu citizen execute a Heba deed in Bangladesh?

No. Heba is a concept exclusive to Muslim personal law. A Hindu citizen transfers property without consideration through a registered Gift Deed (দানপত্র দলিল) under the Transfer of Property Act 1882.

How long does the entire Heba deed registration and mutation take from abroad?

Embassy execution abroad takes 3 to 5 days, MOFA and DC office stamping in Dhaka takes 2 to 3 weeks, Sub-Registry registration takes 1 day, and e-Namjari mutation takes approximately 28 working days.

Can minor children receive a Heba deed in Bangladesh?

Yes. A minor child can lawfully receive property via Heba; acceptance (Qubul) is formally executed on their behalf by their legal guardian (father, paternal grandfather, or court-appointed guardian).

Anticipatory Bail in High Court Bangladesh: Cost, Procedure, Documents & Required Time (2026 Guide)

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-08-15 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

When an individual faces an imminent threat of arrest in a non-bailable, false, or politically/business-motivated criminal case, the legal framework of Bangladesh offers pre-arrest protection known as <strong>Anticipatory Bail (আগাম জামিন)</strong> under <strong>Section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), 1898</strong>. Secured predominantly from the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, anticipatory bail shields innocent individuals from arbitrary detention and police custody until the allegations are properly examined. This definitive 2026 guide by <strong>Advocate Md. Shah Alam</strong>, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, details the legal grounds, procedural steps, mandatory court appearances, and realistic costs involved.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

What Is Anticipatory Bail and How Does Section 498 Cr.P.C. Function?

Anticipatory bail is an extraordinary judicial remedy granting bail in anticipation of arrest. Unlike regular bail under Section 497 Cr.P.C., which is sought after an accused is already arrested or detained by police, anticipatory bail under Section 498 is prayed for prior to formal arrest.

If granted by the High Court Division, the court directs the police that in the event of the petitioner's arrest in connection with the specified case, they must immediately release the individual on furnishing a bail bond.

Grounds for Granting Anticipatory Bail in the High Court Division

The High Court Division exercises discretionary power under Section 498 sparingly and only upon sound judicial principles. Key grounds include:

  • Malafide & Collateral Purpose: Where the First Information Report (FIR) or Complaint Case (C.R. Case) has been filed to harass, humiliate, or extort the accused due to business rivalry, land disputes, or political animosity.
  • Absence of Specific Overt Acts: Where the petitioner is roped in omnibus allegations without any direct role in the alleged offence.
  • Vulnerable Status: Old age, acute medical conditions, women, or individuals of respectable social standing with deep community roots who are unlikely to abscond.
  • Documentary Proof of Innocence: Undeniable alibi or documentary proof showing that the accused was elsewhere or that the dispute is purely of a civil nature.

Mandatory Prerequisite: The Physical Surrender Requirement

A fundamental rule settled by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh is that no person can obtain anticipatory bail while remaining in hiding or through an attorney alone.

The petitioner must be physically present inside the courtroom before the High Court Division Bench when the matter is called for hearing. If the Bench refuses bail, the petitioner risks being handed over to law enforcement officers present in the court premises.

Step-by-Step Procedure to Obtain Anticipatory Bail in the High Court

  1. Step 1: Procurement of Case Documents: Procure a certified copy of the FIR from the concerned Thana or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) / Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) court, or the Complaint Petition in C.R. cases.
  2. Step 2: Drafting the Criminal Miscellaneous Petition: Your High Court advocate drafts a Criminal Miscellaneous (Cr. Misc.) petition detailing the background, grounds of innocence, and persecution threats.
  3. Step 3: Affidavit & Filing: The petitioner or a Tadbirkar deposes an affidavit before the Supreme Court Affidavit Commissioner. The petition is formally filed with the High Court Registry.
  4. Step 4: Bench Placement & Hearing: The application is listed in the Daily Cause List of the designated Criminal Anticipatory Bail Bench. The advocate presents oral submissions while the petitioner stands before the bench.
  5. Step 5: Pronouncement & Bail Order: The Court pronounces the order (typically granting 4 to 8 weeks bail) and directs the petitioner to surrender before the competent Sessions Court upon expiry.

Required Documents & Evidence Checklist

  • Certified copy of the FIR / Ejahar or Complaint Petition (C.R. Case).
  • Forwarding letter, seizure list, and remand rejection copies (if co-accused were earlier arrested).
  • Valid National ID Card (NID) or Passport of the petitioner.
  • Certified medical documents from registered physicians (if bail is sought on medical grounds).
  • Exculpatory documentary evidence (e.g., flight tickets, CCTV logs, employment records establishing an alibi).

Filing Expenses, Court Fees & Realistic Legal Costs in 2026

The total cost of obtaining anticipatory bail consists of government court fees, clerk charges, and professional advocate fees:

  • Government Court Fees & Stamp Duty: Modest statutory costs including Supreme Court welfare stamps, vokalatnama stamp, and affidavit stamps (typically BDT 1,500 – 3,500).
  • Certified Copy Retrieval: Expenses for court clerks and typists at the district registry (BDT 2,000 – 5,000).
  • Professional Advocate Fees: Depending on the severity of charges (e.g., cheating, property dispute vs. murder, cybercrime, or Special Powers Act), professional fees in Dhaka range from BDT 40,000 to BDT 150,000+.

What Happens After Anticipatory Bail is Granted? (Surrender in Lower Court)

Anticipatory bail is transitional. The High Court grants it to protect the petitioner from immediate arrest while directing them to surrender before the concerned Court of Sessions Judge or Metropolitan Sessions Judge within the granted period (e.g., 4 or 6 weeks).

Before the expiration of the granted timeframe, your lawyer will prepare a regular bail application under Section 497 Cr.P.C. before the trial court. Having respected the High Court’s surrender order, trial courts routinely confirm regular bail.

What If Anticipatory Bail is Rejected?

If the High Court Division is not inclined to grant anticipatory bail, the counsel may withdraw the petition before formal rejection to avoid adverse observations on record, or seek direction from the Bench for the petitioner to surrender peacefully before the trial magistrate within 7 days without police harassment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can anyone apply for Anticipatory Bail before an FIR is lodged?

No. The law requires a specific apprehension based on an actual registered FIR or formal complaint (C.R. Case). Anticipatory bail cannot be granted on vague or imaginary fears.

Does the accused have to go to court personally for Anticipatory Bail?

Yes, absolutely mandatory. The petitioner must surrender and be physically present in the High Court courtroom during the hearing.

How long does it take to secure Anticipatory Bail in the High Court?

Under normal circumstances, it takes 2 to 4 working days from receiving the certified FIR copy. In cases of extreme urgency, filings can be expedited within 24 to 48 hours.

Can police arrest someone after Anticipatory Bail is granted?

No. As long as the petitioner holds a valid certified order of anticipatory bail from the High Court Division, law enforcement agencies cannot arrest or detain them in that specified case.

How Heirs Claim Deceased Parent Bank FDR and Savings in Bangladesh: Succession Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-10 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Following the tragic demise of a parent, families face immense emotional grief alongside sudden administrative hurdles. When heirs approach the deceased's bank branch to access savings accounts, Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDR), or treasury bonds, they are frequently met with bureaucratic resistance: bank managers refuse withdrawals, citing outdated regulations, or an estranged sibling nominated on the account claims absolute personal ownership of all funds to the exclusion of other heirs. In Bangladesh, banking operations and inheritance laws are strictly regulated. The Supreme Court has unequivocally established that a nominee is merely a trustee/custodian—not the beneficial owner. Understanding how to navigate Bangladesh Bank regulations and obtain a Succession Certificate from the Joint District Judge Court under the Succession Act 1925 is the definitive legal key to releasing and distributing your rightful family inheritance.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

The Challenge: Accessing Deceased Parents' Bank Accounts

When a parent passes away in Bangladesh, their estate consists not only of immovable lands and homesteads, but frequently of substantial liquid assets: savings accounts, Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDR), current corporate accounts, national savings certificates (Sanchayapatra), and locker contents. Heirs expect that by presenting the deceased's death certificate and the local Chairman's Warishan Certificate (heirship certificate), the bank will promptly divide and disburse the money.

In reality, bank compliance procedures are stringent. Commercial banks fear wrongful disbursement liability and conflicting claims among family members. Under Section 103 of the Bank Company Act 1991, banks operate with immense caution. If the deceased parent did not name a nominee, named an estranged relative who refuses to share, or left a multi-lakh FDR deposit, bank managers immediately freeze operations and issue a formal compliance letter: 'Please obtain and submit a Succession Certificate from the competent civil court.' Understanding the legal pathway to procure this certificate is essential to prevent family assets from languishing indefinitely in frozen bank vaults.

Nominee vs. Legal Heirs: The Supreme Court Settled Law

For decades, a bitter legal controversy raged in Bangladesh: does the nominee named in a bank account form become the absolute owner of the money upon the depositor's death, or are they merely an agent receiving the money for all legal heirs? Selfish nominees routinely argued that Section 103 of the Bank Company Act 1991 gave them exclusive rights, cutting out daughters, elderly mothers, or younger siblings.

This dispute was decisively and permanently settled by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. In landmark judgments of both the High Court Division and the Appellate Division (including the celebrated Bangladesh Bank vs. Bilkis Hossain jurisprudence), the highest court established that a nominee is merely a collector or trustee. The court ruled that nomination does not constitute a gift (Hiba) or a will (Wasiyat). The nominee's sole function is to receive the funds from the bank to give the bank a valid discharge of liability; once received, the money forms part of the deceased's general estate and must be distributed among all statutory heirs strictly according to their religious personal law (Faraiz under Islamic law or Hindu succession rules). Any nominee who appropriates the funds solely for themselves commits criminal breach of trust under Section 406 of the Penal Code 1860.

Bangladesh Bank Regulations on Deceased Depositors

The central bank, Bangladesh Bank, has issued detailed Master Circulars to commercial banks regarding the treatment of deceased depositors' accounts. These regulations balance administrative convenience with heirship protection:

  • Small Balance Protocol (Without Court Certificate): For relatively minor balances (typically amounts under BDT 1,00,000 to BDT 2,00,000, depending on the internal policy of the bank), banks can release funds without a Succession Certificate if all legal heirs appear in person, execute a joint indemnity bond, and submit certified death certificates and Warishan certificates.
  • Substantial Balances & FDRs: Where the balance is substantial (exceeding bank policy thresholds, or involving large term deposits/FDRs), banks are legally mandated to demand an authenticated Succession Certificate issued by the Joint District Judge Court.
  • Disputed Accounts: If any single heir submits a written objection claiming that the nominee is acting fraudulently or that certain heirs are being concealed, the bank must instantaneously place a 'Debit Block' on the account, disallowing any withdrawals until a court order is produced.

Understanding these thresholds prevents heirs from wasting months arguing with branch officers when a civil court petition is the mandatory legal requirement.

What Is a Succession Certificate Under the 1925 Act?

A Succession Certificate is a specialized judicial document granted by a civil court under Part X (Sections 370 to 390) of the Succession Act 1925. It provides official judicial authority to the person(s) named therein to collect debts and securities due to the estate of a deceased individual and to give valid discharge to debtors, including commercial banks, insurance companies, and public institutions.

It is important to distinguish a Succession Certificate from a Letters of Administration or Probate: a Succession Certificate applies exclusively to 'debts and securities'—meaning liquid cash in bank accounts, FDRs, shares, bonds, mutual funds, and government savings certificates. It does not apply to immovable agricultural lands or residential buildings. Once the court grants the certificate, commercial banks are statutorily bound to disburse the specified amounts according to the percentage shares specified in the court's decree.

Step-by-Step Procedure in the Joint District Judge Court

Procuring a Succession Certificate requires a structured judicial procedure before the Court of the Joint District Judge within whose territorial jurisdiction the deceased ordinarily resided or where the bank branch is situated:

  1. Drafting the Petition (Section 372 Succession Act): The petition must specify the exact date and place of death, annex the official death certificate, list all surviving legal heirs with their relationship and ages, provide the Faraiz calculation of shares, and detail the exact bank accounts, FDR numbers, and monetary sums.
  2. Filing and Gazetted Newspaper Notice: Upon admission of the petition, the court orders a public citation published in a widely circulated national Bengali daily newspaper, providing 15 to 30 days for any potential claimant or creditor to file an objection.
  3. Ex Parte Hearing or Contested Evidence: If no objections are filed, the petitioner appears before the judge, submits original documents (FDR receipts, death certificates, Warishan Sanad), and tenders formal oral evidence confirming the family pedigree.
  4. Judicial Grant and Security Bond: The court passes an order granting the Succession Certificate. Upon furnishing the requisite court fees and any indemnity bond required by the court, the official sealed certificate is signed and issued.

Typically, an uncontested Succession Case concludes within 60 to 90 days when handled by experienced banking and succession counsel.

Court Fees and Statutory Costs for Succession Certificates

A common apprehension among heirs is that court fees for releasing bank funds will consume their inheritance. In Bangladesh, court fees for a Succession Certificate are governed by the Court-fees Act 1870 (Schedule I, Article 12) and Ministry of Law statutory notifications.

Under current statutory rates, the ad-valorem court fee is calculated as a small percentage of the total debt/security value, subject to a statutory maximum cap. For modest sums, the court fee is minimal; for multi-million-taka estates, the fee is legally capped to prevent disproportionate burden on grieving families. When weighed against the prospect of leaving tens of lakhs of taka frozen indefinitely or losing the funds entirely to a rogue nominee, statutory court costs represent a modest, structured investment to secure permanent, unchallengeable legal ownership.

How to Freeze an Account If a Nominee Tries to Flee

In crisis situations, heirs discover that an untrustworthy sibling or relative named as nominee is quietly communicating with the bank branch manager to withdraw the entire FDR balance and transfer it to their personal account. If the funds are cashed out and converted into cash, recovering them through years of civil litigation is exceptionally difficult.

To prevent immediate asset flight, legal counsel executes an emergency two-step intervention:

  • Immediate Advocate Notice to Branch Manager: Dispatch an urgent formal legal notice to the bank branch manager, regional head, and managing director, citing the Appellate Division ruling on nominee trusteeship. The notice informs the bank that the depositor has deceased, lists the legal heirs, asserts an active dispute, and warns that if the bank disburses funds solely to the nominee, the bank officers will be held personally liable for aiding criminal breach of trust. Upon receiving this notice, banks immediately freeze withdrawals to protect themselves from liability.
  • Injunction from Civil Court: Concurrently, file an application before the Joint District Judge or Family Court for an interim order of injunction restraining the bank from disbursing funds until the disposal of the Succession Case.

This swift action locks the money safely inside the banking system until the court determines each heir's lawful percentage.

Comparison Table: Nominee Rights vs. Legal Heir Rights

The table below summarizes the exact legal distinctions between a bank nominee and a legal heir under Bangladesh law:

Nature of RightTrustee / custodian for collection onlyTrue beneficial owner of the estate
Legal AuthorityBank Company Act 1991 Section 103Religious personal laws of succession (Faraiz)
Ownership of FundsZero ownership; cannot keep fundsEntitled to statutory percentage share
Remedy If Funds StolenGuilty of Penal Code §406 criminal breachCan prosecute nominee and attach assets
Bank Withdrawal BasisPermitted only if uncontested by heirsAbsolute right via Succession Certificate

Recognizing that nominees are merely custodians protects families from being disinherited by predatory relatives.

Illustrative Scenario: Recovering an FDR from a Hostile Nominee

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) demonstrates how siblings protected their inheritance from a rogue nominee in Dhaka:

A retired government physician passed away in Dhanmondi, leaving behind three children: two married daughters living abroad in London and an unmarried son living with him. The father held BDT 65,00,000 across two Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDR) in a private commercial bank. Unbeknownst to his sisters, the son had persuaded his ailing father to nominate him as the sole nominee on both FDR accounts. Following the father's demise, the son visited the bank, presented the death certificate, and requested the entire BDT 65,00,000 be transferred into his personal account, falsely informing the branch manager that he was the only surviving child.

When the daughters discovered the deception, they contacted an advocate in Dhaka. The advocate immediately drafted an emergency legal notice served by hand to the branch manager and the bank's head of legal. The notice attached the registered Nikahnama, the family's official Warishan Sanad issued by Dhaka South City Corporation proving the existence of the two daughters, and cited Supreme Court rulings establishing that the nominee is strictly a trustee. Fearing legal liability, the bank placed an immediate freeze on both FDRs.

The advocate then filed a Succession Case in the Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka, on behalf of the daughters. The court issued public citations and summoned the bank's account statements. During the hearing, the son's lawyer conceded that under Islamic Faraiz law, the son was entitled to 50% of the estate, while each daughter was entitled to 25%. The Joint District Judge issued a Succession Certificate distributing the BDT 65,00,000 strictly according to the statutory Faraiz shares. The bank disbursed the funds via three separate certified pay orders, ensuring justice and preserving the daughters' lawful inheritance.

Talk to an Advocate

Navigating the release of a deceased parent's bank accounts, FDRs, and securities requires disciplined legal navigation between banking compliance and civil court succession. Attempting to resolve nominee disputes through informal arguments often results in funds being misappropriated or frozen permanently. An experienced succession and banking advocate will immediately freeze unauthorized withdrawals, prepare your Succession Case before the Joint District Judge Court, and ensure that every heir receives their precise statutory inheritance without delay.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a nominee own the bank money after the account holder dies in Bangladesh?

No. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has firmly settled that a nominee is merely a trustee and custodian. The money belongs to all legal heirs according to their personal inheritance laws (Faraiz), and the nominee must distribute the funds among all statutory heirs.

What is a Succession Certificate and why does the bank demand it?

A Succession Certificate is a court order issued by the Joint District Judge Court under the Succession Act 1925 empowering legal heirs to collect debts and securities of a deceased person. Banks require it for large deposits or disputed accounts to protect themselves from wrongful disbursement claims.

How long does it take to get a Succession Certificate in Bangladesh?

An uncontested Succession Case typically takes between 60 to 90 days from filing to certificate issuance, which includes the mandatory 15-30 day public newspaper citation period.

Can an FDR be cashed out without a Succession Certificate?

For smaller sums, some banks may release funds upon submission of a certified Warishan Certificate, death certificate, and an indemnity bond signed by all legal heirs. For substantial FDR amounts, a court Succession Certificate is mandatory.

What should I do if a nominee is secretly trying to withdraw all the money?

Immediately serve a formal Advocate Legal Notice on the bank branch manager and regional office, informing them of the death and the legal heirs. The bank will place an immediate 'Debit Block' on the account to freeze withdrawals.

What documents are required to file a Succession Case in Bangladesh?

You need the official Death Certificate, Chairman/Councillor Warishan Certificate, National ID copies of all heirs, bank statements or FDR certificates with exact account numbers, and the calculated Faraiz distribution shares.

Can overseas Bangladeshi heirs (NRB) claim bank money without traveling to Bangladesh?

Yes. An NRB heir can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the local Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, appointing a trusted representative or lawyer in Bangladesh to file the Succession Case and collect their share.

What happens if the nominee spends the money and refuses to share with other heirs?

The nominee commits criminal breach of trust under Section 406 of the Penal Code 1860, punishable by up to 3 years imprisonment. The legal heirs can file a criminal case in the Magistrate Court and a civil suit for recovery and asset attachment.

How to Quash a False FIR or Criminal Case in High Court Bangladesh (Section 561A CrPC Guide)

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-24 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

False criminal cases, fabricated FIRs, and malicious prosecutions are frequently misused in Bangladesh to settle personal vendettas, land disputes, or business rivalries. Facing a bogus criminal charge under severe sections of the Penal Code can jeopardize your career, reputation, and personal freedom. Fortunately, under Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), the High Court Division has inherent powers to quash (cancel) any illegal or malicious criminal proceeding to prevent abuse of judicial process. For immediate protection, consult Supreme Court Advocate <a href="/advocate-md-shah-alam" style="color:var(--accent);font-weight:600;">Advocate Md. Shah Alam</a>.

What Is Quashment Under Section 561A CrPC?

Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 confers inherent powers upon the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under the CrPC, or to prevent abuse of the process of any court, or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

Quashment is an extraordinary judicial remedy where the High Court steps in to wipe out an illegal FIR, investigation, charge sheet, or trial order right at the threshold, saving innocent citizens from prolonged trial harassment.

When Can You File for Quashment in High Court?

The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has laid down strict parameters regarding when inherent powers under Section 561A may be exercised:

  • No Offence Disclosed: Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint, even if taken at face value, do not constitute any criminal offence under the law.
  • Absence of Material Evidence: Where the police charge sheet contains zero evidence linking the accused to the alleged crime.
  • Barred by Law: Where the prosecution is expressly barred by statutory limitation or lack of required sanction (e.g., prosecution without government sanction under Section 197 CrPC).
  • Civil Dispute Criminalized: Where a purely civil land or contract breach has been given a false criminal color (e.g., converting a land partition dispute into a fraud case under Sections 420/406 IPC).
  • Malicious Intent (Mala Fide): Where the criminal proceeding is manifestly instituted with ulterior motives to exact vengeance.

Quashing FIR vs. Quashing Charge Sheet (Investigation vs. Trial Stage)

Timing is critical when invoking Section 561A CrPC:

  • Quashing FIR (Investigation Stage): Courts are generally cautious about interfering during ongoing police investigation. However, if the FIR is absurd, impossible on its face, or politically motivated, the High Court can stay proceedings and call for records.
  • Quashing Charge Sheet / Framing of Charge (Trial Stage): This is the most effective stage. Once police file a Charge Sheet (Police Report under Section 173 CrPC) or the magistrate takes cognizance, if the evidence is insufficient, a 561A petition is highly maintainable.

Consult a qualified Criminal Defense Lawyer in Dhaka to determine whether to file immediately or after charge sheet submission.

Step-by-Step Procedure to File a 561A Petition

Filing a Quashment Miscellaneous Petition before the High Court Division follows these statutory steps:

  1. Certified Copies: Obtain certified copies of the FIR, General Diary (GD), Seizure List, Charge Sheet, and order sheets from the concerned Magistrate Court.
  2. Drafting 561A Application: Advocate drafts the criminal miscellaneous petition citing specific legal errors and precedents.
  3. Affidavit & Verification: Swear an affidavit before the Oath Commissioner at the High Court.
  4. Filing & Bench Motion: File in the High Court Registry and move the petition before a designated Division Bench dealing with Criminal Miscellaneous matters.
  5. Rule Nisi & Stay Order: The High Court bench hears primary arguments. If satisfied, it issues a Rule Nisi to the State and Complainant, and grants an immediate Stay of Proceedings.
  6. Final Hearing: Upon receiving state counter-affidavit, final arguments take place. If allowed, the High Court passes an order making the Rule Absolute, cancelling the case completely.

Key Precedents & Judgments of Supreme Court of Bangladesh

In landmark decisions such as Ali Akbor vs. The State (45 DLR AD 164) and Habibur Rahman vs. State, the Supreme Court held that where a criminal proceeding is instituted without legal justification, keeping the case pending inflicts irreparable harm upon the citizen's right to liberty (Article 32 of Constitution).

Citing established Appellate Division rulings is vital for winning a 561A motion on the first day of hearing.

How to Obtain an Interim Stay Order against Arrest

When filing a 561A petition, your lawyer will simultaneously pray for an interim stay order (স্থগিতাদেশ). If granted:

  • Police cannot arrest you in connection with that specific case.
  • Trial court proceedings (summons, warrant, trial dates) are completely frozen.
  • You receive full legal protection while the High Court evaluates the petition.

To secure a stay order, present strong documentary evidence proving your innocence (e.g., Alibi proof, passport exit logs showing you were abroad on the date of alleged crime).

Counter-Filing Against False Complainants (Section 211 Penal Code)

Once your criminal case is quashed or discharged, you have full legal authority to hold the false complainant accountable:

  • Section 211 of Penal Code 1860: File a criminal case against the false complainant for making a false charge of offence with intent to injure. Punishable up to 7 years imprisonment.
  • Civil Suit for Damages: File a civil suit in the Sub-Judge Court claiming monetary compensation for malicious prosecution and loss of reputation.

Why Expert High Court Defense Representation Is Essential

Navigating criminal proceedings before the High Court Division demands precise constitutional knowledge, flawless drafting, and persuasive oral argument.

Advocate Md. Shah Alam — Supreme Court Advocate with 10+ years of practice (enrolled advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh since 2015) — has successfully quashed numerous false criminal cases, securing interim stay orders and full discharges for his clients.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can an FIR be quashed before police file a charge sheet in Bangladesh?

Yes. If the FIR allegations on their face disclose no crime or are demonstrably impossible, the High Court Division can stay police investigation and quash the FIR under Section 561A CrPC.

How long does a Section 561A quashment petition take in the High Court?

An interim Stay Order against arrest/proceedings can be obtained on the first day of motion hearing (within 2-4 days of filing). The final Rule hearing takes 3 to 12 months depending on court list.

What is the difference between Discharge (Section 241A/265C) and Quashment (Section 561A)?

Discharge is granted by the local Magistrate/Sessions trial court at the stage of framing charges. Quashment is an inherent power exercised exclusively by the High Court Division to strike down illegal proceedings at any stage.

Do I need anticipatory bail if I file a 561A quashment petition?

If there is an active arrest warrant or immediate risk of arrest, it is best practice to seek Anticipatory Bail alongside or prior to moving a 561A stay petition.

How to Challenge and Quash a False Criminal Case in Bangladesh: Complete Legal Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-12 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

False criminal cases are a serious problem in Bangladesh, often filed out of personal vendettas, business disputes, or to harass opponents. If you have been falsely accused, you have several powerful legal remedies from obtaining anticipatory bail to filing a quashing petition in the High Court Division. This guide explains every step you can take to fight back.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Understanding False Criminal Cases in Bangladesh

False criminal cases in Bangladesh are disturbingly common. They are filed for various reasons:

  • Land disputes where the opponent uses criminal charges to harass the rightful owner
  • Business conflicts where false fraud or misappropriation charges are filed
  • Personal vendettas between family members or neighbors
  • Political persecution where criminal cases are filed against opposition members or activists
  • Extortion by unscrupulous individuals threatening criminal prosecution

The Bangladesh legal system provides multiple remedies for the falsely accused, both at the trial court level and through the constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. Engaging an experienced criminal lawyer in Bangladesh at the earliest stage is critical.

Immediate Steps: Anticipatory Bail and Lawyer Engagement

If you learn that a criminal case has been filed against you or that your arrest is imminent, your first priority is to:

  1. Engage a criminal lawyer immediately: Do not wait until you are arrested. A lawyer can assess the FIR, advise on the strength of the case, and immediately move for anticipatory bail.
  2. Apply for anticipatory bail: Under Section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) 1898, you can apply for anticipatory bail to any Session Court or High Court Division with jurisdiction. This prevents your arrest while the court examines the merits.
  3. Stay calm and do not flee: Fleeing makes you look guilty. Remain accessible to your lawyer and comply with court directions.
  4. Gather initial evidence: Collect documents, messages, or witnesses that establish your innocence or the falsity of the allegations from day one.

Our experienced bail lawyers can file for anticipatory bail within hours of being engaged.

Applying for Regular Bail in a False Case

If you have already been arrested on a false case, securing bail is your first objective. In Bangladesh:

  • Cognizable offenses: Police can arrest without warrant. Bail applications for non-bailable offenses go to the Magistrate's Court, then Sessions Court if rejected.
  • Factors courts consider for bail: Nature of the offense, strength of evidence against you, your ties to the community, risk of flight, and likelihood of tampering with evidence
  • Bail for non-bailable offenses: Under Section 497 CrPC, courts have discretion to grant bail for non-bailable offenses. For a false case, your lawyer should present the lack of a prima facie case, your clean record, your community ties, and the motivated nature of the complaint.
  • High Court Division bail: If Sessions Court denies bail, an immediate appeal to the High Court Division is available under Section 498 CrPC. The High Court has broader powers to grant bail and can also consider the constitutional right to liberty under Article 32 of the Bangladesh Constitution.

Act quickly as prolonged pretrial detention can cause irreparable harm to your reputation and livelihood.

Filing a Quashing Petition in the High Court Division

The most powerful remedy against a false criminal case in Bangladesh is a quashing petition filed in the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, read with Section 561A of the CrPC.

Grounds for Quashing:

  • The FIR or complaint discloses no cognizable offense even if every allegation is taken as true
  • The case is an abuse of process of court filed with malicious intent
  • There is no prima facie case against the accused
  • Manifest injustice would result from continuing the proceedings

Process:

  1. Your lawyer files a writ petition or criminal miscellaneous petition in the High Court Division
  2. The court may issue a Rule Nisi directing the lower court or prosecution to show cause why the case should not be quashed
  3. The High Court may simultaneously stay the lower court proceedings pending its decision
  4. After hearing both sides, the High Court quashes the case if grounds are established

Our Supreme Court lawyers have extensive experience in quashing petitions before the High Court Division.

Challenging the Charge Sheet and Filing for Discharge

After police investigation, they may submit either a final report if no case is found or a charge sheet if they find sufficient grounds. If a charge sheet is filed against you:

Option 1 - Discharge Petition: File an application for discharge before the trial court at the charge framing stage, arguing that the charge sheet does not disclose a sufficient case to proceed to trial. Submit exculpatory evidence, alibi documentation, and legal arguments.

Option 2 - Challenge Investigation: If the investigation was conducted improperly (e.g., no proper inquiry, witnesses fabricated, evidence planted), challenge the investigation itself. Your lawyer can file objections and call for re-investigation by the Criminal Investigation Department (CID).

Option 3 - Demand Further Investigation: You can petition the court to order further investigation if key evidence was ignored or witnesses were not examined, which may change the conclusion of the investigation.

Filing a Counter-Case Against the Complainant

Filing a false criminal case in Bangladesh is itself a criminal offense. If someone has falsely accused you, consider:

  • Filing an FIR for filing a false case: Under Section 211 of the Penal Code 1860, filing a false charge with intent to injure is punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
  • Filing a case for fabricating evidence: Under Sections 191 to 196 and 199 of the Penal Code, fabricating false evidence is a serious offense.
  • Civil suit for malicious prosecution: After the criminal case is dismissed, you can file a civil suit claiming damages for the harm caused by the false prosecution covering legal costs, lost income, reputational damage, and mental distress.
  • Defamation case: If the false allegations were published or widely circulated, a defamation case under Sections 499 to 501 of the Penal Code may also be available.

Counter-litigation strategy should be discussed with your criminal law attorney after assessing the overall case landscape.

Building Your Defense: Evidence and Witnesses

A strong defense against a false criminal case depends on proactive evidence gathering from day one:

  • Alibi evidence: Collect documentary proof that you were elsewhere at the time of the alleged offense such as CCTV footage, phone records, travel tickets, bank ATM records, or hotel receipts
  • Character witnesses: Identify credible witnesses who can testify to your good character and reputation
  • Documentary evidence: Gather contracts, emails, WhatsApp messages, bank statements, or any documents that contradict the prosecution's version of events
  • Expert witnesses: In financial fraud or technical cases, expert testimony can dismantle false allegations
  • Preserve digital evidence: Secure screenshots, email chains, and call logs that support your position

The prosecution bears the burden of proof in criminal cases and must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Your defense only needs to raise reasonable doubt to secure an acquittal.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should I do immediately after a false FIR is filed against me in Bangladesh?

Immediately engage a criminal lawyer, apply for anticipatory bail before your arrest, and gather all evidence that contradicts the allegations. Do not speak to police without your lawyer present.

How long does it take to quash a case in the High Court Division of Bangladesh?

Obtaining a Rule Nisi (stay of proceedings) from the High Court Division can take days to weeks. A final quashing order, after full hearing, typically takes 6 months to 2 years depending on case complexity and court scheduling.

Can I get anticipatory bail for a murder charge in Bangladesh?

Anticipatory bail for non-bailable offenses including murder is available under Section 498 CrPC from the High Court Division. However, courts are very cautious with serious offenses. The merits of the bail application depend heavily on the specific facts and the strength of falsity claims.

What is the punishment for filing a false case in Bangladesh?

Filing a false criminal case to injure another person is an offense under Section 211 of the Penal Code 1860, punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine. Additional charges for fabricating evidence under Sections 191 to 196 may also apply.

Can I travel abroad if I have a pending false criminal case against me in Bangladesh?

If you are on bail, you generally need court permission to travel abroad. Courts may impose travel restrictions as a bail condition. Your lawyer should apply for permission to travel abroad if needed, providing assurances of your return.

Step 1: Decide the Type of Divorce That Applies to You

Before filing, you must determine which divorce process applies to your situation. In Bangladesh, the process depends on your religion and the circumstances:

  • Muslim Talaq (Husband-initiated): The husband sends a written divorce notice to the local Arbitration Council and the wife. A 90-day reconciliation process follows.
  • Muslim Khula (Wife-initiated): The wife relinquishes her dower (mahr) in exchange for divorce. If the husband agrees, the arbitration council processes it; if not, the wife must apply to the Family Court for judicial khula.
  • Mutual Divorce (Mubaarat): Both parties agree to end the marriage. The notice is sent to the Arbitration Council, and 90 days later the divorce is effective.
  • Judicial Divorce: Filed in Family Court for cases involving khula refusal, non-Muslim divorces, or grounds under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939.

Consulting a divorce lawyer in Dhaka before starting will help you select the most appropriate process for your situation.

Step 2: Gather Essential Documents

Before initiating any divorce proceeding, collect the following documents:

  • Kabinnama (Marriage Contract): The original Muslim marriage contract is essential as it contains your dower amount and other terms. Obtain a certified copy from the Kazi office where your marriage was registered if you cannot locate the original.
  • National ID Cards: Both parties National Identity Cards (NID)
  • Birth Certificates: For all minor children, important for custody claims
  • Proof of Address: Current address documentation of both parties
  • Financial Documents: If claiming maintenance or alimony, salary slips, bank statements, or business registration documents
  • Evidence of Grounds: If filing on specific grounds such as cruelty or non-maintenance, medical reports, police complaints, or correspondence
  • Passport-size photographs of both parties

Organize all documents in advance to avoid delays in the arbitration council or court filing process.

Step 3: Drafting and Sending the Divorce Notice

For Muslim divorce (talaq, khula, or mubaarat), a formal written notice must be drafted and sent to:

  1. The Chairman of the Arbitration Council: This is the Chairman of the relevant Union Parishad, City Corporation Ward Councilor, or Paurashava Chairman where the marriage was registered or where the parties last lived together
  2. The Spouse: A copy of the divorce notice must simultaneously be delivered to the other spouse

What the notice must contain:

  • Full names and addresses of both parties
  • Date and place of marriage
  • Reference to the Kabinnama date and registration number
  • A clear statement of the intention to divorce
  • For talaq: the husband's declaration of talaq
  • For khula: the wife's offer to relinquish her dower in exchange for divorce
  • Date of notice and signature of the party giving notice

The notice should be sent by registered mail with acknowledgment receipt to ensure proof of delivery. Your divorce lawyer will draft this notice accurately to avoid procedural errors.

Step 4: Arbitration Council Proceedings

After the Chairman receives the divorce notice, the arbitration process begins:

  1. Formation of Arbitration Council: Within 30 days, the Chairman forms a council comprising the Chairman or his representative, one representative nominated by the husband, and one representative nominated by the wife
  2. Reconciliation Meetings: The council meets to attempt reconciliation. You are not required to agree to reconcile and may attend and formally decline.
  3. If Reconciliation Fails: The council confirms that reconciliation was not achieved and the 90-day period continues running from the date of the Chairman's original receipt of the notice.
  4. 90-Day Completion: Exactly 90 days after the Chairman received the notice (or after the end of iddat if the wife is pregnant), the divorce becomes legally effective.
  5. Collect Documentation: Request a formal acknowledgment and record from the Chairman's office confirming the completion of the arbitration process.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Step 5: Filing in Family Court (If Required)

Court filing is required when the wife seeks judicial khula and the husband refuses to cooperate, disputes arise over dower or maintenance, child custody needs to be formally resolved, the divorce involves non-Muslim parties, or grounds under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939 are being claimed.

How to file in Family Court:

  1. Prepare the court petition (plaint) with a statement of facts, parties' details, grounds for relief, and the specific orders sought
  2. Pay the court fees and stamp duty
  3. File the petition at the Family Court registry. In Dhaka this is at Bakshi Bazar Family Court
  4. The court issues a summons to the other party requiring them to appear and file a response
  5. Both parties appear, evidence is presented, and the court attempts conciliation before proceeding to full hearing

Step 6: Obtaining the Divorce Certificate

After the divorce is finalized either through the arbitration council or by court decree, you must obtain your official divorce certificate:

  • Arbitration Council Certificate: Apply to the Union Parishad or City Corporation Chairman's office for a certificate confirming the divorce. Bring your copy of the divorce notice, acknowledgment receipts, and national ID.
  • Court Decree: If divorce was through Family Court, the court issues a decree. Obtain a certified copy from the court registry as this is your official divorce document.
  • Registration: Under the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974, divorce should also be registered with the local Kazi office.

You will need the divorce certificate for passport applications, remarriage, property transfers, children's educational documents, and any future legal proceedings. Keep multiple certified copies in a safe location.

Common Mistakes to Avoid When Filing for Divorce

These are the most common errors that can complicate or invalidate a divorce filing in Bangladesh:

  • Failing to send notice to the Arbitration Council: Without this step, a Muslim divorce is legally invalid and may be challenged later
  • Not serving notice on the spouse simultaneously: Notice must reach both the Arbitration Council Chairman AND the spouse at the same time
  • Missing the 90-day waiting period: Divorce cannot be effective before 90 days from the date the Chairman received the notice
  • Failing to claim dower in the divorce proceedings: A wife who does not claim her dower during divorce proceedings may face difficulty recovering it later
  • Neglecting custody arrangements: Failing to formalize custody arrangements during divorce proceedings can lead to prolonged disputes later
  • Not registering the divorce: Unregistered divorces can create legal complications for future administrative purposes

Work with an experienced divorce lawyer in Bangladesh from the outset to avoid these costly mistakes.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does a divorce take in Bangladesh?

A mutual Muslim divorce through the Arbitration Council takes a minimum of 90 days. An uncontested Family Court divorce typically takes 6 to 12 months. A contested divorce involving custody, property, and dower disputes can take 2 to 4 years in the trial court, with potential appeals adding further time.

What happens to dower (mahr) when divorcing in Bangladesh?

Upon divorce, the wife is entitled to receive any unpaid dower (mahr) as specified in the Kabinnama. If the husband refuses to pay, the wife can file a dower suit in the Family Court. Courts can enforce dower payment as a debt.

Can I divorce without going to court in Bangladesh?

Yes, for Muslim divorce (talaq or mubaarat) where both parties cooperate, the entire process can be completed through the Arbitration Council without any court involvement. Court is only required for contested matters such as custody disputes, dower claims, or judicial khula.

Do I need to appear in person at the Arbitration Council?

Personal attendance is strongly recommended. While not always mandatory in practice, appearing demonstrates good faith cooperation in the reconciliation process and avoids complications. Your lawyer can accompany you and handle the procedural aspects.

Can I remarry immediately after divorce in Bangladesh?

For men, remarriage is permissible after the divorce becomes effective after the 90-day period. For Muslim women, the iddat period (approximately 3 months or 3 menstrual cycles after divorce) must pass before remarriage. If pregnant, iddat lasts until childbirth.

How to File Divorce Bangladesh – Muslim, Khul & Court Divorce Step-by-Step

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-28 · 14 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Filing for divorce in Bangladesh involves distinct legal procedures depending on who initiates it and the religion of the parties involved. Under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 and the Family Courts Ordinance 1985, Bangladeshi law provides structured pathways for talaq by the husband, khul by the wife, mutual divorce, and court-ordered dissolution of marriage. This comprehensive guide walks you through every step, required documents, costs, and timelines so you can navigate the process with confidence.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

  4. Type 3: Mutual Divorce (Mubarat)
  5. Type 4: Court Divorce via Family Court
  6. Grounds for Court Divorce Under Bangladesh Law
  7. Required Documents for Each Type of Divorce
  8. Divorce Process Flow – Comparison Table

Types of Divorce Under Bangladesh Law

Divorce in Bangladesh is primarily governed by the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (MFLO 1961) for Muslim citizens, and the Family Courts Ordinance 1985 for adjudication of family disputes. Broadly, there are four recognised types of divorce:

  • Talaq – Divorce by the husband (unilateral)
  • Khul – Divorce initiated by the wife, usually by returning the mahr (dower)
  • Mubarat (Mutual Divorce) – Divorce by mutual agreement of both spouses
  • Judicial Dissolution (Court Divorce) – Dissolution of marriage through Family Court on specified legal grounds

Each type follows a different procedural path, involves different documentation, and carries different legal consequences. Understanding which type applies to your situation is the critical first step.

Type 1: Talaq – Divorce by the Husband

Under Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, a husband who wishes to divorce his wife must follow a mandatory statutory procedure. Simply pronouncing talaq verbally three times without notice is legally ineffective in Bangladesh — failure to comply with Section 7 is a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment up to one year or a fine of Tk. 10,000, or both.

Step-by-Step Talaq Procedure:

  1. Pronounce Talaq: The husband pronounces talaq (verbally or in writing). One pronouncement is sufficient to initiate the legal process.
  2. Send Written Notice to Chairman: Within 30 days of pronouncing talaq, the husband must send a written notice to the Chairman of the relevant Union Parishad / Ward Commissioner / Paurashava. A copy of this notice must also be served on the wife.
  3. Arbitration Council Formed: Upon receiving the notice, the Chairman constitutes an Arbitration Council (comprising representatives of both parties) within 30 days and makes efforts for reconciliation over a 90-day period.
  4. Talaq Takes Effect: If reconciliation fails and the 90-day period expires, the talaq becomes effective and legally final. During the 90-day iddat period, the wife is entitled to maintenance.

Important: If the wife is pregnant at the time of talaq, the divorce only takes effect after the delivery of the child, whichever period is longer.

Type 2: Khul – Divorce Initiated by the Wife

Khul is the right of a Muslim wife to obtain a divorce by returning her mahr (dower) or any agreed consideration to the husband. Under Bangladesh law, a wife may seek khul through the Family Court if the husband is unwilling to agree.

Step-by-Step Khul Procedure:

  1. Negotiate with Husband: The wife first requests the husband to accept the return of mahr in exchange for divorce. If the husband agrees, it becomes a mutual (mubarat) divorce.
  2. File a Suit in Family Court: If the husband refuses, the wife files a suit for dissolution of marriage in the Family Court under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939, citing grounds including the husband's failure to treat her equitably, cruelty, or desertion.
  3. Court Issues Decree: The Family Court issues a decree of dissolution. The wife may be required to return the mahr amount, either fully or as determined by the court.
  4. Notice to Arbitration Council: The court's decree is communicated to the relevant Union Parishad Chairman, and the standard 90-day period may apply depending on circumstances.

A wife does not need to prove fault in a pure khul — her sincere desire to end the marriage and willingness to return dower is generally sufficient grounds before a sympathetic court.

Type 3: Mutual Divorce (Mubarat)

Mubarat refers to a divorce by mutual consent, where both husband and wife agree to end the marriage. This is the fastest and least adversarial form of divorce in Bangladesh.

Step-by-Step Mutual Divorce Procedure:

  1. Execute a Mutual Divorce Deed: Both parties sign a mutual divorce agreement (mubarat deed) drafted by a lawyer, addressing mahr, maintenance, child custody, and property.
  2. Husband Sends Talaq Notice: Even in a mutual divorce, the husband must send a written notice to the Union Parishad Chairman under Section 7 of the MFLO 1961, with a copy to the wife.
  3. 90-Day Period: The standard 90-day reconciliation window applies, after which the divorce is final.
  4. Registration (Optional but Recommended): The mutual divorce deed can be registered at the Sub-Registrar's office for a permanent legal record.

Mutual divorce is strongly recommended when both parties are in agreement, as it avoids prolonged litigation, reduces costs, and allows the parties to negotiate terms amicably — particularly regarding child custody and financial settlement.

Type 4: Court Divorce via Family Court

When a wife seeks divorce but the husband refuses to cooperate, or in cases of severe matrimonial breakdown, the Family Court (established under the Family Courts Ordinance 1985) has exclusive jurisdiction to hear and decide divorce petitions. The wife (or husband) files a suit for dissolution of marriage.

Court Divorce Filing Steps:

  1. Engage a Family Lawyer: Consult a lawyer to evaluate your grounds and prepare the plaint (petition).
  2. File the Plaint in Family Court: Submit the plaint to the Family Court in the district where either party resides. Pay the court filing fee (based on the claim amount).
  3. Summons to Defendant: The court issues summons to the other spouse.
  4. Pre-Trial Conciliation: Under Section 10 of the Family Courts Ordinance 1985, the judge attempts reconciliation between the parties.
  5. Trial and Evidence: If conciliation fails, the case proceeds to trial. Both parties submit evidence and witnesses are examined.
  6. Decree of Dissolution: The court passes a decree dissolving the marriage. The decree becomes effective after the appeal period lapses.

A Family Court divorce typically takes 6 months to 2 years, depending on the complexity of the case, cooperation of the parties, and court backlog.

Grounds for Court Divorce Under Bangladesh Law

Under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939, a Muslim wife may seek judicial dissolution of marriage on the following grounds:

  • Whereabouts of the husband have been unknown for 4 years
  • Husband has failed to provide maintenance for 2 years
  • Husband has been sentenced to imprisonment for 7 years or more
  • Husband has failed to perform marital obligations for 3 years without reasonable cause
  • Husband was impotent at the time of marriage and remains so
  • Husband has been insane for 2 years or suffers from leprosy or venereal disease
  • Wife was married before the age of 15 and repudiates the marriage before age 18 (option of puberty)
  • Husband treats the wife with cruelty (physical or mental)
  • Any other ground recognized by Islamic law (residual ground)

A husband may also file for dissolution citing the wife's desertion or other valid grounds. The court examines all evidence before issuing a decree.

Required Documents for Each Type of Divorce

Having the correct documents ready speeds up the divorce process significantly. Below is a breakdown by divorce type:

Document Talaq Khul Mutual Court

Written Talaq Notice (Section 7 MFLO) Yes No Yes No
Proof of Mahr payment / return No Yes Optional Optional
