6. Summary Matrix: CIB Loan Status Codes, Impact & Legal Solutions

Understanding CIB classification codes and corresponding legal remedies is vital for navigating credit rehabilitation. The following matrix synthesizes the operational classifications:

CIB Classification Code Overdue Period Threshold Impact on Borrowing & Directorship Recommended Remedial Pathway
STD (Standard) Regular payment; overdue < 60 days Full access to credit, credit cards, and directorships Maintain normal debt servicing schedules
SMA (Special Mention) Overdue 60 to 89 days Early warning alert; banks scrutinize fresh credit limits Clear overdue installments before formal classification
SS (Sub-Standard) Overdue 90 to 179 days Classified defaulter; no fresh loans or LCs permitted Apply for restructuring under BRPD guidelines with down payment
DF (Doubtful) Overdue 180 to 269 days Severe default; bank issues Artha Rin legal notices Negotiate comprehensive debt rescheduling or OTS package
BL (Bad / Loss) Overdue 270+ days Total credit freeze, directorship bar, Artha Rin lawsuit High Court Article 102 writ stay or formal settlement

7. Step 3: High Court Division Writ Petitions (Article 102) for Immediate Stays

When commercial banks act in bad faith—refusing to update CIB after full payment, blacklisting an individual without required prior demand notices, or holding directorships hostage over disputed interest computations—the High Court Division provides powerful constitutional relief.

Under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, the aggrieved citizen or corporate director can file a Writ Petition against Bangladesh Bank (specifically the General Manager of CIB) and the lending commercial bank. The petition demonstrates that the ongoing negative reporting violates fundamental rights to engage in lawful trade and business under Article 40 and equality before the law under Article 27.

The High Court Division bench routinely issues a Rule Nisi accompanied by an interim direction staying the operation of the negative CIB classification for a specified period (typically 3 to 6 months), commanding Bangladesh Bank to exclude the petitioner's name from the defaulter list. This judicial stay enables the company to immediately open letters of credit, renew industrial trade licenses, and participate in commercial tenders. For writ protocols, explore our guide on Supreme Court writ litigation services.

8. Illustrative Scenario: Managing Director Clearing a 12 Crore BDT Default Record

To illustrate how CIB de-listing unfolds in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

The Managing Director of a ready-made garment (RMG) export enterprise in Gazipur applied for a 20 Crore BDT working capital facility to fulfill European purchase orders. To his shock, the prospective bank rejected the application, revealing that he was flagged as a Bad/Loss (BL) defaulter on Bangladesh Bank's CIB database for a 12 Crore BDT term loan originally taken by a company in which he held a minority directorship eight years earlier.

The director had formally resigned from that board in 2018, and the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RJSC) had certified Form XII recording his exit. However, the lending bank had negligently failed to update its internal sanction records and continued listing him as an active guarantor. With export deadlines approaching and factory payroll in jeopardy, the director retained a Supreme Court corporate advocate.

The advocate served an emergency statutory legal notice, and within three days filed a Writ Petition under Article 102 before the High Court Division. The High Court observed that keeping a resigned director on CIB for third-party defaults violated natural justice and central bank circulars. The bench issued an interim direction commanding Bangladesh Bank to suspend the petitioner's CIB default status within 48 hours and directed the lending bank to show cause why the record should not be permanently erased. The CIB status was cleared, the export credit lines were approved, and the factory avoided shutdown.

9. Practical Credit Health Checklist for Business Executives & Importers

Maintaining a clean credit profile is as essential as commercial profitability. Follow these practical safeguards to protect against unexpected CIB blacklisting in Bangladesh:

  • Conduct Periodic CIB Inquiries: Request an annual CIB report through your primary commercial bank to verify that all loan limits, guarantees, and credit cards are accurately categorized.
  • Formally Revoke Guarantees Upon Exit: When resigning from any corporate directorship or partnership, issue a formal registered notice under Section 130 of the Contract Act 1872 revoking your personal guarantee for future transactions and obtain a written discharge certificate.
  • Demand 'No Due' Certificates (NOC): Whenever a term loan or credit card is settled, never assume the file is closed. Insist on a formal written NOC confirming that the account balance is zero and that CIB has been updated.
  • Monitor Facility Reschedulings: Verify that your bank promptly transmits BRPD restructuring approvals to Bangladesh Bank; delayed data entry can leave you classified even after paying down-payment installments.
  • Challenge Irregular Notices Immediately: If a bank serves an advocate notice threatening CIB blacklisting over disputed interest, issue an immediate written rebuttal putting the bank on formal notice to prevent arbitrary reporting.

For strategic representation in banking litigation and corporate governance, consult our specialized company and corporate legal counsel and tax and commercial advisors.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a Banking & High Court Advocate in Dhaka: To challenge arbitrary CIB blacklisting before the High Court Division under Article 102, negotiate one-time debt settlements under Bangladesh Bank circulars, or compel banks to issue CIB clearance certificates, reach out on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call +880 1712-655546. Specialized counsel for corporate directors, business owners, and expatriates.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is CIB in Bangladesh Bank?

The Credit Information Bureau (CIB) is the central credit information registry operated by Bangladesh Bank that tracks the repayment history, loan classifications, and credit defaults of all borrowers and guarantors across the financial system.

How long does a default record stay on the CIB report in Bangladesh?

A default classification remains visible as long as the loan remains unsettled. Even after settlement or rescheduling, the historical repayment trend may appear for twelve months, but the active default tag (BL/DF/SS) is converted to unclassified status upon bank update.

Can an individual remove their name from CIB without paying the bank?

If the CIB record is the result of clerical error, identity confusion, or unauthorized guarantor listing, you can compel the bank or obtain a High Court writ to remove your name without paying. Genuine loans must be restructured or settled.

What is the role of Bangladesh Bank BRPD circulars in CIB clean-up?

BRPD circulars establish the statutory guidelines for loan rescheduling, one-time settlements (OTS), and down payment requirements, which allow banks to legally regularize a borrower's CIB status from Bad/Loss to Unclassified.

How can the High Court Division help if a bank refuses to clear my CIB?

Under Article 102 of the Constitution, the High Court Division can issue a Writ of Mandamus staying the negative CIB status and commanding Bangladesh Bank to suspend the default listing so you can operate accounts and open letters of credit.

Can a company director be removed from their position due to a personal CIB default?

Yes. Under Section 17 of the Banking Companies Act 1991, an individual classified as a loan defaulter is legally disqualified from holding directorships in banking companies and listed financial institutions.

How long does it take for Bangladesh Bank to update CIB after loan payment?

Banks upload electronic CIB data on a monthly batch basis. However, in urgent situations, the lending bank can submit a manual urgent correction request, or a High Court order can compel de-listing within 48 to 72 hours.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi check their CIB status from abroad?

Yes. An overseas Bangladeshi can authorize an advocate or representative in Bangladesh via a power of attorney or bank authorization letter to run an official CIB inquiry through a scheduled commercial bank.

How to Form a 100% Foreign-Owned Company in Bangladesh 2026: BIDA Registration & Tax Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-24 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Bangladesh is one of South Asia's fastest-growing economies, offering lucrative incentives for foreign direct investment (FDI). Under the Companies Act 1994 and BIDA Guidelines 2026, foreign investors, NRBs, and multinational corporations can set up a 100% foreign-owned Private Limited Company, Branch Office, or Liaison Office in Bangladesh without any local shareholding requirement. For full corporate incorporation and tax licensing support, consult Supreme Court Advocate <a href="/advocate-md-shah-alam" style="color:var(--accent);font-weight:600;">Advocate Md. Shah Alam</a>.

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Registration Fee & Stamp Duty1% Registration Fee + 1.5% Stamp Duty on deed value
Local Government Tax & VAT2%–3% Local Govt Tax + 1.5%–4.5% VAT (varies by City/Pourosova/Union)

  5. Step 3: RJSC Incorporation Certificate & Form XII Filing

  7. Post-Incorporation Licenses: Trade License, TIN, BIN (VAT) & RJSC Annual Compliance
  8. Profit Repatriation & Dividend Transfer Rules in Bangladesh

Legal Vehicles for Foreign Investors in Bangladesh

Foreign companies and entrepreneurs can enter the Bangladesh market through three primary corporate structures:

  • 100% Foreign-Owned Private Limited Company: A separate legal entity incorporated under the Companies Act 1994. Best for long-term commercial operations, manufacturing, tech startups, and trading.
  • Branch Office: An extension of a foreign parent company. Permitted to undertake commercial activities approved by BIDA.
  • Liaison / Representative Office: Permitted only for market research and customer coordination; prohibited from generating local revenue or invoices.

Consult a qualified Corporate Lawyer in Dhaka to choose the optimal legal entity based on your business strategy.

Key Advantages of a 100% Foreign-Owned Subsidiary

Bangladesh offers significant legal and fiscal benefits for Foreign Direct Investment (FDI):

  • 100% foreign equity ownership permitted in almost all industrial sectors (excluding defence, minting, forest reserve, and nuclear energy).
  • Unrestricted repatriation of net profits, dividends, and invested capital under Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947.
  • Tax holidays (up to 5–10 years) for companies established in Economic Zones (BEZA) or High-Tech Parks (BHTPA).
  • Protection of foreign investments under Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs).

Step 1: RJSC Name Clearance & Statutory Drafting

Incorporation begins at the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RJSC):

  1. Name Clearance: Submit proposed company name online at roc.gov.bd. Fee: BDT 230 per name. Valid for 180 days.
  2. Drafting MOA & AOA: Prepare the Memorandum of Association (MOA) and Articles of Association (AOA) setting out business clauses, authorized capital, and share distribution.

Step 2: Capital Inflow & Encashment Certificate from Bangladesh Bank

To complete 100% foreign company registration, equity money must originate from abroad:

  • Open a temporary bank account in the proposed company name at a commercial bank in Bangladesh (e.g., Standard Chartered, HSBC, City Bank).
  • Remit paid-up capital from the foreign investor's overseas bank account to this Bangladesh account via official banking channel.
  • The bank issues an official Encashment Certificate (অবকাশিক এনক্যাশমেন্ট সনদ) verifying foreign currency inflow. This is mandatory for RJSC filing.
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Step 3: RJSC Incorporation Certificate & Form XII Filing

Once encashment is received, submit incorporation documents online to RJSC:

  • MOA & AOA signed by foreign subscribers.
  • Encashment Certificate & Bank Statement.
  • RJSC statutory forms: Form I (Declaration), Form VI (Notice of Situation), Form IX (Consent of Director), Form XII (Particulars of Directors).
  • Pay RJSC registration fees based on Authorized Capital scale.
  • Upon review, RJSC issues the digital Certificate of Incorporation.

Step 4: BIDA Registration & Work Permit for Foreign Directors

After incorporation, register the entity with the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA) via oss.bida.gov.bd.

BIDA Registration provides:

  • Eligibility for B-Visa (Business Visa) and Work Permits for foreign directors and expatriate executives.
  • Approval for foreign commercial loan technology transfer fees, and royalties.
  • Import registration certificate (IRC) & Export registration certificate (ERC) recommendations.

Post-Incorporation Licenses: Trade License, TIN, BIN (VAT) & RJSC Annual Compliance

To commence commercial operations, secure post-incorporation operational approvals:

  • E-TIN (Tax Identification Number): Obtained online free of charge from NBR.
  • Trade License (ট্রেড লাইসেন্স): Issued by local City Corporation (e.g., DNCC/DSCC).
  • BIN / VAT Registration (ভ্যাট নিবন্ধন): Mandatory 9-digit e-VAT number from NBR portal.
  • RJSC Annual Return Filing: Submit audited financial statements and Form Schedule X annually to maintain active corporate status.

Profit Repatriation & Dividend Transfer Rules in Bangladesh

Under Foreign Exchange Circulars issued by Bangladesh Bank, foreign investors can easily repatriate profits:

  • Dividends declared after paying applicable corporate tax can be remitted through an authorized dealer bank without prior Bangladesh Bank approval.
  • Required documents: Audited Balance Sheet, Board Resolution declaring dividend, Tax Clearance Certificate, and Auditor Certificate.
  • Capital gains upon exit or share sale can also be remitted after valuation assessment by Bangladesh Bank.

Advocate Md. Shah Alam — Supreme Court Advocate in Dhaka — provides end-to-end corporate setup, RJSC filing, BIDA approvals, and foreign investment structuring for international clients.

⚖️ Planning Foreign Direct Investment in Bangladesh? Contact Supreme Court Advocate Advocate Md. Shah Alam for complete RJSC incorporation and BIDA approval services. Visit our Corporate Legal Services Page or Contact Us Directly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a foreign national be the sole director of a Bangladesh company?

Under the Companies Act 1994, a Private Limited Company requires a minimum of 2 directors. Both directors can be foreign nationals; no resident Bangladeshi director is legally required.

What is the minimum paid-up capital for a foreign company in Bangladesh?

Legally, there is no statutory minimum paid-up capital requirement under the Companies Act. However, to obtain BIDA work permits for foreign staff, a minimum paid-up capital of USD 50,000 is generally required.

How long does it take to register a 100% foreign-owned company in Dhaka?

With proper documentation, RJSC incorporation takes approx 7–14 days. Full post-incorporation setup (BIDA, Trade License, VAT) takes 3 to 4 weeks.

Are foreign companies allowed to buy commercial land in Bangladesh?

Yes. A Bangladeshi Private Limited Company (even if 100% foreign-owned) is a local corporate entity and has the legal right to acquire and register land in its corporate name.

Falsely Accused of a Crime Bangladesh? Your Step-by-Step Legal Defence

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-04-16 · 14 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

⚡ Quick Answer: If you are falsely accused in Bangladesh, your most powerful tools are: (1) anticipatory bail before arrest, (2) quashing petition to the High Court to cancel the FIR entirely, and (3) counter-case against the complainant for malicious prosecution. Act fast — the first 48 hours are critical. — False criminal cases are a serious problem in Bangladesh, used as tools of harassment, business rivalry, or personal revenge. You have strong legal options, but you must act quickly.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order
Official Portalssupremecourt.gov.bd, judiciary.gov.bd, pcc.police.gov.bd & land.gov.bd
Supreme Court ChamberAdvocate Md. Shah Alam — Uttara & Dhaka Judge Court (+880 1712-655546)
📋 In This Article
  1. Why False Cases Are Filed in Bangladesh
  2. Step 1: Secure Bail Immediately
  3. Step 2: File for Quashing of the FIR
  4. Grounds That Court Accepts for Quashing
  5. Step 3: File a Counter-Case
  6. Step 4: Collect Evidence to Disprove the FIR
  7. Step 5: Challenge the Charge Sheet
  8. Cost and Timeline for Fighting a False Case
  9. Protecting Your Employment and Reputation During a False Case
  10. Your 48-Hour Action Checklist After a False FIR

Why False Cases Are Filed in Bangladesh

In Bangladesh, FIRs (First Information Reports) can be filed with relative ease at a police station. This has been misused in many contexts:

  • Business disputes: A rival files a criminal complaint to paralyse a competitor's business
  • Land disputes: A party with a weak title claim uses criminal cases to pressure the rightful owner
  • Family conflicts: Divorce or inheritance disputes escalate to criminal complaints
  • Personal revenge: A neighbour or acquaintance files false allegations out of spite
  • Extortion: A false FIR is used to extract money under threat of continued prosecution

All of these are abuses of the criminal justice system. The High Court Division of Bangladesh has consistently condemned false FIRs as a misuse of the process. A criminal lawyer in Dhaka can help you identify the correct remedy immediately.

Step 1: Secure Bail Immediately

Your first and most urgent priority is securing your freedom. Do not wait for the case to 'go away' on its own — an FIR in the police system will escalate.

  • Anticipatory bail (before arrest): If you have not yet been arrested, immediately apply for anticipatory bail at the Sessions Court or High Court Division. This temporarily protects you from arrest while the matter is heard. See our guide: Anticipatory Bail in Bangladesh.
  • Regular bail (after arrest): If you have already been arrested, apply for bail at the Magistrate Court immediately, then escalate to Sessions Court or High Court if refused. See: How to Get Bail in Bangladesh Fast.

Running from a false case or hiding only makes it worse. Engage a lawyer and face the case through legal channels — starting with bail.

Step 2: File for Quashing of the FIR

Under Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, you can apply to the High Court Division to quash (permanently cancel) a false FIR. The High Court has inherent power to prevent abuse of the criminal process and to ensure justice.

A successful quashing petition terminates the case entirely — before a trial even begins. This is the most powerful remedy available against a false case and should be pursued simultaneously with securing bail.

The quashing application is heard by a Judge of the High Court Division. An interim stay on further proceedings (preventing the police from arresting you or taking further steps in the case) is routinely sought along with the main application.

Grounds That Court Accepts for Quashing

The High Court will quash an FIR when:

  1. No cognizable offence disclosed: Even if the FIR allegations are taken as true, they do not constitute a criminal offence under any law
  2. Manifestly absurd or improbable allegations: The story in the FIR is physically impossible or internally contradictory
  3. Mala fide (bad faith) filing: The FIR is clearly filed as a pressure tactic in a civil dispute — courts are particularly alert to land and business disputes dressed up as criminal cases
  4. Compoundable offence with no public interest: The parties have already settled and there is no public interest in continued prosecution
  5. Abuse of process: Serial filing of FIRs against the same person on similar allegations — a pattern of harassment

Each ground requires documentary evidence and careful legal argument. Your lawyer will identify which applies and build the petition accordingly.

Step 3: File a Counter-Case

If the false case is part of deliberate, sustained harassment, you and your lawyer should consider counter-action:

  • Section 211 Penal Code (False charge with intent to injure): File a complaint against the person who filed the false FIR. This is a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment.
  • Section 182 Penal Code (False information to police): If the FIR contained knowingly false information, the complainant committed an offence.
  • Civil suit for malicious prosecution: If you suffer financial losses because of a false case, you can sue the complainant for damages (compensation) in a Civil Court.
  • Contempt petition: If the false case violated a court order that was already in place (e.g., an injunction in a civil dispute), file a contempt petition.

Counter-cases serve as a powerful deterrent — they put the complainant on the defensive and often accelerate settlement negotiations.

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Step 4: Collect Evidence to Disprove the FIR

Start building your factual defence from day one — before evidence disappears. Focus on:

  • Alibi evidence: If the FIR says you were somewhere committing a crime, gather CCTV footage, travel records, hotel bills, or witness statements showing you were elsewhere
  • Motive evidence: Preserve WhatsApp/SMS conversations, emails, or social media messages showing the complainant's real motive (disputes, threats, previous demands)
  • Contradicting physical facts: Medical reports, property documents, or financial records that contradict the FIR's narrative
  • CCTV footage: Request this immediately — most cameras overwrite footage within 7–30 days

Present all gathered evidence to your lawyer immediately. The earlier this is compiled, the stronger your defence at every stage.

Step 5: Challenge the Charge Sheet

After investigating, police submit a charge sheet (or final report) to the Magistrate. If the charge sheet is filed against you, your lawyer can:

  • File a discharge application before the Magistrate — arguing the evidence in the charge sheet is insufficient to frame a charge. If the Magistrate agrees, you are discharged before trial even begins.
  • File a writ petition in the High Court challenging the charge sheet as wholly without basis
  • If the police file a 'final report' (concluding no case), and the Magistrate still takes cognizance against you, file a revision challenging that decision

For complex false case defence involving multiple stages, consult an experienced criminal lawyer in Uttara or Dhaka who handles both trial courts and High Court practice.

Cost and Timeline for Fighting a False Case

Fighting a false case requires stamina and financial planning. Here is a realistic outlook:

  • Anticipatory bail: ৳20,000–৳50,000 lawyer fee. Obtained within 1–2 weeks.
  • Quashing petition (High Court): ৳30,000–৳80,000 lawyer fee. Interim stay within 1–2 weeks; final hearing in 3–6 months.
  • Full trial defence (if quashing is not successful): ৳50,000–৳2,00,000+. Timeline: 1–5 years depending on offence and court.
  • Counter-case filing: ৳10,000–৳30,000 (lawyer fee for drafting complaint and filing).

The total cost of fighting a serious false case can be significant, but the cost of losing — a criminal record, imprisonment, and reputational damage — is far greater. Early investment in an experienced lawyer almost always pays off.

Protecting Your Employment and Reputation During a False Case

A false FIR can damage your reputation, employment, and social standing even before any court verdict. Proactive reputation management is as important as the legal defence itself.

Impact on Employment

A pending criminal case may appear in police verification reports required for government jobs, professional licenses, and financial sector employment. However, important distinctions apply:

  • A pending case (not yet convicted) should not, by law, be treated as equivalent to a conviction.
  • If your employer asks about pending criminal cases, disclose with context and your lawyer's letter explaining the baseless nature of the complaint.
  • A High Court quashing order completely removes the FIR from the record — making it as if the case never existed.
  • An acquittal at trial also results in a clean record, though it takes longer.

Managing Social and Community Reputation

  • Avoid publicly discussing the case on social media — anything you say can be used against you or complicate the legal proceedings.
  • Inform close family and trusted colleagues of the true facts calmly and factually — without attacking the complainant in public.
  • If the complaint has been widely publicized falsely, a defamation case against the complainant may be available alongside the counter-FIR.
  • Keep all communications with police, prosecutors, and courts exclusively through your lawyer.

NRB (Non-Resident Bangladeshi) Considerations

For Bangladeshis living abroad, a false FIR in Bangladesh can create complications with visa renewals, foreign employment background checks, and passport renewals. If you live abroad and face a false FIR in Bangladesh, a Dhaka-based criminal lawyer can represent you in all proceedings without you needing to return to Bangladesh in many cases — through properly executed power of attorney. Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam in Uttara for NRB false case representation.

Your 48-Hour Action Checklist After a False FIR

The first 48 hours after you discover a false FIR has been filed against you are the most critical. Here is your action checklist — follow it immediately:

Within the First 2 Hours

  1. Do NOT go to the police station alone. Never voluntarily appear at a police station without a lawyer present if you believe you may be arrested.
  2. Call a criminal lawyer immediately. Share the FIR details, your relationship with the complainant, and any background on the dispute. Request an urgent appointment.
  3. Do NOT make any statement — oral or written — to anyone including friends, relatives, or police until you have spoken to your lawyer.

Within 24 Hours

  1. Obtain a certified copy of the FIR — your lawyer will know how to access this from the relevant police station.
  2. Brief your lawyer fully — every fact, every dispute, every communication with the complainant. Lawyers cannot help what they do not know.
  3. Begin collecting evidence — screenshots of all relevant WhatsApp/SMS messages, photos, video recordings, and financial documents that contradict the FIR.
  4. Identify witnesses who can support your version of events.

Within 48 Hours

  1. File for anticipatory bail if arrest is imminent — your lawyer files this in Sessions Court or High Court.
  2. Assess quashing prospects — your lawyer reviews the FIR for legal defects, jurisdictional issues, and evidence of malicious intent.
  3. Consider counter-case filing — your lawyer files a counter-FIR against the complainant if there is clear evidence of malicious prosecution.

Remember: the criminal justice system rewards those who act quickly and decisively. Delay is your enemy. Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam in Uttara immediately for same-day consultation on false criminal cases.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I file a counter-FIR against someone who filed a false case against me?

Yes. Under Section 211 of the Penal Code (false charge with intent to injure) and Section 182 (false information to police), your lawyer can file a criminal complaint against the person who filed the false FIR. This is itself a cognizable offence.

What is the success rate of quashing petitions in Bangladesh?

There is no published statistic, but well-prepared quashing petitions on solid grounds — particularly those showing clear mala fide intent or no cognizable offence — have a good success rate in the Bangladesh High Court. The key is quality of legal argument and evidence.

Can a police officer be held accountable for filing a false FIR?

Yes. A police officer who files or abets a false FIR can face departmental action, a complaint to the Police Headquarters (PHQ), and a writ petition to the High Court. Human rights organisations can also be involved in systematic cases of police misconduct.

What happens if the complainant withdraws the false case?

For compoundable offences, withdrawal with the complainant's consent is straightforward — the case is compounded in court. For non-compoundable offences (such as serious criminal charges), even if the complainant wants to withdraw, the state must consent to discontinue prosecution.

Does a false FIR affect future employment or background checks?

A pending FIR may appear in a police verification report. This can affect government jobs and certain professional licences. A quashing order from the High Court removes this entirely. Managing the case urgently is therefore important even if the trial outcome would eventually be an acquittal.

Can I travel abroad while a false criminal case is pending?

Generally yes — a pending FIR alone does not prevent travel unless a court has specifically issued a travel ban or the accused person is on a court bail condition prohibiting travel. However, you should consult your lawyer before making international travel arrangements while a case is pending.

How to Trace a Scammer Phone Number Legally in Bangladesh (Number to NID)

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-10 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

When financial fraud, blackmail, or cyber harassment strikes, victims often possess only a single lead: the perpetrator's mobile phone number. Finding the real individual behind that number is crucial for justice, but unauthorized database lookups are illegal in Bangladesh. Here is the authoritative legal guide on how police, the Cyber Tribunal, and mobile network operators extract subscriber identities through lawful court orders.

: · Cyber Crime & Criminal Defense Lawyer Dhaka

The Dilemma: Cyber Scams and Anonymous Numbers

In Bangladesh, mobile financial services, e-commerce transactions, and messaging applications have expanded rapidly. Alongside this growth, fraudulent schemes have multiplied. Victims encounter deceptive job offers, investment platforms, lottery swindles, or malicious blackmail where the only point of contact is an unfamiliar eleven-digit mobile number. The immediate objective of every victim is straightforward: identify the real person who owns the number, locate their registered National Identity (NID) details, and recover stolen assets or stop ongoing harassment.

However, discovering who registered a SIM card is not as simple as performing an internet search. Because mobile phone numbers are inextricably linked to biometric identity verification under Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) mandates, access to this data is tightly controlled. Victims often feel desperate when a fraudster blocks their calls, leading some to search online for quick database lookups. Understanding the clear legal boundary between lawful judicial evidence-gathering and illegal private data hunting is the critical first step toward achieving an enforceable legal outcome.

Telecom Laws: Why Private Lookups Are Illegal

Under the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulation Act 2001 and the Cyber Security Act 2023, telecommunications data is protected personal information. Mobile network operators (such as Grameenphone, Robi, Banglalink, and Teletalk) are strictly prohibited from sharing subscriber records, biometric verification logs, or National ID numbers with private citizens, commercial organizations, or independent legal counsel.

Section 97A of the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulation Act provides explicit authority for lawful interception and subscriber data extraction exclusively to designated government security and law enforcement agencies. No private investigator, software vendor, or social media group possesses lawful authorization to pull an NID server copy or subscriber registration form on demand. Individuals who purchase unauthorized database extracts from underground brokers not only waste money on falsified data, but also expose themselves to criminal liability for possessing stolen electronic records. Evidence obtained through unlawful backdoors is inadmissible in a court of law and can compromise an otherwise solid criminal complaint.

Evidentiary Records: Linking Phone to Person

To establish criminal culpability before a Magistrate Court or the Cyber Tribunal of Bangladesh, the prosecution must construct an unbroken evidentiary chain linking the physical mobile handset, the SIM card, the registered subscriber identity, and the transaction. In formal telecommunication forensics, three distinct categories of records are requisitioned:

  • Subscriber Registration Form (SAF) & Biometric Log: The official application containing the subscriber's name, parentage, permanent address, photograph, verified NID number, and biometric fingerprint timestamp captured at the point of sale.
  • Call Detail Records (CDR): A comprehensive chronological log recording outgoing and incoming voice calls, SMS exchanges, call durations, and cell tower identifications for both originating and terminating endpoints.
  • Mobile Financial Services (MFS) KYC: If money was transferred via bKash, Nagad, Rocket, or Upay, the associated MFS wallet registration documents confirm the National ID, linked bank accounts, cash-out agent locations, and transaction timestamps.

When an investigating agency compiles these three records through formal statutory channels, the identity of the perpetrator is established on an objective, verifiable basis that meets the strict evidentiary standards of the Evidence Act 1872.

Need legal representation to file a cyber fraud case or requisition digital evidence in Bangladesh? Send your complaint details or transaction proofs on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007. Overseas clients and local victims can arrange an initial legal assessment remotely.

How Police and CID Lawfully Extract Subscriber Data

When a victim submits a formal complaint to law enforcement, specialized units step in to execute the digital investigation. In Bangladesh, the principal specialized bodies include the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) Cyber Police Centre, the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI), and the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime (CTTC) cyber division.

Once an investigating officer (IO) is assigned, they follow an institutional verification protocol. The IO prepares a formal requisition memorandum addressed to the focal officers of the relevant telecommunication operator and the National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC) or BTRC. The operator cross-checks the target mobile number against the Central Biometric Verification System (CBVS). The operator then transmits a sealed, digitally signed compliance report containing the subscriber's registered NID card details, registration date, and customer profile directly to the investigating agency. This process preserves the chain of custody, ensuring that every page of digital evidence submitted to court is certified and admissible.

CrPC Section 94 and Judicial Orders

Section 94(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 serves as the primary statutory engine for compelling the disclosure of telecommunications and banking records during a judicial proceeding. The section stipulates that whenever any Court or police officer considers that the production of any document or other thing is necessary or desirable for the purposes of any investigation, inquiry, trial, or other proceeding, such court may issue a summons, or such officer may issue a written order, directing the person in whose possession or power such document or thing is believed to be, to attend and produce it.

In practice, when an advocate files a formal petition before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, or the Cyber Tribunal under Section 94 CrPC, the court evaluates the prima facie relevance of the target number to the alleged offense. Upon satisfaction, the court issues a formal judicial direction instructing the telecom operator's authorized nodal officer to produce the certified subscriber registration form, biometric match certificate, and CDR. The judicial order ensures compliance within a specified deadline, overcoming bureaucratic delays and ensuring that telecom providers release confidential records under statutory compulsion.

Essential Digital Evidence Victims Must Preserve

The success of any legal action hinges upon the quality of evidence provided at the initial filing. Because digital records are volatile, victims must systematically document and preserve all interactions before the perpetrator deletes accounts or switches SIM cards. Key evidentiary elements include:

  1. Complete Uncropped Screenshots: Capture full screen captures showing the scammer's mobile number, profile name, conversation text, dates, and precise timestamps. Do not crop out battery, network, or status bars.
  2. Transaction Identifiers (TrxID): For monetary transfers via bKash, Nagad, or bank accounts, record the transaction ID number, the originating wallet number, the recipient wallet number, and the official electronic SMS receipt.
  3. Electronic Statements: Download certified monthly account statements directly from your bank or mobile financial service app demonstrating the debit transaction.
  4. Audio and Media Files: Preserve voice calls, WhatsApp voice notes, and sent media files in their original electronic format. Export chat logs directly from messaging applications to maintain metadata integrity.
  5. Device Information: Document your own handset IMEI, operating system version, and SIM serial number to demonstrate that you were the lawful recipient of the communications.

These materials form the factual annexures attached to the initial legal complaint drafted by your advocate.

Step-by-Step Legal Procedure to File and Prosecute

Navigating the legal pathway to uncover a fraudster's identity requires following a disciplined statutory progression:

Step 1: General Diary (GD) or Thana Complaint
The victim files a General Diary at the nearest police station or via the online police portal (gd.police.gov.bd), detailing the fraudulent phone number, date, time, and financial loss. If the offense is cognizable (such as extortion, cheating under Section 420 of the Penal Code, or cyber blackmail), the Thana registers a formal First Information Report (FIR).

Step 2: Complaint Register (CR) Case at the Cyber Tribunal
If the local police station delays or declines to register an FIR, the victim's advocate files a direct complaint petition under Section 190 of the CrPC before the jurisdictional Cyber Tribunal or Metropolitan Magistrate Court. The court examines the complainant under Section 200 CrPC, reviews the annexed digital evidence, and orders a formal judicial inquiry by the CID or PBI.

Step 3: Section 94 CrPC Judicial Requisition
The assigned investigating officer or the presiding judge issues a formal directive to the mobile network operator and BTRC, compelling the production of the subscriber's biometric registration details and NID documents.

Step 4: Identification, Freezing, and Arrest
Upon receiving the certified NID data, the investigating agency verifies the perpetrator's permanent address, traces the active cell tower location through lawful tracking protocols, obtains an arrest warrant from the court, and proceeds with apprehension and asset recovery.

Comparison: Legal Requisition vs. Illegal Scams

The table below highlights the operational and evidentiary differences between authorized court-mandated subscriber extraction and illegal private lookup services:

ParameterOfficial Court/Police RequisitionIllegal Black-Market Lookup
Statutory AuthoritySection 94 CrPC & Telecom Act §97ANone; violates Cyber Security Act 2023
Data SourceDirect from BTRC & Operator Biometric DBLeaked obsolete databases or fabricated data
Court Admissibility100% admissible certified documentary proofInadmissible; risks criminal liability for buyer
ActionabilityEnables arrest warrants, bank freezes, recoveryUseless for official arrest or court recovery
Confidentiality & SafetyProtected by judicial oversight and police secrecyHigh risk of blackmail or secondary extortion

Relying on formal court procedures is the only path that yields enforceable warrants, financial restitution, and criminal convictions.

Illustrative Scenario: Tracing a Scammer Through Court

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) demonstrates how a structured legal approach resolves an anonymous fraud case:

A business proprietor in Uttara, Dhaka, was contacted by an individual claiming to represent a commercial machinery supplier. Over the course of three days, the caller negotiated the sale of equipment and requested an advance payment of BDT 1,85,000 via two bKash merchant numbers. Once the funds were transferred, the caller's phone was switched off, and the WhatsApp business profile was deleted. The victim possessed only the mobile number and the bKash transaction confirmation messages.

Rather than contacting unverified online tracing groups, the business owner retained an advocate to draft a formal petition before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court in Dhaka. The advocate filed a Complaint Register (CR) case under Sections 406 (criminal breach of trust) and 420 (cheating) of the Penal Code 1860, accompanied by a petition under Section 94 CrPC requesting subscriber identity and transaction disclosure.

The Magistrate examined the complainant, took cognizance of the offense, and directed the CID Cyber Police to conduct an inquiry. Under formal court requisitions, Grameenphone and bKash supplied the certified biometric registration forms, the registered NID number, and the corresponding cash-out agent logs located in Bogura. The investigation revealed that the funds were withdrawn at a specific market agent. Armed with official records, the CID team apprehended the perpetrator, seized the handset used in the offense, and recovered BDT 1,20,000 of the stolen funds. The official NID extract provided the cornerstone evidence for the subsequent formal charge sheet.

Defenses and Complexities: Fake SIMs and Mules

While telecommunications tracing is powerful, practical complexities frequently arise during cyber investigations in Bangladesh. Experienced cybercriminals often utilize sophisticated evasion tactics that require nuanced legal handling:

  • SIM Registered Under Stolen NID: In many syndicate operations, the SIM card is registered using the National ID and biometric data of an unwitting rural villager or daily wage earner whose identity was compromised during fake promotional campaigns. In such circumstances, tracing the NID alone does not immediately reveal the mastermind, but it provides the investigating officer with the physical point-of-sale retail location where the registration occurred.
  • Money Mules and Layered Transfers: Fraudulent funds are rarely held in the primary receiving wallet. Criminals rapidly disperse funds across multiple secondary accounts before cashing out. The advocate must petition the court for a comprehensive financial trail disclosure covering all secondary recipient wallets.
  • Handset IMEI vs. SIM Swapping: Criminals frequently discard SIM cards after a single operation. However, every mobile handset possesses a unique 15-digit International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) number. When police requisition operator logs, they obtain the IMEI linked to the target number. Even when the perpetrator inserts a new SIM card, the network registers the handset, allowing authorities to track the active number currently operating in that device.

Overcoming these complexities requires persistent judicial follow-up and close coordination between your legal counsel and the investigating authority.

Talk to an Advocate

Recovering from cyber fraud, harassment, or financial swindles requires immediate, disciplined legal action. Attempting to navigate the system alone or relying on unauthorized data brokers can jeopardize your case and cause unnecessary financial loss. A competent cyber crime advocate ensures that your complaint is drafted with precision, that digital evidence is preserved according to statutory rules, and that court requisitions under Section 94 CrPC are expedited through police channels.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I pay a private service or website to trace a scammer's phone number to their NID?

No. Private individuals, forensic consultants, and commercial websites do not have lawful access to telecommunication subscriber databases in Bangladesh. Anyone offering instant 'Number to NID' lookups operates illegally, often using leaked or falsified data. Evidence obtained from unauthorized sources is inadmissible in court and purchasing it can expose you to legal liability.

How do Bangladesh mobile operators verify a subscriber's NID before issuing a SIM card?

Under BTRC mandates, every SIM card issued in Bangladesh requires biometric verification. The customer's National ID number and date of birth are validated against the Election Commission database, and live fingerprint biometric scans are cross-checked before network activation.

What is the procedure if a scammer used a SIM card registered under someone else's stolen NID?

If the SIM card was registered fraudulently under an innocent third party's NID, the investigating officer traces the point of sale, retail agent logs, and handset IMEI records. By identifying the physical device and subsequent financial cash-outs, police can locate the actual user rather than the innocent identity victim.

How does Section 94 of the Code of Criminal Procedure help unmask a cyber criminal?

Section 94 CrPC empowers courts and police investigating officers to issue written summons or orders compelling any individual or corporation—including mobile operators and banks—to produce necessary documents, subscriber registration files, and digital records relevant to an investigation.

How can I check how many SIM cards are registered under my own National ID card?

Citizens can easily verify all mobile numbers registered against their own NID by dialing *16001# from any mobile phone in Bangladesh. When prompted, enter the last four digits of your NID card to receive an official SMS listing all registered numbers across all mobile networks.

Can Call Detail Records (CDR) and tower locations be retrieved through this legal process?

Yes. Once an FIR is registered or a court order is granted under Section 94 CrPC, the investigating officer can lawfully requisition Call Detail Records (CDR) and historical cell tower locations from the network provider to establish the perpetrator's geographic movements and communication patterns.

What should I do immediately after sending money to a fraudulent phone number via bKash or Nagad?

Immediately call the official customer care helpline of the respective mobile financial service (16247 for bKash or 16167 for Nagad) to report the transaction ID and request an urgent security hold. Concurrently, preserve all transaction messages and file a General Diary (GD) at the nearest police station.

Will evidence obtained through police requisition be sufficient to convict a scammer in the Cyber Tribunal?

Yes. Certified subscriber application forms, biometric registration timestamps, and official operator CDRs meet the statutory requirements of the Evidence Act 1872 and the Cyber Security Act. When combined with victim testimony and financial transaction records, they form formidable documentary evidence in court.

Husband Refusing to Register Divorce After Talaq: Wife Legal Rights in Bangladesh

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-10 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

A common and deeply traumatic situation occurs across Bangladesh: a husband utters verbal talaq three times in anger, throws his wife out of the house, and declares the marriage terminated, yet steadfastly refuses to serve an official written notice to the local Arbitration Council or register the dissolution with a licensed Muslim Marriage Registrar (Kazi). This deliberate inaction leaves the wife trapped in legal limbo—unable to remarry, unable to obtain her official divorce certificate, and facing social stigma. Under the statutory laws of Bangladesh, verbal talaq without written notice is legally ineffective, and wives possess robust civil and criminal remedies to compel registration, demand immediate dower and maintenance, and hold delinquent husbands accountable.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

The Nightmare of Unregistered Verbal Talaq in Bangladesh

Across Bangladesh, countless women endure an agonizing legal dilemma: their husbands verbally pronounce divorce—often during an explosive domestic argument or via a casual telephone call—and then abandon them, refusing to take any formal legal steps. The husband frequently tells relatives, 'I have divorced her under Sharia law,' but deliberately avoids filing a notice with the local authorities or registering the deed with a licensed Muslim Marriage Registrar (Kazi). This tactic is often deployed maliciously to evade paying the wife's registered dower (Denmohar) and spousal maintenance, or to prevent her from moving on with her life.

For the wife, this informal limbo creates acute vulnerability. If she treats the marriage as dissolved and attempts to remarry, she faces allegations of bigamy under Section 494 of the Penal Code 1860. If she applies for a government passport, visa, or inheritance certificate, official authorities demand an authenticated divorce certificate (Talaqnamah) and Chairman certificate, which do not exist. Understanding that statutory legislation in Bangladesh overrides unilateral verbal pronouncements is the foundation of protecting your legal dignity and financial security.

MFLO Section 7: Mandatory Statutory Talaq Rules

The governing statute regulating Muslim divorce in Bangladesh is the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (MFLO). Section 7 of this Ordinance completely eliminated the traditional instantaneous triple talaq (Talaq-e-Bid'ah) from the legal framework of Bangladesh. The statute establishes a strict, non-negotiable legal procedure:

  • Mandatory Written Notice: Under Section 7(1), any man who wishes to divorce his wife must, as soon as may be after the pronouncement of talaq in any form whatsoever, give the Chairman of the Union Parishad or City Corporation Ward Councillor notice in writing of his having done so, and must supply a copy thereof to the wife.
  • Statutory 90-Day Cooling-off Period: Under Section 7(3), a talaq does not take effect until the expiration of ninety (90) days from the day on which notice under sub-section (1) is delivered to the Chairman.
  • Mandatory Arbitration Council: Under Section 7(4), within thirty days of the receipt of the notice, the Chairman must constitute an Arbitration Council consisting of himself and a representative of each of the parties, for the purpose of bringing about a reconciliation between the parties.

Judicial precedent established by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh confirms that if the husband fails to send written notice to the Chairman, the verbal talaq is null and void in the eyes of the law. The marital tie remains legally intact, and the husband's full marital liabilities continue unabated.

Criminal Penalties for Failure to Serve Notice

To deter husbands from abandoning wives through informal verbal pronouncements, the legislature instituted explicit criminal sanctions. Section 7(2) of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 provides that whoever contravenes the provisions of sub-section (1)—meaning any husband who pronounces talaq but willfully fails to serve written notice upon the Chairman and his wife—shall be punishable with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one (1) year, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand taka (BDT 10,000), or with both.

An aggrieved wife can file a formal complaint petition before the Judicial Magistrate Court or Metropolitan Magistrate Court under Section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC). Once the magistrate examines the complainant and inspects the registered Kabinnama, the court can issue a summons or warrant against the husband. Facing a criminal trial and potential incarceration often compels delinquent husbands to either formally retract their verbal pronouncements or execute formal registered notices through proper statutory channels.

Wife's Strategic Options: Exercising Talaq-e-Tawfeez

When a husband refuses to regularize an informal separation, a wife does not have to remain a passive victim waiting for his cooperation. Under Bangladesh law, she possesses proactive legal pathways to terminate the marriage on her own terms:

  1. Delegated Right of Divorce (Talaq-e-Tawfeez): Examine Clause 18 of your registered Nikahnama (Kabinnama). In almost all modern Bangladeshi Muslim marriages, the husband delegates the unconditional right of divorce to the wife under Clause 18. If this clause is answered affirmatively (e.g., 'Yes' or 'Unconditionally delegated'), the wife can appear before any licensed Kazi, pronounce Talaq-e-Tawfeez, execute a formal registered Talaqnamah, and serve official notice upon the Chairman herself.
  2. Judicial Dissolution via Family Court (Khula / Faskh): If Clause 18 was left blank or struck out, the wife can file a suit for dissolution of marriage before the Family Court under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939 and Section 5 of the Family Courts Act 2023, citing desertion, non-maintenance for over two years, or mental cruelty.

Exercising her own statutory right of divorce liberates the woman from her husband's games and initiates the official 90-day statutory countdown.

Dealing with an uncooperative spouse, verbal talaq, or dower dispute in Bangladesh? Send your marriage documents and dispute details on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007. Overseas clients and local wives can arrange a confidential document review.

Recovering Full Dower and Maintenance in Family Court

A primary financial weapon against a husband who refuses to register talaq is instituting a comprehensive suit in the Family Court under the Family Courts Act 2023. Because the husband's refusal to serve notice keeps the marriage legally alive, his financial liabilities accumulate every month:

  • Arrears of Maintenance (Past Khorposh): The wife can claim past unpaid maintenance for up to three years prior to the filing of the suit, establishing that the husband expelled her from the marital residence and neglected his maintenance duties under Section 9 MFLO.
  • Ongoing Monthly Maintenance: The Family Court orders the husband to pay monthly maintenance pendente lite (during the pendency of the litigation) for both the wife and any minor children residing with her.
  • Acceleration of Entire Dower (Denmohar): Under Muslim law, dower is a debt upon the husband. The prompt portion (Mu'ajjal) is payable immediately on demand, while the deferred portion (Mu'wajjal) becomes instantaneously due upon the dissolution of the marriage or upon the husband's expulsion of the wife.

Family Courts in Bangladesh act decisively in dower and maintenance suits. If the husband fails to pay the decreed sums, the court issues civil execution warrants, attachments of his salary or bank accounts, and civil jail warrants under Section 16 of the Family Courts Act 2023.

Bigamy Risk: Husband Remarrying Without Notice

Many husbands who verbally divorce their wives mistakenly believe they are free to marry another woman immediately. In Bangladesh, this misconception leads directly to severe criminal consequences. Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 explicitly prohibits any man from contracting another marriage during the subsistence of an existing marriage without the prior written permission of the local Arbitration Council.

Furthermore, because the verbal talaq is null and void without Section 7 notice, the husband's first marriage legally continues. If he contracts a second marriage without completing the 90-day statutory notice period, the first wife can institute criminal prosecution under Section 494 of the Penal Code 1860 for bigamy, which carries a maximum penalty of seven (7) years rigorous imprisonment and monetary fines. Additionally, the Kazi who registers such an illegal marriage without verifying previous divorce compliance faces criminal prosecution and revocation of his registration license.

Arbitration Council Proceedings and the 90-Day Rule

Once an official notice of talaq is delivered to the Chairman of the Union Parishad or Ward Councillor, the statutory 90-day countdown commences. The procedural progression before the Arbitration Council is structured as follows:

  1. Issuance of Summons: Within thirty days of receipt, the Chairman issues formal notices to both parties requesting them to nominate authorized representatives (usually a family member or advocate) to form the Arbitration Council.
  2. Three Conciliation Sessions: The Chairman convenes up to three reconciliation meetings during the 90-day period to ascertain if the marital discord can be resolved. If the wife was coerced or the husband wishes to revoke the pronouncement, reconciliation is formally recorded.
  3. Failure Certificate / Effectiveness: If reconciliation fails or the husband persists, the talaq becomes legally effective upon the exact completion of the 90th day. The Chairman issues an official Certificate of Effectiveness under his official seal.
  4. Kazi Registration: Armed with the Chairman's 90-day Certificate, the divorce is formally registered in the Muslim Divorce Register (Volume Book) under Section 6 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974, and official Talaqnamah certificates are issued to both parties.

This documented sequence provides the only legally recognized proof of divorce for all government and foreign embassy requirements.

Comparison Table: Verbal Talaq vs. Registered Dissolution

The table below highlights the crucial legal contrasts between informal verbal divorce and lawful statutory dissolution under Bangladesh law:

Legal ParameterVerbal Talaq (Unregistered)Statutory Talaq (MFLO §7 & Kazi)
Legal ValidityVoid ab initio; marriage legally continues100% valid upon completion of 90 days
Maintenance RightsWife remains entitled to monthly maintenanceMaintenance payable during 90-day Iddat period
Dower (Denmohar)Immediately demandable in full as debtMust be settled in full prior to or upon completion
Right to RemarryWife risks bigamy charges under Penal Code §494Both parties completely free to remarry legally
Embassy / Passport UseRejected outright by all official authoritiesAccepted globally as official proof of divorce

Relying on informal verbal claims leaves women defenseless, whereas statutory registration secures full legal freedom and financial rights.

Illustrative Scenario: Compelling Registration and Dower

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how an experienced advocate breaks the deadlock of an unregistered divorce:

A schoolteacher in Sylhet was married for four years with a registered dower of BDT 8,00,000. Following a dispute over money, her husband verbally pronounced talaq three times in front of his parents, threw her suitcases onto the street, and told her never to return. For six months, the husband ignored her calls, refused to give her a single taka for maintenance, and boasted to neighbours that he was a bachelor again, preparing to marry an expatriate woman. However, he refused to serve notice to the local Ward Councillor because he did not want to pay her BDT 8,00,000 dower.

Devastated and unable to remarry or update her passport, she consulted an advocate. The advocate obtained a certified copy of her Kabinnama, which clearly contained delegated divorce under Clause 18. First, the advocate filed a suit in the Sylhet Family Court under Section 5 of the Family Courts Act 2023 claiming BDT 1,20,000 in past maintenance and the full BDT 8,00,000 prompt dower. Concurrently, the advocate filed a criminal complaint under Section 7(2) MFLO for failure to serve talaq notice.

The Magistrate issued a summons against the husband, while the Family Court attached his bank account to secure the dower claim. Confronted with imminent criminal penalties and a frozen bank balance, the husband retained counsel. Through court-mediated conciliation, the husband agreed to pay the entire BDT 8,00,000 dower in two certified pay orders, signed the official Talaqnamah before the licensed Kazi, and submitted the notice to the Ward Councillor. Within ninety days, the wife received her official Chairman Certificate and registered divorce decree, restoring her legal freedom and financial dignity.

Talk to an Advocate

If your husband has verbally pronounced divorce, abandoned you, or refused to provide an official registered Talaqnamah, do not remain in painful uncertainty. You are not without legal recourse. An experienced family law advocate will inspect your Kabinnama, institute targeted Family Court proceedings for full dower and maintenance, and enforce criminal accountability under Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961. Protecting your financial entitlements and legal status requires swift, professional action.

Need an advocate for a divorce, dower, or family court matter in Bangladesh? Send your marriage documents and case details on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: remote document reviews and court representation available.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a verbal talaq legally valid in Bangladesh without paper notice?

No. Under Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, any verbal talaq is completely invalid and ineffective in law unless written notice is served upon the local Union Parishad Chairman or Ward Councillor, and ninety days have elapsed.

Can my husband be jailed for giving verbal talaq without sending notice?

Yes. Section 7(2) of the MFLO 1961 makes it a punishable offense for a husband to pronounce talaq without giving written notice to the Chairman and the wife, carrying a penalty of up to 1 year simple imprisonment or a fine of up to BDT 10,000, or both.

Can I remarry if my husband verbally divorced me but did not register it?

No. Because the marriage legally subsists until the 90-day statutory notice period has officially expired and a Kazi registration is completed, remarrying based only on verbal talaq exposes you to bigamy charges under Section 494 of the Penal Code 1860.

What happens to my dower (Denmohar) if my husband refuses to register talaq?

Your dower rights remain fully protected. In fact, you can file a lawsuit in the Family Court immediately demanding the prompt portion of the dower and all accumulated monthly maintenance, which the court can enforce through asset attachment.

How can a wife divorce her husband if he refuses to issue a notice?

If Clause 18 of the registered Kabinnama confers delegated divorce (Talaq-e-Tawfeez), the wife can execute the divorce before a licensed Kazi and serve notice to the Chairman herself. If Clause 18 is absent, she can file a suit for dissolution of marriage in the Family Court.

How long does it take for a talaq to become final after notice is served?

Under Section 7(3) MFLO, talaq becomes legally final exactly ninety (90) days from the date the Chairman receives the written notice, provided the parties do not reconcile before the Arbitration Council.

Can a husband revoke a talaq notice during the 90-day period?

Yes. Under Muslim family law, the husband has the legal right to revoke the talaq at any point before the expiration of the 90 days, either expressly in writing to the Chairman or by resuming conjugal relations.

Can an overseas wife (NRB) pursue these legal remedies from abroad?

Yes. A wife residing in the UK, USA, Canada, or elsewhere can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy, appointing a trusted representative in Bangladesh and retaining an advocate to file Family Court and criminal petitions on her behalf.

Husband Taking a Second Wife Bangladesh – First Wife's Legal Rights & What to Do

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-08 · 9 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Discovering that your husband intends to take a second wife is one of the most emotionally and legally complex situations a Bangladeshi woman can face. While polygamy is permitted under Bangladesh's Muslim personal law in limited circumstances, the first wife has significant legal protections — including the right to arbitration, financial rights, and the right to divorce. This guide explains everything you need to know.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

📋 In This Article

  2. The Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 and Second Marriage
  3. Does the Husband Need the First Wife's Permission?
  4. What Happens If the Husband Marries Without Permission?
  5. First Wife's Right to Divorce After Second Marriage
  6. First Wife's Financial Rights When Husband Remarries
  7. What Is the Arbitration Council Process?
  8. Can the First Wife Stop the Second Marriage?
  9. Legal Steps for a First Wife to Take Immediately
  10. Second Wife's Legal Status in Bangladesh

Is Polygamy Legal in Bangladesh?

Under Islamic law as applied in Bangladesh, a Muslim man is permitted to have up to four wives simultaneously — subject to strict conditions including ability to treat all wives justly and equally. However, Bangladesh law has significantly restricted this right through the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (MFLO).

Practically speaking, while polygamy is not absolutely prohibited, the MFLO imposes a mandatory procedural requirement — obtaining permission from an Arbitration Council — before contracting a second marriage. This requirement is meant to protect existing wives and ensure fairness.

In reality, however, the enforcement of these protections depends on the first wife knowing her rights and actively invoking them. Many first wives are unaware of the protections available under the MFLO until it is too late. This guide aims to change that.

The Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 and Second Marriage

Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (MFLO) is the key provision governing second marriages in Bangladesh:

  • A Muslim man who wishes to contract another marriage while already married must first obtain permission from the Arbitration Council of the Union Parishad or City Corporation where he ordinarily resides.
  • To apply for permission, he must submit an application stating the reasons for the proposed marriage and whether the existing wife's consent has been obtained.
  • The Arbitration Council must give notice to the existing wife and provide her an opportunity to be heard.
  • The Council must satisfy itself that the proposed marriage is necessary and just before granting permission.

The penalty for marrying without permission: Under Section 6(5) MFLO, a husband who contracts a second marriage without Arbitration Council permission is liable to:

  • Immediate payment of the entire outstanding deferred dower (mahr) to the existing wife
  • A fine of BDT 10,000 (under the criminal provisions)
  • In some interpretations, the existing wife's right to seek divorce crystallises automatically

Does the Husband Need the First Wife's Permission?

Under the MFLO 1961, the husband does not technically need the first wife's consent — but he must notify her and allow her to appear before the Arbitration Council. The Arbitration Council then makes an independent decision on whether permission should be granted.

However, there is an important practical consideration: many Kabin Namas (Muslim marriage contracts) include a clause delegating the wife the right of talaq if the husband remarries. If your Kabin Nama contains this clause (talaq-e-tafweez conditional on second marriage), then a second marriage by the husband automatically triggers your delegated right to divorce without any court proceedings.

Always check your Kabin Nama with a divorce lawyer in Bangladesh to understand what protections you already have by contract.

What Happens If the Husband Marries Without Permission?

If a husband contracts a second marriage without obtaining Arbitration Council permission — which unfortunately is common in practice — several consequences follow:

  • The second marriage is still legally valid in Bangladesh: The absence of Arbitration Council permission does not void the second marriage under current Bangladesh Supreme Court interpretation. This is a significant gap in the protective framework.
  • Criminal liability: The husband can be prosecuted under Section 6(5) MFLO and fined.
  • Entire deferred mahr becomes immediately due: The first wife can immediately file a suit to recover her full outstanding deferred dower — this becomes due immediately upon the illegal second marriage.
  • First wife's divorce right arises: The first wife can seek divorce from the Family Court, with the unauthorised second marriage as a ground.
  • Criminal complaint: The first wife can file a criminal complaint against the husband for contracting an unauthorised marriage.

Act immediately if this happens. Every day of delay affects your practical position. Contact Adv. Shah Alam to take urgent steps.

First Wife's Right to Divorce After Second Marriage

A Muslim woman in Bangladesh has a right to seek divorce from the Family Court when her husband takes or intends to take a second wife, on the following grounds:

  • Under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939: A wife can seek a court decree of dissolution of marriage if the husband has taken another wife in contravention of the provisions of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (Section 2(viii)(d) of the Act).
  • Via Khul: Regardless of any specific ground, the wife can seek Khul divorce through the Family Court if the marriage has irretrievably broken down following the husband's second marriage.
  • Via Talaq-e-Tafweez: If the Kabin Nama includes a delegated right of divorce triggered by the husband's second marriage, the wife can invoke this right immediately — notifying the Union Parishad/City Corporation as with any talaq.

The financial settlement in such divorces must be carefully handled — the wife is entitled to full outstanding dower, iddah maintenance, and appropriate child maintenance. A divorce proceeding following a husband's second marriage often involves significant negotiation.
