First Wife's Financial Rights When Husband Remarries

Whether or not the first wife divorces after the husband's second marriage, her financial rights include:

  • Full outstanding dower: If the second marriage was contracted without Arbitration Council permission, the entire outstanding deferred dower (including the deferred portion that would normally be payable only upon divorce or death) becomes immediately payable to the first wife.
  • Equal maintenance: Under Islamic law (applied in Bangladesh), a husband with multiple wives must provide each wife with equal maintenance. If he is neglecting the first wife's maintenance in favour of the second, the first wife can file a maintenance case in Family Court.
  • Equal housing: Each wife must be provided with separate, equal housing. If the first wife is being displaced from the marital home by the second wife, she has legal remedies.
  • Child support: All children — from any marriage — are entitled to maintenance from their father. This does not diminish based on additional marriages.

What Is the Arbitration Council Process?

The Arbitration Council is a committee constituted under the MFLO 1961, typically comprising the Union Parishad Chairman (or his nominee) and representatives nominated by each party. Its role in second marriage applications is:

  1. Husband submits application to the Union Parishad/City Corporation Chairman with his reasons for seeking a second marriage.
  2. The Chairman constitutes an Arbitration Council.
  3. The Council notifies the first wife and invites her to appear.
  4. The Council holds a hearing where both the husband and first wife (or their representatives) can present their positions.
  5. The Council examines whether the proposed second marriage is necessary and just — considering the husband's financial capacity, the first wife's health, and other relevant factors.
  6. The Council grants or refuses permission. If permission is refused, the husband cannot legally remarry without going through further legal proceedings to challenge the Council's decision.

Appearing before the Arbitration Council with a lawyer significantly improves the first wife's ability to present her case and oppose the granting of permission for the second marriage.

Can the First Wife Stop the Second Marriage?

Practically, it is very difficult to permanently prevent a determined husband from taking a second wife in Bangladesh — the MFLO's Arbitration Council mechanism can delay but not permanently prevent a second marriage. However, the first wife has significant leverage:

  • Opposing at the Arbitration Council: A strong, well-argued case before the Council can result in permission being refused — at least temporarily.
  • Filing a writ petition in the High Court: If the Arbitration Council wrongly grants permission, the first wife can challenge the decision by filing a writ petition before the High Court Division.
  • Invoking Talaq-e-Tafweez: If the Kabin Nama includes a conditional delegated right of divorce, the first wife can immediately divorce the husband as soon as the second marriage is contracted — removing herself from the situation on her own terms and securing her financial rights.

Rather than attempting to prevent what cannot ultimately be stopped, many first wives focus on securing the best possible financial settlement and custody arrangement. This strategic approach — with the help of a skilled divorce lawyer — often produces better outcomes than a bitter legal battle over the fact of the second marriage itself.

Legal Steps for a First Wife to Take Immediately

If you have just discovered your husband is planning or has contracted a second marriage, take these steps immediately:

  1. Secure your Kabin Nama: Get a certified copy of your Kabin Nama from the Nikah Registrar. Check for any delegated right of divorce (Talaq-e-Tafweez) clauses.
  2. Engage a family lawyer immediately: Time is critical. Contact a divorce lawyer in Dhaka on the same day.
  3. File at the Arbitration Council: If the husband has filed or is about to file for second marriage permission at the Arbitration Council, file your opposition with supporting documents.
  4. File for immediate maintenance: File a maintenance application in the Family Court to secure financial support — do not wait for the second marriage question to be resolved before securing your income.
  5. Consider your divorce options: Discuss with your lawyer whether pursuing divorce on your own terms — with full dower and maintenance — is the right strategy for your situation.
  6. Document everything: Keep records of all communications from your husband, any evidence of the second marriage preparations, and your own financial position.

Second Wife's Legal Status in Bangladesh

While this guide focuses on the first wife's rights, it is important to note the legal status of the second wife:

  • If the second marriage was contracted with Arbitration Council permission (or even without it), it is generally treated as legally valid in Bangladesh — both under statutory and Islamic law.
  • The second wife has the same marital rights as the first wife — dower, maintenance, and rights in the marriage.
  • Children of the second marriage are fully legitimate and have the same inheritance rights as children of the first marriage.
  • The husband's estate (upon death) is divided equally among all legal heirs from all marriages.

This reality underscores why it is important for a first wife to focus on her own rights and financial security rather than on challenging the legal validity of the second marriage itself.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a second marriage without Arbitration Council permission valid in Bangladesh?

Bangladesh courts have generally held that the second marriage itself remains valid even without Arbitration Council permission — but the husband faces criminal liability and financial consequences to the first wife. This is a controversial area and the Supreme Court's position has evolved over time.

What if my Kabin Nama has a clause allowing me to divorce if my husband remarries?

This is called Talaq-e-Tafweez (delegated right of divorce conditional on second marriage). If your Kabin Nama contains this clause, your right to divorce crystallises the moment the husband contracts a second marriage — you can invoke it immediately by notifying the relevant authority, without going to court.

Can a non-Muslim man legally take a second wife in Bangladesh?

No. Only Muslim men are permitted to practice polygamy under Bangladesh's personal law framework. For Hindus and Christians, polygamy is illegal and the second marriage of a non-Muslim man while the first wife is alive is a criminal offence.

How quickly can I file for divorce if my husband takes a second wife?

You can file immediately — the second marriage is a recognised ground for divorce under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939. With urgent representation, an application can be filed in Family Court within days of learning of the second marriage.

Will I lose child custody if I divorce my husband because of his second marriage?

Not automatically. Child custody is determined by the Family Court based on the child's best interests. Under hizanat, a mother retains custody of sons until age 7 and daughters until puberty — regardless of the reason for divorce. However, if you remarry (someone other than the child's father), your custody right may be affected.

Husband Transferring Property to Evade Dower? Legal Remedies

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-10 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

When marital discord surfaces or divorce notices are served in Bangladesh, husbands frequently resort to a dishonest tactic: hastily transferring, selling, or gifting their valuable real estate, residential flats, and commercial shares to trusted family members (such as mothers, brothers, or close friends). The malicious objective is to present themselves as assetless 'paupers' before the Family Court, thereby frustrating the wife's statutory claim to her promised dower (Denmohar) and ongoing child maintenance. Under the Transfer of Property Act 1882, the Family Courts Act 2023, and the Code of Civil Procedure 1898, a wife is legally recognized as an accrued creditor. The law provides decisive legal remedies to set aside sham transfers, freeze husband assets before judgment, and execute recovery against fraudulently conveyed properties.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)

📋 In This Article
  1. 1. The Legal Status of Dower: An Unconditional Statutory Debt in Muslim Law
  2. 2. The Statutory Shield: Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882
  3. 3. Identifying Sham Transactions: Nominal Heba Deeds and Benami Transfers
  4. 4. Freezing Assets Fast: Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC
  5. 5. Temporary Injunctions under Order 39: Restraining Immovable Transfers
  6. 6. Summary Matrix: Asset Protection Remedies, Prerequisites & Fora
  7. 7. Setting Aside Fraudulent Deeds: Section 39 Specific Relief Act Lawsuits
  8. 8. Illustrative Scenario: Recovering 30 Lakh BDT Dower Against a Sham Heba Deed
  9. 9. Essential Evidentiary Checklist for Wives Facing Asset Dissipation
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate

1. The Legal Status of Dower: An Unconditional Statutory Debt in Muslim Law

In Islamic jurisprudence as codified and applied in Bangladesh, dower (Denmohar) is not a customary wedding gift or voluntary gratuity. It is an unconditional statutory debt owed by the husband to the wife arising immediately upon the solemnization of the marriage under the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937.

Dower is categorized into Prompt Dower (Mu'ajjal), which is payable on demand at any time during marriage, and Deferred Dower (Muwajjal), which becomes payable upon dissolution of marriage by divorce or the husband's death. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly established that the wife holds the status of an unsecured creditor in respect of her unpaid dower.

Because the dower liability represents an existing legal obligation, a husband cannot defeat this debt by impoverishing himself through fictitious transactions. When a husband transfers property knowing that divorce is imminent or that the wife has demanded prompt dower, the transfer is presumed under law to be intended to delay and defeat the wife's financial recovery.

2. The Statutory Shield: Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882

The primary statutory weapon against bad-faith debtors attempting to hide real estate is Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 ('Fraudulent Transfer').

Section 53(1) establishes the foundational legal rule: every transfer of immovable property made with intent to defeat or delay the creditors of the transferor shall be voidable at the option of any creditor so defeated or delayed. The section expressly protects bona fide purchasers who acquired property for valuable consideration without notice of the fraudulent intention, but provides zero immunity to gratuitous transferees or colluding family members.

Where a husband gifts or nominally transfers his property to a parent, sibling, or close relative shortly before or immediately after marital breakdown without receiving genuine fair market consideration, the law establishes a strong presumption of fraudulent intent. The affected wife is entitled to file a civil suit to declare the transfer voidable and restore the property to the husband's execution estate.

3. Identifying Sham Transactions: Nominal Heba Deeds and Benami Transfers

Husbands seeking to evade dower almost never sell their property to genuine arms-length third parties; doing so would deprive the family of the asset. Instead, they execute sham transactions within their immediate trusted circle.

The two most common devices deployed are:

  • Fraudulent Heba Deeds (Gifts): The husband executes a registered Heba deed gifting his apartment or land to his mother, brother, or second wife for nominal government registration fees. Crucially, the husband often retains physical possession, collects rental income, and continues residing on the property, proving the gift was a sham without delivery of possession.
  • Benami / Fictitious Sale Deeds: The husband executes a registered Saf Kabala deed to a trusted friend or distant relative showing a fictitious sale price. Banking records reveal that no actual money transferred between the parties, or that cash withdrawn was immediately redeposited into the husband's secret accounts.

Is your husband secretly transferring, gifting, or selling properties to defeat your dower (Denmohar) claim in Bangladesh? Immediate legal action before the properties pass to third parties is vital to freeze the assets. Message our family law advocates on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for confidential guidance.

Courts pierce these colorable transactions by analyzing the proximity of dates between marital disputes and deed registrations, the absence of real consideration, and the retention of physical possession by the husband. For insights on Heba cancellations, review our analysis on Heba deed cancellation laws in Bangladesh.

4. Freezing Assets Fast: Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC

When a wife initiates a suit for recovery of dower and maintenance in the Family Court under the Family Courts Act 2023, waiting for the final judgment (which may take 12 to 24 months) creates an acute risk that the husband will dispose of all immovable properties during the trial.

To eliminate this threat, the wife's advocate must immediately file an emergency application for Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38, Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The application demonstrates that the defendant husband, with intent to obstruct or delay the execution of any decree that may be passed against him, is about to dispose of the whole or part of his property.

The Family Court issues a notice commanding the husband to either furnish sufficient financial security (such as a bank guarantee) to satisfy the dower claim or appear and show cause why his properties should not be attached. If the husband fails to furnish security, the court issues a formal attachment order. A copy of the attachment order is transmitted to the relevant Sub-Registry Office and AC Land office, legally prohibiting any deed registration or mutation pending final trial.

5. Temporary Injunctions under Order 39: Restraining Immovable Transfers

In addition to attachment before judgment, an application for a temporary injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the CPC provides vital interim protection. While an attachment creates an official government encumbrance, an injunction directly restrains the husband personaliter.

To obtain an injunction, the wife must establish the three classic equitable tests: a prima facie case (proven by the registered Nikahnama showing unpaid dower), irreparable financial injury if the husband becomes assetless, and the balance of convenience lying in favor of preserving the status quo.

The court passes an ad-interim or temporary injunction restraining the husband, his agents, and nominees from selling, transferring, gifting, mortgaging, or changing the physical character of the specified properties. Disobedience of an injunction order exposes the husband to civil detention under Order 39, Rule 2A CPC, providing powerful leverage to preserve assets.

6. Summary Matrix: Asset Protection Remedies, Prerequisites & Fora

Wives facing fraudulent asset dissipation can evaluate the operational distinctions between emergency protective mechanisms in the following comparative matrix:

Legal Remedy Governing Statute / Rule Prerequisites for Relief Effect on Husband's Property
Attachment Before Judgment Order 38 Rule 5 CPC Proof of attempt to dispose of property to defeat decree Registry encumbrance; property cannot be sold or mortgaged
Temporary Injunction Order 39 Rules 1 & 2 CPC Prima facie title, balance of convenience, irreparable injury Restrains husband from executing deeds; violation triggers jail
Section 53 Fraudulent Transfer Suit Transfer of Property Act (Sec 53) Proof of gratuitous/collusive transfer defeating creditor debt Civil court declares sham deed void and cancels registration
Execution by Auction Sale Family Courts Act & Order 21 CPC Final decree for unpaid dower and failure to satisfy debt Court auctions attached properties to pay dower to wife

7. Setting Aside Fraudulent Deeds: Section 39 Specific Relief Act Lawsuits

If the wife discovers that the husband has already registered a sham Heba deed or fictitious sale deed before she could obtain an injunction, all hope is not lost. The transaction can be directly annulled through a declaratory title suit.

The wife, as an aggrieved creditor, files a suit under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act 1877 read with Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 in the competent Assistant Judge or Joint District Judge Court. The plaint impleads both the husband and the colluding transferee (e.g., the mother-in-law or brother-in-law), detailing that the transfer was nominal, lacked consideration, and was engineered solely to defeat the accrued dower debt.

Upon evaluating the evidence and finding that the transfer was fraudulent, the civil court enters a decree adjudging the deed void, commands the Sub-Registry Office to make an entry of cancellation in the official Balam Boi records, and restores title to the husband's name, rendering the asset available for execution. For broader insights on dower litigation, review our guide on dower and maintenance recovery in Bangladesh.

8. Illustrative Scenario: Recovering 30 Lakh BDT Dower Against a Sham Heba Deed

To understand how this dual litigation strategy operates in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A corporate director in Dhanmondi, Dhaka, entered into a registered Nikahnama stipulating a dower of 30 Lakh BDT. After eight years of marriage, the husband served a notice of divorce under Section 7 of the MFLO. Simultaneously, he executed a registered Heba deed gifting his primary asset—a 4-story commercial building in Mirpur valued at 4 Crore BDT—exclusively to his elderly mother, while claiming before the Family Court that he had zero immovable property and could only afford 5,000 BDT monthly maintenance.

The wife engaged a Supreme Court family advocate. The advocate immediately obtained a certified copy of the Heba deed from the Sub-Registry Office, confirming that the transfer occurred exactly fourteen days after the divorce notice was issued. The legal team filed a suit in the Family Court for recovery of the 30 Lakh BDT dower, accompanied by an Order 38 Rule 5 application for attachment before judgment over the Mirpur property.

Concurrently, the advocate filed a suit under Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act and Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act to cancel the sham Heba deed. The court observed that the mother paid zero consideration, the husband continued collecting commercial rents, and the transfer was executed solely to defeat the wife's debt. The court cancelled the Heba deed, decreed the full 30 Lakh BDT dower, and attached the commercial building. Confronted with an impending court auction, the husband satisfied the entire dower decree in cash.

9. Essential Evidentiary Checklist for Wives Facing Asset Dissipation

Wives suspecting that their husbands are preparing to conceal assets should take immediate, proactive legal steps to preserve evidence:

  • Procure Certified Nikahnama & Kazi Records: Obtain certified copies of the registered Kabinnama detailing the prompt and deferred dower figures and any property pledged as dower.
  • Document Real Estate Identifiers: Secure plot numbers, Mouza names, Khatian numbers, and Sub-Registry details of all lands, apartments, and commercial holdings owned by the husband.
  • Track Corporate & Banking Assets: Identify company names, directorship records from the RJSC, bank branches, and vehicle registration numbers registered in the husband's name.
  • Act Before Deeds Are Registered: File an emergency Family Court petition seeking Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC at the very first indication of marital breakdown.
  • Challenge Sub-Registry Transfers Immediately: If a deed is executed, obtain certified copies (Nokol) immediately and file a Section 53 cancellation suit before third-party rights intervene.

For dedicated representation in matrimonial property litigation, explore our specialized divorce and family lawyer services and land dispute advocacy.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a Family & Property Advocate in Dhaka: To file emergency attachment before judgment applications under Order 38 CPC, cancel sham Heba deeds under Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act, or execute Family Court decrees, reach out via WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call our chamber at +880 1712-655546. Specialized counsel for domestic and non-resident wives.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a husband legally gift all his property to his mother to avoid paying dower?

No. Under Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882, transfers made with intent to defeat or delay creditors (including a wife owed dower) are voidable. A court can declare the gift deed fraudulent and set it aside.

Is a wife considered a creditor of her husband under Bangladeshi law?

Yes. Islamic law and Bangladeshi judicial precedents establish that unpaid dower (Denmohar) is an unconditional debt, placing the wife in the legal position of a creditor against her husband's estate.

What is Attachment Before Judgment under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC?

Attachment Before Judgment is an emergency court order that freezes the defendant's immovable properties during an ongoing trial, preventing them from selling or transferring assets to evade satisfying a future decree.

Can the Family Court auction a husband's property to pay unpaid dower?

Yes. In execution proceedings under the Family Courts Act 2023 and Order 21 CPC, if the husband fails to pay the decreed dower, the court can seize, attach, and auction his properties to satisfy the debt.

What happens if a husband transfers land to a stranger for nominal value?

If the transfer was made to a colluding third party for nominal or fictitious consideration with notice of the dispute, it can be cancelled under Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act and Section 39 Specific Relief Act.

Can a wife freeze her husband's bank accounts for dower recovery?

Yes. A wife can apply to the Family Court or High Court to attach the husband's commercial bank accounts, salary, and company dividends to secure payment of her dower and child maintenance.

What should I do if my husband threatens to divorce me without giving my dower?

Immediately retain counsel to file a Family Court suit for recovery of prompt dower and maintenance, accompanied by an Order 38 Rule 5 petition to attach his real estate before divorce notices take effect.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi wife sue her husband for dower from abroad?

Yes. An overseas wife can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission, authorizing an advocate in Dhaka to file the suit and attach properties without returning to Bangladesh.

Income Tax Audit Notice Defense in Bangladesh: New Income Tax Act 2023 Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-13 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Opening a registered official envelope from the National Board of Revenue (NBR) to find a formal Audit Notice under Section 182 or a Show-Cause Notice under Section 212 of the new Income Tax Act 2023 is an alarming experience for any taxpayer. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes (DCT) questions your declared bank deposits, points to discrepancies between your declared wealth statement and property purchases, challenges source of funds, or alleges unexplained cash credits, threatening punitive tax penalties of up to 200%. Taxpayers often panic, ignoring the notice or paying unregulated intermediaries who make false promises of 'fixing the file.' The Income Tax Act 2023 (Aykor Ain 2023) introduced sweeping modernizations, strict evidentiary standards, and comprehensive statutory appeal rights. Understanding how to structure your written reply, compile lawful asset documentation, and defend your return before the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Taxes Appellate Tribunal is the definitive key to eliminating arbitrary tax assessments.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

  2. Decoding the Audit Notice: Sections 182, 183, and 212
  3. The Dreaded Wealth Mismatch: IT-10B Asset Statements
  4. Unexplained Cash Credits and Bank Deposit Scrutiny
  5. Drafting the Written Reply and Compiling Evidence
  6. Best Judgment Assessment Under Section 184
  7. The Appeal Hierarchy: Commissioner (Appeals) & Tribunal

  9. Illustrative Scenario: Defeating an Arbitrary BDT 25 Lakh Tax Claim
  10. Talk to an Advocate

The New Tax Landscape Under the Income Tax Act 2023

In June 2023, the Parliament of Bangladesh enacted the historic Income Tax Act 2023 (Aykor Ain 2023), completely replacing the four-decade-old Income Tax Ordinance 1984. The new enactment shifted Bangladesh's direct tax system toward universal self-assessment, mandatory digital reporting, and widespread data cross-matching between the National Board of Revenue (NBR), commercial banks, Sub-Registry offices, and vehicle registration portals.

While universal self-assessment allows taxpayers to file returns smoothly, it expanded the scope of post-filing tax audits. The NBR's automated Risk Management Engine now flags returns exhibiting substantial bank turnover, major real estate acquisitions, or sharp variances in net wealth. When an audit notice arrives, taxpayers often assume the tax officer is accusing them of criminal fraud. In reality, a tax audit is a statutory fact-finding proceeding. Knowing how to present verifiable documentary evidence under the new Act protects your hard-earned assets from arbitrary tax demands.

Decoding the Audit Notice: Sections 182, 183, and 212

When you receive a tax notice, the first critical step is identifying the exact statutory section cited by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes (DCT). Under the Income Tax Act 2023, tax inquiries fall into distinct statutory categories:

  • Section 182 (Audit Selection): Under Section 182, the NBR or Commissioner selects a return for comprehensive audit based on automated risk parameters. The DCT is legally required to explain the specific risk factors triggering the audit.
  • Section 183 (Audit Assessment): Once selected, the DCT issues notice under Section 183 requiring the taxpayer to produce books of accounts, bank statements, sales registers, and asset purchase deeds.
  • Section 212 (Re-Opening / Escape Assessment): If the DCT discovers that income has escaped assessment, was under-assessed, or that excessive reliefs were claimed in any past assessment year, a notice under Section 212 can be issued to re-open the file within statutory limitation windows.

Understanding which section governs your notice dictates the scope of documents required and the statutory deadlines for compliance.

The Dreaded Wealth Mismatch: IT-10B Asset Statements

The single most frequent trigger for tax audit notices in Bangladesh is a mathematical mismatch in the Statement of Assets and Liabilities (Form IT-10B). Under the Income Tax Act 2023, submission of a wealth statement is mandatory for any individual whose gross wealth exceeds BDT 40,00,000, or who owns motor vehicles, or possesses real estate in municipal areas.

Audit notices routinely highlight discrepancies: for example, your net wealth increased by BDT 50,00,000 during the financial year, but your declared business income was only BDT 15,00,000, leaving an unexplained accretion of BDT 35,00,000. In their written reply, the taxpayer must scientifically reconcile this gap: demonstrating non-taxable receipts such as foreign remittances received through formal banking channels (exempt under Schedule 6), agricultural income, capital gains from exempted securities, registered inheritance from parents, or lawful gifts from family members backed by formal tax filings.

Unexplained Cash Credits and Bank Deposit Scrutiny

Another primary focus of tax audits is bank account turnover. Under automated data-sharing agreements with Bangladesh Bank's Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU), the NBR receives automated reports of large banking transactions. If your declared business revenue is BDT 30,00,000, but your personal or corporate bank statements show total credits of BDT 1,20,00,000, the DCT will issue a show-cause notice treating the entire BDT 90,00,000 difference as 'unexplained cash credit' and adding it directly to your taxable income under the new Act.

To defeat this presumption, your tax advocate must conduct a detailed bank ledger reconciliation: demonstrating that credits represent business loan disbursements, inter-account transfers between your own accounts, customer advances subsequently adjusted, or funds held temporarily as an agent. Presenting bank statements with clear narration and supporting commercial vouchers successfully dismantles the allegation of hidden income.

Drafting the Written Reply and Compiling Evidence

The written response submitted to the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes forms the permanent factual backbone of your tax file. An informal or evasive reply practically guarantees an adverse assessment. A professional tax defense dossier requires:

  1. Point-by-Point Clarification: Address every query in the DCT's notice systematically, cross-referencing specific bank entries, purchase vouchers, and balance sheet items.
  2. Documentary Annexures: Attach certified bank statements, registered property deeds (Saf Kabala), loan sanction letters, audited balance sheets, and copies of previous years' assessment orders.
  3. Citing Statutory Exemptions: Cite specific sections and schedules of the Income Tax Act 2023 and NBR Statutory Regulatory Orders (SROs) confirming the tax-exempt status of specific incomes.
  4. Time Extension Applications: If assembling documents takes longer than the notice period, your advocate must file a formal application under the Act requesting a 15-day extension before the deadline expires, preventing unilateral orders.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Best Judgment Assessment Under Section 184

The greatest catastrophe a taxpayer can bring upon themselves is ignoring an audit notice. Under Section 184 of the Income Tax Act 2023, if a taxpayer fails to make a return, fails to comply with all the terms of a notice under Section 183, or fails to produce books of accounts, the DCT is legally empowered to make a Best Judgment Assessment.

In a Best Judgment Assessment, the DCT determines your total income based on their own estimation and available market data, without requiring your consent. The DCT routinely doubles or triples your estimated income, disallows legitimate business deductions, and imposes severe penalties and statutory interest. Once a Best Judgment order is passed, the tax becomes a certified government debt recoverable through bank account freezing under Section 275 and property attachment. Prompt legal representation before assessment finalization is critical.

The Appeal Hierarchy: Commissioner (Appeals) & Tribunal

If the DCT passes an arbitrary, unjust assessment order despite your documentary evidence, the Income Tax Act 2023 provides an independent, structured judicial appeal hierarchy:

  • First Appeal to Commissioner (Appeals): Under Section 285 of the Act, any taxpayer objecting to an assessment order can file a formal memorandum of appeal before the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeals) within forty-five (45) days of receiving the assessment order and demand notice. Under the new law, the appellant must deposit ten percent (10%) of the disputed tax before filing. The Commissioner (Appeals) can confirm, reduce, enhance, or annul the assessment.
  • Second Appeal to Taxes Appellate Tribunal: If dissatisfied with the appellate order, the taxpayer can file an appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal under Section 293 within sixty (60) days. The Tribunal is an independent judicial body comprising judicial and accountant members, providing impartial scrutiny of complex corporate accounting disputes.
  • High Court Division Reference: On questions of pure law, the taxpayer can approach the High Court Division under Section 309 of the Act.

Comparison Table: Income Tax Act 2023 vs. 1984 Ordinance

The table below summarizes the key procedural differences between the old 1984 Ordinance and the modern Income Tax Act 2023 regarding audits and appeals:

ParameterNew Income Tax Act 2023Old Income Tax Ordinance 1984
Language of LawStandard modern Bengali statutory textEnglish statutory text
Audit Selection SectionSection 182 (Automated risk engine)Section 82BB / 83 audit selection
First Appeal ForumSection 285 Commissioner (Appeals)Section 153 Appellate Commissioner
Pre-Appeal Deposit Rule10% of disputed tax payable before appeal10% to 15% deposit requirements
Digital Cross-MatchingAutomated bank, NID, and land registry linksPrimarily manual document inspection

Mastering the new 2023 statutory structure ensures that tax disputes are defended on solid, up-to-date legal grounds.

Illustrative Scenario: Defeating an Arbitrary BDT 25 Lakh Tax Claim

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how an experienced tax advocate resolved an audit dispute in Dhaka:

A commercial importer in Gulshan filed his income tax return under Universal Self-Assessment for the assessment year 2024-2025, declaring a net business income of BDT 28,00,000 and paying BDT 4,20,000 in income tax. Six months later, he received an Audit Notice under Section 182 followed by a Show-Cause Notice under Section 183 from the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes (Circle 45, Taxes Zone 2, Dhaka). The DCT pointed out that during the year, the taxpayer purchased a residential flat in Dhanmondi valued at BDT 1,20,00,000, and personal bank accounts showed credit deposits of BDT 85,00,000, proposing to treat BDT 70,00,000 as unexplained investment and demanding BDT 24,50,000 in additional tax and penalties.

The taxpayer retained a Supreme Court tax advocate. The advocate inspected the client's past five years of tax returns and compiled a comprehensive evidence file: (1) bank statements showing BDT 45,00,000 received as a home loan from a private commercial bank; (2) certified proceeds realization certificates (PRC) proving BDT 20,00,000 received as foreign remittance from the taxpayer's brother in Canada (fully tax-exempt under Schedule 6); and (3) previous year accumulated savings. The advocate drafted a comprehensive Written Explanation under the Income Tax Act 2023 cross-referencing each transaction.

During the personal hearing before the DCT, the advocate presented the loan sanction letters and remittance certificates. Confronted with an airtight documentary audit trail, the DCT accepted the explanation, dropped the unexplained investment allegation, and passed an assessment order accepting the declared income with zero additional tax liability, saving the taxpayer BDT 24,50,000 and permanently regularizing his tax profile.

Talk to an Advocate

Navigating complex legal disputes in Bangladesh requires uncompromising documentary preparation, precise statutory drafting, and experienced courtroom representation. Whether you are seeking to buy back ancestral land through pre-emption, stay an unlawful bank auction, prosecute fraudulent recruitment brokers, restrain violent death threats, or resolve high-stakes income tax audit notices, procedural delays can extinguish your statutory remedies. A qualified advocate protects your interests, files emergency petitions, and enforces your legal entitlements across civil, criminal, revenue, and constitutional tribunals.

Need an advocate for this legal matter in Bangladesh? Send your documents on WhatsApp to +880 1712-655546, or call +880 1955-802007. Overseas clients: remote consultation and courtroom representation available.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should I do first if I receive an Income Tax Audit Notice in Bangladesh?

Never ignore the notice. Check the specific section cited (Section 182, 183, or 212 of the Income Tax Act 2023) and note the compliance date. Contact an experienced tax advocate immediately to examine your return, bank statements, and draft a formal written response.

Can I get more time to respond to a Deputy Commissioner of Taxes (DCT) notice?

Yes. You or your authorized tax advocate can submit a formal written application to the DCT requesting a 15-day extension to gather bank statements, deeds, or audited accounts. It must be filed before the original deadline expires.

What happens if I fail to respond to an Income Tax Audit notice?

Under Section 184 of the Income Tax Act 2023, the DCT can pass a unilateral 'Best Judgment Assessment', estimating your income arbitrarily, disallowing expenses, and imposing heavy taxes, interest, and penalties.

How do I explain a wealth mismatch in my tax return?

You must provide documentary evidence reconciling the increase in assets, such as formal bank home loans, tax-exempt foreign remittances (with PRC certificates), agricultural income, capital gains, or inheritance and gift deeds.

What is the deadline to appeal an adverse tax assessment in Bangladesh?

Under Section 285 of the Income Tax Act 2023, you must file a formal memorandum of appeal before the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeals) within forty-five (45) days of receiving the assessment order and demand notice.

Do I have to pay tax before filing an appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals)?

Yes. Under the Income Tax Act 2023, an appellant is generally required to pay ten percent (10%) of the disputed tax before the appeal can be admitted for hearing by the Commissioner (Appeals).

What is the Taxes Appellate Tribunal in Bangladesh?

The Taxes Appellate Tribunal is an independent second-appellate judicial authority established under Section 293 of the Act, consisting of judicial and accountant members, that hears appeals against orders passed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

Can an overseas non-resident Bangladeshi (NRB) defend a tax audit from abroad?

Yes. An NRB taxpayer can authorize a tax lawyer or Income Tax Practitioner (ITP) in Bangladesh through a formal Power of Attorney or Letter of Authority (Form IT-33) to attend hearings and represent them before the tax authorities.

Income Tax Case Procedure Bangladesh: How to Handle NBR Disputes

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-05-12 · 9 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Receiving an income tax notice from the National Board of Revenue (NBR) is a stressful experience — whether you are an individual or a company. An incorrect tax assessment, a penalty notice, or a demand for back taxes can have serious financial and legal consequences if not handled correctly. Understanding the income tax dispute procedure in Bangladesh — and your rights at each stage — is essential to protecting yourself and your business.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Overview: Income Tax Disputes in Bangladesh

Income tax disputes in Bangladesh arise when there is a disagreement between a taxpayer and the National Board of Revenue (NBR) regarding the amount of tax owed, allowable deductions, tax exemptions, or penalties. The Income Tax Act 2023 (replacing the Income Tax Ordinance 1984) governs all income tax proceedings in Bangladesh.

The dispute resolution process in Bangladesh's income tax system follows a multi-stage hierarchy: NBR assessment → Commissioner's objection → Taxes Appellate Tribunal → High Court Division. A tax lawyer in Dhaka can represent you at every stage to protect your financial interests.

Types of NBR Income Tax Notices You May Receive

The NBR issues several types of income tax notices in Bangladesh:

  • Section 163 Notice (return submission): Requiring you to submit an income tax return if you have not done so
  • Section 176 Notice (audit/assessment): Notifying you that your tax return is being audited and you must produce books of accounts and documents
  • Demand Notice (after assessment): A formal demand for additional tax based on the completed assessment order
  • Penalty Notice: Imposing a penalty for late filing, concealment of income, or failure to deduct TDS
  • TDS Default Notice: Against employers or businesses that failed to deduct and deposit withholding tax
  • Show Cause Notice: Asking you to explain why a penalty or additional tax should not be imposed

Each type of notice requires a specific, timely response. Missing the response deadline can result in an adverse order issued ex parte (without hearing your side).

How to Respond to an Income Tax Notice

When you receive any income tax notice from NBR, the most important step is to respond within the stated deadline. Here is the general approach:

  1. Identify the notice type and deadline. Read the notice carefully. Note the response deadline — typically 15–30 days from the notice date.
  2. Gather all relevant documents. Depending on the notice: income tax returns for the relevant years, audited financial statements, bank statements, evidence of allowable deductions, TDS certificates, and any other documents referenced in the notice.
  3. Draft a written response. Address every point in the notice factually and with supporting documentation. Vague or incomplete responses invite follow-up notices and adverse orders.
  4. Attend the hearing if required. Some notices require a personal or representative appearance before the Inspecting Joint Commissioner or Tax Circle. Your lawyer can attend as your authorised representative.
  5. File the response within the deadline. Late responses are treated as defaults and the tax authority can proceed ex parte.

The Tax Assessment Process

The NBR conducts tax assessments through the Tax Circle Officer (Tax Commissioner's designated representative). The assessment process involves:

  • Review of your filed return (if filed) or estimation based on available information (if not filed)
  • A notice for production of books of accounts, statements, and relevant documents
  • Examination of your income sources, claimed deductions, and any discrepancies
  • Preliminary findings are communicated and you are given an opportunity to respond (a Show Cause notice)
  • A final assessment order is issued specifying the total income assessed and the tax demand

The assessment order sets out the tax officer's conclusions. If you disagree with the assessment, you have the right to appeal — but this right must be exercised within the specified limitation period, typically 45–90 days from the assessment order date.

Objecting to a Tax Assessment: Filing an Appeal

Under the Income Tax Act 2023, a taxpayer who disagrees with a tax assessment order can file an appeal before the Tax Commissioner (Appeals) — also known as a first appeal:

  1. File a written objection (appeal petition) within the prescribed time limit from the assessment order date
  2. Pay the prescribed amount of disputed tax as a condition of appeal admission (currently one-third or as directed)
  3. Attach supporting documents, accounts, and legal arguments
  4. The Commissioner (Appeals) hears both parties and issues an order

Key grounds for first appeal: calculation errors in the assessment, improper disallowance of legitimate deductions, failure to consider submitted evidence, assessment based on estimated income without basis, and procedural irregularities in the assessment process.

Taxes Appellate Tribunal: Second Level of Appeal

If the first appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) does not resolve the dispute, the taxpayer can file a further appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal — a quasi-judicial body constituted under the Income Tax Act with independent members.

The Tribunal reviews questions of fact and law. Proceedings are more formal — legal arguments and written submissions are presented, and both parties may be represented by lawyers. The Tribunal's decision is authoritative on factual matters.

Beyond the Tribunal, further appeals on questions of law go to the High Court Division — making it the final stage for legal questions about tax law interpretation.

High Court Division: Final Legal Remedy

Appeals from the Taxes Appellate Tribunal on questions of law go to the High Court Division under Section 160 of the Income Tax Act (previously Section 158 of the Ordinance 1984). The High Court:

  • Considers questions of law — not fresh factual disputes
  • Can set aside, modify, or uphold the Tribunal's decision
  • Issues authoritative rulings that bind tax authorities on the legal question

Additionally, a writ petition before the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution is available where the NBR has acted without jurisdiction, violated fundamental rights, or acted in breach of natural justice. This is a powerful and often faster remedy in clear cases.

An experienced Supreme Court advocate handles High Court tax appeals and writ petitions in income tax cases.

Common Grounds for Successful Tax Appeals

Experienced tax lawyers in Bangladesh know which arguments are most effective in the appeals process:

  • Addition without basis: The tax officer added income without any documentary or credible evidence — a common and successful ground for appeal
  • Improper disallowance of deductions: Legitimate business expenses, depreciation, or bad debts wrongfully disallowed
  • Double taxation: The same income taxed twice — at withholding and again at assessment
  • Statute of limitations: Assessment issued after the limitation period expired
  • Procedural failures: Assessment made without proper notice, hearing denied, or fair opportunity to present evidence not given
  • Incorrect application of tax rate or exemption: Wrong tax bracket applied or available exemption not granted

How a Tax Lawyer Helps in Income Tax Cases

Advocate Md. Shah Alam's law chambers provides full-spectrum income tax dispute representation in Bangladesh including:

  • Drafting responses to NBR notices and show cause notices
  • Attending tax circle hearings on your behalf
  • Filing first appeals before the Commissioner (Appeals)
  • Representation before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal
  • High Court income tax appeals on questions of law
  • Writ petitions against unlawful NBR actions
  • Tax compliance review to prevent future disputes

Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam for a confidential consultation on your income tax dispute today.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should I do if I receive an income tax notice from NBR in Bangladesh?

Read the notice carefully, note the response deadline, gather all relevant financial documents, and consult a tax lawyer immediately. File a written response within the deadline. Missing the deadline allows the tax authority to proceed ex parte, usually resulting in an adverse assessment.

Can I appeal against a NBR income tax assessment in Bangladesh?

Yes. File a first appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) within the limitation period from the assessment order date. Pay the prescribed portion of the disputed tax as a condition of admission. A tax lawyer can identify the strongest grounds for your appeal.

What is the Taxes Appellate Tribunal in Bangladesh?

The Taxes Appellate Tribunal is a quasi-judicial appellate body that hears appeals from Commissioner (Appeals) decisions in income tax cases. It is independent of the NBR and has the authority to modify or set aside tax assessments. Further appeals from its decisions go to the High Court Division on questions of law.

Can I go to the High Court against an NBR income tax decision?

Yes — through two routes. First, an appeal on a question of law from the Taxes Appellate Tribunal. Second, a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution if the NBR acted without jurisdiction or violated your legal rights. The High Court can set aside unlawful tax demands.

How long does an income tax appeal take in Bangladesh?

First appeal (Commissioner Appeals): 3–12 months. Taxes Appellate Tribunal: 1–3 years. High Court appeal: 2–5+ years. These are estimates — actual timelines depend on case complexity and court scheduling. An experienced tax lawyer can accelerate hearings through proper case management.

Inheritance Law Bangladesh: How Property Is Divided After Death

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-03-02 · 8 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

When a family member passes away, how their property and assets are distributed can either bring the family together or trigger prolonged, expensive legal disputes. Understanding inheritance law in Bangladesh — and acting promptly — protects your rights as a legal heir.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

📋 In This Article

  2. Shares of Major Heirs Under Muslim Law
  3. Inheritance for Non-Muslims in Bangladesh
  4. Wills (Wasiyat) Under Bangladesh Law
  5. The Heirship Certificate: What It Is and Why You Need It
  6. Obtaining a Heirship Certificate in Bangladesh
  7. Common Inheritance Disputes and How to Avoid Them
  8. Inheritance Tax in Bangladesh

Muslim Inheritance Law: The Faraid System

For Muslims in Bangladesh — the majority of the population — inheritance is governed by Muslim personal law, specifically the system of faraid (obligatory shares prescribed by Islamic law). These rules apply automatically upon death regardless of what the deceased may have said verbally during their lifetime.

The faraid system divides heirs into two main categories: Quranic heirs (Sharers) who receive fixed fractional shares, and Agnatic heirs (Residuaries) who take the remainder after the Sharers have received their portions. A property lawyer in Dhaka can help calculate precise shares for each heir in your family situation.

Shares of Major Heirs Under Muslim Law

Key inheritance shares for common family situations in Bangladesh:

  • Wife: 1/8 if she has children with the deceased, 1/4 if he had no children. She receives this share even if she has remarried.
  • Husband: 1/4 if his wife has children, 1/2 if she had no children.
  • Daughter: 1/2 if the sole heir (no sons), 1/3 each if two daughters and no sons. If there are sons, daughters receive half the son's share.
  • Son: Sons are residuary heirs — they receive equal shares of whatever remains after Sharers are paid. Each son takes double the share of a daughter.
  • Mother: 1/6 if there are children or multiple siblings, 1/3 if there are no children and not more than one sibling.
  • Father: 1/6 with children; if no children, he is both a Sharer and a Residuary heir.

These are simplified illustrations — actual calculations depend on exactly which relatives survive the deceased. Always have a lawyer calculate the shares properly before distributing in an estate with multiple heirs.

Inheritance for Non-Muslims in Bangladesh

Non-Muslims in Bangladesh inherit under their personal laws or the Succession Act 1925:

  • Hindus: Governed by Hindu personal law (Dayabhaga school prevails in Bangladesh). Property typically passes to sons, with daughters receiving shares in some circumstances.
  • Christians and others: The Succession Act 1925 applies. This broadly follows a spouse-plus-children distribution, with detailed rules for more distant relatives.

For non-Muslim inheritance disputes, a lawyer with expertise in the relevant personal law is essential — the rules are complex and community-specific.

Wills (Wasiyat) Under Bangladesh Law

Under Muslim law in Bangladesh, a person can make a will (wasiyat) but with important limitations:

  • A Muslim can only bequeath by will up to 1/3 of their estate — the remaining 2/3 must pass under the faraid rules to legal heirs.
  • A Muslim cannot make a will in favour of a legal heir who is already entitled to an inheritance share (to prevent favouring one child over others) — unless all other heirs consent after death.
  • Wills for non-Muslims have more flexibility under the Succession Act 1925 — generally a person can bequeath their entire estate by will.

Wills in Bangladesh do not require registration, but registered wills are more difficult to challenge. Store your will safely and tell your executor where it is kept.

The Heirship Certificate: What It Is and Why You Need It

A heirship certificate (also called a legal heirship certificate or inheritance certificate) is a document issued by a court certifying who the legal heirs of a deceased person are and in what proportions they inherit. In Bangladesh, this certificate is essential for:

  • Transferring bank accounts and fixed deposits of the deceased to heirs
  • Filing for land mutation (namjari) of inherited property
  • Claiming provident fund, gratuity, or pension benefits of a deceased employee
  • Collecting insurance proceeds
  • Registering inherited vehicles

Without a heirship certificate, institutions will typically refuse to deal with the heirs. Don't wait — apply promptly after a death occurs.

Obtaining a Heirship Certificate in Bangladesh

A heirship certificate is obtained from the Civil Court (typically the Assistant Judge's Court at District level). The process:

  1. File an application petition with the court listing all legal heirs and their relationship to the deceased.
  2. Attach: the death certificate of the deceased, National Identity Cards of all heirs, and supporting documents of relationship (birth certificates, Kabinnama).
  3. The court issues notice and verifies the list of heirs.
  4. A heirship certificate is issued — typically within a few weeks to a few months depending on the court's workload.

All major heirs must cooperate in the process. If there is a dispute about who the legal heirs are — for example, claims of secret marriage or disputed paternity — the matter escalates to contested litigation. A property lawyer can manage this process efficiently.

Common Inheritance Disputes and How to Avoid Them

Most inheritance disputes in Bangladesh arise from:

  • Undisclosed second marriages creating competing sets of heirs
  • Pre-death transfers — land gifted or sold to one child, allegedly unfairly, before death
  • Fraudulent mutation — one heir secretly mutating all land in their name after death
  • Exclusion of female heirs — daughters being informally told they have no share (contrary to law)
  • Disputed wills — wills challenged as forged or made under undue influence

Prevention: keep all title documents updated, have clear records of all family relationships, and if you own significant property, consult a lawyer about whether to formalise your estate planning with a will and clear record of your assets.

Inheritance Tax in Bangladesh

Bangladesh does not currently have a general inheritance tax or estate duty. Heirs inherit the deceased's assets without a specific tax on the inheritance itself. However:

  • Stamp duty and registration fees apply when inherited land is formally transferred through a heba (gift) deed or other registered document.
  • Inherited assets become part of the heir's income tax return going forward — any income generated from inherited property is taxable income of the heir.
  • If you sell inherited property, capital gains may be taxable depending on the circumstances.

For complex estates involving significant assets, consulting a tax lawyer alongside a property lawyer ensures proper compliance with all legal requirements.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can daughters inherit property in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under Muslim law, daughters are legal heirs with specific shares. However, they receive half of what sons receive in the same category. Daughters cannot legally be denied their inheritance share.

What happens to inherited property if the heir dies before distribution?

The share of the deceased heir passes to their own heirs under the faraid rules. All heirs' shares are determined as of the date of the original owner's death.

Can I contest a will that I believe is fraudulent?

Yes. A will can be challenged in court on grounds of forgery, undue influence, mental incapacity of the testator, or violation of the 1/3 rule for Muslim estates. File promptly — delay weakens your challenge.

Is a verbal promise of property before death enforceable?

Generally not enforceable as an inheritance right. Only formal gifts (heba) completed during the owner's lifetime with delivery of possession, or registered wills, create legal rights.

What if one heir refuses to cooperate in the heirship certificate application?

File the application with all cooperative heirs listed. The court may issue a notice to all potential heirs. A persistently uncooperative heir can be compelled through court orders.

How long do I have to file an inheritance claim?

Limitation periods apply to inheritance suits. Generally, a suit for a declaration of inheritance rights should be filed within the applicable limitation period from the time of dispossession or refusal of your share — consult a lawyer promptly.

Injunction Procedure Bangladesh: How to Stop Illegal Action by Court Order

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-03-18 · 7 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Someone is constructing on your land. A business partner is about to sell shared assets without your consent. A former employee is breaching a non-compete clause. In each of these situations, money compensation after the fact may be useless — you need the action stopped now. An injunction is a court order that compels a party to do something (mandatory injunction) or prevents them from doing something (prohibitory injunction). This guide explains how to obtain one in Bangladesh.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

  8. Civil Lawyer's Role in Injunction Applications

What is an Injunction in Bangladesh Law?

An injunction is a judicial order requiring a party to do (or refrain from doing) a specific act. In Bangladesh, injunctions are governed by the Specific Relief Act 1877 (Sections 52–57) for perpetual injunctions, and the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (Order 39) for temporary injunctions.

Injunctions are equitable remedies — courts grant them at their discretion when they determine that ordinary monetary remedies would be inadequate or that irreparable harm would result without the order. Contact a civil lawyer in Dhaka immediately if you need urgent injunctive relief.

Types of Injunctions Available in Bangladesh

Bangladesh courts issue two broad categories of injunction:

  • Prohibitory (Restrictive) Injunction: Prevents the defendant from doing something — the most common type. E.g., stop selling disputed property, stop using a trademark, stop construction on land in dispute.
  • Mandatory Injunction: Orders the defendant to do something positive — e.g., restore possession of property, remove an illegal structure built in violation of a court order. Courts grant mandatory injunctions more rarely and only in clear cases.

Temporary vs. Perpetual Injunction

These differ in duration and purpose:

  • Temporary (Interim) Injunction: Granted at the beginning of a case to preserve the status quo until the final hearing. It is not a final determination of rights — just a holding order. Governed by Order 39 CPC.
  • Perpetual Injunction: Granted at the end of a suit as a final remedy, permanently restraining the defendant. Governed by the Specific Relief Act 1877.

Most urgent situations require a temporary injunction first. The court will fix a date for both sides to be heard to determine if the injunction should continue through the trial.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Conditions the Court Considers for an Injunction

Bangladesh courts apply the three-pronged test before granting a temporary injunction. The plaintiff must establish all three:

  1. Prima Facie Case: There is a serious question to be tried — the plaintiff's claim appears to have merit on preliminary examination.
  2. Balance of Convenience: The harm to the plaintiff if the injunction is refused outweighs the harm to the defendant if the injunction is granted.
  3. Irreparable Injury: The plaintiff would suffer harm that cannot be adequately compensated by money damages if the injunction is not granted.

The applicant typically must provide an undertaking as to damages — a promise to compensate the defendant for losses if the injunction is later found to have been wrongly granted.

How to Apply for a Temporary Injunction in Bangladesh

The procedure for obtaining a temporary injunction:

  1. File the main suit: A temporary injunction cannot be obtained standalone — it is an interlocutory application within a main civil suit.
  2. File the injunction application: Simultaneously or very soon after filing the suit, file an application under Order 39 CPC stating the grounds for urgency and the three-pronged test.
  3. Affidavit in support: Attach a sworn affidavit verifying the facts and the urgency of the situation.
  4. Court hearing: The court can hear both parties (inter partes) or issue an ex parte order if the case is urgent.
  5. Show Cause: If an ex parte order is granted, the defendant is given a date to appear and show cause why the injunction should not continue.

A Dhaka civil lawyer can prepare and file an injunction application on an emergency basis — sometimes within a single day when the urgency is dire.

Consequences of Breaching an Injunction Order

Breach of a court injunction order is treated as contempt of court in Bangladesh — a serious matter with significant consequences:

  • Imprisonment for a term determined by the court
  • Fine imposed by the court
  • Attachment and sale of assets
  • In property cases: the breaching construction may be ordered demolished

If someone is defying an existing court injunction order against you, apply immediately to the court that issued the order to initiate contempt proceedings. Our civil lawyers handle urgent contempt applications in Dhaka civil courts.

Frequently Asked Questions

How quickly can I get an emergency injunction in Bangladesh?

In urgent cases, a court can issue an ex parte temporary injunction on the same day the application is filed. The defendant is then given notice and a date to contest the order.

Can I get an injunction without filing a full lawsuit?

No. A temporary injunction is an interlocutory application within a main civil suit. You must file the suit and apply for the injunction simultaneously or shortly after.

What if someone ignores a court injunction against them?

Non-compliance with a court injunction constitutes contempt of court. Apply to the court that issued the order for contempt proceedings, which can result in the defendant's imprisonment and/or fine.

Can I get an injunction to stop a bank from recovering a loan?

It is very difficult to obtain injunctions against banks executing security for loans. Courts are generally reluctant to prevent legitimate banking operations. However, injunctions may be available in cases of clear procedural error.

How long does a temporary injunction last?

A temporary injunction remains in force until the final disposal of the suit, unless vacated earlier by the court on an application by either party.

entries.body:
INTERPOL Red Notice in Bangladesh: Extradition Act 1974 & Cross-Border Defense Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-08 · 19 minutes

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In an interconnected global financial and political environment, cross-border criminal proceedings, mutual legal assistance requests, and INTERPOL Red Notices have become potent instruments. For dual citizens, Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs), and foreign nationals residing in or visiting Bangladesh, discovering an active INTERPOL Red Notice or facing an extradition request is an acute legal emergency. An INTERPOL Red Notice is not an international arrest warrant; it is an electronic request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. In Bangladesh, formal surrender to foreign nations is strictly governed by the Extradition Act 1974 (Act No. LVIII of 1974) and constitutional safeguards under Articles 31 and 32. This definitive legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate and criminal defense practitioner in Uttara and Dhaka, details the statutory extradition framework, substantive legal defenses, INTERPOL CCF deletion petitions, and emergency High Court writ remedies.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

📋 In This Article
