How Widespread Is Land Fraud in Bangladesh?

Land fraud in Bangladesh is extraordinarily common. The country's complex land recording system — with colonial-era records, multiple layers of government databases, and a land sub-registry process that has historically been vulnerable to corruption — creates fertile ground for fraudsters.

Common victims include:

  • Property buyers who purchase land from people who do not have clear title
  • NRBs (Non-Resident Bangladeshis) who cannot monitor their ancestral property in Bangladesh
  • Heirs who discover that their family property has been fraudulently transferred by a dishonest co-heir or relative
  • Landowners whose boundaries have been encroached upon through false mutations
  • Flat buyers who purchase apartments built on land the developer did not have clear title to

A property lawyer in Dhaka who conducts thorough due diligence before purchase is the single most effective protection against land fraud.

Most Common Types of Land Fraud in Bangladesh

The most prevalent forms of land fraud in Bangladesh include:

  • Forged deeds (deed fraud): A fraudster creates a fake sale deed, gift deed, or power of attorney — sometimes using counterfeit stamps and forged signatures — to transfer land they do not own.
  • Double selling: The same piece of land is sold to two or more buyers simultaneously. The fraudster takes money from multiple buyers before disappearing.
  • Fraudulent Power of Attorney (POA): A dishonest agent or relative uses a forged or improperly obtained POA to sell the owner's land without their knowledge or consent.
  • Fraudulent mutation (namjari): Through bribery or forged documents, a fraudster causes the land records (khatian) to be changed to their name — effectively stealing the mutation record even though the land deed remains with the true owner.
  • Encroachment with fraudulent RS/CS records: By submitting falsified survey records to government offices, encroachers create paper records supporting their false claim to land they have physically occupied.
  • Undisclosed encumbrances: A seller fails to disclose that the property is mortgaged, subject to a court injunction, or has other charges — transferring the problem to the buyer.
  • Developer fraud: Real estate developers sell flats on land that has title disputes, insufficient RAJUK approval, or multiple mortgage charges — leaving buyers with legally defective properties.

How to Detect Land Fraud Before Buying Property

The most effective protection against land fraud is thorough due diligence before purchase. Your property lawyer should conduct:

  • Title search: Review of at least 25–30 years of ownership history in the Sub-Registrar's deed index books. Every transfer of the property should be traceable through registered deeds.
  • Mutation record check (namjari): Obtain certified copies of the current and historical khatian (land registration record) from the AC Land office. This should match the deed chain.
  • Survey record check (CS, SA, RS, BS): Review the relevant survey records (Colonial Settlement, State Acquisition, Revisional Survey, Bangla Survey) to confirm the property's recorded area, location, and ownership history at each survey stage.
  • Physical inspection: Verify that the physical boundaries of the land match the deeds and survey records. Identify any encroachers or structures that suggest disputed possession.
  • Court case search: Search the local courts for any pending civil suits (title suits, partition suits, injunctions) or criminal cases involving the property or the seller.
  • RAJUK/Development Authority clearance: For urban properties, check RAJUK (or RJSC for converted land) records for any development plan violations, restrictions, or pending notices.
  • Encumbrance search: Check whether the property has been mortgaged to a bank or financial institution and whether any such mortgage remains outstanding.

How to Check Land Records Online in Bangladesh

Bangladesh has made significant progress in digitising land records. Key online resources for land record verification include:

  • Land Records Portal (land.gov.bd): Check the national land portal for khatian (plot register) information including ownership, area, and classification of plots by district and mouza.
  • eporcha.gov.bd: The e-porcha system provides official digital copies of land records (RS, SA, CS records) for most districts. You can purchase official digital copies online.
  • Online Mutation Check: Check the status of pending mutation applications at the relevant AC Land office's online portal (varies by district).
  • Sub-Registrar Deed Registry: Registered deeds can be checked (in person or sometimes online) at the relevant Sub-Registrar's office for the district where the land is located.

While online checks are a useful first step, they are not a substitute for professional legal due diligence. Many fraud documents have not yet been detected and entered into the database as fraudulent. A property lawyer who physically inspects the original records can catch discrepancies that online checks miss.

Red Flags: Warning Signs of Property Fraud

Be alert to these warning signs that may indicate property fraud:

  • Rushed transaction: The seller is pushing for an unusually fast sale — often a sign they want to complete the fraud before discovery.
  • Reluctance to produce original documents: A genuine seller will readily produce original deeds, khatian, mutation records, and tax payment receipts. Hesitation or only producing photocopies is a warning sign.
  • Price significantly below market rate: Fraudsters often sell at a discount to attract buyers who do not ask too many questions.
  • Multiple owners claiming the same land: Someone tells you "there's a small court case, but it will be resolved" — this is a serious warning. Do not buy contested property.
  • Deeds with erasures, corrections, or poor printing: Original deeds are stamped and printed in specific ways. Any alterations, corrections, or quality inconsistencies in the deed document are red flags.
  • NRB seller with very limited knowledge of the property: When an overseas seller knows almost nothing about the physical property they are selling, this may indicate they are not the true owner.
  • Agent or third party only — seller never meets you: Fraudsters often operate through intermediaries to avoid direct identification.

What to Do If You Are a Victim of Land Fraud

If you have already been defrauded, act immediately — delay reduces your ability to recover the property or money. The steps to take are:

  1. Engage a property lawyer immediately: Contact Adv. Shah Alam immediately. A property lawyer will assess your position and recommend the fastest legal remedies.
  2. Gather all documents: Collect every document you have relating to the transaction — the sale deed, money receipts, correspondence, photographs, and any communications with the fraudster.
  3. Obtain an injunction: If the fraudster is attempting to further transfer or mortgage the property, your lawyer can file an emergency application in the Civil Court for an injunction to stop any further dealing with the land.
  4. File a criminal complaint: Land fraud involves criminal offences — cheating (Section 420 Penal Code), forgery (Sections 463–471 Penal Code), and criminal breach of trust (Section 406 Penal Code). File a complaint at the police station or directly before the Magistrate's Court.
  5. File a civil title suit: A civil suit for declaration of title, cancellation of fraudulent deeds, and injunction is the primary civil remedy to reclaim the land.
  6. Report to the AC Land office: If fraudulent mutation has occurred, file a complaint with the AC Land office to freeze further mutations pending court proceedings.

Criminal and Civil Remedies for Land Fraud

Victims of land fraud in Bangladesh have both criminal and civil remedies available simultaneously — you do not have to choose one over the other.

Criminal remedies:

  • Section 420 Penal Code (Cheating): A person who induces another to deliver property by deception is liable to imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
  • Sections 463–471 Penal Code (Forgery): Creating, using, or possessing a forged document is punishable with imprisonment of up to 2–10 years depending on the type of document. Forging a valuable security or property deed carries the harshest penalties.
  • Section 406 Penal Code (Criminal Breach of Trust): An agent or attorney who misappropriates property entrusted to them (e.g., a dishonest Power of Attorney holder) is liable to up to 3 years imprisonment.

Civil remedies:

  • Title Suit (Declaration Suit): Seeking a court declaration that you are the true owner of the property and that the fraudulent deed is null and void.
  • Cancellation of Deed: An application under Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act to cancel a fraudulent deed or document.
  • Injunction: Preventing the fraudster from dealing with the property while court proceedings are pending.
  • Suit for specific performance: If you paid for land and the seller refuses to execute the deed, a specific performance suit can compel them to do so.
  • Damages: A civil suit for money damages (compensation) for financial loss caused by the fraud.

How to File a Land Fraud Case in Bangladesh

Land fraud cases involve both the criminal and civil court systems. Your lawyer will advise which route — or combination of routes — is most appropriate for your situation.

Criminal complaint process:

  1. File an FIR (First Information Report) at the police station of the jurisdiction where the fraud occurred.
  2. If police refuse or are slow to act, file a direct complaint (naraji petition) before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM).
  3. The court may take cognizance and direct an investigation, or issue a process against the accused directly.

Civil suit process:

  1. File a Civil Suit (Title Suit) in the Civil Court of the district where the land is located.
  2. Simultaneously apply for a temporary injunction to stop further dealing with the property.
  3. The court will hear both parties and ultimately determine ownership — a process that can take several years, though interim protection orders are available immediately.

Engaging a property lawyer in Dhaka who has experience specifically in land fraud cases is essential. These cases require simultaneous management of criminal and civil proceedings.

How a Property Lawyer Protects You from Land Fraud

The most important protection against land fraud is engaging a property lawyer in Bangladesh before any transaction. Here is what an expert property lawyer does:

  • Pre-purchase due diligence: Conducts a comprehensive title search, mutation check, and court search — typically requiring 1–2 weeks and producing a written title opinion confirming whether the land is safe to buy.
  • Deed drafting: Prepares a legally sound sale deed that protects the buyer's interests and includes warranties by the seller regarding title and freedom from encumbrances.
  • Registration supervision: Attends the Sub-Registrar's office to oversee the registration of the deed and ensure it is correctly executed, stamped, and registered.
  • Mutation and possession: Assists with post-purchase mutation (namjari) to ensure the buyer's name is entered in the land records.
  • Fraud detection: Identifies discrepancies in documents, suspicious patterns, and red flags that an untrained buyer would miss.

The cost of legal due diligence is a tiny fraction of the property price — and an absolute necessity in Bangladesh's land market. Contact Adv. Shah Alam for pre-purchase legal due diligence on any property you are considering buying.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I recover land that was sold by a fraudster without my knowledge in Bangladesh?

Yes, but you must act quickly. File both a criminal complaint and a civil title suit. The courts can declare the fraudulent deed void and order the land returned to the true owner. An injunction can prevent further transfers while the case is pending.

Is it safe to buy land from an NRB (Non-Resident Bangladeshi) via Power of Attorney?

POA-based sales are high-risk in Bangladesh. Ensure the POA is genuinely executed by the owner (authenticated by the Bangladesh Embassy/Consulate abroad), is registered in Bangladesh, and has not been revoked. Your lawyer must independently verify the POA's authenticity before proceeding.

How do I know if a land mutation has been done fraudulently in my name being changed?

Regularly check the land records (khatian) at the AC Land office or online at land.gov.bd and eporcha.gov.bd. If you discover an unauthorised mutation, file an immediate complaint with the AC Land office and engage a property lawyer to challenge the fraudulent mutation and restore the original record.

What should I check before buying a flat or apartment in Bangladesh?

Key checks include: the developer's RAJUK (or relevant authority) approved plan, the developer's registered deed for the land, any existing mortgages on the land, RJSC registration status, and whether the developer has sold the same flat to other buyers. A pre-purchase legal checklist is essential.

Can police help with land fraud cases in Bangladesh?

Yes — land fraud is a criminal matter under the Penal Code. You can file an FIR at the local police station. If police are uncooperative, you can file a direct complaint before the Magistrate's Court. However, be aware that civil proceedings (title suits) are also essential to recover the property itself.

Launched by the Ministry of Land, it has transformed how citizens interact with land administration in Bangladesh. What Is land.gov.bd (ভূমি সেবা)?

land.gov.bd is the official digital land services portal of Bangladesh, operated by the Ministry of Land (ভূমি মন্ত্রণালয়). It provides citizens with online access to land records, mutation services, tax payment, and document ordering — without requiring repeated visits to the AC Land office (উপজেলা ভূমি অফিস).

The portal is part of Bangladesh's broader Digital Bangladesh initiative and integrates multiple sub-systems:

  • land.gov.bd — Main citizen portal for land record search and services
  • bl.land.gov.bd — BhoomiPRO: integrated land management system for administration
  • eporcha.gov.bd — Certified digital porcha (khatian copy) purchase portal
  • mutation.land.gov.bd — Dedicated mutation application tracking

Whether you are buying land, settling an inheritance dispute, or applying for a bank mortgage, land.gov.bd is your first stop for verifying land ownership in Bangladesh. A land lawyer in Uttara, Dhaka uses these portals as a starting point for all property due diligence.

Khatian Search Online – CS, SA, RS & BS Records

The khatian search function on land.gov.bd lets you view historical and current land ownership records across all four major surveys of Bangladesh.

Step-by-step to search a khatian:

  1. Go to land.gov.bd and click "খতিয়ান তথ্য" (Khatian Information) from the services menu
  2. Select the Survey Type from the dropdown: CS, SA, RS, or BS
  3. Select your Division (বিভাগ)
  4. Select your District (জেলা)
  5. Select your Upazila/Thana (উপজেলা)
  6. Select your Mouza (মৌজা) — the lowest land administrative unit
  7. Enter either the Khatian Number (খতিয়ান নম্বর) or the Owner's Name (মালিকের নাম)
  8. Click Search (খুঁজুন)

The result shows the khatian record including owner name(s), dag numbers, land area per plot, and land classification. If the mouza is not yet digitised, no result will appear — in that case, visit the AC Land office directly.

⚠️ Tip: The mouza name can be found in any existing registered deed or land tax receipt. If you don't know it, ask your local UP member or the AC Land office.

RS Porcha Check by Dag Number

The RS Porcha (Revisional Survey Plot Record) shows detailed information about a specific plot (dag number) — including its area, land classification, and all khatians that include that dag.

How to check RS Porcha by Dag Number:

  1. On land.gov.bd, select "RS পর্চা" or "Plot Information"
  2. Select Division, District, Upazila, and Mouza
  3. Enter the Dag Number (দাগ নম্বর) of the specific plot
  4. Click Search — the porcha shows area, land type, and all associated khatian numbers

Why this matters:

  • If a single dag appears in two or more khatians, it signals a potential fraudulent double-entry or ownership dispute
  • Verifying the dag number against the seller's deed prevents purchasing non-existent or misrepresented land
  • Banks require confirmed dag and khatian details before approving a mortgage against land

If you spot anomalies in the porcha data, consult a property lawyer in Dhaka before proceeding with any transaction.

Online Mutation (Namjari) Application

Mutation (নামজারি/মিউটেশন) is the process of updating the khatian to reflect a new owner after a land purchase, inheritance, or gift. In several districts, Bangladesh now allows online mutation applications through land.gov.bd.

How to apply for mutation online:

  1. Go to land.gov.bd → Select "নামজারি আবেদন" (Mutation Application)
  2. Register or log in with your mobile number (OTP verification)
  3. Fill in the applicant details: name, NID number, contact
  4. Enter the land details: Division, District, Upazila, Mouza, Dag No., Khatian No.
  5. Upload required documents (see table below)
  6. Pay the application fee online via mobile banking or card
  7. Submit and receive your mutation case number (নামজারি কেস নম্বর)
Document Required For
Registered sale deed (দলিল)Purchase-based mutation
Succession certificate / heirship documentInheritance-based mutation
Applicant's NID copyAll applications
Previous khatian copy (certified)All applications
Land tax payment receipt (khajna)All applications
Court decree (if mutation follows a court order)Court-ordered mutation

Online mutation is currently available in most upazila land offices in Dhaka, Chittagong, Sylhet, Rajshahi, and Khulna divisions. For other areas, applications may still need to be filed in person.

Tracking Mutation Application Status Online

Once you have filed a mutation application and received a case number, you can track its progress at any time through land.gov.bd.

Steps to track mutation status:

  1. Go to land.gov.bd → Select "নামজারি অবস্থান" or "Mutation Status"
  2. Select Division, District, and Upazila
  3. Enter your Mutation Case Number (নামজারি কেস নম্বর)
  4. Click Search

Status stages you may see:

  • প্রাপ্ত (Received): Application lodged, awaiting assignment
  • তদন্তাধীন (Under Inspection): Field inspection by an AC Land officer scheduled or ongoing
  • আপত্তি দাখিল (Objection Filed): A third party has filed an objection — a hearing is needed
  • শুনানির তারিখ (Hearing Scheduled): Date set for both parties to appear before AC Land
  • আদেশ পাস (Order Passed): AC Land has ruled — either approving or rejecting mutation
  • খতিয়ান ইস্যু (Khatian Issued): New khatian issued in the applicant's name — mutation complete

If your status has been stuck at "Under Inspection" for more than 60 days with no update, a land lawyer in Dhaka can follow up formally with the AC Land office to unblock the process.

Paying Land Tax (Khajna) Online

Annual land development tax — commonly known as khajna (খাজনা) — can now be paid online through land.gov.bd in most districts, eliminating the need to queue at the Union Land Office (ইউনিয়ন ভূমি সহকারী কার্যালয়).

How to pay khajna online:

  1. Go to land.gov.bd → Select "ভূমি উন্নয়ন কর" (Land Development Tax)
  2. Select your Division, District, Upazila, and Union
  3. Enter your Holding Number (হোল্ডিং নম্বর) or search by owner name
  4. View outstanding khajna balance
  5. Pay via bKash, Nagad, Rocket, debit/credit card, or internet banking
  6. Download or print the Digital Khajna Receipt (ডিজিটাল দাখিলা)

⚠️ Important: Keep all khajna receipts safely — they are required when filing a mutation application, selling land, or producing evidence of peaceful possession in a land dispute.

Online khajna payment is currently operational in most upazilas in the eight divisions. If your holding is not found online, visit the Union Land office and request to have your holding number registered in the digital system.

BhoomiPRO – bl.land.gov.bd Integrated Land System

BhoomiPRO (accessible at bl.land.gov.bd) is Bangladesh's integrated digital land management system, connecting AC Land offices, Sub-Registrar offices, and the Ministry of Land into a single platform.

For citizens, BhoomiPRO provides:

  • Real-time mutation processing status linked directly to the AC Land office workflow
  • Integrated deed registration verification — deeds registered at the Sub-Registrar office are linked to BhoomiPRO
  • District-level land record management for government administrators
  • An advanced search interface for cross-referencing khatian, deed, and mutation records

BhoomiPRO is particularly useful for verifying whether a recently registered deed has been correctly reflected in the land administration system — an important check when purchasing land in Dhaka or other major cities where fraud is more common.

eporcha.gov.bd – Ordering Certified Digital Copies

eporcha.gov.bd is the dedicated portal for purchasing certified digital copies of khatian records (porcha). Unlike the free viewing on land.gov.bd, a certified digital porcha from eporcha.gov.bd carries an official digital signature and is accepted for most formal purposes.

How to order a certified porcha from eporcha.gov.bd:

  1. Go to eporcha.gov.bd and register with your NID and mobile number
  2. Search for your khatian using Division, District, Upazila, Mouza, and Khatian Number
  3. Select the porcha and add to your order
  4. Pay the government fee online (typically BDT 100–300 per porcha depending on type)
  5. Download your digitally signed certified porcha immediately after payment

Acceptance of eporcha certified copies:

  • ✅ Accepted for mutation applications at most AC Land offices
  • ✅ Accepted for bank mortgage documentation in most banks
  • ✅ Accepted for Sub-Registrar office deed registration purposes
  • ⚠️ For court evidence, a physical certified copy with wet stamp from AC Land office may still be required — confirm with your lawyer

Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam at our Uttara, Dhaka chamber for guidance on which type of certified document is required for your specific legal matter.

Free vs Paid Services on land.gov.bd

Understanding which services are free and which require payment saves time and avoids surprises:

Service Cost Notes

Online khajna paymentActual tax amountNo extra portal fee

Physical certified copy (AC Land office)BDT 100–200Required for court proceedings

Limitations of the Portal & When to Visit AC Land Office

Despite significant improvements, land.gov.bd has limitations you should know:

  • Digitisation gaps: Many rural mouzas, especially in Barisal, Mymensingh, Rangpur, and Sylhet hill districts, are not yet fully digitised. Searches will return no results for these areas.
  • Delayed updates: The online system can lag weeks or months behind the physical AC Land office records. A recently completed mutation may not yet appear online.
  • Not legally authoritative: For court proceedings, banks, and formal applications, certified physical copies from the AC Land office remain the gold standard — online printouts are supplementary only.
  • Server downtime: The portal occasionally experiences downtime, especially during peak hours. Try early mornings or off-peak times.
  • Registration required for applications: While viewing is open, submitting applications requires NID-linked registration via OTP.

When you MUST visit the AC Land office in person:

  • Your mouza is not available on the online portal
  • You need a physical certified khatian copy for court submission
  • Your mutation application has been rejected and you want to appeal
  • There is an objection to your mutation that requires a hearing before the AC Land officer
  • You need to correct an error in the khatian record

A land and property lawyer in Uttara, Dhaka can represent you at the AC Land office for all these matters, saving you time and ensuring the process follows legal procedure correctly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is land.gov.bd free to use?

Basic khatian and porcha viewing is free. Certified digital copies via eporcha.gov.bd cost BDT 100–300. Mutation applications have a government fee of BDT 100–500 depending on the district and land value.

What is the difference between land.gov.bd and eporcha.gov.bd?

land.gov.bd is the main portal for searching records, tracking mutation status, and paying khajna for free. eporcha.gov.bd is a paid sub-portal specifically for purchasing digitally signed certified khatian copies that carry official validity for most formal purposes.

Can I use the online khatian printout in court?

No. Bangladesh courts require certified physical copies with official stamps from the AC Land office or a digitally signed certified porcha from eporcha.gov.bd (acceptance varies by court). Confirm with your lawyer before submitting any land documents as evidence.

My mouza is not found on land.gov.bd. What should I do?

Not all mouzas are fully digitised yet. If your mouza doesn't appear, you must visit the AC Land office (ভূমি অফিস) of the relevant upazila in person and request records from the physical record room.

How long does online mutation take after I apply?

Online mutation applications are typically processed within 30–90 days depending on the upazila. The timeline includes field inspection, notice to adjoining landholders, and a hearing if anyone objects. If the AC Land office is busy, it can take longer — a land lawyer can help follow up to keep the process on track.

Is there a mobile app for land.gov.bd?

The Ministry of Land has released a mobile app called 'ভূমি সেবা' (Bhumi Seba) available on Google Play and Apple App Store. It provides the same core khatian search and khajna payment functions. However, the web portal is more complete for full mutation applications.

Land Law Bangladesh: Your Complete Guide to Property Rights & Disputes

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-04-16 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

⚡ Quick Answer: In Bangladesh, land ownership is proven through three things: a registered deed + khatian (land record) + mutation (namjari). Without all three, your ownership is incomplete in the eyes of government and courts. — Land disputes are the most common civil litigation in Bangladesh. Whether you are buying property, inheriting land, or caught in a title dispute, this complete guide will protect your investment and your rights.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

How Land Ownership Works in Bangladesh

Bangladesh operates a khatian-based land records system inherited from the colonial era. Ownership is established through a chain of three elements:

  1. Registered deed — executed at the Sub-Registrar's office under the Registration Act 1908
  2. Khatian — the government land revenue record showing your name as owner
  3. Mutation (namjari) — the process of updating the khatian in your name after acquisition

A registered deed without mutation is legally valid but practically incomplete. A khatian without a registered deed is not sufficient to prove ownership in most cases. You need both, and you need them to be consistent with each other. Consult a land lawyer in Dhaka to verify your full chain of title.

The Three Surveys You Must Know (CS, SA, RS)

Bangladesh land records come from three government survey periods. Understanding them is essential for any land transaction:

  • CS (Cadastral Survey, 1888–1940): The original colonial-era record. CS khatian is the historical root of title — courts often go back to CS to trace the ownership chain.
  • SA (State Acquisition Survey, 1956–1963): Created after land reform (Zamindari abolition). Most land was transferred to occupants at this stage.
  • RS (Revisional Survey, 1960s–ongoing): The most current record. RS khatian is given the most weight in modern courts and government offices.

The RS khatian is your most important document, but all three may be needed to trace a complete chain of title — especially in inheritance or title dispute cases.

Buying Land – The Essential Checklist

Before purchasing any land in Bangladesh, verify these items independently:

  • CS/SA/RS khatian consistency: The seller's name must appear in the latest khatian. Verify the chain from CS → SA → RS.
  • No mortgage or encumbrance: Check the Sub-Registrar's office for any registered mortgage, lien, or lis pendens (pending court case) on the property.
  • No mutation dispute: Verify no rival claims or objections have been filed at the Land Office (AC Land).
  • Identity verification: Confirm the seller's NID matches the name in the khatian and deed.
  • Physical inspection: Visit and measure the land. Confirm boundaries match the porcha (land plot information sheet).
  • Revenue dues (khajna): Confirm no outstanding land revenue is owed to the government.

For high-value purchases, always hire a property lawyer in Dhaka to conduct a title search before paying any advance.

Land Registration – Process and Fees

All land transactions must be registered at the office of the Sub-Registrar in the area where the land is located. Unregistered transfers of immovable property are void against third parties.

Registration process:

  1. Execute the deed of transfer (sale deed, gift deed, etc.) drafted by a lawyer
  2. Both buyer and seller appear at the Sub-Registrar's office
  3. Pay stamp duty and registration fees (calculated on deed value)
  4. Submit all supporting documents (khatian copy, NID, porcha, khajna receipt)
  5. The Sub-Registrar registers the deed and returns a certified copy

Fees (approximate):

  • Stamp duty: approximately 3% of the declared deed value
  • Registration fee: approximately 1–2% of the declared deed value
  • Local government tax (LGT): approximately 2% of the declared deed value
  • Total: approximately 6–8% of the declared value

After registration, proceed immediately to land mutation (namjari) at the Union Land Office.

Mutation (Namjari) – Updating the Record

Mutation is the process of updating the government khatian in your name after acquiring land. Without mutation:

  • Your name does not appear in government records as owner
  • You cannot pay land revenue (khajna) in your own name
  • Banks will not accept the land as mortgage collateral
  • Courts give less weight to your ownership claim

The mutation application is filed at the Union Land Office / AC Land office with your registered deed, khatian copy, NID, and khajna receipt. The process takes 2–6 months and costs ৳500–৳2,000 in government fees. For the complete step-by-step guide, see our article on land mutation (namjari) in Bangladesh.

Inheritance and Land

When a landowner dies, the land passes to their heirs according to:

  • Muslim personal law (Hanafi school): For most Bangladeshis — specific shares for sons, daughters, spouse, parents
  • Hindu succession law: For Hindu Bangladeshis
  • Succession Act 1925: For Christians and certain others

After the owner's death, heirs must complete an inheritance mutation — they apply jointly at the Land Office, submitting the deceased owner's death certificate and a court-issued legal heirship certificate. Without inheritance mutation, heirs cannot independently deal with the land (sell, mortgage, or use as collateral).

Disputes between co-heirs over inheritance shares are resolved through a partition suit in Civil Court. For detailed guidance, see our guide on inheritance law in Bangladesh.

Common Land Disputes and How to Win

1. Title Dispute (Swattwo Mamla)
When two parties both claim ownership. File a title declaration suit in Civil Court. The party with the stronger chain of title — better khatian record + registered deed + possession — typically wins. Engage a land dispute lawyer immediately upon notification of a rival claim.

2. Fraudulent Mutation
If someone has fraudulently mutated your land in their name: (a) file for cancellation of mutation with the AC Land office, (b) file a criminal complaint for forgery, and (c) consider a writ petition to the High Court for an emergency stay order.

3. Partition Dispute
When co-owners (usually co-heirs) cannot agree on division of jointly owned land, file a partition suit in Civil Court. The court may order physical partition or sale and equal division of proceeds.

4. Illegal Dispossession (Beadakhali)
If someone is physically occupying your land without authority: (a) file a GD with police, (b) apply for an injunction/stay order from Civil Court, and (c) file a title/possession suit. Time is critical — courts favour the party in actual possession.

Your Strongest Defence: Physical Possession

In Bangladesh courts, actual physical possession of land combined with a registered deed is the strongest possible combination. Courts have consistently held that a person in peaceful possession cannot be arbitrarily dispossessed even by a person claiming better title.

If someone is attempting to dispossess you:

  1. Call police immediately and file a GD (General Diary) or FIR if violence is used
  2. Apply for an injunction (stay order) from Civil Court — this preserves the status quo
  3. File a title and possession suit to establish your legal ownership

Do not abandon possession voluntarily even during litigation. Physical possession combined with a registered deed is extremely difficult for any opponent to overcome in Bangladesh courts.

When to Call a Land Lawyer

You should contact a property lawyer in Dhaka immediately if:

  • You are buying land above ৳10 lakh — a title search is essential
  • You notice someone else's name in the khatian for your land
  • A rival claimant has appeared or filed a case
  • Your mutation application has been refused or is stalled
  • You are a co-heir and other heirs are not cooperating on partition
  • You have received a court notice or summons related to land
  • You want to mortgage land but the bank is raising title questions

Land law in Bangladesh is complex and highly fact-specific. An early consultation saves far more than it costs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a registered deed enough to prove land ownership in Bangladesh?

A registered deed is strong proof but must be corroborated by the khatian (land record) and supported by mutation. All three together constitute the strongest case of ownership. A deed alone, without khatian support, can be challenged.

Can oral transfer of land be valid in Bangladesh?

No. Under the Transfer of Property Act, transfers of immovable property must be in writing and registered at the Sub-Registrar's office. Oral transfers are void against third parties.

What is 'baina' (advance/booking) and is it legally binding?

A baina (advance payment for land purchase) creates a contractual right but does not transfer ownership. A registered sale deed is still required. If the seller backs out unjustifiably, you can sue for specific performance of the deed.

How do I stop a fraudulent sale of my land?

File for an injunction in Civil Court immediately. Also file a complaint with the Sub-Registrar's office to flag the property and consider a writ petition in the High Court for an emergency stay order preventing registration of any fraudulent deed.

What is a 'porcha' and do I need it?

A porcha is an information sheet about your land plot showing the dag (plot) number, area, RS khatian reference, and owner details. It is needed for mutation and registration. Obtain it from the AC Land office or the land records portal (land.gov.bd).

Can NRBs (non-resident Bangladeshis) buy land in Bangladesh?

Yes. NRBs can purchase land in Bangladesh. They typically use a Power of Attorney (POA) authorising a trusted local representative to complete the registration. The POA must itself be registered to be legally effective.

What is the difference between a title suit and a partition suit?

A title suit (declaration suit) asks the court to declare who owns the land. A partition suit asks the court to divide jointly owned land among co-owners. Both are filed in Civil Court, but they address different problems.

How long does a land dispute case take in Bangladesh?

Land cases at the district Civil Court level typically take 3–7 years, depending on the complexity and backlog. Appeals can extend this further. Interim orders (injunctions, stay orders) can be obtained much faster — often within weeks.

Why Mutation Matters

Registration transfers title on paper, but the revenue office keeps a separate record to collect land development tax and to certify possession. Banks, developers and buyers all check the mutation record. If you only have a deed, a later buyer may doubt your possession. See how to check land records online to review your current status.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Documents Required

  • Registered sale deed (or gift deed / heirship certificate with death certificate for inheritance).
  • Previous mutation Khatian and CS/SA/RS/BS Khatian.
  • Land development tax (Dakhila) receipt of the seller.
  • Applicant's NID or passport copy and photograph; for NRBs a passport copy is often accepted.
  • Mouza and plot details: dag number, area, khatian number.
  • Power of Attorney if an attorney applies (see our Power of Attorney guide).

Step-by-Step Process

  1. Open the official e-Mutation portal and create an account with a phone number.
  2. Select the division, district, upazila, mouza and enter dag and khatian details.
  3. Fill in applicant details and upload scanned documents.
  4. Pay the application fee online through the supported payment method. The official fee is modest; confirm the current amount on the portal.
  5. The Assistant Land Office inspects the documents, may visit the land, and issues a notice to interested persons.
  6. A hearing is held; if there is no objection, the Assistant Commissioner (Land) approves the mutation.
  7. You pay land development tax and receive the new mutation Khatian and Dakhila.

The rules aim for a decision within a defined period, but delays happen. Track the case number regularly through your attorney.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Can I Do It Without Travelling?

Mostly yes. The application is online and your representative can attend hearings with a valid Power of Attorney. If an objection is raised, the Assistant Commissioner may want to see you or take evidence. You can also ask to attend via video link or send an affidavit, but this is at the officer's discretion.

Common Problems and Solutions

  • Seller's name does not match the record: first correct the earlier mutation.
  • Inheritance mutation with missing heirs: all heirs must be named; get a correct heirship certificate.
  • Objection by a neighbour or relative: the officer will hear both sides; bring deeds and possession evidence.
  • Area mismatch: request survey or correct in the same application.
  • Delay: follow up through your attorney and, if needed, petition the Deputy Commissioner.

Appeal if Mutation Is Rejected

If the Assistant Commissioner (Land) rejects the application, you can appeal to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) within the time specified in the rules (usually about 30 days), and further to the Divisional Commissioner. For disputes about title, the Civil Court remains available. An advocate can prepare the appeal quickly.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is mutation compulsory after buying land?

It is not required to make the sale valid, but it is essential for proving possession, paying tax and selling later.

How much does mutation cost?

There is a modest official fee payable online. Confirm the current amount on the portal; avoid paying unofficial charges.

Can an NRB apply for mutation online?

Yes. You or your attorney can apply through the e-Mutation system with scanned documents and passport details.

How long does mutation take?

The rules set a target period of weeks, but real cases may take longer if there is an objection or missing documents.

What if mutation is cancelled?

You can appeal to higher revenue officers or file a civil suit for declaration of title.

Land Mutation Rejection & Namjari Appeal in Bangladesh: AC (Land) Miss Case & ADC Revenue Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-02 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In Bangladesh's land administration system, purchasing real estate or inheriting ancestral property remains legally incomplete until the owner completes **Namjari (Mutation)**—the official process of recording the new owner's name in the government Record of Rights (Khatian) and opening a separate holding (Jamabandi) to pay land development tax (Khajna). However, hundreds of thousands of applicants, particularly Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) and urban property buyers in Dhaka, face unexpected administrative blockades when their online **e-Namjari** applications are summarily rejected by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) [AC Land]. Rejections often cite vague grounds such as 'chain deed mismatch', 'unverified CS/SA/RS khatian', or spurious third-party objection letters. Under the **State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (SAT Act)** and the **Land Management Manual**, an applicant is not helpless. This exhaustive guide explains how to file a **Review / Miss Case** before the AC (Land), institute a statutory **Mutation Appeal** before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) under Section 150 of the SAT Act, and escalate to the Divisional Commissioner, Land Appeal Board, or the High Court Division.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Official Government Portalsland.gov.bd, mutation.land.gov.bd, dlrms.land.gov.bd & eporcha.gov.bd
Total Official E-Namjari FeeBDT 1,170 (Court fee 20 + Notice 50 + Record fee 1,000 + Khatian 100)
Standard Processing Time28 Working Days (9–12 working days for NRB / expatriate applicants)
National Land Helpline16122 (24/7 Ministry of Land Call Center)
📋 In This Article
  1. 1. Common Grounds for e-Namjari Rejection by AC (Land)
  2. 2. The Statutory Hierarchy: Section 147 to 150 of the SAT Act 1950
  3. 3. Filing a Review / Miss Case Before the Assistant Commissioner (Land)
  4. 4. Step-by-Step Appeal Before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue)
  5. 5. Escalation: Revision Before Divisional Commissioner & Land Appeal Board
  6. 6. Comparative Matrix: Revenue Forums, Deadlines, Powers & Reliefs
  7. 7. High Court Division Remedy: Article 102 Writ of Mandamus
  8. 8. Curing Chain of Title Defects: Bia Deeds, Porcha & Warishan Certificates
  9. 9. How NRBs Can Pursue Mutation Appeals Remotely via Power of Attorney
  10. 10. Real-Life Case Study: Overturning a Fraudulent Mutation Rejection in Savar
  11. 11. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1. Common Grounds for e-Namjari Rejection by AC (Land)

When submitting an online e-Namjari application through the Ministry of Land portal (mutation.land.gov.bd), rejections typically arise from four recurring administrative triggers:

  • Chain Deed (Bia Dalil) Incompleteness: Failure to submit certified copies establishing an unbroken 25-year title chain connecting the original survey record owner (CS/SA/RS) to the present seller.
  • Fictitious Third-Party Objections: Corrupt local land grabbers or estranged distant relatives file frivolous written objection petitions alleging joint tenancy or forged signatures, causing timid AC (Land) officers to reject applications with the stock phrase 'Dispute of title; refer to Civil Court'.
  • Khatian Area Discrepancy: The physical land measured on the ground or in the registered deed slightly exceeds the share recorded in the latest BS/City survey khatian.
  • Vested / Khas Property Allegations: Erroneous classification by the Union Land Assistant Officer (Tahsilder) asserting that the property falls under Government Khas land or Vested (Enemy) Property lists.

2. The Statutory Hierarchy: Section 147 to 150 of the SAT Act 1950

The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (SAT Act) provides an autonomous, self-contained judicial hierarchy for challenging revenue orders without immediately entering the lengthy civil court pipeline:

  • Section 147 (Appeals): Confers the statutory right of appeal against any original order passed by a Revenue Officer under Chapter XVII of the Act.
  • Section 148 (Limitation Period): Mandates that an appeal to the Collector or Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) must be filed within thirty (30) days from the date of the order appealed against.
  • Section 149 (Revision): Grants revisional jurisdiction to the Divisional Commissioner to call for the records and revise orders passed by the ADC (Revenue).
  • Section 150 (Review): Permits the AC (Land) or Revenue Officer to review their own decision within 30 days if new, vital documentary evidence is brought to light that could not be produced earlier.

3. Filing a Review / Miss Case Before the Assistant Commissioner (Land)

Where an application was rejected purely due to a procedural irregularity—such as non-appearance at a hearing due to illness, server glitch, or a missing land development tax receipt—filing a Mutation Review Miss Case directly before the same AC (Land) is the quickest remedy:

  • Application Grounds: The petition must specify that the rejection occurred without examining essential title records or that new certified documents (e.g., rectified deed, updated Dakhila, or civil court decree) are now available.
  • Notice to Opposite Parties: The AC (Land) registers the matter as a Mutation Miss Case, issues notices to all interested co-sharers, calls for a fresh field report from the Tahsilder, and conducts a formal hearing.
  • Timeline: An uncontested review miss case is usually resolved within 30 to 60 days.

4. Step-by-Step Appeal Before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue)

If the AC (Land) issued a biased, erroneous, or contentious rejection order, the applicant should immediately file a formal Revenue Appeal before the Court of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue):

  1. Procure Certified Copy of the Rejection Order: Obtain certified copies of the AC (Land)'s final rejection order and the Tahsilder's field inquiry report from the Land Office record room.
  2. Drafting the Memorandum of Appeal: Prepared by an enrolled advocate setting forth precise legal grounds demonstrating why the AC (Land)'s order is arbitrary, legally unsustainable, and contrary to the registered deeds.
  3. Court Fee Stamping: Affix non-judicial stamps as prescribed under the Court-Fees Act 1870.
  4. Admit Hearing & Record Call: The ADC (Revenue) hears the advocate, admits the appeal (registered as a Mutation Appeal Case), calls for the lower court records (LCR) from the AC (Land) office, and issues stay orders preventing third-party mutations over the plot.
  5. Final Hearing & Remand/Direct Order: The ADC (Revenue) delivers a judgment either setting aside the rejection and directly ordering the AC (Land) to open a mutation khatian, or remanding the case for fresh field verification.

5. Escalation: Revision Before Divisional Commissioner & Land Appeal Board

If an aggrieved party suffers an adverse order from the ADC (Revenue), the statutory escalation ladder continues:

  • Revision Before the Divisional Commissioner: Under Section 149 of the SAT Act, an application for Revision must be instituted before the Divisional Commissioner (e.g., Dhaka Divisional Commissioner Office in Segunbagicha) within sixty (60) days. The Commissioner examines whether lower revenue courts committed jurisdictional errors or misapplied the law.
  • Final Revision Before the Land Appeal Board (Bhumi Appeal Board): Established under the Land Appeal Board Act 1989, the Board sits in Dhaka as the apex administrative tribunal for revenue disputes. Under Section 149(3), decisions of the Land Appeal Board are conclusive within the revenue administrative hierarchy.

6. Comparative Matrix: Revenue Forums, Deadlines, Powers & Reliefs

Understanding the statutory deadlines and scope of each revenue forum is vital to avoid fatal limitation dismissals:

Revenue ForumStatutory BasisFiling DeadlinePrimary PowersSubsequent Recourse
Review Miss CaseSAT Act 1950, Sec 15030 Days from orderAC (Land) reconsiders clerical or procedural rejectionsAppeal to ADC (Revenue)
Mutation AppealSAT Act 1950, Sec 147-14830 Days from orderADC (Revenue) sets aside AC Land order and orders NamjariRevision to Divisional Commissioner
Revenue RevisionSAT Act 1950, Sec 14960 Days from orderDivisional Commissioner rectifies legal and jurisdictional flawsRevision to Land Appeal Board
Land Appeal BoardLand Appeal Board Act 198990 Days from orderApex revenue ruling; final administrative authorityHigh Court Division (Writ Petition)

7. High Court Division Remedy: Article 102 Writ of Mandamus

When land revenue officials act corruptly, sit on appeal files for years, or arbitrarily refuse mutation despite a citizen holding unassailable registered title deeds and final civil court decrees, the administrative remedy becomes exhausted or ineffective.

Under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, the owner can file a Writ Petition (Writ of Mandamus) before the High Court Division. The Supreme Court routinely issues binding directions commanding the AC (Land) and ADC (Revenue) to open the mutation khatian and accept land development tax within 30 to 60 days, threatening delinquent officers with contempt of court proceedings if they disobey.

8. Curing Chain of Title Defects: Bia Deeds, Porcha & Warishan Certificates

To win a mutation appeal, an applicant must systematically cure documentary gaps:

  • Reconstructing Missing Bia Deeds: If intermediate title deeds from 1980 or 1995 are missing, obtain certified copies directly from the relevant District Sub-Registry Office Volume Books.
  • Certified Khatians: Procure official certified copies (Porcha) of CS, SA, RS, and City Survey records from the Deputy Commissioner Record Room (DC DC Record Room), complete with official watermark stamps.
  • Warishan (Succession) Certificates: In cases of inherited land, submit certified Warishan Sanad issued by the City Corporation Councillor or Union Parishad Chairman, accompanied by a sworn Family Genealogical Affidavit.
  • Tahsilder Field Report Vetting: Scrutinize the Union Tahsilder's written report to ensure no fraudulent assertions regarding possession or government reservation were falsely inserted.

9. How NRBs Can Pursue Mutation Appeals Remotely via Power of Attorney

Expatriates living in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, or Australia face constant harassment because corrupt land grabbers exploit their absence to cancel ancestral mutations. An NRB is not required to travel to Dhaka to conduct revenue appeals.

Under the Power of Attorney Act 2012, an overseas owner can execute a Special Power of Attorney before the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, appointing an enrolled Supreme Court advocate or trusted family member in Bangladesh. Once validated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) in Segunbagicha and the DC Treasury Office in Dhaka, the attorney can file review miss cases, depose before the ADC (Revenue), and secure the final Namjari khatian.

10. Real-Life Case Study: Overturning a Fraudulent Mutation Rejection in Savar

An NRB software architect residing in Sydney, Australia, purchased a 10-decimal residential plot in Savar, Dhaka, through a registered sale deed in 2021. In late 2023, his online e-Namjari application was abruptly rejected by the Savar AC (Land) citing 'Third-party objection alleging SA record mismatch'. In reality, a local land broker had submitted a forged handwritten deed from 1974 to extort money.

The Sydney-based owner retained our law chamber. Our legal team executed the following strategic workflow:

  1. Drafted a Special Power of Attorney in Sydney, authenticated by the Bangladesh High Commission, Canberra, and stamped by MOFA and DC Dhaka.
  2. Secured certified copies of the 1974 Volume Book from the Sub-Registry office, proving through forensic evidence that the broker's deed number corresponded to a completely different mouza and was an outright forgery.
  3. Filed a formal Mutation Appeal Case before the Court of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka, within the statutory 30-day window under Section 148 SAT Act.
  4. The ADC (Revenue) called for the lower court records, examined our certified chain deeds, and issued an interim order restraining any third-party mutation over the plot.
  5. At final hearing, the ADC (Revenue) set aside the AC (Land)'s rejection order, reprimanded the Union Tahsilder, and issued a peremptory direction commanding the Savar AC (Land) to issue the mutation khatian and Dakhila in the Sydney client's name within 15 working days.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the statutory deadline to appeal a rejected mutation in Bangladesh?

Under Section 148 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, a Mutation Appeal must be filed before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) within thirty (30) days from the date of the AC (Land) rejection order.

Can I file a Miss Case before the same AC (Land) who rejected my application?

Yes. Under Section 150 of the SAT Act, an AC (Land) has the legal authority to review their own decision within 30 days if new documentary evidence or procedural omissions are properly presented.

What happens if both the AC (Land) and ADC (Revenue) reject my mutation?

You can file an application for Revision before the Divisional Commissioner within 60 days under Section 149 SAT Act, followed by a final administrative revision before the Land Appeal Board in Dhaka.

Can the High Court Division order land officials to approve a mutation?

Yes. Under Article 102 of the Constitution, the High Court Division can issue a Writ of Mandamus commanding land revenue officials to approve mutation and accept land taxes when registered title deeds are indisputable.

Why do land offices reject mutation saying 'chain deed mismatch'?

This happens when the applicant fails to provide certified copies of intermediate sale deeds (Bia deeds) showing how the title transferred from the original survey recorded owner down to the present seller over the preceding 25 years.

Can an NRB living abroad challenge a mutation rejection without coming to Bangladesh?

Yes. An expatriate can execute a Special Power of Attorney authenticated by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, empowering a Supreme Court advocate or representative in Bangladesh to manage the entire appeal process.

Is land ownership secure if I have a registered deed but no mutation khatian?

No. Without a mutation khatian, you cannot pay annual government land development tax (Khajna), obtain a Dakhila, secure a bank loan against the land, or sell the property in the future. Mutation is essential to protect possession.

What is the role of the Land Appeal Board (Bhumi Appeal Board)?

The Land Appeal Board in Dhaka is the highest administrative tribunal for land revenue disputes in Bangladesh. It hears final revisions against orders passed by Divisional Commissioners.

Land Registration Fee Calculator Bangladesh 2026 | Cost Chart

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-09-21 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Buying land or property in Bangladesh involves several statutory fees, taxes, and registry expenses. Under the latest Finance Act and Land Registration Rules 2026, the total registration cost typically ranges between 10% to 14% of the deed value, depending on whether the property is located within a City Corporation, Municipality, or Union Parishad. Understanding these exact rates prevents overpayment and protects buyers from fraudulent sub-registry middleman charges. For expert land verification and deed drafting, consult Supreme Court Advocate <a href="/advocate-md-shah-alam" style="color:var(--accent);font-weight:600;">Advocate Md. Shah Alam</a>.

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Registration Fee & Stamp Duty1% Registration Fee + 1.5% Stamp Duty on deed value
Local Government Tax & VAT2%–3% Local Govt Tax + 1.5%–4.5% VAT (varies by City/Pourosova/Union)
Source Tax (Gain Tax / TDS)1% to 8% depending on mouza classification under Income Tax Act 2023

📋 In This Article

  4. Capital Gain Tax & Advance Income Tax (AIT) Rules

Overview of Land Registration Cost Components in 2026

When registering a land purchase deed (Saf Kabala / সাফ কবালা দলিল) in Bangladesh, the registration cost is not a single lump sum. It comprises multiple Government duties, local municipality taxes, and statutory processing fees payable under the Registration Act 1908 and the Stamp Act 1899.

The primary components include:

  • Stamp Duty (স্ট্যাম্প ডিউটি): Revenue stamp fee collected by the National Board of Revenue (NBR).
  • Registration Fee (রেজিস্ট্রেশন ফি): Statutory fee for registering the document in the Sub-Registry Office.
  • Local Government Tax (স্থানীয় সরকার কর): Tax payable to City Corporations, Municipalities (Paurashava), or Zilla Parishads.
  • Capital Gain Tax / Advance Income Tax (উৎস কর / এআইটি): Tax levied on the seller's property transaction under Income Tax Act.
  • E-Namjari Fee (ই-নামজারি ফি): Online mutation fee payable to the AC Land Office.

Consulting an experienced Land Lawyer in Dhaka before deed registration ensures all tax chalans and pay orders are accurately calculated.

Detailed Percentage Breakdown of Registry Fees

Below is the standard statutory fee table for land deed registration in Bangladesh for 2026:

Fee Head Percentage / Rate Payable To
Stamp Duty 1.5% to 3.0% of Deed Value NBR (Treasury Chalan)
Registration Fee 1.0% of Deed Value Sub-Registry Office
Local Govt Tax 2.0% (City Corp) / 3.0% (Paurashava) Local Government Body
Gain Tax (AIT) 2.0% to 5.0% (Location Dependent) Tax Zone / NBR
E-Namjari Fee BDT 1,170 (Fixed) Land Ministry Portal

Location-Based Tax Rate Variations (Dhaka vs Outside)

The total registration cost varies significantly depending on the geographical location of the property:

  • Dhaka, Chittagong, Gazipur City Corporation Areas: Highest AIT rates apply (up to 5% or fixed rate per Katha depending on commercial/residential zone like Gulshan, Banani, Motijheel, Uttara).
  • Other City Corporations & District Municipalities: Moderate AIT rates (3% to 4%) and 2% Local Govt Tax.
  • Rural / Union Parishad Areas: Lowest AIT rate (2%) and 1% Zilla Parishad Tax. Total registration cost is lowest in rural areas (approx 8.5% to 10%).

Capital Gain Tax & Advance Income Tax (AIT) Rules

Under the Income Tax Act 2023 and updated Finance Rules, Gain Tax (Source Tax under Section 53H) is legally the seller's responsibility, though in commercial practice buyers often negotiate this in the total contract value.

Key Gain Tax rules include:

  • Property sold within 5 years of acquisition may attract higher tax rates.
  • Commercial land in prime Dhaka hubs (Motijheel, Kawran Bazar, Dhanmondi, Uttara) has fixed per-katha tax rates set by the National Board of Revenue.
  • Exemption applies to specific inherited properties or gift transfers between primary family members under Heba Bil Ewaz.

E-Namjari (Mutation) Fees & Online Process

After registering the deed, property ownership is incomplete without E-Namjari (ই-নামজারি) at the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Office. The Government of Bangladesh has automated this via land.gov.bd.

Statutory Breakdown of the BDT 1,170 Mutation Fee:

  • Application Fee: BDT 70
  • Notice Issue Fee: BDT 50
  • Khatian Fee: BDT 100
  • Mutation Fee (DCR Fee): BDT 950
  • Total Official Charge: BDT 1,170

Never pay excessive illegal charges for online mutation. If an AC Land office rejects or delays your application, consult a qualified lawyer to file a Miss Case or Appeal.

Sub-Registry Office Additional Official Fees & Cartridge Paper

Besides percentage fees, minor fixed statutory charges apply during deed presentation:

  • E-Fee: BDT 100 per deed.
  • N-Fee (Search Fee): BDT 20 to BDT 100 per volume book search.
  • Cartridge Paper & Writing Charge: BDT 300 to BDT 500.
  • Deed Writer (দলিল লেখক) License Commission: Governed by official scale or mutual agreement.

How to Calculate Total Cost: Practical Examples

Example Scenario: Purchasing a Flat / Land in Uttara, Dhaka valued at BDT 1,00,00,000 (1 Crore):

  • Stamp Duty (1.5%): BDT 1,50,000
  • Registration Fee (1%): BDT 1,00,000
  • Local Govt Tax (2%): BDT 2,00,000
  • Gain Tax / AIT (approx 4%): BDT 4,00,000
  • Misc Stamps & Charges: BDT 5,000
  • Estimated Total Registration Cost: BDT 8,55,000 (approx 8.55%)

Crucial Legal Checklist Before Registering Land in Dhaka

Before depositing bank pay orders for land registration, ensure your advocate conducts complete due diligence:

  1. Verify CS, SA, RS, and BS Khatians at the District Record Room.
  2. Check if the land is listed as Khas (Government), Vested Property, or Wetlands.
  3. Verify original deed title flow (Via Deed / বায়া দলিল) for 25 years.
  4. Verify seller's online E-Namjari and latest Land Development Tax (Khajna) receipt.
  5. Obtain non-encumbrance certificate (NEC) from the Sub-Registry office.

Advocate Md. Shah Alam — Supreme Court Advocate with 10+ years experience (enrolled since 2015) — provides complete land title verification, deed drafting, and sub-registry representation in Uttara and across Dhaka.

⚖️ Need Expert Land Legal Verification? Contact Supreme Court Advocate Advocate Md. Shah Alam for title vetting, deed registration, and mutation support. Visit our Land Legal Services Page or Contact Us Directly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is legally responsible for paying land registration fees in Bangladesh?

By law and custom, the buyer pays the Stamp Duty, Registration Fee, and Local Government Tax. The seller is responsible for the Capital Gain Tax (AIT), though contract terms may specify otherwise.

What happens if I register land at a lower deed value than actual market value?

Under-invoicing to evade tax is illegal. Sub-registrars verify official government minimum land rates (Mouza Rate). Registration below the Mouza Rate will be rejected or impounded for penalty.

How long after deed registration must I complete E-Namjari?

E-Namjari should be filed immediately after receiving the deed copy. Delaying mutation leaves your property vulnerable to illegal sale or double registration by fraudsters.

Can non-resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) register land via Power of Attorney?

Yes. NRBs can execute an Irrevocable Power of Attorney authenticated by the Bangladesh Embassy/High Commission abroad, attested by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) in Dhaka.

Land Survey, Dag & Mouza Bangladesh – How Land is Measured & Mapped

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-06 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Understanding your land's dag number, mouza, and the survey record it belongs to is the foundation of property ownership in Bangladesh. With approximately 70,000 mouzas across the country and successive government surveys creating multiple sets of records, navigating the system can be bewildering for landowners. This guide demystifies the entire land mapping and measurement system — from reading a mouza map to finding your property online and resolving discrepancies between CS and RS records.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

What is a Mouza — The Basic Land Administrative Unit

A mouza (মৌজা) is the smallest revenue and administrative unit of land in Bangladesh. The entire territory of Bangladesh is divided into approximately 70,000 mouzas, each with a unique name and a Jurisdiction List (JL) number assigned by the government. Every piece of land in Bangladesh — whether urban or rural, agricultural or built-up — falls within a specific mouza.

The mouza system was established during the British colonial period as part of the land revenue administration. Each mouza has a defined boundary (mouza boundary marker, or আইল) that separates it from adjacent mouzas. A mouza can be as small as a few acres (in densely built-up urban areas) or as large as thousands of acres (in remote rural areas).

Key facts about mouzas in Bangladesh:

  • Each mouza has a unique combination of: District name → Upazila name → Union name → Mouza name → JL Number
  • The JL number is used in all official land records, court documents, and deeds to identify the mouza
  • Within each mouza, each individual plot of land is identified by its unique dag number
  • The mouza is the unit at which government surveys are conducted and mouza maps (মৌজা ম্যাপ) are prepared
  • Mouza names are in Bengali and reflect the historical, geographical, or community characteristics of the area

When dealing with any land-related document — a deed, a court case, a mutation application — you will always need to specify the mouza name and JL number in addition to the dag number and khatian number.

What is a Dag Number — Identifying Your Plot

A dag number (দাগ নম্বর) is the unique identification number assigned to a specific plot of land within a particular mouza. Think of the mouza as a village or neighbourhood, and the dag number as the house/plot address within that neighbourhood. Every distinct parcel of land within a mouza has its own dag number.

Key characteristics of dag numbers:

  • Mouza-specific: Dag numbers are unique only within a mouza. The same dag number can exist in two different mouzas — so a dag number is always stated together with the mouza name and JL number.
  • Survey-specific: Different surveys (CS, SA, RS, BS) can assign different dag numbers to the same physical plot of land. This is a common source of confusion and disputes. A property may have a CS dag number and a different RS dag number referring to the same piece of land.
  • Sub-divided dags: When a plot is partitioned, the original dag is subdivided into new dags. For example, dag 123 might be divided into dags 123/1, 123/2, and 123/3 after partition.
  • Amalgamated dags: When adjacent plots are merged, they receive a new combined dag number.
  • Area of dag: Each dag has a specific land area recorded in the survey records (in decimals, kathas, or acres depending on the region and survey era).

When purchasing land, always verify that the dag number in the sale deed matches the dag number in the seller's khatian (Record of Rights), and that both match the mouza map. Discrepancies between these records are a common cause of post-purchase disputes.

The Khatian (Record of Rights) — Linking Owner to Land

A khatian (খতিয়ান), also called the Record of Rights (RoR), is the official government document that records the ownership (or occupancy rights) of land. It is the legal link between the owner's name and the specific dag numbers they own.

A khatian contains:

  • The khatian number (a unique number within the mouza for that survey)
  • The owner's name, father's/husband's name, and address
  • The dag numbers owned by that owner within the mouza
  • The area of each dag owned
  • The type of tenancy or ownership (ownership, tenancy, government khas, etc.)
  • Classification of land use (agricultural, homestead, pond, fallow, etc.)
  • Land development tax (LDT) assessment

The relationship between mouza, dag, and khatian can be visualised as follows:

MOUZA (e.g., Mouza: Uttara, JL No. 42, Dhaka District)
├── DAG 101 — Area: 10 decimals — Owner: Khatian 55
├── DAG 102 — Area: 15 decimals — Owner: Khatian 55
├── DAG 103 — Area: 8 decimals — Owner: Khatian 78
└── DAG 104 — Area: 20 decimals — Owner: Khatian 55

KHATIAN 55 (Owner: Md. Karim, S/O Md. Rahim)
├── Dag 101 — 10 decimals
├── Dag 102 — 15 decimals
└── Dag 104 — 20 decimals
Total: 45 decimals

This means if you know someone's khatian number, you can find all their dags in that mouza. Conversely, if you know a dag number, you can find the khatian and thus the owner's name. Both dag and khatian numbers are mouza-specific and survey-specific.

Survey History in Bangladesh — CS, SA, RS, and BS

Bangladesh has had multiple government land surveys since the 19th century, each producing its own set of maps and khatians. Understanding which survey applies to your land is critical for resolving discrepancies.

Survey NameFull Name / PeriodCoverageLegal Status
CSCadastral Survey (1888-1940)Most of undivided Bengal; foundation surveyOldest; used as reference baseline
SAState Acquisition Survey (1956-1962)Conducted after land reform; East Pakistan eraImportant for ownership after abolition of zamindari system
RSRevisional Survey (1966-present)Ongoing; updating CS/SA recordsMost current survey where completed; RS khatian is generally the operative record
BSBangladesh Survey / City Survey (1990s-present)Urban areas, particularly Dhaka, ChattogramMost current for covered urban areas; replaces RS where completed

Which survey applies to your land? The most recently completed survey for your area is the operative one. In much of Dhaka city, the BS (Bangladesh Survey) is operative. In rural areas, the RS khatian is usually the current operative record. However, where RS or BS surveys have not yet been completed, the CS or SA khatian remains the operative record. Your Sub-Registrar's office and local AC (Land) office can confirm which survey is current for your specific mouza.

How to Read a Mouza Map — Sheet Number, Scale and Plot Boundaries

A mouza map (মৌজা ম্যাপ) is the official cadastral map that shows all the plots (dags) within a particular mouza, their boundaries, shape, and relative positions. Reading a mouza map correctly is essential for verifying land boundaries and identifying your plot.

Key Elements of a Mouza Map

  • Map Sheet Number: Each mouza map has a unique sheet number. A large mouza may span multiple sheets. The sheet number is printed in the top corner of the map.
  • Scale: Older CS maps are typically at scales of 1:3,960 (16 inches to a mile) or 1:7,920 (8 inches to a mile). RS maps are usually at 1:3,960. BS (urban) maps may be at larger scales (1:1,000 or 1:2,000) for greater detail. Knowing the scale allows you to calculate approximate areas from the map.
  • Plot Numbers (Dag Numbers): Each plot is shown as a polygon with its dag number written inside. The size of the polygon corresponds to the area of the plot at the given scale.
  • Boundary Features: Roads (রাস্তা), canals (খাল), rivers (নদী), embankments (বাঁধ), and railways are shown as natural boundaries.
  • North Direction Indicator: All maps have a north arrow. Orient the map with north to verify the actual direction of plot boundaries on the ground.
  • Adjacent Mouza Boundaries: The boundary with adjacent mouzas is shown as a heavy line.

How to Identify Your Plot on the Map

Once you have the dag number and mouza map, locate the dag number on the map sheet. The polygon showing that dag number represents your plot's shape and boundaries. Check the adjacent dag numbers (as stated in the deed) to confirm you are looking at the correct plot. If the physical boundary on the ground does not match the map, this may indicate encroachment, survey error, or boundary erosion — all of which require legal attention.

Land Measurement in Bangladesh — Decimal, Katha, Bigha and Acre

Land area in Bangladesh is measured using traditional units that vary somewhat by region, alongside the metric system increasingly used in urban areas. The following table provides the standard conversions used in land records and deeds across Bangladesh:

UnitBengali NameEquivalentNotes
1 Acreএকর100 Decimals = 4,840 sq. yards = 4,046.86 sq. mStandard unit; used in official records
1 Decimalডেসিমাল / শতাংশ1/100 of an acre = 435.6 sq. ft = 40.47 sq. mMost commonly used unit in deeds and records
1 Bighaবিঘা33 Decimals (standard) = 0.33 acresVaries regionally; some areas use 20-katha bigha
1 Kathaকাঠা1.65 Decimals = 720 sq. ft (standard)20 kathas = 1 bigha (standard); varies by region
1 Chatakছটাক1/16 of a katha = 45 sq. ftUsed for very small plots; 16 chataks = 1 katha
1 Gondaগন্ডা1/4 of a katha = 1/80 of a bighaTraditional unit; less common in modern records
1 Sq. Metreবর্গমিটার0.0247 Decimals = 10.764 sq. ftUsed in urban/apartment contexts; increasingly common

Regional Variations: It is important to note that the katha and bigha measurements can vary significantly by region. In Sylhet, a katha is different from a Dhaka katha. In Chittagong Hill Tracts, different traditional units may apply. Always confirm the local definition of the unit with the AC (Land) office or a local land lawyer when dealing with property outside familiar areas.

How area is recorded in deeds: Official deeds and khatians express land area in acres, roods, and decimals format, e.g., 0 acres 0 roods 15 decimals (= 15 decimal). Older CS/SA records may use bighas and kathas. Always verify the unit being used before calculating area.
