How to Find Your Dag and Mouza Online — land.gov.bd and eporcha.gov.bd

The Government of Bangladesh has digitised significant land records and made them available online through two primary portals, making it easier for citizens to verify their land records from anywhere:

1. land.gov.bd — Ministry of Land Portal

The official website of the Ministry of Land (minland.gov.bd and land.gov.bd) provides access to:

  • Land mutation status and application tracking
  • Land development tax payment portal
  • Information about land-related government services
  • Links to district land offices and AC (Land) offices
  • Online mutation application submission (Namjari e-service)

2. eporcha.gov.bd — Digital Land Records Portal

The eporcha (ই-পর্চা) portal is the primary online platform for accessing digitised land records in Bangladesh. Through eporcha.gov.bd, you can:

  • Search by Khatian Number: Enter the district, upazila, mouza, survey type (CS/SA/RS/BS), and khatian number to view the full khatian record (Record of Rights) showing all dags owned under that khatian.
  • Search by Dag Number: Enter the district, upazila, mouza, survey type, and dag number to find which khatian the dag falls under and who the recorded owner is.
  • Download certified digital copies: Certified copies of khatians can be downloaded from eporcha.gov.bd for a nominal fee, paid online. These certified digital copies are accepted as evidence in courts and at the Sub-Registrar's office.
  • Mouza Map View: Some districts have digitised mouza maps available for online viewing.

How to use eporcha.gov.bd step by step:

  1. Visit eporcha.gov.bd in your browser.
  2. Select your Division, District, Upazila, and Mouza from the dropdown menus.
  3. Select the survey type (CS / SA / RS / BS).
  4. Enter the Khatian Number or Dag Number in the search box.
  5. Click Search — the matching khatian record will be displayed.
  6. To download a certified copy, click the download/purchase option and pay the nominal fee via mobile banking or debit card.

Important note: Not all mouzas across Bangladesh have been fully digitised. If your mouza's records are not available on eporcha, you must visit the local AC (Land) office (সহকারী কমিশনার ভূমি) physically to obtain certified copies of khatians and mouza maps.

When Dag Numbers Don't Match Between CS and RS Records

One of the most frequent land-related problems in Bangladesh is a mismatch between dag numbers in different survey records (e.g., CS dag number ≠ RS dag number for the same physical plot). This occurs because:

  • Land was sub-divided or amalgamated between the two surveys
  • Survey boundaries were redrawn during the revision process
  • Clerical or mapping errors were made in one or both surveys
  • Land characteristics changed (e.g., river erosion, accretion of char land) between surveys

How to Identify Whether Your CS and RS Dags Refer to the Same Land

The mutation khatian (নামজারি খতিয়ান) maintained by the AC (Land) office serves as the current operative record that cross-references different survey dag numbers. A cross-reference table (পারস্পরিক সম্পর্ক তালিকা) is also maintained by the Survey Department. You can also overlay the CS and RS mouza maps for your mouza to see how the dag boundaries evolved.

Legal Consequences of Dag Mismatches

When a seller's deed references a CS dag number but the current RS record shows a different dag number (or no matching record), the buyer faces significant risks:

  • The Sub-Registrar may refuse to register the sale deed
  • A third party may claim ownership based on the RS record
  • Government mutation may be refused

Solutions

  • File an application before the AC (Land) office for a cross-survey verification (পর্চা সংশোধন)
  • Obtain a Land Tribunal order under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 correcting the record
  • Commission an independent survey (আমিন সার্ভে) to establish the physical boundaries and link to both CS and RS records
  • Consult a property lawyer before proceeding with any purchase where dag number mismatches exist

Survey Errors, Boundary Disputes and Their Legal Resolution

Survey errors and boundary disputes are among the most common land-related legal problems in Bangladesh. The causes and remedies are as follows:

Type of DisputeCommon CauseLegal RemedyForum
Boundary encroachment by neighbourPhysical shifting of boundary pillars; gradual encroachmentTitle suit with survey commission; injunctionCivil Court (District Judge / Assistant Judge)
Incorrect area in survey recordMeasurement error by surveyorApplication for record correction; new field surveySettlement Officer / AC (Land)
Wrong name recorded in khatianClerical error; fraudKhatian correction application; Land Tribunal suitAC (Land) / Land Tribunal
Land absorbed by river (erosion)Natural river changes; char land formationClaim for re-emerged char land; government applicationDC office / Land Ministry
Overlapping claims on same dagMultiple deeds; fraud; partition disputeTitle suit; declaration of titleCivil Court

Civil Court Suit for Declaration of Title: Under the Specific Relief Act 1877 and the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, a person whose title to land is disputed can file a suit for declaration of title and injunction against interference. The court may appoint a Commissioner (usually a qualified land surveyor / amin) to conduct a fresh demarcation survey and report to the court.

Land Tribunal: Bangladesh has established Land Tribunals under the Land Reforms Ordinance 1984 and related legislation to handle specific types of land disputes faster than regular civil courts. Cases involving vested property, khas land claims, and certain title disputes fall under Land Tribunal jurisdiction.

How to Request a Field Survey or Mutation

When your land records need to be updated — after purchase, partition, inheritance, or to correct errors — you need to apply for mutation (নামজারি / খারিজ) and/or a field survey. Here is how:

Mutation (Namjari) — Updating Ownership in Government Records

  1. Obtain the registered deed or inheritance documents (court order, death certificate, etc.)
  2. Prepare a mutation application (নামজারি দরখাস্ত) with required annexures
  3. Submit the application to the Assistant Commissioner (Land) / Tahsildar office of the concerned upazila
  4. Pay the required government fees via challan
  5. An inspector (তহসিলদার) will visit the site and verify the claim
  6. After verification, the AC (Land) issues a mutation order (নামজারি আদেশ) and the khatian is updated with the new owner's name

Currently, mutation applications can also be submitted online through the land.gov.bd portal's namjari e-service. Processing time is generally 28 working days from date of application, though delays are common in practice.

Requesting a New Field Survey (আমিন সার্ভে)

If you need to resolve a boundary dispute, verify your land area on the ground, or establish physical boundaries after purchase, you can request a field survey by a licensed government amin (land surveyor):

  • File an application with the AC (Land) office or the local Settlement Officer
  • Pay the survey fee (based on area and complexity)
  • The amin conducts the field measurement using a chain and offset method (or increasingly, modern digital instruments)
  • A field report (খসড়া খতিয়ান) is prepared and circulated to all interested parties for objection
  • After the objection period, the Settlement Officer finalises the record

Common Land Map Problems and Practical Solutions

The following are the most frequently encountered problems related to land maps and records in Bangladesh, along with actionable solutions:

ProblemSymptomImmediate Action
Dag number in deed does not exist in RS recordsSearch on eporcha returns no resultVerify with AC (Land) office; check if it is a CS dag without RS equivalent; consult a property lawyer
Different persons recorded as owners in CS and RS khatiansCompeting ownership claimsConsult a land lawyer immediately; file title suit in Civil Court before further dealing with the property
Mouza map not available on eporchaMouza not yet digitisedVisit the local Settlement Office or District Records Room to obtain physical copy of the mouza map
Physical land area differs from deed areaGround measurement inconsistencyEngage a licensed amin for fresh measurement; identify cause (encroachment, survey error, or natural change)
Mutation refused by AC (Land)Conflicting claims; missing documentsObtain written reason for refusal; appeal before the Additional DC (Revenue); consult a lawyer

Get Expert Legal Help for Land Survey Disputes

Land survey disputes in Bangladesh — whether involving dag number mismatches, boundary encroachments, survey errors, or contested khatians — are technically complex matters that require both legal expertise and familiarity with land revenue procedures. The stakes are high: an unresolved survey dispute can cloud your title, make your land unsaleable, and expose you to protracted court litigation.

Advocate Md. Shah Alam, practising from his chamber in Uttara, Dhaka, has extensive experience handling land survey and boundary disputes across Bangladesh, including:

  • Verifying dag numbers, khatians, and mouza maps across CS, SA, RS, and BS surveys
  • Filing and managing mutation applications and appeals
  • Conducting title searches and encumbrance checks before property purchase
  • Filing civil suits for declaration of title, injunction, and recovery of possession
  • Liaising with the Survey Department and AC (Land) office for field surveys and record corrections
  • Representing clients before Land Tribunals and civil courts at all levels

Before buying any land in Bangladesh, invest in a thorough title and survey verification. It costs a fraction of what a court case will cost later. Contact our office for a comprehensive land verification and legal opinion.

Consult Our Expert Property and Land Lawyer

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I find my land's dag number and khatian number in Bangladesh?

You can find your land's dag number and khatian number through several means: (1) Check your existing registered deed — it will state the mouza name, JL number, dag number, and khatian number. (2) Visit eporcha.gov.bd and search by district, upazila, mouza, and survey type. (3) Check the certified copy of the mouza map at the local AC (Land) office. (4) The local Tahsildar office (তহসিল অফিস) maintains current mutation khatians and can assist with searches.

What is the difference between CS, SA, RS, and BS survey records?

These represent four different government land surveys conducted at different times in Bangladesh: CS (Cadastral Survey, 1888-1940) is the oldest; SA (State Acquisition Survey, 1956-1962) was done after the zamindari system was abolished; RS (Revisional Survey, 1966-ongoing) is the most widely operative current survey; and BS (Bangladesh Survey, 1990s-present) applies to urban areas including Dhaka. The most recently completed survey for your area is generally the operative one. A property may have different dag numbers in different surveys for the same physical plot.

How many decimals are in one katha and one bigha?

In standard Bangladesh measurement: 1 katha = 1.65 decimals (720 sq. ft). 20 kathas = 1 bigha = 33 decimals. 3 bighas = 1 acre = 100 decimals. Note that these measurements can vary by region — particularly the katha, which may differ in Sylhet, Chittagong Hill Tracts, and other areas from the Dhaka standard. Always confirm local definitions when dealing with property outside familiar regions.

Can I download a certified copy of my khatian online in Bangladesh?

Yes, certified digital copies of khatians can be downloaded from the eporcha.gov.bd portal for most digitised mouzas in Bangladesh. You need to search by district, upazila, mouza, survey type, and khatian or dag number. A nominal fee (usually Tk 100-200 per khatian) is payable online via mobile banking or debit card. These certified digital copies are accepted as evidence in courts and official proceedings. However, not all mouzas have been digitised yet — if yours has not been, you must obtain physical certified copies from the local AC (Land) office.

What should I do if my neighbour has encroached on my land?

If you discover a boundary encroachment by a neighbour, take these steps: (1) Obtain a certified copy of the mouza map and your khatian from eporcha.gov.bd or the AC (Land) office. (2) Engage a licensed amin (land surveyor) to measure the actual boundaries on the ground. (3) Send a formal legal notice to the encroaching neighbour through a lawyer, demanding removal of encroachment. (4) If the encroachment is not voluntarily removed, file a civil suit for injunction and recovery of possession before the competent civil court. Do not attempt to forcibly remove the encroachment yourself — this can lead to criminal charges against you.

How long does the mutation process take in Bangladesh?

Under current government rules, a mutation (namjari) application should be processed within 28 working days from the date of submission to the AC (Land) office. However, in practice, due to workload and administrative delays, it can take 2-6 months or longer. Online applications through land.gov.bd may be processed somewhat faster. If your application is unreasonably delayed, you can file a complaint with the Additional DC (Revenue) or approach the Land Reforms Board. A lawyer can help expedite the process by following up formally with the concerned authorities.

The final publication of the Bangladesh Survey (BS), City Jarip, or Dhaka Metropolitan Survey (DMS) records of rights (Khatians) has created widespread property crises for millions of landowners across Bangladesh. In numerous instances, survey officers erroneously recorded privately owned ancestral land in the name of total strangers, adjacent neighbors, or falsely entered the land into government Khas, abandoned, or vested property schedules. Under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (SAT Act), once a record of rights is finally published under Section 144, the Assistant Commissioner (Land) loses statutory power to alter ownership. The exclusive judicial forum to rectify final survey errors is the Land Survey Tribunal (LST) established under Section 145A of the Act.

1. The Anatomy of Survey Errors: How Wrong BS Khatians Are Created

The cadence of land revenue administration in Bangladesh relies on periodic cadastral field surveys. Following the historical Cadastral Survey (CS), State Acquisition Survey (SA), and Revisional Survey (RS), the government launched the Bangladesh Survey (BS) and specialized City Jarip across Dhaka, Chittagong, and other urban hubs.

Due to corruption among field Kanungos, lack of landowner attendance during field verification (Khanapuri and Bujharat), or deliberate fraud by unscrupulous neighbors, massive errors infected the draft records. Landowners frequently discover that their purchased or inherited property has been recorded in the name of an adjacent owner, that the recorded acreage is drastically curtailed, or that private freehold land has been entered into Government Khas Khatian No. 1 or Vested Property lists.

When the final Gazette notification is issued and the BS volume is deposited in the Collectorate record room, the record becomes final. Relying on an incorrect BS Khatian exposes the property to wrongful mutation, illegal encroachment, and mortgage rejections by commercial banks.

2. The Legal Framework: Section 145A of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act 1950

Prior to 2004, aggrieved landowners had to file regular title suits in the ordinary civil courts under the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) to challenge incorrect survey entries. Because civil suits took decades to resolve, parliament amended the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 via the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act 2004, inserting Sections 145A through 145I.

Section 145A(1) empowers the government to establish one or more Land Survey Tribunals in each district. The tribunal is presided over by a judicial officer not below the rank of Joint District Judge. Section 145A(5) vests the tribunal with the exclusive jurisdiction to entertain, hear, and dispose of suits arising out of the final publication of the record of rights prepared under Section 144.

Under this statutory mandate, ordinary Assistant Judge civil courts are barred from entertaining suits challenging finally published survey records where an operational tribunal exists, making the Land Survey Tribunal the primary statutory courthouse for khatian rectification.

3. Why the AC Land Cannot Rectify a Finally Published BS Khatian

A widespread and costly mistake made by property owners is filing a mutation review application (Miss Case) before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) requesting the AC Land to 'correct' a wrong BS Khatian. Landowners often waste years petitioning Upazila land offices only to have their applications rejected.

Under the Tenancy Rules and Ministry of Land circulars, the Assistant Commissioner (Land) possesses administrative power to conduct mutation (Namjari) based upon existing, legally recognized records and registered transfer deeds. However, the AC Land possesses zero judicial authority to declare a finally published BS Khatian void or cancel an entry made by the Directorate of Land Records and Surveys (DLRS).

Discovered an error in your BS or City Jarip Khatian in Bangladesh? Immediate legal action before the Land Survey Tribunal or High Court is essential before limitation expires. Message our land litigation team on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for professional file vetting.

The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly ruled that once a record of rights is finally published under Section 144 of the SAT Act 1950, it carries a statutory presumption of correctness. Only a decree passed by a competent court or the Land Survey Tribunal under Section 145A can legally rebut this presumption and command the land administration to rewrite the record. To understand mutation procedures, see our guide on land mutation Miss Case appeals in Bangladesh.

4. The Strict Limitation Period: One-Year Rule and Condonation of Delay

Statutory limitation is the most critical hurdle in Land Survey Tribunal litigation. Under Section 145A(2) of the SAT Act 1950, any person aggrieved by the final publication of any record of rights may, within one (1) year from the date of such publication, file a suit before the Land Survey Tribunal.

The proviso to Section 145A(2) grants the tribunal limited discretion: the tribunal may entertain a suit after the expiration of the one-year period, but not exceeding a further period of one (1) year, if it is satisfied that the plaintiff had sufficient cause for not filing the suit within the initial timeframe.

This creates a strict statutory limitation ceiling of two years from the final publication date. Because many district survey publications occurred years ago and landowners only discover the error when attempting to sell or construct, strict application of limitation often bars the suit. In such instances, specialized advocacy relies on Section 5 of the Limitation Act 1908 or shifts the battle to the constitutional writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division.

5. Step-by-Step Procedure for Filing and Contesting an LST Suit

Filing a suit before the Land Survey Tribunal follows the formal evidentiary standards of the Code of Civil Procedure 1898. The procedural stages encompass:

  1. Drafting the Plaint: The plaintiff drafts a comprehensive plaint impleading the person wrongly recorded in the BS Khatian, the Deputy Commissioner (representing the government), and the relevant AC Land. The plaint specifies the exact plot, khatian numbers, acreage, and the relief sought—namely, declaration of plaintiff's title and direction to correct the BS record.
  2. Documentary Annexures: The plaintiff must produce certified copies of the unbroken chain of title: CS Khatian, SA Khatian, RS Khatian, registered deeds (Saf Kabala, Heba, or Bonton-nama), mutation porchas, and land development tax receipts (Dakhila).
  3. Service of Summons: Summons are served on the recorded defendants and government revenue officers. The government typically files a pro-forma written statement through the Government Pleader (GP).
  4. Trial and Evidence: The plaintiff gives oral testimony (PW-1) and tenders original or certified documentary records into evidence. The tribunal examines whether the plaintiff established continuous physical possession and lawful devolution from historical records.
  5. Final Judgment and Decree: Upon finding in favor of the plaintiff, the Joint District Judge delivers a judgment declaring the erroneous BS Khatian void and directs the revenue authority to prepare a corrected Khatian in the plaintiff's name.

6. Summary Matrix: Record Correction Forums, Powers & Limitations

Understanding which legal forum holds jurisdiction over land record corrections saves years of futile litigation. The following comparative matrix outlines key statutory venues:

Legal Forum Governing Authority Scope of Rectification Power Limitation Period
Land Survey Tribunal (LST) Joint District Judge (Sec 145A SAT Act) Exclusive jurisdiction over finally published BS/City Khatians 1 year + 1 year condonation (Sec 145A)
High Court Division (Writ) Supreme Court Bench (Article 102) Mandamus to correct records when LST is vacant/non-functional No strict limitation; reasonable promptness

7. Enforcing LST Decrees: Section 145B Directions to Deputy Commissioners

Obtaining a favorable judgment and decree from the Land Survey Tribunal is a major triumph, but the decree must be practically executed in the government revenue books to enable smooth mutation and land tax payments.

Under Section 145B of the SAT Act 1950, when the Land Survey Tribunal passes a decree for the correction of a record of rights, a certified copy of the decree is transmitted directly to the Collector (Deputy Commissioner) of the district. The Deputy Commissioner is statutorily mandated to cause the necessary corrections to be made in the master record of rights maintained in the Collectorate record room.

The DC then forwards an operational direction to the relevant Assistant Commissioner (Land) and Union Land Assistant Officer (Tahsildar). The AC Land opens a dedicated execution mutation file, enters the corrected Khatian in the digital land ledger, generates a corrected Porcha in the plaintiff's name, and accepts land development taxes. If local land officers delay implementation, the plaintiff can file an execution case before the tribunal or issue a formal contempt notice.

8. High Court Writ Remedies (Article 102) When LST Benches Are Vacant

A widespread systemic failure across Bangladesh is that in numerous districts, Land Survey Tribunals have remained physically vacant or non-functional for years due to judicial vacancy crises. Furthermore, while Section 145E of the SAT Act contemplated Land Survey Appellate Tribunals (LSAT), the government failed to establish functional appellate tribunals in most divisions.

This structural void creates a grave denial of access to justice. In landmark decisions, the High Court Division established that where an aggrieved citizen has no functional statutory tribunal to approach within the limitation window, or where an LST decree remains unexecuted due to administrative apathy, the citizen cannot be left without a remedy.

Landowners can approach the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution for a Writ of Mandamus. The High Court examines the undisputed historical records (CS, SA, RS) and registered deeds, observes that the petitioner's fundamental right to property under Article 42 is violated, and directly commands the Deputy Commissioner and AC Land to correct the khatian records. For writ strategies, consult our practice overview on Supreme Court writ litigation in Bangladesh.

9. Illustrative Scenario: Recovering Ancestral Land from a Fraudulent BS Entry

To illustrate how LST litigation unfolds in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A family in Mirpur, Dhaka, held title to 12 decimals of commercial land continuously owned since the 1962 SA survey and recorded in their father's name in the RS survey. During the final publication of the City Jarip in Dhaka, the family discovered that their entire plot had been recorded under City Khatian No. 892 in the name of an influential local developer who possessed zero title deeds.

The family engaged a Supreme Court land advocate. The advocate immediately obtained certified copies of the CS, SA, and RS Khatians, the original 1958 purchase deed, and 50 years of uninterrupted Dakhila receipts. Within ten months of the final City Jarip gazette publication, the advocate filed an LST Suit before the Dhaka Land Survey Tribunal under Section 145A of the SAT Act 1950.

During trial, the developer failed to produce any registered deed explaining how title passed from the original RS record owners. The Joint District Judge decreed the suit in the family's favor, declaring City Khatian No. 892 void and fraudulent. Pursuant to Section 145B, the certified decree was transmitted to the Deputy Commissioner of Dhaka. Within sixty days, the AC Land Mirpur generated a corrected City Jarip Khatian in the family's name, restoring their market title.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a Land Survey Advocate in Dhaka: To file an LST suit, enforce a tribunal decree before the DC and AC Land offices, or petition the High Court Division under Article 102 when tribunals are non-functional, message our chamber on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call our chamber at +880 1712-655546. Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Land Survey Tribunal (LST) in Bangladesh?

The Land Survey Tribunal is a specialized statutory court established under Section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, presided over by a Joint District Judge, with exclusive jurisdiction to rectify errors in finally published BS and City Jarip Khatians.

What is the deadline to file a suit in the Land Survey Tribunal?

Under Section 145A(2) of the SAT Act, the suit must be filed within one year from the date of final publication of the record of rights. The tribunal may extend this period by a maximum of one additional year upon proof of sufficient cause.

Can the Assistant Commissioner (Land) correct a wrong BS Khatian directly?

No. The AC Land has no judicial power to cancel or correct a finally published BS Khatian. Rectification requires a formal decree from the Land Survey Tribunal or a writ order from the High Court Division.

What can I do if the Land Survey Tribunal in my district is vacant or non-functional?

If the district LST is vacant or not sitting, you can file a Writ Petition before the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution, which can issue mandatory directions to the Deputy Commissioner to correct the record.

What documents are required to file an LST suit for BS khatian correction?

You must provide certified copies of the erroneous BS Khatian, the correct historical CS, SA, and RS Khatians, registered title deeds, mutation records, land tax receipts (Dakhila), and field trace maps proving continuous ownership and possession.

How is an LST decree enforced after winning the case?

Under Section 145B of the SAT Act, a certified copy of the decree is transmitted to the Deputy Commissioner (Collector), who directs the relevant AC Land to correct the master record and issue a corrected Khatian to the decree-holder.

Can an ordinary civil court entertain a suit to cancel a BS Khatian?

Where a functional Land Survey Tribunal exists, ordinary Assistant Judge civil courts are barred from entertaining suits challenging finally published survey records under Section 145A(5) of the SAT Act.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi file an LST suit from abroad without returning to Dhaka?

Yes. An overseas Bangladeshi can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission in their country of residence, empowering an advocate or relative to file and conduct the LST case in Bangladesh.

Death Threats & Breach of Peace in Bangladesh: Section 107 CrPC Peace Bond Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-13 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

A common and alarming situation arises across Bangladesh: following an unresolved boundary dispute, family inheritance squabble, tenancy confrontation, or political disagreement, an aggressive neighbor, relative, or local hoodlum begins issuing overt death threats (Pran Nasher Humki). They shout abuse, threaten to break limbs, vandalize your property, or assemble armed thugs outside your gate. When you visit the local police station to report the terror, the duty officer often advises: 'This is a non-cognizable civil dispute; file a General Diary (GD).' However, a standard GD does not arrest the aggressor or provide physical protection. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, the law provides a swift, preventative criminal judicial remedy: filing a proceeding under Section 107 of the CrPC before the Executive Magistrate Court to bind the aggressor down under a Peace Bond (Muchleka) with heavy sureties.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

The Reality of Threats and Intimidation in Bangladesh

In Bangladesh's crowded neighborhoods and semi-urban commercial centers, disputes over property boundaries, shop rentals, family partitions, or personal rivalries often cross the line from civil disagreements into open terror. Unscrupulous parties frequently hire local musclemen or assemble gangs to intimidate peaceable families. They issue explicit death threats, warn victims that their children will be harmed, and threaten to dismantle boundary fences at night.

Victims who rush to the local police station frequently encounter procedural inertia: because verbal threats (criminal intimidation under Section 506 of the Penal Code) are technically classified as non-cognizable offenses, the police cannot arrest the aggressor without a court order, merely recording an entry in the General Diary (GD). Relying solely on a passive GD leaves the family in acute physical danger. The Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 anticipated this exact administrative vacuum, providing a powerful preventative weapon under Section 107 before actual bloodshed occurs.

Understanding Preventive Criminal Justice: Section 107 CrPC

Criminal jurisprudence in Bangladesh is divided into punitive justice (punishing crimes after they occur) and preventative justice (stopping crimes before they happen). Section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC) is the cornerstone of preventative criminal administration.

Section 107(1) stipulates: 'Whenever an Executive Magistrate is informed that any person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquility, or to do any wrongful act that may probably occasion a breach of the peace, the Magistrate may... require such person to show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond, with or without sureties, for keeping the peace for such period not exceeding one year as the Magistrate thinks fit to fix.' This provision does not aim to brand the aggressor as a convicted criminal; its objective is to place a heavy judicial leash around their neck, compelling them to furnish substantial financial sureties that will be immediately forfeited if they misbehave.

Role and Jurisdiction of the Executive Magistrate Court

Following the historic separation of the judiciary from the executive in 2007 (the Masdar Hossain case), judicial powers under the CrPC were divided between Judicial Magistrates and Executive Magistrates. While Judicial Magistrates conduct criminal trials, the maintenance of public order, breach of peace, and preventative security under Sections 107, 144, and 145 CrPC are assigned exclusively to Executive Magistrates.

In Dhaka, Chattogram, and metropolitan areas, Executive Magistrate Courts operate under the District Administration (headed by the District Magistrate / Deputy Commissioner) or specialized Metropolitan Executive Magistrate benches. In upazilas, the Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) or Assistant Commissioner (Land) functions as an Executive Magistrate. These courts possess summary authority to summon parties, direct the local Thana police to submit expedited inquiry reports, and issue binding orders maintaining peace.

Section 117: Interim Peace Bonds for Urgent Protection

The standard inquiry under Section 107 requires examining witnesses, which can take several weeks. If the victim faces imminent threat of physical violence tonight, waiting for the final order offers little solace. To solve this emergency, the legislature enacted Section 117(3) of the CrPC.

Section 117(3) provides an extraordinary emergency remedy: 'The Magistrate may, if he considers that immediate measures are necessary for the prevention of a breach of the peace or disturbance of the public tranquility or the commission of any offence or for the public safety, for reasons to be recorded in writing, direct the person in respect of whom the order under section 112 has been made to execute a bond, with or without sureties, for keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour until the conclusion of the inquiry, and may detain him in custody until such bond is executed.' An advocate files an emergency interlocutory application under Section 117(3) alongside the main petition, securing an immediate interim bond on the very first day of appearance.

Police Inquiry Reports and Thana Investigation Protocols

Upon receiving a petition under Section 107 CrPC, the Executive Magistrate issues an official order directing the Officer-in-Charge (OC) of the local Thana to depute a Sub-Inspector (SI) to conduct an on-site field inquiry. The police officer visits the disputed locality, interviews neighbors, examines boundary lines, and inspects recorded General Diaries.

The police officer then prepares a formal Police Inquiry Report submitted directly to the Executive Magistrate Court. If the report confirms that the opposite party is aggressive, maintains armed associates, and that an imminent breach of the peace exists, the Magistrate immediately issues a Show Cause Order under Section 112 CrPC. This official police verification strips the aggressor of any plausible deniability, compelling the court to demand high financial sureties.

Consequences of Violating a Bond: Forfeiture and Jail

A Peace Bond executed under Section 107 CrPC is not a hollow piece of paper; it carries severe financial and physical penalties. When an aggressor executes a bond, they must submit personal recognizance alongside two reputable local sureties (such as solvent business owners or municipal councillors) who pledge substantial financial sums (typically BDT 50,000 to BDT 2,00,000 each).

Under Section 122 and Section 514 of the CrPC, if the bound person violates the peace during the one-year bond period—by uttering fresh death threats, assaulting the complainant, or trespassing on their land—the consequences are swift:

  1. Immediate Forfeiture of Money: The Magistrate passes a summary order forfeiting the entire bond amount. If the sureties fail to pay, the court attaches and sells their immovable property through public distress warrants.
  2. Remand to Jail Custody: Under Section 123 CrPC, if the aggressor refuses to execute the bond or breaches the peace, the Magistrate orders the offender remanded directly to central jail for the entire unexpired duration of the bond period.

Combining Section 107 with Penal Code Section 506

To build an impenetrable legal defense, an experienced criminal advocate adopts a two-pronged strategy: combining preventative administrative proceedings with formal criminal prosecution. Parallel to the Section 107 petition before the Executive Magistrate Court, the advocate files a Complaint Register (CR) case under Section 506 of the Penal Code 1860 (Criminal Intimidation) before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) Court.

Under the second part of Section 506, if the threat is to cause death or grievous hurt, or to cause the destruction of any property by fire, the offense is punishable with imprisonment for up to seven (7) years, or with fine, or with both. Prosecuting under Section 506 alongside Section 107 exposes the aggressor to long-term criminal prison sentences while simultaneously binding them under an immediate peace bond, completely disarming their aggressive posture.

Comparison Table: General Diary (GD) vs. Section 107 CrPC

The table below summarizes the operational differences between relying solely on a police General Diary versus pursuing a Section 107 CrPC court proceeding:

ParameterPolice General Diary (GD) AloneSection 107 CrPC Court Case
Judicial AuthorityNone; purely an internal police station logJudicial proceeding before Executive Magistrate
Power to Compel OpponentNone; police cannot compel appearanceCourt summons & non-bailable warrants
Financial SuretiesZero financial deterrenceSurety bonds of BDT 50,000–2,00,000
Jail Detention PowerNone without registering formal FIRDirect imprisonment under §123 for non-compliance
Speed of ReliefPassive; often archived without actionInterim peace bond under §117(3) within days

A General Diary merely records an allegation; a Section 107 court case enforces immediate legal deterrence that restrains aggressive opponents.

Illustrative Scenario: Stopping a Land Grabber's Threats in Mirpur

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how an emergency Section 107 proceeding neutralized a violent threat in Mirpur, Dhaka:

A retired government school headmaster lived in a modest residential house in Mirpur-12, Dhaka. An influential local real estate developer purchased an adjacent plot and demanded that the headmaster sell his front driveway at a nominal price to allow road widening for a commercial building. When the headmaster refused, the developer sent armed thugs who banged on his iron gates at night, shouted obscenities, and verbally warned him that if he did not sign a deed within seven days, 'his body would be found floating in the Turag River.' The terrified family lodged two GDs at Pallabi Thana, but the threats only escalated.

The headmaster consulted a criminal defense advocate. The advocate drafted an urgent petition under Section 107 of the CrPC, filed directly in the Court of the Executive Magistrate, Dhaka, accompanied by an interlocutory petition under Section 117(3) for an interim peace bond. The petition annexed the two stamped GD entries, audio recordings of telephone threats, and photographs of the developer's associates outside the gate.

The Executive Magistrate took immediate cognizance, issued a Show Cause Notice under Section 112 CrPC, and directed the Officer-in-Charge of Pallabi Thana to submit an expedited inquiry report within three days. The police visited the site, warned the developer, and confirmed the threat to the Magistrate. On the return date, the Magistrate ordered the developer to execute an immediate Interim Peace Bond of BDT 1,00,000 with two solvent local sureties, warning him that any further harassment would result in immediate remand to Dhaka Central Jail. Confronted with immediate imprisonment and financial forfeiture, the developer dismissed his thugs and abandoned his unlawful demands, restoring complete peace to the family.

Talk to an Advocate

Navigating complex legal disputes in Bangladesh requires uncompromising documentary preparation, precise statutory drafting, and experienced courtroom representation. Whether you are seeking to buy back ancestral land through pre-emption, stay an unlawful bank auction, prosecute fraudulent recruitment brokers, restrain violent death threats, or resolve high-stakes income tax audit notices, procedural delays can extinguish your statutory remedies. A qualified advocate protects your interests, files emergency petitions, and enforces your legal entitlements across civil, criminal, revenue, and constitutional tribunals.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in Bangladesh?

Section 107 CrPC is a preventative criminal law provision that empowers Executive Magistrates to order any person who threatens a breach of the peace or public tranquility to execute a Peace Bond (Muchleka), with financial sureties, for keeping the peace for up to one year.

Which court handles Section 107 cases in Bangladesh?

Section 107 proceedings are heard exclusively by Executive Magistrate Courts operating under the District Administration in metropolitan cities and district headquarters, or by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) in upazila jurisdictions.

Is filing a General Diary (GD) enough to stop death threats?

No. A General Diary is merely an administrative record in the police register. To legally force the aggressor to stop threats under threat of imprisonment and financial forfeiture, you must file a formal case under Section 107 CrPC before the Executive Magistrate.

What is an Interim Peace Bond under Section 117(3) CrPC?

An Interim Peace Bond is an emergency order granted by the Magistrate at the initial stage of the proceeding, requiring the aggressor to immediately sign a financial bond keeping the peace while the full inquiry is ongoing.

What happens if a person violates a Section 107 Peace Bond?

Under Section 122 and Section 514 CrPC, the court will forfeit the entire bond money, attach the properties of the sureties, and remand the offender directly to central jail under Section 123 for the remaining bond period.

Can Section 107 be used in neighbor boundary or land disputes?

Yes. When land or boundary disputes escalate into verbal death threats, physical intimidation, or assembling armed men, Section 107 is the standard legal mechanism to maintain the peace while civil title suits proceed.

Can an accused person be jailed under Section 107 CrPC?

While Section 107 is preventative rather than punitive, if the summoned person refuses to execute the required peace bond or violates its conditions, the Magistrate has full statutory authority to order them detained in jail.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi (NRB) file a Section 107 case for family safety in Bangladesh?

Yes. An NRB can execute a Power of Attorney or authorize family members residing in Bangladesh to institute Section 107 proceedings through an advocate to protect elderly parents and ancestral homes from local intimidation.

Lost Land Deed in Bangladesh? How to Get Certified Copy (Nokol)

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-09 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Losing an original registered land title deed (Saf Kabala, Heba, Partition, or Exchange deed) is an alarming experience for property owners in Bangladesh. Whether the deed was misplaced during relocation, damaged by environmental elements, or deliberately withheld by disputing relatives, property owners worry that they have lost their legal title. Under Bangladeshi property jurisprudence, ownership resides in the underlying lawful registration and record of rights, not solely in the physical document. The Registration Act 1908 provides a well-defined statutory procedure to inspect official archives, search volume books (Balam Boi), and procure an authentic certified copy (Nokol) possessing full evidentiary validity in all courts and government land offices.

1. Immediate Protective Steps: Police GD and Newspaper Notice

The moment you realize an original registered deed is missing, stolen, or misplaced, your immediate priority is to create an official evidentiary record of the loss. This prevents dishonest third parties or fraudulent family members from attempting to create unauthorized mortgage liens or sham powers of attorney using your physical document.

The first mandatory step is filing a General Diary (GD) with the police station (thana) having territorial jurisdiction over the location where the document was misplaced. The GD must state the precise details of the registered deed—including the deed number, date of execution, name of the Sub-Registry Office, mouza, khatian, plot (dag) numbers, and the registered owner's full particulars. If you require guidance on lodging police station records, examine our practical guide on how to file a GD at a Bangladesh police station.

Following the GD, property owners should publish a brief loss announcement in a widely circulated national Bengali or English daily newspaper. The published notice serves as public notice to financial institutions and prospective purchasers that the original deed is missing and that any transaction conducted on the basis of the missing physical document is unauthorized and subject to legal challenge.

2. The Archive System: Understanding Balam Boi and Registry Indexes

Many landowners assume that if the paper deed in their custody is gone, proof of ownership disappears. In reality, Bangladesh maintains a centralized, permanent archival recording system under the Registration Act 1908. Every Sub-Registry Office maintains physical and increasingly digitized record books known as Balam Boi (Volume Books).

When a deed is registered, the Sub-Registry Office copies the entire text and hand-drawn property sketch verbatim into Book No. 1 ('Register of non-testamentary documents relating to immovable property'). The volume is bound into permanent books and assigned a specific Volume (Balam) number, Book number, and Page numbers. These historical volumes are permanently preserved in the district record rooms (Record Mahal) under the authority of the District Registrar.

To enable public retrieval, the registry office maintains statutory cross-reference indexes pursuant to Section 54 of the Registration Act 1908. Index I records the names of all executing parties and claimants in alphabetical order. Index II records the property particulars arranged by Mouza, sheet, and plot numbers. These indexes allow records to be traced even when original paperwork has been lost for decades.

3. How to Search When Deed Number or Year Is Unknown

A frequent challenge arises when property was purchased decades ago by parents or grandparents, and the heirs know the plot location but have no record of the deed number or exact registration year. In this scenario, obtaining a certified copy requires an official archive search (Talashi).

Under Section 57(1) of the Registration Act 1908, any person may inspect Book No. 1 and its related indexes upon payment of the statutory inspection fees. To initiate an index search, you must submit an application identifying the relevant Sub-Registry Office (such as Tejgaon, Uttara, Dhanmondi, or a specific Upazila registry), the Mouza name, and the approximate year or multi-year range of the transaction.

Lost your original land deed or facing record search delays in Bangladesh? Our legal team assists domestic and overseas landowners in tracing Sub-Registry volume books and procuring certified copies. Message our chamber on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for professional assistance.

The registry searcher reviews Index II for the specified Mouza and plot number across the designated years. When a matching entry is discovered, the index discloses the exact registered deed number, volume number, and page range. Once these reference numbers are established, the path is clear to apply for the certified copy.

4. Step-by-Step Procedure to Apply for a Certified Copy (Nokol)

Once the deed number, volume number, and year of registration are identified, obtaining the official certified copy (Nokol) proceeds through a structured statutory workflow:

  1. Submission of Form No. 36: Procure and complete the prescribed statutory application form (Form No. 36) addressed to the Sub-Registrar. Detail the deed number, year, volume, page number, donor/donee names, and property description.
  2. Affixing Court Fees: Affix the required Court Fee stamp to the application header as mandated by the Court Fees Act 1870.
  3. Payment of Search and Inspection Fees: Pay the statutory search fees covering the relevant archive years under Section 78 of the Registration Act 1908.
  4. Payment of Copying Stamp Fees: Deposit the requisite non-judicial stamps and copying fees. Currently, certified copies require non-judicial stamps under Article 24 of Schedule I of the Stamp Act 1899, plus fixed government folios (cartridge paper fees).
  5. Transcription and Comparison: The Sub-Registry copying section (Nokol Nobish) transcribes the deed from the master Balam Boi onto official stamped folios. A comparison officer (Taqabila) reads and verifies the transcript against the original book record.
  6. Certification and Seal: The Sub-Registrar applies the official embossed seal, certifies the document as a true copy of the record under Section 57(5) of the Registration Act 1908, signs the certification, and issues the document to the applicant.

5. Government Fee Schedule for Inspections and Certified Copies

All fees for searching archives and procuring certified copies of registered deeds are determined by government statutory regulatory orders (SROs) promulgated under Section 78 of the Registration Act 1908 and the Stamp Act 1899. The following fee ranges reflect official government schedules as verified for the 2026 operational year:

  • Application Court Fee: Nominal court fee stamp (typically 20 to 50 BDT) affixed to the initial application.
  • Search Fee (Deed Number Known): Searching records for a single specified year incurs an official fee of approximately 50 BDT.
  • Multi-Year Index Search Fee (Deed Number Unknown): When a multi-year search across Index I or II is required, the statutory fee is charged per year searched (typically 50 to 100 BDT per year).
  • Non-Judicial Stamp for Certified Copy: Non-judicial stamp duty under the Stamp Act 1899 (currently 50 BDT for non-testamentary instruments) must be deposited.
  • Folio / Transcription Fees: A per-page transcription fee (calculated per 300 words or per cartridge folio, roughly 100 to 200 BDT per folio) covers copying and comparison.
  • Urgent Processing Surcharge: An optional expedited processing fee can be deposited for urgent deliveries within 3 to 7 working days.

Always ensure that official government receipts (Dakhila) are collected for all fees deposited at the registry treasury counter. Confirm current fee schedules with your advocate before filing.

6. Summary Matrix: Document Types, Search Protocols & Timeline

Different types of missing real estate records require slightly different search workflows. The following matrix outlines the procedural roadmap across common property deed categories in Bangladesh:

Document Type Lost Primary Record Custodian Information Needed to Retrieve Typical Processing Timeline
Saf Kabala (Outright Sale Deed) Sub-Registry Office (Book No. 1) Deed No., Year, Mouza, Buyer/Seller Names 5 to 14 working days
Heba / Gift Deed (Blood Relation) Sub-Registry Office (Book No. 1) Deed No., Year, Donor & Donee Names 5 to 14 working days
Power of Attorney (Am-Moktarnama) Sub-Registry Office (Book No. 1 or 4) Deed No., Principal & Attorney Names, Year 5 to 12 working days
Partition Deed (Bonton-nama) Sub-Registry Office (Book No. 1) Deed No., All Co-sharer Names, Mouza 7 to 20 working days

7. Evidentiary Value of a Certified Copy in Civil Court and AC Land Mutation

A widespread concern among landowners who hold a certified copy instead of the original deed is whether the copy carries identical legal validity. The statutory framework provides complete reassurance on this point.

Under Section 57(5) of the Registration Act 1908, a certified copy given under the official hand and seal of the registering officer 'shall be admissible for the purpose of proving the contents of the original document.' In civil litigation, while Section 64 of the Evidence Act 1872 establishes that documents must generally be proved by primary evidence (the original document itself), Section 65(f) expressly permits secondary evidence when the document is a public record within the meaning of Section 74, or when it is a certified copy permitted by the Registration Act.

Similarly, the Ministry of Land and the Assistant Commissioner (Land) offices across Bangladesh routinely accept certified Nokols for the purposes of mutation (Namjari), creation of new Khatians, and payment of land development taxes (Khajna). A certified copy, accompanied by the police GD number confirming loss of the primary document, is fully recognized by commercial banks for title verification and property conveyancing. For title vetting insights, review our guide on remote land title search and vetting in Bangladesh.

8. Illustrative Scenario: Tracing a 30-Year-Old Missing Saf Kabala

To demonstrate how an archive search and Nokol procurement unfold in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

An expatriate living in Sydney inherited two plots of prime residential land in Uttara, Dhaka, originally purchased by his late father in 1994. While organizing family affairs following the father's death, the family discovered that the physical Saf Kabala deed was missing from the family safe, and no relative possessed a photocopy noting the registration serial number. Without the deed, the AC Land office declined to process the mutation into the heirs' names.

The heir retained an advocate in Dhaka to conduct a comprehensive archival retrieval. The legal team first obtained the original RS and City Jarip Khatians from the Dhaka Collectorate record room to establish the exact Mouza name, CS/SA/RS plot numbers, and the late father's recorded name. Armed with these property coordinates, the advocate submitted an application under Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908 at the relevant Sub-Registry Office for an Index II inspection spanning the years 1992 through 1996.

Within ten days, the registry searchers located the entry in the 1994 Index II, revealing Deed No. 4582 recorded in Volume 48, pages 112 through 126 of Book No. 1. The advocate deposited the required statutory cartridge paper fees and non-judicial stamps. Within one week, the Sub-Registrar issued an official certified Nokol bearing the embossed government seal. Using this certified document and a succession certificate, the heirs successfully mutated the land records into their names without dispute.

9. Remote Deed Procurement Protocols for Non-Resident Bangladeshis

Non-resident Bangladeshis residing in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and the Middle East face unique logistical barriers when deeds are misplaced in Bangladesh. Traveling to Bangladesh merely to attend registry counters is both expensive and unnecessary.

To safely procure a certified copy of a missing land deed from abroad without international travel, follow these established legal steps:

  • Gather Baseline Land Identifiers: Review existing Khatians (CS, SA, RS, BS), land tax receipts (dakhila), or municipal tax bills to note the Mouza, Upazila/Thana, and plot numbers.
  • Engage a Licensed Advocate via Remote Consultation: Retain an advocate practicing in the relevant district to represent your interests before the Sub-Registry Office.
  • File an Online Police GD: In many metropolitan jurisdictions including Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP), a General Diary for lost property can be filed through the official DMP Online GD portal, providing immediate digital GD verification.
  • Authorize Record Searches: Instruct your advocate to conduct the Balam Boi search under Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908.
  • Secure Attested Courier Dispatch: Once certified by the Sub-Registrar, the advocate can have the certified document apostilled or attested by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) in Dhaka if required for foreign embassy submissions, and securely dispatched to your overseas address via tracked international courier.

For additional assistance with remote property management, review our specialized services for land dispute resolution and NRB legal services in Bangladesh.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a Land Advocate in Dhaka: To conduct volume book (Balam Boi) searches, draft missing deed GDs, or obtain certified Nokols across Dhaka and all district Sub-Registry offices, contact our office via WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients can request remote searches and direct international couriers.

Frequently Asked Questions

If I lose my original land deed, do I lose ownership of my property in Bangladesh?

No. Ownership is established by the legal registration of the document in the government registry and the recorded title in the Khatians, not solely by physical possession of the original paper. A certified copy issued by the Sub-Registry Office legally proves your ownership.

What is a Nokol (নকল) in Bangladeshi property law?

A Nokol is an official certified copy of a registered deed transcribed directly from the master volume book (Balam Boi) and certified under the seal and signature of the Sub-Registrar pursuant to Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908.

Can someone fraudulently sell my land if they possess my lost original deed?

It is illegal to sell property without valid title. However, dishonest individuals may attempt fraud or take private loans. Filing an immediate police GD and publishing a newspaper notice legally invalidates unauthorized transactions based on the missing deed.

How can I find my lost deed if I do not know the deed number or year of registration?

You can apply for an archival search under Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908. The Sub-Registry Office will search Index I (by parties' names) or Index II (by Mouza and plot numbers) across the estimated years to identify the deed number and volume.

Is a certified copy accepted by banks for mortgage loan applications in Bangladesh?

Yes. Most commercial banks accept a certified Nokol accompanied by the police GD, newspaper publication, and complete chain of title records, subject to verification against the Sub-Registry Balam Boi by the bank's panel lawyer.

Can I mutate (Namjari) my land using a certified copy of a lost deed?

Yes. Assistant Commissioner (Land) offices across Bangladesh routinely accept certified copies of registered deeds for mutation applications, provided the document is certified by the Sub-Registrar and verified in the registry records.

How long does it take to obtain a certified copy of a deed from the Sub-Registry Office?

If the deed number and year are known, it generally takes 5 to 14 working days. If an archive index search is required across multiple historical years, the process typically takes two to four weeks.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi obtain a certified deed without returning to Bangladesh?

Yes. An overseas Bangladeshi can authorize an advocate in Bangladesh to conduct the search and retrieve the certified copy under Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908, with documents dispatched abroad via tracked courier.

entries.body:
Mahr (Dower) Rights Wife Bangladesh – Amount, Recovery & Legal Remedies

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-06 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Mahr (also written as mehr or dower) is one of the most important financial rights of a wife under Muslim personal law as applied in Bangladesh. It is an obligatory payment from the husband to the wife — a debt of honour and law — that cannot be taken away without the wife's free and voluntary consent. Despite its fundamental nature, mahr is among the most frequently violated rights of Muslim women in Bangladesh. This guide explains everything a wife (or her family) needs to know about mahr — from setting the amount to recovering unpaid mahr through the courts.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

What is Mahr (Dower) Under Muslim Law?

Mahr (مهر) — variously transliterated as mehr or dower — is a mandatory financial gift or payment that a Muslim husband is obligated to give his wife upon marriage under Islamic law. In Bangladesh, mahr is governed by Muslim personal law as preserved and applied through secular legislation.

Mahr is distinct from other concepts in several important ways:

  • It is not a bride price: Mahr belongs exclusively to the wife — not to her parents or family. She has absolute ownership and control over her mahr once received.
  • It is not a gift: Unlike a gift (which the giver may choose to make or not), mahr is a legal obligation on the husband. The wife has an enforceable legal right to demand it.
  • It is a debt: If the husband fails to pay mahr, the wife can sue him in court to recover it as she would sue for any other debt. The husband's estate is liable for unpaid mahr even after his death.
  • It is consideration for the marriage (in a legal sense): Classical Islamic jurisprudence regards mahr as one of the essential elements that gives the marriage contract (nikah) legal validity, though the marriage is not void merely because mahr is not specified at the time of the nikah.

The concept of mahr is recognised and enforceable in Bangladesh under the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937, which directs that in matters of Muslim personal law (including marriage, dower, divorce, and inheritance), the rule of decision shall be Muslim personal law (shariat).

Types of Mahr — Prompt (Mu'ajjal) and Deferred (Mu'akhkhar)

Muslim law and the nikah contract in Bangladesh (kabinnama) can divide mahr into two portions based on when they become payable:

Type of MahrArabic TermBengali TermWhen PayableKey Features
Prompt DowerMu'ajjal (معجل)নগদ দেনমোহরImmediately upon demand; wife can demand at any time after marriageWife can refuse to live with husband until paid; she can leave the marital home
Deferred DowerMu'akhkhar (مؤخر)বাকি দেনমোহর / উশুল দেনমোহরUpon dissolution of marriage (divorce or death of husband)Automatically becomes due and payable when marriage ends; priority debt of estate

In Bangladesh, the kabinnama (nikah registration certificate) issued by the Nikah Registrar (কাজি) typically specifies both a prompt mahr amount (নগদ উশুল) and a deferred mahr amount (বাকি আদায়). The kabinnama is the primary documentary evidence of the agreed mahr amount.

Practical reality in Bangladesh: In many marriages, particularly in rural areas, the entire mahr is listed as deferred — meaning the wife cannot demand it until divorce or the husband's death. However, the portion listed as prompt becomes immediately payable upon the wife's demand. A well-advised wife (or her family) should negotiate for a significant portion of the mahr to be classified as prompt dower (mu'ajjal).

Legal Basis for Mahr in Bangladesh

The legal framework governing mahr in Bangladesh is built on several overlapping sources of law:

  • Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937: This Act directs that Muslim personal law shall apply in all matters of marriage, dower, maintenance, divorce, and inheritance for Muslims in Bangladesh. It makes the rules of Islamic jurisprudence (as interpreted by the courts) enforceable through secular courts.
  • Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (MFLO 1961): This Ordinance governs nikah registration, talaq procedures, polygamy rules, and other aspects of Muslim family law. While it does not directly specify mahr amounts, it requires all nikahs to be registered with the Nikah Registrar, who must record the agreed mahr amount in the kabinnama. This makes mahr a matter of official record.
  • Family Courts Ordinance 1985: This legislation established Family Courts (পারিবারিক আদালত) in Bangladesh with jurisdiction over matrimonial disputes including recovery of mahr and maintenance. The Family Court is the primary forum for mahr recovery suits.
  • Muslim law jurisprudence: Bangladesh courts apply the Hanafi school of Islamic jurisprudence (the dominant school in South Asia) in matters of personal law. Under Hanafi law, the minimum mahr is 10 dirhams (a nominal silver-based amount), though there is no maximum. Courts have also recognised the concept of 'proper dower' (مهر المثل, Mahr al-Mithl) when no mahr is specified in the kabinnama.
  • Evidence Act 1872: Governs how mahr claims are proved in court — the kabinnama, witness testimony, and other evidence.

How Mahr Amount is Set — Kabinnama and Negotiation

The mahr amount is typically agreed between the parties (or their families) at the time of the nikah and recorded in the kabinnama (কাবিননামা) — the official nikah registration certificate. The kabinnama is prepared by the licensed Nikah Registrar (কাজি) who officiated or registered the marriage.

What the Kabinnama Records About Mahr

The standard government-issued kabinnama form in Bangladesh contains specific columns for recording:

  • Total mahr amount (মোট দেনমোহর)
  • Amount paid as prompt mahr (নগদ উশুল / পরিশোধিত)
  • Amount deferred (বাকি / আদায়যোগ্য)
  • Whether prompt mahr was paid in cash, gold, or other property

What Happens If the Kabinnama is Lost or Destroyed?

If the kabinnama is lost (a common problem in Bangladesh due to floods, fires, and poor document preservation), the mahr claim does not disappear. The wife can prove the mahr amount through:

  • Testimony of persons present at the nikah (witnesses, family members)
  • Certified copy of the kabinnama from the Nikah Registrar's office (all Nikah Registrars are required to maintain a register)
  • If the registered copy is also unavailable, the court may apply the concept of proper dower (Mahr al-Mithl) — an amount equivalent to what was settled for the wife's paternal female relatives of similar social standing at the time of their marriages

Negotiating Mahr Amount

There is no legally prescribed minimum mahr in Bangladesh beyond the classical Hanafi minimum (10 dirhams — now a negligible symbolic amount). In practice, mahr amounts range from a few thousand taka to crores, depending on the financial standing of the parties and family negotiations. A higher mahr provides stronger financial security for the wife. Given that mahr is often the wife's only guaranteed financial asset from the marriage, families are well-advised to negotiate a meaningful amount.

Minimum and Maximum Mahr — What Does the Law Say?

One of the most frequently asked questions about mahr is whether there is a legally prescribed minimum or maximum amount. Here is the position under Bangladesh law:

  • Minimum Mahr: Under Hanafi jurisprudence (which Bangladesh courts apply), the minimum mahr is 10 silver dirhams — historically equivalent to approximately 30.6 grams of silver. In modern Bangladesh, courts have not enforced a specific taka equivalent for this minimum, and any amount agreed upon between the parties is generally upheld. However, courts will not enforce a mahr of zero (i.e., the complete absence of mahr is not permissible under Muslim law, though it does not void the marriage).
  • Maximum Mahr: There is no maximum mahr under Muslim law or Bangladesh legislation. The amount is entirely at the discretion of the parties. However, courts have noted in some cases that an extremely high mahr amount that appears to have been agreed under duress may be subject to reduction if the husband can prove duress — this is an exceptional circumstance and the burden of proof is on the husband.
  • Proper Dower (Mahr al-Mithl): If no mahr was agreed at the time of the nikah, or if the kabinnama is silent on the amount, the wife is entitled to proper dower — an amount that the court determines based on the mahr settled for the wife's paternal female relatives (sisters, paternal aunts) of similar social position, age, and educational background. This is a judicially determined amount that varies case by case.

Courts across Bangladesh have upheld significant mahr amounts in recovery suits, treating mahr as an enforceable debt. The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court has consistently held that mahr is a legal right of the wife that cannot be defeated by informal agreements or social pressure.

Can Mahr Be Waived or Reduced?

This is a critical question with significant legal nuance. The general principle is:

Mahr can only be validly waived or reduced by the wife herself, voluntarily, freely, and after having received or been in a position to receive the mahr.

Specific rules under Hanafi law as applied in Bangladesh:

  • Voluntary remission by wife: A wife of full legal capacity (adult, of sound mind) can voluntarily forgive (remit) all or part of her mahr. This is called ibra (إبراء). Once validly remitted, the wife cannot later claim the remitted portion.
  • Conditions for valid remission: The remission must be: (a) made freely and without coercion or undue influence; (b) made by the wife herself (not by her guardian or family members); and (c) made with full knowledge of the amount being remitted.
  • Coerced remission is void: If the husband (or his family) pressures, threatens, or coerces the wife into signing a document waiving her mahr, or if the wife signs under threats of violence, the waiver is void under both Muslim law and general contract law principles (see Section 15-19 of the Contract Act 1872 on coercion and undue influence).
  • Remission before receiving mahr: Under classical Hanafi law, a wife's remission of mahr before it becomes payable (before marriage is consummated, for example) requires additional caution — some scholars hold such pre-payment remission invalid as the wife cannot truly consent to foregoing something she has not yet received.
  • Social pressure is not consent: Bangladesh courts have repeatedly held that social pressure, family mediations, or verbal agreements to 'settle' mahr disputes outside court do not constitute valid legal remission if the wife later claims the mahr was not freely waived.

Recovering Unpaid Mahr — Legal Remedies Available

When a husband refuses or fails to pay mahr, the wife has several powerful legal remedies available under Bangladesh law:

Option 1 — Family Court Suit (Most Common)

Under the Family Courts Ordinance 1985, the Family Court (পারিবারিক আদালত) at the district level has jurisdiction to hear mahr recovery suits. The Family Court process is:

  1. File a plaint (আর্জি) in the Family Court of the district where the wife resides or where the marriage was registered
  2. Produce the kabinnama or other evidence of mahr amount
  3. The court attempts reconciliation first (within 30 days)
  4. If reconciliation fails, trial proceeds — usually faster than regular civil courts
  5. Court passes decree for recovery of mahr as a money decree
  6. If unpaid, the wife can execute the decree against the husband's property (attach and sell his assets)

Option 2 — Civil Suit

A mahr recovery suit can also be filed as a regular civil suit (money suit) in the Civil Court. However, since the Family Courts Ordinance 1985 gives Family Courts exclusive jurisdiction over mahr matters, a separate civil suit for mahr alone is not generally maintainable.

Option 3 — Refusing to Cohabit (for Prompt Dower)

For unpaid prompt dower (mu'ajjal), the wife has a classical Muslim law right of non-consummation / refusal of cohabitation — she can refuse to live with the husband and cannot be compelled to do so until the prompt mahr is paid. If the husband files a restitution of conjugal rights suit against her, the court will take the unpaid mahr into account as a defence.

Option 4 — Mahr as Defence in Divorce Proceedings

When the husband files for divorce (talaq), the wife can raise the unpaid mahr as a claim, and the court will pass a decree for mahr recovery alongside or as part of the divorce decree. This gives the wife significant leverage.
