Frequently Asked Questions

What minimum shareholding is needed to file an oppression petition in Bangladesh?

Under Section 233(1)(a) of the Companies Act 1994, the petitioner or petitioners must hold at least one-tenth (10%) of the issued share capital of the company. Multiple minority shareholders can combine their holdings to meet this statutory threshold.

Which court hears corporate oppression cases in Bangladesh?

Company petitions under Section 233 are filed exclusively before the Company Bench of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, which exercises specialized original company jurisdiction.

Can the High Court freeze company bank accounts in a shareholder dispute?

Yes. The High Court has wide discretionary powers under Section 233(2) to pass ad-interim orders freezing corporate bank accounts or requiring joint signatures to prevent the majority from siphoning funds while litigation is pending.

Can a board of directors remove a director without a shareholder meeting?

No. Under Section 106 of the Companies Act 1994, a director can only be removed by an extraordinary resolution passed by shareholders at a properly convened general meeting after special notice. A board of directors has no statutory power to remove a peer.

What happens if majority directors dilute my shareholding without my knowledge?

If the majority issues new shares without offering pre-emptive rights to existing shareholders, the High Court will examine the bona fides of the transaction and can declare the share allotment illegal and cancel the RJSC return of allotment under Section 43.

Can the High Court order the majority to buy out my shares?

Yes. One of the most common and practical remedies granted under Section 233 is an order directing the majority shareholders or the company itself to purchase the minority's shares at a fair market valuation determined by an independent court-appointed auditor.

How long does a Section 233 Company Petition take in the High Court?

Initial ad-interim protective orders (such as bank freezes and status quo orders) can be secured within 1 to 2 weeks of filing. Full hearing and final disposal typically take between 6 to 18 months, depending on the complexity of forensic audits.

Can an overseas non-resident Bangladeshi (NRB) shareholder file a Section 233 petition?

Yes. An NRB shareholder residing abroad can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the local Bangladesh High Commission or Embassy, empowering an advocate in Bangladesh to institute and prosecute the company petition on their behalf.

Mobile Banking Fraud Bangladesh: Legal Action Against bKash, Nagad Scams

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-03-31 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Mobile banking fraud — particularly involving bKash, Nagad, and Rocket — has become one of the most common financial crimes in Bangladesh. Fraudsters use SIM swapping, phishing, fake customer service calls, and social engineering to empty mobile wallets in minutes. If you have been victimised, swift legal action is critical — money recovery becomes significantly harder with each passing hour.

: · Cyber Crime & Criminal Defense Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing LawCyber Security Act, 2023 & Penal Code, 1860 (Bangladesh)
First Step at Police StationFile an Online or In-Person General Diary (GD) at gd.police.gov.bd / local Thana
Police Cyber Support for Women (PCSW)Helpline: 01320-000888 | Email: cybersupport.women@police.gov.bd
CID / CTTC Cyber Crime Unit24/7 Emergency: 999 | Police Headquarters & Cyber Tribunal Dhaka
Required Digital EvidenceFull URLs, unedited screenshots, transaction IDs (bKash/Nagad), and call logs
📋 In This Article
  1. Common Types of Mobile Banking Fraud in Bangladesh
  2. Which Laws Apply to Mobile Banking Fraud?
  3. Immediate Steps After Mobile Banking Fraud
  4. How to File a Complaint: Step-by-Step
  5. Can You Recover Your Money?
  6. DSA and Penal Code: Which Case to File?
  7. How to Recover Money Lost to Mobile Banking Fraud
  8. Protecting Yourself from Future Mobile Banking Fraud
  9. Role of a Cyber Law Lawyer

Common Types of Mobile Banking Fraud in Bangladesh

Mobile banking fraud in Bangladesh typically takes one of these forms:

  • Fake customer service calls: Fraudsters impersonate bKash/Nagad agents, claim your account is being blocked, and ask for your PIN or OTP.
  • SIM swap fraud: The fraudster convinces the telecom operator to transfer your SIM to their device, gaining access to OTPs.
  • Phishing links: Fake bKash or Nagad websites/apps steal your login credentials.
  • Online marketplace fraud: For items sold on Facebook or local platforms, payment is initiated and then reversed.
  • Lottery and prize scams: Victims are told they have won a prize and asked to send money for "processing fees".

Immediate Steps After Mobile Banking Fraud

Act within the first few hours for the best chance of recovery:

  1. Call bKash (16247), Nagad (16167) or Rocket (16216) immediately and report the fraud — request a transaction freeze or reversal.
  2. Screenshot all transaction records from your mobile banking app.
  3. Note the fraudster's mobile number if you have it.
  4. Contact your telecom operator if you suspect SIM swap.
  5. File a GD or FIR at the nearest police station — include the fraudster's number and all transaction details.
  6. Contact a cyber law lawyer immediately — a court order can freeze the recipient account before funds are withdrawn.

How to File a Complaint: Step-by-Step

For mobile banking fraud in Bangladesh, file complaints at multiple levels simultaneously:

  1. Mobile Banking Provider: File a fraud complaint through their helpline and follow up in writing. Ask for all transaction records (sender, receiver, timestamps).
  2. Police Station (FIR): File an FIR under Penal Code Section 420 (cheating) and DSA Section 24 (online fraud). Attach transaction screenshots, fraudster's number, and your statement.
  3. Bangladesh Bank: If a bank account was involved in the transfer chain, Bangladesh Bank's Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) can freeze funds.
  4. Cyber Tribunal: For DSA-specific complaints, file directly or through your lawyer before the Cyber Tribunal in Dhaka.

A cyber law lawyer in Dhaka can draft all these complaints simultaneously and obtain emergency court orders to freeze suspect accounts.

Can You Recover Your Money?

Money recovery is possible but time-sensitive:

  • If funds have not yet been withdrawn from the recipient's mobile wallet, an emergency court order can freeze the account and direct the MFS provider to reverse the transaction.
  • If already withdrawn as cash, tracing is much harder — though not impossible with police digital forensics.
  • Bangladesh Bank has issued directives requiring licensed MFS providers to cooperate with fraud investigations.

Courts in Bangladesh have granted emergency injunctions freezing mobile wallet accounts within 24–48 hours in fraud cases. Speed is everything. Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam in Uttara immediately for emergency legal intervention.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

DSA and Penal Code: Which Case to File?

Both laws apply simultaneously — and you should use both:

  • Penal Code 1860, Section 420: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property — up to 7 years' imprisonment.
  • Digital Security Act 2018, Section 24: Online fraud and cheating — up to 7 years' imprisonment and BDT 5 lakh fine, or both.

Filing under both laws strengthens your case. DSA cases go to the Cyber Tribunal (faster process); Penal Code cases go to regular Magistrate courts. An experienced Uttara cyber lawyer will structure your complaint to maximize legal pressure.

How to Recover Money Lost to Mobile Banking Fraud

Recovering money lost to mobile banking fraud in Bangladesh requires a multi-track approach — legal intervention alone is rarely sufficient without also working with the mobile financial service (MFS) provider and Bangladesh Bank's regulatory mechanisms. Here is a comprehensive recovery strategy:

Track 1: Emergency Court Order (Most Effective)

The most powerful recovery tool is an emergency injunction from a civil court ordering the MFS provider to freeze the recipient's account before the fraudster withdraws the funds. This requires:

  1. Immediate lawyer engagement — within hours, not days, of the fraud.
  2. Your lawyer files an emergency application before the Civil Court or Cyber Tribunal.
  3. The court issues an ex-parte (one-sided, without notice to the fraudster) injunction ordering bKash/Nagad to freeze the specific account to which the money was transferred.
  4. The MFS provider complies and the funds are frozen pending further court orders.
  5. Following the FIR and police investigation, the frozen funds can be released to you through a court order for return.

Courts in Bangladesh have issued such emergency injunctions within 24–48 hours in documented fraud cases. Speed is everything — every hour allows the fraudster to withdraw and dissipate the funds.

Track 2: Bangladesh Bank Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU)

Bangladesh Bank's Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) has authority under the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012 to freeze accounts involved in financial crime. For large fraud amounts (over BDT 1 lakh), engaging the FIU through your complaint to Bangladesh Bank adds an additional layer of regulatory pressure on the MFS provider to cooperate with recovery efforts.

Track 3: MFS Provider Fraud Policy

File a formal written complaint with the MFS provider's fraud investigation team (not just customer service) with: your mobile number and account details; the fraudster's number to which money was transferred; exact transaction reference numbers, amounts, and timestamps; copy of the FIR you filed with police; and a formal demand for transaction freeze and reversal. The provider can freeze the recipient account at their level even without a court order in clear fraud cases.

Realistic Recovery Chances

  • If caught within 1–2 hours: 70–80% chance of recovery through emergency freeze
  • If reported within 24 hours (funds still in wallet): 40–60% chance with court order
  • If funds already withdrawn as cash: Less than 20% chance of full recovery — but partial recovery through criminal case compensation is possible

Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam in Uttara immediately — our firm has experience in emergency cyber fraud interventions. Do not wait, do not try to resolve it yourself. Every minute lost reduces your chances of recovery.

Protecting Yourself from Future Mobile Banking Fraud

Prevention is far better than recovery. Once you have addressed an immediate fraud incident — or even before it happens — taking protective measures significantly reduces your vulnerability to future mobile banking fraud in Bangladesh.

Security Best Practices

  • Never share your PIN or OTP: bKash, Nagad, Rocket, and Upay will never call you and ask for your PIN or OTP. Any such request is 100% fraud — hang up immediately.
  • Enable all available security features: Set up biometric login, enable transaction alerts for every transaction, and use a strong, unique PIN that you change regularly.
  • Register SIM in your own name: Ensure your mobile SIM is registered to your own NID. Contact your telecom operator to verify. Fraudsters exploit SIM registrations under others' names for SIM swap attacks.
  • Beware of fake apps: Only download bKash, Nagad, and Rocket apps from official sources (Google Play Store or Apple App Store). Verify the developer name carefully — fake apps with near-identical names are a growing threat.
  • Set transaction limits: Enable low daily transaction limits on your mobile banking account and only increase them temporarily when you need a large transfer.

If Your SIM Is Swapped or Lost

If you suddenly lose mobile signal or cannot access your SIM, immediately: call your telecom operator from another phone to report SIM compromise; call bKash (16247) / Nagad (16167) / Rocket (16216) to freeze your mobile banking account temporarily; visit the nearest telecom office with your NID to restore your SIM; and file a GD at the nearest police station as a precautionary measure.

Bangladesh has enacted the Digital Security Act 2018 (now Cyber Security Act 2023) specifically to address digital financial crimes. The penalties for mobile banking fraud are severe — up to 7 years imprisonment and BDT 5 lakh fine under DSA Section 24. Consult a cyber crime lawyer in Dhaka for emergency legal intervention.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the success rate for mobile banking fraud cases in Bangladesh?

Cases where the fraudster's mobile number is identified, and complaints are filed within 24-48 hours, have a significantly higher recovery rate. Cases with strong digital evidence (transaction logs, call records) are most successful.

Can I get my money back if it was already withdrawn?

Once cash is withdrawn, recovery is difficult. However, courts can order asset recovery proceedings against identified fraudsters, and Bangladesh Bank fraud liability guidelines may require MFS providers to contribute to compensation in certain circumstances.

Will bKash or Nagad refund my money automatically?

Not automatically for fraud cases. You must file a formal complaint with the provider. If you can demonstrate the transaction was unauthorized, and they cooperate with police, funds in their system may be frozen and returned through a court order.

What if the fraudster used a fake SIM?

Police can obtain call data records (CDR) from the telecom operator to trace the physical location where the SIM was activated and used. CCTV evidence and tower location data have been used successfully in Bangladesh fraud cases.

Mobile Court Bangladesh – Powers, Offences, Fines & Your Rights

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-06 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

The mobile court (ভ্রাম্যমাণ আদালত) is one of the most visible arms of enforcement law in Bangladesh — appearing at markets, restaurants, construction sites, and public spaces to impose on-the-spot fines and even imprisonment for regulatory violations. Understanding the Mobile Court Act 2009, what powers these courts actually have, your rights when facing one, and how to legally challenge an unjust order can make all the difference. This guide covers everything you need to know.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

📋 In This Article

  2. Legal Basis: The Mobile Court Act 2009
  3. Which Magistrates Can Run a Mobile Court?
  4. List of Offences Covered by Mobile Courts
  5. Maximum Sentence Limits Under the Act
  6. Table of Common Offences vs Penalties
  7. Your Rights When Facing a Mobile Court
  8. How to Challenge or Appeal a Mobile Court Order
  9. High Court Writ Against Unfair Mobile Court Action
  10. Important Limitations and Criticisms of Mobile Courts
  11. Get Legal Help Today

What Is a Mobile Court in Bangladesh?

A mobile court (ভ্রাম্যমাণ আদালত) is a special summary court that operates outside the traditional courtroom — moving to the location where an offence is being committed or where regulatory violations are suspected. Rather than waiting for a case to go through the ordinary criminal justice process, the mobile court enables an executive magistrate to investigate, try, convict, and sentence a person on the spot, often within minutes.

Mobile courts currently operate across Bangladesh in sectors including:

  • Food safety and adulteration (bazaars, restaurants, food factories)
  • Weights and measurements fraud (shops, markets)
  • Environmental pollution (industrial areas, brick kilns)
  • Consumer protection violations (shops overcharging or selling expired goods)
  • Building code violations (construction sites)
  • Drug laws (pharmacies selling medicines without prescription)
  • Road transport regulations (vehicles without proper documents)
  • Public health and sanitation violations

While mobile courts serve a genuine enforcement function, they have also been criticised for procedural shortcuts that sometimes violate the constitutional rights of accused persons. Understanding the law is essential whether you are a business owner, consumer advocate, or individual citizen.

Legal Basis: The Mobile Court Act 2009

The Mobile Court Act 2009 (Act No. LIX of 2009), known in Bangla as the ভ্রাম্যমাণ আদালত আইন ২০০৯, provides the formal statutory basis for mobile courts in Bangladesh. Prior to this Act, mobile courts operated under a 2007 executive order during the caretaker government. The 2009 Act converted them into a permanent feature of Bangladesh law.

Key structural features of the 2009 Act include:

  • Section 3: Authorises the government to empower executive magistrates to conduct mobile court proceedings.
  • Section 4: Specifies which laws can be enforced through mobile courts. These are listed in a Schedule attached to the Act and can be expanded by government notification.
  • Section 5: Sets out trial procedure — the magistrate must allow the accused to make a statement before imposing any sentence.
  • Section 6: Imposes a ceiling on punishment — mobile courts cannot impose imprisonment exceeding 2 years or fines exceeding Taka 2,00,000 (two lakh) for any single offence, regardless of what the parent law provides.
  • Section 7: Provides for appeal against mobile court orders.
  • Section 10: Bars courts from taking cognizance of an offence already dealt with by a mobile court (protection against double jeopardy).

The Schedule to the Act, as currently in force, lists over 40 laws under which mobile court proceedings can be initiated, covering food, environment, consumer protection, narcotics, building safety, road transport, and more.

Which Magistrates Can Run a Mobile Court?

Not every government officer can conduct a mobile court. The Mobile Court Act 2009 specifically limits this power to executive magistrates who have been assigned mobile court powers by the government under Section 3 of the Act. The key points are:

  • Only Executive Magistrates (not Judicial Magistrates) are empowered to conduct mobile courts. The distinction matters — Bangladesh separated the executive and judicial magistracy under the Supreme Court directives in 2007. Judicial Magistrates handle criminal cases under the CrPC; executive magistrates handle regulatory enforcement.
  • Executive Magistrates are officers of the district administration under the Deputy Commissioner (DC). They are typically Assistant Commissioners (AC), Upazila Nirbahi Officers (UNO), or Additional District Magistrates (ADM).
  • The government specifies which officers have mobile court powers by gazette notification. An executive magistrate conducting a mobile court without proper authorisation is acting ultra vires, which can be challenged in the High Court.
  • In practice, mobile courts are often conducted jointly with the police, army (during special drives), or sector-specific enforcement agencies (e.g., BSTI for weights and measures, BFSA for food safety).

It is important to verify the identity and authorisation of any magistrate conducting a mobile court action against you or your business. Failure of the magistrate to disclose their authority is itself grounds for challenge.

List of Offences Covered by Mobile Courts

The Schedule to the Mobile Court Act 2009 currently covers enforcement actions under the following categories of law (the list is non-exhaustive as the government can add by notification):

  • Food Safety: The Food Safety Act 2013 — sale of adulterated, rotten, or expired food products; use of harmful preservatives; operating food businesses without licence.
  • Weights and Measures: The Weights and Measures Ordinance 1982 — using fraudulent or uncertified weighing equipment in commercial transactions.
  • Consumer Protection: The Consumer Rights Protection Act 2009 — overcharging, deceptive advertising, selling goods below quality, refusing to give receipts.
  • Environment: The Environment Conservation Act 1995 — releasing pollutants, operating polluting industries without clearance, brick kilns without proper licence.
  • Narcotics and Drugs: The Drugs Act 1940 — pharmacies selling controlled medicines without prescription, stocking counterfeit medicines.
  • Building Code: The Building Construction Act 1952 — construction without permission, violation of approved plan, unsafe structures.
  • Road Transport: The Motor Vehicles Ordinance 1983 — driving without licence, overloading, unfit vehicles.
  • Tobacco Control: The Smoking and Tobacco Products Usage (Control) Act 2005 — smoking in public places, selling tobacco to minors.
  • Public Health: The Infectious Disease Prevention and Elimination Act 2018 — violations of public health orders.
  • Land and Property: Certain provisions relating to illegal occupation of government land or encroachment on water bodies.

Note that the mobile court cannot try any offence not listed in the Schedule. Attempting to do so renders the conviction void and open to challenge.

Maximum Sentence Limits Under the Act

This is one of the most important safeguards in the Mobile Court Act 2009. Regardless of the penalty prescribed in the parent law, a mobile court is constitutionally capped at:

  • Imprisonment: Maximum 2 years (rigorous or simple) for any single offence. If the parent law prescribes a longer sentence, the mobile court can only impose up to 2 years. The remainder of the sentence would require a regular court proceeding.
  • Fine: Maximum Taka 2,00,000 (two lakh) for any single offence. Again, if the parent law prescribes a higher fine, the mobile court is capped at two lakh.
  • A mobile court cannot impose the death penalty, life imprisonment, or any sentence of imprisonment exceeding 2 years, no matter the gravity of the offence.
  • Mobile courts cannot try scheduled offences of a serious nature listed under the First Schedule of the CrPC, such as murder, rape, or kidnapping. These require Judicial Magistrate or Sessions Court proceedings.

In practice, most mobile court penalties are fines rather than imprisonment. When imprisonment is ordered, it is typically for a matter of days or weeks for repeat or flagrant offenders. The immediacy and certainty of the penalty is the mobile court primary deterrent tool.

Table of Common Offences vs Penalties

The table below shows common mobile court offences, the governing law, and the typical penalties that can currently be imposed:

Consumer rights violation (overcharging)Consumer Rights Protection Act 20091 yearTk. 50,000
Environmental pollutionEnvironment Conservation Act 19952 years (mobile court cap)Tk. 2,00,000
Driving without licenceMotor Vehicles Ordinance 19833 monthsTk. 25,000

Your Rights When Facing a Mobile Court

Many people are unaware that they have meaningful legal rights even in the rapid-fire environment of a mobile court proceeding. The Mobile Court Act 2009 and the Constitution of Bangladesh both guarantee certain protections:

Right to Make a Statement (Section 5)

Before imposing any penalty, the magistrate must give you an opportunity to make a statement in your defence. This is not optional — it is a mandatory procedural requirement. If you are convicted without being given this opportunity, the conviction is procedurally defective and can be challenged on appeal.

Right to Know the Charge

The magistrate must inform you of the specific offence you are accused of committing and the law under which the charge is brought. A vague or unspecified charge is legally invalid.

Right to Verify Authorisation

You have the right to ask the executive magistrate to identify themselves and confirm their authorisation to conduct a mobile court under Section 3 of the Mobile Court Act 2009. A mobile court conducted by an unauthorised officer is void.

Right Against Self-Incrimination

Under Article 35(4) of the Constitution of Bangladesh, no person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. While mobile court proceedings are summary in nature, this constitutional protection still applies. You cannot be forced to confess.

Right to Pay Fine Instead of Imprisonment

In most mobile court proceedings, the magistrate has discretion to impose a fine rather than imprisonment. You may request that the magistrate exercise this discretion in your favour, particularly for first-time or minor offences.

Right of Appeal

Any mobile court conviction can be appealed. This is perhaps the most important right — and it is discussed in detail in the next section.

How to Challenge or Appeal a Mobile Court Order

A mobile court conviction is not the end of the road. Bangladesh law provides a clear appeals mechanism under Section 7 of the Mobile Court Act 2009:

  1. Who hears the appeal? An appeal against a mobile court order lies before the Sessions Judge of the relevant district. The Sessions Judge has full power to confirm, modify, or set aside the mobile court conviction and sentence.
  2. Time limit for appeal: The appeal must be filed within 30 days of the mobile court order. Missing this deadline can result in the appeal being barred, though courts have discretion to condone delay in exceptional circumstances.
  3. Grounds for appeal: Common grounds include: (a) the offence was not in the Schedule of the Mobile Court Act; (b) you were not given an opportunity to make a statement; (c) the magistrate was not authorised; (d) the fine or imprisonment exceeded the statutory cap; (e) the facts did not constitute an offence under the charged law.
  4. Stay of sentence: Upon filing the appeal, you can apply to the Sessions Judge for a stay of the sentence pending appeal — particularly important if you have been ordered to pay a large fine or undergo imprisonment.
  5. Legal representation: Unlike the summary mobile court proceeding itself (where lawyers are not typically present on the spot), you are fully entitled to be represented by an advocate in the appeals proceedings before the Sessions Judge.

It is advisable to consult a criminal lawyer immediately after receiving a mobile court order that you intend to challenge, given the 30-day limitation period.

High Court Writ Against Unfair Mobile Court Action

Beyond the appeal to the Sessions Judge, persons who believe that a mobile court action was fundamentally unlawful — rather than merely factually wrong — can approach the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh for constitutional relief under Article 102 of the Constitution.

Grounds for a High Court writ (certiorari or mandamus) against a mobile court include:

  • The magistrate was not legally authorised to conduct a mobile court (ultra vires).
  • The offence is not covered by the Schedule to the Mobile Court Act 2009.
  • The penalty imposed exceeded the statutory caps (over 2 years or over Tk. 2 lakh).
  • The proceeding violated a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution (e.g., right against self-incrimination, right to equality).
  • The mobile court action was politically motivated or conducted in bad faith.

The High Court has historically been willing to scrutinise mobile court actions carefully. In several notable cases, the court has quashed mobile court convictions where procedural requirements were not followed. Filing a writ petition requires the assistance of an advocate enrolled in the High Court Division.

Additionally, if a mobile court action results in unlawful arrest or detention, a habeas corpus petition under Article 102(2)(b) of the Constitution is available to secure immediate release.

Important Limitations and Criticisms of Mobile Courts

Despite their utility as enforcement tools, mobile courts in Bangladesh have attracted significant criticism from legal scholars, civil society organisations, and the courts themselves:

  • No lawyers present: Accused persons in mobile court proceedings typically have no access to legal counsel at the time of the proceeding, compromising their ability to defend themselves effectively.
  • Summary procedure risks injustice: The entire process from accusation to sentence can occur in minutes. There is no examination of witnesses in the traditional sense and no opportunity to present documentary evidence.
  • Executive, not judicial: The separation of the executive and judicial magistracy means that mobile courts are run by executive officers who may face political pressure, creating risk of misuse.
  • Expansion beyond original intent: Critics argue that mobile courts have expanded far beyond their original enforcement role and are sometimes used for purposes that should properly go through the ordinary criminal justice system.
  • Constitutional tension: The Bangladesh Constitution guarantees the right to a fair trial under Article 31 and 35. Summary mobile court proceedings have been criticised as incompatible with these guarantees in certain applications.

These concerns make it especially important that anyone subjected to an unfair or illegitimate mobile court action knows their right to appeal and to seek High Court review.

Get Legal Help Today

If you or your business has been subjected to a mobile court order — whether a fine, closure notice, or imprisonment — it is important to act quickly. The 30-day appeal deadline under Section 7 of the Mobile Court Act 2009 is strict, and early legal advice can mean the difference between a conviction becoming permanent or being overturned.

Advocate Md. Shah Alam, operating from his Uttara, Dhaka chamber, has represented clients in mobile court appeal proceedings before Sessions Judges and in High Court writ petitions challenging unlawful mobile court actions. His team can assess the legality of any mobile court order, advise on grounds for challenge, and represent you at every level of the legal process.

Contact us today for an urgent consultation. Speak with our criminal lawyer to protect your rights against mobile court overreach.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a mobile court send me to jail immediately in Bangladesh?

Yes, under the Mobile Court Act 2009, an executive magistrate can impose on-the-spot imprisonment for up to 2 years for Schedule offences. However, in practice, mobile courts predominantly impose fines. Imprisonment is reserved for serious or repeat violations. You have the right to make a statement before any sentence is imposed.

What is the maximum fine a mobile court can impose in Bangladesh?

The maximum fine a mobile court can impose is Taka 2,00,000 (two lakh), regardless of what the parent law prescribes. Similarly, imprisonment cannot exceed 2 years, even if the parent law provides for a longer sentence. These caps are set by Section 6 of the Mobile Court Act 2009.

How do I appeal a mobile court decision in Bangladesh?

Under Section 7 of the Mobile Court Act 2009, you can appeal to the Sessions Judge of the relevant district within 30 days of the mobile court order. The Sessions Judge can confirm, modify, or set aside the conviction and sentence. You should engage a criminal lawyer immediately to file the appeal within the deadline.

Can I challenge a mobile court action in the High Court?

Yes. If the mobile court action was fundamentally unlawful — for example, the offence was not in the Schedule, the magistrate was not authorised, or the penalty exceeded statutory caps — you can file a writ petition in the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. The High Court has quashed several mobile court convictions on such grounds.

Do I have the right to a lawyer during a mobile court proceeding?

The Mobile Court Act 2009 does not guarantee the right to have a lawyer present during the on-the-spot summary proceeding. However, you have the right to make a statement in your defence. If the case goes to appeal before the Sessions Judge, you are fully entitled to legal representation.

Can a mobile court close my business permanently?

A mobile court can order temporary closure of a business premises as part of its enforcement action. However, permanent closure or cancellation of trade licences typically requires separate administrative or regulatory proceedings, not a mobile court order alone. A lawyer can help you understand the scope of any closure order made against your business.

Bank Account Freeze in Bangladesh: BFIU Rules, Money Laundering Act & Court Remedies

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-08 · 19 minutes

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Discovering that your commercial or personal bank account has been suddenly frozen in Bangladesh without advance warning is a critical operational crisis for businesses, overseas investors, and Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs). Cheques bounce, payrolls halt, and inward trade remittances are blocked. In most cases, these freezes are initiated by the Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU) or the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) under the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012 (Act No. V of 2012). However, statutory agencies must strictly adhere to statutory time limits and due process. Indefinite administrative freezes without court confirmation violate constitutional protections under Articles 31 and 42. This exhaustive legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate and criminal litigation practitioner in Uttara and Dhaka Court, explains the legal mechanisms of account freezes, statutory limitation windows, and actionable procedures to unfreeze funds through the Special Judge Court and High Court Division.

1. Statutory Framework: Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012

In Bangladesh, financial asset freezing is governed by the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012 (Act No. V of 2012) along with the Anti-Terrorism Act 2009. The statutory architecture aims to curb illicit financial flows, bribery, extortion, trade-based money laundering, and tax evasion. However, aggressive application often ensnares legitimate commercial enterprises, export-import firms, and non-resident investors.

The law creates a strict division between administrative inquiry powers and judicial authority. Under Section 23, the Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU), housed within Bangladesh Bank, serves as the central national agency responsible for analyzing Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) and Cash Transaction Reports (CTRs) submitted by commercial scheduled banks. While the BFIU has executive authority to freeze transactions provisionally, it cannot confiscate property or freeze funds indefinitely without judicial scrutiny. The ultimate authority to try offences and order substantive property attachments resides with the designated Senior Special Judge Courts established under the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1958.

Understanding this distinction is vital. When an account holder receives a generic freeze notice from their branch manager, identifying whether the action stems from an administrative BFIU directive, a police investigatory desk, or a formal court order determines the appropriate judicial countermeasure. Consult our guide on quashing false criminal cases in Bangladesh for related trial procedures.

2. BFIU Powers Under Section 23: The 30-Day & 6-Month Limits

The power of the BFIU to restrict banking operations is strictly defined by Section 23(1)(c) of Act No. V of 2012. Under this provision, if the BFIU has reasonable grounds to suspect that an account is linked to money laundering or predicate offences, it may issue an executive order directing the scheduled bank to suspend transactions in that account.

The statute imposes rigorous temporal constraints on this emergency power:

  • Initial 30-Day Validity: The initial administrative freezing order issued by the BFIU is legally effective for a period not exceeding thirty (30) days from the date of issuance.
  • Incremental Extension Up to 6 Months: If the inquiry requires further analysis, the BFIU may extend the suspension period. However, Section 23(1)(c) establishes that the total cumulative period of such administrative extensions cannot exceed six (6) months (180 days).
  • Mandatory Referral to Law Enforcement: During the six-month window, the BFIU must transmit its investigative report to an authorized investigatory agency—such as the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC), the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) of Police, or the National Board of Revenue (NBR)—to institute a formal criminal case.

If the six-month period expires without the investigating agency obtaining a formal judicial attachment order from a court, the legal basis of the BFIU freeze lapses automatically. Continuing the freeze thereafter constitutes an unlawful administrative act.

3. Judicial Attachment Under Section 14: Special Judge Court Orders

To freeze or attach a bank account beyond the six-month administrative threshold, the investigating agency must transition the matter to a judicial forum. Under Section 14 of the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012, the investigating officer must submit a formal written application before the competent Senior Special Judge Court having territorial and subject-matter jurisdiction.

Section 14 mandates that the court must be satisfied on judicial grounds that:

  1. A formal FIR or criminal proceeding has been instituted regarding a scheduled money laundering predicate offence.
  2. There is tangible, prima facie evidence indicating that the funds deposited in the targeted bank account represent proceeds of crime or properties derived from illegal activities.
  3. There is a genuine, imminent danger that the account holder will withdraw, transfer, or dissipate the funds before the conclusion of trial.

The Special Judge Court issues an order of attachment (freezing) and serves it officially upon the Head Office and branch of the scheduled bank. Crucially, an order passed under Section 14 is a judicial proceeding. The affected account holder is entitled to retain an advocate, inspect the case docket, file an application for recall or modification, and present legitimate financial evidence demonstrating lawful origins of the funds.

4. Common Triggers for Bank Account Freezes in Bangladesh

Facing a frozen bank account or BFIU notice in Bangladesh? Contact our Supreme Court chamber immediately on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007. Overseas clients and business directors can arrange rapid emergency document review.

In practice, commercial scheduled banks trigger algorithmic compliance flags that generate STRs resulting in BFIU intervention. The most frequent triggers include:

  • Unmatched Foreign Inward Remittances: Rapid inward transfers from foreign jurisdictions into personal or commercial accounts where the beneficiary cannot produce a matching export form, commercial invoice, or approved service agreement. Expatriates sending family funds without clear remittance memos frequently encounter this barrier.
  • High-Frequency Digital Wallet Transfers: Accounts receiving numerous daily transfers from mobile financial services (MFS) platforms such as bKash, Nagad, or Rocket, which compliance algorithms flag for suspected informal currency remittance (Hundi) or unauthorized currency exchange.
  • Discrepancies with NBR Tax Returns: Sudden massive deposits that vastly exceed the annual income or gross assets declared in the account holder's latest income tax acknowledgment receipt under the Income Tax Act 2023.
  • Inclusion in Political or Commercial Inquiries: Account holders named in generalized FIRs, corporate shareholder disputes, or ACC preliminary fact-finding inquiries.

5. Legal Comparison: BFIU Administrative Freeze vs. Judicial Attachment

Distinguishing between administrative directives and judicial freezing orders is essential for structuring an effective legal challenge:

6. Step-by-Step Legal Protocol to Unfreeze a Bank Account

When your account is restricted, implementing a disciplined legal protocol prevents unnecessary delays:

  1. Obtain Written Confirmation from the Bank: Visit your branch and submit a formal written demand letter requesting the branch manager to specify the exact legal basis of the freeze, including the issuing authority's reference memo number, date of directive, and specific statutory section.
  2. Assemble Financial Evidence: Compile full bank statements, audited company accounts, proof of legitimate business transactions, commercial contracts, tax returns (IT-10B), and foreign remittance encashment certificates.
  3. Submit a Representation to BFIU: If the freeze is an administrative action under Section 23 and within the initial 30 days, your advocate can submit a comprehensive written representation to the Director General of the BFIU demonstrating the legitimate origin of the funds and requesting immediate release.
  4. File a Petition Before the Special Judge: If an attachment order was issued under Section 14, file an application for recall or de-freezing before the Senior Special Judge, establishing that the seized funds bear no connection to the alleged predicate offence.
  5. Move the High Court Division: If administrative agencies maintain the freeze beyond statutory deadlines without judicial confirmation, file an emergency Writ Petition before the High Court Division.

7. High Court Writ Remedies Under Article 102 for Indefinite Freezes

In numerous instances, banks keep accounts frozen for a year or longer simply because an agency sent an exploratory letter and never sent a follow-up cancellation notice. In these scenarios, the High Court Division provides effective constitutional relief under Article 102 of the Constitution.

A Writ of Mandamus or Certiorari is instituted on the grounds that:

  • Violation of Fundamental Rights: Freezing an account without statutory authority violates Article 31 (right to be treated in accordance with law) and Article 42 (right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property).
  • Breach of Statutory Deadlines: The BFIU has exceeded the six-month statutory ceiling mandated by Section 23(1)(c) of Act No. V of 2012 without obtaining a Section 14 judicial attachment order.
  • Deprivation of Livelihood: Freezing entire commercial operating accounts containing legitimate business funds to investigate an isolated transaction is disproportionate and punitive.

The High Court Division routinely issues a Rule Nisi calling upon Bangladesh Bank, the BFIU, and the inquiring agency to explain the illegality of the freeze, while concurrently granting an Ad-Interim Order directing the commercial bank to immediately restore operational access to the account.

8. Safeguards for Expatriates, NRBs and Corporate Entities

Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) and international business entities can adopt proactive compliance safeguards to mitigate the risk of account freezes:

  • Execute Formal Remittance Contracts: Whenever remitting substantial foreign exchange into Bangladesh for real estate, business equity, or family support, retain certified Inward Remittance Encashment Certificates from authorized dealer banks. See our guide on remittance and tax scrutiny for NRB property purchases.
  • Maintain Segregated Commercial and Personal Accounts: Never mix business turnover funds with personal savings accounts. Commercial transactions should always flow through corporate accounts registered with an updated trade license and e-TIN.
  • Respond Promptly to Bank KYC Audits: When your bank requests updated Know Your Customer (KYC) documentation, Transaction Profiles (TP), or sources of funds, reply promptly through official written channels to prevent automatic compliance suspension.
  • Appoint an Advocate via Special Power of Attorney: Overseas clients who discover an account freeze while abroad can empower a Supreme Court advocate to access bank records, communicate with the BFIU, and represent them in court proceedings.

9. Illustrative Scenario: Lifting an Arbitrary Commercial Account Freeze

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): An NRB entrepreneur operating an export-import consultancy in Birmingham, UK, maintained an operational current account in Gulshan, Dhaka, to fund local software development teams. In early 2025, following a series of foreign inward remittances totaling 1.8 Crore BDT, the bank suddenly dishonored payroll cheques and informed the client that the account was 'frozen under central bank regulatory instructions.'

Unable to pay salaries and facing commercial catastrophe, the entrepreneur instructed Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber. Our legal team took swift action:

  1. Issued an immediate advocate's legal demand letter to the branch manager, forcing the bank to disclose that the freeze originated from a provisional BFIU memo issued five months earlier, which had never been confirmed by any court.
  2. Ascertained that no FIR or formal money laundering proceedings had been instituted before any Senior Special Judge Court.
  3. Drafted and moved an emergency Writ Petition under Article 102 before a Division Bench of the High Court Division, demonstrating that the BFIU suspension had surpassed the statutory limits of Section 23(1)(c) of Act No. V of 2012 and infringed Articles 31 and 42 of the Constitution.
  4. The High Court Division issued a Rule Nisi and passed an immediate Ad-Interim Order directing the commercial bank to unfreeze the current account within 48 hours.
  5. Served the certified court order on the bank's head office and legal department, successfully restoring full transactional access and enabling the client to resume operations without disruption.

10. Talk to an Advocate: Bank Account Freeze Defense

If your personal or commercial bank account has been frozen by the BFIU, ACC, or CID in Bangladesh, securing experienced legal counsel is essential to protect your assets and restore commercial liquidity. Advocate Md. Shah Alam and his dedicated team of Supreme Court and Dhaka Court advocates provide rapid intervention before banking compliance desks, Special Judge Courts, and the High Court Division.

Need an advocate for this matter in Bangladesh? Send your documents on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: a first document review can be done remotely.

Our principal chamber is situated in Uttara, Dhaka, minutes from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, alongside our daily litigation chamber at the Supreme Court Bar Association and Dhaka Judge Court.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the BFIU freeze a bank account permanently without a court order?

No. Under Section 23(1)(c) of the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012, BFIU administrative freezes are valid for an initial 30 days and can be extended up to a maximum cumulative limit of six months. Freezing beyond six months requires a formal judicial attachment order from a Senior Special Judge Court.

What is the difference between an account freeze and an account debit block?

A debit block permits deposits but restricts outward payments and cash withdrawals. A total account freeze immobilizes both inward credits and outward debits. Both measures represent statutory restrictions that must comply with procedural due process under banking and criminal laws.

Can I withdraw living expenses or salary payments from a frozen account?

If an account is frozen under a judicial order, the account holder can submit an application before the Senior Special Judge Court requesting permission to withdraw specific, documented living expenses, medical treatment costs, or staff salary disbursements from legitimate balances.

How long does it take to unfreeze an account through a High Court Writ Petition?

In urgent matters where an administrative freeze has exceeded statutory time limits without a formal criminal charge, the High Court Division can hear the petition and grant an ad-interim de-freezing direction within 3 to 7 working days.

Does having a frozen account mean I will be arrested?

Not necessarily. Many freezes occur purely on automated algorithmic flags or preliminary suspicious transaction reports (STRs) where no criminal case exists. However, it indicates an active inquiry, making immediate legal consultation vital to prevent formal criminal charges.

Can overseas Bangladeshis (NRBs) challenge an account freeze from abroad?

Yes. An overseas account holder can instruct a Supreme Court advocate remotely through an embassy-authenticated Special Power of Attorney or authorized local representative to access bank records, make representations, and file petitions in court.

What documents are required to prove funds are legitimate to the BFIU?

Essential documents include foreign remittance encashment certificates, tax acknowledgment receipts (IT-10B), commercial contracts, audited financial statements, invoices, and bank statements establishing a verifiable, lawful chain of funds.

Can the police freeze a bank account directly without BFIU or court permission?

Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (Section 102/103) and Money Laundering Prevention Act, police officers cannot independently freeze accounts without written authorization from a magistrate or the competent Senior Special Judge Court.

Money Suit & Order 37 CPC in Bangladesh: Debt Recovery, Cheques & Summary Suits

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-08 · 19 minutes

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In Bangladesh's dynamic commercial landscape, unpaid business invoices, defaulted commercial loans, dishonored bank cheques, and unfulfilled contractual advances represent serious operational hazards. When a trading partner, corporate debtor, or individual borrower refuses to satisfy their financial liabilities, relying purely on criminal cheque bounce proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 is often insufficient to secure full financial recovery. To legally compel the physical attachment and recovery of funds, creditors must institute civil recovery proceedings. Governed by the **Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC)**, plaintiffs have two potent judicial mechanisms: an **Ordinary Money Suit** before the Joint District Judge Court, or a fast-track **Summary Suit under Order 37 CPC** based on written contracts, bills of exchange, or promissory notes. This comprehensive legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate and civil litigation specialist in Dhaka, explains the statutory procedures, limitation deadlines, court fee caps, and execution tactics to recover debts in Bangladesh.

1. Statutory Framework: Civil Debt Recovery Under CPC

In Bangladesh, recovering monetary dues arising from commercial transactions, goods supplied, unpaid loan facilities, or broken business agreements is fundamentally governed by the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (Act No. V of 1908), the Contract Act 1872, and the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881.

Creditors frequently confuse criminal prosecutions with civil asset recovery. While filing a criminal complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act or Sections 406/420 of the Penal Code can lead to the arrest of the debtor, a criminal court's primary mandate is punitive punishment rather than executing asset attachments. To secure a binding judicial decree that directly attaches the debtor's commercial bank accounts, factories, and immovable properties, a creditor must institute a formal civil proceeding.

The CPC provides two distinct structural avenues: the conventional Ordinary Money Suit governed by Section 26 and Order 7, and the accelerated Summary Procedure under Order 37. Choosing the correct forum depends on the nature of the underlying documentation, whether negotiable instruments exist, and the urgency of preventing asset dissipation. Review our analysis on breach of contract damages and specific performance in Bangladesh for related contractual claims.

2. Order 37 CPC: Fast-Track Summary Suits for Cheques & Notes

Order 37 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 is a specialized procedural fast-track designed to prevent dishonest debtors from dragging out commercial claims through frivolous defenses and endless adjournments.

Under Order 37 Rule 1, summary suits are strictly restricted to claims founded upon:

  • Bills of Exchange (Hundis).
  • Promissory Notes (Demand Promissory Notes / DP Notes).
  • Cheques dishonored upon presentation to commercial banks.
  • Written contracts where the debt sought to be recovered is a fixed liquidated sum of money or a liquidated demand arising under an express covenant.

The defining procedural characteristic of an Order 37 suit is that upon being served with court summons, the defendant has no automatic right to file a written statement. Unlike ordinary suits where a defendant can file routine denials, in an Order 37 suit the allegations in the plaint are legally deemed to be admitted unless the defendant formally petitions the court and is granted special judicial leave to defend.

3. The Leave to Defend Standard & Security Deposit Rules

Under Order 37 Rule 2 and Rule 3 of the CPC, when the defendant is served with summons in Form No. 4 of Appendix B, a strict procedural timeline is triggered:

  1. The 10-Day Appearance Mandate: The defendant must enter an appearance within ten (10) days of receiving summons and file an application supported by a sworn affidavit for Leave to Defend the suit.
  2. Substantiating Triable Issues: The defendant's affidavit must disclose specific factual and legal grounds establishing a bona fide, plausible defense. Vague or general denials will be summarily rejected by the court.
  3. Conditional vs. Unconditional Leave: If the defense appears genuine and substantial, the court may grant unconditional leave to defend. However, if the defense appears questionable, illusory, or intended merely to delay, the court routinely grants Conditional Leave, directing the defendant to deposit the entire claimed debt amount (or a substantial percentage thereof) in cash or bank guarantee into the court registry within a stipulated timeframe.
  4. Immediate Decree on Default: If the defendant fails to apply for leave to defend within 10 days, or if leave is refused, or if the defendant fails to satisfy the court's deposit condition, the court immediately pronounces final judgment and passes a decree in favor of the plaintiff for the full claimed amount plus contractual interest.

4. Ordinary Money Suits Before the Joint District Judge Court

Need an advocate for commercial debt recovery or an Order 37 suit in Bangladesh? Contact our civil litigation chamber on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas businesses can arrange remote document vetting.

Where a debt is not anchored in a formal negotiable instrument or signed promissory note—such as claims arising from running account ledgers, oral agreements with delivery receipts, disputed invoice valuations, or complex construction claims—the appropriate legal avenue is an Ordinary Money Suit.

Key procedural dimensions of an Ordinary Money Suit include:

  • Pecuniary Jurisdiction: Under the Civil Courts Act 1887 (as amended), jurisdiction is determined strictly by claim valuation. Claims exceeding 25 Lakh BDT fall within the exclusive original jurisdiction of the Court of the Joint District Judge. Claims between 15 Lakh and 25 Lakh BDT are heard by Senior Assistant Judges, while claims up to 15 Lakh BDT are tried by Assistant Judges.
  • Pre-Suit Legal Demand Notice: A formal Legal Notice drafted by a Supreme Court advocate must be served via registered post demanding payment within 15 to 30 days. This notice establishes demand, default, and statutory interest accrual.
  • Full Trial Stages: An ordinary money suit proceeds through standard civil trial stages: Plaint submission, Written Statement, Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR mediation under Section 89A CPC), Framing of Issues, Peremptory Hearing (witness examination and cross-examination), and Final Arguments.

5. Legal Matrix: Order 37 CPC vs. Ordinary Money Suit vs. Section 138 NI Act

6. Court Fee Calculation & Statutory Maximum Caps (Court-Fees Act 1870)

A critical consideration for corporate creditors filing recovery suits is calculating the mandatory judicial court fee. In Bangladesh, court fees for money suits are governed by the Court-Fees Act 1870 (Act No. VII of 1870).

Key statutory fee rules include:

  • Ad Valorem Scale: For suits seeking money recovery, court fees are calculated on an ad valorem (proportional) basis according to the total claimed debt valuation.
  • Statutory Maximum Ceiling: To facilitate commercial access to justice and prevent exorbitant barriers, the Legislature introduced a statutory maximum cap on ad valorem court fees. For any civil suit—regardless of whether the claim is 5 Crore BDT or 50 Crore BDT—the maximum court fee payable in Bangladesh is statutorily capped at 50,000 BDT (plus nominal welfare stamps and process fees).
  • Fee Recovery from Debtor: Under Section 35 of the CPC, the court routinely awards full costs of the suit against the defaulting debtor, enabling the successful plaintiff to recover all paid court fees and reasonable legal expenses upon final decree.

7. Limitation Deadlines Under the Limitation Act 1908

In debt recovery litigation, time is of the essence. The Limitation Act 1908 (Act No. IX of 1908) establishes strict statutory limitation windows that extinguish the right to file suit if neglected.

Critical limitation schedules in Bangladesh include:

  1. Debts on Promissory Notes or Bills: Under Articles 64, 73, and 80 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act 1908, a suit on a promissory note or bill of exchange must be filed within three (3) years from the date when the instrument becomes payable or is dishonored.
  2. Price of Goods Sold and Delivered: Under Article 52, a suit for the price of goods sold where no specific credit period was agreed must be filed within three (3) years from the date of delivery of the goods.
  3. Breach of Written Contracts: Under Article 115, a suit for compensation or debt arising from the breach of any contract must be instituted within three (3) years from when the breach occurred.
  4. Extension via Written Acknowledgment: Under Section 19 of the Limitation Act 1908, if the debtor signs a written acknowledgment of liability or makes a partial payment on account of principal or interest (Section 20) before the expiration of the 3-year period, a fresh 3-year limitation window commences from the date of that acknowledgment.

8. Executing Money Decrees: Bank Garnishment & Asset Auctions

Securing a judgment is meaningless unless converted into physical cash. Execution of money decrees is governed by Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (Jari Mamla).

The execution court provides robust statutory enforcement mechanisms:

  • Attachment of Bank Accounts (Order 21 Rule 46): The court serves prohibitory orders on scheduled banks freezing the judgment debtor's current, savings, and fixed-deposit accounts, directing bank managers to transfer funds into court.
  • Attachment and Sale of Movable Property (Order 21 Rule 43): Commercial vehicles, factory machinery, inventory stocks, and corporate assets are seized and sold at public auction.
  • Attachment of Immovable Property (Order 21 Rule 54): Lands, commercial buildings, and corporate real estate are formally attached, precluding any sale or mortgage, and subsequently auctioned under court supervision.
  • Civil Imprisonment (Section 51 & Order 21 Rule 37): If a debtor who possesses financial capacity deliberately avoids satisfying the decree, the court can issue a warrant of civil arrest and commit the debtor to civil prison for up to six months. Civil detention does not extinguish the underlying debt.

9. Illustrative Scenario: Recovering BDT 45 Lakhs via Order 37 CPC

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): A Dhaka-based textile chemical importer supplied industrial auxiliaries valued at 45 Lakh BDT to a garment washing factory in Gazipur. The buyer issued three post-dated cheques backed by a signed corporate memorandum. Upon presentation, all three cheques were dishonored due to 'insufficient funds'. The buyer offered vague verbal assurances but refused payment for seven months.

Facing cash flow strain, the supplier engaged Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber. Our litigation team executed a coordinated civil recovery strategy:

  1. Dispatched a formal statutory Legal Notice demanding 45 Lakh BDT plus commercial interest within 15 days. Concurrently, filed a criminal complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 to initiate criminal pressure.
  2. Simultaneously instituted a Summary Suit under Order 37 CPC before the Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka, depositing the capped statutory court fee of 50,000 BDT.
  3. The Joint District Judge issued summons in Form No. 4. The defaulting buyer appeared on the ninth day and filed an application for Leave to Defend, falsely claiming the chemical supplies were substandard.
  4. Our advocates argued before the court that the buyer had signed receipt vouchers without raising any contemporaneous quality disputes and had utilized the goods in export production.
  5. The court granted Conditional Leave to Defend on the strict condition that the defendant deposit 50% of the claimed debt (22.5 Lakh BDT) into the court registry within 30 days. When the debtor failed to deposit the security, the court struck off the defense and passed a summary decree for the full 45 Lakh BDT plus interest, subsequently executing the decree by attaching the debtor's commercial bank balances in Motijheel.

10. Talk to an Advocate: Commercial Debt Recovery Litigation

Recovering commercial debts, unpaid corporate invoices, and defaulted business loans in Bangladesh requires assertive civil litigation and rigorous procedural execution. Advocate Md. Shah Alam and his experienced civil litigation team represent corporate creditors, suppliers, and overseas trading entities before Joint District Judge Courts and the Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

Our principal chamber is located in Uttara, Dhaka, minutes from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, alongside our daily litigation chamber at the Dhaka Judge Court.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between an Ordinary Money Suit and an Order 37 Summary Suit?

In an Ordinary Money Suit, the defendant has an automatic right to file a written statement and undergo full trial. In an Order 37 Summary Suit (based on cheques or bills), the defendant must apply for and obtain Leave to Defend within 10 days, or a summary decree is passed immediately.

Can I file both a criminal cheque bounce case and a civil Money Suit at the same time?

Yes. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has established that a Section 138 NI Act criminal prosecution and a civil Money Suit under Order 37 CPC are parallel, concurrent remedies that can be pursued simultaneously.

What is the time limit for filing a Money Suit in Bangladesh?

Under the Limitation Act 1908, a Money Suit must be instituted within three (3) years from the date of debt default, cheque dishonor, or written acknowledgment of liability.

What is the maximum court fee for filing a Money Suit?

Under the Court-Fees Act 1870, ad valorem court fees for money suits in Bangladesh are statutorily capped at a maximum of approximately 50,000 BDT, regardless of multi-crore claim valuations.

What is 'Leave to Defend' in an Order 37 case?

Leave to Defend is formal permission granted by the civil court allowing the defendant to contest the suit. It is granted only if the defendant demonstrates genuine, triable factual or legal issues through a sworn affidavit.

Which court hears commercial money suits in Dhaka?

Claims exceeding 25 Lakh BDT are heard by the Court of the Joint District Judge. Claims between 15 Lakh and 25 Lakh BDT are tried by Senior Assistant Judges, and claims under 15 Lakh BDT by Assistant Judges.

Can a civil court send a debtor to prison for failing to pay a money decree?

Yes. Under Section 51 and Order 21 Rule 37 CPC, if the judgment debtor possesses financial means but deliberately refuses to pay, the execution court can order civil imprisonment for up to six months.

Can foreign companies or overseas creditors file a Money Suit in Bangladesh?

Yes. International companies and non-resident creditors can institute money suits in Bangladesh through a duly authorized advocate via an embassy-authenticated Special Power of Attorney.

entries.body:
Mortgage Law Bangladesh – Types, Foreclosure & Redemption Rights

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-05-21 · 9 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Mortgaging property is a common practice in Bangladesh — whether to secure a bank loan, borrow from a private lender, or receive agricultural finance. However, many property owners enter mortgage agreements without fully understanding their rights and the risks involved. This guide explains all types of mortgages, foreclosure rules, and the mortgagor's right of redemption under Bangladesh's Transfer of Property Act 1882.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

📋 In This Article

  2. Types of Mortgages Recognised in Bangladesh
  3. Rights and Duties of the Mortgagor
  4. Rights and Duties of the Mortgagee
  5. Foreclosure of Mortgage in Bangladesh
  6. Right of Redemption – Mortgagor's Protection
  7. Mortgage Disputes and Legal Remedies in Bangladesh

What Is a Mortgage Under Bangladesh Law?

Under Section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 (which applies in Bangladesh), a mortgage is defined as:

"The transfer of an interest in specific immoveable property for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or the performance of an engagement which may give rise to a pecuniary liability."

Key elements of a valid mortgage under Bangladesh law:

  • Immovable property: The security must be specific immovable property (land, buildings)
  • Transfer of interest: The mortgagor transfers a limited interest in the property to the mortgagee — not full ownership
  • Securing a debt or obligation: The transfer is made as security, not as a sale
  • The parties: The mortgagor is the borrower/property owner; the mortgagee is the lender/creditor

A mortgage is distinct from a sale (which transfers full ownership) and a pledge (which applies to movable goods). Mortgages of immovable property above BDT 100 in value must be by a registered mortgage deed (except for deposit of title deeds). For any mortgage transaction, consult a property lawyer in Dhaka to ensure your rights are protected.

Types of Mortgages Recognised in Bangladesh

The Transfer of Property Act 1882 recognises six types of mortgages in Bangladesh:

1. Simple Mortgage (Section 58(b))

The mortgagor does not deliver possession of the property to the mortgagee. The mortgagor personally undertakes to repay the loan, and if they fail, the mortgagee has the right to have the property sold (but not to take possession). This is the most common form used by banks and financial institutions in Bangladesh.

2. Mortgage by Conditional Sale (Section 58(c))

The property is ostensibly sold to the mortgagee with a condition that on payment of the loan the sale becomes void (i.e., the mortgagor can reclaim the property), or on default the sale becomes absolute. The key distinction from an actual sale is that the condition of reconveyance must be contained in the same document as the sale deed.

3. Usufructuary Mortgage (Section 58(d)) — বন্দকি বন্ধক

This is the most common form of private/informal mortgage in rural Bangladesh. The mortgagor delivers possession of the property to the mortgagee, who is entitled to enjoy the usufruct (rents, income, produce) of the property in lieu of interest. The mortgagee retains possession until the mortgage money is fully paid. No personal obligation to repay exists — the mortgagee recovers the loan from the property's income.

4. English Mortgage (Section 58(e))

The mortgagor transfers absolute ownership to the mortgagee, with a personal covenant to repay, and an agreement that on repayment the mortgagee will retransfer the property. Common in formal commercial lending in Bangladesh.

5. Mortgage by Deposit of Title Deeds (Equitable Mortgage) (Section 58(f))

The mortgagor deposits the original title documents of the property with the mortgagee (usually a bank) as security, with an oral or written agreement creating a charge. No registration is required. Very commonly used by banks in Dhaka and major cities as a quick, low-cost mortgage security.

6. Anomalous Mortgage (Section 58(g))

Any mortgage that does not fall neatly into the above categories. Often encountered in rural areas with customary local practices.

Understanding which type of mortgage you have entered into is essential because the remedies available to the mortgagee and the protections available to the mortgagor differ significantly between types. Consult a property lawyer in Bangladesh to review your mortgage deed.

Rights and Duties of the Mortgagor

The mortgagor (borrower/property owner) retains several important rights under Bangladesh law:

  • Right of redemption (Section 60): The mortgagor's most fundamental right — the right to pay off the mortgage money and reclaim full ownership of the property at any time before the mortgage is foreclosed or the property sold. This right cannot be validly clogged (restricted) by the mortgage deed.
  • Right to inspect and produce documents (Section 60A): The mortgagor can inspect and produce for copying all documents of title relating to the mortgaged property in the mortgagee's possession.
  • Right to add to the security (Section 62): In a usufructuary mortgage, the mortgagor may add further security if the court directs.
  • Right to redeem separately or simultaneously (Section 61): Where there are several mortgages on the same property, the mortgagor can redeem any one mortgage without being required to redeem all simultaneously.

The mortgagor's key duties include:

  • To repay the loan as agreed
  • To not commit waste that would impair the mortgagee's security
  • To pay government taxes and charges on the property
  • To keep the property insured (if required by the deed)
  • In a simple mortgage: to defend the mortgagee's title against third-party claims

Rights and Duties of the Mortgagee

The mortgagee (lender/bank) also has defined rights and obligations under the Transfer of Property Act:

Rights of the Mortgagee

  • Right to foreclosure or sale (Section 67): On default of repayment, the mortgagee may file a mortgage suit for foreclosure (in a mortgage by conditional sale) or for sale of the mortgaged property (in a simple mortgage or English mortgage).
  • Right to sue for mortgage money (Section 68): In certain mortgages, the mortgagee can sue the mortgagor personally for the mortgage money when the mortgagor is personally liable and the security has become insufficient.
  • Right to accession (Section 70): Any accession (improvement or addition) to the mortgaged property after the mortgage accrues to the benefit of the mortgagee's security.
  • Right to spend on repairs (Section 72): The mortgagee in possession can spend on necessary repairs and insurance and add such amounts to the principal mortgage debt.
  • Right of a mortgagee in possession: In a usufructuary mortgage, the mortgagee has the right to receive rents and profits of the property and apply them first to interest and then to principal.

Duties of the Mortgagee

  • To manage the mortgaged property (if in possession) as a person of ordinary prudence
  • Not to commit waste or damage the property
  • To account for all rents and profits received from the property
  • To retransfer the property upon payment of the mortgage money (Section 60)
  • Not to create a new mortgage or encumbrance on the property without the mortgagor's consent

If a mortgagee (bank or private lender) is mismanaging your mortgaged property or refusing to accept repayment and reconvey, contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam immediately for legal intervention.
