1. The Legal Concept of Joint Ownership & Co-Sharership (সহ-অংশীদারিত্ব)

Under both Islamic jurisprudence (ফারায়েজ / Farayez) and Hindu personal law (Dayabhaga School), the death of a property owner instantly transforms the surviving legal heirs into co-owners in joint tenancy. Key legal principles that every overseas heir must understand include:

  • Undivided Interest across Every Square Inch: Until a registered deed of partition (রেজিস্ট্রিকৃত আপস বন্টননামা) is executed or a civil court passes a partition decree, no single heir owns a specific demarcated physical plot. Every co-sharer holds an undivided fractional interest in every square inch of the ancestral estate.
  • Illegal Unilateral Transfers: If a resident brother purports to sell the 'front 5 decimals' of road-facing land to a developer, the transfer is legally defective. Under Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882, the buyer only steps into the shoes of the co-sharer's undivided interest and cannot claim exclusive possession without a partition suit.
  • Constructive Possession: Possession of one co-sharer is legally regarded as possession on behalf of all co-sharers (সহ-দখল), unless an active, overt ouster has occurred.

2. Statutory Framework: Partition Act 1893 & Code of Civil Procedure 1908

Partition litigation is anchored primarily in three statutory pillars:

  1. The Partition Act, 1893 (Act No. IV of 1893): Governs the judicial division of property among co-sharers. Section 2 of the Act provides that where property cannot reasonably or conveniently be divided into physical shares, the court may order a public or private auction among co-sharers, distributing the monetary proceeds. Section 4 allows a family member to buy out a stranger who purchased an undivided share in a family dwelling house.
  2. The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC): Governs the pleadings, discovery, preliminary decree under Order XX Rule 18, appointment of commissioners under Order XXVI Rule 13, and execution under Order XXI.
  3. The Court-fees Act, 1870: Regulates the statutory stamp duty payable on the plaint depending on whether title is disputed.

3. Grounds for Filing: Recognizing Co-Sharer Fraud & Ouster

Expats should never wait passively when family negotiations stall. Instituting a partition suit becomes urgent in the following scenarios:

  • Monopolization of Commercial Income: Resident relatives collect rents from ancestral markets, shopping complexes, or multi-story apartments and refuse to wire the expat's rightful share.
  • Unequal Physical Possession: Local siblings occupy high-value commercial frontage while attempting to relegate overseas heirs to low-value, water-logged, or rear-inaccessible land.
  • Attempts to Deprive Female Heirs: In many rural areas, brothers pressure overseas sisters to 'surrender' their shares or falsely claim an oral gift (Heba) was made prior to the father's demise.
  • Impending Developer Contracts: Relatives sign unauthorized Memorandums of Understanding (MoU) with real estate developers to demolish ancestral structures without your consent.

4. How an NRB Can Litigate Entirely from Abroad (Order III Rule 1 CPC)

A prevalent myth is that an expatriate plaintiff must continuously attend court hearings in Bangladesh. This is legally untrue:

Order III Rule 1 of the CPC: Expressly permits any suit, application, or appearance in a civil court to be instituted and prosecuted by the party's 'recognized agent' or an enrolled pleader. An expatriate living in New York, London, or Toronto executes a Special Power of Attorney in Form 1 before the Bangladesh Embassy, completes MOFA and DC office stamping, and empowers their attorney to sign the plaint, verification, and affidavits.

The expat's physical presence is generally required only at the final evidence stage (examination-in-chief and cross-examination), and even this can frequently be handled through commission under Order XXVI or through short visits coordinated with counsel.

5. Mathematical Farayez Share Distribution Matrix (Muslim Succession)

To claim your share, you must understand your statutory entitlement under Islamic succession law (ফারায়েজ). The following table illustrates fractional shares under standard Sunni Hanafi rules:

Surviving Legal HeirsStatutory Share of Mother/WidowStatutory Share of SonsStatutory Share of Daughters
Widow, 2 Sons, 2 Daughters1/8 (12.5%)Residuary: Each Son receives 2 parts (~29.17% each)Residuary: Each Daughter receives 1 part (~14.58% each)
Widow & Only 1 Daughter (No Sons)1/8 (12.5%)NoneFixed 1/2 (50%) + Residuary via Radd (رد)
Widow & 3 Daughters (No Sons)1/8 (12.5%)NoneShare 2/3 equally (~22.2% each) + Radd
Husband, 1 Son, 1 DaughterHusband gets 1/4 (25%)Son receives 2/3 of remainder (50%)Daughter receives 1/3 of remainder (25%)

6. Step 1 — Serving the Mandatory Pre-Suit Legal Notice

Prior to instituting the suit, an enrolled Supreme Court advocate must issue a formal Legal Notice for Amicable Partition (বন্টনের আইনি নোটিশ) to all co-sharers via Registered Post with A/D:

  • Sets out the pedigree of the family (বংশলতিকা) and the complete property schedule.
  • Identifies the plaintiff's exact mathematical fractional share under personal succession law.
  • Calls upon the defendants to execute a registered Partition Deed (আপস বন্টননামা) within 15 to 30 days.
  • Warns that failure to partition mutually will compel the plaintiff to seek judicial partition, court costs, and an injunction.
  • Serving the legal notice is essential evidence proving that cause of action has arisen and mutual settlement was refused.
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

7. Step 2 — Drafting the Plaint & Determining Court Fees (Fixed vs Ad-Valorem)

The plaint must be instituted in the court having territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction:

  • Court Jurisdiction: Up to BDT 15 Lakh = Senior Assistant Judge Court; BDT 15 Lakh to BDT 25 Lakh = Sub-Judge Court; Above BDT 25 Lakh = Joint District Judge Court.
  • Court Fees: Under Schedule II Article 17(vi) of the Court-fees Act 1870:
    • Constructive Joint Possession: If title is undisputed and the plaintiff claims joint constructive possession, a nominal fixed court fee of BDT 300 to BDT 1,000 is payable.
    • Disputed Title or Complete Ouster: If the defendants deny your title or have forcefully evicted you, ad-valorem court fees based on property market value (up to statutory ceilings, currently BDT 50,000 to BDT 75,000) must be paid.

8. Step 3 — Securing an Injunction (Order 39 CPC) to Freeze Construction & Sale

The single most dangerous threat during litigation is defendants hurrying to alter the character of the land or transferring parcels to innocent third parties. To counter this:

Emergency Order 39 Petition: Simultaneously with the plaint, your advocate files an application for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1 & 2 read with Section 151 CPC. The court must be satisfied on three criteria: (1) Strong prima facie case, (2) Balance of convenience, and (3) Irreparable injury. The judge issues an ad-interim injunction restraining defendants from alienating, encumbering, or changing the physical condition of the suit land until disposal.

9. Step 4 — The Preliminary Decree: Adjudicating Title & Saham Fractions

Unlike ordinary civil suits, a Partition Suit proceeds through two distinct judicial stages:

  1. Summons & Written Statement: Defendants file their defense (Written Statement under Order VIII Rule 1 CPC).
  2. Settlement of Issues & Trial: The court frames issues regarding pedigree, legality of documents, and respective shares.
  3. Passing of Preliminary Decree: Under Order XX Rule 18 CPC, the judge delivers judgment declaring the title of the parties and their specific fractional share (Saham / সাহাম). No physical land demarcation takes place at this stage; it is purely a judicial declaration of legal ownership.

10. Step 5 — The Final Decree: Advocate Commissioner Survey & Allotment

Once the Preliminary Decree is sealed, parties are given a brief window to divide the land amicably. If they fail, the plaintiff applies for a Final Decree (চূড়ান্ত ডিক্রি):

  • Appointment of Advocate Commissioner: Under Order XXVI Rule 13 CPC, the court appoints an independent Advocate Commissioner accompanied by a licensed government Amin (surveyor).
  • On-Site Physical Survey: The Commissioner visits the land after serving notice to all parties, measures the boundaries with modern GPS/theodolite equipment, and draws an exact allotment map (চিঠাকাটা নকশা).
  • Balancing Road Access & Valuation: The Commissioner ensures that every Saham receives fair road frontage, drainage access, and equalized property value. If one plot has higher commercial value, compensation adjustments (Owelty / ক্ষতিপূরণ) are calculated.
  • Final Decree Confirmation: The court hears objections, approves the Commissioner's allotment report, and seals the Final Decree.

11. Step 6 — Execution Suit (জারী মামলা) & Demarcation with Police Assistance

If stubborn relatives refuse to surrender physical possession of the demarcated plot following the final decree:

  1. File an Execution Case (বন্টন ডিক্রি জারী মামলা) under Order XXI of the CPC.
  2. The court issues a Writ of Delivery of Possession (দখলনামা পরোয়ানা) directed to the Court Nazir.
  3. The Nazir, accompanied by police forces, attends the land, removes illegal obstructions, erects permanent boundary pillars (সীমানা পিলার), and delivers vacant physical possession to your attorney.
  4. Resistance constitutes criminal trespass and contempt of court.

12. Real-World Case Study: UK Expat Securing His 3-Katha Share in Sylhet

Background: Mr. Joynal Abedin, living in Birmingham, UK, was denied his 3-katha share in an ancestral plot worth BDT 1.8 Crore in Dargah Gate, Sylhet by his two resident brothers. The brothers began constructing a commercial market covering the entire frontage.

Chamber Action:

  1. Executed an embassy-attested Special Power of Attorney appointing his cousin in Sylhet.
  2. Filed Partition Suit No. 84/2024 before the Joint District Judge Court, Sylhet, with an emergency Order 39 injunction petition.
  3. Secured an immediate stay order halting commercial construction within 7 days of filing.
  4. Proved title via original 1962 CS/SA Khatians and father's registered title deed. Obtained a Preliminary Decree declaring Mr. Joynal's 1/3rd share.
  5. Advocate Commissioner surveyed the land, carving out a dedicated 3-katha road-front commercial plot with independent egress.
  6. Final Decree confirmed, and physical possession delivered with police presence. Mr. Joynal is now developing his parcel independently.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I file a partition suit in Bangladesh if I do not possess original land deeds?

Yes. An advocate can inspect Sub-Registry Volume Books to obtain certified copies (সার্টিফাইড নকল) of all historical deeds, as well as official certified Porchas from the DC office.

How long does a contested Partition Suit take from filing to final possession?

An average partition suit takes between 2 to 4 years to complete both the preliminary and final decree stages in the trial court. However, protective injunctions are issued in the very first weeks.

Can my brothers sell my deceased father's land while I live in the USA?

No. Under Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882, any sale executed without other legal heirs only conveys the seller's personal share; they cannot lawfully transfer your share.

Do married daughters have equal rights to claim partition under Bangladesh law?

Yes. Under Muslim succession law, daughters inherit specific fixed shares, and have full statutory standing to institute an independent partition suit in civil court.

What is Owelty in a partition decree?

Owelty is monetary compensation ordered by the court when physical property cannot be divided equally in value, requiring the party receiving the prime plot to compensate other co-sharers.

Can a Partition Suit be settled out of court through Solenama?

Yes. At any point before the final decree, parties can enter into a Solenama (আপসনামা) under Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC, and the court will issue a decree based entirely on the amicable compromise.

What happens if the property is too small to be physically divided?

Under Section 2 of the Partition Act 1893, if the property is indivisible (such as a tiny commercial shop), the court orders a public or private auction among co-sharers and divides the cash proceeds.

Does paying land revenue tax (Khajna) prove title in a partition suit?

No. Dakhilas prove payment of revenue but do not establish substantive title. Title must be proved through registered deeds and unbroken Khatian records.

Power of Attorney from USA, UK & Canada for Bangladesh Property: Embassy Attestation & MOFA Stamping Guide (2026)

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-26 · 18 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

For Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) residing in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, or Australia, managing ancestral land, selling real estate, executing development agreements, or representing family interests in court without physically travelling to Bangladesh requires a legally unimpeachable Power of Attorney (আমমোক্তারনামা). Under the Power of Attorney Act 2012 (পাওয়ার অব অ্যাটর্নি আইন, ২০১২) and the Power of Attorney Rules 2015, any instrument executed outside Bangladesh is subject to a rigorous, non-negotiable three-tier authentication regime: Consular attestation abroad, Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) verification in Dhaka, and stamp duty adjudication by the District Collector (DC Office). A single procedural error—such as an incomplete property schedule, missing photograph seals, or missing statutory deadlines under the Stamp Act 1899—renders the deed void ab initio, unregistrable at the Sub-Registry, and legally inadmissible in Bangladeshi civil courts. This comprehensive guide walks expatriate landowners through the exact legal framework, drafting requirements, embassy workflows, domestic stamping protocols, and revocation mechanisms.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

1. Statutory Framework: Power of Attorney Act 2012 & 2015 Rules

Executing an overseas Power of Attorney is strictly governed by Section 6 of the Power of Attorney Act, 2012 (Act No. 35 of 2012) read with Rule 13 of the Power of Attorney Rules, 2015. Prior to the 2012 Act, fraudulent powers of attorney executed on plain paper or via informal notary endorsements caused rampant land litigation across Bangladesh. The 2012 legislative overhaul established unambiguous statutory safeguards to protect both absent landowners and third-party buyers.

Key statutory provisions that every Non-Resident Bangladeshi must understand include:

  • Section 6(1) of the 2012 Act: Mandates that any Power of Attorney executed outside Bangladesh must be executed before an authorized officer of the Bangladesh Foreign Mission stationed in that foreign country.
  • Rule 13(1) of the 2015 Rules: Prescribes that the deed must strictly adopt Form 1 of the Schedule. Any substantive omission of statutory declarations renders the document invalid.
  • Section 18 of the Stamp Act, 1899: Stipulates that every instrument executed out of Bangladesh chargeable with duty must be stamped by the Collector within three months (extended to four months in administrative practice) after it has been first received in Bangladesh.
  • Sections 17 and 33 of the Registration Act, 1908: Dictate when a Power of Attorney must be compulsorily registered before a Sub-Registrar to confer legal capacity to convey title or execute sale deeds.

Without full compliance across all four statutes, the document cannot be presented in any court of law, land revenue office (AC Land), or Sub-Registry in Bangladesh.

2. Three Types of Powers: General, Special, and Irrevocable

Expatriates must exercise utmost legal precision when selecting the nature of the power granted. Confusing these categories can result in an untrustworthy agent selling off ancestral assets without permission:

A. Special Power of Attorney (নির্দিষ্ট আমমোক্তারনামা)

A Special Power of Attorney confers limited, explicitly demarcated authority for a designated legal act. Examples include:

  • Filing or defending a specific partition suit (বাটোয়ারা মামলা) or title suit in a Civil Court.
  • Applying for e-Mutation (ই-নামজারি) and paying Land Development Tax before the Assistant Commissioner (Land).
  • Applying for certified copies of Khatians (CS, SA, RS, BS) and Registered Deeds from the Sub-Registry.
  • Overseeing building renovations or collecting commercial rents.

Once the specified purpose is fulfilled, the authority automatically extinguishes. This is the safest, most recommended instrument for expatriates managing family land affairs from abroad.

B. General Power of Attorney (সাধারণ আমমোক্তারনামা)

Under Section 2(1) of the 2012 Act, a General Power confers comprehensive administrative powers over all properties or multiple assets of the Principal. While an agent holding a General Power can sign lease agreements, supervise caretakers, and pay municipal taxes, a General Power does NOT automatically authorize the agent to sell, gift, mortgage, or execute a registered transfer deed unless express, unambiguous language granting power of alienation is explicitly written into the deed and registered at the Sub-Registry.

C. Irrevocable Power of Attorney for Land Transfer (অপ্রত্যাহারযোগ্য পাওয়ার অব অ্যাটর্নি)

Under Section 2(2) and Section 6 of the 2012 Act, an Irrevocable Power of Attorney is an instrument executed in connection with a contract for sale (বায়না চুক্তি), financial consideration, or a real estate joint-venture development agreement with a developer. Key attributes:

  • It cannot be cancelled or revoked unilaterally by the Principal without court intervention or mutual registered deed.
  • It requires mandatory registration at the competent Sub-Registry office upon arrival in Bangladesh.
  • If the Principal dies, the power does not automatically lapse; the legal heirs remain bound by the obligations under Section 14 of the 2012 Act.

3. Comparison Matrix: Power of Attorney Types & Requirements

The following table outlines the comparative legal requirements, registration necessity, and risks associated with each instrument:

FeatureSpecial Power (নির্দিষ্ট)General Power (সাধারণ)Irrevocable Power (অপ্রত্যাহারযোগ্য)
Scope of AuthoritySingle specific act (e.g. partition suit, mutation)General management, maintenance, leasingSale, conveyance, joint venture development
Sub-Registry RegistrationNot mandatory unless authorizing deed executionOptional for management; Mandatory for saleMandatory under Section 6 of 2012 Act
RevocabilityFreely revocable at any time by PrincipalFreely revocable by executing Deed of RevocationIrrevocable without formal Court Decree or consent
Effect of Principal's DeathExtinguished immediately upon deathExtinguished immediately upon deathSurvives; binding on legal heirs (Sec 14)
Recommended For NRBsHighly Recommended (Lowest risk)Moderate (Only with trusted close family)High Caution (Requires strict legal drafting)

4. Step 1 — Drafting the Deed in Statutory Form 1

A Power of Attorney drafted in colloquial English or relying on standard Western notary templates will be outright rejected by Bangladeshi revenue authorities. Under Rule 13 of the Power of Attorney Rules 2015, the draft must strictly incorporate Form 1. Drafting should be carried out by an advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh or experienced land counsel.

Mandatory drafting components include:

  1. Principal's Identification: Full name, Bangladeshi Passport Number (or foreign passport with NVR endorsement), Overseas Residential Address, Permanent Address in Bangladesh, Father's and Mother's names.
  2. Attorney's Identification: Full name, Bangladeshi National ID (NID) number (mandatory), Father's and Mother's names, permanent address, and active telephone/email.
  3. Exhaustive Property Schedule (তফসিল):
    • District, Sub-Registry Office, Police Station (Thana), and Union/Ward.
    • Mouza name and JL Number.
    • Khatian Numbers: CS, SA, RS, and City Survey / BS (as applicable).
    • Dag / Plot Numbers: CS, SA, RS, and BS.
    • Exact area of land in Acres, Decimals (শতাংশ), or Square Feet, along with physical boundaries (চৌহদ্দি: North, South, East, West).
  4. Specific Operative Clauses: Itemized list of authorized actions. Avoid general blanket statements like 'to do all lawful acts'; specify whether the agent can sign plaints, appear before the AC Land, compromise disputes, receive money, or execute sale deeds.
  5. Affidavit of Execution: The statutory declaration confirming that the Principal is executing the instrument voluntarily, of sound mind, and without undue influence.

5. Step 2 — Consular Signing & Attestation at Bangladesh Missions Abroad

Once the deed is drafted, the Principal must personally attend the diplomatic mission having territorial consular jurisdiction over their residence.

Mandatory Procedure at the Embassy or High Commission:

  1. Personal Appearance: Under Section 6(1) of the Act, all Principals granting the power must appear physically. Postal or mail-in signing without personal appearance is prohibited.
  2. Photographs: Affix passport-sized color photographs of both the Principal and the nominated Attorney at the designated locations on the first page of the deed.
  3. Signature in Consular Presence: The Principal must sign every page of the deed and append their signature/thumb impression in the direct presence of the Consular Officer.
  4. Cross-Stamping: The Consular Officer signs and places the official metal embossed seal and rubber stamp partly across the photograph and partly across the page. This prevents fraudulent photo substitution.
  5. Consular Fee Receipt: Obtain the official consular fee receipt and keep a scanned digital backup of the attested deed before physical dispatch.

7. Step 3 — Verification at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) in Dhaka

Following embassy attestation abroad, the original document must be dispatched to Bangladesh via secure courier (DHL or FedEx). Under Bangladeshi law, consular signatures abroad are not automatically judicially recognized until endorsed by the central executive government.

Section 18 Limitation Warning: The deed must be presented to the Consular and Welfare Wing of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), 1st Building, Segunbagicha, Dhaka within 4 months of its physical receipt in Bangladesh. Failure to submit within statutory limitation requires a cumbersome condonation application accompanied by postal tracking proofs.

MOFA Authentication Protocol:

  • The attorney or their engaged advocate submits the original deed at the MOFA Consular Counter between 9:30 AM and 12:30 PM on government working days.
  • MOFA officials match the embassy seal and signature against the official Diplomatic Signature Registry maintained by the Ministry.
  • Upon authentication, MOFA places an official barcode sticker, endorsement stamp, and authorized signature on the reverse of the deed.
  • Standard turnaround time is 24 to 48 hours with zero government fee.

8. Step 4 — Adjudication of Stamp Duty by the District Collector (DC Office)

Under Section 18 read with Sections 31 and 32 of the Stamp Act, 1899, every instrument executed outside Bangladesh chargeable with stamp duty must be adjudicated and validated by the Collector (Deputy Commissioner / DC Office) of the district where the property is situated or where the attorney resides.

The DC Office Adjudication Procedure:

  1. Filing the Adjudication Petition: The attorney submits a formal petition under Section 31 to the Treasury / Revenue Branch of the DC Office, attaching the MOFA-endorsed deed, property Khatians, and NID copies.
  2. Assessment of Duty: The Collector assesses the appropriate stamp duty under Schedule I of the Stamp Act:
    • Special Power of Attorney: Fixed stamp duty ranging from BDT 500 to BDT 1,000 depending on the nature of court or administrative representation.
    • General Power for Management: BDT 1,000 to BDT 2,000 fixed stamp duty.
    • Power Authorizing Land Sale: Ad-valorem stamp duty or statutory fixed stamp duty (typically BDT 2,000 to BDT 5,000 depending on jurisdiction).
  3. Deposit via Treasury Chalan: The duty is deposited through an official Treasury Chalan (ট্রেজারি চালান - Code 1-1101-0025-2681) at Bangladesh Bank or designated branches of Sonali Bank.
  4. Collector's Certificate & Embossing: The Collector endorses a formal Certificate of Adjudication under Section 32 on the deed and affixes an embossed seal, certifying that full stamp duty has been collected.

9. Step 5 — Registration at the Sub-Registry Office

Is registration at the Sub-Registry mandatory for all overseas powers? This depends strictly on the legal objective of the document:

  • When Registration is NOT Required: A Special Power of Attorney authorizing an attorney to represent the NRB in a civil lawsuit (partition suit, recovery suit) or handle administrative mutation before the AC Land does NOT require Sub-Registry registration once DC Office adjudication is complete. The DC-embossed deed is immediately valid and acceptable in all civil courts under Section 85 of the Evidence Act 1872.
  • When Registration IS Mandatory: Under Section 6 of the Power of Attorney Act 2012 read with Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908, any Power of Attorney that authorizes the attorney to execute, register, or convey a deed of transfer (sale, gift, mortgage, or lease exceeding one year) MUST be registered at the Sub-Registry Office having local jurisdiction over the land within 4 months of DC office adjudication.

10. Fatal Drafting & Procedural Defects That Cause Rejection

Attorneys at Advocate Md. Shah Alam Chamber routinely encounter invalid overseas deeds executed by expatriates without professional guidance. The most common fatal mistakes include:

  • Vague or Incomplete Property Schedule: Stating 'My 10 decimals land in Uttara, Dhaka' without specifying Mouza, JL Number, CS/SA/RS/BS Khatian numbers, and Dag numbers. Sub-Registrars will summarily refuse registration.
  • Signing Before a Foreign Public Notary: An attestation by a US Notary Public, UK Solicitor, or Canadian Commissioner of Oaths has zero validity under Section 6 of the 2012 Act. The deed MUST be executed before a Bangladeshi Consular Officer.
  • Missing Photo Seal Across Face: If the consular officer signs below the photo instead of stamping across the photograph and the paper, the DC office will reject the document on suspicion of photo substitution.
  • Expiration of the 4-Month Window: Allowing more than 4 months to elapse between arrival in Bangladesh and submission to MOFA or DC Office without formal legal condonation.
  • Conflict of Interest: Appointing an attorney who is simultaneously the prospective buyer in a contract for sale without express disclosure.

11. Real-World Case Study: NRB Land Sale from New York to Dhaka

Background: Mr. Tariq Ahmed, a permanent resident of Queens, New York, inherited an undivided 6-decimal residential plot in Uttara Sector 11, Dhaka following his father's demise. A local developer offered BDT 2.5 Crore for the plot. Mr. Tariq could not travel to Bangladesh due to his employment.

Legal Strategy Implemented:

  1. Our chamber drafted a customized Special Power of Attorney in statutory Form 1, conferring specific authority to his elder brother in Dhaka to sign the development agreement, apply for RAJUK plan clearance, and receive consideration through account-payee banking channels.
  2. Mr. Tariq attended the Consulate General of Bangladesh in New York with his valid Bangladeshi passport and NID, executing the deed before the Consular Officer.
  3. The attested deed was dispatched to Dhaka via DHL. Our team completed MOFA authentication at Segunbagicha within 48 hours.
  4. We submitted the adjudication petition to the Dhaka Deputy Commissioner's Revenue branch, paid the statutory treasury chalan duty, and secured the Collector's embossing.
  5. The deed was presented to the Uttara Sub-Registry Office for formal registration under Section 17. The entire transaction was concluded safely in 24 business days without Mr. Tariq booking a single flight.

12. Legal Procedure for Revoking an Overseas Power of Attorney

If an expatriate discovers that their appointed attorney is acting against their financial interests, attempting unauthorized encumbrances, or misrepresenting rental proceeds, the power can be extinguished immediately:

  1. Draft a Deed of Revocation (আমমোক্তারনামা বাতিল দলিল): Must conform to Form 4 of the Power of Attorney Rules 2015, stating the original deed number, date, and reasons for cancellation.
  2. Consular Execution Abroad: The Principal executes the cancellation deed before the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad following the identical authentication procedure.
  3. Service of Formal Legal Notice: An enrolled Supreme Court advocate serves a formal Legal Notice under Section 11 of the 2012 Act to the Attorney via registered post with A/D, immediately terminating all legal agency.
  4. Notification to Authorities: Formal intimation copies are dispatched to the Sub-Registrar, Assistant Commissioner (Land), and relevant Civil Courts.
  5. Public Notice in National Dailies: Publish a formal notice of revocation in one Bengali national daily (e.g. Daily Ittefaq/Prothom Alo) and one English national daily (e.g. The Daily Star) to notify the public and invalidate third-party dealings.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I execute a Power of Attorney if my Bangladeshi Passport has expired?

Yes. If your Bangladeshi passport is expired, you can present your foreign passport (US, UK, Canadian) provided it carries a valid 'No Visa Required' (NVR) seal or you produce your original 10-digit/17-digit Bangladeshi National ID (NID) card or Dual Nationality Certificate.

Can I execute a Power of Attorney for property sale without going to the Embassy?

No. Under Section 6 of the Power of Attorney Act 2012, personal appearance before a Consular Officer of the Bangladesh Mission abroad is mandatory. Remote notary or digital execution is invalid under Bangladeshi real estate law.

What is the penalty if an Attorney misuses their power or sells land illegally?

Under Section 13 of the Power of Attorney Act 2012 and Section 406/420 of the Penal Code 1860, fraudulent misuse of power of attorney is punishable with rigorous imprisonment up to 5 years, along with separate criminal liability under the Land Crime Prevention and Redress Act 2023.

How long does the entire Power of Attorney process take from USA/UK to Bangladesh?

Consular attestation abroad takes 2 to 5 working days. International courier takes 3 to 4 days. MOFA authentication in Dhaka takes 2 days, and DC office adjudication takes 7 to 15 business days. The complete cycle takes approximately 3 to 4 weeks.

Does a Power of Attorney remain valid after the death of the Principal?

A Special or General Power of Attorney automatically terminates upon the death of the Principal. However, under Section 14 of the 2012 Act, an Irrevocable Power of Attorney executed for consideration survives and binds the legal heirs.

Can I appoint two Attorneys simultaneously to act jointly or severally?

Yes. You can appoint multiple attorneys in Form 1, specifying whether they must act jointly (যৌথভাবে - both must sign all documents) or severally (পৃথকভাবে - either attorney can act independently).

Can a foreign national spouse be appointed as an Attorney for Bangladesh land?

While legally permissible, it is highly impractical. The Attorney must physically attend land revenue offices, sub-registries, and courts in Bangladesh. Appointing a Bangladeshi citizen resident in Bangladesh with a valid NID is strongly advised.

What happens if I miss the 4-month limitation deadline for MOFA or DC office stamping?

Your advocate must file a formal application under Section 18 of the Stamp Act 1899 showing 'sufficient cause' (such as medical emergency or postal delay) accompanied by courier receipts to secure condonation of delay from the Collector.

Online Fraud and Cheating Case Under Bangladesh Law: Your Legal Options

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-04-07 · 8 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Online fraud is surging in Bangladesh — fake e-commerce shops, advance fee scams, fake job offers, and investment fraud are causing significant financial losses. Bangladesh law provides multiple legal routes to pursue both criminal prosecution and civil recovery of your money. This guide walks you through your options.

: · Cyber Crime & Criminal Defense Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing LawCyber Security Act, 2023 & Penal Code, 1860 (Bangladesh)

📋 In This Article

  2. Common Types of Online Fraud in Bangladesh
  3. Laws That Apply to Online Fraud
  4. Criminal vs. Civil Routes
  5. How to File a Fraud Case
  6. Can You Recover Your Money?

What is Online Fraud Under Bangladesh Law?

Online fraud involves using digital channels — websites, social media, messaging apps — to deceive a person into parting with money or valuables under false pretences. Under Bangladesh law, this falls under:

  • Penal Code 1860, Section 420: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property — up to 7 years' imprisonment and fine.
  • Digital Security Act 2018, Section 25: Publishing false, menacing, or offensive information through digital means — up to 5 years.
  • DSA Section 24: Identity theft and impersonation online — up to 5 years.

Contact a cyber law lawyer in Dhaka to determine which laws apply to your specific fraud situation.

Common Types of Online Fraud in Bangladesh

The most reported online fraud types in Bangladesh include:

  • Fake e-commerce shops: Facebook pages or websites that take payment and never deliver goods.
  • Advance fee scams: Promises of large sums of money, lottery wins, or job offers requiring upfront payment.
  • Investment fraud: Fake investment platforms (cryptocurrency, stock trading) promising unrealistic returns.
  • Impersonation fraud: Scammers posing as government officials, bank employees, or trusted persons to extract money.
  • Romance scams: Building fake romantic relationships online to eventually extort money.
  • Fake job offers: Charging fees for non-existent jobs, especially targeting overseas employment seekers.
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

How to File a Fraud Case

Steps to take after falling victim to online fraud:

  1. Collect and preserve all evidence: Screenshots of conversations, payment receipts, the website/page URL, bank transfer records, and any contact information used by the fraudster.
  2. File an FIR at your nearest police station under sections 420 of the Penal Code and relevant DSA provisions.
  3. Report to the Cyber Crime Unit of the Bangladesh Police (Cyber Support for Women Desk for women victims) or file directly at the Cyber Tribunal.
  4. Report to your bank immediately if you made a bank transfer — they may be able to freeze the recipient's account if you act within 24-48 hours.
  5. File a civil suit for recovery of the fraudulently obtained money.

Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam in Uttara for immediate legal action on online fraud cases.

Can You Recover Your Money?

Recovery is possible but depends on speed of action:

  • Bank transfers (within 24-48 hours): Contact your bank and the fraudster's bank immediately to request a freeze. Courts can compel banks to reverse fraudulent transactions if acted upon quickly.
  • Mobile banking fraud (bKash/Nagad): Report immediately to the MFS provider — they have fraud departments and can sometimes reverse transactions if the money has not been withdrawn.
  • Court recovery order: Once a criminal case is filed and assets of the fraudster are identified, courts can order attachment and recovery.

The single most important factor in financial recovery is speed — every hour of delay reduces the chance of recovery significantly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get my money back from a Facebook page scam?

If the Facebook page operator can be identified and their bank account or MFS wallet traced, courts can order recovery. Reporting to police quickly and engaging a lawyer for an urgent court order gives the best chance of recovery.

Is it worth filing a case for a small fraud amount?

Even small amounts should be reported — patterns of fraud by the same operator can be established across multiple complaints, making prosecution much stronger. Filing a case also creates an official record that supports insurance or tax claims.

Can I sue a fake e-commerce website anonymously?

You can file an FIR. The police or Cyber Tribunal can compel Facebook, domain registrars, and payment processors to reveal the owner's identity through court orders.

Online Harassment and Cyberstalking Law Bangladesh: What Victims Can Do

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-04-04 · 8 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Online harassment in Bangladesh has reached alarming levels — threatening messages, relentless tagging, fake profiles circulating personal information, and digital stalking that invades every aspect of a victim's life. If you are being harassed online, Bangladesh law provides criminal charges, protective orders, and emergency relief. This guide explains your rights and legal options.

: · Cyber Crime & Criminal Defense Lawyer Dhaka

What is Online Harassment Under Bangladesh Law?

Online harassment includes any pattern of digital behaviour intended to frighten, distress, intimidate, humiliate, or control another person. Under Bangladesh law, this covers:

  • Repeated threatening or abusive messages.
  • Creating fake accounts to impersonate or mock the victim.
  • Spreading intimate images or private information.
  • Coordinated harassment by groups (dogpiling or mass tagging).
  • Repeated unwanted contact after being asked to stop.
  • Monitoring a person's movements, location, or activity online.

If you are experiencing any of these, you have legal remedies available in Bangladesh courts. Contact a cyber law lawyer in Uttara or Dhaka immediately.

Laws That Protect Victims of Online Harassment

Multiple laws provide protection:

  • Digital Security Act 2018, Section 25: Sending offensive, menacing, or false information through digital means — up to 5 years' imprisonment.
  • DSA Section 29: Online defamation accompanying the harassment — up to 3 years.
  • DSA Section 26: Distributing intimate images (revenge porn, sextortion) — up to 7 years.
  • Penal Code 1860, Section 506: Criminal intimidation — up to 7 years for threats of grievous harm.
  • Penal Code Section 354A (as applicable): Sexual harassment including in digital spaces.

Bangladesh also has general provisions under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000 that cover harassment through digital means.

How to Document Online Harassment

Proper documentation is critical before filing any complaint. Do this immediately:

  • Screenshot everything — messages, posts, profiles, notifications. Include timestamps and URLs.
  • Do not delete or block immediately — blocking destroys evidence. Screenshot first, then block.
  • Record dates and times of each incident in a written log.
  • Save any phone numbers or email addresses used to contact you.
  • Preserve digital evidence — do not edit or alter screenshots, as this can undermine their credibility in court.

A cyber law lawyer can apply to court for an order preserving digital evidence from platforms before it disappears.

Can You Get a Protection Order?

Yes. Bangladesh courts can issue interim orders (injunctions) requiring the harasser to:

  • Cease all contact with the victim.
  • Delete posts, profiles, or content used to harass.
  • Stay away from the victim's physical locations.

In urgent cases — particularly threats of violence or ongoing distribution of intimate images — the court can grant emergency interim relief within days. Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam in Uttara for emergency court proceedings.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get the harasser's identity from their fake account?

Yes. Through a court order, you can compel the platform (Facebook, Instagram, etc.) to disclose account registration data, IP addresses, and linked phone numbers. Police digital forensics can also trace anonymous accounts.

What if the harasser is in another city or country?

Bangladesh courts have jurisdiction over cyber harassment directed at Bangladesh residents regardless of where the harasser is located. International enforcement is an additional step but domestic court orders against platforms are immediately enforceable.

What should I do if I receive threats of violence online?

Treat it as an emergency. Screenshot the threats and contact the police immediately for a safety assessment. Also engage a lawyer to seek an emergency court order. Do not assume online threats are just words.

Overseas Job Visa Fraud and Human Trafficking in Bangladesh: Legal Actions Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-13 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Every year across Bangladesh, hundreds of thousands of aspiring workers and youth dream of securing employment in Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Malaysia, Italy, or Eastern Europe to build a secure future for their families. Tragically, this migration desperation is exploited by predatory manpower syndicates, unlicensed sub-agents (Dalals), and rogue recruiting agencies. Victims sell ancestral lands, borrow money at exorbitant interest, and hand over BDT 5,00,000 to BDT 15,00,000 for promised high-paying jobs, only to receive fake tourist visas, face severe exploitation abroad, or find themselves abandoned in transit camps in Dubai or Libya. In Bangladesh, taking money under false promises of foreign employment is not a mere civil breach of contract—it constitutes severe, non-bailable criminal offenses under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012 and the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013, punishable by life imprisonment. Here is the comprehensive legal guide to prosecuting visa fraudsters, opposing bail, and recovering stolen funds.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

  3. Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013: Licensing Rules

  5. Anti-Human Trafficking Tribunals: Process and Warrants

  7. Bail Opposition and Compelling Financial Restitution
  8. Comparison Table: Human Trafficking (§2012) vs. Cheating (§420)
  9. Illustrative Scenario: Recovering BDT 12 Lakh from a Visa Broker
  10. Talk to an Advocate

The Scourge of Overseas Visa Fraud in Bangladesh

Remittances sent by Bangladeshi migrant workers constitute a primary pillar of the national economy. Yet, the migration corridor remains fraught with deception. Unscrupulous middlemen operating out of rural villages and urban recruitment hubs routinely deceive aspiring workers with promises of 'free visas,' 'direct government work permits,' or 'guaranteed European factory jobs.'

Workers borrow money against high-interest informal loans or sell ancestral farmland to pay sums ranging from BDT 4,00,000 to BDT 12,00,000. Once the funds are pocketed, the brokers deliver counterfeit visas, send workers on tourist visas that result in immediate airport deportation, or route them through illegal transit networks where they face kidnapping and torture in transit countries. When victims demand their money back, brokers respond with threats, claiming political protection. Understanding that modern statutory enactments classify overseas job deception as serious human trafficking is the critical key to bringing these syndicates to justice.

Prevention of Human Trafficking Act 2012: Core Provisions

The premier statutory instrument combating cross-border recruitment fraud is the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012 (Manob Pachar Protirodh O Daman Ain 2012). The Act provides an expansive statutory definition of trafficking that specifically captures fraudulent foreign employment schemes.

Under Section 3 of the Act, trafficking includes recruiting, transporting, transferring, harboring, or receiving a person for the purpose of exploitation by means of threat, force, fraud, deception, or abuse of power. Section 7 prescribes severe punishments: whoever commits human trafficking shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven (7) years and may extend to life imprisonment, and with fine which shall not be less than five lakh taka (BDT 5,00,000). Furthermore, under Section 8, any person who attempts, abets, or conspires to commit trafficking faces identical rigorous sentences. Offenses under this Act are cognizable, non-bailable, and non-compoundable.

Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013: Licensing Rules

Operating parallel to criminal trafficking laws is the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013, which regulates the licensing and operations of recruiting agencies in Bangladesh. The Act makes it a severe criminal offense for any individual or agency to recruit or attempt to send migrant workers abroad without a valid recruiting license issued by the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment.

Under Section 31 of the 2013 Act, carrying out overseas recruitment without a valid license is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for up to five (5) years and heavy fines. Under Section 33, publishing false advertisements or making fraudulent representations regarding foreign jobs carries imprisonment for up to seven (7) years. Crucially, the Act empowers the government to cancel the operating license of any recruiting agency and forfeit their mandatory security deposit (typically BDT 50,00,000 or more held with the Ministry) to compensate defrauded workers.

Essential Evidence: Receipts, Bank Slips, and Chat Logs

To build an impenetrable criminal prosecution against a visa fraudster, documentary and electronic proof must be assembled before confronting the suspect:

  • Financial Audit Trail: Bank deposit slips, cheque counterfoils, RTGS advice, or bKash/Nagad transaction statements showing payments to the broker, agency, or their nominees.
  • Written Agreements and Money Receipts: Any signed money receipt, non-judicial stamp agreement, or handwritten commitment paper signed by the broker acknowledging receipt of funds for foreign employment.
  • Passports and Counterfeit Visas: Photocopies of the victim's passport surrendered to the broker, along with printouts of the fraudulent e-visas, job appointment letters, or fictitious flight tickets.
  • Digital Communications: Audio recordings of phone conversations where the broker promises job placement, and WhatsApp messages detailing visa promises, salary rates, and flight dates.

These exhibits form the core annexures attached to the initial criminal complaint.

Need professional legal advice or urgent court representation in Bangladesh? Send your case documents or dispute details on WhatsApp to +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients and local litigants can arrange an immediate confidential document review.

Anti-Human Trafficking Tribunals: Process and Warrants

To ensure speedy trials, the government established specialized Anti-Human Trafficking Offence Tribunals (Manob Pachar Daman Tribunal) across Bangladesh, presided over by Sessions Judges. Victims have two procedural avenues to institute proceedings:

  1. Filing an FIR at the Thana: The victim lodges a written complaint at the local police station under Sections 7, 8, and 10 of the 2012 Act. Police are mandated to register the FIR, initiate an investigation, and arrest the accused Dalal immediately.
  2. Direct Complaint Petition Before the Tribunal: If the local Thana refuses to register an FIR due to the broker's local influence, an advocate files a Complaint Register (CR) case directly before the Anti-Human Trafficking Offence Tribunal. The judge examines the complainant, inspects bank slips, and issues direct arrest warrants or directs the CID or PBI to investigate.

Cases before these specialized tribunals are fast-tracked, putting immense pressure on human trafficking syndicates.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

BMET Complaints and Agency Security Deposit Claims

In addition to criminal prosecution, victims should initiate administrative recovery proceedings before the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) and the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment.

Every licensed recruiting agency (RL holder) in Bangladesh is required by law to maintain a substantial cash security deposit and bank guarantee with the government. When a formal complaint is submitted to the Director General of BMET detailing that an agency took money but failed to provide genuine visas, the BMET summons the agency managing director for a summary arbitration hearing. If the agency fails to refund the money, BMET has the statutory power to encash the agency's security deposit, disburse the funds directly to the victims, and suspend the agency's license on the government server.

Bail Opposition and Compelling Financial Restitution

Because offenses under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012 are strictly non-bailable, when the accused broker is arrested and produced before the Magistrate or Tribunal, their defense counsel routinely moves for bail. This is the pivotal moment in the litigation.

The victim's advocate must vigorously oppose bail, presenting the bank deposit slips and demonstrating that the accused defrauded poor migrant families of their life savings and that the stolen proceeds remain unrecovered. Because tribunals are exceptionally strict in human trafficking matters, bail is frequently denied. Facing prolonged incarceration in central jail, the accused broker's family is almost invariably compelled to approach the victim to negotiate an out-of-court settlement, refunding the full stolen amount via certified bank pay orders to secure conditional bail.

Comparison Table: Human Trafficking (§2012) vs. Cheating (§420)

The table below summarizes the critical strategic advantages of prosecuting visa fraudsters under the Human Trafficking Act 2012 versus general cheating under the Penal Code:

ParameterHuman Trafficking Act 2012 (§7)Penal Code 1860 (Section 420 Cheating)
Punishment Severity7 years to Life Imprisonment + BDT 5L fineUp to 7 years imprisonment or fine
Bail ClassificationStrictly non-bailable (Hard to obtain)Non-bailable but bail granted routinely
Trial ForumSpecialized Anti-Human Trafficking TribunalRegular Magistrate / Assistant Sessions Court
Burden of ProofReverse burden on broker to prove legalityProsecution must prove every element
Compensation PowersCourt can order victim compensation directlyMust file separate civil Money Suit for money

Invoking the Human Trafficking Act 2012 transforms a slow civil dispute into a high-stakes criminal proceeding that prioritizes financial restitution.

Illustrative Scenario: Recovering BDT 12 Lakh from a Visa Broker

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how specialized criminal prosecution recovered stolen migration funds in Tangail:

Two young brothers from Tangail wished to travel to Romania for warehouse employment. A local manpower broker in Dhaka promised them work permits and visas within four months, collecting BDT 12,00,000 across two bank transfers and two cash installments backed by handwritten money receipts. Six months passed without visas; the broker produced two suspicious PDF documents that Romanian embassy verification revealed were forged. When the brothers demanded their money back, the broker threatened to implicate them in false criminal cases through his political connections.

The brothers retained an advocate specializing in human trafficking litigation. The advocate bypasses general cheating charges and drafted a formal criminal complaint under Sections 3, 7, and 8 of the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012, filed directly before the Anti-Human Trafficking Offence Tribunal in Tangail. The petition annexed the bank transfer statements, handwritten receipts, and the embassy forgery confirmation. Concurrently, the advocate filed an administrative complaint before the Director General of BMET in Dhaka.

The Tribunal took immediate cognizance and issued non-bailable arrest warrants. Police arrested the broker at his Dhaka office and transferred him to Tangail jail. When the broker moved for bail, the brothers' advocate fiercely opposed it, highlighting the unrecovered BDT 12,00,000 and the life-destroying impact on the rural family. After two months in jail with multiple bail rejections, the broker's family approached the brothers: the broker paid the full BDT 12,00,000 back via three certified pay orders, achieving complete financial recovery and ending the family's nightmare.

Talk to an Advocate

Navigating complex legal disputes in Bangladesh requires uncompromising documentary preparation, precise statutory drafting, and experienced courtroom representation. Whether you are seeking to buy back ancestral land through pre-emption, stay an unlawful bank auction, prosecute fraudulent recruitment brokers, restrain violent death threats, or resolve high-stakes income tax audit notices, procedural delays can extinguish your statutory remedies. A qualified advocate protects your interests, files emergency petitions, and enforces your legal entitlements across civil, criminal, revenue, and constitutional tribunals.

Need an advocate for this legal matter in Bangladesh? Send your documents on WhatsApp to +880 1712-655546, or call +880 1955-802007. Overseas clients: remote consultation and courtroom representation available.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is taking money for a fake foreign visa considered human trafficking in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under Section 3 of the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012, recruiting, transporting, or receiving money from any person for overseas employment through deception or fraudulent promises constitutes human trafficking.

What is the punishment for a visa broker (Dalal) under the Human Trafficking Act?

Under Section 7 of the 2012 Act, human trafficking is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for not less than seven (7) years and up to life imprisonment, along with a mandatory fine of at least five lakh taka (BDT 5,00,000).

Can I get my money back from a fraudulent recruiting agency through BMET?

Yes. Licensed recruiting agencies must maintain cash security deposits with the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare. If BMET finds the agency guilty of fraud during arbitration, it has the statutory power to forfeit the agency's security deposit and compensate victims directly.

What evidence is needed to prove visa fraud against an agent?

You need bank transfer receipts, money receipts, WhatsApp chat messages, audio recordings of promises, passport copy handovers, and printouts of any fake visas or job appointment letters provided by the broker.

What should I do if the local police station refuses to file my case against a visa broker?

If the local Thana refuses to register an FIR, your advocate can file a direct criminal petition before the specialized Anti-Human Trafficking Offence Tribunal (Manob Pachar Daman Tribunal) in your district, which can issue direct arrest warrants.

Can an unlicensed sub-agent (Dalal) be prosecuted if they claim they gave the money to an agency?

Yes. Under Section 8 of the 2012 Act, abetting, assisting, or acting as an intermediary in human trafficking carries the same severe penalty. The sub-agent cannot escape liability by blaming an upstream agency.

How long does an Anti-Human Trafficking Tribunal case take in Bangladesh?

Under the 2012 Act, trials before Anti-Human Trafficking Tribunals are fast-tracked. Because offenses are strictly non-bailable, most fraudulent brokers seek an early financial compromise within 2 to 6 months of being remanded to custody.

Can an expatriate worker stranded abroad file a trafficking case in Bangladesh?

Yes. The stranded worker's family members in Bangladesh, or the worker acting through a Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy abroad, can file criminal cases against the recruiting syndicate in Bangladesh.

Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) in Bangladesh: Preliminary Decree, Advocate Commissioner & Court Partition Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-02 · 14 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In Bangladesh, undivided ancestral real estate and joint property ownership are notorious breeding grounds for multi-generational familial warfare. When co-sharers (brothers, sisters, cousins, or paternal uncles) refuse to amicably demarcate land, block legitimate inheritance shares, or unlawfully attempt to construct commercial buildings on the most valuable roadside frontage, the only definitive legal mechanism to legally sever joint ownership is instituting a **Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla / বাটোয়ারা মামলা)** in the Civil Court. Governed by the **Partition Act 1893**, the **Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC)**, and the **Court-Fees Act 1870**, a partition lawsuit is a unique, two-stage judicial procedure: obtaining a **Preliminary Decree** declaring each co-sharer's legal fractional share, followed by the appointment of a court-deputed **Advocate Commissioner** who physically surveys the ground, drafts separate lot allocations (Saham), and delivers a binding **Final Decree**. This guide details the step-by-step litigation roadmap, preventing co-sharer obstruction, court fees, and remote management for overseas heirs.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

  3. 3. Stage Two: The Advocate Commissioner, Amin Survey & Saham Allotment
  4. 4. Stage Three: The Final Decree, Registration & Delivery of Possession
  5. 5. Section 4 of the Partition Act: Buying Out Outside Strangers
  6. 6. Comparative Matrix: Partition Stages, Timeframes, Fees & Required Actions

  8. 8. Court Fees & Valuation: Fixed Partition Fee vs. Ad Valorem Dispute Fee
  9. 9. How NRBs Living Abroad Can Successfully Prosecute a Partition Suit
  10. 10. Real-Life Case Study: Resolving a 40-Year Family Land Dispute in Gazipur
  11. 11. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1. Nature of Partition Suits: Joint Title, Possession & Causes of Action

A Partition Suit (বাটোয়ারা মামলা) is distinct from all other civil litigations in Bangladesh. In an ordinary property lawsuit, one party wins and the other loses. In a partition suit, every co-sharer is simultaneously a plaintiff and a defendant, because the court's decree definitively settles the boundaries of all parties involved.

  • Undivided Co-Ownership: Every co-sharer owns a mathematical fraction of every square foot of the land until a legal partition occurs. One co-sharer cannot unilaterally sell off the prime roadside corner without the written consent of all other joint heirs.
  • Cause of Action: Arises the moment the plaintiff demands an amicable, registered partition deed (Aposh Batwara Dalil) and the other co-sharers refuse, delay, or attempt to grab more than their lawful share.
  • Filing Forum: Governed by the Civil Courts Act 1887. Filed in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge (for properties valued up to 25 Lakh BDT) or the Court of the Joint District Judge (for properties exceeding 25 Lakh BDT).

2. Stage One: The Preliminary Decree & Share Determination (Order XX Rule 18)

The initial phase of a partition lawsuit strictly adjudicates legal title and entitlement under Order XX, Rule 18 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908:

  1. Institution of Plaint: The plaintiff submits a plaint setting out the complete pedigree genealogy (Khatiyan Warishan tree), the chain of title deeds (CS, SA, RS, BS khatians), and the specific property schedules.
  2. Written Statement (W.S.): Defendants submit their written statements either admitting the pedigree or alleging previous oral partition, heba deeds, or lifetime sales.
  3. Trial & Evidence: The court examines documentary exhibits and records oral depositions (P.W.s and D.W.s) regarding the legitimacy of the heirs.
  4. Pronouncement of Preliminary Decree: The judge delivers a formal preliminary judgment declaring the exact arithmetic share of every co-sharer (e.g., Plaintiff No. 1 gets 0.250 share, Defendant No. 1 gets 0.375 share) and grants the parties thirty (30) days to partition the property amicably based on those declared shares.

3. Stage Two: The Advocate Commissioner, Amin Survey & Saham Allotment

When co-sharers fail to execute an amicable partition within the court-stipulated window, the plaintiff files a petition for the appointment of a Pleader Commissioner / Advocate Commissioner under Order XXVI, Rule 13 of the CPC:

  • Writ of Commission: The court issues a formal writ commanding an enrolled advocate commissioner, accompanied by a government-licensed land surveyor (Amin), to visit the suit land.
  • Notice of Field Survey: The Commissioner serves written notices upon all parties specifying the date and time of the physical field measurement.
  • Allotment of Saham (Lots): The Commissioner measures the land on the ground, prepares an accurate topographical map (Poshani Map), and divides the property into distinct, numbered allotments (Saham). In doing so, the Commissioner must balance frontage, road access, depth, and preserve existing residential structures wherever equitable.
  • Filing Commissioner's Report: The Commissioner submits a comprehensive written report, field map, and valuation schedule to the court. If any party is dissatisfied, they may file formal written objections under Order XXVI Rule 14.

4. Stage Three: The Final Decree, Registration & Delivery of Possession

Following the hearing of objections to the Commissioner's report, the civil court enters the final decree stage:

  • Final Decree (Order XX Rule 18): The judge confirms or modifies the Commissioner's allotment report and signs the Final Decree. The partition map prepared by the Commissioner forms an integral part of the decree.
  • Mandatory Stamp Duty & Registration: Under the Stamp Act 1899, non-judicial stamp paper must be deposited by the parties based on the net valuation of their allotted shares to engrave the final decree. The decree is then forwarded to the Sub-Registry Office for official entry into Book 1.
  • Execution of Decree (Title Execution Case): If stubborn co-sharers refuse to vacate the newly demarcated lots, the plaintiff files a Title Execution Case (Jari Mamla) under Order XXI CPC. The court deputes the Civil Court Nazir, who visits the land with police assistance, dismantles illegal fences, plants government demarcation boundary pillars, and hands over exclusive physical possession to the decree-holder.

5. Section 4 of the Partition Act: Buying Out Outside Strangers

One of the most aggressive predatory tactics in Bangladesh is when a rogue co-sharer secretly sells their undivided share in an ancestral family home to a violent local land grabber or outside developer to intimidate the remaining family members.

To counteract this, Section 4 of the Partition Act 1893 provides an extraordinary statutory shield:

'Where a share of an undivided dwelling-house belonging to an undivided family has been transferred to a person who is not a member of such family, and such transferee sues for partition, the Court shall, if any member of the family being a shareholder shall undertake to buy the share of such transferee, make a valuation of such share... and direct the sale of such share to such shareholder.'

Under settled Appellate Division rulings, the family member can compel the outsider to sell the share back to the family at the market value determined by the court, completely expelling the stranger from the ancestral home.

6. Comparative Matrix: Partition Stages, Timeframes, Fees & Required Actions

The judicial trajectory of a partition suit is outlined in the comparative table below:

Stage of SuitStatutory ProvisionCore Judicial PurposeAverage DurationKey Documentation
Preliminary StageCPC Order XX, Rule 18(2)Adjudication of title, genealogy & declaration of shares12 to 24 monthsPlaint, Warishan Sanad, CS/SA/RS khatians, Bia deeds
Advocate CommissionCPC Order XXVI, Rule 13Field survey, measurement & Saham allotment4 to 8 monthsWrit of commission, field book, Poshani partition map
Final Decree StageCPC Order XX, Rule 18Judicial confirmation of allotment & decree engraving3 to 6 monthsNon-judicial stamp papers, Sub-Registry registration copy
Title ExecutionCPC Order XXI, Rule 35Physical demarcation, pillar setting & delivery of possession3 to 6 monthsNazir execution report, police escort requisition

7. Emergency Relief: Obtaining Injunctions Against Construction & Tree Cutting

A classic menace during pending partition cases is the aggressive co-sharer who brings bricks, cement, and labourers onto the suit land to construct a multi-story building on the best commercial portion, attempting to create 'settled possession' that the court will hesitate to demolish later.

Under Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2 of the CPC, the plaintiff must file an emergency application for a Temporary Injunction on Day 1 of instituting the suit. The Supreme Court has firmly established that no co-sharer has the right to alter the nature and character of joint property or construct permanent structures until a final decree of partition is signed. The court will grant an immediate Status Quo or Injunction order restraining all construction.

8. Court Fees & Valuation: Fixed Partition Fee vs. Ad Valorem Dispute Fee

A major financial advantage of a partition suit in Bangladesh is the favorable court fee structure under the Court-Fees Act 1870:

  • Fixed Court Fee (Constructive Possession): If the plaintiff is in joint, actual, or constructive possession of any portion of the joint property, the court fee payable on the plaint is a fixed statutory fee of approximately 300 to 1,000 BDT under Article 17(vi) of Schedule II. The plaintiff does not have to pay expensive ad valorem fees on the multi-crore value of the ancestral estate.
  • Ad Valorem Fee (Complete Ouster): If the plaintiff admits that they have been completely ousted and dispossessed from the entire property, the court will treat the suit as one for declaration of title and recovery of possession, demanding ad valorem court fees up to the statutory cap. Skillful legal drafting must emphasize joint constructive possession to preserve the fixed court fee status.

9. How NRBs Living Abroad Can Successfully Prosecute a Partition Suit

Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) in the United States, UK, Canada, and Australia are disproportionately targeted by resident relatives who consume all rental income and refuse to demarcate land. An overseas heir does not need to abandon their employment to pursue a partition suit in Bangladesh.

Under the Power of Attorney Act 2012, the expatriate executes a Special Power of Attorney before the Consular Wing of the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, appointing an advocate or trusted representative in Dhaka. Once verified by MOFA and the DC Treasury, the attorney signs the plaint, adduces documentary evidence, attends the Advocate Commissioner's survey, and secures the final registered decree without the overseas heir ever needing to set foot in Bangladesh.

10. Real-Life Case Study: Resolving a 40-Year Family Land Dispute in Gazipur

Three expatriate sisters residing in Birmingham, UK, inherited a 2.5-acre prime highway-facing commercial land parcel in Gazipur following their father's demise. For over 35 years, their resident elder brother managed the entire property, collected commercial rents from truck terminals, and adamantly refused to divide the land, falsely claiming that their late father had gifted him the entire front section via an unrecorded oral Heba.

Engaging our legal chamber from the UK, our legal intervention proceeded as follows:

  1. Executed a Special Power of Attorney in London, authenticated by the Bangladesh High Commission, London, and cleared MOFA and DC Gazipur stamping.
  2. Filed Partition Suit No. 118/2022 before the 1st Court of the Joint District Judge, Gazipur, securing an immediate Ad-Interim Injunction restraining the brother from erecting new warehouse structures.
  3. At trial, our advocates dismantled the fraudulent oral Heba claim under Islamic jurisprudence, demonstrating that no change of possession or registered deed existed.
  4. The Joint District Judge pronounced a Preliminary Decree declaring the three sisters' combined 0.600 legal share in the estate.
  5. Upon the brother's refusal to demarcate amicably, our team secured the appointment of an Advocate Commissioner who surveyed the 2.5 acres, valued the frontage, and carved out a 1.5-acre independent commercial Saham with direct highway access for the three sisters.
  6. The court confirmed the Commissioner's report, passed the Final Decree, and executed the decree with police assistance, successfully planting permanent boundary pillars and allowing the sisters to lease their independent commercial plot to a multinational logistics corporation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between a Preliminary Decree and a Final Decree in a partition suit?

A Preliminary Decree declares the exact legal arithmetic shares of each co-sharer in the property. A Final Decree physically demarcates the land on the ground through an Advocate Commissioner, assigns numbered lots (Saham), and delivers separate registered title.

What is the court fee for filing a Partition Suit in Bangladesh?

If the plaintiff is in joint or constructive physical possession of any part of the land, the court fee is a fixed nominal fee of approximately 300 to 1,000 BDT under Article 17(vi) of Schedule II of the Court-Fees Act 1870.

Can a co-sharer construct a building on joint land while the case is pending?

No. Under Order XXXIX of the CPC, any co-sharer can obtain a temporary injunction restraining other parties from constructing permanent structures, cutting trees, or altering the physical state of joint land until the final decree is issued.

What does an Advocate Commissioner do in a partition suit?

The Advocate Commissioner is an independent officer of the court who visits the land with a licensed surveyor (Amin), measures the property, prepares a partition map, divides the land into separate Sahams (lots) based on road frontage and value, and files a report with the court.

What happens if an outside stranger buys land in our joint family home?

Under Section 4 of the Partition Act 1893, family members have the legal right to buy back the stranger's share at a court-determined market valuation, completely ejecting the outsider from the family dwelling house.

Can an NRB living in USA or UK file a partition suit without traveling to Bangladesh?

Yes. An overseas citizen can execute a Special Power of Attorney authenticated by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, empowering a Supreme Court advocate or representative in Bangladesh to institute and manage the entire lawsuit.

How long does a Partition Suit take in a Bangladeshi civil court?

A standard partition suit typically takes 18 to 36 months to progress through both the preliminary decree and final commissioner demarcation phases, depending on the number of co-sharers and court backlogs.

How is the final partition decree enforced on the ground?

If co-sharers refuse to honor the final decree, the decree-holder files a Title Execution Case under Order XXI CPC. The court deputes the Civil Court Nazir with police assistance to physically install boundary pillars and deliver possession.

Partition Suit & Joint Family Property Division Bangladesh – Legal Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-05-21 · 9 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

When multiple co-owners or family members share property but cannot agree on how to divide it, a partition suit is the legal remedy available under Bangladesh law. Whether you are dealing with ancestral land, inherited property, or jointly purchased real estate, understanding the partition process under the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 is essential to protect your rightful share.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka
