📋 In This Article
  1. What Is a Partition Suit in Bangladesh?
  2. Who Can File a Suit for Partition?
  3. Procedure for Filing a Partition Suit Under CPC
  4. Preliminary Decree and Final Decree in Partition
  5. Partition of Muslim Joint Family Property
  6. Pre-emption Rights in Property Partition
  7. Practical Tips and When to Hire a Lawyer

What Is a Partition Suit in Bangladesh?

A partition suit is a legal action filed in the civil court by a co-owner or co-sharer of property to compel the physical division (or separation of ownership interests) of jointly held property. In Bangladesh, partition suits are governed primarily by:

  • The Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC) — particularly Order XX Rule 18 (decree for partition)
  • The Partition Act 1893 — specifically applicable to partition of immovable property held by co-owners
  • Personal law (Muslim, Hindu) for family property disputes regarding inheritance shares
  • The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 for agricultural land

Any person holding an undivided share in property — whether through inheritance, purchase, gift, or co-ownership — has an absolute right to demand partition. This right cannot be contractually waived permanently, though parties may agree to postpone division for a reasonable period.

Partition can be either physical (the property is actually divided into separate portions) or by division of sale proceeds (where physical division is impractical, the court may order the property sold and proceeds distributed). If you are a co-sharer facing difficulties dividing ancestral or jointly owned land, consult a land and property lawyer in Dhaka.

Who Can File a Suit for Partition?

Any co-owner or co-sharer of property can file a partition suit, including:

  • Heirs who have inherited undivided shares in ancestral property
  • Joint purchasers of property
  • Donees who received an undivided share through gift or heba
  • Beneficiaries of a bequest under a will who hold an undivided share
  • A person who purchased a co-sharer's undivided interest from them

The suit must be filed in the Civil Court (usually the Assistant Judge's Court or Joint District Judge's Court, depending on the value of the suit) within the jurisdiction where the property is situated. All other co-owners/co-sharers must be named as defendants in the partition suit.

There is a limitation period for partition suits. Under the Limitation Act 1908, a suit for partition of immovable property generally must be filed within 12 years from the date the right to seek partition accrued. However, when a co-sharer is in actual possession, the limitation period may run differently — early legal advice is essential.

A minor co-sharer's interests are protected through a court-appointed guardian (Next Friend or Guardian ad litem), and the court must specifically protect their share when passing a partition decree. For complex family property disputes, seek guidance from a property lawyer in Bangladesh.

Procedure for Filing a Partition Suit Under CPC

Filing a partition suit in Bangladesh involves the following steps:

  1. Engage a lawyer and gather documents: Collect all title deeds, mutation records (namjari), CS/RS/BS khatian (land records), inheritance documents (succession certificate, heirship certificate, or Muslim family law declarations), and any court documents related to the property.
  2. Draft and file the plaint: The plaint must state the plaintiff's share, describe the property in detail (mouza, dag number, area, boundaries), list all defendants (other co-sharers), and pray for a decree of partition. Court fees are paid based on the valuation of the plaintiff's share.
  3. Service of summons: The court issues summons to all defendants to appear and file written statements.
  4. Framing of issues: The court identifies the disputed points — typically: (a) whether the plaintiff has the claimed share, (b) whether partition should be granted, and (c) how the property should be divided.
  5. Evidence and hearing: Both parties present documentary and oral evidence. Expert witnesses (amins/surveyors) may be appointed to assess the property.
  6. Preliminary Decree: The court first passes a preliminary decree determining the shares of all parties.
  7. Final Decree: After the preliminary decree, the court carries out the actual partition — either through a court-appointed commissioner/amin who physically divides the land, or by ordering sale of the property and distribution of proceeds.

Partition suits can take several years if contested. However, courts often encourage parties to settle through compromise partition, which can be recorded as a compromise decree (under Order XXIII CPC) and is much faster. An experienced land lawyer in Dhaka can help negotiate an amicable partition.

Preliminary Decree and Final Decree in Partition

The two-stage decree system in partition suits is a key procedural feature under Bangladesh law:

Preliminary Decree

The preliminary decree (under Order XX Rule 18 CPC) declares the rights of the parties — specifically, each party's fractional share in the property. It does not yet physically divide anything. The preliminary decree is important because:

  • It conclusively determines the ownership shares of each co-sharer
  • It can be appealed to the higher court if a party disputes the declared share
  • It forms the basis for the subsequent physical partition

Final Decree

After the preliminary decree, a court-appointed Commissioner (Amin) surveys the property and prepares a scheme of partition dividing the land into separate lots, allocating one lot to each co-sharer according to their declared share. The Commissioner's report is presented to the court, objections are heard, and the court then passes the final decree which physically allots specific portions to each party.

If physical division is impractical (e.g., a single-room building, or a very small plot of land that cannot be usefully divided), the court can order the property to be put up for sale by auction and the proceeds distributed proportionally. One co-sharer may also buy out the others at a court-fixed price.

Once the final decree is passed, each party can register their separately allotted portion and apply for mutation (namjari) in their individual name. Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam for expert guidance on partition proceedings in Dhaka and across Bangladesh.

Partition of Muslim Joint Family Property

In Bangladesh, the majority of partition disputes involve Muslim family property. Several special rules apply:

Inheritance Shares Under Muslim Law

n

Muslim inheritance law (derived from the Quran and Hadith, and applied through personal law in Bangladesh) prescribes specific fractional shares for each heir. For example:

  • A son receives twice the share of a daughter (asbah principle in Sunni law)
  • A widow receives 1/8 if there are children, 1/4 if there are none
  • Parents and siblings have defined shares under the rules of residuaries and sharers

Before filing a partition suit, it is advisable to obtain a Succession Certificate or a declaration of heirship from the family court. This document establishes who the legal heirs are and their respective shares.

Joint Family vs. Self-Acquired Property

Under Muslim law in Bangladesh, there is no concept of a joint family estate (as exists in Hindu law). Each Muslim owns their property individually, and on death it devolves instantly to the heirs in their prescribed fractional shares — creating a co-ownership situation. This co-ownership can be dissolved through partition at any time.

Pre-Death Gift and Exclusion

A Muslim may make a heba (gift) of property during their lifetime to one or more heirs. Such gifts, if properly made and delivered, reduce the estate available for partition. Disputes about pre-death gifts frequently arise in partition suits. An experienced property lawyer in Bangladesh can advise on challenging or defending such gifts in court.

Pre-emption Rights in Property Partition

Pre-emption is a critically important right in Bangladesh property law that intersects with partition proceedings. Under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (Section 96), a co-sharer in agricultural land has the right to pre-empt — that is, to purchase the share of another co-sharer who sells it to a stranger (third party) at the same price the stranger paid.

This right exists to keep agricultural land within the family/co-sharer group and prevent fragmentation of holdings among outsiders. Key points about pre-emption:

  • The pre-emption right must be exercised by filing a suit in the civil court within 4 months of the date of registration of the sale deed
  • The pre-emptor must deposit the full sale price and applicable duties with the court
  • Pre-emption applies to agricultural land held in co-sharership; it does not apply to urban non-agricultural land in the same way
  • If multiple co-sharers all claim pre-emption, the court distributes the purchased share proportionally among all the pre-emptors according to their existing shares

Pre-emption suits are separate from partition suits but are frequently related — a co-sharer who sells their share to a stranger triggers the pre-emption right of other co-sharers, which may then lead to a full partition proceeding. If a co-owner is selling their share to an outsider without your knowledge, act immediately — the 4-month deadline is strict. Contact a land lawyer in Dhaka without delay.

Practical Tips and When to Hire a Lawyer

Partition proceedings involve complex intersections of land law, personal law, civil procedure, and registration law. Here are practical tips for anyone involved in a partition dispute in Bangladesh:

  • Collect all land records early: Obtain the CS, SA, RS, and BS khatians, all mutation records, and copies of relevant deeds from the Sub-Registry Office and AC Land Office before filing suit
  • Verify all heirs: In a family partition, all legal heirs must be included as parties — missing a co-sharer can make the decree unenforceable against that person
  • Consider a family settlement: A mutually agreed partition recorded through a registered partition deed (ভাগ দলিল — bhag dalil) is faster and cheaper than court litigation. All co-sharers sign the deed before a Sub-Registrar.
  • Do not sell or encumber your share pending suit: Transferring your undivided share while a partition suit is pending complicates the proceedings and may trigger pre-emption claims
  • Monitor the mutation after final decree: After the final decree, ensure you promptly apply for mutation (namjari) in your name to perfect your individual title
  • Act on pre-emption quickly: If a co-sharer sells to a stranger, file the pre-emption suit within 4 months — courts are strict about this deadline

Partition suits require deep expertise in both civil procedure and property law. For professional legal representation in a partition suit anywhere in Bangladesh, contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam — an experienced land and property lawyer and Supreme Court advocate based in Uttara, Dhaka.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a co-owner be forced to accept partition in Bangladesh?

Yes. Every co-owner has an absolute legal right to demand partition of jointly held property. No co-sharer can be permanently forced to remain in co-ownership. If other co-sharers refuse to partition, you can file a partition suit in the civil court and the court will order partition.

What is the difference between a preliminary decree and a final decree in a partition suit?

The preliminary decree declares each party's fractional share (e.g., 1/3, 1/4) but does not physically divide the property. The final decree, passed after a court-appointed commissioner surveys and divides the land, allots specific plots to each co-sharer. Both decrees can be appealed.

How long does a partition suit take in Bangladesh?

A contested partition suit can take 3–7 years depending on the complexity, court backlog, and whether parties appeal. A mutually agreed partition through a registered bhag dalil (partition deed) can be completed in a few weeks. Mediation or compromise during the suit can also significantly shorten the timeline.

What is a bhag dalil and is it sufficient for partition?

A bhag dalil (partition deed) is a registered document through which co-sharers voluntarily agree to divide the property and record each person's allotted portion. It is registered at the Sub-Registry Office, after which each party can apply for mutation in their own name. It is fully sufficient and legally effective for voluntary partition.

Does a daughter have the right to demand partition of ancestral property in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under Muslim personal law (applicable to the majority of Bangladeshis), daughters inherit a defined share (typically half that of a son) in their parents' estate. They are co-owners of that share and have a full legal right to demand partition and obtain their allotted portion.

What is the court fee for filing a partition suit in Bangladesh?

Court fees for a partition suit are calculated on the value of the plaintiff's share (as declared in the plaint) under the Court Fees Act 1870. The rate varies but is generally a percentage of the declared value. Additional commissioner fees and other costs apply during the actual measurement and division.

Can I file a partition suit if there is an existing mortgage on the property?

Yes, you can file a partition suit on mortgaged property. However, the mortgage must be addressed in the partition proceedings — typically, the mortgage is paid off from the proceeds before distribution, or the mortgaged portion is allotted to the co-sharer who assumes the mortgage liability.

Partnership Business Law Bangladesh – Complete Legal Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-05-21 · 14 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Partnership is one of the most common business structures in Bangladesh, yet it is also one of the most legally misunderstood. Disputes between partners — over profit sharing, decision-making, or dissolution — can destroy a business overnight. Understanding your rights and obligations under the Partnership Act 1932 before entering or exiting a partnership can save you significant time, money, and legal hardship.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

📋 In This Article

  2. How to Form a Valid Partnership in Bangladesh
  3. Rights and Duties of Partners
  4. Liability of Partners to Third Parties
  5. Types of Partners: Active, Sleeping, and Nominal
  6. Dissolution of Partnership in Bangladesh
  7. Resolving Partnership Disputes in Court
  8. What to Include in a Partnership Deed: Essential Clauses
  9. Converting a Partnership to a Company in Bangladesh

What Is a Partnership Under Bangladesh Law?

Under the Partnership Act 1932 (applicable in Bangladesh), a partnership is defined as the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. Three essential elements must be present:

  • An agreement: A contract (oral or written) between two or more persons
  • A business: The partnership must carry on a lawful business activity, not merely hold property jointly
  • Sharing of profits: Profit must be shared among the partners (though loss sharing is implied)

A partnership is distinct from a company. Unlike a private limited company registered under the Companies Act 1994, a partnership does not have a separate legal personality — the firm itself cannot sue or be sued independently of its partners in Bangladesh law (though the firm name is used in practice).

The maximum number of partners allowed in a general trading partnership in Bangladesh is 20, and for banking partnerships 10. Beyond these limits, the entity must be incorporated as a company under the Companies Act 1994. For advice on choosing the right business structure, consult a company and corporate lawyer in Dhaka.

How to Form a Valid Partnership in Bangladesh

A partnership can be formed orally or through a written Partnership Deed (also called Articles of Partnership). While a written deed is not legally mandated, it is strongly recommended to avoid future disputes. A well-drafted partnership deed should include:

  • Name of the firm and its principal place of business
  • Names and addresses of all partners
  • Nature and scope of the business
  • Capital contribution of each partner
  • Profit and loss sharing ratio
  • Duties, rights, and powers of each partner
  • Salary or commission of managing partners (if any)
  • Rules for admission of new partners and retirement of existing ones
  • Procedure for dissolution and accounts settlement
  • Dispute resolution mechanism (arbitration or court)

Registration of the partnership in Bangladesh is optional under the Partnership Act 1932, but unregistered firms face significant disadvantages. An unregistered partnership firm cannot file a suit in a court of law to enforce rights arising out of the partnership contract. Partners of an unregistered firm also cannot sue each other for partnership rights. Registration is done with the Registrar of Firms under the Department of Registration.

To register, the partners submit the Statement of Partnership (Form I) signed by all partners, along with the partnership deed, identity documents, and prescribed fees. Upon registration, the Registrar issues a Certificate of Registration.

Rights and Duties of Partners

The Partnership Act 1932 grants partners several important rights (subject to the partnership deed):

Rights of Partners

  • Right to take part in management: Every partner is entitled to participate in the conduct of the firm's business
  • Right to be consulted: Ordinary business matters are decided by majority vote; extraordinary matters (e.g., changing the nature of the business) require unanimous consent
  • Right to access books: Every partner may inspect and copy the firm's accounts and books at any time
  • Right to share profits: Partners share profits in the agreed ratio; in the absence of agreement, equally
  • Right to indemnity: A partner is entitled to be indemnified for payments made and liabilities incurred in the ordinary conduct of business
  • Right to interest on capital/advances: Unless agreed otherwise, partners are entitled to 6% per annum interest on advances to the firm (but not on capital)

Duties of Partners

  • Duty of good faith (uberrima fides): Partners must act with absolute good faith toward each other — this is the cornerstone of partnership law
  • Duty to render true accounts: Every partner must keep proper accounts and share all information relating to the firm's business
  • Duty not to compete: A partner may not carry on a competing business without the consent of all other partners
  • Duty to work diligently: Active partners must devote time and effort to the partnership's business
  • Duty to account for secret profits: Any profit made by a partner through use of firm property or business opportunity must be disclosed and paid to the firm

Breach of these duties can give rise to a dissolution suit or a claim for accounts in the civil court. Contact a corporate lawyer in Bangladesh if a partner is breaching fiduciary obligations.

Liability of Partners to Third Parties

One of the most significant legal features of a partnership — and the biggest risk — is the doctrine of unlimited joint and several liability. Every partner is personally liable, jointly with all other partners and also severally (individually), for all acts of the firm done while the partner is a partner.

This means:

  • If the firm incurs a debt or faces a judgment, each partner's personal assets (home, savings, investments) can be used to satisfy the liability
  • A creditor can sue any one partner for the entire amount of the firm's debt
  • Even an incoming partner can become liable for pre-existing firm debts if they agree to assume them
  • A retiring partner remains liable for all debts incurred before retirement, unless creditors agree to release them

For acts of a partner that are wrongful (torts, fraud, misapplication of money) committed in the ordinary course of business or with the authority of other partners, the firm and all partners are jointly liable. This unlimited liability is the primary reason why many businesses prefer to incorporate as a private limited company. Consult a company lawyer in Dhaka to understand which structure best protects you.

Types of Partners: Active, Sleeping, and Nominal

Not all partners have the same role in the firm. Bangladesh partnership law recognises several types of partners:

  • Active (working) partner: Takes an active part in managing the firm's business. Has actual authority to bind the firm in ordinary business matters.
  • Sleeping (dormant) partner: Contributes capital but does not participate in day-to-day management. Still liable to third parties for firm acts.
  • Nominal partner: Lends their name to the firm without contributing capital or participating in management. Still fully liable to third parties who deal with the firm on the faith of their name.
  • Partner in profits only: Shares in profits but not in losses. This arrangement is valid between partners but does not shield them from liability to third parties.
  • Sub-partner: Shares in another partner's profits but has no direct relationship with the firm.
  • Partner by estoppel (holding out): A person who represents themselves (or allows themselves to be represented) as a partner, even if they are not one. They become liable to third parties who deal with the firm on the faith of that representation.

Understanding the type of partnership interest you hold is critical — especially when disputes arise. Sleeping partners often believe they are insulated from liability, which is incorrect under Bangladesh law. Always have your partnership structure reviewed by a business lawyer in Bangladesh.

Dissolution of Partnership in Bangladesh

A partnership can be dissolved in several ways under the Partnership Act 1932:

1. Dissolution by Agreement

Partners can dissolve the firm at any time by mutual consent. This is the simplest and most amicable method. All partners sign a dissolution agreement, accounts are settled, assets are distributed, and liabilities are discharged.

2. Compulsory Dissolution

A partnership is automatically dissolved if:

  • All partners (or all but one) are declared insolvent
  • The business becomes unlawful (e.g., the activity is banned by law)

3. Dissolution on Happening of Contingency

Unless the deed provides otherwise, dissolution occurs on:

  • Expiry of the fixed term for which the partnership was formed
  • Completion of the specific venture (for a partnership formed for a single project)
  • Death of a partner
  • Insolvency of a partner

4. Dissolution by Notice (at Will)

In a partnership at will (no fixed term), any partner can dissolve the firm by giving written notice to all other partners.

5. Dissolution by Court Order (Section 44)

A partner can file a suit in the civil court for dissolution on any of the following grounds:

  • A partner has become of unsound mind
  • Permanent incapacity of a partner to perform their duties
  • Willful or persistent breach of the partnership agreement
  • Conduct likely to prejudicially affect the business
  • Transfer/charge of a partner's share to a third party
  • The business can only be carried on at a loss
  • Any other just and equitable ground

After dissolution, partners must settle accounts in the following priority: (1) debts to third-party creditors, (2) advances by partners, (3) capital contributions, (4) residual profits shared in agreed ratio. If you are facing a contested dissolution, contact a Supreme Court lawyer for guidance.

Resolving Partnership Disputes in Court

Partnership disputes in Bangladesh are civil matters heard before the Civil Court having jurisdiction over the place where the partnership business is carried on. The main reliefs available include:

  • Suit for accounts and dissolution: The most common partnership suit — a partner seeks a court-supervised winding up of the firm, rendering of accounts, and distribution of assets
  • Injunction: To restrain a partner from misappropriating firm property, acting outside authority, or competing illegally
  • Appointment of receiver: The court can appoint a receiver to manage the firm's assets during ongoing litigation
  • Damages for breach of fiduciary duty: A partner who profits secretly or causes loss through bad faith can be sued for damages

It is critical to remember that only a registered partnership firm can file a suit to enforce rights arising from the partnership contract against other partners or third parties. An unregistered firm's partners cannot maintain a suit against co-partners for enforcement of partnership rights — though they can still be sued by third-party creditors.

Where the partnership deed contains an arbitration clause, disputes must first go to arbitration under the Arbitration Act 2001 of Bangladesh before proceeding to court. Arbitration is often faster and more confidential than litigation for commercial disputes. For expert legal representation in a partnership dispute, contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam, a Supreme Court lawyer with extensive experience in commercial litigation in Dhaka.

What to Include in a Partnership Deed: Essential Clauses

A well-drafted partnership deed is the foundation of any successful partnership in Bangladesh. Disputes arise most often when the deed is silent or ambiguous on critical issues. Every partnership deed should address the following essential clauses:

1. Name and Nature of the Firm

The firm name, the nature and scope of the business, and the registered address of the principal place of business.

2. Capital Contributions

Each partner's exact contribution (cash, property, services, or goodwill) and how additional capital may be required in the future (call obligations). Specify what happens if a partner fails to make a required capital call.

3. Profit and Loss Sharing Ratio

The exact ratio in which profits and losses are shared. If the ratio differs from the capital contribution ratio, state this clearly. Also address: treatment of drawings, interest on capital, and remuneration for working partners (if any).

4. Management and Decision-Making

Who manages day-to-day operations? Which decisions require unanimous consent vs. majority vote? How are disputes between managing partners resolved? Address the authority limits of each partner to bind the firm.

5. Banking and Finance

Bank account operation rules (joint signing requirements, spending limits), borrowing authority limits, and financial reporting obligations.

6. Partner Entry and Exit

Conditions for admitting new partners; how a partner may resign (notice period, settlement terms); what happens upon death, incapacity, or insolvency of a partner; whether surviving partners can continue the firm.

7. Non-Compete and Confidentiality

Prohibitions on partners engaging in competing businesses during and after the partnership; protection of firm trade secrets and client lists.

8. Arbitration Clause

A mandatory arbitration clause for partnership disputes can save enormous time and cost compared to civil court litigation. Specify the number of arbitrators and applicable rules (e.g., Bangladesh International Arbitration Centre — BIAC).

Have your partnership deed professionally drafted and reviewed by a corporate lawyer in Dhaka — the cost of proper drafting is trivial compared to the cost of resolving disputes arising from poor drafting.

Converting a Partnership to a Company in Bangladesh

As a partnership business grows, the unlimited personal liability of partners and the inability to raise external capital often make conversion to a private limited company the logical next step. Bangladesh law permits this conversion.

Why Convert?

  • Limited liability: Shareholders in a company are only liable to the extent of their unpaid share capital — protecting personal assets from business debts.
  • Perpetual existence: A company continues regardless of changes in membership — unlike a partnership that can dissolve on a partner's death.
  • Access to capital: A company can issue shares to investors; a partnership cannot.
  • Credibility: Many government contracts, large clients, and banks prefer or require dealing with a registered company rather than a partnership.

How to Convert a Partnership to a Company

  1. Dissolution of the partnership: Pass a formal resolution to dissolve the partnership firm and document the settlement of accounts.
  2. Incorporate the company: File for incorporation of a private limited company with RJSC under the Companies Act 1994. The former partners become shareholders and directors.
  3. Transfer assets: Execute proper transfer documents (registered sale deed for property, bill of sale for business assets) from the partnership to the new company.
  4. Notify creditors and regulatory bodies: Inform all creditors, banks, and relevant regulatory bodies of the conversion. Update all business registrations (trade licenses, tax, VAT, etc.) to the new company name.
  5. Update contracts: Existing contracts in the partnership name should be novated (transferred) to the new company with the agreement of the counterparty.

For professional guidance on partnership-to-company conversion and drafting all necessary documents, contact a company and corporate lawyer in Dhaka. The process typically takes 2–6 weeks from start to company registration.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it mandatory to register a partnership firm in Bangladesh?

Registration is optional under the Partnership Act 1932, but highly recommended. An unregistered firm cannot file a suit in court to enforce rights arising from the partnership contract, which severely limits your legal remedies in case of a dispute.

How many partners can a partnership have in Bangladesh?

A general trading partnership can have a maximum of 20 partners. For banking businesses the maximum is 10. If you need more members, you must form a company under the Companies Act 1994.

Can a sleeping partner be held personally liable for firm debts in Bangladesh?

Yes. All partners — including sleeping (dormant) partners — are personally liable, jointly and severally, for all debts and obligations of the firm incurred while they are partners. A sleeping partner's personal assets are at risk.

How is profit shared between partners in Bangladesh if no deed is signed?

If there is no partnership deed or if the deed is silent on profit sharing, profits and losses are shared equally among all partners under Section 13(b) of the Partnership Act 1932.

Can a partner be expelled from the firm in Bangladesh?

A partner can be expelled only if: (a) the partnership deed expressly provides for expulsion, (b) the power is exercised in good faith for the benefit of the firm, and (c) a majority of partners agree. Expulsion without these conditions is invalid and challengeable in court.

What is the difference between partnership and a private limited company in Bangladesh?

A private limited company under the Companies Act 1994 has a separate legal identity from its shareholders, limits liability to paid-up capital, and requires more formalities (Memorandum & Articles, RJSC registration). A partnership has no separate legal identity and partners have unlimited personal liability, but it is simpler to form and manage.

How do I dissolve a partnership if my co-partner refuses to agree?

If your co-partner refuses to dissolve the firm, you can file a dissolution suit in the civil court under Section 44 of the Partnership Act 1932 on grounds such as willful breach of agreement, misconduct, or 'just and equitable' grounds. The court may order dissolution and appoint a receiver to wind up the firm.

Partnership Firm Disputes and Fund Misappropriation in Bangladesh: Suits for Accounts, Dissolution, and Criminal Penalties

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-14 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Entering into a partnership firm begins with shared commercial ambitions and mutual trust. However, when a managing partner begins siphoning revenues into personal bank accounts, concealing transaction books, or operating parallel competing businesses, the firm faces imminent financial ruin and bitter legal warfare.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

The Anatomy of Partnership Breakdowns in Bangladesh

Imagine investing tens of lakhs of taka into a promising commercial partnership in Dhaka, Chattogram, or Narayanganj—perhaps an import-export trading concern, an IT agency, or a readymade garments manufacturing unit. As an investing partner, you relied on the managing partner to supervise daily operations, maintain billing records, and manage commercial banking channels.

Over time, revenue distributions mysteriously dry up. The managing partner claims market downturns and heavy operational losses, yet arrives in luxury vehicles and acquires prime residential plots. When you demand to inspect the firm's ledgers and bank statements, you are stonewalled, physically barred from the office premises, or threatened with false criminal litigation.

This betrayal is one of the most destructive commercial disputes in Bangladesh. However, the legal system does not permit a dishonest partner to hide behind informal accounting tricks. The Partnership Act 1932 and the Code of Civil Procedure provide comprehensive, coercive tools to audit stolen funds, freeze corporate assets, appoint independent court receivers, and hold rogue partners criminally responsible.

Fiduciary Duties Under the Partnership Act 1932

Under the Partnership Act 1932, the relationship between partners is fundamentally rooted in uberrima fides—the highest standard of good faith and mutual fiduciary duty. The Act establishes several non-negotiable statutory mandates:

  • General Duties of Partners (Section 9): Partners are bound to carry on the business of the firm to the greatest common advantage, to be just and faithful to each other, and to render true accounts and full information of all things affecting the firm.
  • Duty to Indemnify for Fraud (Section 10): Every partner must indemnify the firm for any loss caused to it by their fraud in the conduct of the business of the firm.
  • Accountability for Personal Profits (Section 16(a)): If a partner derives any personal profit for themselves from any transaction of the firm, or from the use of the property or business connection of the firm or the firm name, they are legally bound to account for that profit and pay it into the firm.
  • Prohibition on Competing Businesses (Section 16(b)): If a partner carries on any business of the same nature as and competing with that of the firm without consent, they must account for and surrender all profits made in that competing business.

Any managing partner who secretly diverts clients or revenues into a side enterprise commits a direct statutory breach of Section 16.

Investigating and Documenting Fund Misappropriation

Before rushing into court, an aggrieved partner must systematically build an airtight evidentiary portfolio. Courts decide commercial disputes on verifiable paper trails, not emotional accusations:

  1. Banking and Transactional Forensics: Obtain copies of the firm's official bank account statements. Compare incoming payments from major clients against the invoices recorded in company books. Trace electronic transfers routed to the personal accounts of the managing partner or their relatives.
  2. VAT and Tax Reconciliation: Scrutinize the firm's monthly VAT Mushak 6.3 invoices and annual income tax returns filed with the National Board of Revenue (NBR). Discrepancies between declared taxable turnover and actual sales records provide conclusive proof of suppressed revenue.
  3. Digital Communications and Audit Records: Preserve all email correspondence, WhatsApp chats, vendor delivery challans, and signed internal vouchers confirming operational transactions and disputed asset purchases.

Serving a formal Advocate Legal Notice demanding access to the firm's books under Section 12(d) of the Partnership Act establishes a statutory record of non-compliance if the managing partner refuses access.

Suit for Dissolution and Rendition of Accounts (Section 44)

When negotiations fail and the partnership is hopelessly compromised, the definitive civil remedy is filing a Suit for Dissolution of Partnership and Rendition of Accounts in the Joint District Judge Court under Section 44 of the Partnership Act 1932.

Section 44 empowers the civil court to dissolve a partnership firm upon the petition of a partner on several statutory grounds:

  • Section 44(c) - Prejudicial Misconduct: Where a partner is guilty of conduct which is calculated to prejudicially affect the carrying on of the business.
  • Section 44(d) - Persistent Breach of Agreement: Where a partner willfully or persistently commits breach of agreements relating to the management of the firm or conducts themselves such that it is not reasonably practicable for the other partners to carry on business with them.
  • Section 44(g) - Just and Equitable Grounds: The court possesses broad equitable discretion to dissolve a firm whenever circumstances render continued partnership impossible.

Upon hearing the preliminary stage, the court pronounces a Preliminary Decree for Accounts, appointing a qualified Advocate Commissioner or Chartered Accountant to examine all ledgers, determine total misappropriated funds, and submit a formal audit report to the court.

Facing a similar legal dispute in Bangladesh? Don't fight it alone. Contact Advocate MD Shah Alam for expert legal consultation, tactical dispute evaluation, and courtroom representation. WhatsApp: +880 1955-802007 or Call: +880 1712-655546.

Injunctive Relief and Freezing Firm Bank Accounts

The moment a rogue partner realizes a lawsuit has been filed, their instinctive reaction is often to empty company bank accounts, liquidate warehouse stock at distressed prices, and transfer machinery to third parties. Preventing this dissipation requires immediate injunctive relief.

Under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, your legal counsel must file an urgent application for an ad-interim temporary injunction concurrently with the plaint:

  • Restraining Bank Withdrawals: Impleading the firm's commercial banks as pro-forma defendants and seeking a restraining order against the rogue partner operating the accounts unilaterally.
  • Restraining Disposal of Firm Assets: Prohibiting the sale, mortgage, or transfer of factory premises, machinery, vehicles, patents, or trade inventories.
  • Maintaining Status Quo: Freezing existing commercial operations to preserve the firm's capital until the court adjudicates the preliminary decree.

Securing an injunction immediately shifts leverage back to the aggrieved partner, forcing the wrongdoer to the negotiating table.

Order XL CPC: Appointment of a Court Receiver

In severe disputes where partners are physically fighting or where the managing partner continues to embezzle daily cash flows, an injunction alone may be insufficient. The ultimate protective measure is the Appointment of a Receiver under Order XL Rule 1 CPC.

Where it appears to the court to be 'just and convenient,' the Joint District Judge has statutory power to appoint a Court Receiver to take immediate physical custody and management of the partnership business:

  1. Seizure of Books and Assets: The Receiver immediately enters the firm's offices, seizes all physical ledgers, servers, chequebooks, and keys to warehouses.
  2. Neutral Day-to-Day Management: The Receiver oversees ongoing operations, collects outstanding debts from clients, pays staff salaries, and deposits all operational revenues into a dedicated court-supervised bank account.
  3. Exclusion of Rogue Partners: The delinquent partner is stripped of administrative authority and physically excluded from handling company money.

Bangladeshi courts readily appoint receivers in partnership disputes where prima facie evidence of gross financial diversion and waste of assets is presented.

Criminal Remedies: Sections 406, 409, and 420 Penal Code

While partnership disputes are primarily civil matters, siphoning firm money frequently crosses the boundary into serious criminal offenses under the Penal Code 1860:

  • Section 406 Penal Code (Criminal Breach of Trust): A partner is an agent of the firm and holds company funds in a fiduciary capacity. If a partner dishonestly misappropriates or converts to their own use money belonging to the partnership, they are punishable with imprisonment for up to 3 years, or fine, or both.
  • Section 409 Penal Code (Criminal Breach of Trust by Banker, Merchant, or Agent): Where the partner acted as a managing agent or commercial trustee, penalties extend up to 10 years or life imprisonment.
  • Section 420 Penal Code (Cheating and Dishonestly Inducing Delivery of Property): Applicable where a partner induced investments based on fabricated profit projections or false capital contributions, carrying up to 7 years imprisonment.
  • Section 477A Penal Code (Falsification of Accounts): Penalizes any partner who willfully alters, mutilates, or falsifies firm account books with intent to defraud.

Filing a Complaint Register (CR) case before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or Thana FIR creates intense criminal liability that accelerates settlement.

Comparison Table: Civil Suit for Accounts vs. Criminal Action

Deploying both civil and criminal strategies requires an understanding of their respective objectives, procedures, and outcomes:

Strategic MetricSuit for Dissolution and AccountsCriminal Prosecution (Sec 406/420)
Governing ForumJoint District Judge Court (Civil Jurisdiction).Chief Metropolitan Magistrate / Sessions Court.

Primary ObjectiveDissolution of firm, formal audit, recovery of capital.Penal retribution, arrest warrants, criminal deterrence.
Immediate Interim ReliefInjunctions (Order 39) & Court Receiver (Order 40).Non-bailable arrest warrants (WA) & police seizure.
Standard of ProofPreponderance of probabilities based on audit ledgers.Strict proof beyond reasonable doubt of fraudulent intent.
Final ResolutionFinal money decree distributing assets and debts.Imprisonment and criminal fines paid to state/victim.

Illustrative Scenario: Recovering Misappropriated Capital in Dhaka

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): Kamrul and Navid established a partnership logistics firm in Motijheel, Dhaka, with a registered deed specifying equal 50-50 shareholding. Kamrul invested BDT 50 Lakh in cash, while Navid managed daily fleet operations. By the end of 2025, Navid claimed the company was running at a steep loss, demanding that Kamrul inject an additional BDT 20 Lakh to maintain vehicle leases.

Suspicious of the sudden deficit, Kamrul covertly engaged an independent forensic accountant. An audit revealed that Navid had opened a secret bank account under a nearly identical trade name in Uttara, diverting corporate transport contracts worth BDT 85 Lakh directly into his private account, while using Kamrul's capital to cover fuel and repair expenses.

Kamrul's advocate immediately moved the Joint District Judge Court with a Suit for Dissolution and Rendition of Accounts, concurrently filing an application for an ad-interim injunction and the appointment of a Court Receiver. Concurrently, a CR case under Section 406/420 Penal Code was lodged before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court.

The civil judge promptly granted an injunction freezing the firm's commercial accounts and issued a show-cause notice for a Receiver. Facing criminal arrest warrants and frozen operational cash flows, Navid conceded, signing a formal Solenama (compromise agreement) returning BDT 65 Lakh to Kamrul and dissolving the partnership peacefully.

Talk to an Advocate

A partnership dispute left unaddressed can rapidly deplete your lifetime capital, destroy your commercial reputation, and leave you saddled with fraudulent vendor liabilities. Allowing a rogue partner to continue controlling company ledgers invites wholesale destruction of evidence. An experienced corporate dispute advocate intervenes swiftly to secure freezing orders, place the business under court supervision, and recover your rightful profits.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can an unregistered partnership firm file a suit for accounts in Bangladesh?

Under Section 69(1) and (2) of the Partnership Act 1932, an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties or enforce contractual claims. However, Section 69(3)(a) provides an explicit exception: any partner can sue for the dissolution of the firm and for the rendition of accounts of a dissolved firm, regardless of whether the firm is registered with RJSC.

Can a partner be held criminally liable for stealing firm money under Section 406 Penal Code?

Yes. While partners hold joint ownership of assets, when a partner is entrusted with specific funds or books and dishonestly misappropriates them for personal enrichment to the exclusion of other partners, the Supreme Court has affirmed that criminal prosecution under Section 406 and 420 Penal Code is fully maintainable.

How does the court determine the exact share of profits if the partnership deed is silent?

Under Section 13(b) of the Partnership Act 1932, in the absence of any contract to the contrary, all partners are presumed to be entitled to share equally in the profits earned and must contribute equally to the losses sustained by the firm, regardless of differing capital contributions.

What happens to the partnership assets and liabilities upon court-ordered dissolution?

Under Section 48 of the Partnership Act, upon dissolution, firm assets are applied first to pay the debts and liabilities of the firm to third parties, second to repay advances made by partners beyond capital, third to pay each partner rateably what is due to them for capital, and any surplus is divided among partners in profit-sharing proportions.

Can the court appoint a Receiver before the final judgment of the dissolution lawsuit?

Yes. Under Order XL Rule 1 CPC, the court can appoint an interim Receiver at any stage of the proceedings, even immediately after the suit is filed, if the applicant demonstrates a strong prima facie case of fund diversion, asset dissipation, or gross mismanagement.

What is the time limit for an expelled or retired partner to file a suit for accounts?

Under Article 106 of the Limitation Act 1908, a suit for an account and a share of the profits of a dissolved partnership must be filed strictly within <strong>3 years</strong> from the date of the dissolution of the firm.

Can an aggrieved partner freeze the firm's bank accounts immediately through an injunction?

Yes. By submitting bank statements, partnership deeds, and evidence of unauthorized personal withdrawals, your advocate can petition the Joint District Judge Court under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 CPC for an ex-parte ad-interim injunction restraining the banks from honoring cheques signed unilaterally by the rogue partner.

What happens if a partner secretly starts a competing business using firm trade secrets?

Under Section 16(b) of the Partnership Act 1932, any partner who operates a competing business of the same nature without the consent of the other partners is statutorily obligated to account for and surrender all personal profits derived from that competing enterprise to the original firm.

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-02 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

For entrepreneurs, professional consultants, commercial trading houses, and joint-venture founders in Bangladesh, establishing a **Partnership Business (অংশীদারি কারবার)** offers a flexible, low-overhead alternative to incorporating a private limited company. However, a catastrophic mistake made by thousands of business owners across Dhaka, Chattogram, and Sylhet is operating an **unregistered partnership firm** on informal verbal understandings or basic notarized stamp paper. Under the **Partnership Act 1932**, failing to formally register the partnership with the **Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RJSC)** under Section 58 triggers devastating legal consequences under **Section 69**: the firm cannot sue third-party clients or suppliers to recover unpaid invoices, cannot enforce contractual rights in court, and partners cannot sue each other to settle accounts or dissolve the firm. This master business guide outlines the legal drafting of an unassailable Partnership Deed, stamp duty requirements, RJSC digital filing, municipal trade licensing, firm taxation, and risk mitigation.

1. Legal Definition & Essential Elements of a Partnership Under the 1932 Act

Section 4 of the Partnership Act 1932 defines a partnership as: 'the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.' To constitute a legally recognized partnership in Bangladesh, three foundational elements must co-exist:

  • Contractual Agreement: A partnership arises strictly from a voluntary contract, not from status, inheritance, or family kinship (Section 5). Joint Hindu family businesses or undivided heirs sharing rental income do not constitute a partnership.
  • Sharing of Profits: There must be an express agreement to distribute the net profits (and impliedly losses) generated by the commercial venture.
  • Mutual Agency: The hallmark test of a partnership. Every partner is simultaneously a principal and an agent for all other partners. Any lawful business contract signed by one partner in the ordinary course of the firm's business legally binds all other partners personally.

2. The Fatal Risks of Unregistered Partnerships: Section 69 Explained

While registration with RJSC is technically optional at the moment of inception, Section 69 of the Partnership Act 1932 imposes crippling statutory disabilities upon an unregistered firm:

  • Bar on Suing Third Parties: An unregistered firm cannot institute any suit in any civil court against a customer, client, or supplier to enforce a contract or recover unpaid business debts exceeding a trivial sum of 100 BDT. If a client defaults on a 50 Lakh BDT invoice, an unregistered firm's plaint will be summarily rejected by the court.
  • Bar on Partner vs. Partner Suits: No partner can sue the firm or fellow partners to enforce rights under the partnership deed or claim their lawful share of profits without simultaneously petitioning for the complete dissolution of the firm.
  • Bar on Set-Off: If a third party sues the unregistered firm, the firm cannot claim a legal set-off or counterclaim in court.

3. Partnership Firm vs. Private Limited Company: Pros & Cons

Choosing between a partnership firm and a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act 1994 involves balancing operational flexibility against liability:

  • Advantages of Partnership: Minimal compliance costs; no mandatory requirement to conduct formal statutory annual general meetings (AGM); freedom to draw capital without dividend withholding taxes; simple dissolution procedures without High Court winding-up petitions.
  • Major Disadvantages: Unlimited Personal Liability: Unlike limited company shareholders whose liability is capped at their unpaid shares, partners are jointly and severally liable down to their personal bank accounts, homes, and ancestral lands for the firm's debts; inability to raise venture capital or foreign direct investment (FDI); statutory cap of maximum 20 partners.

4. Essential Clauses in an Unassailable Partnership Deed & Stamp Duty

The Partnership Deed (Partnership Agreement) forms the constitutional charter of the business. Executed on non-judicial stamp paper of 2,000 BDT under the Stamp Act 1899, it must contain:

  • Firm Name & Principal Place: The registered trading name and official office address in Bangladesh.
  • Capital Contribution: Exact financial capital invested by each partner and whether interest on capital is payable.
  • Profit & Loss Ratio: Precise percentage split (e.g., 50:50 or 60:40). In the absence of an explicit clause, Section 13(b) mandates that profits and losses must be shared equally regardless of capital differences.
  • Management & Banking Powers: Designating managing partners authorized to operate commercial bank accounts, sign tenders, and bind the firm.
  • Dispute Resolution & Arbitration: Mandatory arbitration clause under the Arbitration Act 2001 to resolve intra-firm disputes without paralysing the business in civil court.

5. Step-by-Step RJSC Registration Workflow: Form I Submission

Securing official registration from the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RJSC) follows an established administrative procedure:

  1. Name Clearance: Apply for and secure formal Name Clearance for the proposed firm through the RJSC digital portal (rjsc.gov.bd).
  2. Execution & Notarization of Deed: Execute the Partnership Deed on 2,000 BDT stamp paper, signed by all partners before two witnesses and notarized by an authorized Notary Public.
  3. Filing Form I (Statement of Particulars): Submit Form I under Section 58 of the Partnership Act, specifying: (a) Firm name; (b) Nature of business; (c) Principal and branch addresses; (d) Full names and permanent addresses of all partners; (e) Date of joining of each partner; and (f) Duration of the firm.
  4. Payment of Registration Fees: Deposit statutory government registration fees and filing charges through designated bank branches via treasury challan.
  5. Issuance of Certificate of Registration: RJSC scrutinizes the dossier, records the particulars in the official Register of Firms, and issues the formal Certificate of Registration of Firm bearing the seal of the Registrar.
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

6. Comparative Matrix: Sole Proprietorship vs. Partnership vs. Private Limited

Understanding the statutory trade-offs across business vehicles in Bangladesh is critical for commercial founders:

Entity TypeGoverning StatuteLiability ProfileRegistration AuthorityThird-Party Suing Capacity
Sole ProprietorshipCity Corporation / Municipal Acts100% Unlimited Personal LiabilityLocal City Corporation / Union ParishadProprietor sues personally in own name
Registered PartnershipPartnership Act 1932Joint & Several Unlimited LiabilityRJSC (Registrar of Joint Stock Companies)Full capacity to sue under firm name
Unregistered PartnershipPartnership Act 1932Joint & Several Unlimited LiabilityNone (Unregistered)BARRED under Section 69; cannot sue
Private Limited CompanyCompanies Act 1994Limited Liability (Shields personal assets)RJSC (Corporate Registry)Independent legal entity; full capacity to sue

7. Post-Registration Compliances: Municipal Trade License, e-TIN & Bank Account

Securing the RJSC Certificate of Registration is followed by establishing the operating infrastructure:

  • Firm e-TIN Registration: Under the Income Tax Act 2023, a partnership firm must obtain a separate 12-digit electronic Tax Identification Number (e-TIN) from the National Board of Revenue (NBR), distinct from the personal e-TINs of the partners.
  • Municipal Trade License: Apply to the relevant City Corporation (e.g., DNCC, DSCC) or Union Parishad for a commercial Trade License issued in the official name of the partnership firm, submitting the RJSC certificate and deed.
  • Commercial Bank Account: Open a partnership current account by submitting the certified deed, RJSC certificate, trade license, partner NIDs, and a formal partnership mandate resolution specifying bank operating powers.
  • VAT (BIN) Registration: If engaged in manufacturing, trading, or importing, secure a Business Identification Number (BIN) through the NBR VAT online portal.

8. Handling Partner Disputes: Admission, Retirement & Dissolution of the Firm

When commercial partnerships face internal friction, the Act sets forth strict protocols:

  • Admission of a New Partner (Section 31): Requires unanimous consent of all existing partners unless the deed explicitly allows majority admission.
  • Retirement of a Partner (Section 32): A partner may retire in accordance with an express agreement or with the consent of all other partners. Mandatory public notice must be given under Section 72; failure to publish public notice leaves the retired partner personally liable for all future debts incurred by the firm.
  • Dissolution of the Firm (Chapter VI): May occur by agreement, compulsory bankruptcy, or by court order under Section 44 on grounds of partner insanity, permanent incapacity, or continuous deadlock.

9. NRB & Foreign Investor Participation in Bangladeshi Partnerships

Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) and foreign citizens can enter partnership firms in Bangladesh, subject to regulatory constraints under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 (FERA):

  • While foreign direct investment (FDI) generally flows through private limited companies, foreign individuals can join a partnership firm provided all inward capital contributions enter through official Authorized Dealer (AD) banking channels with an Inward Remittance Encashment Certificate.
  • NRBs can execute partnership deeds abroad through Consular Attestation at Bangladesh Embassies and manage their interests via a registered Special Power of Attorney.
  • Profit repatriation abroad is subject to NBR tax clearance and Bangladesh Bank regulatory guidelines.

10. Real-Life Case Study: Saving an Unregistered Dhaka Logistics Firm from 70-Lakh Default

Three logistics entrepreneurs in Tejgaon, Dhaka, operated an unregistered partnership firm for four years, relying merely on a notarized deed. A major corporate manufacturer defaulted on freight invoices amounting to 70 Lakh BDT. When the partners consulted a commercial lawyer to file a Money Suit, they were shocked to learn that under **Section 69 of the Partnership Act**, their suit was legally barred and would be dismissed with costs because the firm was unregistered with RJSC.

The partners retained our corporate legal chamber. Our tactical recovery strategy was executed as follows:

  1. Immediately initiated an expedited RJSC Registration campaign, securing Name Clearance, executing a fresh restated deed on 2,000 BDT stamps, and filing Form I before the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies.
  2. Obtained the official RJSC Certificate of Registration of Firm within 14 working days, effectively curing the statutory incapacity.
  3. Dispatched a devastating 15-day statutory Legal Notice to the corporate debtor under the firm's newly registered RJSC identity, demanding payment of the 70 Lakh BDT debt plus commercial interest.
  4. Concurrently drafted a Money Suit Plaint before the Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka, citing the newly issued RJSC registration certificate and establishing full compliance with Section 69.
  5. Faced with an airtight lawsuit and imminent court attachment of their corporate bank accounts, the defaulting manufacturer agreed to settle before trial, issuing Bank Pay Orders for the full 70 Lakh BDT within 30 days.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is registration with RJSC mandatory for a partnership firm in Bangladesh?

While not technically mandatory at the moment of creation, registration with RJSC under Section 58 of the Partnership Act 1932 is practically essential. An unregistered firm cannot sue third parties in civil court to recover debts or enforce contracts under Section 69.

What is the maximum number of partners allowed in a partnership firm in Bangladesh?

Under Bangladeshi law, a general partnership business can have a maximum of twenty (20) partners. If the firm is engaged in the business of banking, the maximum limit is ten (10) partners.

What is the stamp duty payable on a Partnership Deed in Bangladesh?

Under the Stamp Act 1899, a Partnership Deed must be executed on non-judicial stamp paper of exactly 2,000 BDT, signed by all partners before two witnesses and notarized.

What is the consequence of Section 69 of the Partnership Act 1932?

Section 69 bars an unregistered firm or its partners from filing any lawsuit in a civil court against third parties to enforce contractual rights or recover debts exceeding 100 BDT, rendering the firm legally powerless in disputes.

Do partners have limited liability in a partnership firm?

No. In a general partnership in Bangladesh, partners have joint and several unlimited personal liability. If the firm cannot pay its commercial debts, creditors can attach and auction the partners' personal homes, lands, and private bank accounts.

Can a partnership firm obtain its own separate e-TIN and Trade License?

Yes. A registered partnership firm must obtain its own 12-digit e-TIN from the National Board of Revenue (NBR) and a municipal Trade License from the local City Corporation or Union Parishad in the firm's name.

Can an NRB living abroad be a partner in a Bangladeshi firm?

Yes. A Non-Resident Bangladeshi (NRB) can become a partner by executing the partnership deed before the Consular Wing of the Bangladesh Embassy abroad and remitting capital through banking channels.

How can a partnership firm be dissolved in Bangladesh?

A firm can be dissolved in accordance with an express agreement in the deed, by unanimous consent of all partners, by compulsory dissolution upon bankruptcy, or by court decree under Section 44 of the Partnership Act.

entries.body:
Lost, Stolen or Expired Passport Bangladesh – Step-by-Step Legal Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-06 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Losing your passport — whether through theft, misplacement, or damage — is a stressful experience that requires immediate and correct legal action. In Bangladesh, there is a clear process governed by the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP) for replacing a lost or stolen passport, and failure to follow proper procedures can lead to delays, legal complications, or even criminal liability. This comprehensive guide walks you through every step, from filing the initial police report to collecting your new passport, including what to do if you are stranded abroad.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order
Official Portalssupremecourt.gov.bd, judiciary.gov.bd, pcc.police.gov.bd & land.gov.bd
