  3. Who Sits on the Arbitration Council?
  4. Consequences of Marrying Without Permission
  5. First Wife's Rights When Husband Seeks Second Marriage
  6. Can the First Wife Prevent the Second Marriage?
  7. Divorce Rights Triggered by Second Marriage
  8. Maintenance and Dower After Second Marriage

MFLO 1961: The Permission Requirement

The Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (MFLO) — which applies to all Muslim men in Bangladesh — requires that a man obtain prior written permission from the Arbitration Council before contracting a second (or subsequent) marriage. Key provisions:

  • The man must submit a written application to the Chairman of the Union Parishad (or equivalent local authority) where he resides.
  • The application must state reasons for seeking a second marriage and confirm the existing wife's written consent.
  • The Chairman convenes an Arbitration Council consisting of one representative of each party (the husband and the first wife).
  • The Council determines whether the second marriage is necessary and just.
  • Only after receiving a Certificate of Permission from the Council may the second Nikah proceed.

For legal advice on your specific situation, consult a family lawyer in Dhaka.

Consequences of Marrying Without Permission

If a man contracts a second marriage without the Arbitration Council's permission, the consequences under MFLO 1961 are severe:

  • Criminal offence: Punishable by up to one year imprisonment, a fine of Tk. 10,000, or both.
  • Immediate payment of full dower: The entire unpaid dower (mehr) of the first wife becomes immediately payable.
  • First wife's right to divorce: The first wife acquires an immediate right to divorce through Talaq-e-Tafwid (delegated divorce) if this was included in the Nikahnama, or through Khula or judicial divorce.

Importantly, the second marriage itself is not void under Bangladesh law — it remains a valid marriage — but the man faces the above legal consequences for proceeding without permission.

First Wife's Rights When Husband Seeks Second Marriage

The first wife has several legal protections and options:

  • Right to participate in the Arbitration Council: She must be notified and given the opportunity to appoint a representative.
  • Right to object: Her objection carries significant weight — the Council is unlikely to grant permission without good reason shown by the husband.
  • Right to immediate divorce: If a divorce right was delegated to her in the Nikahnama (Kabinname), she can exercise it immediately upon the second marriage.
  • Right to full unpaid dower: The remainder of the dower becomes immediately payable upon the second marriage contracted without permission.
  • Right to maintenance: The first wife retains her right to maintenance even if the husband takes a second wife — provided she is obedient and not in breach of marital duties.

Can the First Wife Prevent the Second Marriage?

The first wife cannot obtain a court injunction preventing the second Nikah ceremony itself — courts generally do not intervene in private religious ceremonies. However, she can:

  • Participate in the Arbitration Council and vigorously oppose the grant of permission.
  • File a criminal complaint if the husband proceeds without permission.
  • Immediately file for divorce on the grounds of the unauthorized second marriage.
  • Demand full payment of her dower.

A Dhaka family lawyer can help a first wife assert all these rights promptly and effectively.

Maintenance and Dower After Second Marriage

Financial rights after a second marriage:

  • Maintenance: A husband with multiple wives must treat them with justice — providing equal maintenance is a duty under Islamic law. Failure to maintain either wife is grounds for divorce through court.
  • Dower (Mehr): Each wife retains her individual dower right. The second marriage does not reduce or eliminate the first wife's dower.
  • Inheritance: Both wives and all children from all marriages have inheritance rights from the husband's estate under Muslim personal law.

If you are a first wife facing this situation, contact an Uttara family lawyer to protect your financial rights immediately.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is second marriage legal in Bangladesh without the first wife's consent?

Second marriage without Arbitration Council permission is a criminal offence under MFLO 1961 — but the marriage itself is not void. The man faces imprisonment, fine, and immediate obligation to pay full first-wife's dower.

Can the first wife get a divorce if her husband marries again?

Yes. If she has delegated divorce rights in the Nikahnama, she can exercise them immediately. Otherwise, she can pursue Khula or judicial divorce — the second unauthorized marriage is strong grounds.

Does the MFLO apply to all Muslim men in Bangladesh?

Yes, MFLO 1961 applies to all Muslim citizens of Bangladesh. There are very limited exceptions.

What if the second marriage was performed abroad (e.g., in Malaysia or the Middle East)?

MFLO technically applies to Bangladeshi Muslim citizens abroad. However, enforcement against overseas marriages is practically challenging. First wives should seek legal advice on their options.

Can a husband grant the first wife divorce rights in the Nikahnama before the second marriage question arises?

Yes. Including delegated divorce rights (Talaq-e-Tafwid) in the Nikahnama at the time of the first marriage is a standard legal protection that gives the wife autonomy if the husband takes a second wife.

Power of Attorney for Bangladesh Property: How to Make One from the UK, USA, UAE or Canada

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-04 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

A Power of Attorney (PoA) is the single most powerful and most abused document in NRB property matters. A good PoA lets a trusted person manage your land, pay taxes and defend cases while you stay abroad. A careless one can let someone sell your property without you ever signing a deed. This guide is written by <a href="/advocate-md-shah-alam" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">Advocate Md. Shah Alam</a>, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, for Bangladeshis living in the UK, USA, UAE, Canada and elsewhere. For case-specific help you can call the chamber on <a href="tel:01712655546" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">01712655546</a> or WhatsApp the same number.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

  2. General vs Special Power of Attorney

  6. Registration in Bangladesh and Use of the PoA
  7. Risks and How to Reduce Them
  8. Cancelling or Revoking a PoA

What a Power of Attorney Does

A Power of Attorney is a written authority by which you (the principal) authorise another person (the attorney or agent) to act for you in legal and financial matters. In property matters, an attorney can:

  • Pay land development tax and obtain Dakhila.
  • Apply for mutation (Namjari).
  • Appear before Sub-Registrar and, if authorised, sign a sale deed.
  • File or defend suits and engage a lawyer on your behalf.

The attorney acts as you, so everything he does within the powers binds you.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

General vs Special Power of Attorney

General PoA: broad authority over many matters. Convenient, but dangerous in unreliable hands.

Special PoA: limited to a defined act (for example: "to sell Plot 15, Dag No. 456, Mouza X, for not less than Tk Y"). It is safer and is what most advocates recommend.

You can give several special PoAs for different tasks instead of one all-powerful document.

Step-by-Step: Making a PoA from Abroad

  1. Ask your Bangladeshi advocate to draft the PoA in line with Bangladesh law (language, stamp, property description).
  2. Print on plain paper (or stamp paper if your advocate advises) and take it, with your passport/ID, to a Notary Public (or Solicitor/Commissioner for Oaths) in your country.
  3. Sign in front of the notary, who verifies your identity and attests the signature.
  4. Take the notarised PoA to the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission for consular attestation (some countries also require prior legalisation by the foreign ministry).
  5. Courier the original attested PoA to your attorney in Bangladesh.
  6. Your advocate then presents it before the Sub-Registrar or the court as needed, and registers it if required.

Requirements and fees differ for each mission, so check the website or call the consular section before you go.

Embassy and Notary Requirements by Country

Every country has a slightly different process, but the pattern is consistent:

  • UK: notary public or solicitor, and sometimes legalisation by the FCDO, then Bangladesh High Commission attestation.
  • USA: notary public (state), and sometimes county/state authentication, then Embassy/Consulate attestation.
  • UAE: approved notary / Ministry process, then Bangladesh Embassy in Abu Dhabi or Consulate in Dubai.
  • Canada: Canadian notary public, then the High Commission in Ottawa (or consulate) attestation.

Always bring original passport, a recent photo and a copy of the Bangladeshi NID or passport. Allow a few days to weeks for the process.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

What to Write in the PoA

  • Full identification of principal and attorney: names, parents' names, NID/passport numbers, addresses and photographs.
  • Exact property description: district, upazila, mouza, dag, khatian and area.
  • A list of specific powers granted.
  • Limits: minimum price, validity period and whether the attorney may sub-delegate.
  • Reporting duty: ask the attorney to send copies of documents and receipts within a fixed time.
  • Termination clause.

Never sign a blank or partly filled document, and never let the attorney keep the only copy.

Registration in Bangladesh and Use of the PoA

Under Section 33 of the Registration Act 1908, a PoA executed outside Bangladesh and properly authenticated by a notary public or consular officer is recognised for registration of documents. In practice, many Sub-Registrar offices expect the PoA to be registered locally and consider the facts of each case carefully, especially for sales.

Your advocate will advise whether to register the PoA and how long it will be valid. Keep a certified copy of everything the attorney files.

Risks and How to Reduce Them

  • Attorney sells without your knowledge: use a special PoA with price floor and an express requirement to inform you.
  • Forged PoA: keep the attested original and verify that the embassy record matches.
  • Death or dispute of the attorney: a PoA ends on the death of the principal or the attorney; appoint a backup.
  • "Irrevocable" PoA: these are sometimes used to disguise a sale. Do not sign one without legal advice.
  • Poor accounting: insist on receipts and bank-only payment.

Cancelling or Revoking a PoA

You can revoke a PoA at any time unless it is genuinely coupled with the attorney's own interest. The usual steps are:

  1. Sign a revocation deed before a notary abroad, attested like the original.
  2. Register the revocation in Bangladesh and inform the Sub-Registrar office where the PoA was used.
  3. Give written notice to the attorney, banks, tenants and anyone who dealt with him, and consider a newspaper notice.
  4. Consult a lawyer immediately if the attorney has already misused it. Criminal and civil remedies may be available.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a Power of Attorney from the UK/USA/UAE/Canada valid in Bangladesh?

Yes, if it is properly notarised and authenticated by the Bangladesh Embassy/High Commission and complies with Bangladesh law and the Registration Act.

Can an attorney sell my land in Bangladesh?

Only if the PoA expressly authorises sale and the deed is registered properly. To be safe, give a special PoA with precise conditions.

How long is a Power of Attorney valid?

Until its stated expiry, revocation, completion of the task, or the death of the principal or attorney. Add a clear validity period.

Can I cancel a PoA from abroad?

Yes, through a notarised and attested revocation deed that is registered in Bangladesh and communicated to relevant parties.

Do I need a lawyer to prepare a PoA?

It is strongly advisable. A wrongly drafted PoA can be rejected by the Sub-Registrar or abused by the attorney.

Power of Attorney From Abroad for a Bangladesh Land Sale: Embassy Attestation, MOFA Verification and Registration Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-10 · 14 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Selling land in Bangladesh while you live in the UK, USA, Canada or the EU depends on one document: a power of attorney that survives every checkpoint from a foreign notary to a Sub-Registrar in Bangladesh. This pillar guide walks through the full chain, including drafting, signing abroad, Embassy or High Commission attestation, MOFA verification in Dhaka, stamp duty, registration, buyer due diligence, revocation and fraud red flags. It is written by <a href="/advocate-md-shah-alam" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">Advocate Md. Shah Alam</a>, Supreme Court of Bangladesh. For case-specific help call or WhatsApp the chamber on <a href="tel:01712655546" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">01712655546</a>, or start at the <a href="/nrb-legal-help" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">NRB legal help hub</a>.

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

  9. Step-by-Step Checklist: POA From Abroad for a Land Sale

  11. Buyer Due Diligence: What a Careful Purchaser Checks
  12. Revocation, Death and Incapacity: How a POA Can Fail After You Sign

Why a Power of Attorney From Abroad Is the Riskiest Document in a Land Sale

For most non-resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) in the UK, USA, Canada or the EU, a land sale in Bangladesh cannot wait for a personal visit. The usual solution is a power of attorney (POA, also called mukhtarnama or attorney deed) in favour of a trusted relative or lawyer. The same document that makes the sale possible is also the document most often used to defraud absent owners.

The reason is simple: the Sub-Registrar who registers a sale deed never meets you. He or she relies on a paper trail that begins in a foreign notary's office, passes through a Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission, and ends in Dhaka. If any link in that chain is weak, the buyer's title can be challenged years later, often at the exact moment the property has become valuable or a family dispute has started.

This guide follows the whole chain end to end: drafting, signing abroad, consular attestation, Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) verification in Dhaka, stamp duty, registration under the Registration Act 1908, buyer due diligence, revocation risk and fraud red flags. For shorter overviews, see our guides on POA for property from abroad and POA for land transfer. For the wider picture of services for Bangladeshis overseas, visit the NRB legal help hub.

Disclaimer: This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Statutes, forms, fees, consular rules and registry practice change and differ between countries and offices. Confirm the current requirements with the relevant Bangladesh Mission, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Sub-Registrar's office, and consult a qualified advocate before you sign or rely on any document.

The Full Chain at a Glance: From Your Desk Abroad to the Sub-Registry

A POA executed abroad becomes usable for a land sale only after it clears several checkpoints. The exact requirements differ by country and by office, so treat the table below as a map, not as a rulebook.

StageWho is involvedWhat happensWhat to verify
1. DraftingAdvocate in Bangladesh (preferably) and youDeed is drafted in clear terms naming the land, the agent and the exact powersLand details match the latest records; powers are specific, not vague
2. Signing abroadNotary public, or a consular officer of the Bangladesh MissionYou sign in person, with identity checked, and the notary or officer authenticates itName spelling matches your passport and your land records; every page is initialled
3. Mission attestationBangladesh Embassy or High CommissionThe Mission verifies the notary's signature and seal, or records its own authenticationWhether a prior step (such as local foreign-ministry authentication) is required first
4. MOFA verificationMinistry of Foreign Affairs, Dhaka (consular or attestation section)Mission attestation is checked and countersigned for use inside BangladeshWhether the receiving Sub-Registry currently insists on it; current procedure and fee
5. Stamp and registrationYour agent, the Sub-Registrar, and the buyerAgent presents the POA, and later the sale deed, for registrationStamp paid correctly; POA registered or recognised under the Registration Act 1908
6. Post-sale stepsBuyer and assistant commissioner (land)Mutation (namjari) and record updatesDeed number, volume and date are recorded correctly

Notice that the buyer's lawyer will check each of these steps. If you are the seller, a POA that is complete and well documented will make your buyer more confident and can help the deal complete faster.

The Legal Framework: Powers of Attorney Act 1882, Registration Act 1908 and Related Laws

Several statutes work together. You do not need to memorise them, but your advocate should be able to explain how each applies to your file.

  • Powers-of-Attorney Act 1882: deals with how a person holding a power of attorney may execute documents and act for the principal, and gives certain protections to those who act in good faith. Read the current text with your advocate for the exact provisions.
  • Contract Act 1872 (agency provisions): an agent's authority can end when the principal revokes it (section 201 deals with termination of agency), and revocation takes effect against third persons only when it becomes known to them (section 208). This is why revocation must be communicated and, ideally, registered.
  • Registration Act 1908, sections 32 and 33: section 32 lists who may present a document for registration, including an agent holding a power of attorney. Section 33 sets out which powers of attorney the registering officer must recognise. For a principal who lives outside Bangladesh, a power of attorney executed before and authenticated by a notary public, a court, a judge, a magistrate or a Bangladesh consular representative is of the kind the section contemplates. Ask your advocate to confirm the current wording and any amendments.
  • Transfer of Property Act 1882, section 54: a sale of immovable property of the value prescribed in that section can be made only by a registered instrument. A sale deed signed by an agent still has to be registered.
  • Evidence Act 1872, section 85: courts presume that a power of attorney executed before and authenticated by a notary public, court, judge, magistrate or consular officer was duly executed. That presumption is useful in later litigation but can still be rebutted by proof of forgery or fraud.
  • Stamp Act 1899 and the Penal Code 1860: the first governs stamp duty on the deed, and the second punishes cheating and forgery (for example sections 420, 467, 468 and 471).

One practical point: the statutes do not use the words "MOFA verification". That step comes from administrative practice and government circulars, which is why it can change. Always ask the Sub-Registry and the Mission what they require at the moment you start.

Step 1: Drafting the POA - Special or General, and the Clauses That Matter

Most disputes begin with a badly drafted deed. If you are selling one specific plot, a special power of attorney is usually safer than a general one. Our guide to POA types and registration explains the difference in detail.

A strong land-sale POA normally contains:

  • Full identity of the principal: name as in your passport, father's and mother's names, Bangladeshi NID or old passport details where available, current foreign address and nationality. Mismatches between spellings are a leading cause of rejection.
  • Full identity of the agent: name, parentage, NID number, address and relationship to you.
  • Exact schedule of property: district, upazila, mouza, plot (dag) numbers by each survey record (CS, SA, RS, BS as applicable), khatian numbers, area, boundaries and how you acquired the land. Copy these from the latest records, not from memory.
  • Specific powers: to negotiate, to receive earnest money, to sign the sale agreement and the sale deed, to appear before the Sub-Registrar, to admit execution, to receive the price, to apply for mutation, and to pay taxes. If you do not want the agent to receive money, say so and arrange payment into your own account.
  • Price floor or conditions: a minimum price, an approved buyer, or a requirement for your written approval before the final deed. This is your best protection against under-value sales.
  • Duration and revocation language: a clear end date or event, and a statement that you may revoke the deed.
  • Caution on "irrevocable" clauses: these draw heavy scrutiny. Do not use them unless an advocate has explained the consequences, especially where money has been paid to you.

Draft the deed in Bangladesh with your advocate, send it to you as a PDF, and print it on plain paper abroad for signing. Do not accept a half-filled template from a broker. For a clean transfer, also see our overview of legal checks for buying land from abroad, which a buyer's lawyer will use against your documents.

Step 2: Signing Abroad Before a Notary or Consular Officer

You have two routes. Which is better depends on the country where you live and the Mission's current services.

Route A: Sign before a local notary public. You appear in person with passport or national identity, sign in front of the notary, and the notary signs, stamps and records the act. In the UK this is usually a notary public or solicitor with notarial powers; in the USA it may be a notary public with state-specific rules; in Canada, a notary or a lawyer who is a commissioner. This route is common because notaries are easy to find.

Route B: Sign directly before the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission. Many Missions can authenticate a deed signed before their consular officer. This often shortens the chain because the Mission's own authentication replaces the foreign notary and the later check of the notary's seal. Whether the Mission offers it, whether an appointment is needed, and what fee applies are matters to confirm directly with the Mission.

Whichever route you choose:

  • Sign only in front of the notary or officer. Never pre-sign.
  • Bring your valid passport and, if possible, documents showing your Bangladeshi identity (NID, old passport, birth certificate).
  • Initial every page and make sure any annexed land schedule is attached and referred to in the main deed.
  • Ask that the deed be in English, or in Bengali with an accurate English translation, according to the Mission's rules. If a translation is required, use a competent translator and keep the certificate.
  • Ask for the notary's registry or serial number and keep a copy of the full signed set.

Step 3: Embassy or High Commission Attestation

If you signed before a foreign notary, the next stage is attestation by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission that covers your country. The Mission does not rewrite or approve the contents of your deed. It authenticates the signature and seal of the notary or the foreign authority, so that offices in Bangladesh can trust the document's origin.

Points to confirm with your Mission before you travel or post documents:

  • Prior authentication: some Missions ask that the notary's signature first be authenticated by a local government body, such as a foreign ministry, a state authority or a county office. Requirements differ by country, so ask rather than assume.
  • Apostille is not the same as consular attestation: an apostille is a certificate under an international convention, and it is a different process from consular attestation. Do not assume that an apostille alone satisfies a Bangladesh office. Ask the Mission whether it is needed as a preliminary step.
  • Appointment, mailing and original documents: whether you must appear in person, whether postal submission is accepted, and whether originals or photocopies are needed.
  • Fees: check the current fee schedule on the Mission's website. Do not rely on agents' quoted amounts.
  • Return of the document: how and to whom the attested deed will be handed back or couriered.

Keep the attestation page, the notary's page and the deed together as one bound set. Loose attachments cause suspicion at the registry.

Step 4: MOFA Dhaka Verification

After attestation abroad, the document is sent to Bangladesh. Many registry offices, banks and courts expect the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Dhaka to verify the Mission's attestation and add its own stamp or signature, confirming that the Mission's seal and the officer's signature are genuine. This is often what people mean by "MOFA attestation".

Practical points:

  • Who submits: usually your agent, a lawyer or a representative, using the original attested set. Ask the ministry whether authorisation or ID is required from the person submitting.
  • Timing and fee: processing times and fees are set by the ministry and may change. Check the current fee schedule and expected time before relying on any date.
  • Is it always required? Practice varies between sub-registry offices and also depends on the purpose. For a land sale, a prudent plan is to complete MOFA verification unless the Sub-Registry and your advocate confirm in writing that it is not needed for your case.
  • Keep copies: make colour scans of the deed, the notary page, the Mission page and the MOFA page before anything is submitted.

Where the deed was signed directly before a consular officer, the pathway may be shorter. The exact route is a question for both the Mission and the ministry, so confirm in advance rather than discover a missing step on the day of registration.

Stamp Requirements and Registration With the Sub-Registrar

The deed must carry the stamp duty (non-judicial stamp) required under the Stamp Act 1899 and the current schedule. The amount depends on the type of deed and how it is structured, for example whether it covers one or several agents and one or several properties. I am deliberately not quoting a figure because schedules and e-stamp arrangements change. Ask your advocate or the registry to compute it and check the current fee schedule.

A deed executed abroad is often stamped after it arrives in Bangladesh, within the period allowed by the stamp law. Ask your advocate about the time limit and the correct procedure so that the deed does not become liable to penalty.

Then comes the registry:

  1. Registration of the POA: for a POA that authorises the sale of land, registry offices expect it to be registered or at least presented for recognition under section 33 of the Registration Act. The Sub-Registrar examines the notary or consular authentication and the attestation chain.
  2. Presentation of the sale deed: the agent signs the sale deed in your name as attorney, and presents it under section 32 along with the POA. Identification of the agent is checked, and registry staff usually take photographs and fingerprints or biometric data under the current system.
  3. Payment of registration fee and taxes: registration fee, source tax, local government tax and other charges as presently prescribed. Check the current fee schedule on the day.
  4. Return of the registered deed: keep the receipt and later obtain the certified copy.
  5. Mutation (namjari): the buyer then applies for mutation. Our guide to mutation from abroad explains the usual steps.

Which Sub-Registry has jurisdiction is determined by where the land is situated. Registration in the wrong office can be a basis for challenge, so confirm this before you book a date.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Step-by-Step Checklist: POA From Abroad for a Land Sale

Use this as a working checklist, and tick off each line only when you hold the document in your hand.

  1. Collect the land documents: deed of ownership, latest khatian, mutation record, land development tax receipts, and any heirship certificate if the land was inherited.
  2. Appoint an advocate in Bangladesh to verify the title and to prepare the draft POA.
  3. Decide on the agent. Choose someone reliable and, preferably, a person who is not in a conflict of interest with you.
  4. Fix the powers: special POA for one specific sale, with a price floor and a ban on any other transaction.
  5. Review the draft carefully and check every spelling against your passport and land records.
  6. Print the final text, then sign in person before a notary public or a consular officer abroad.
  7. Obtain any preliminary authentication required by the Mission (confirm in writing or by email).
  8. Submit the deed for Embassy or High Commission attestation and pay the fee shown on the Mission's site.
  9. Courier the full attested set to your agent and keep scanned copies and tracking records.
  10. Have MOFA Dhaka verify the attestation, unless your advocate confirms in writing that it is not necessary.
  11. Pay the stamp duty and have the POA registered or presented for recognition at the proper Sub-Registry.
  12. Agree the sale in writing with the buyer, with part-payment into your bank account or by an auditable route.
  13. Have the sale deed registered under sections 32 and 33 of the Registration Act and receive the receipt.
  14. Obtain the certified copy of the registered deed and confirm that the buyer has applied for mutation.
  15. Arrange lawful remittance of proceeds through banking channels and check with Bangladesh Bank rules or a bank officer on repatriation requirements.
  16. Revoke the POA formally once the transaction is complete, and send written notice to the agent.

Comparison Table: Four Ways to Authorise a Land Sale From Abroad

A POA is not the only option. This table compares the main routes at a high level; your advocate can tell you which fits your property, family and timeline.

RouteStrengthsWeaknessesBest used when
Special POA signed before a foreign notary, then Mission attestation and MOFA verificationCommon, flexible, widely understood by registriesMore steps, more documents to match, forgery risk if drafting is looseYou live abroad and need to sell one defined property
Special POA signed before a Bangladesh consular officerFewer checkpoints; authentication by the Mission itselfDepends on the Mission's services and appointment availabilityThe Mission near you offers this service and you can travel there
General POA covering all your Bangladesh affairsOne document for banking, rent, tax and litigationWide authority, high abuse risk; registries may ask for more proof for a saleLong-term management, not a single sale; use with strong safeguards
Signing the deed yourself on a visit to BangladeshNo agent risk, clean registry recordNeeds travel and time in the countryHigh-value land or a contested family property

Where family members share the land, consider also the position of co-heirs, because a sale of the whole by one co-owner or his agent invites dispute. Our guide to types of POA covers the extent of authority in more depth.

Buyer Due Diligence: What a Careful Purchaser Checks

If you are the seller, think like the buyer's lawyer and answer these questions before they are asked. If you are the buyer, insist on each of them.

  • Is the owner alive and does he or she still stand behind the POA? A POA ends on death of the principal. Ask for a recent confirmation, preferably recorded in writing or on a video call that the buyer's lawyer attends, and ask whether there has been any revocation.
  • Does the POA match the land? Compare plot numbers, khatian, mouza and area in the POA with the title deed, the mutation record and the current online record.
  • Was the deed properly authenticated abroad? Look at the notary or consular authentication, the Mission attestation, the MOFA verification and the stamping. Check names, dates and seals for any inconsistency.
  • Is the POA registered, and is there any registered revocation? Ask the relevant Sub-Registry whether a revocation deed has been recorded, and obtain a certified copy of the POA register entry.
  • Does the agent hold the power to receive money? If not, pay only to the owner's bank account.
  • Is the price reasonable? A big gap below market value, or a POA with a very high-speed process, is a warning sign.
  • Are there other claims? Check for pending suits, mortgages, acquisition, vested or abandoned property claims and co-sharer rights. See our buyer checklist.
  • Is the agent's identity genuine? Compare NID, photograph and signature, and be wary of a person who is evasive about how to reach the owner.

Buyers should avoid paying any large sum before the deed is registered. The sale is complete only on registration, and earnest money should be documented in a written agreement with a clear refund clause.

Revocation, Death and Incapacity: How a POA Can Fail After You Sign

A POA is not permanent. Understanding how it ends protects both sides.

  • Revocation by the principal: you can generally revoke the authority of your agent, subject to any legal protection for rights coupled with an interest. To protect yourself, make revocation in writing, register it where the original POA was registered, notify the agent in writing and notify known third parties such as the buyer, banks and the Sub-Registry.
  • Notice to third parties: under the agency rules of the Contract Act, revocation binds a third person only once it is known to that person. Until the buyer knows, the buyer may be protected if he acts in good faith. Unrecorded revocation is therefore risky.
  • Death of the principal: the authority normally ends on the death of the person who granted it. A sale deed signed by an agent after the principal's death, even if both sides are unaware of it, creates serious doubt over title and may be void. Heirs must act quickly to inform the registry and close the file.
  • Unsoundness of mind: if the principal loses capacity, the agent's authority generally ends as well.
  • Completion of the task: a special POA for one sale ends once the sale is complete.
  • Agent's death or resignation: authority also ends on the agent's death or renunciation.
  • Expiry: if the deed contains an end date, it lapses on that date.

If you suspect your agent has acted beyond the powers granted, a civil suit for cancellation of the deed and a prohibitory injunction can be filed under the Specific Relief Act 1877 and the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, and a criminal complaint may be considered where forgery or cheating is suspected. Speed matters, because third-party rights can arise quickly.

Fraud Red Flags and the Reality of Remote or Video Signing

Fraud involving absent owners is a recurring pattern. Watch for the following red flags.

  • Pressure and secrecy: an agent who insists on speed, discourages you from contacting your advocate, or refuses to share copies.
  • Inconsistent documents: a notary seal from one country with a date that does not match the Mission stamp, spelling differences between pages, or pages that look re-typed.
  • A POA you never signed: if someone tells you that a POA exists in your name and you do not remember signing it, treat it as an emergency.
  • Photographs of "you" that are low quality or edited, or a foreign identity paper that cannot be verified.
  • Broker quotes for "fast attestation": middlemen who promise to obtain attestation without your appearance should be avoided. A genuine authentication needs the real participation of the notary or consular officer.
  • Payment to a third-party account: never accept the price into an account that is not yours or that of a clearly authorised person.

Video-call or electronic signing. Many NRBs ask whether they can sign over video. Bangladeshi practice on remote notarisation and electronic signatures on land documents is still evolving, and registry offices differ in how they treat them. Whether a given Mission or ministry accepts a remotely notarised or electronically signed POA must be checked with them directly. If you cannot obtain written confirmation, do not use that method for a land sale. A video call can still be useful for something else: a short recorded confirmation to the buyer's lawyer that you have granted the POA, which supports the paperwork but never replaces it.

If you discover forgery, consult an advocate immediately about a criminal complaint (the Penal Code deals with cheating and forgery, for example sections 420, 467, 468 and 471), a civil suit to cancel the document, and a prompt injunction to stop further transfers.

Common Mistakes NRBs Make With a POA for Land Sale

  • Using a template from the internet without a Bangladeshi advocate reviewing the property schedule and the powers.
  • Granting a general POA when only a single sale is intended.
  • Spelling mismatches between the passport, the deed and the land records, leading to rejection or later challenge.
  • Skipping the preliminary authentication that the Mission requires, then discovering the delay after the notary visit.
  • Assuming an apostille or notary seal alone is enough for Bangladesh. The consular attestation step and any ministry verification are separate.
  • Forgetting stamp duty or stamping late, which can bring penalty and delays.
  • No price floor and no buyer approval clause, leaving the agent free to sell low.
  • Giving the agent power to collect all the money with no audit trail.
  • Not revoking the POA after the sale or after losing trust in the agent.
  • Ignoring heirs and co-owners and their rights to the same property.
  • Never checking the registry afterwards for any transaction under your name or for unexpected recorded POAs.

For a smoother process, prepare the full document set in advance and cross-check each name and number against the originals. If you are an NRB with a complex family property or suspect misuse of an existing POA, you can speak to a land lawyer through NRB legal help.

Related Reading and When to Get Legal Help

These guides on this site expand on parts of the process:

  • Power of attorney for Bangladesh property from abroad
  • Power of attorney for land transfer in Bangladesh
  • Types of POA and registration in Bangladesh
  • Land mutation (namjari) from abroad, step by step
  • Buying land in Bangladesh from abroad: legal checklist
  • NRB legal help hub

Consider engaging an advocate when the property is of high value, when co-heirs exist, when the land has a history of litigation, when you did not personally prepare the POA, or when you suspect that a deed has been used without your consent. A lawyer can verify title, supervise drafting, liaise with the Mission and the ministry, attend registration, and file urgent court applications if needed.

Disclaimer: This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Statutes, forms, fees, consular rules and registry practice change and differ between countries and offices. Confirm the current requirements with the relevant Bangladesh Mission, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Sub-Registrar's office, and consult a qualified advocate before you sign or rely on any document.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I sell my Bangladesh land from the UK, USA or Canada using a power of attorney?

Yes, in principle. You execute a POA abroad before a notary or consular officer, have it attested by the Bangladesh Mission, complete any ministry verification in Dhaka, stamp it and have your agent present it to the Sub-Registrar along with the sale deed. The sale deed itself must still be registered.

Is Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission attestation mandatory?

For a deed signed before a foreign notary, practice in Bangladesh is to require attestation by the Bangladesh Mission so that the notary's signature and seal can be trusted. If you sign directly before a Bangladesh consular officer, the authentication may be performed by the Mission itself. Confirm the current requirement with the Mission and the Sub-Registry.

What is MOFA verification and do I need it?

It is verification by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Dhaka of the Mission attestation, so that offices inside Bangladesh can rely on it. Practice varies by office and purpose, so ask your advocate to confirm with the Sub-Registry whether it is required for your case. Check the current procedure and fee schedule before you apply.

Does a POA signed abroad have to be registered in Bangladesh?

Where the POA authorises sale of land, registry offices expect it to be registered or presented for recognition under sections 32 and 33 of the Registration Act 1908. Ask your advocate how the Sub-Registry handles it at present.

How much stamp duty and what fees will I pay?

Amounts depend on the type of deed, the number of agents and properties, and on current schedules and e-stamp rules. Check the current fee schedule with the Sub-Registry and the Mission instead of relying on quotes from brokers.

How long does the whole attestation chain take?

It depends on the country, the Mission's appointment queue, courier time, ministry processing and the registry. No reliable fixed period can be promised, so plan generously and ask each office for its current time frame.

Can I sign a POA over a video call?

Treat this with caution. Rules on remote notarisation and electronic signatures differ and the Mission, ministry and registry may not accept them. Do not use this route for a land sale unless each of those offices confirms acceptance in writing.

What happens if the owner dies after signing the POA?

The agent's authority normally ends on the principal's death. A deed signed after death can be challenged as void. Heirs should inform the registry and any buyer immediately and take legal advice.

How do I cancel a POA I gave to a relative?

Prepare a written deed of revocation, have it executed and authenticated in the proper manner, register it where the original POA was recorded, notify the agent and give written notice to buyers, banks and the Sub-Registry. Revocation binds third persons only once they know of it.

Can the buyer rely on the POA alone?

A careful buyer will also verify the owner's identity and continuing consent, the match between POA and land records, the registry entry, the absence of any recorded revocation and the payment route. A POA alone is not a guarantee of valid title.

Power of Attorney Land Transfer Bangladesh: Complete Legal Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-03-13 · 7 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Thousands of Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) and property owners in Bangladesh rely on Power of Attorney to manage land transactions from a distance. But a poorly drafted or improperly registered POA can be misused, invalidated, or used to defraud the principal. Understanding the legal framework is essential before you sign.

What Is a Power of Attorney in Bangladesh Law?

A Power of Attorney (POA) is a legal document through which one person (the principal or donor) authorises another person (the attorney or donee) to act on their behalf in specified legal matters. In the context of land and property, a POA authorises the attorney to sign deeds, execute sale agreements, receive payments, or take possession of land on the principal's behalf.

In Bangladesh, Powers of Attorney relating to immovable property must comply with the Power of Attorney Act 2012, the Registration Act 1908, and the Stamp Act 1899. An improperly executed or unregistered POA cannot be used for property transactions. For guidance specific to your situation, consult a land and property lawyer in Dhaka or Uttara.

Types of Power of Attorney for Land

There are two broad types of Power of Attorney relevant to land transactions in Bangladesh:

  • General Power of Attorney (GPA): Grants broad authority to the attorney to handle a wide range of matters on behalf of the principal — including executing sale deeds, managing tenants, collecting rents, and registering documents.
  • Special Power of Attorney (SPA): Authorises the attorney for a specific, defined purpose — such as executing a single sale deed for a particular plot on a specific date. The SPA expires once the specific act is completed.

For property transactions of significant value, a Special Power of Attorney is generally safer — it limits the attorney's authority to a defined transaction and reduces the risk of misuse.

Irrevocable vs. Revocable Power of Attorney

A standard Power of Attorney is revocable — the principal can cancel it at any time before the attorney acts under it. An Irrevocable Power of Attorney is one that the principal expressly states cannot be revoked — typically because it is given as security for a financial obligation or is coupled with an interest.

  • Irrevocable POA: Remains valid even after the principal's death or mental incapacity (in some circumstances). Often used in property development agreements where the developer needs certainty that the POA will not be withdrawn mid-project.
  • Revocable POA: Can be cancelled by the principal at any time by executing a Deed of Revocation and registering it at the Sub-Registrar's office.

An irrevocable POA must be carefully drafted to specify exactly what acts are covered. Courts will scrutinise irrevocable POAs carefully where disputes arise. Always take legal advice before granting an irrevocable POA over valuable property.

Registration Requirements for a Land POA

Under the Power of Attorney Act 2012 and the Registration Act 1908, a Power of Attorney for immovable property transactions must be registered at the Sub-Registrar's office. Key requirements:

  • The document must be executed on proper stamp paper of the value prescribed by the Stamp Act.
  • Both the principal and attorney may need to appear before the Sub-Registrar (or the principal may execute before a notary if abroad).
  • For POAs executed abroad, attestation by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission in the country of execution is required before registration in Bangladesh.
  • The POA must include: full identity details of both parties, specific property description, exact powers granted, duration (if limited), and the principal's NID or passport details.

An unregistered POA cannot be used to transfer title to immovable property in Bangladesh. It may still have contractual force between the parties but cannot create a registered deed of sale or mortgage in the principal's name.

How to Execute a POA from Abroad (NRBs)

Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) frequently issue Powers of Attorney to manage property in Bangladesh from abroad. The standard procedure is:

  1. Draft the Power of Attorney document — ideally by a licensed lawyer in Bangladesh who understands the legal requirements.
  2. Send the draft to the NRB abroad for review.
  3. The NRB executes (signs) the document before a Notary Public in the country of residence.
  4. The NRB attests the document before the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission in that country — this step is mandatory for use in Bangladesh.
  5. The original attested document is sent to Bangladesh (by courier or through a trusted person).
  6. The attorney registers the POA at the relevant Sub-Registrar's office in Bangladesh, on the appropriate stamp paper.

The entire process typically takes 2–4 weeks. For urgent land transactions, it is possible to expedite Embassy attestation at some missions. Contact a property lawyer in Dhaka to prepare the correct document before the NRB executes.

What an Attorney Can and Cannot Do

A POA attorney's authority is strictly limited to what is expressly stated in the document. An attorney can:

  • Execute and register sale deeds, gift deeds, and mortgage documents (if expressly authorised).
  • Collect rent, manage tenants, and receive payments on behalf of the principal.
  • Appear before land offices and courts as representative of the principal.
  • Execute agreements for sale (baina) and complete the transaction.

An attorney cannot:

  • Transfer the property to themselves (self-dealing is prohibited and voidable).
  • Make gifts of the principal's property (unless expressly authorised).
  • Execute a Will on behalf of the principal — a Will is a personal act.
  • Act beyond the scope of the POA's express terms.

Any act of the attorney that exceeds their authority under the POA is void and can be challenged in court by the principal or their heirs.

Risks of Misuse and How to Protect Yourself

Power of Attorney fraud — particularly involving land — is regrettably common in Bangladesh. Known misuse patterns include:

  • An attorney selling the property to a third party for their personal benefit without informing the principal.
  • Using a forged or expired POA to transfer property.
  • Granting multiple POAs to different persons for the same property.
  • An attorney accepting a lower price for the property and pocketing the difference.

To protect yourself as a principal:

  • Issue a Special POA for specific transactions only — not a broad General POA.
  • Set a short duration with an explicit expiry date.
  • Require the attorney to report and provide documentation of every transaction.
  • Conduct periodic checks of the land mutation records and Registration Office records to detect any unauthorised transfers.
  • Consider requiring that any sale proceeds be deposited directly into your bank account abroad.

If you discover that your POA has been misused, immediately consult a land and property lawyer to cancel the POA, challenge the fraudulent deed, and file the appropriate legal actions.

Cancelling a Power of Attorney

To revoke a registered Power of Attorney in Bangladesh:

  1. Execute a Deed of Revocation on appropriate stamp paper, clearly identifying the original POA (registration number, date, Sub-Registrar's office).
  2. Register the Deed of Revocation at the same Sub-Registrar's office where the original POA was registered.
  3. Serve written notice of revocation on the attorney personally (by registered post with acknowledgement).
  4. Inform any third parties (banks, courts, etc.) who may be relying on the POA of its revocation.

From the date of registration of the Deed of Revocation, the attorney has no further authority to act under the cancelled POA. Any act done after valid notice of revocation is void and unenforceable against the principal. If the attorney refuses to cooperate, a court injunction can be obtained preventing them from acting further on the revoked POA.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a Power of Attorney for land need to be registered in Bangladesh?

Yes. A POA for immovable property transactions must be registered at the Sub-Registrar's office. An unregistered POA cannot be used to create or transfer property rights through a registered deed.

Can an NRB grant a Power of Attorney from abroad?

Yes. The NRB must execute the POA before a Notary Public, then have it attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission. The attested document is then registered at a Sub-Registrar's office in Bangladesh.

Is an irrevocable Power of Attorney binding in Bangladesh?

An irrevocable POA coupled with an interest is binding and cannot be cancelled by the principal alone. Courts will enforce it, but scrutinise its terms strictly.

What happens if the principal dies while a POA is in force?

A regular POA is automatically revoked by the death of the principal. An irrevocable POA coupled with an interest may survive the principal's death in limited circumstances. The principal's heirs should be notified and legal advice sought.

Can an attorney sell property to themselves?

No. Self-dealing by an attorney is prohibited and the transaction is voidable by the principal or their estate. Courts will not uphold such transactions.

How long is a Power of Attorney valid in Bangladesh?

A POA is valid until it is revoked, the purpose is completed, or the principal dies (for revocable POAs). A time-limited POA expires on the specified date. Always specify an expiry date for security.

Can I cancel a Power of Attorney if the attorney is misusing it?

Yes. Execute and register a Deed of Revocation immediately and serve notice on the attorney. Then take legal action to undo any unauthorized transactions the attorney has already completed.

Do I need a lawyer to draft a Power of Attorney?

Legally you don't have to, but given the risks involved in property POAs, professional legal drafting is strongly recommended to ensure the document is correctly worded, registered, and limited to safe parameters.

What is a Power of Attorney in Bangladesh?

A Power of Attorney (POA) is a legal document authorizing one person (the agent or attorney-in-fact) to act on behalf of another (the principal) in legal, financial, or property matters. In Bangladesh, POAs are governed by:

  • Powers of Attorney Act 2012
  • Registration Act 1908
  • Transfer of Property Act 1882

A properly executed POA can authorise the agent to buy/sell land, file court cases, sign contracts, manage bank accounts, and engage in almost any legal act — within the scope defined in the document. Consult a civil lawyer in Dhaka before granting broad powers to any agent.

General vs. Special Power of Attorney

The two core types differ in scope:

  • General Power of Attorney (GPA): Grants the agent broad authority over the principal's affairs — typically covering all property transactions, legal proceedings, and financial matters. GPAs are often used by NRBs (Non-Resident Bangladeshis) to manage affairs back home.
  • Special Power of Attorney (SPA): Restricts the agent to a specific, defined act — for example, "to execute the sale deed for Plot No. X" or "to appear in Case No. Y." An SPA expires once the specific purpose is fulfilled.

Key rule: For property transactions, always use a Special POA specifying the exact property and transaction. Broad GPAs are a major source of fraud in Bangladesh.

When is POA Registration Mandatory?

Under the Registration Act, POAs are mandatory to register when they relate to:

  • Transfer of immovable property (land, flat, building).
  • Receiving consideration (payment) for property.
  • Filing suits relating to immovable property.

Unregistered POAs for property transactions are legally invalid and will not be accepted by the Sub-Registrar's office for executing deeds. Registration fees apply based on the value of the property or transaction covered.

NRB Power of Attorney: Overseas Authentication

For Bangladeshis abroad (NRBs), the POA must go through additional authentication steps:

  1. Draft the POA in Bangladesh or abroad.
  2. Have it notarized by a local notary or court in the foreign country.
  3. Get it authenticated (apostilled or attested) at the Bangladeshi Embassy or High Commission in that country.
  4. Upon arrival in Bangladesh, submit it to the Sub-District (Upazila) Land Registry for local verification if property matters are involved.

Countries that are signatories to the Hague Apostille Convention can use apostille stamps; others require full embassy attestation. Advocate Md. Shah Alam in Uttara assists NRB families with the full POA authentication and registration process.

Common POA Fraud in Bangladesh

POA fraud is rampant in Bangladesh. Common schemes include:

  • Forged POAs: Fake documents presented to Sub-Registrars to sell land without the owner's knowledge.
  • Broad GPAs exploited: An agent with a General POA sells or mortgages property that was not intended to be touched.
  • POAs from deceased persons: Using old POAs after the principal has died — legally void but fraudulently misused.

If you suspect your POA has been forged or misused, take immediate legal action — file FIR and apply for a court injunction to halt any resultant transaction.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a Power of Attorney be used after the principal dies?

No. A POA automatically terminates on the death of the principal. Any act performed by the agent after the principal's death is invalid and potentially fraudulent. Heirs should immediately cancel any outstanding POAs upon a principal's death.

Can someone revoke a Power of Attorney in Bangladesh?

Yes. A POA can be revoked by the principal at any time (unless it is an "irrevocable POA" coupled with an interest). Revocation should be in writing, registered, and notice given to third parties who relied on the POA.

Can an NRB in Canada or UK grant a POA for Bangladesh property?

Yes. The NRB executes the POA abroad, has it notarized locally, authenticates it at the Bangladesh Embassy, and it becomes valid in Bangladesh after local verification. Most major cities have Bangladesh Embassies or High Commissions to assist with this.

Pre-Emption Lawsuit in Bangladesh: How Co-Sharers Forcibly Buy Back Sold Land

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-13 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Few family shocks are as infuriating as discovering that your brother, uncle, or joint co-sharer has secretly sold an undivided piece of your ancestral land to an outside stranger without giving you the opportunity to purchase it. The first time you learn about the transfer is when an aggressive third party arrives with surveyors, planning to build a boundary wall through your family holding. In Bangladesh, the law strictly disfavors outside interlopers disrupting joint land holdings. Under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (SAT Act), co-sharers possess an extraordinary statutory power called the Right of Pre-emption (Ogrokroy). By filing a pre-emption lawsuit in the Civil Court and depositing the purchase consideration plus statutory compensation, you can compel the court to cancel the stranger's deed and forcibly transfer the title directly into your name.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

  9. Illustrative Scenario: Recovering Ancestral Land in Cumilla

What Is the Right of Pre-emption (Ogrokroy) in Bangladesh?

The right of pre-emption—historically known in Bengal as Haq Shufa under Islamic jurisprudence and codified as Ogrokroy in modern statutory law—is a legal right conferred upon existing landowners to acquire property in preference to an outside stranger. The legislative purpose behind pre-emption is grounded in sound social policy: preventing the fragmentation of agricultural holdings, protecting the privacy and security of family residential compounds, and excluding hostile third-party speculators from disrupting joint holdings.

When a joint owner sells land without offering it first to co-heirs, the transaction is not automatically void, but it remains permanently defeasible. That means the sale stands subject to the superior right of the non-consenting co-sharers to step into the buyer's shoes. By invoking statutory pre-emption, you do not need to prove that the seller committed fraud or that the land was undervalued; the mere fact that you are a legitimate co-sharer by inheritance and were bypassed gives you the statutory power to buy back the property through judicial mandate.

Section 96 State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950

The primary governing statute for pre-emption of agricultural land in Bangladesh is Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (SAT Act). The section underwent a major legislative overhaul through the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act 2006, which introduced streamlined rules to curb frivolous litigation while reinforcing the primacy of family co-heirs.

Under Section 96(1), if a portion or share of a holding of land is transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding may apply to the court for the portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves. The statute mandates that the application must be instituted in the civil court of the lowest grade having territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction (typically the Senior Assistant Judge or Joint District Judge Court). Once the statutory conditions are met, the court has no discretion to refuse; granting pre-emption is a mandatory statutory duty.

Who Is Eligible: Co-Sharers by Inheritance vs. Purchase

A pivotal reform introduced by the 2006 Amendment to Section 96 SAT Act was clarifying the hierarchy of eligible applicants. Prior to 2006, adjacent landowners (contiguous plot owners) could also file pre-emption suits, creating endless litigation among neighbors. Today, the law establishes strict eligibility:

  • Co-sharer by Inheritance (Primary Right): A person who inherited an undivided share of the land from a common ancestor. Co-sharers by inheritance enjoy the highest, indisputable priority. If a co-sharer by inheritance applies, their claim defeats all other classes of claimants.
  • Co-sharer by Purchase: A person who acquired an undivided share in the holding through a registered deed of purchase. Under the amended law, a co-sharer by purchase can only claim pre-emption if no co-sharer by inheritance applies.
  • Exclusion of Contiguous Neighbors: Under the amended Section 96, adjacent/neighboring plot owners who do not share title in the holding can no longer claim pre-emption over agricultural land, preventing predatory boundary lawsuits.

Mandatory Court Deposit: Consideration Plus 25% Compensation

The single most critical procedural requirement of a Section 96 pre-emption case is the statutory deposit. Unlike general civil lawsuits where court fees are nominal, pre-emption requires the applicant to put their money on the table immediately upon filing.

Under Section 96(3) of the SAT Act, the application will not be entertained unless the applicant, at the time of making the application, deposits in the court:

  1. The Consideration Amount: The exact purchase price stated on the face of the registered sale deed executed in favor of the stranger.
  2. 25% Statutory Compensation: An additional statutory compensation equal to twenty-five percent (25%) of the stated consideration value, awarded to the purchaser for being deprived of the land.
  3. 8% Annual Interest: Simple interest calculated at eight percent (8%) per annum on the consideration amount from the date of deed execution to the date of filing the application.

If the applicant fails to deposit the full statutory sum via treasury challan concurrently with the application, the petition is summarily rejected as legally incompetent. No extension of time is granted for this deposit.

Strict Statutory Limitation Deadlines: The Two-Month Rule

The law of limitation in pre-emption cases is unforgiving. Under Section 96(1) of the SAT Act, an application for pre-emption must be made within:

  • Two (2) Months: Within two months from the date of the service of official notice of transfer under Section 89 of the SAT Act. When a deed is registered at the Sub-Registry Office, the Sub-Registrar is legally required to issue a formal transfer notice to all recorded co-sharers.
  • Two Months from Knowledge (Max 3 Years): If the seller and buyer colluded to conceal the sale and no official notice was served, the co-sharer must file within two (2) months from the date they first acquired knowledge of the fraudulent sale. However, the application must in all events be filed within three (3) years from the date of registration of the deed.

Waiting even one day past the two-month deadline from the date of confirmed knowledge can prove fatal to your claim. Your advocate must plead the exact date and mode of gaining knowledge in the plaint with meticulous precision.

Pre-Emption for Non-Agricultural Land: Section 24 NAT Act

While Section 96 SAT Act governs agricultural holdings, urban real estate (commercial shops, residential plots in cities and municipalities) is governed by Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 (NAT Act). While the underlying objective remains the same, several procedural distinctions apply:

Under Section 24 of the NAT Act, the statutory compensation deposited with the court is five percent (5%) of the purchase consideration, accompanied by interest at the rate of 6.25% per annum. Furthermore, under the NAT Act, contiguous landowners (neighbors whose land touches the boundary of the transferred plot) retain the legal standing to claim pre-emption if no co-sharer exercises their right. Understanding whether the land is classified in the government Khatian as agricultural (Nal, Doba) or non-agricultural (Bastu, Dukan, Commercial) dictates which statute must be invoked.

Step-by-Step Civil Court Procedure and Reconveyance

The judicial progression of a pre-emption lawsuit follows a structured timeline:

  1. Filing and Challan Deposit: The advocate files a Miscellaneous Case under Section 96 SAT Act, annexing certified copies of the deed, Khatian, and the treasury challan proving deposit of the consideration plus 25% compensation.
  2. Service of Summons: The court issues notices to the purchaser (transferee) and the seller (transferor), requiring them to show cause within a specified date.
  3. Injunction Against Possession & Construction: Concurrently, the advocate moves an application under Order 39 CPC for a temporary injunction restraining the purchaser from constructing structures, digging foundations, or transferring the land to fourth parties.
  4. Evidence & Final Order: The court examines proof of co-sharership (CS, SA, RS, and City/BS Khatians) and verifies the limitation timeline. Upon satisfaction, the court allows the pre-emption case.
  5. Deed Execution by Court: The court directs the purchaser to execute and register a re-conveyance deed in favor of the applicant. If the purchaser refuses to sign, the judge executes and registers the deed under the official court seal, and the court bailiff delivers physical possession to the applicant.

Comparison Table: Section 96 SAT Act vs. Section 24 NAT Act

The table below summarizes the vital legal distinctions between pre-emption of agricultural versus non-agricultural land in Bangladesh:

Legal FeatureSection 96 SAT Act 1950 (Agricultural)Section 24 NAT Act 1949 (Non-Agricultural)
Land ClassificationAgricultural land (Nal, Chala, Crop fields)Urban, homestead, commercial, shop plots
Statutory Compensation25% of registered purchase consideration5% of registered purchase consideration
Annual Interest Rate8% simple interest per annum6.25% simple interest per annum
Adjacent Neighbor RightsCompletely abolished by 2006 AmendmentPermitted if no co-sharer applies
Primary PriorityCo-sharer by inheritance has absolute priorityCo-sharer tenant holds primary priority

Accurately identifying the land classification ensures that your pre-emption deposit and petition are legally unassailable from day one.

Illustrative Scenario: Recovering Ancestral Land in Cumilla

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how an aggrieved co-sharer used Section 96 to buy back stolen family land in Cumilla:

Three brothers jointly inherited an undivided 30-decimal agricultural parcel in Debidwar, Cumilla. Two brothers lived in Dhaka working in private firms, while the youngest brother remained in the village. In early 2024, the youngest brother, facing gambling debts, secretly sold his undivided 10-decimal share to an influential local brickfield owner for BDT 12,00,000, registering the deed at Debidwar Sub-Registry Office. The buyer deliberately omitted serving notice to the two elder brothers. Four months later, when the elder brothers visited the village for Eid, they found laborers digging soil across the plot.

The brothers engaged a civil litigation advocate. Within 48 hours, the advocate obtained a certified copy of the sale deed from the Sub-Registry Office. The deed stated a consideration of BDT 12,00,000. Working swiftly to meet the strict two-month limitation from the date of knowledge, the advocate filed a Miscellaneous Case under Section 96 of the SAT Act in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Debidwar. Concurrently, the brothers deposited BDT 12,00,000 (consideration) plus BDT 3,00,000 (25% statutory compensation) plus statutory interest into the government treasury via court challan.

The advocate immediately secured an ad-interim injunction under Order 39 CPC restraining the brickfield owner from excavating soil. In court, the buyer argued that the brothers knew of the sale earlier, but could produce no proof of written notice under Section 89. The court held that the elder brothers were co-sharers by inheritance with superior statutory rights. The Senior Assistant Judge allowed the pre-emption case, directed the deposit to be paid to the buyer, and ordered the buyer to execute a deed of re-conveyance. When the buyer evaded, the judge executed the registered deed under the court's official seal, successfully returning the 10 decimals to the ancestral family.

Talk to an Advocate

Navigating complex legal disputes in Bangladesh requires uncompromising documentary preparation, precise statutory drafting, and experienced courtroom representation. Whether you are seeking to buy back ancestral land through pre-emption, stay an unlawful bank auction, prosecute fraudulent recruitment brokers, restrain violent death threats, or resolve high-stakes income tax audit notices, procedural delays can extinguish your statutory remedies. A qualified advocate protects your interests, files emergency petitions, and enforces your legal entitlements across civil, criminal, revenue, and constitutional tribunals.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a Pre-emption (Ogrokroy) lawsuit in Bangladesh?

Pre-emption is a statutory lawsuit where a co-sharer of land exercises their legal right to forcibly buy back a portion of the property sold by another co-heir to an outside stranger, upon depositing the purchase price plus statutory compensation into court.

How much money must be deposited to file a pre-emption case under Section 96 SAT Act?

You must deposit the exact consideration money written on the registered deed, plus 25% statutory compensation, plus 8% annual interest calculated from the date of deed registration to the date of filing.

What is the time limit to file a pre-emption case in Bangladesh?

Under Section 96 of the SAT Act, you must file within two (2) months of receiving official notice of transfer, or within two months of learning of the sale, subject to an outside maximum cap of three (3) years from the date of deed registration.

Can an adjacent neighbor claim pre-emption on agricultural land?

No. The State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act 2006 abolished pre-emption rights for contiguous/adjacent neighbors over agricultural land. Only co-sharers by inheritance and co-sharers by purchase can claim pre-emption under Section 96.

Can an outside buyer refuse to sell the land back if pre-emption is granted?

No. Once the civil court passes a pre-emption decree, the buyer is legally obligated to execute a re-conveyance deed. If the buyer refuses or evades, the civil court judge executes and registers the deed under the court's official seal.

What happens if the seller wrote an artificially high price on the deed to block pre-emption?

If the parties inflated the registered deed price to discourage pre-emption, the applicant must initially deposit the stated deed amount, but can challenge the valuation during trial. The court can order an inquiry to determine true market value and order a partial refund.

Can I stop the buyer from building structures while the pre-emption case is ongoing?

Yes. Your advocate will file an application for a Temporary Injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 CPC. The court will issue an injunction restraining the buyer from constructing buildings, digging soil, or transferring the land until final judgment.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi (NRB) file a pre-emption lawsuit from abroad?

Yes. An NRB co-heir can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, empowering a trusted relative or lawyer in Bangladesh to file the petition and deposit the treasury funds.

Probate of Will & Letters of Administration in Bangladesh: Succession Act 1925 Guide for NRBs & Heirs

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-02 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

When a family member passes away leaving immovable property, land, commercial buildings, bank accounts, or corporate equity in Bangladesh, foreign heirs and Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) in the United States, UK, Canada, and Australia frequently face insurmountable administrative hurdles. Banks freeze deceased accounts, the Assistant Commissioner (Land) rejects mutation applications, and Sub-Registrars refuse title transfers without a conclusive court order. Under the Succession Act 1925, obtaining a Probate of Will or Letters of Administration from the District Judge Court is the only legally binding mechanism to establish testamentary title or administer an un-willed estate. This exhaustive legal guide breaks down the statutory differences between Muslim testamentary limits (Wasiyat) and Christian/Hindu wills, the filing procedure in the Court of the District Judge, court fee structures, citation requirements, and step-by-step estate resolution for expatriates.
