1. Distinguishing Probate, Letters of Administration, and Succession Certificates

One of the most persistent misconceptions among beneficiaries and legal practitioners alike in Bangladesh is confusing a Succession Certificate with a Probate or Letters of Administration. Under the Succession Act 1925, the legal nature of the deceased's assets dictates the specific judicial instrument required:

  • Probate (Section 222 & 276): A grant issued exclusively by the District Judge to an executor appointed under a Will, establishing the authenticity of the testamentary document and conferring absolute authority over both movable and immovable assets.
  • Letters of Administration (Section 218 & 278): Granted when a person dies intestate (leaving no Will), or where a Will fails to name an executor, or the nominated executor renounces or predeceases the testator. This empowers an administrator to manage and distribute the entire real estate and financial holdings.
  • Succession Certificate (Section 370): Issued by a Senior Assistant Judge Court strictly for debts and securities (bank deposits, national savings certificates, shares, and bonds). A Succession Certificate conveys no jurisdiction or authority whatsoever over immovable real estate or land. Attempting to use a Succession Certificate to mutate land or sell apartment properties is rejected by Land Revenue officers.

2. Muslim Wasiyat Limits vs. Non-Muslim & Expat Wills

Bangladesh operates under a dual system of secular statutory procedure and personal religious inheritance laws. For Muslim citizens and foreign Muslims owning property in Bangladesh, testamentary freedom is strictly circumscribed by classical Islamic jurisprudence as codified in Bangladeshi precedent:

  • The One-Third (1/3) Limitation: Under Sunni Hanafi law, a Muslim testator cannot bequeath more than one-third of their net estate (after paying funeral expenses and legitimate debts) via a Will (Wasiyat) without the explicit consent of the natural legal heirs.
  • No Bequest to a Legal Heir: Under the famous principle of 'La wasiyata li-warith' (no bequest to an heir), a Muslim cannot execute a Will giving extra property to one son or daughter to the exclusion of others. If such a will is executed, it remains invalid unless all other co-heirs grant their express, unequivocal consent after the death of the testator. Consent given during the testator's lifetime has no legal force.
  • Hindu, Christian, and Secular Foreign Testators: Under the Succession Act 1925, Hindus, Christians, Parsis, and non-Muslim foreign investors have unlimited testamentary capacity. They may bequeath 100% of their self-acquired and ancestral property to any person, trust, or charitable foundation, entirely bypassing biological heirs if explicitly stated in a legally executed Will.

3. Court Jurisdiction & Filing Forum Under Succession Act 1925

Section 270 of the Succession Act 1925 vests testamentary jurisdiction in the Court of the District Judge. Where property is situated in multiple districts or the deceased died outside Bangladesh (e.g., in London, New York, Toronto, or Sydney), identifying the correct territorial jurisdiction is critical to avoid jurisdictional dismissals:

  • Primary Territorial Forum: The District Judge within whose territorial jurisdiction the deceased had a permanent or fixed place of abode at the time of death.
  • Ancillary Property Forum: If the deceased had no fixed residence in Bangladesh at the time of death (common for long-term expatriates), the petition must be instituted before the District Judge within whose jurisdiction any portion of the immovable property or financial asset is situated (e.g., Dhaka District Judge Court for assets in Gulshan, Dhanmondi, or Uttara).
  • Delegation to Additional District Judge: While original filings land in the District Judge Court, cases without contentious dispute are frequently transferred to an Additional District Judge for recording testimony and issuing final decrees.

4. Step-by-Step Court Procedure for Probate in Bangladesh

Obtaining a certified Probate decree requires rigorous judicial scrutiny to prevent estate hijacking. The procedural stages proceed as follows:

  1. Preparation & Drafting of Petition: The executor files a formal petition under Section 276 of the Succession Act 1925, verified by affidavit, attaching the original Will, original Death Certificate (registered with city corporation/Union Parishad or consular post), schedule of all immovable properties with CS/SA/RS/BS khatian numbers, and a complete schedule of liabilities.
  2. Attestation Affidavit: At least one surviving attesting witness who signed the Will must submit an affidavit swearing that the testator executed the Will in their presence while in sound mind and disposing capacity (Section 281).
  3. Court Registration & Inspection: The petition is registered as a Probate Miscellaneous Case (Probate Misc. Case). The original Will is placed in safe judicial custody in the court's vault.
  4. Issuance of Citations: The court issues notices to all natural legal heirs and orders general public citation.
  5. Recording of Deposition: If no caveat or objection is entered, the court records the oral deposition of the executor and the attesting witness.
  6. Payment of Ad Valorem Fees: The court orders calculation of court fees based on property valuation.
  7. Grant of Probate: Upon payment of court fees and execution of an administration bond, the court issues the formal grant bearing the seal of the District Court.

5. General & Special Citations: Handling Caveats and Objections

To protect absent heirs and prevent fraudulent probate grants, Section 283 of the Succession Act empowers the District Judge to issue two types of judicial citations:

  • Special Citations: Direct court summons served personally by process server or registered postal courier upon all immediate natural heirs (spouse, children, parents, siblings) who would have inherited the property under intestate rules had the Will not existed.
  • General Public Citation: A court-mandated public notification published in two widely circulated national daily newspapers (one Bengali daily, e.g., The Daily Ittefaq, and one English daily, e.g., The Daily Star). The notice informs the global public that any person having interest or claim against the estate must lodge a formal Caveat within 30 to 45 days.
  • Effect of a Caveat: If an aggrieved heir files a Caveat contesting the genuineness of the Will (alleging forgery, undue influence, fraud, or mental incompetence), the proceeding is instantly converted from a non-contentious miscellaneous case into a regular Testamentary Civil Suit under Section 295, tried identically to a regular civil lawsuit with full framing of issues, documentary discovery, cross-examination, and judicial trial.

6. Comparative Overview: Estate Instruments, Fees & Timelines

Selecting the incorrect legal vehicle leads to years of stalled administrative processing. The table below delineates the essential comparative metrics under Bangladeshi statutory law:

Legal InstrumentApplicable StatuteAsset CoverageTarget BeneficiaryEstimated Timeline
Probate of WillSuccession Act 1925, Sec 276All Immovable Land & Movable AssetsNamed Executor in a written Will6 to 12 months (uncontested)
Letters of AdministrationSuccession Act 1925, Sec 278Entire Real & Personal EstateStatutory Heirs (Intestate / No Executor)8 to 14 months
Succession CertificateSuccession Act 1925, Sec 370Debts, Bank Deposits & Securities ONLYSurviving Legal Heirs3 to 6 months
Civil Partition SuitPartition Act 1893 & CPC 1908Immovable Real Estate Partition & DemarcationCo-sharer Heirs in Joint Title18 to 36+ months

7. How NRBs Living in USA, UK, Canada & Australia Can File Remotely

Expatriates and dual nationals residing in London, New York, Toronto, or Sydney are not legally required to reside in Bangladesh throughout probate proceedings. The law provides an established extraterritorial mechanism under the Power of Attorney Act 2012 and the Power of Attorney Rules 2015:

  • Drafting the Special Power of Attorney: A comprehensive Special Power of Attorney must be drafted specifically empowering a trusted relative or an enrolled Supreme Court advocate in Bangladesh to file the probate petition, depose on behalf of the principal, and sign verification affidavits.
  • Consular Attestation Abroad: The foreign-based executor must execute the Power of Attorney before the Consular Officer at the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission in their host country (e.g., London High Commission, Bangladesh Consulate in New York or Los Angeles, Ottawa or Canberra missions).
  • Home Ministry & DC Office Stamping: Once mailed to Bangladesh, the power of attorney document must be counter-attested by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Consular Wing) in Segunbagicha, Dhaka, and subsequently validated and stamped by the Collector (Deputy Commissioner's Treasury Branch) within statutory deadlines.
  • Appearance via Video Conferencing: Under current judicial digitalization circulars issued by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, witness depositions can in exceptional cases be requested via recorded digital conferencing upon formal court application.

8. Executor Rights, Estate Duties, and Submitting the 6-Month Inventory

A grant of probate does not make the executor the absolute owner of the estate; rather, it clothes them with fiduciary responsibility as a trustee for all legitimate beneficiaries. Under Section 317 of the Succession Act 1925, the executor assumes stringent statutory duties:

  • Filing of Formal Inventory (6 Months): Within six (6) months from the grant of probate or letters of administration, the executor must exhibit in court a complete, itemized inventory containing an accurate appraisal of all real and personal property, credits, and debts of the deceased.
  • Filing Final Estate Accounts (1 Year): Within twelve (12) months from the date of the grant, the administrator must submit a verified formal account of the estate, displaying all collections, disbursements, tax payments, and distributed shares to beneficiaries.
  • Devastavit & Civil Liability: If an executor wastes estate funds, sells land below market price without beneficiary authorization, or misappropriates bank balances, they are personally liable under Section 368 for devastavit (misapplication of assets) and can face immediate revocation of probate under Section 263, alongside criminal breach of trust proceedings under Section 406 of the Penal Code.

9. Common Pitfalls: Forged Wills, Unattested Codicils & Mutation Roadblocks

Substantial delays and litigation disasters occur when estates stumble into predictable legal potholes:

  • Relying on Unregistered Wills: While an unregistered will is not automatically void under the Succession Act, it faces severe evidentiary suspicion. Sibling rivals frequently challenge unregistered wills alleging mental illness or post-mortem forgery. Registering a will during the testator's lifetime at the Sub-Registry Office establishes almost incontrovertible legal validity.
  • Failing to Prove Attestation (Section 68, Evidence Act): Under Section 68 of the Evidence Act 1872, a Will cannot be used as evidence until at least one attesting witness has been called to prove its execution. If all attesting witnesses are deceased or untraceable, Section 69 mandates proving the handwriting of at least one witness and the signature of the testator through forensic handwriting examination.
  • Attempting Land Sale Before AC (Land) Mutation: Merely holding a certified Probate decree does not instantly allow an executor to sell land. The executor must first submit the probate decree along with the original title deed to the Assistant Commissioner (Land) to mutate the property in the executor's name (or the beneficiaries' names) in the online Namjari portal and clear all ground rents (Khajna).

10. Real-Life Expat Case Study: Resolving Disputed Gulshan Property Probate

A senior physician who migrated to the United Kingdom passed away in Manchester, leaving behind a 5-katha residential plot in Gulshan-2, Dhaka, and commercial bank accounts in Sonali Bank. In his registered 2018 Will executed in Dhaka, he appointed his London-based elder daughter as sole executrix, bequeathing the property equally between his two daughters while explicitly excluding an estranged son who had previously taken his entire UK share during lifetime.

Upon the physician's death, the London-based executrix engaged our chamber. Our legal team executed the following strategic workflow:

  1. Drafted a Special Power of Attorney in London, authenticated by the Bangladesh High Commission, London, and cleared MOFA and DC Dhaka stamping.
  2. Filed a petition for Probate under Section 276 before the District Judge Court, Dhaka (Probate Misc. Case No. 84/2024).
  3. Secured personal appearance affidavits from two retired senior civil servants in Dhaka who had signed as attesting witnesses to the 2018 registered Will.
  4. Published mandatory general citations in The Daily Star and Prothom Alo. When the estranged son attempted to lodge an informal complaint with the Gulshan AC (Land), our advocates established before the court that no formal Caveat had been instituted within the statutory 30-day window.
  5. Calculated the maximum statutory court fee cap, deposited the treasury challan, executed the judicial administrative bond, and secured the final sealed Grant of Probate within 7 months.
  6. Successfully executed online mutation and tax clearances, enabling the overseas daughters to legally lease out the commercial ground floor to a multinational bank with full repatriation rights.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is probate mandatory for all wills in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under Section 213 of the Succession Act 1925, no right as executor or legatee can be established in any Court of Justice unless a Court of competent jurisdiction has granted probate of the will under which the right is claimed or has granted letters of administration. Without probate, title cannot be transferred at the Sub-Registry office.

Can a Muslim in Bangladesh give their entire property away through a will?

No. Under Muslim personal law in Bangladesh, a Muslim can bequeath at most one-third (1/3) of their net surplus estate to persons who are not their natural legal heirs. Any bequest exceeding one-third, or any bequest made to a legal heir, is legally invalid unless all other natural heirs grant explicit consent after the testator has died.

What is the difference between Probate and Letters of Administration?

A Probate is granted exclusively to an executor named inside a valid Will. Letters of Administration are granted when the deceased died without leaving a Will (intestate), or when the Will failed to nominate an executor, or the nominated executor died or refused to act.

Can an NRB living in the US or UK apply for probate without traveling to Dhaka?

Yes. Under the Power of Attorney Act 2012, an overseas executor can execute a Special Power of Attorney before the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, appointing an attorney or Supreme Court advocate in Bangladesh to file the petition, manage citations, and complete all court proceedings.

What happens if someone files a Caveat objecting to the Will?

If an heir or interested person files a Caveat within the citation window, the non-contentious probate proceeding is immediately converted into a regular Testamentary Civil Suit under Section 295 of the Succession Act. The court then conducts a formal trial with evidence, cross-examination, and judicial judgment.

How long does it take to obtain a Probate decree in Dhaka District Court?

For an uncontested probate case with cooperative attesting witnesses, the process typically takes between 6 to 10 months in Dhaka. If an objection or Caveat is lodged, converting it into a contentious suit, litigation can take 18 to 36 months depending on court backlogs.

Does a Succession Certificate allow heirs to take possession of deceased family land?

No. Section 370 of the Succession Act explicitly restricts Succession Certificates to debts and securities (bank funds, stock shares, national savings certificates). It confers zero authority or title over immovable landed property. Immovable land requires Probate, Letters of Administration, or a Partition Suit.

What are the court fees for probate in Bangladesh?

Court fees for probate and letters of administration are assessed ad valorem based on the net valuation of the estate under the Court-Fees Act 1870, subject to statutory maximum caps and exemptions for low-value estates. A treasury challan must be deposited prior to the final grant being issued.

Property Inheritance in Bangladesh for NRBs: Muslim, Hindu and Christian Law

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-04 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

When a parent dies in Bangladesh, the children abroad often hear that "everything is already settled" and discover years later that their share was sold, transferred by a forged deed or occupied by one sibling. Knowing how inheritance works, and acting early, is the best protection. This guide is written by <a href="/advocate-md-shah-alam" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">Advocate Md. Shah Alam</a>, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, for Bangladeshis living in the UK, USA, UAE, Canada and elsewhere. For case-specific help you can call the chamber on <a href="tel:01712655546" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">01712655546</a> or WhatsApp the same number.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

📋 In This Article

  2. Muslim Inheritance: Fixed Shares
  3. Hindu Inheritance (Dayabhaga)
  4. Christian and Other Inheritance
  5. Heirship Certificate, Mutation and Documents
  6. Disputes, Partition and Fraud
  7. Special Issues for NRBs
  8. Steps to Protect Your Share

Which Law Applies?

Bangladesh has no single inheritance statute for everyone. The religion of the deceased decides which law applies:

  • Muslims: Muslim personal law (Sharia, mainly Hanafi), supplemented by the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (for example, the rights of orphaned grandchildren).
  • Hindus: Dayabhaga school (mostly in Bangladesh), with the Hindu Women's Right to Property Act 1937.
  • Christians and others: the Succession Act 1925.

A will can also change the picture, but a Muslim can leave only up to one-third of the estate by will to a non-heir without the consent of the other heirs.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Muslim Inheritance: Fixed Shares

Muslim law fixes the shares of the main heirs. The exact result depends on who survives the deceased, and you should always have your advocate calculate it, but the following are the commonly applied rules:

  • Wife: 1/8 if there are children, 1/4 if there are no children (shared among wives).
  • Husband: 1/4 if there are children, 1/2 if there are none.
  • Sons and daughters: the residue after fixed shares, with each son receiving twice a daughter's share.
  • Only daughter: 1/2; two or more daughters (no sons): 2/3 together.
  • Mother: 1/6 if there are children, otherwise 1/3.
  • Father: 1/6 if there are children plus residue in some cases.

Heirs living abroad have exactly the same rights as heirs who live in Bangladesh. Debts, funeral expenses and valid bequests are paid first.

Hindu Inheritance (Dayabhaga)

Under the Dayabhaga system, the sons, widow and daughters inherit on the death of the owner. In general, sons take the property equally; a widow can inherit a share equal to a son in the absence of other heirs and holds a limited interest; and a daughter inherits mainly in the absence of sons or widow. The rules are complex, and recent reform proposals are not yet complete, so get advice for your specific family.

Christian and Other Inheritance

Under the Succession Act 1925, if a Christian dies without a will, the spouse and children take specified shares: one-third to the widow and two-thirds to the children, equally (if there is no child, shares go to other kin). If there is a valid will, probate or letters of administration are obtained from the District Judge.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Heirship Certificate, Mutation and Documents

  1. Obtain the death certificate of the deceased.
  2. Get the heirship certificate (Warish Sanad) from the City Corporation / Union Parishad / Pourashava, naming all legal heirs.
  3. Collect the land documents: deeds, Khatian, tax receipts.
  4. Apply for mutation (Namjari) by inheritance, naming all heirs and their shares.
  5. Pay land development tax in the names of all heirs.

For banks, savings certificates or insurance, a Succession Certificate from the Civil Court may be needed.

Disputes, Partition and Fraud

Disputes usually arise when one heir takes control of the property. Typical problems include:

  • One heir sells the whole property or mutates it solely in his name.
  • Forged heirship certificates omitting heirs abroad.
  • Forged gift deeds or wills.
  • Occupation by a sibling without paying other heirs.

Remedies include an application for cancellation of mutation, a suit for declaration and partition (the Partition Act 1893), injunction and, where documents have been forged, a criminal complaint. Courts take time, so act as soon as you learn of a problem.

Special Issues for NRBs

  • Appoint a trusted advocate with a limited Power of Attorney to represent you.
  • Make sure your name, parents' names and NID/passport details match the heirship certificate.
  • Do not sign "no objection" or relinquishment papers without independent legal advice.
  • If you wish to give up your share, do it by a properly registered deed.
  • Keep proof of your relationship (birth certificate, NID, passport).

Steps to Protect Your Share

  1. Obtain the heirship certificate with all heirs' names.
  2. Verify the current mutation and tax records.
  3. Get a deed search to ensure no transfer has been made without your consent.
  4. Reach a written, registered partition agreement if the family agrees.
  5. If not, file a partition suit with an injunction against sale.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do heirs living abroad have inheritance rights in Bangladesh?

Yes. Residence abroad does not reduce an heir's legal share under Muslim, Hindu or Christian succession law.

How much does a daughter get under Muslim law?

A daughter receives half of a son's share when there are sons. A sole daughter gets 1/2 of the estate, and two or more daughters together get 2/3 if there are no sons.

How do I get an heirship certificate in Bangladesh?

Apply to the Union Parishad, Pourashava or City Corporation with the death certificate, NIDs and family information. They issue a Warish Sanad naming the heirs.

Can a brother sell inherited property without my consent?

He can only sell his own share. A sale of the entire property without co-heirs' consent can be challenged, and you can seek injunction and cancellation in court.

What if my siblings refuse to divide the property?

You can file a partition suit in the Civil Court to have the property divided according to each heir's legal share.

Property Inheritance & Distribution Law Bangladesh – Muslim, Hindu & Succession Rights

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-28 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

When a person dies in Bangladesh, the distribution of their property among surviving family members is governed by a complex interplay of personal laws — primarily Islamic Shariat law for Muslims, Hindu personal law for Hindus, and the Succession Act 1925 for Christians and other non-Muslims. Understanding your rightful share in a deceased parent's or spouse's estate, and knowing how to legally enforce that right, is one of the most important aspects of family law in Bangladesh. This comprehensive guide covers all you need to know about property inheritance and distribution law in Bangladesh in 2026.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

📋 In This Article

  2. Muslim Inheritance Law in Bangladesh: The Hanafi Framework
  3. Who Inherits When a Father Dies Under Muslim Law?
  4. The 2:1 Ratio – Sons vs Daughters in Islamic Inheritance
  5. Shares of Spouse, Mother, and Siblings Under Muslim Law
  6. Situations Where Daughters Are Illegally Deprived of Inheritance
  7. Hindu Succession Law in Bangladesh
  8. The Succession Act 1925: Christians and Other Non-Muslims
  9. Inheritance Share Comparison Table
  10. Partition Suits (Bonton Mamla) in Bangladesh
  11. Succession Certificate: When and How to Obtain It
  12. How a Family Lawyer Can Protect Your Inheritance Rights

Overview of Inheritance Law in Bangladesh

Bangladesh does not have a uniform civil code governing inheritance. Instead, the applicable law depends on the religion of the deceased at the time of death. The three primary legal frameworks are:

  • Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937 – Governs inheritance for Muslims, applying the principles of the Quran and Hanafi jurisprudence as the default rule.
  • Hindu personal law (Dayabhaga school, applicable in Bangladesh) – Governs inheritance for Hindus, though there is no comprehensive codified Hindu succession act in Bangladesh unlike in India.
  • The Succession Act 1925 – Applies to Christians, Buddhists, Parsis, and others who are neither Muslims nor Hindus. This Act also governs succession certificates regardless of religion.

A deceased person's property is classified into two broad types for inheritance purposes:

  1. Self-acquired property: Property the deceased acquired through their own efforts (purchase, profession, business).
  2. Inherited (ancestral) property: Property passed down from prior generations.

In Bangladesh, both types of property are subject to the same personal law rules upon the death of the owner, unless the owner made a valid will (wasiyat). Under Muslim law, a will cannot dispose of more than one-third (1/3) of the total estate to non-heirs — the remaining two-thirds must be distributed among legal heirs according to Quranic shares.

Muslim Inheritance Law in Bangladesh: The Hanafi Framework

Bangladesh being approximately 90% Muslim, Muslim inheritance law is by far the most widely applied. The Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937 (Act XXVI of 1937) mandates that in all matters of succession, inheritance, and distribution of property, the rule of decision shall be Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) for Muslims in Bangladesh.

The Hanafi school of jurisprudence — which predominates in South Asia — divides heirs into two categories:

  • Dhawul Faraid (Sharers): Heirs entitled to fixed, Quranically specified fractional shares of the estate. These are: spouse (husband or wife), daughters, father, mother, grandfather, grandmother, full sister, half-sister, and uterine siblings. Their shares are fixed regardless of the number of other heirs.
  • Asabah (Residuaries): Heirs who inherit what remains after the Dhawul Faraid have received their fixed shares. Sons are the primary Asabah. Sons do not have a fixed fraction — they divide the residue among themselves (and with daughters in a 2:1 ratio).

The basic Hanafi inheritance rules follow the principle of proximity of relationship: closer relatives exclude more distant ones from inheriting. For example, a son excludes a grandson from inheriting.

Importantly, non-Muslims cannot inherit from a Muslim, and a Muslim cannot inherit from a non-Muslim under classical Hanafi law. A murderer is also excluded from inheriting from their victim under Bangladeshi courts' application of this principle.

Who Inherits When a Father Dies Under Muslim Law?

The death of a father is the most common inheritance scenario in Bangladesh. Under Hanafi Muslim law, the following persons are entitled to share in the father's estate:

HeirCategoryShareConditions
Wife (or wives)Dhawul Faraid1/4 (if no children); 1/8 (if children exist)All wives share equally within the allotted fraction
Son(s)Asabah (Residuary)Residue after sharers, double the daughter's shareSons exclude grandsons from inheriting
Daughter(s)Mixed (Sharer/Asabah)1/2 if only one daughter; 2/3 if two or more daughters (when no son); joins residue with son in 2:1 ratioSons and daughters jointly share residue in 2:1 ratio
FatherDhawul Faraid1/6 (if son exists); inherits rest as Asabah (if no son)Father of the deceased
MotherDhawul Faraid1/6 (if children or two+ siblings exist); 1/3 (if no children)Mother of the deceased

Practical Example: A father dies leaving behind a wife, two sons, and one daughter, with a net estate worth BDT 80,00,000 (80 lakhs):

  1. Wife's share (1/8 as children exist): BDT 10,00,000
  2. Remaining residue: BDT 70,00,000
  3. Distributed among 2 sons + 1 daughter in 2:1:1 ratio (5 parts total): Each part = BDT 14,00,000
  4. Each son receives: BDT 28,00,000; daughter receives: BDT 14,00,000

The 2:1 Ratio – Sons vs Daughters in Islamic Inheritance

Perhaps the most widely known — and most frequently disputed — rule in Muslim inheritance law is the 2:1 ratio between sons and daughters. This principle derives directly from the Quran (Surah An-Nisa, 4:11): "For the male the equivalent of the portion of two females."

Under Hanafi law applied in Bangladesh, this means:

  • When both sons and daughters survive the deceased father, they share the residuary estate together, with each son receiving twice the share of each daughter.
  • This ratio applies only to the residue after fixed sharers (Dhawul Faraid) have received their portions.
  • The ratio applies regardless of the number of sons or daughters — it is per capita within each gender group.

Many families in Bangladesh — particularly in rural areas — misunderstand or deliberately misapply this rule to deprive daughters entirely of inheritance. It must be clearly stated: under Muslim law, daughters have an enforceable, constitutionally protected right to inherit. The 2:1 ratio does not mean daughters inherit nothing — it governs only the relative proportion.

The Constitution of Bangladesh (Article 28) prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth, and the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has upheld daughters' rights to their lawful share as a constitutional right enforceable through civil courts.

Shares of Spouse, Mother, and Siblings Under Muslim Law

Beyond sons and daughters, several other family members hold significant inheritance rights under Muslim law in Bangladesh:

Spouse's Share:

  • A husband inherits 1/2 of the wife's estate if there are no children; 1/4 if there are children.
  • A wife (or all wives collectively) inherit 1/4 of the husband's estate if there are no children; 1/8 if there are children.

Mother's Share:

  • The mother receives 1/3 of the estate if there are no children and no more than one sibling of the deceased.
  • The mother receives 1/6 if there are children or two or more siblings of the deceased.

Full Siblings' Share:

  • Full brothers and sisters are excluded from inheriting when the deceased has a surviving son, father, or paternal grandfather.
  • Where siblings inherit, full brothers are Asabah (residuaries); full sisters are Dhawul Faraid (1/2 for one sister; 2/3 for two or more sisters).
  • Where a full brother and full sister co-inherit, they share in a 2:1 ratio, similar to sons and daughters.

Grandchildren's Share:

A key rule in Hanafi law is that grandchildren are excluded by their uncles or aunts when a son or daughter of the deceased is alive. If a son of the deceased predeceased the grandfather, his children (the grandchildren) receive nothing — this is a major source of injustice in Bangladesh that has been addressed in some Muslim-majority countries through obligatory bequest (wasiyat-i-wajiba) provisions, though Bangladesh has not yet enacted such legislation.

Situations Where Daughters Are Illegally Deprived of Inheritance

Despite clear Quranic injunctions and legal provisions, daughters in Bangladesh are frequently — and illegally — deprived of their rightful inheritance. Common methods of deprivation include:

  • Premature or fraudulent property transfer: A father transfers all or most property to sons (via gift deed or sham sale deed) during his lifetime, leaving nothing to be inherited by daughters after his death. If such transfers are made without adequate consideration and with intent to deprive daughters, they may be challenged in court.
  • Forged will (wasiyat): A will is produced after the father's death, purportedly bequeathing the entire estate to sons. Under Muslim law, a will cannot validly dispose of more than 1/3 of the estate to non-heirs. A will that purports to disinherit daughters entirely is void under Shariat.
  • Social pressure and family agreements: Daughters are pressured to sign away inheritance rights in exchange for gifts, marriages expenses, or social acceptance. Such agreements may be challenged as unconscionable contracts under the Contract Act 1872.
  • Delay in mutation: Brothers who take possession of the property quickly apply for mutation in their own names, leaving daughters' names off the record. Daughters must act promptly to assert their rights before mutation is finalized.
  • Concealment of assets: Brothers conceal the existence of certain assets from sisters and the court.

A daughter who has been deprived of inheritance has the following legal remedies:

  • Filing a partition suit (bonton mamla) before the civil court under the Partition Act 1893
  • Filing a declaration suit to establish her title to the inherited property
  • Challenging fraudulent transfers under the Transfer of Property Act 1882, Section 53 (transfer to defraud creditors/heirs)
  • Filing a complaint about mutation fraud before the AC Land office or the Land Appeal Board
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Hindu Succession Law in Bangladesh

For Hindus in Bangladesh, inheritance is governed by the Dayabhaga school of Hindu personal law, which is the applicable school in Bengal (as opposed to the Mitakshara school prevalent in most of India). Key features of Dayabhaga succession include:

  • No coparcenary concept: Under Dayabhaga, a son does not acquire a birth-right interest in the father's property. The father has absolute ownership of self-acquired property and may dispose of it freely during his lifetime, including by will.
  • Inheritance upon death only: Sons, daughters, and other heirs acquire rights only upon the father's death — not at birth (unlike Mitakshara).
  • Widow's rights: A Hindu widow has the right to inherit her husband's property, though traditionally her interest was a "limited estate" that could not be alienated. The Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act 1937 (applicable in Bangladesh) expanded widows' rights significantly.
  • Daughter's position: Under Dayabhaga, unmarried daughters and widowed daughters have inheritance rights. However, married daughters traditionally had weaker claims, though this position has evolved through court decisions.

It is important to note that unlike India (which enacted the Hindu Succession Act 1956 and its 2005 amendment giving daughters equal coparcenary rights), Bangladesh has not enacted a corresponding statute. Hindu succession in Bangladesh remains governed by uncodified personal law, leading to significant uncertainty and litigation. Consulting a lawyer with expertise in Hindu personal law is essential for Hindu families dealing with inheritance matters.

Hindu families in Bangladesh also frequently use family partition deeds (bonton deed) registered before the Sub-Registrar to formally divide ancestral property among heirs.

The Succession Act 1925: Christians and Other Non-Muslims

The Succession Act 1925 (Act XXXIX of 1925) governs the succession of Christians, Buddhists, Parsis, and other non-Muslims in Bangladesh. It provides a codified scheme of inheritance. Key provisions include:

  • Where there is a will: The deceased's property is distributed according to the will (testamentary succession), subject to the court's grant of Probate.
  • Where there is no will (intestate succession):
    • If the deceased leaves a spouse and lineal descendants (children/grandchildren): The spouse receives 1/3 and the descendants share 2/3 equally.
    • If the deceased leaves a spouse but no lineal descendants: The spouse receives 1/2 and the other half goes to kindred (relatives).
    • If no spouse but lineal descendants survive: The entire estate goes to the lineal descendants equally (sons and daughters take equal shares — unlike Muslim law).
  • Succession Certificate: The Succession Act 1925 also governs the issuance of Succession Certificates by courts for debts and securities — applicable to all religions.

A significant distinction from Muslim law is that under the Succession Act 1925, sons and daughters inherit equally — there is no 2:1 differential.

Inheritance Share Comparison Table

The following table compares the inheritance shares of key family members under the three primary legal frameworks applicable in Bangladesh:

HeirMuslim Law (Hanafi)Hindu Law (Dayabhaga)Succession Act 1925
SonResidue; double daughter's share (2:1 ratio)Primary heir; takes full shareEqual share with siblings
DaughterHalf of son's share (1:2 ratio)Inherits; share varies by status (married/widowed/unmarried)Equal share with siblings
Wife (Widow)1/4 (no children); 1/8 (with children)Inherits husband's share (limited estate historically)1/3 (with children); 1/2 (without children)
Husband1/2 (no children); 1/4 (with children)Inherits wife's property1/3 (with children); 1/2 (without children)
Father1/6 (with son); residue if no sonGenerally excluded by sonsNo specific share; takes under kindred rules
Mother1/6 (with children/2+ siblings); 1/3 (no children)Inherits in some circumstancesIncluded in kindred distribution
GrandchildrenExcluded by surviving childrenInherit per stirpes in some casesInherit per stirpes if parent predeceased

Note: This table provides a simplified overview. Actual inheritance calculations depend on the specific combination of surviving heirs and must be computed for each family situation individually. Consult a qualified family lawyer for advice specific to your circumstances.

Partition Suits (Bonton Mamla) in Bangladesh

When co-owners of inherited property cannot agree on how to divide it, any co-owner may file a partition suit (bonton mamla) before the competent civil court under the Partition Act 1893. This is one of the most common categories of civil litigation in Bangladesh.

Key aspects of partition suits in Bangladesh:

  • Who can file: Any co-owner (sharer in inheritance) has the right to file a partition suit, including daughters, widows, and minor heirs (through a guardian).
  • Court jurisdiction: Partition suits involving immovable property are filed before the Assistant Judge (Civil) of the district where the property is located. Appeals lie to the District Judge and then to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court.
  • Procedure: The plaintiff files a plaint describing the property, their share, and all co-owners. The court may appoint a Commissioner to inspect and value the property. The court then passes a preliminary decree establishing shares, followed by a final decree for actual partition (physical division or sale and division of proceeds).
  • Time limit (Limitation): A partition suit must be filed within 12 years of the date when the right to sue first accrued (i.e., the date of the deceased's death), under the Limitation Act 1908.
  • Interim orders: The court may grant an injunction preventing co-owners from alienating or encumbering the property during the pendency of the suit.

It is advisable to attempt family mediation (salish) before resorting to litigation. Many families successfully resolve inheritance disputes through facilitated negotiation and a registered family settlement deed, avoiding the cost and time of court proceedings.

Succession Certificate: When and How to Obtain It

A Succession Certificate is a court-issued document authorising the holder to collect debts and securities owed to a deceased person. It is governed by Part X of the Succession Act 1925 and is relevant across all religious communities in Bangladesh.

A Succession Certificate is typically required when:

  • Claiming money from a bank account of a deceased person
  • Receiving insurance proceeds, provident fund, or gratuity of a deceased employee
  • Collecting dividends or transferring shares held by the deceased
  • Claiming dues from government or private entities owed to the deceased

How to obtain a Succession Certificate in Bangladesh:

  1. File a petition before the District Judge of the district where the deceased ordinarily resided or where the property is located.
  2. The petition must describe all legal heirs, the nature of the debts/securities, and the relationship of the applicant to the deceased.
  3. The court issues a notice fixing a hearing date and calling for objections (usually published in a newspaper).
  4. If no valid objections are raised, the court grants the Succession Certificate after the applicant pays court fees (ad valorem, calculated as a percentage of the value of the estate).
  5. The certificate is issued within 2 to 6 months typically, though complex cases may take longer.

A Succession Certificate does not determine inheritance rights conclusively — it is merely an administrative authorisation to collect debts. For a conclusive determination of title to immovable property, a declaration suit before the civil court or a probate proceeding (for will-based succession) is required.

How a Family Lawyer Can Protect Your Inheritance Rights

Inheritance disputes in Bangladesh are among the most emotionally charged and legally complex matters. Whether you are a daughter seeking your rightful share, a widow protecting your portion of the marital estate, or a son ensuring equitable distribution among siblings, the assistance of an experienced family lawyer is invaluable.

A qualified family lawyer can assist you in:

  • Calculating your exact inheritance share under the applicable personal law based on the specific surviving heirs
  • Filing or defending a partition suit (bonton mamla) before the civil court
  • Obtaining a Succession Certificate to collect bank deposits, insurance proceeds, and other financial assets
  • Challenging fraudulent gift deeds or sham sales made to deprive heirs of their rightful share
  • Filing mutation (namjari) applications to record the inherited property in the heirs' names
  • Drafting family settlement deeds to avoid protracted litigation
  • Appealing erroneous decisions of lower courts to the High Court Division or Appellate Division of the Supreme Court

Advocate Md. Shah Alam, practicing from his Uttara chamber in Dhaka and available for consultations across Bangladesh, has handled numerous complex inheritance and partition matters for Muslim, Hindu, and Christian families. His expertise spans the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937, the Succession Act 1925, Hindu personal law, and the Partition Act 1893. Advocate Shah Alam is also associated with the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, enabling him to represent clients in inheritance appeals at the highest level.

Do not let family pressure or ignorance of the law deprive you of your legal inheritance. Contact our office today for a confidential consultation on your inheritance rights.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a daughter be legally deprived of her inheritance in Bangladesh?

No. Under Muslim law in Bangladesh, a daughter has a legally enforceable right to inherit from her father's estate — she is entitled to half the share of a son. Any attempt to deprive her through fraudulent gifts, forged wills, or family pressure is illegal and can be challenged in court. A daughter may file a partition suit before the civil court to claim her rightful share within 12 years of the father's death.

What is the wife's share in her husband's property under Muslim law in Bangladesh?

Under Hanafi Muslim law applicable in Bangladesh, a wife receives 1/4 of her husband's estate if there are no children, or 1/8 if there are children. If the husband had multiple wives, they share this fraction equally among themselves. These shares are fixed Quranic entitlements that cannot be taken away by will or family pressure.

How is a father's property divided in Bangladesh when there are only daughters and no sons?

If a father dies leaving two or more daughters but no sons (and no other residuary heirs), the daughters together receive 2/3 of the estate. If there is only one daughter, she receives 1/2. The remaining portion (1/3 or 1/2) goes to other fixed sharers such as the mother, father, and spouse of the deceased. If there are no other sharers or residuaries, the daughters may take the remainder by return (radd).

What is a succession certificate and who needs it in Bangladesh?

A succession certificate is a court order under the Succession Act 1925 that authorises a legal heir to collect debts and financial assets (such as bank accounts, insurance money, or provident funds) belonging to a deceased person. It is obtained by filing a petition before the District Judge. All heirs — Muslim, Hindu, or Christian — may need a succession certificate to access the financial assets of a deceased family member.

What is the time limit for filing a partition suit in Bangladesh?

Under the Limitation Act 1908, a partition suit for immovable property must be filed within 12 years of the date on which the right to sue first arose — typically the date of the deceased person's death or the date a co-owner first excluded other co-owners from possession. It is advisable to act promptly rather than waiting near the limitation deadline.

Do Hindu daughters have inheritance rights in Bangladesh?

Yes, under the Dayabhaga school of Hindu personal law applicable in Bangladesh, daughters (especially unmarried and widowed daughters) have inheritance rights. However, unlike India which enacted the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 giving daughters equal rights, Bangladesh does not have a codified Hindu succession statute. As a result, the rights of Hindu daughters remain governed by older case law and uncodified personal law, creating significant uncertainty. Consulting a lawyer experienced in Hindu personal law is essential.

Family Property Partition Suit in Bangladesh: How to Divide Joint Land & Inheritance

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-09-21 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Joint family property disputes and inheritance distribution conflicts are among the most common civil court litigations in Bangladesh. When siblings, relatives, or co-sharers (সহ-শরীক) refuse to divide inherited land amicably or attempt to sell specific prime portions without mutual consent, filing a <strong>Partition Suit (বাটোয়ারা মামলা)</strong> under the Partition Act 1893 and Code of Civil Procedure 1908 is the ultimate legal remedy. For expert civil representation, consult Supreme Court Advocate <a href="/advocate-md-shah-alam" style="color:var(--accent);font-weight:600;">Advocate Md. Shah Alam</a>.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order
Official Portalssupremecourt.gov.bd, judiciary.gov.bd, pcc.police.gov.bd & land.gov.bd
Supreme Court ChamberAdvocate Md. Shah Alam — Uttara & Dhaka Judge Court (+880 1712-655546)
📋 In This Article

  2. When Should You File a Partition Suit?
  3. Pre-Filing Requirements & Title Document Checklist
  4. Understanding the Two Stages of Partition Suit: Preliminary & Final Decree
  5. Role of Advocate Commissioner & Saham (সহম) Allocation
  6. Obtaining an Injunction to Stop Co-Sharers from Selling Joint Land
  7. Court Fees & Valuation Rules for Partition Lawsuits
  8. Why You Need a Senior Civil Advocate in Dhaka

What Is a Partition Suit (বাটোয়ারা মামলা) under Bangladesh Civil Law?

A Partition Suit is a civil lawsuit filed by a co-owner or legal heir seeking judicial division and separate physical possession of their rightful share in joint land, building, or ancestral estate.

Governing Laws:

  • The Partition Act 1893: Provides for judicial sale or buyout of property if physical partition is impossible.
  • Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC): Governs suit procedure, injunctions (Order 39), and commissioner appointment (Order 26 Rule 13).
  • Personal Inheritance Laws: Muslim Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937 or Hindu Law governing share ratios.

Consult a skilled Land & Property Lawyer in Dhaka before filing.

When Should You File a Partition Suit?

You should immediately file a partition suit if:

  • Co-sharers refuse to execute a registered Deed of Amicable Partition (আপস বাটোয়ারা দলিল).
  • One co-sharer forcibly occupies the best commercial roadside portion of joint land.
  • A co-sharer secretly attempts to sell specific land plots to a third-party developer or buyer.
  • There is a dispute over exact inheritance share ratios under CS, SA, RS, or BS Khatians.

Pre-Filing Requirements & Title Document Checklist

Before filing the suit, compile complete title flow records:

  • Ancestral Khatian records (CS, SA, RS, BS Khatian copies).
  • Original Death Certificate of ancestor and official Warishan Certificate.
  • Via Deeds (বায়া দলিল) showing how ancestors acquired the property.
  • Latest E-Namjari and Land Development Tax (Khajna) receipts.
  • Site map/sketch showing current joint possession.

Understanding the Two Stages of Partition Suit: Preliminary & Final Decree

A partition suit is unique because it proceeds in two distinct judicial stages:

  1. Stage 1: Preliminary Decree (প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি): The Court evaluates title documents and passes a judgment declaring the exact legal percentage/fractional share of each co-sharer (e.g., 1/4th or 2/16th share).
  2. Stage 2: Final Decree (চূড়ান্ত ডিক্রি): After the preliminary decree, the Court appoints a Commissioner to physically measure the ground area and draw up specific boundary lots (Saham). Once approved, the Court signs the Final Decree granting exclusive possession.
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Role of Advocate Commissioner & Saham (সহম) Allocation

During the Final Decree stage, an official Advocate Commissioner (অ্যাডভোকেট কমিশনার) along with a professional government surveyor (আমিন) visits the land:

  • Measures exact plot dimensions, road access, and building structures.
  • Prepares individual Saham (সহম) maps demarcating exact plots for each co-sharer.
  • Submits a Commissioner Report to the Court. Parties can file written objections if dissatisfied with the proposed division.

Obtaining an Injunction to Stop Co-Sharers from Selling Joint Land

Under Order 39 Rules 1 & 2 of CPC, your advocate can file an urgent application for Temporary Injunction (অস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞা) at the time of filing the suit.

If granted:

  • Co-sharers are legally prohibited from transferring, selling, or mortgaging joint land.
  • All ongoing illegal construction work on the disputed plot is frozen by court order.
  • Sub-Registry offices are notified not to register any third-party deeds for the property.

Court Fees & Valuation Rules for Partition Lawsuits

Court fee for a partition suit depends on possession status:

  • If Plaintiff is in Joint Possession: Fixed nominal court fee (BDT 300 to BDT 1,000) applies under Court Fees Act 1870.
  • If Plaintiff has been completely dispossessed (Out of Possession): Ad Valorem court fee applies based on the market value of the plaintiff's share.

Why You Need a Senior Civil Advocate in Dhaka

Partition lawsuits involve intricate boundary math, khatian vetting, and commissioner advocacy.

Advocate Md. Shah Alam — Supreme Court Advocate practicing at Civil Courts Dhaka — has successfully represented hundreds of families in resolving joint land partition suits and securing exclusive title decrees.

⚖️ Need to Divide Joint Family Property? Contact Supreme Court Advocate Advocate Md. Shah Alam for expert civil partition suit representation. Visit our Land Legal Services Page or Contact Us Directly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a co-sharer sell their specific plot before a partition suit is finalized?

A co-sharer can legally sell only their undivided fractional share, but CANNOT transfer a specific physical plot or portion without an executed partition deed or court final decree. Any such sale is subject to court injunction.

How long does a partition suit take in Bangladesh courts?

An uncontested partition suit takes approx 1 to 2 years. A contested suit involving multiple appeals can take 3 to 5 years to reach Final Decree.

What if physical partition of land or building is impossible?

Under the Partition Act 1893, if a building or narrow plot cannot be physically divided without destroying its value, the court can order an auction sale among co-sharers or to the public, distributing money according to share ratios.

What is an Amicable Partition Deed (আপস বাটোয়ারা দলিল)?

If all co-sharers agree mutually, they can avoid court by drafting an Amicable Partition Deed, getting it registered at the Sub-Registry office, and mutating individual Khatians.

Property Registration Process in Bangladesh 2026: Complete Step-by-Step Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-12 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Registering property in Bangladesh is a mandatory legal step that protects your ownership rights. An unregistered sale deed is not admissible as evidence of ownership in court. This complete 2026 guide covers the entire property registration process — from preparing documents to paying stamp duty, registration at the Sub-Registrar's office, and completing mutation at the AC Land office.

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Registration Fee & Stamp Duty1% Registration Fee + 1.5% Stamp Duty on deed value
Local Government Tax & VAT2%–3% Local Govt Tax + 1.5%–4.5% VAT (varies by City/Pourosova/Union)
Source Tax (Gain Tax / TDS)1% to 8% depending on mouza classification under Income Tax Act 2023
Official Land & Mouza Portalsland.gov.bd, dlrms.land.gov.bd, and eporcha.gov.bd
📋 In This Article
  1. Why Property Registration Is Mandatory in Bangladesh
  2. Step 1: Due Diligence and Title Verification
  3. Step 2: Preparing the Sale Deed
  4. Step 3: Calculating and Paying Stamp Duty & Registration Fees
  5. Step 4: Registration at the Sub-Registrar's Office
  6. Step 5: Mutation (Namjari) at the AC Land Office
  7. Common Property Registration Frauds and How to Avoid Them

Why Property Registration Is Mandatory in Bangladesh

Under the Registration Act 1908 (Section 17), any transfer of immovable property worth more than BDT 100 must be registered. For practical purposes, all property transactions of value must be registered. The consequences of failing to register include:

  • An unregistered deed cannot be used as evidence of ownership in any court of law
  • The transfer of ownership is legally ineffective against third parties
  • The buyer is vulnerable to the seller transferring the same property to another buyer who registers first
  • Difficulty in obtaining bank loans or mortgages against unregistered property
  • Problems passing the property to heirs or future buyers

Registration creates a public record of ownership that protects buyers. Always complete registration promptly after purchase. For assistance with title verification and registration, consult our property law specialists.

Step 1: Due Diligence and Title Verification

Before registering a property, conduct thorough due diligence to ensure the seller has a clear title and the property is free from disputes or encumbrances:

  1. Obtain certified copies of khatians: CS, SA, and RS khatians from the District Record Room or AC Land office — these confirm the land's survey history and rightful owner
  2. Verify the deed chain: Obtain certified copies of all previous registered deeds for the property from the Sub-Registrar's office. Trace ownership back at least 25–30 years.
  3. Check for encumbrances: Search the Sub-Registrar's record for any mortgage (bandez), charge, or other encumbrance on the property
  4. Verify mutation records: Check whether the seller's name appears in the mutation (namjari) records at the AC Land office
  5. Inspect the physical property: Visit the property to verify boundaries match the documents and confirm there are no adverse possessors or encroachers
  6. Check for pending litigation: Ask the seller for a disclosure of any pending cases involving the property

Hiring a qualified land lawyer to conduct due diligence is strongly recommended before committing to a property purchase.

Step 2: Preparing the Sale Deed

The sale deed (dastabon) is the primary legal document that transfers ownership. It must be prepared carefully to include:

  • Full details of both parties: Buyer and seller names, father's names, addresses, and National ID numbers
  • Complete property description: CS/SA/RS dag numbers, khatian numbers, mouza name, upazila, district, total area, and boundaries (north, south, east, west)
  • Purchase price: The agreed consideration amount (must be accurate — under-declaring price is a common but illegal practice)
  • Previous deed references: Reference to the seller's own title deed(s)
  • Warranty clause: The seller's warranty that the property is free from encumbrances and they have full authority to sell
  • Witness details: At least two witnesses are required

The deed must be typed/printed on appropriate stamp paper. Your lawyer will draft the deed to ensure legal accuracy and compliance with current registration requirements. Errors in the deed description can cause serious problems in future transfers or legal proceedings.

Step 3: Calculating and Paying Stamp Duty & Registration Fees

Stamp duty and registration fees are significant costs in Bangladesh property transactions. As of 2026:

Stamp Duty: Calculated on the higher of the stated consideration price or the government-published upazila/district market value (mouza rate). Typical rates range from 3% to 4% of property value depending on the area.

Registration Fee: Typically 1% of the property value.

Local Government Tax: An additional local government tax (Dhaka City Corporation area typically 2%) applies in many urban areas.

Gain Tax (Capital Gains Tax): On the seller's side, a source tax on property transfer income applies. The rate depends on the seller's category (individual, company) and property location.

How to Pay:

  1. Stamp duty is paid by purchasing stamp paper (non-judicial) from authorized stamp vendors or through the e-Porcha/online payment system
  2. Registration fee is paid at the Sub-Registrar's office treasury or by bank draft
  3. Obtain payment receipts — these are essential for the registration appointment

Total transaction costs (stamp duty + registration + taxes) typically range from 7% to 12% of property value in Bangladesh. Budget for this significant additional cost when purchasing property.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Step 4: Registration at the Sub-Registrar's Office

Property registration in Bangladesh is completed at the Sub-Registrar's office having jurisdiction over the location of the property. Here is the process:

  1. Book an Appointment: Visit or contact the relevant Sub-Registrar's office to schedule a registration appointment. Some offices now accept applications online or through the District e-Service center.
  2. Attend with All Parties: Both buyer(s) and seller(s) must be physically present at the Sub-Registrar's office on the registration date, along with two witnesses.
  3. Submit Documents: Present the prepared deed, stamp papers, payment receipts, national ID copies of all parties, photographs, khatian copies, and previous deed copies.
  4. Sub-Registrar Verification: The Sub-Registrar examines documents, verifies identities, and records thumb impressions/signatures of all parties and witnesses.
  5. Registration Completion: The deed is officially registered and given a unique book number, volume number, and serial number in the register. This number is your registration reference.
  6. Collect Registered Deed: After registration (which may take a few days to process), collect the registered original deed from the Sub-Registrar's office. The deed is now an official government record.

Step 5: Mutation (Namjari) at the AC Land Office

After registration of the deed, the next critical step is mutation (namjari) — updating the government land records to reflect the new owner's name. Without mutation, the government records still show the previous owner, creating complications for future sales, inheritance, and tax payments.

Where to Apply: The AC Land (Assistant Commissioner Land) office at the Upazila level having jurisdiction over the property location.

Documents Required for Mutation:

  • Certified copy of the registered deed
  • CS/SA/RS khatian copies
  • National ID of the buyer
  • Application form (available at AC Land office)
  • Court fee stamp (nominal amount)
  • Land development tax payment receipt (up-to-date)

Process: After filing the mutation application, the AC Land office issues a notice to neighboring landholders. If no objection is received, the mutation is approved and the land records are updated. The entire process takes approximately 30–90 days.

Importance of Mutation: Mutated land records allow you to pay land development tax (khajna) in your own name and use the mutation certificate as additional evidence of ownership in any future legal proceedings.

Common Property Registration Frauds and How to Avoid Them

Property fraud is common in Bangladesh. Protect yourself by knowing these warning signs:

  • Selling land without title: The seller has no registered deed tracing back to a khatian — verify the complete deed chain before purchase
  • Forged Power of Attorney: A fraudster sells property using a fabricated power of attorney from the real owner — always verify POA authenticity directly with the original owner
  • Multiple sale of same property: The seller sells the same land to multiple buyers — check Sub-Registrar records for recent transactions involving the same property
  • Under-declared price: Parties declare a lower price to reduce stamp duty — this is illegal and creates risks if the transaction is ever challenged in court
  • Encumbered property: The seller has a mortgage or pending case on the property but conceals it — always conduct a thorough encumbrance search at the Sub-Registrar's office
  • Fake khatians: Fraudulent or altered khatian documents — verify all khatians against original records at the District Record Room

Working with an experienced land lawyer in Bangladesh for due diligence before any property purchase is the most effective protection against these frauds. Read our guide on handling land disputes in Bangladesh if you encounter problems after purchase.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does property registration take in Bangladesh?

The actual registration appointment at the Sub-Registrar's office typically takes a few hours. However, receiving the registered deed (after processing) can take 3–10 working days. The subsequent mutation process at the AC Land office takes approximately 30–90 days.

What is the stamp duty rate for property in Dhaka, Bangladesh?

Stamp duty in Dhaka varies by area and property type. For residential property in Dhaka City Corporation, total transfer costs (stamp duty, registration fee, local government tax, and capital gains tax) typically amount to 7–12% of the transaction value. Confirm current rates with a land lawyer as rates may be updated by the national budget.

Can I register property online in Bangladesh?

Bangladesh has been gradually introducing digital registration processes. Some districts offer online appointment booking and pre-submission of documents. However, physical attendance at the Sub-Registrar's office by both buyer and seller is still required for final deed execution and thumb impression verification.

What happens if I buy property that is not registered in my name?

Without registration, your title is not legally effective against third parties. An unregistered deed cannot be used as evidence of ownership in court. If the seller later sells the same property to another buyer who registers it, that buyer may have superior legal rights. Always register immediately after purchase.

Is mutation (namjari) the same as registration?

No. Registration at the Sub-Registrar's office creates the legal transfer of title between buyer and seller. Mutation (namjari) at the AC Land office updates the government land records to reflect the new owner's name. Both steps are necessary — registration establishes the legal transfer, while mutation updates the administrative record used for tax purposes.

Quashing False Criminal Cases in Bangladesh: Section 561A CrPC High Court Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-02 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In Bangladesh, the weaponization of the criminal justice system to settle civil scores, land disputes, commercial contract disagreements, and family inheritances is an alarming reality. Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs), business founders, and prominent citizens frequently find themselves slapped with fabricated First Information Reports (FIRs) or direct Magistrate Court complaints (C.R. Cases) alleging cheating (Section 420), criminal breach of trust (Section 406), extortion (Section 385), or fraudulent transactions. Facing harassment, arrest warrants, or airport look-out notices, the primary constitutional and statutory shield available in the higher judiciary is invoking the inherent power of the High Court Division under <strong>Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC)</strong>. This master legal guide explains when and how a criminal proceeding can be quashed, landmark Supreme Court jurisprudence, the difference between quashment, revision, and discharge, and practical steps to secure an immediate Stay of Proceedings.

1. The Inherent Power of the High Court: Statutory Scope of Section 561A

Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 does not confer any new legislative power upon the High Court Division; rather, it expressly preserves and recognizes the inherent judicial power that the apex court has always possessed to ensure that justice is not defeated by procedural manipulation. The section explicitly provides:

'Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent power of the High Court Division to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.'

This power is extraordinary and exercisable ex debito justitiae (from a debt of justice). It serves as a constitutional safeguard against malicious prosecution, rogue complainants, and subordinate magistrates who mechanically take cognizance without judicial application of mind.

2. Established Judicial Grounds for Quashing Criminal Proceedings

Through decades of settled jurisprudence established by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, Section 561A intervention is strictly guided by well-defined legal parameters. The High Court Division will quash a criminal proceeding under the following established circumstances:

  • No Offence Disclosed on the Face of the Record: Taking all allegations in the FIR or petition of complaint as true and accepted in their entirety, they do not prima facie constitute any criminal offence known to law.
  • Pure Civil Breach of Contract: Where the dispute arises out of a commercial sale, loan, lease, or land agreement where no dishonest intention or fraudulent inducement existed at the inception of the transaction.
  • Absence of Competent Sanction or Statutory Bar: Where the law requires prior government sanction (such as prosecutions under the Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2004 or against public servants under Section 197 CrPC) and no valid sanction was obtained before taking cognizance.
  • Blatant Abuse of Court Process: Where criminal prosecution is instituted maliciously with the ulterior motive of wreaking personal vengeance, extorting money, or forcing an out-of-court compromise in a pending civil land suit.
  • Frivolous and Vexatious Charges: Where uncontroverted documentary evidence demonstrates that the proceeding is absurd, contradictory, and legally unsustainable.

3. The 'Civil Dispute Dressed Up as Crime' Doctrine (406/420 IPC Analysis)

The single most common ground for invoking Section 561A in corporate and property disputes is challenging charges framed under Section 406 (Criminal Breach of Trust) and Section 420 (Cheating and Dishonestly Inducing Delivery of Property) of the Penal Code 1860.

The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly affirmed that a mere failure to perform a contract, non-payment of a commercial invoice, or delay in delivering property does not amount to criminal cheating unless it is proved that the accused had a fraudulent or dishonest intention right at the very inception of the transaction. If the transaction was initially genuine and subsequent commercial disagreements arose, the only remedy open to the complainant is filing a civil suit for damages or specific performance in a Civil Court, not instituting a criminal case to put police pressure on the defendant.

4. Comparative Distinction: Section 561A vs. Section 241A/265C vs. Revision

Navigating the procedural hierarchy of criminal remedies requires precision. The table below delineates the statutory differences between quashment, discharge, and criminal revision:

5. Procedural Roadmap: Filing a 561A Petition in the High Court Division

Filing a Section 561A criminal miscellaneous application demands meticulous procedural compliance:

  1. Obtaining Certified Copies: Counsel must secure certified copies of the initial FIR, Ejahar, C.R. petition of complaint, police investigation report (Charge Sheet or Final Report), and the order of cognizance passed by the Magistrate Court.
  2. Drafting the 561A Criminal Misc. Petition: The petition must set forth concise grounds demonstrating lack of mens rea, statutory violations, or malicious abuse of process, accompanied by an affidavit sworn before the High Court Affidavits Commissioner.
  3. Filing Before the High Court Section: The case is assigned a Criminal Miscellaneous (Criminal Misc.) Case number and listed before the competent High Court Motion Bench hearing Section 561A matters.
  4. Motion Hearing: Senior Supreme Court advocates present oral arguments during motion. If a prima facie case is established, the bench issues an interim stay of trial court proceedings and grants a Rule Nisi.
  5. Service of Rule Nisi: The petitioner serves formal court notices upon the State (through the Attorney General's Office) and the private complainant/opposite party.
  6. Final Hearing & Judgment: Upon hearing both sides, if the court finds the proceeding untenable, it makes the Rule absolute, permanently quashing the criminal case.
