Remittance, Tax and NBR Scrutiny When NRBs Buy Property in Bangladesh

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-10 · 14 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

For many Non-Resident Bangladeshis, buying land or a flat at home is a lifetime goal, but the money trail behind that purchase is what tax and financial-intelligence authorities look at first. This pillar guide explains why scrutiny arises at registration, why the banking channel matters, what documents to keep for each way of funding the purchase, and how tax residency and foreign-side reporting fit in. It is written by <a href="/advocate-md-shah-alam" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">Advocate Md. Shah Alam</a>, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, for Bangladeshis living in the UK, USA, UAE, Canada and elsewhere. For case-specific help call or WhatsApp the chamber on <a href="tel:01712655546" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">01712655546</a>.

Why a Property Purchase Draws Scrutiny at Registration

Buying land, a house or a flat is usually the largest single financial transaction a Non-Resident Bangladeshi (NRB) makes in Bangladesh. It is also one of the very few transactions that leaves a permanent, public, stamped record: the registered deed. Because the deed states the buyer, the seller, the price and the date, it gives tax and financial-intelligence authorities a ready-made starting point for a simple question: where did the money come from?

For a buyer living in Bangladesh, that question is normally answered by tax returns and bank statements. For an NRB, the answer sits partly in another country, in another currency and under another tax system. That is where problems begin. The money may have passed through a friend's account, a family member's account or an exchange house; it may have been sent in several small instalments; or it may have been carried in cash. None of these facts is automatically unlawful, but each one makes the paper trail harder to explain.

This guide is a deeper companion to our general pieces on sending money to Bangladesh legally and the NRB land-buying legal checklist. Its focus is narrow: how to arrange and document the funding of a property purchase so that, if anyone asks, you can answer calmly and completely.

A word on tone. Most NRBs who run into trouble did nothing dishonest. They simply did not keep records, or they used an informal route because it was convenient. The goal here is prevention: build the file before you pay, not after a notice arrives.

Who Can Ask Questions: NBR, BFIU, ACC and Your Bank

Several bodies can have an interest in a property purchase funded from abroad. Their roles are different, and it helps to understand each one at a high level.

  • National Board of Revenue (NBR). The tax authority. It is concerned with whether income has been declared, whether the right tax has been paid at the right time, and whether your assets are consistent with your declared income. Property purchases, bank deposits and other third-party data can be used to test that consistency.
  • Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU). Housed within Bangladesh Bank, BFIU receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports and similar information from banks and other reporting institutions, under the anti-money-laundering framework. Large, unusual or poorly explained inflows are the kind of pattern that can generate a report.
  • Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC). The ACC has powers to inquire into assets that appear disproportionate to known sources of income, usually in connection with allegations of corruption or abuse of position. It is far less likely to be relevant to an ordinary salaried NRB, but it can become relevant if a purchase is made in the name of, or with money linked to, a public official or politically exposed person.
  • Your own bank. Banks have their own customer due diligence duties. A bank that sees an unusually large credit may ask for the source of funds before it processes a payment order or releases money. That request is routine, not an accusation.
  • Registration offices. The sub-registrar checks the deed, the price against the applicable minimum value and the payment of government charges. Information from registration offices and banks can be shared with the tax authority under the rules in force at the time.

Two practical points follow. First, you will not always meet these bodies at the same moment. A purchase made today may be queried years later during a tax assessment, an audit or a dispute with a seller or relative. Second, the burden of explaining the funds usually falls on the person who owns the asset. Records are therefore your protection, and they should be kept for the long term.

Banking-Channel Remittance vs Hundi or Hawala

The single most important decision you make is how the money travels. In Bangladesh the lawful route is the formal banking channel: money sent through a bank, an authorised exchange house or a licensed mobile financial service arrangement that credits a bank account in Bangladesh with a traceable record.

Hundi (also called hawala) is an informal value-transfer system. Typically you hand local currency to an agent abroad, and a counterpart in Bangladesh pays taka to your relative or to the seller, with no money formally crossing the border. It can look cheaper and faster, and the rate offered is sometimes better. It is also, at a high level, unlawful in Bangladesh: dealing in foreign exchange outside authorised channels is prohibited under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947, and moving or concealing funds of unclear origin can attract the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012. Penalties under these laws can include imprisonment and forfeiture, and the offence can sit with the person who uses the route as well as the agent who runs it.

Beyond the legal risk, hundi has a practical cost that NRBs rarely consider until later: it produces no paper. There is no bank advice, no remittance record, no evidence that the taka in the seller's hands came from your foreign earnings. If a question is ever asked, you may have nothing to show. Money received informally also cannot be easily claimed as lawful inward remittance when you want to document the purchase, and it may complicate any later wish to repatriate sale proceeds.

A banking-channel remittance, by contrast, creates a chain of documents: your foreign bank debit, the transfer instruction, the intermediary or exchange-house record, and the credit advice in Bangladesh. Where your Bangladesh bank issues a remittance or encashment advice, ask for it and keep it. Whether a particular certificate is issued, and what it is called, depends on the bank and current practice, so ask your Authorised Dealer bank what proof it provides.

If you have already used an informal channel in the past, do not try to hide it or paper over it with invented documents. Get advice before you make any statement to an authority. Forged or back-dated documents turn a manageable explanation problem into a criminal one.

Bangladesh Bank Rules for Buying Property with Foreign Currency

Foreign-exchange control in Bangladesh is administered by Bangladesh Bank through its Foreign Exchange Regulation framework and circulars issued to Authorised Dealer (AD) banks. These rules are detailed and are updated from time to time. Always check the current Bangladesh Bank and Authorised Dealer rules before you move money. The points below are a high-level orientation, not a substitute for that check.

  • Use an Authorised Dealer bank. Inward remittances should reach your Bangladesh account through an AD bank or an approved channel so that the inflow is recorded as a foreign-exchange receipt.
  • Foreign-currency accounts. NRBs may be able to hold foreign-currency accounts in Bangladesh, commonly referred to as NFCD (Non-Resident Foreign Currency Deposit) accounts, and residents may hold RFCD (Resident Foreign Currency Deposit) accounts under defined conditions. Who is eligible, what can be credited and how the balance can be used for a property purchase are matters governed by current circulars. Do not assume that money in such an account can be paid directly to a seller; ask your bank to confirm in writing.
  • Purpose of remittance. Banks often ask you to state the purpose of an inward transfer. Choose the purpose that is truthful. A transfer labelled as family support but used to pay a land seller creates an inconsistency that you may later have to explain.
  • Payment to the seller. In most transactions, the price should be paid by an account-payee instrument or bank transfer that appears on the deed or in a payment schedule, not in cash. Cash payments of large amounts are hard to prove and invite questions.
  • Foreign nationals and dual citizens. The rules on who may buy property depend on citizenship status. If you hold a foreign passport, read our guide on foreigners and dual citizens owning property first, because your status affects both the permission to buy and the exchange-control treatment of the funds.

If a bank officer gives you an oral answer about what is permitted, ask for it in writing or by email on bank letterhead. Policies are interpreted differently across branches, and a written confirmation is much better evidence of good faith than a conversation.

Tax Residency and NRB Status for Income Tax

"NRB" is a practical label; for income tax what matters is tax residency, which is determined by the law for each income year, not by your passport or your intention. In general terms, residency under Bangladeshi tax law depends on the number of days you were physically present in Bangladesh in the income year, with a basic threshold of about half a year and additional tests that look at earlier years. The exact thresholds and wording are set out in the Income Tax Act 2023 and can be amended, so check the current text or ask a tax professional.

Why does this matter?

  • A non-resident is generally taxed in Bangladesh on income that arises, accrues or is received in Bangladesh, not on income earned and kept abroad.
  • A resident is generally taxed on worldwide income, which can include foreign salary, foreign rent and foreign investment returns, subject to any relief for foreign tax paid.

An NRB who returns to Bangladesh for long periods, for example to supervise construction, may unintentionally cross the threshold and become a tax resident for that year. Keep a simple travel log from your passport stamps, boarding passes and e-gate records. It is the cheapest piece of evidence you will ever create, and it is exactly what an assessing officer will ask for when deciding which category you fall in.

Residency also interacts with foreign tax law. You may be a tax resident of the UK, the USA, Canada, the UAE or another country for that country's purposes while being a non-resident for Bangladesh. The two tests are independent. Do not assume that being "non-resident" in one place answers the question in the other.

Finally, status can change from year to year. A year spent largely in Bangladesh may be treated differently from the years either side of it, so review your position annually rather than relying on a past conclusion.

Source Tax, Wealth Statement and Disclosure at Registration

When a deed is registered, several government charges and advance taxes are collected on the transaction. These typically include stamp duty, registration fee, local government tax and a tax collected at source in connection with the transfer, along with other charges depending on the location and type of property. The rates and the way they are calculated are set by law and are often changed by the Finance Act or by NBR orders each year, so we do not quote numbers here. Your deed writer or lawyer should obtain the current schedule from the sub-registry office, and our separate registry cost guide (in Bengali) explains the cost heads in more detail.

It is important to understand a point many buyers miss: paying source tax at registration does not, by itself, settle your tax position. It is generally an advance or adjustable amount, and it does not prove that the money used for the purchase was lawfully earned or properly declared. Those are separate questions.

Disclosure of the asset itself is dealt with through your income tax return. Where you are required to file a return and the law requires a statement of assets and liabilities (often called a wealth statement), a newly bought property should appear in it, with its acquisition cost and the source of funds. If you are tax-resident in Bangladesh, or if you have Bangladesh-source income that brings you into the return system, check whether the asset statement is required for you. The thresholds and forms are updated regularly, so verify them for the current assessment year.

If you are not required to file a Bangladesh return, you should still keep the full source-of-fund file described below. A person who is outside the return system may be asked to explain a purchase if a notice is issued or an enquiry is opened. For a related discussion of notices triggered after land transactions, see our Bengali article on tax notices after buying and selling land.

Finally, remember that the declared deed value, the actual price paid and the amount shown as remitted should tell the same story. Large gaps between them are a common reason for follow-up questions.

Documents to Keep for Each Funding Route

Your documentary needs depend on how the money reached the seller. The table below summarises the usual file for each route, the purpose it serves and the typical risk if the proof is missing. It is a guide, not an exhaustive list, and your bank or adviser may ask for more.

Funding routePurpose of the documentTypical proof to keepRisk if missing
Banking-channel remittanceShows the funds entered Bangladesh lawfully and are traceable to you.Foreign bank statement showing the debit; transfer instruction or receipt; Bangladesh bank credit advice; remittance or encashment advice if your bank issues one; your account statement showing the credit and onward payment.Cannot link your foreign earnings to the taka paid; weak answer to a source-of-fund query.
Wage-earner remittance (salary sent home)Connects the remittance to a real job and real income abroad.Employment contract or letter; payslips; foreign tax return or tax statement; work permit or residence permit; monthly bank statements showing salary and transfers.Remittance looks unexplained or out of proportion to declared income; inconsistent purpose statements.
Foreign-currency account (NFCD/RFCD)Shows the balance came from lawful foreign-currency sources and was used within the account rules.Account opening documents; deposit records and their origin; bank written confirmation that the balance may be used for the purchase; statements showing conversion and payment.Bank refuses the payment or the use of funds is questioned; origin of deposits cannot be shown.
Gift from relativesShows a genuine gift and that the donor had lawful funds.Signed gift letter naming donor, recipient and amount; donor identity and relationship proof; donor bank statement; evidence of donor source of funds; proof of transfer through a banking channel; tax treatment note from an adviser.Treated as unexplained money; donor funds themselves may be questioned; possible gift or tax issues on either side.
Sale of a foreign assetShows the funds came from a documented disposal abroad.Sale contract; completion statement or closing statement; evidence of title and prior purchase; foreign tax filing for the gain, if any; bank statement showing proceeds received; transfer records to Bangladesh.Source looks undocumented; foreign tax may be unpaid; difficulty proving the amount and timing.
Mixed funding (for example, savings plus a family loan)Shows each part separately.A reconciliation sheet listing each amount, its source and its proof; loan agreement and repayment plan; matching bank records.One weak part can contaminate the whole file; the totals do not match the price.

Whatever the route, keep both the original documents and clean scanned copies. If a document is in a foreign language, keep a certified translation. Documents from abroad that you intend to use formally in Bangladesh may require attestation or legalisation, so ask early.

Step-by-Step Documentation Checklist

Use this sequence from the moment you decide to buy. It is designed so that each payment can be traced from your foreign income to the seller's receipt.

  1. Decide your status. Confirm whether you are a Bangladeshi citizen, a dual citizen or a foreign national, and keep proof such as passport, NVR endorsement or NID. This affects what you may buy and how funds are treated.
  2. Open or confirm the right bank account. Speak to an Authorised Dealer bank branch about the account type, and ask in writing what the bank needs for inward funds meant for a property purchase.
  3. Build a source-of-fund file before you send anything. Gather employment proof, payslips, foreign tax returns, savings statements and any sale or gift documents, matched to the amounts you plan to send.
  4. Send money only through banking channels. Avoid cash, third-party accounts and informal agents. State the true purpose of each transfer.
  5. Keep every transfer document. Retain the foreign debit record, transfer receipt and Bangladesh credit advice for each instalment, and note the exchange rate used.
  6. Verify the property and seller. Do title checks, khatian and mutation history and any pending dispute before paying. Our guide on buying land from abroad sets out the legal checks.
  7. Pay the seller by traceable means. Use account-payee cheque or bank transfer, record each payment, and make sure the paid amount matches the deed and the payment receipts.
  8. Pay government charges through the official channel. Keep the challans, payment orders and receipts for the stamp duty, registration fee and taxes collected at registration.
  9. Register the deed and collect the certified copy. Check the price, party details and schedule on the deed before leaving the office.
  10. Complete mutation. Apply for mutation so the record shows your name. See land mutation (namjari) from abroad.
  11. Update tax records. Include the asset in any return or asset statement that applies to you in Bangladesh, and discuss your foreign-side reporting with a tax professional in the country where you are resident.
  12. Archive the file. Create one folder, physical and digital, with an index. Keep it for as long as you own the property and for a long period after any sale, since tax questions can arise years later.

Double Taxation Treaties and Foreign-Side Reporting

Bangladesh has entered into double taxation avoidance agreements (DTAs) with a number of countries. A treaty may allocate taxing rights between the two states, provide a method for relief or credit for tax paid in the other country, and set out rules for resolving residency conflicts. Whether a treaty exists between Bangladesh and your country of residence, and what it says about the type of income you have, must be checked individually. A treaty never removes the duty to file or to disclose; it only reduces the risk of being taxed twice on the same income.

Equally important is reporting in the country where you live. Many countries require residents and citizens to report foreign assets and foreign accounts, even where no tax is due. Examples that NRBs commonly meet include:

  • United States: reporting of foreign financial accounts (FBAR) and foreign financial assets under FATCA rules, which may be relevant if you are a US person.
  • United Kingdom: disclosure of overseas income and gains through the self-assessment system administered by HMRC, and rules on residence and domicile or its replacement concepts.
  • Canada, Australia, the Gulf states and others: each has its own regime on foreign income, foreign property and bank accounts.

Failure to report on the foreign side can be penalised heavily, and information is increasingly exchanged between tax authorities under international reporting standards. A purchase that is perfectly tidy in Bangladesh can still create a problem abroad if it is never mentioned. We are Bangladesh-law advisers and do not advise on foreign tax. Please engage a qualified tax professional in your country of residence, and ask them to coordinate with a Bangladeshi adviser so that the two filings are consistent in amounts, dates and exchange rates.

Repatriating Sale Proceeds: A High-Level View

Many NRBs ask at the time of buying whether they can later take the money back out. The honest answer is that it depends on your status, on how the purchase was funded and on the Bangladesh Bank rules in force at the time of sale. In general, outward remittance of sale proceeds is controlled, and the ability to repatriate is far stronger when you can prove two things: that the original purchase was funded by lawful inward remittance, and that the relevant taxes were paid on both the purchase and the sale.

That is one more reason to use the banking channel. An NRB whose purchase was funded through documented inward remittance is in a much better position to apply for approval to remit proceeds than one whose money arrived informally and cannot be traced. Any approval, conditions and limits are matters for Bangladesh Bank and your Authorised Dealer bank, so check the current requirements and, if the sum is large, take advice before the sale rather than after.

Sale itself carries tax consequences: the seller's side may involve tax at the time of transfer and capital gain or other income tax rules. Those depend on the holding period, the type of asset and the current law. Plan the sale paperwork with the same discipline as the purchase: sale deed, payment records, tax payment proof and a clear trail from the buyer's money to your account.

Common Mistakes NRBs Make

  • Using hundi because it is convenient. The saving is small compared with the legal exposure and the loss of documentary proof.
  • Sending money through a relative's account without a record. If the relative then pays the seller, your link to the funds depends on informal understanding. Use a written gift or authority letter and keep bank evidence.
  • Structuring payments into small amounts to avoid attention. Splitting transfers to stay under a notional limit can itself look suspicious and may attract reports.
  • Understating the deed value. Declaring a lower price to reduce charges creates a gap between the deed and the money trail, with consequences for both the buyer and the seller. The deed value must also respect the applicable minimum value.
  • Paying part in cash. Cash cannot be traced. If a seller insists on cash, treat it as a warning sign.
  • Giving a false or vague purpose to the bank. A remittance labelled with an untrue purpose will not match later documents.
  • Ignoring tax residency. Spending long periods in Bangladesh without tracking days may change your status for the year.
  • Forgetting the foreign-side filing. A Bangladesh purchase may need disclosure abroad.
  • Relying on a power of attorney without safeguards. If an agent handles payments and registration for you, make sure every payment still passes through your documented channel.
  • Throwing records away. Tax questions can be raised long after the purchase. Keep records for the life of the asset.
  • Creating documents after the fact. Back-dated gift letters or invented receipts can lead to criminal liability for forgery. If something is missing, obtain a genuine replacement from the bank or counterparty.

What to Do If You Receive a Notice or Query

If a tax office, bank or other authority sends you a notice asking about the source of funds for a property purchase, do not panic and do not ignore it. A notice is a request for information; it is not a finding that you did anything wrong.

  1. Read the notice carefully. Note the issuing office, the legal provision cited, the property or transaction mentioned and the deadline.
  2. Do not miss the deadline. If you need more time, ask for it in writing before the date passes.
  3. Collect your file. Use the table and checklist above to assemble remittance advices, statements and supporting documents.
  4. Prepare a short chronology. One page showing dates, amounts, sources and payments is more persuasive than a pile of papers.
  5. Respond in writing and keep proof of delivery. Do not give oral assurances you cannot support with documents.
  6. Take advice before admitting anything. A lawyer and tax adviser can help you frame the response and, where necessary, correct a past position properly.

If your difficulty is a land dispute, a missing record or a question about mutation rather than tax, you may also want to read the broader material in our NRB legal help hub.

Disclaimer and Next Steps

Cross-border purchases combine exchange-control law, anti-money-laundering rules, income tax law, registration law and foreign tax law. No single article can cover your exact facts. The most protective steps are consistent and simple: use the banking channel, tell the truth about the purpose and amount, keep a complete source-of-fund file, pay the government charges officially, and report on both sides of the border.

For more on lawful transfers, see our guide to sending money to Bangladesh legally, and for the overall NRB library visit the NRB legal help hub.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms, tax rates and procedures change, often with each annual Finance Act or Bangladesh Bank circular; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate and tax professional before acting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does the tax office ask about my source of funds when I buy property?

A registered deed is a permanent record of a high-value transaction. Tax authorities use such records to check whether declared income can reasonably explain an asset. For an NRB, the explanation usually sits partly abroad, so documentary proof of the foreign income and the remittance trail matters.

Is hundi or hawala illegal in Bangladesh?

At a high level, yes. Dealing in foreign exchange outside authorised channels is prohibited under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947, and moving funds of unclear origin can attract the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012. Use banks and authorised exchange houses instead.

What proof should I keep for a banking-channel remittance?

Keep your foreign bank debit record, the transfer receipt, the Bangladesh bank credit advice, any remittance or encashment advice your bank issues, and statements showing the onward payment to the seller. Ask your Authorised Dealer bank which documents it provides.

Can I use money in a foreign-currency (NFCD or RFCD) account to buy property?

It may be possible, but it depends on the current Bangladesh Bank and Authorised Dealer rules and on your status. Ask your bank to confirm in writing how the balance may be used before you proceed.

Can a relative gift me the money for a property purchase?

A gift can be legitimate, but it needs a signed gift letter, proof of relationship, evidence of the donor's lawful source of funds and a banking-channel transfer. There may also be tax consequences on either side, so take advice.

Does paying tax at registration mean my source of funds is accepted?

No. Source tax and other charges collected at registration are separate from the question of whether the money used was lawfully earned and properly declared. Keep your source-of-fund file regardless.

How is an NRB treated for income tax in Bangladesh?

It depends on tax residency, which is generally determined by days of physical presence in the income year under the current law, not by passport. A non-resident is generally taxed on Bangladesh-source income. Check the current Income Tax Act 2023 thresholds or consult a tax professional.

Do I need to report my Bangladesh property in the country where I live?

Possibly. Many countries require residents to report foreign assets or income, and some exchange information with other tax authorities. Speak to a qualified tax professional in your country of residence.

Can I take the sale proceeds of my Bangladesh property back abroad?

Outward remittance of sale proceeds is controlled and depends on your status, how the purchase was funded and current Bangladesh Bank rules. Documented inward remittance and proof of tax payments make approval easier. Check the current requirements before selling.

Remote Land Due Diligence in Bangladesh: How Expats in USA, UK & Canada Can Verify Khatians & Namjari Online (2026)

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-26 · 19 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Hard-earned foreign remittances earned through years of labor by Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia are frequently targeted by predatory housing societies, rogue real estate developers, and unscrupulous relatives selling disputed, encumbered, or non-existent land. In Bangladesh's real estate ecosystem, physical possession does NOT guarantee legal title. Fraudulent sellers routinely manufacture counterfeit deeds (ভুয়া দলিল), forge mutation slips, sell mortgaged plots, or sell the same parcel to multiple overseas buyers. Thanks to Bangladesh's modernized digital land governance (land.gov.bd, e-Porcha, and DLRS map portals), overseas investors can now conduct rigorous preliminary due diligence from London, New York, or Toronto. However, digital checks cover only half the risk; sealing an investment demands physical Sub-Registry Volume Book searches, Non-Encumbrance Certificate (NEC) audits, and a formal written **Title Search & Legal Opinion Report (স্বত্ব মতামত প্রতিবেদন)** by an enrolled Supreme Court advocate. This exhaustive guide provides the complete legal vetting blueprint for overseas property investors.

  11. 11. Real-Life Case Study: Saving a UK Expat BDT 3.5 Crore from a Forged Plot Deal
  12. 12. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1. The Core Peril: Why Physical Possession Does Not Mean Legal Title in Bangladesh

In Western real estate markets (USA, UK, Canada), title guarantees and title insurance protect buyers from hidden encumbrances or defective registries. In Bangladesh, the doctrine of Caveat Emptor (ক্রেতা সাবধান / Buyer Beware) applies with absolute rigor.

A seller can physically stand on a plot in Dhaka or Sylhet, show you boundary walls, and introduce local caretakers, while possessing zero marketable title in law. Common fraudulent traps targeting expatriates include:

  • Secret Bank Mortgages: The seller deposited the original title deeds with a commercial bank to secure a BDT 5 Crore loan, then used a 'lost deed' police GD to obtain a certified copy and sell the land to an unsuspecting expat.
  • Double Sale (একাধিক বিক্রয়): The seller executed a registered deed to Buyer A, and before Buyer A completed mutation, hurriedly sold the identical Dag/plot to an overseas Buyer B.
  • Un-Partitioned Joint Land: Selling a specific road-facing plot that legally belongs to an undivided ancestral estate where other co-sharers have not partitioned.
  • Unapproved Developer Projects: Private housing companies carving up low-lying flood retention zones without RAJUK or DOE clearance.

2. The 25-Year Unbroken Chain of Title (বায়া দলিল / Baya Dalil) Rule

Under established legal standards practiced by banks and the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, an unassailable title search requires tracing ownership back a minimum of twenty-five (25) years through the chain of previous title deeds (বায়া দলিল / Baya Dalil):

  1. Root of Title: Tracing the land back to the recorded tenant (রায়ত) in the State Acquisition (SA) or Cadastral Survey (CS) Khatian.
  2. Every Intervening Transfer: Inspecting every single Sale Deed (সাফ কবলা), Gift Deed (হেবা), Partition Deed (বন্টননামা), or Succession Inheritance occurring over the last 25 years.
  3. Mathematical Acreage Consistency: Ensuring that the acreage transferred in each deed exactly matches the acreage owned. If an ancestor owned 20 decimals but historical deeds show transfers totaling 30 decimals, the excess 10 decimals are completely void.
  4. Absence of Ownership Gaps: Any missing link in the chain creates a cloud on title, leaving the purchaser vulnerable to future ejectment suits.

3. Four Generations of Land Surveys: CS, SA, RS, and City Survey / BS Explained

Understanding the historical progression of land revenue surveys is mandatory for every serious real estate investor:

  • CS (Cadastral Survey 1888–1940): The foundational British-era survey. Highly accurate, accompanied by hand-drawn mouza maps. Regarded in courts as the primary baseline of title.
  • SA (State Acquisition Survey 1956): Prepared following the abolition of the Zamindari system under the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. Crucial for establishing who held lawful tenancy after 1950.
  • RS (Revisional Survey 1965–1990): The revisional survey conducted across Bangladesh to correct SA errors and reflect modern possession. Holds immense evidentiary weight in civil courts.
  • City Survey / BS (Bangladesh Survey 1990–Present): The ongoing modern survey. In Dhaka, it is known as City Survey (ঢাকা মহানগরি জরিপ). While modern, City Survey records frequently contain bureaucratic errors; a City Survey Khatian alone does NOT confer title unless supported by RS and SA title deeds.

4. Step-by-Step Remote Verification of Digital Khatians (eporcha.gov.bd)

The Ministry of Land's official portal eporcha.gov.bd allows expats to inspect and order certified copies of land survey records online from anywhere in the world:

  1. Access Portal: Visit eporcha.gov.bd or land.gov.bd.
  2. Geographical Navigation: Select Division (বিভাগ), District (জেলা), Upazila/Thana, and Mouza (মৌজা with JL Number).
  3. Survey Selection: Choose the Khatian type: CS, SA, RS, or BS/City Survey.
  4. Search Query: Search by Khatian number, Dag (Plot) number, or Owner's name (মালিকের নাম).
  5. Data Cross-Check: Verify: (a) Does the seller's ancestor appear as the recorded tenant? (b) Does the recorded land share (অংশ) equal the land being sold? (c) Are there adverse remarks (মন্তব্য কলাম) indicating acquisition, vested property, or government mortgage?
  6. Certified Copy Application: Submit an online application for an official Certified Copy (সার্টিফাইড কপি) bearing digital QR-code verification, delivered locally to your advocate.

5. How to Detect Forged e-Namjari Mutations & Counterfeit DCR Receipts

One of the most dangerous frauds encountered by expatriates is the production of counterfeit manual mutation slips by sellers:

The Absolute Rule: Since 2021, manual paper mutation (ম্যানুয়াল নামজারি) has been completely abolished across Bangladesh. ANY MUTATION THAT DOES NOT EXIST ON THE CENTRAL SERVER (mutation.land.gov.bd) IS FORGED AND VOID.

Digital Verification Protocol:

  • Visit mutation.land.gov.bd. Navigate to 'Application Tracking' (আবেদন ট্র্যাকিং).
  • Input Division, District, Upazila, Application Number, and NID.
  • A genuine mutation displays the complete digital approval workflow, signed orders of the Assistant Commissioner (Land), and a valid Duplicate Carbon Receipt (DCR) showing BDT 1,150 paid into the government treasury.
  • Scan the QR code on the Mutation Khatian. It must redirect directly to the official government server displaying the identical plot and owner particulars.

6. Digital Land Development Tax Verification (ldtax.gov.bd)

Never purchase property where Land Development Tax (ভূমি উন্নয়ন কর) is delinquent or unpaid:

  1. Access ldtax.gov.bd.
  2. Enter the owner's Holding Number, Mouza, and Khatian Number.
  3. A genuine tax profile displays the updated digitized Holding (ডিজিটাল হোল্ডিং), owner's name, and historical payment ledger.
  4. Ensure taxes are cleared up to the current fiscal year. If an owner claims they have paid tax but produces old paper Dakhilas without an online record, the holding is un-digitized or disputed.

7. The Vital Sub-Registry Physical Audit: Volume Books & NEC Form 41

While online checks verify revenue records, they cannot detect secret bank mortgages or prior sales. A qualified advocate must conduct physical searches at the Sub-Registry Office:

A. Volume Book Inspection (বালাম বই তল্লাশি)

The advocate inspects the physical Volume Book where registered deeds are hand-bound and archived. The advocate matches the deed serial, registration date, stamp duty value, and vendor/vendee signatures and thumbprints against the seller's photocopy. If the Volume Book shows a different deed on that page, the seller's deed is an outright counterfeit.

B. Non-Encumbrance Certificate (NEC - দায়মুক্ত সনদ)

Under Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908 and Form 41 of the Registration Rules, your advocate files an application for a formal 12 to 25-year Search and Non-Encumbrance Certificate:

  • The Sub-Registrar conducts a comprehensive search across all transaction registers for that specific Mouza, Khatian, and Dag.
  • If no prior sales, mortgages, or court attachments exist, the Sub-Registrar issues an official seal-embossed Non-Encumbrance Certificate (Form 41) certifying that the property is unencumbered.

8. Vetting Developers & Housing Societies (RAJUK, CDA, RDA Clearances)

If purchasing an apartment or housing plot in Dhaka from a real estate developer, verify the following mandatory regulatory clearances:

  • REHAB Membership: Verify that the developer is an enrolled member of the Real Estate & Housing Association of Bangladesh.
  • RAJUK / Development Authority Project Approval: Under the Private Residential Land Development Rules 2004, no developer can advertise or sell plots without formal layout approval from RAJUK (Dhaka), CDA (Chattogram), or RDA (Rajshahi).
  • Building Plan Sanction (অনুমোদিত নকশা): Verify the approved architectural drawing, building height, floor area ratio (FAR), and fire/civil aviation NOCs.
  • Landowner-Developer Power of Attorney: If buying from a developer developing land on joint-venture, verify the registered Irrevocable Power of Attorney executed by the landowner in favor of the developer. Ensure the specific flat being purchased falls within the developer's allocated share.

9. Red-Flag Categories: Khas, Vested Property, Waqf, and LA Cases

Immediately abort the transaction if your due diligence reveals any of the following fatal encumbrances:

  • Government Khas Land (সরকারি খাস জমি): Land owned exclusively by the government under Section 86 of the SAT Act 1950. Any private deed for Khas land is void ab initio.
  • Vested Property 'Ka' Schedule: Encumbered under Vested Property legislation. Cannot be sold without a formal Tribunal release decree.
  • Waqf / Debottar Religious Property: Islamic Waqf or Hindu Debottar land cannot be alienated without prior sanction from the Waqf Administrator or District Judge.
  • Land Acquisition (L.A. Case - অধিগ্রহণ): Check whether the Deputy Commissioner's Land Acquisition Branch has issued gazette notifications under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Act 2017 for roads, metro rail, or public infrastructure.
  • Wetland / Flood Retention Zone: Land classified as water-body or flood retention zone under the Natural Water Reservoir Conservation Act 2000 cannot be land-filled or developed.

10. Standard Advocate Title Search & Legal Opinion Report Structure

Before remitting any earnest money from abroad, demand a formal written Legal Search Report & Title Opinion (স্বত্ব মতামত প্রতিবেদন) signed by an enrolled advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. The report must contain:

  1. Executive Summary: Unambiguous opinion stating whether the title is Marketable, Free from Encumbrance, and Safe for Purchase.
  2. Chain of Title Analysis: Chronological table linking CS & SA Khatians to present ownership deeds.
  3. Survey & Mutation Verification: Analysis of RS, City Survey, e-Namjari, DCR, and online tax Dakhilas.
  4. Sub-Registry Search Findings: Report on Volume Book inspection and NEC Form 41 status.
  5. Statutory Clearances: Verification of RAJUK/CDA, environmental, and non-acquisition status.
  6. Specific Cautions & Recommendations: Mandatory conditions precedent to be inserted in the contract for sale (বায়নাপত্র).

11. Real-Life Case Study: Saving a UK Expat BDT 3.5 Crore from a Forged Plot Deal

Background: Mr. Shafiqul Alam, a businessman in Manchester, UK, negotiated to purchase a prime 5-katha commercial plot in Uttara Sector 14, Dhaka for BDT 3.5 Crore. The seller produced impressive manual deeds, an RS Porcha in his name, and a recent tax receipt, demanding a BDT 50 Lakh non-refundable booking advance.

Chamber Due Diligence Uncovered:

  1. Our advocate conducted an e-Porcha search, discovering that the seller's RS Porcha was counterfeit; the actual recorded tenant in government archives was the Ministry of Housing and Public Works (Khas land).
  2. A physical Volume Book search at the Sub-Registry revealed that the seller's 1994 registered deed number actually corresponded to a completely different plot in Savar.
  3. The seller was operating under a forged manual mutation slip that had zero presence on mutation.land.gov.bd.
  4. We halted the wire transfer immediately, saving Mr. Shafiqul BDT 3.5 Crore ($300,000 USD) and referred the fraud syndicate to the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) for prosecution under the Land Crime Prevention and Redress Act 2023.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I verify land ownership in Bangladesh online without hiring a lawyer?

You can perform preliminary checks on eporcha.gov.bd and mutation.land.gov.bd, but online databases do not show secret bank mortgages or prior un-mutated sales. A physical Sub-Registry Volume Book search and NEC by an advocate are indispensable.

What is the difference between a Khatian and a Dalil in Bangladesh?

A Dalil (Deed) is the legal transfer contract executed between parties at the Sub-Registry. A Khatian (Record of Rights / Porcha) is the official government land revenue survey record reflecting title, plot boundaries, and tax assessment.

How do I know if a property is mortgaged to a commercial bank in Bangladesh?

An advocate must conduct a Non-Encumbrance Certificate (NEC Form 41) search at the Sub-Registry Office and cross-verify through bank panel lawyers with Credit Information Bureau (CIB) records.

What is a Baya Dalil (বায়া দলিল)?

A Baya Dalil (previous deed / chain deed) is any historical registered transfer deed through which the current seller or their predecessor acquired title. A complete chain spanning 25 years is required to prove unclouded title.

Can a housing developer sell a plot without RAJUK approval in Dhaka?

No. Under the Private Residential Land Development Rules 2004, selling or advertising unapproved housing plots is illegal and punishable with criminal imprisonment and demolition.

How much does a professional Title Search and Legal Opinion report cost?

Depending on the complexity of the chain of title, number of previous deeds, and registry searches, advocate fees typically range from BDT 25,000 to BDT 60,000 ($250–$600 USD).

What is a DCR receipt in land mutation?

DCR (Duplicate Carbon Receipt) is the official government treasury receipt issued upon paying the BDT 1,150 mutation fee, proving that the mutation was processed lawfully through the Assistant Commissioner (Land) office.

Can I buy land in Bangladesh if the seller has not completed e-Namjari?

Never. Under Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908, Sub-Registrars are legally barred from registering a sale deed unless the seller's name is mutated in the government e-Namjari database with an up-to-date Khatian.

Road Accident Death and Injury Compensation in Bangladesh: Trust Fund Claims, Civil Damages, and Criminal Prosecution

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-14 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

A split-second act of reckless driving on a Bangladeshi highway or urban thoroughfare can instantly destroy a family's future. When a sole earning parent is killed or a child suffers permanent catastrophic injury, transport owners and syndicates routinely vanish, leaving grieving families crushed under funeral expenses and intensive care bills.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

The Devastation of Road Accidents and Legal Rights in Bangladesh

Imagine your spouse, parent, or child setting off on a routine inter-district bus journey or daily commute in Dhaka, only for your family to receive a devastating phone call from a highway police outpost. A speeding long-haul bus or overloaded heavy truck operating without a valid fitness certificate lost control, resulting in a fatal collision. In an instant, the family's sole economic breadwinner is gone, leaving dependents overwhelmed by grief and looming financial catastrophe.

Historically in Bangladesh, victims of road crashes and their families were left entirely abandoned. Transport owners and powerful transport worker federations routinely protected reckless drivers, while insurance companies used cumbersome procedures to evade third-party liability claims under the outdated Motor Vehicles Ordinance 1983.

However, modern statutory enactments have transformed this legal terrain. With the operationalization of the Road Transport Act 2018 and the landmark compensation precedents established by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, victims possess powerful, enforceable legal rights to demand immediate statutory financial relief, substantial tort damages, and stringent criminal accountability.

Statutory Framework: Road Transport Act 2018 Overview

The enactment of the Road Transport Act 2018 (Act No. 47 of 2018) replaced the colonial-era Motor Vehicles Ordinance 1983, establishing a rigorous legal framework for road safety, vehicle fitness, driver accountability, and victim rehabilitation.

Crucially, the Act created two distinct legal mechanisms for accident victims:

  • Statutory Financial Assistance Fund (Section 53): An institutionalized, permanent compensation fund established under the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA) to disburse immediate financial assistance to accident victims and their families without requiring lengthy courtroom trials.
  • Stringent Criminal Penalties (Sections 66, 84, 98, and 105): Substantially heightened criminal sanctions for reckless driving, driving without valid licenses, operating unfit vehicles, and causing death or grievous hurt.

By decoupling basic financial compensation from the outcome of criminal trials, the law ensures that impoverished families do not have to wait a decade for criminal convictions before receiving emergency financial aid.

The Financial Assistance Fund: Statutory Compensation Rates

Under Section 53 of the Road Transport Act 2018, read with the Road Transport Rules 2022, the government established the Financial Assistance Fund (Aarthik Shohayota Tohobil), managed by an independent Board of Trustees headquartered at the BRTA.

The rules establish guaranteed statutory compensation ceilings for road accident casualties:

  • Fatal Accidents (Death): A mandatory lump-sum payment of BDT 5,00,000 (Five Lakh Taka) payable directly to the legal heirs and dependents of the deceased victim.
  • Permanent Disability or Loss of Limb: A lump-sum payment of BDT 3,00,000 (Three Lakh Taka) for victims suffering permanent paralysis, amputation of limbs, loss of eyesight, or traumatic brain injury.
  • Grievous Physical Injury: Up to BDT 1,00,000 (One Lakh Taka) for major surgical treatments, prolonged hospitalization, and medical rehabilitation.

These statutory payments are non-repayable grants funded through mandatory annual contributions paid by commercial motor vehicle owners during vehicle registration and fitness renewals.

Step-by-Step Claim Procedure Before the Trustee Board

Securing compensation from the Financial Assistance Fund requires adhering to a strict administrative procedure established under the Road Transport Rules 2022:

  1. Strict 30-Day Limitation Window: Under Rule 151, the victim or their legal heirs must submit their formal compensation application to the Chairman of the Trustee Board (BRTA) within 30 days of the accident. If delayed due to medical hospitalization, an application for extension with medical certificates must be filed.
  2. Prescribed Application Form: The claim must be submitted on Form-39, specifying accident details, vehicle registration numbers, police station FIR numbers, hospital admission records, and applicant bank details.
  3. Inquiry by Inquiry Committee: The Trustee Board forwards the claim to a local inquiry committee comprising the Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) or Executive Magistrate, the local police officer-in-charge (OC), and a government medical officer.
  4. Verification and Recommendation: The committee inspects the accident scene, verifies the police report, and submits an assessment report to the Trustee Board within 30 days.
  5. Disbursement via Bank Transfer: Upon approval, the Trustee Board issues an account-payee cheque or direct electronic fund transfer (BEFTN) to the victim or legal heirs within 30 days of receiving the inquiry report.

Mandatory Documents & Evidence Gathering Checklist

A compensation claim will be summarily rejected if the supporting evidentiary portfolio is incomplete. Your legal team must systematically secure the following documents:

  • Police Documentation: A certified copy of the Thana FIR, General Diary (GD) entry, or Highway Police seizure list confirming the date, time, location, and involved vehicle registration numbers.
  • Medical Evidence: Original hospital discharge certificates, surgical notes, medication receipts, and a permanent disability certificate issued by a government Medical Board or Civil Surgeon.
  • Post-Mortem & Death Certificate: In fatal cases, the official autopsy report from a government medical college hospital and the municipal or Union Parishad death certificate.
  • Proof of Heirship: An authentic Succession Certificate from the civil court or Warishan Sanad (Heirship Certificate) issued by the local Ward Councilor or Union Parishad Chairman, accompanied by NID cards of all legal heirs.

Civil Lawsuits for Substantial Tort Damages: Fatal Accidents Act

While BDT 5 Lakh from the BRTA Trust Fund provides immediate emergency assistance, it is utterly inadequate to compensate for the loss of a young parent or professional whose lifetime earnings would have exceeded crores of taka. Fortunately, claiming Trust Fund aid does not forfeit your right to pursue substantial civil damages.

Under the Fatal Accidents Act 1855 and common-law tort principles, surviving dependents can institute a comprehensive civil damage suit in the Joint District Judge Court against the transport company, the bus owner, and the driver. In the historic, precedent-setting judgment of Catherine Masud vs. Md. Kashed Miah and Others (2017), the High Court Division awarded over BDT 4.61 Crore in compensation to the family of renowned filmmaker Tareque Masud, establishing landmark legal rules:

  1. Strict Vicarious Liability: Transport companies are financially responsible for the negligent and reckless driving of their employed drivers.
  2. Calculation of Lifetime Loss: Courts calculate compensation based on the deceased's monthly income, future career promotions, dependency multiplier, and personal living expenditures.
  3. Joint and Several Decrees: Decrees can be executed directly against the bank accounts, commercial vehicle fleets, and immovable properties of the transport owners.

Criminal Prosecution Against Reckless Drivers and Owners

Simultaneously with financial claims, criminal accountability must be pursued to prevent the offending driver and transport owner from escaping justice:

  • Section 105 Road Transport Act 2018: Any person causing death or grievous injury through reckless or negligent driving shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to 5 years, or with a substantial fine, or with both. This offense is strictly non-bailable.
  • Section 98 RTA 2018 (Dangerous Driving): Penalizes speeding, dangerous overtaking, and driving in contravention of road signals with up to 3 years imprisonment.
  • Owner Liability (Sections 66 & 77): Vehicle owners who knowingly assign an unfit vehicle, an unlicensed driver, or permit overloaded passenger transit can be prosecuted as criminal co-accused.
  • Vehicle Seizure and Custody: The offending vehicle is impounded by the police under a formal seizure list (Jobdo-talika) and cannot be released without court permission, providing immense leverage during settlement negotiations.

Comparison Table: Trust Fund vs. Civil Tort Suit vs. Criminal Case

Victims must coordinate all three legal tracks to achieve maximum financial restitution and criminal justice:

Legal TrackBRTA Trust Fund ClaimCivil Tort Suit (Fatal Accidents Act)Criminal Case (Section 105 RTA)

Maximum Financial CapBDT 5 Lakh for death; BDT 3 Lakh for disability.No statutory limit; crores of taka based on earnings.Criminal fines deposited primarily to the state.
Statutory DeadlineStrictly within 30 days of the accident date.Within 1 year under Fatal Accidents Act 1855.No strict limit, but immediate FIR strongly recommended.
Time to ResolutionTypically 2 to 4 months.Typically 2 to 5 years through trial.Typically 1 to 3 years through police charge sheet.

Illustrative Scenario: Securing Trust Fund and Civil Compensation

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): Mahbub, a 36-year-old marketing manager and father of two young children, was traveling from Cumilla to Dhaka on the highway when a reckless inter-district passenger bus, racing another vehicle, slammed head-on into his microbus. Mahbub was killed instantly, while two other passengers suffered severe spinal fractures. The bus driver fled the scene, but highway police impounded the bus.

Devastated and facing immediate mortgage and school fee defaults, Mahbub's widow consulted a specialized accident litigation advocate within two weeks of the tragedy. Her legal counsel took swift, synchronized action:

First, within 25 days of the crash, a complete Form-39 claim was submitted to the BRTA Financial Assistance Fund, accompanied by the police FIR, highway seizure list, post-mortem report, and heirship certificates. Within 75 days, the Trustee Board disbursed BDT 5,00,000 directly into the widow's bank account, providing essential immediate relief.

Second, her advocate filed a comprehensive civil tort lawsuit under the Fatal Accidents Act 1855 in the Joint District Judge Court, claiming BDT 1.85 Crore in loss of lifetime dependency against the bus company and its primary shareholders. Concurrently, criminal prosecution under Section 105 RTA 2018 prevented the transport company from retrieving the impounded BDT 90 Lakh luxury bus without securing significant court bail bonds, ultimately compelling the transport syndicate to settle the civil damage claim for BDT 75 Lakh.

Talk to an Advocate

Surviving the aftermath of a catastrophic road traffic accident requires disciplined, compassionate, and aggressive legal advocacy. Missing the strict 30-day statutory deadline to apply for the BRTA Trust Fund or failing to prevent the release of an impounded commercial vehicle can permanently compromise your family's financial recovery. A dedicated accident compensation lawyer ensures that police reports are properly framed, emergency government funds are secured, and multi-crore civil damage claims are pursued relentlessly.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the deadline to apply for financial assistance from the Road Transport Trust Fund?

Under Rule 151 of the Road Transport Rules 2022, the application for financial assistance must be submitted to the Chairman of the Trustee Board (BRTA) strictly within <strong>30 days</strong> from the date of the road accident. If the victim was unconscious or hospitalized, an application for extension with certified medical records must be submitted.

Does receiving BDT 5 Lakh from the Trust Fund prevent the family from filing a civil damages lawsuit?

No. Statutory financial assistance received from the BRTA Trust Fund under Section 53 of the Road Transport Act 2018 is an emergency welfare grant and does not forfeit or extinguish the legal heirs' right to file a civil lawsuit for substantial tort compensation under the Fatal Accidents Act 1855.

What documents are strictly required to prove a road accident compensation claim?

The mandatory documents include: (1) Certified copy of the Thana FIR or General Diary (GD), (2) Police accident seizure list, (3) Post-mortem / autopsy report or medical board disability certificate, (4) Original medical bills and treatment vouchers, (5) Death certificate and Warishan Sanad (Heirship Certificate), and (6) National ID copies of legal heirs.

Can the family sue the bus or truck company directly if the driver fled the scene?

Yes. Under the doctrine of vicarious liability, the registered owner and transport company are legally liable for damages caused by vehicles operated under their commercial management. The family can file a civil suit for damages in the Joint District Judge Court against the registered owner regardless of whether the driver was arrested immediately.

How do courts calculate lifetime loss of earnings in a road accident tort suit?

Following the Supreme Court precedent in the <em>Catherine Masud</em> case, courts assess the victim's monthly income, calculate expected future promotions and career longevity up to retirement age (typically 60 to 65 years), deduct personal living expenses (typically one-third), and apply an actuarial dependency multiplier.

Can a passenger injured inside a public bus or ride-sharing car claim compensation?

Yes. Passengers injured while traveling inside buses, minibuses, ride-sharing vehicles, or auto-rickshaws have full legal standing to claim statutory medical compensation from the BRTA Trust Fund and sue both the transport operator and the other colliding vehicle for civil damages.

What criminal charges can be brought against a driver who drove without a valid driving license?

Under Section 66 of the Road Transport Act 2018, driving without a valid professional license is punishable with imprisonment for up to 6 months, or fine up to BDT 25,000, or both. If reckless driving without a license results in death, the driver faces prosecution under Section 105, carrying up to 5 years non-bailable imprisonment.

How can a family obtain a certified copy of the police accident report (FIR and Charge Sheet)?

The family or their engaged advocate can apply directly to the Officer-in-Charge (OC) of the concerned Thana or Highway Police Outpost, or submit a formal court application to the Chief Judicial or Metropolitan Magistrate Court where the police station records are submitted.

entries.body:
RS Khatian Online Check Bangladesh – How to Verify Your RS Land Record

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-23 · 7 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

The RS Khatian (Revisional Survey Khatian) is one of the most important land record documents in Bangladesh — used in property disputes, mutation applications, bank mortgages, and title verification. With the launch of land.gov.bd, you can now check your RS Khatian online without visiting the AC Land office. This step-by-step 2026 guide shows you exactly how to find, verify, and download your RS Khatian record.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Official Government Portalsland.gov.bd, mutation.land.gov.bd, dlrms.land.gov.bd & eporcha.gov.bd
Total Official E-Namjari FeeBDT 1,170 (Court fee 20 + Notice 50 + Record fee 1,000 + Khatian 100)
Standard Processing Time28 Working Days (9–12 working days for NRB / expatriate applicants)
National Land Helpline16122 (24/7 Ministry of Land Call Center)
📋 In This Article
  1. What Is an RS Khatian?
  2. Difference Between CS, SA, RS and BS Khatian
  3. Why RS Khatian Is the Most Important Survey Record
  4. How to Check RS Khatian Online at land.gov.bd (Step-by-Step)
  5. How to Search RS Khatian by Dag (Plot) Number
  6. What Information the RS Khatian Shows
  7. Downloading Your RS Khatian Certificate Online
  8. When the Online Record Is Missing – What to Do
  9. RS Khatian in Property Disputes and Court Cases

What Is an RS Khatian?

An RS Khatian (Revisional Survey Khatian — রিভিশনাল সার্ভে খতিয়ান) is the land record produced during the Revisional Survey conducted across most districts of Bangladesh between the 1940s and 1970s. It was prepared to update the older CS (Colonial Survey) records to reflect ownership changes after the Partition of Bengal in 1947 and the State Acquisition of 1956.

Each RS Khatian contains:

  • Khatian number — the unique identifier for the owner's land account
  • Owner's name(s) — as recorded in the survey
  • Dag (plot) numbers — each individual plot of land listed under that khatian
  • Area of each dag — in decimal, katha, or bigha
  • Land classification — agricultural (কৃষি), homestead (বাস্তু), pond (পুকুর), etc.

If you are involved in a land dispute, mutation, or property purchase, a land lawyer in Dhaka will always cross-reference the RS Khatian as a primary record.

Difference Between CS, SA, RS and BS Khatian

Bangladesh land records are organised by the survey in which they were created. Understanding the differences is essential:

Survey Full Name Period Significance
CSCadastral Survey1888–1940Oldest official record; baseline for all subsequent surveys
SAState Acquisition Survey1956–1962Recorded ownership after zamindari system abolished
RSRevisional Survey1940s–1970sUpdated SA records; most widely used for current disputes
BSBangladesh Survey1977–presentOngoing; most current record in completed districts

Which is most important? In most parts of Bangladesh, the RS Khatian is the most widely referenced record because: (1) BS surveys are still incomplete in many districts; (2) RS records are fully digitised in most areas; (3) courts and banks commonly require RS certified copies. In Dhaka, Chittagong, Sylhet, and other cities, RS Khatian is the primary reference document.

Why RS Khatian Is the Most Important Survey Record

The RS Khatian carries significant legal weight in Bangladesh for several reasons:

  • Bank mortgage: Most banks require a certified RS Khatian copy before approving a land mortgage loan
  • Mutation (Namjari): The AC Land office uses the RS Khatian as the base record when processing mutation applications
  • Title suits: Courts frequently refer to the RS Khatian as the primary title document in land dispute cases
  • Property purchase due diligence: Lawyers verify the RS Khatian to confirm that the seller's name is correctly recorded before advising clients to buy
  • Land registration: Sub-Registrar offices cross-reference RS Khatian details when registering deeds

A mismatch between the RS Khatian and what a seller claims — such as a different dag number, area discrepancy, or the seller's name not appearing — is a serious red flag that requires investigation by a property lawyer in Dhaka before any transaction proceeds.

How to Check RS Khatian Online at land.gov.bd (Step-by-Step)

The Bangladesh government's official land records portal at land.gov.bd allows you to check RS Khatian records for most districts. Follow these steps:

  1. Go to land.gov.bd in your browser (or search "Bangladesh land record online" on Google)
  2. Click on "নাগরিক সেবা" (Citizen Services) from the top menu
  3. Select "খতিয়ান তথ্য" (Khatian Information) or "পর্চা দেখুন"
  4. From the survey type dropdown, select "RS"
  5. Select your Division (বিভাগ) from the dropdown
  6. Select your District (জেলা)
  7. Select your Upazila/Thana (উপজেলা)
  8. Select your Mouza (মৌজা) — this is the lowest administrative land unit
  9. Enter the Khatian Number (খতিয়ান নম্বর) — you can find this in any existing deed or previous land document
  10. Click Search/খুঁজুন

The system will display the RS Khatian record. If you don't have the khatian number, you can search by owner name — enter part of the name and browse the results.

⚠️ Tip: If you don't know the Mouza name, check any existing deed for the land — the Mouza is always mentioned in the property description.

How to Search RS Khatian by Dag (Plot) Number

If you know the dag (plot) number but not the khatian number, you can do a reverse search:

  1. At land.gov.bd, select "RS Porcha" (RS পর্চা) instead of Khatian
  2. Select Division, District, Upazila, and Mouza
  3. Enter the Dag Number (দাগ নম্বর)
  4. Click Search — the system shows all khatians that include this dag number

This is particularly useful when:

  • You have a registered deed showing only a dag number and need to find the matching khatian
  • You want to verify that no one else has a competing claim on the same dag
  • You are checking a property you are considering buying and want to identify all khatian entries for that plot

If a single dag number appears in multiple khatians, this indicates a potential dispute or fraudulent double-recording — consult a land lawyer immediately before proceeding with any transaction.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

What Information the RS Khatian Shows

A typical RS Khatian online record contains the following information:

  • কতিয়ান নং (Khatian Number): The unique RS khatian number for that mouza
  • মৌজা নং ও নাম (Mouza Number and Name): The specific land administrative unit
  • জেলা / উপজেলা (District/Upazila): Location details
  • মালিকের নাম ও পিতার নাম (Owner Name and Father's Name): As recorded at the time of RS survey
  • দাগ নং (Dag Number): Each individual plot number under this khatian
  • শ্রেণী (Classification): Land type — agricultural (আবাদি), homestead (বাস্তু), pond (পুকুর), fallow (পতিত), etc.
  • পরিমাণ (Area): Land area in decimal, katha, or bigha per dag
  • মোট পরিমাণ (Total Area): Sum of all dags in the khatian

Note: The RS Khatian shows ownership as it was at the time of survey. If the land was sold, gifted, or inherited since the RS survey, the BS Khatian or a registered mutation certificate would show the updated owner — not the RS record.

Downloading Your RS Khatian Certificate Online

Once you have found your RS Khatian on land.gov.bd:

  1. Click on the khatian record to open the full details page
  2. Use the Print (মুদ্রণ) button to save or print the record
  3. For a certified digital copy, look for the option to download a digitally signed certificate — this is available in select districts that have fully migrated to the digital system

Important distinction:

  • Online printout (unofficial): Useful for your own reference. NOT accepted as evidence in courts or for bank mortgage purposes.
  • Certified copy from AC Land Office: Required for courts, banks, mutation applications, and formal transactions. You obtain this by visiting the AC Land office (ভূমি অফিস) and paying the prescribed fee.

A property lawyer in Uttara, Dhaka can obtain certified RS Khatian copies from the relevant AC Land office on your behalf, saving you multiple trips and potential delays.

When the Online Record Is Missing – What to Do

If your RS Khatian is not showing up on land.gov.bd, don't panic. Several reasons explain this:

  • Mouza not yet digitised: Many rural mouzas, especially in Barisal, Mymensingh, and parts of Rangpur, are not yet fully digitised in the online system
  • Wrong Mouza selected: One district may have dozens of mouzas with similar names — double-check the mouza number if available
  • Khatian number mismatch: The khatian number in old deeds may use a different format than what's in the online system
  • Data entry error: Digitisation errors can cause records to be filed under slightly incorrect names or numbers

If the record is genuinely missing online, you must:

  1. Visit the AC Land office (ভূমি অফিস) of the relevant Upazila in person
  2. Request a certified copy of the RS Khatian from the physical record room (রেকর্ড রুম)
  3. Ask about the status of digitisation for your mouza

For legal proceedings, always get a certified physical copy regardless of what is available online. Contact Advocate Md. Shah Alam for assistance with land record retrieval and verification.

RS Khatian in Property Disputes and Court Cases

The RS Khatian plays a central role in land dispute litigation in Bangladesh:

  • Title suits (স্বত্ব মামলা): The plaintiff typically submits CS, SA, and RS Khatian copies to establish an unbroken chain of title going back to the original survey
  • Partition suits (বণ্টন মামলা): RS Khatian establishes who the co-owners are and what share each holds
  • Mutation disputes: When a mutation is challenged, the AC Land office and courts refer to the RS Khatian to verify who should be recorded as owner
  • Injunction applications: Courts may grant stay orders preventing land transactions when RS Khatian ownership is in dispute
  • Succession matters: The RS Khatian in the deceased's name is a key document in estate administration

If your RS Khatian shows a discrepancy — wrong owner name, wrong area, or a dag that is missing — this must be corrected through a formal correction application before the AC Land office, or through court if the error is contested. An experienced land and property lawyer in Dhaka can guide you through the correction or dispute resolution process.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I find my mouza name to search for RS Khatian online?

The mouza name (মৌজা নাম) is mentioned in any existing registered deed for the land. You can also find it by looking at old land tax receipts (খাজনার রশিদ) or by asking the local UP (Union Parishad) member or AC Land office for your location.

Can I search RS Khatian online without knowing the khatian number?

Yes. On land.gov.bd, you can search by the owner's name instead of the khatian number. Enter the full or partial name of the landowner and select the correct mouza — the system will list matching khatians for you to browse.

Is RS Khatian the same as BS Khatian?

No. RS (Revisional Survey) and BS (Bangladesh Survey) are different surveys done in different time periods. RS was conducted 1940s–1970s; BS is the ongoing modern survey starting 1977. In districts where BS is complete, the BS Khatian reflects the most current ownership. Where BS is incomplete, the RS Khatian remains the primary reference.

My name is not in the RS Khatian even though I bought the land. Why?

The RS Khatian shows ownership at the time of the RS survey. If you purchased the land after the RS survey was conducted, your name will only appear in the BS Khatian (after mutation) or in the registered deed — not in the RS record. This is normal and does not affect your ownership if you have a valid registered deed and completed mutation (namjari).

Can I use a printed RS Khatian from land.gov.bd in court?

No. For court proceedings, you need a certified copy from the AC Land office with official stamp and signature. A printout from the online portal is useful for reference only — it is not legally admissible as evidence in Bangladesh courts.

Is land.gov.bd available in English?

The portal is primarily in Bengali. However, the interface is navigable even if you are not fluent in Bengali, as the form fields follow a standard geographical hierarchy (division → district → upazila → mouza). You can also ask your land lawyer to run the search on your behalf.

Legal Disclaimer: The information provided in this article is for general legal awareness and educational purposes only. It does not constitute formal legal advice and does not establish an attorney-client relationship. For specific legal remedies tailored to your case, please consult directly with an enrolled advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh or the Judges Court.

entries.body:
RS Survey Bangladesh – What It Is, Districts Covered & How It Affects Your Land

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-06-28 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

The Revisional Survey (RS) is one of the most legally significant land surveys conducted in Bangladesh, forming the backbone of property records in dozens of districts across the country. Understanding the RS Khatian and its standing in property disputes, mutation applications, and inheritance claims is essential for any landowner in Bangladesh. This comprehensive guide explains what the RS survey means, which districts are covered, and how it directly impacts your land rights in 2026.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order
Official Portalssupremecourt.gov.bd, judiciary.gov.bd, pcc.police.gov.bd & land.gov.bd
Supreme Court ChamberAdvocate Md. Shah Alam — Uttara & Dhaka Judge Court (+880 1712-655546)
📋 In This Article
