  2. Historical Background of Land Surveys in Bangladesh
  3. CS, SA, RS, and BS: A Comparative Overview
  4. Purpose and Legal Significance of the RS Survey
  5. RS Khatian: What It Contains and Why It Matters
  6. Districts Where RS Survey Has Been Completed
  7. RS Survey and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950
  8. How RS Survey Affects Property Disputes and Mutation
  9. Checking Your RS Khatian Online: eporcha.gov.bd
  10. Common Legal Issues Arising from RS Survey Records
  11. How a Land Lawyer Can Help You

What Is the RS Survey in Bangladesh?

The Revisional Survey (RS) is a government-mandated cadastral land survey conducted in Bangladesh primarily during the 1960s and 1970s, aimed at revising and updating earlier Colonial-era CS (Cadastral Survey) records. The term "RS" stands for Revisional Settlement or Revisional Survey, and it produced a new set of land records known as the RS Khatian.

In simple terms, the RS survey corrected errors in older records, re-mapped land parcels (dags or plots), and brought property ownership records in line with the realities on the ground following the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, which abolished the zamindari system. Every RS Khatian contains:

  • The Khatian number – a unique folio identifier for each owner group
  • The Dag number(s) – plot numbers associated with that Khatian
  • The name(s) of recorded owner(s) and their shares
  • The classification of land (agricultural, homestead, pond, etc.)
  • The area in decimals or acres
  • Annual land revenue (khajna) payable

The RS record serves as a primary evidentiary document in land ownership disputes, mutation applications, partition suits, and succession matters across Bangladeshi courts and revenue offices.

Historical Background of Land Surveys in Bangladesh

To understand the RS survey, one must appreciate the sequential history of land surveys conducted in the Bengal region that now constitutes Bangladesh:

  1. Cadastral Survey (CS) – 1888 to 1940: The first systematic, plot-by-plot survey of British India, conducted under the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885. CS records formed the original land register and remain the oldest legally admissible survey record.
  2. State Acquisition Survey (SA) – 1956 onwards: Following the abolition of the zamindari system under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (East Bengal Act XXVIII of 1951), the SA survey recorded raiyati (tenant) rights directly under the state. SA Khatians reflect post-zamindari ownership.
  3. Revisional Survey (RS) – 1960s to 1990s: Conducted to revise and correct SA records, incorporating sub-divisions, transfers, and ground-level changes since the SA survey. The RS is the most relied-upon record in central and northern districts of Bangladesh.
  4. Bangladesh Survey (BS) – 1980s to present: The most recent urban and peri-urban survey, most prominent in Dhaka, Chittagong, and other rapidly developing areas. In many districts, the BS has superseded the RS as the primary record.

This historical layering means that in a property dispute, courts and revenue offices must trace a chain of title across CS to SA to RS to BS records to establish conclusive ownership.

CS, SA, RS, and BS: A Comparative Overview

Landowners frequently become confused about which survey record is most authoritative. The answer depends on the district and time period. The table below provides a direct comparison:

FeatureCS SurveySA SurveyRS SurveyBS Survey
Full NameCadastral SurveyState Acquisition SurveyRevisional SurveyBangladesh Survey
Period1888–19401956–1960s1960s–1990s1980s–present
Legal BasisBengal Tenancy Act 1885SA&T Act 1950SA&T Act 1950 (Revision)Land Survey Act
Recorded OwnerZamindars/Tenure-holdersRaiyats (post-zamindari)Revised raiyati ownersCurrent possessors
Primary Use TodayHistorical title chainTitle verificationPrimary record (many districts)Primary record (urban areas)
Availability OnlinePartial (eporcha)Partial (eporcha)Yes (eporcha.gov.bd)Yes (eporcha.gov.bd)

In practice, courts in Bangladesh generally treat the most recent survey record as the strongest presumptive evidence of title, though earlier CS records can override later ones where fraud or error in subsequent surveys is demonstrated.

Purpose and Legal Significance of the RS Survey

The RS survey carries substantial legal weight under Bangladeshi law. Key points illustrating its importance include:

  • Prima facie evidence of title: Under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, an RS Khatian constitutes prima facie evidence of the rights it records. Courts presume the recorded person to be the lawful owner unless proven otherwise.
  • Basis for mutation (namjari): When property is transferred by sale, inheritance, or gift, the new owner must apply for mutation at the local AC Land office. The mutation is recorded against the existing RS or BS Khatian.
  • Required for deed registration: Sub-registrar offices require applicants to cite the relevant Khatian number (RS or BS) during deed registration, linking the deed to the survey record.
  • Land development tax: The RS Khatian determines the annual land development tax (khajna) assessed on a landholding.
  • Partition suits: In partition suits (bonton mamla) before civil courts, the RS record is exhibited to establish the undivided shares of co-owners.

The legal standing of the RS Khatian has been affirmed in numerous decisions of the Bangladesh Supreme Court, where the Appellate Division has held that a person recorded in the Khatian is presumed to hold valid title unless a competitor establishes a superior chain of title.

RS Khatian: What It Contains and Why It Matters

An RS Khatian is the official folio document summarising who owns what land and under what classification. Understanding its contents helps landowners verify and protect their rights.

Key components of an RS Khatian include:

  • Mouza Name and JL Number: Identifies the revenue village (mouza) and its jurisdiction list (JL) number within the upazila.
  • Khatian Number: The unique identifier for the group of owners sharing the folio.
  • Owner's Name and Father's Name: Recorded owners as surveyed at the time of the RS.
  • Dag Numbers and Area: Each plot (dag) linked to the Khatian with its area in acres-decimals.
  • Class of Land: Whether the land is agricultural (aabadi), homestead (bari), water body (pukur), fallow, etc.
  • Share: Where multiple owners share a Khatian, their fractional shares are recorded (e.g., 1/2, 1/3).
  • Annual Rent (Khajna): The amount of land development tax payable annually.

A certified copy of the RS Khatian, obtained from the AC Land office or downloaded from eporcha.gov.bd, is admissible as evidence before Bangladeshi courts under the Evidence Act 1872 and the Registration Act 1908.

Districts Where RS Survey Has Been Completed

The RS survey has not been uniformly conducted across all 64 districts of Bangladesh. In many districts – particularly urban Dhaka – the BS has been conducted instead of or alongside the RS. The following table provides an overview of survey coverage as of 2026:

DivisionDistricts with RS CompletedDistricts with BS (No Separate RS)Primary Record in Use
RajshahiRajshahi, Natore, Chapainawabganj, Naogaon, Pabna, Sirajganj, Bogura, Joypurhat—RS Khatian
RangpurRangpur, Dinajpur, Thakurgaon, Panchagarh, Nilphamari, Kurigram, Lalmonirhat, Gaibandha—RS Khatian
MymensinghMymensingh, Jamalpur, Sherpur, Netrokona—RS Khatian
SylhetSylhet, Moulvibazar, Habiganj, Sunamganj—RS Khatian
KhulnaNarail, Magura, Jhenaidah, Kushtia, Chuadanga, Meherpur, Jessore (partial)Khulna City, BagerhatRS / SA Khatian
BarisalPatuakhali, Bhola, Jhalokati, Pirojpur, Barguna, Barisal (partial)Barisal City (BS)RS / BS Khatian
ChittagongCumilla, Chandpur, Brahmanbaria, Noakhali, Lakshmipur, Feni, Cox's Bazar, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, BandarbanChattogram Metropolitan (BS)RS / BS Khatian
DhakaFaridpur, Gopalganj, Madaripur, Shariatpur, Rajbari, Kishoreganj, Munshiganj, Tangail (partial)Dhaka City, Gazipur, Narayanganj (BS)BS (urban); RS (rural)

Note: Survey completion status can vary at the upazila and mouza level. Always verify the applicable record at your local AC Land office or via eporcha.gov.bd before initiating any legal proceeding.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

RS Survey and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950

The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (East Bengal Act XXVIII of 1951, the SA&T Act) is the foundational legislation governing land tenure and surveys in Bangladesh. The RS survey was conducted as a revisional settlement exercise under this Act. Key provisions relevant to the RS survey include:

  • Section 143: Empowers the government to conduct settlement operations, including cadastral surveys and preparation of record-of-rights (Khatians).
  • Section 144: Provides for the preparation of a draft record-of-rights during settlement operations, to which objections can be filed.
  • Section 145: Governs the publication of the final record-of-rights (i.e., the Khatian) and confers on it the status of prima facie evidence.
  • Section 149: Allows for revision of the record-of-rights upon application to the Settlement Officer where errors are found.
  • Section 90A: Restricts the maximum ceiling on agricultural land ownership; the RS survey was used partly to identify and vest surplus lands in the government.
  • Section 96: Protects raiyats (recorded owners) against dispossession without due process – the RS Khatian is primary proof of raiyati status.

Landowners whose holdings exceeded the ceiling had surplus land vested in the state — sometimes reflected in the RS Khatian by a government-vested dag entry. Correcting such entries requires legal proceedings under the appropriate provisions of the SA&T Act.

How RS Survey Affects Property Disputes and Mutation

The RS survey record has direct, practical consequences in day-to-day land transactions and disputes in Bangladesh.

1. Property Purchase and Sale

When buying land, a prudent purchaser must verify the vendor's name in the RS or BS Khatian, cross-reference with the deed chain (baina and kabala deeds), and confirm there is no encumbrance or government vesting. Failure to verify the RS Khatian has led to countless fraudulent sales where sellers lacked recorded title.

2. Mutation (Namjari) Applications

After acquiring land by purchase, inheritance, or gift, the new owner must apply for mutation (namjari) at the AC Land office. Required documents typically include:

  • Certified copy of the existing RS/BS Khatian
  • Registered deed of transfer (kabala deed)
  • Succession certificate or waris certificate (for inheritance cases)
  • Up-to-date land development tax (khajna) payment receipt
  • NID copies of applicant and seller/transferor

3. Land Disputes and Litigation

In title suits (dakhol-khilafat mamla) and partition suits before civil courts, the RS Khatian is the centrepiece exhibit. A plaintiff who cannot produce or link to the RS Khatian faces a significantly weaker claim. Conversely, a defendant whose name appears in the RS Khatian benefits from the statutory presumption of title under the SA&T Act.

4. Government Acquisition

When the government acquires land under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Act 2017, the RS/BS Khatian determines who is entitled to receive compensation and in what proportion.

Checking Your RS Khatian Online: eporcha.gov.bd

The Government of Bangladesh has digitised land records – including RS Khatians – through the e-Porcha platform at eporcha.gov.bd, managed under the Ministry of Land (land.gov.bd). This system allows landowners to:

  • Search for RS, CS, SA, and BS Khatians by district, upazila, mouza, Khatian number, or owner name
  • Download a certified copy (porcha) of the Khatian for a nominal fee (currently BDT 100–150 per copy)
  • Search by Dag number to find all Khatians associated with a particular plot
  • Track mutation application status via the e-namjari system

Step-by-step process to check your RS Khatian on eporcha.gov.bd:

  1. Visit eporcha.gov.bd
  2. Select "খতিয়ান" (Khatian) from the menu
  3. Choose the Survey Type as RS
  4. Select your Division, District, Upazila, and Mouza
  5. Enter the Khatian number or owner name and click Search
  6. View the record online or pay BDT 100 via mobile banking (bKash/Nagad/Rocket) to download a certified copy

Not all districts and mouzas are fully digitised yet. If your RS Khatian is not available online, you must obtain a certified copy in person from the AC Land office or the district Collectorate land record room. The government's ongoing Digital Land Management System (DLMS) project aims to complete full digitisation across all districts by 2027.

Common Legal Issues Arising from RS Survey Records

Despite its importance, the RS survey is not without flaws. Several common legal problems arise from RS records in Bangladesh:

  • Incorrect names or shares: Survey officers sometimes recorded names incorrectly or missed co-owners. These errors require a formal correction petition before the Settlement Officer.
  • Phantom plots classified as khas land: Some privately owned plots were erroneously recorded as government khas land during the RS. Reclaiming such land requires filing a suit in civil court or an application to the district administration.
  • Discrepancy between RS and registered deed: A common problem where the area or owner recorded in the RS does not match the registered deed. This often arises due to unrecorded mutations over several generations.
  • Vested property issues: Some Hindu-owned properties were erroneously recorded as vested (enemy) property in the RS Khatian. The Vested Property Return Act 2001 provides a mechanism for reclaiming such lands.
  • Forged RS Khatians: Document fraud is a serious concern. Fraudsters sometimes produce forged certified copies of RS Khatians. Always verify by cross-referencing with the AC Land office records.
  • RS not updated post-partition: Where land was physically divided but the RS Khatian was never updated through mutation, all co-owners remain recorded jointly, creating title complications when one owner sells.

How a Land Lawyer Can Help You

Navigating RS survey records, Khatian disputes, and mutation proceedings in Bangladesh can be extraordinarily complex – especially when multiple survey records, inheritance chains, and registered deeds must be reconciled. A qualified land lawyer in Bangladesh provides invaluable assistance in:

  • Conducting a full title search across CS, SA, RS, and BS records to verify the authenticity of a seller's claim
  • Filing and following up on mutation (namjari) applications at the AC Land office
  • Drafting and filing objections to erroneous RS records before the Settlement Officer
  • Representing clients in title suits, partition suits, and land recovery cases before civil courts
  • Advising on vested property reclaims under the Vested Property Return Act 2001
  • Assisting with land acquisition compensation claims under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Act 2017

Advocate Md. Shah Alam, operating from his Uttara chamber in Dhaka, has extensive experience in land law matters including RS Khatian disputes, mutation proceedings, partition suits, and title verification across multiple districts of Bangladesh. With a deep understanding of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 and the digitised land record systems at eporcha.gov.bd, Advocate Shah Alam provides practical, result-oriented legal counsel to landowners, purchasers, and heirs.

If you are facing a land dispute, need to verify RS records before a property purchase, or require assistance with mutation, contact our office today for a confidential consultation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does RS Survey mean in Bangladesh?

RS stands for Revisional Survey (or Revisional Settlement). It is a government land survey conducted primarily in the 1960s–1990s to revise and update earlier CS and SA survey records. The RS produced RS Khatians — official land ownership folios — that are currently the primary land record in most rural and semi-urban districts of Bangladesh.

Is an RS Khatian sufficient proof of land ownership in Bangladesh?

An RS Khatian constitutes prima facie (presumptive) evidence of title under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. However, it is not conclusive proof by itself. Courts also examine the registered deed chain and any subsequent mutations. For complete title assurance, the RS Khatian should be cross-referenced with CS/SA records and all registered deeds in the title chain.

Which is more important – RS Khatian or registered deed?

Both documents are important and complement each other. The registered deed proves the transaction (transfer of ownership), while the RS Khatian records the survey-based ownership. Bangladeshi courts generally require both. Where there is a conflict, the court examines the entire chain of title. A Khatian without a supporting deed chain, or a deed without RS Khatian linkage, can both lead to title challenges.

How can I check my RS Khatian online in Bangladesh?

You can check your RS Khatian online at eporcha.gov.bd (the official e-Porcha portal of the Ministry of Land). Select the RS survey type, choose your district, upazila, and mouza, then search by Khatian number or owner name. Certified copies can be downloaded by paying BDT 100 via mobile banking (bKash, Nagad, or Rocket).

What is the difference between RS and BS survey in Bangladesh?

The RS (Revisional Survey) was conducted from the 1960s to 1990s to revise earlier records and covers most rural districts. The BS (Bangladesh Survey) is more recent (1980s–present) and is primarily conducted in rapidly urbanising areas such as Dhaka, Chittagong, and Narayanganj. Where a BS Khatian exists, it generally supersedes the RS as the most current record of title.

What should I do if my land is incorrectly recorded in the RS Khatian?

If your land is incorrectly recorded in the RS Khatian — wrong owner name, incorrect area, or wrong classification — you can file a correction application before the Settlement Officer or the AC Land office. If the error is due to a fraudulent entry, a civil suit for declaration and injunction before the appropriate court may be necessary. It is strongly advisable to consult a land lawyer before taking action.

Second Wife Rights Bangladesh – Is a Second Marriage Legal? What Are Her Rights?

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-04-16 · 8 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In Bangladesh, a Muslim man may marry more than once — but the law imposes strict procedural requirements. Ignoring them is a criminal offence. Whether you are a first wife whose husband has taken a second wife, or a second wife uncertain of your legal status, this guide explains your rights under Bangladesh law.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

📋 In This Article
  1. Is a Second Marriage Legal in Bangladesh?
  2. The MFLO 1961 — The Law Governing Second Marriages
  3. What Is the Arbitration Council and What Does It Do?
  4. What Happens If a Man Marries Without Permission?
  5. Rights of the First Wife After Husband's Second Marriage
  6. Legal Status and Rights of the Second Wife
  7. Maintenance — Can Both Wives Claim Equal Support?
  8. Inheritance — Do Children of Both Wives Have Equal Rights?
  9. How to Enforce Your Rights Through Court

Is a Second Marriage Legal in Bangladesh?

Under Muslim personal law as applied in Bangladesh, a Muslim man may have up to four wives simultaneously — provided he can treat them equitably. However, the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (MFLO) significantly restricts this classical permission by requiring government approval before contracting a second or subsequent marriage.

This means: legally permissible in principle, but procedurally restricted in practice. Ignoring the procedure is a criminal offence, not merely a civil wrong. If you need urgent legal advice on a polygamy situation, contact a family lawyer in Dhaka or Uttara immediately.

The MFLO 1961 — The Law Governing Second Marriages

Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 provides that no man who is already married can contract another marriage without the prior permission in writing of the Arbitration Council. The relevant provisions:

  • The man must submit a written application to the Chairman of the Union Parishad (or Pourashava/City Corporation) where he resides
  • The application must state the reasons for seeking a second marriage and confirm that the existing wife or wives have been informed
  • The Arbitration Council (chaired by the Union Parishad Chairman) must convene and decide whether to grant or deny permission
  • The Council considers whether the proposed marriage is necessary and just

Grounds the Council typically accepts: first wife incurably ill, physically incapacitated, or unable to bear children — though these are not automatic grounds; the Council exercises discretion.

What Is the Arbitration Council and What Does It Do?

The Arbitration Council is a statutory body established under the MFLO 1961 at the local government level. For a second marriage application, it must:

  1. Receive the man's written application
  2. Give notice to the existing wife or wives and invite their response
  3. Convene a formal hearing where both sides can appear and speak
  4. Issue a written decision granting or refusing the permission

If the Council refuses permission, the man cannot legally contract the second marriage. If he does so anyway, it is a criminal offence. The first wife can challenge any Council decision she is unhappy with.

What Happens If a Man Marries Without Permission?

A man who marries a second, third, or fourth time without Arbitration Council permission commits a criminal offence under Section 6(5) of the MFLO 1961:

  • Punishment: Imprisonment up to 1 year AND/OR fine up to BDT 10,000
  • He is also required to immediately pay the full deferred mahr to any existing wife
  • The first wife gains an automatic right to seek divorce if she chooses

⚠️ Critically: The second marriage itself is NOT automatically void under Bangladesh law. It may still be valid under Islamic law even if the MFLO procedure was not followed — the criminal liability attaches to the man, not the marriage's religious validity. This distinction is important for the second wife's rights.

Rights of the First Wife After Husband's Second Marriage

Upon the husband contracting a second marriage (with or without Arbitration Council permission), the first wife immediately gains these rights:

  • Immediate payment of deferred mahr: Any component of mahr deferred to the future becomes payable immediately upon the second marriage
  • Right to divorce (khula or talaq-i-tafwid): If her Kabinnama contained a delegated right of divorce clause (tafwid), she can immediately divorce herself without the husband's agreement
  • Right to equal maintenance: The husband must maintain both wives equally — he cannot reduce the first wife's maintenance on remarriage
  • Right to file criminal complaint: If the husband married without Arbitration Council permission, she can file a police complaint or private complaint in Magistrate Court for the MFLO offence

A family lawyer in Dhaka can advise on the fastest route to protect your rights when your husband has taken a second wife.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Legal Status and Rights of the Second Wife

If the second marriage was registered through a licensed Kazi, the second wife has full legal status under Bangladesh law, including:

  • Right to mahr: As stated in her Kabinnama — fully enforceable in Family Court
  • Right to maintenance: Equal maintenance from the husband as the first wife receives
  • Rights under domestic violence law: Full protection under the Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act 2010
  • Inheritance rights: Her children are full legal heirs of the husband with equal inheritance rights to children of the first marriage
  • Right to divorce: Full rights to seek khula or court divorce through the same procedures as any married woman

A second wife's legal position is NOT weaker simply because she is a second wife — her rights under Bangladesh law are equal once the marriage is registered.

Maintenance — Can Both Wives Claim Equal Support?

Under Islamic law and Bangladesh Family Court practice, a husband who has more than one wife must maintain all wives equally. This means:

  • Each wife is entitled to comparable financial support — housing, food, clothing appropriate to the family's financial position
  • If a husband is maintaining the second wife better than the first, the first wife can apply to Family Court for a maintenance order
  • The husband's total income is the basis for calculating what is 'fair' maintenance for each wife

Maintenance cases are filed in the Family Court of the area where the wife resides. The court can issue an interim maintenance order quickly to prevent financial hardship pending a full hearing.

Inheritance — Do Children of Both Wives Have Equal Rights?

Under the Muslim faraid (inheritance) system as applied in Bangladesh, all children of all wives have equal inheritance rights. The father's estate is divided by the faraid rules equally among sons (with daughters getting half a son's share) regardless of which wife is their mother.

A father cannot legally disinherit a child in favour of another wife's children through a will — the faraid rules take precedence. Only gifts (heba) made and completed during the father's lifetime can benefit one child over another.

The property lawyers at our Uttara chambers regularly assist families navigating inheritance from multi-wife households.

How to Enforce Your Rights Through Court

Whether you are a first wife or second wife, the legal routes to enforce rights are:

  1. Family Court: For maintenance, mahr recovery, child custody — file a suit in the Family Court of your area
  2. Criminal Complaint (MFLO offence): If the second marriage was without Arbitration Council permission — file at the Magistrate Court
  3. Divorce proceedings: File through the Union Parishad/Kazi for talaq or through Family Court for khula
  4. Domestic Violence Act: File for a protection order if you are experiencing abuse, economic exploitation, or harassment

Act quickly — delays in asserting family law rights can complicate your legal position. Contact a family lawyer in Uttara, Dhaka for a confidential consultation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a Muslim man in Bangladesh marry a second wife without his first wife's knowledge?

No. MFLO 1961 requires the man to apply to the Arbitration Council AND give notice to the existing wife. Marrying without this process is a criminal offence punishable by up to 1 year imprisonment and/or fine.

Is the second marriage automatically invalid if Arbitration Council permission was not obtained?

Not necessarily. Under Islamic law the second marriage may still be religiously valid even without MFLO compliance. However, the husband faces criminal liability, and the first wife can claim deferred mahr immediately and seek divorce.

Can a first wife stop her husband from marrying a second time?

She can object through the Arbitration Council process and the Council may refuse permission. However, she cannot legally prevent the marriage entirely if the Council grants permission or the husband proceeds anyway (accepting criminal liability).

Does the first wife automatically get divorced when her husband takes a second wife?

No. Divorce only occurs if she exercises her rights — either through delegated divorce rights in the Kabinnama (tafwid), or by filing for khula. She may choose to remain married.

Can a second wife claim inheritance from her husband's estate?

Yes — she inherits as a wife (1/8 share with children, 1/4 without), shared equally with any other surviving wife. Her children inherit equally with children from other wives.

What if my husband is paying more maintenance to his second wife than to me?

Apply to Family Court for a maintenance order. The husband must provide equal maintenance to all wives proportional to his income. The court can enforce equality and order arrears to be paid.

Section 133 CrPC in Bangladesh: Boundary Wall, Drainage & Public Nuisance Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-08 · 19 minutes

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In both densely populated urban neighborhoods of Dhaka and rural village homesteads across Bangladesh, conflicts between adjacent property owners frequently escalate over blocked drainage lines, unauthorized boundary walls, and obstructed access pathways. When an uncooperative neighbor unlawfully builds a brick wall across a shared road, redirects toxic sewage runoff into an adjacent compound, or constructs a hazardous structural overhang that threatens collapse, victims face an immediate threat to health, safety, and property value. While filing an easement suit in a civil court can take years, the **Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC)** provides a rapid, summary legal remedy under **Section 133**. Empowering Executive Magistrates to issue conditional orders for the immediate removal of public nuisances and illegal obstructions, Section 133 is one of the most effective community dispute resolution tools in Bangladesh. This practical legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate and property law practitioner in Uttara and Dhaka Court, explains how to petition the Executive Magistrate, enforce municipal demolition orders, and protect neighborhood rights.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

📋 In This Article

  2. 2. Actionable Nuisances: Blocked Roads, Boundary Walls & Drainage
  3. 3. The Conditional Order Mechanism Under Section 133(1)
  4. 4. Section 139A Procedure: Denying the Existence of a Public Right
  5. 5. Legal Matrix: Section 133 CrPC vs. Civil Easement Suit vs. Section 144
  6. 6. The Role of Police Spot Reports & Municipal Engineer Inspections
  7. 7. Making the Order Absolute & Criminal Penalties Under Section 188
  8. 8. Demolition Protocol & Recovering Costs from the Offender
  9. 9. Illustrative Scenario: Removing an Illegal Wall Blocking a Pathway in Dhaka
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate: Neighbor Dispute & Section 133 Litigation

1. Statutory Foundation: Public Nuisance Powers Under Chapter X CrPC

In Bangladesh, while private boundary encroachments between two individuals can be resolved through civil boundary suits, actions that compromise public health, common pathways, sanitation, and neighborhood safety fall within the criminal public nuisance jurisdiction codified in Chapter X of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC).

Under Section 133 of the CrPC, Parliament vested summary administrative and quasi-judicial authority in Executive Magistrates (specifically the Additional District Magistrate in metropolitan cities and Upazila Nirbahi Officers in rural upazilas) to order the immediate cessation or demolition of public nuisances. The section is not punitive; it is preventive and remedial, aimed at swiftly restoring public convenience and safety before civil litigation can unfold.

The statutory definition of a public nuisance is linked to Section 268 of the Penal Code 1860: an act or omission that causes common injury, danger, or annoyance to the public or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity. Because Section 133 proceedings are swift, cost-effective, and backed by direct police enforcement, they are widely utilized by citizens facing unyielding neighbors and illegal construction cartels.

2. Actionable Nuisances: Blocked Roads, Boundary Walls & Drainage

Section 133(1) of the CrPC identifies specific categories of actionable public nuisances that empower an Executive Magistrate to intervene:

  • Unlawful Obstruction of Public Ways: Any unauthorized construction of a brick wall, bamboo barricade, iron gate, or earth filling that narrows or completely blocks any public road, shared lane, alleyway, or village pathway lawfully used by the public.
  • Illegal Drainage and Sewage Discharges: Redirecting household sewage, septic overflow, or contaminated factory chemical wastewater into neighboring private compounds, public surface drains, or open roads, creating grave public health hazards.
  • Dangerous Structural Overhangs: Old, dilapidated walls, unapproved building projections, decaying concrete parapets, or tilted structures adjoining a public street that threaten imminent collapse on passersby.
  • Noxious Occupations & Industrial Hazards: Operating unauthorized chemical storage facilities, illegal tanneries, noisy industrial workshops, or hazardous sawmills in residential zones in violation of zoning regulations.
  • Unenclosed Wells and Excavations: Leaving deep construction excavations, open water wells, or quarry pits unfenced near public thoroughfares.

3. The Conditional Order Mechanism Under Section 133(1)

When an aggrieved citizen or neighborhood community submits a petition under Section 133, accompanied by a police report or personal affidavit, the Executive Magistrate does not immediately issue a final demolition order. The statute enforces strict procedural due process through a Conditional Order.

Under Section 133(1), the Magistrate issues an order directing the person causing the obstruction or nuisance, within a fixed time to be specified in the order:

  1. To remove such obstruction or nuisance; or
  2. To desist from carrying on, or to remove or regulate such trade or occupation; or
  3. To repair, support, or remove such dangerous building or structure; or
  4. The Show Cause Option: If they object to doing so, to appear before the Magistrate at a fixed time and place to show cause why the conditional order should not be made absolute.

Under Section 134, the conditional order is officially served on the respondent in the manner provided for serving a summons, or by public notice posted at the site of the nuisance.

4. Section 139A Procedure: Denying the Existence of a Public Right

Dealing with an obstructed pathway, illegal boundary wall, or drainage nuisance? Contact our land litigation chamber on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. We coordinate magistrate petitions and police reports.

When an obstruction concerns a pathway, road, or water channel, the respondent frequently appears and argues that the land is private property and that no public right exists. To resolve this threshold challenge, the CrPC provides a mandatory statutory mechanism: Section 139A.

Under Section 139A, the Magistrate must follow a two-tier inquiry:

  • Questioning the Respondent: The Magistrate must specifically ask the respondent whether they deny the existence of any public right in respect of the way, river, or channel.
  • Inquiry into Reliable Evidence: If the respondent denies the public right, the Magistrate must inquire into the matter before proceeding further. The respondent must produce reliable evidence (such as original title deeds, CS/RS/BS Khatians showing private ownership without public easement notations) supporting their denial.
  • Outcome of the Inquiry: If the Magistrate finds there is reliable evidence supporting the denial, the court must stay all proceedings until the matter of public right is decided by a competent civil court. If, however, the respondent produces no reliable evidence or merely raises frivolous objections, the Magistrate rejects the denial and proceeds with the nuisance inquiry under Section 137.

5. Legal Matrix: Section 133 CrPC vs. Civil Easement Suit vs. Section 144

A comparative overview of legal avenues for resolving neighbor and obstruction conflicts in Bangladesh:

FeatureSection 133 CrPCCivil Suit for Easement (Civil Court)Section 144 CrPC
Competent ForumExecutive Magistrate Court (ADM / UNO)Civil Court (Assistant Judge)Executive Magistrate Court (ADM / UNO)
Nature of DisputePublic nuisance; obstruction of public way/drainPrivate right of way; easement by prescription/necessityImminent breach of peace & armed violence
Order TypeConditional order leading to Absolute DemolitionDeclaratory decree & permanent mandatory injunctionTemporary status quo restraining order
Maximum DurationPermanent until set aside by civil courtPermanent civil decree60 Days (Strict statutory ceiling)
Enforcement PowerDirect police and municipal bulldozer demolitionExecution under Order 21 CPC via court bailiffPolice patrol and Section 188 arrest
Average Timeline1 to 3 Months2 to 5 YearsSame day to 14 days
⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

6. The Role of Police Spot Reports & Municipal Engineer Inspections

When a Section 133 proceeding is initiated, the Executive Magistrate directs institutional field investigations to ascertain the ground reality:

  1. Police Station Spot Report (Todontoprotibedon): The local police station Officer-in-Charge directs an investigating officer to visit the locus in quo. The officer prepares an on-site sketch map (Noksha), records statements from neighboring residents, examines whether public access has been interrupted, and reports whether the obstruction poses an imminent public hazard.
  2. Municipal or Union Parishad Inspection: In urban areas (such as Dhaka City Corporation or Gazipur City Corporation), the Magistrate calls for an inspection report from the City Corporation Zonal Executive Officer or Assistant Engineer. The municipal engineer verifies approved master plan roads, official drainage lines, and determines whether the structure violates building setbacks.

Securing an accurate, photographic spot report is the single most critical factor in achieving a successful Section 133 order. An advocate guides the client in providing municipal road maps and photographic evidence directly to the investigating officers.

7. Making the Order Absolute & Criminal Penalties Under Section 188

If the respondent appears and shows cause against the conditional order, the Magistrate proceeds to take evidence in the matter as in a summons case under Section 137 of the CrPC.

The legal transition to final enforcement involves:

  • Making the Order Absolute (Section 137(3)): If the Magistrate is satisfied that the conditional order is reasonable and proper, the order is made Absolute. The Magistrate delivers a formal judgment commanding the respondent to perform the specified act (e.g. demolish the wall or clear the drain) within a fixed deadline.
  • Criminal Penalty Under Section 188 Penal Code: Under Section 136 and Section 140 of the CrPC, if the respondent fails to perform the act within the time specified in an absolute order, they become liable to the criminal penalties prescribed in Section 188 of the Penal Code 1860 (Disobedience to an order duly promulgated by a public servant), punishable with imprisonment up to six months and fines.
  • Criminal Revision Before Sessions Judge: An aggrieved party against whom an absolute order is passed can challenge the legality by filing a Criminal Revision under Section 435/439A CrPC before the Sessions Judge Court.

8. Demolition Protocol & Recovering Costs from the Offender

A uniquely powerful dimension of Section 133 is that the court does not rely on the goodwill of the offender to carry out demolition. Under Section 140 of the CrPC, if the absolute order is not obeyed within the specified time, the Magistrate may cause the act to be performed directly by state machinery.

The statutory enforcement mechanism operates as follows:

  1. Direction to Police and Municipal Authorities: The Magistrate issues a formal demolition requisition to the local Police Station and City Corporation / Pourashava engineering department.
  2. State-Supervised Demolition: Law enforcement personnel and municipal demolition crews enter the land, tear down the illegal brick wall, clear the obstructed drainage ditch, or dismantle the hazardous structure under police protection.
  3. Recovery of Demolition Expenses: Under Section 140(2), the entire financial cost incurred by the government in carrying out the demolition may be recovered from the offender either by the sale of any building materials removed, or by the distress and sale of any other movable property belonging to the offender as if it were a fine.

9. Illustrative Scenario: Removing an Illegal Wall Blocking a Pathway in Dhaka

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): In an established residential sector in Uttara, Dhaka, a 12-foot wide shared access road had been utilized by ten residential households for over thirty years to connect to the main avenue. An influential local plot owner purchased a corner parcel and constructed a 7-foot brick boundary wall extending 6 feet into the shared road, preventing emergency ambulances and vehicles from reaching neighboring houses, and severing the underground surface drainage pipe.

Facing intolerable nuisance and stagnant sewage flooding, the affected residents retained Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber. Our legal team launched a decisive Section 133 action:

  1. Drafted and filed an emergency petition under Section 133 CrPC before the Court of the Additional District Magistrate (ADM), Dhaka, submitting historical layout maps, City Corporation tax holding records, and photographs of the blocked passage and sewage overflow.
  2. The ADM issued an immediate Conditional Order directing the plot owner to demolish the wall within 10 days or show cause, while directing the local police station to submit an emergency Spot Report.
  3. Accompanied the police Sub-Inspector during the on-site inquiry, presenting statements from eight neighborhood residents confirming continuous public use of the road for three decades.
  4. When the plot owner appeared and claimed under Section 139A that the road was his private land, our advocates demonstrated that his own purchase deed referenced the 12-foot shared boundary road, disproving any reliable evidence of private ownership.
  5. The ADM rejected the Section 139A objection and made the conditional order Absolute under Section 137. When the owner failed to demolish the wall within 7 days, the Magistrate dispatched municipal bulldozers and police personnel under Section 140, completely demolishing the illegal wall, restoring the drainage line, and recovering all demolition costs from the offender.

10. Talk to an Advocate: Neighbor Dispute & Section 133 Litigation

Resolving contentious neighbor disputes, illegal road obstructions, and drainage nuisances in Bangladesh requires assertive advocacy before the Executive Magistracy and civil courts. Advocate Md. Shah Alam and his dedicated property litigation team provide complete representation across Uttara, Dhaka Metropolitan Courts, and the High Court Division.

Need an advocate for this matter in Bangladesh? Send your documents on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: a first document review can be done remotely.

Our principal chamber is located in Uttara, Dhaka, minutes from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, alongside our daily litigation chamber at the Dhaka Judge Court.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Section 133 of the CrPC in Bangladesh?

Section 133 CrPC is an emergency statutory mechanism empowering Executive Magistrates to issue conditional orders for the swift removal of public nuisances, blocked pathways, and hazardous drainage discharges.

Which court hears public nuisance cases under Section 133?

Section 133 petitions are heard by the Court of the Additional District Magistrate (ADM) in metropolitan districts or Upazila Nirbahi Officers (UNO) in rural upazilas.

What happens if a neighbor denies that a pathway is a public road?

Under Section 139A CrPC, the Magistrate inquires whether reliable evidence supports the denial. If reliable evidence exists, proceedings are stayed for civil court determination; if absent, the nuisance inquiry proceeds.

Can the magistrate order the demolition of an illegal wall under Section 133?

Yes. If the conditional order is made absolute under Section 137 and the offender fails to remove it, the magistrate can direct police and municipal bulldozers to demolish the wall under Section 140 CrPC.

Who pays for the cost of demolishing an illegal obstruction under Section 140?

Under Section 140(2) CrPC, all expenses incurred by the government in executing the demolition are recovered directly from the offender through the distress and sale of their property.

What is the penalty for disobeying a final order under Section 133?

Disobeying an absolute order under Section 133 CrPC constitutes a criminal offence under Section 188 of the Penal Code 1860, punishable with simple imprisonment up to six months and fines.

Can private drainage overflow be resolved under Section 133?

Yes. Discharging contaminated sewage or wastewater onto neighboring land or shared alleys creates a public health nuisance directly actionable under Section 133 CrPC.

Can an overseas property owner file a Section 133 petition from abroad?

Yes. An expatriate landowner whose property access is blocked in Bangladesh can file a Section 133 petition through an advocate or authorized local power of attorney.

1. Legal Anatomy of Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act 1881

Section 138 penalizes any person who draws a cheque on a bank account maintained by them for the discharge of debt or liability, and such cheque returns unpaid due to insufficiency of funds or exceeding agreed overdraft limits.

2. Is Cheque Bounce a Bailable Offence in Bangladesh?

Yes, offences under Section 138 NI Act are bailable by law. Upon issuance of summons or arrest warrants, an accused represented by an advocate can surrender before the Sessions Judge / Joint Metropolitan Sessions Court and obtain regular bail upon furnishing bail bonds.

3. Strict Statutory Timelines: Dishonour to Filing

The legal procedure is time-barred by strict limitation rules: (1) Cheque must be deposited within 6 months of validity; (2) Legal notice served within 30 days of dishonour memo; (3) 30-day grace period for payment; (4) Formal petition filed within 30 days after expiration of grace period.

4. Mandatory 50% Pre-Deposit Requirement for Appeal

Under Section 138A of the NI Act, if a convicted debtor intends to appeal against a conviction judgment, they must deposit at least 50% of the awarded cheque sum with the trial court before the appeal is admitted.

6. Section 138 NI Act vs Section 420 Penal Code

While Section 420 of the Penal Code 1860 deals with general cheating and fraud, Section 138 NI Act is a specialized commercial recovery mechanism providing direct monetary compensation to the victim alongside penal deterrence.

entries.body:
Section 144 & 145 CrPC in Bangladesh: Land Possession & Emergency Injunction Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-08 · 19 minutes

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

When rival claimants, land grabbers, or corrupt syndicates attempt to trespass onto private property, commence unauthorized boundary wall construction, or forcibly dispossess rightful occupants in Bangladesh, civil litigation often moves too slowly to prevent physical dispossession. Instituting a Title Suit in an Assistant Judge Court can take years to yield a final decree. To prevent immediate bloodshed, breach of the public peace, and unlawful encroachment, the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC) equips land owners with urgent quasi-criminal statutory remedies before the Executive Magistrate Court under Section 144 and Section 145. These provisions empower magistrates to issue restraining orders, direct emergency police spot inquiries, maintain actual physical possession, and attach disputed properties under Section 146. This comprehensive legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate and land law specialist in Uttara and Dhaka Court, explains how to petition the Executive Magistrate, enforce police restraining orders, and transition to civil court title defense.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

  3. 3. Section 145 CrPC: Determining and Restoring Actual Possession
  4. 4. The Two-Month Forcible Dispossession Rule Under Section 145(4)
  5. 5. Legal Matrix: Section 144 vs. Section 145 vs. Civil Injunction
  6. 6. The Role of Police Spot Inquiry & AC Land Revenue Reports
  7. 7. Section 146 CrPC: Attachment of Disputed Property & Receivership
  8. 8. Transitioning from Magistrate Orders to Civil Court Title Suits
  9. 9. Illustrative Scenario: Thwarting Commercial Land Grabbing in Dhaka
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate: Emergency Land Protection & CrPC Petitions

1. Statutory Foundation: Emergency Land Powers Under CrPC

In Bangladesh, property disputes routinely present dual dimensions: the underlying legal title (proprietary ownership) and physical de facto possession on the ground. While the determination of title belongs exclusively to civil courts under the Specific Relief Act 1877, the maintenance of public order and preservation of physical possession falls within the emergency statutory jurisdiction of the Executive Magistracy under the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC).

Under Chapter XII of the CrPC (Sections 144 to 148), Parliament empowered Executive Magistrates—specifically the Additional District Magistrate (ADM) in metropolitan districts and Upazila Nirbahi Officers (UNO) in upazilas—to intervene decisively when real estate disputes threaten public tranquility. These provisions do not adjudicate who owns the land; their statutory purpose is to prevent parties from taking the law into their own hands, enforcing an immediate freeze on violence, and identifying who was in physical occupancy.

Understanding how to deploy Section 144 and Section 145 enables landowners to protect ancestral homesteads, commercial plots, and vacant boundaries from sudden physical invasion while preparing permanent civil suits. For comprehensive title vetting protocols, examine our guide on land registration and title procedures in Bangladesh.

2. Section 144 CrPC: Urgent Injunctions to Prevent Breach of Peace

Section 144 of the CrPC confers sweeping summary powers upon an Executive Magistrate in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger. In the context of real estate disputes, Section 144 is invoked when an opposing party brings armed laborers, bulldozers, or construction materials to forcefully alter the boundary line, demolish fences, or harvest standing agricultural crops.

Key procedural features of a Section 144 land petition include:

  • Ex-Parte Restraining Order: If the danger of violence is immediate, the Magistrate can pass an emergency ex-parte order on the same day the petition is filed, directing both parties to maintain strict status quo and refrain from entering the disputed land.
  • Police Direction for Enforcement: The Magistrate directs the Officer-in-Charge (OC) of the local police station to physically serve the order on the trespassers, maintain strict surveillance, and prevent any construction activity.
  • Statutory 60-Day Ceiling: Under Section 144(6), an order issued by an Executive Magistrate remains in force for a maximum duration of sixty (60) days, unless extended by the Government by notification in the official Gazette.
  • Show Cause Hearing: The opposing party is issued a show-cause notice to appear within 7 to 15 days to present their documents, allowing the magistrate to rescind, modify, or convert the proceedings.

3. Section 145 CrPC: Determining and Restoring Actual Possession

While Section 144 provides temporary 60-day emergency relief, Section 145 of the CrPC is the dedicated statutory mechanism for resolving active possession disputes concerning land, water, or building premises. Section 145 is triggered whenever the Magistrate is satisfied from a police report or private application that a dispute likely to cause a breach of the peace exists concerning any immovable property.

The statutory proceeding under Section 145 unfolds through strict legal steps:

  1. Preliminary Order (Section 145(1)): The Magistrate passes a formal order in writing stating the grounds of being satisfied regarding the breach of peace, requiring the parties to attend court and submit written statements of their respective claims regarding the fact of actual physical possession.
  2. Inquiry Solely on Fact of Possession: Under Section 145(4), the Magistrate's jurisdiction is strictly confined to inquiring into which party was in actual physical possession on the date of the preliminary order. The Magistrate is statutorily prohibited from inquiring into or determining the legal title of the parties.
  3. Final Declaration of Possession (Section 145(6)): If the Magistrate determines that one party was in lawful possession, the court issues an order declaring that party entitled to possession until evicted therefrom in due course of law by a competent civil court, and strictly forbidding all disturbance of such possession in the interim.

4. The Two-Month Forcible Dispossession Rule Under Section 145(4)

Facing imminent land grabbing, trespass, or boundary encroachment? Contact our land dispute litigation team immediately on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007. We provide emergency magistrate filings and police coordination.

A crucial legal safeguard that protects vulnerable landowners who have already suffered physical violence is the proviso to Section 145(4) of the CrPC. Land grabbers frequently invade property at midnight, erect tin-shed structures, and then falsely claim to the court that they are in peaceful current possession.

The law explicitly anticipates and defeats this tactic:

  • The Statutory 2-Month Window: Under the first proviso to Section 145(4), if it appears to the Magistrate that any party has been forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed from the property within two (2) months next before the date of the preliminary order, the Magistrate may treat the party so dispossessed as if they had been in possession on such date.
  • Restoration of Physical Possession: Under Section 145(6), the Magistrate possesses full statutory authority to direct the local police to physically evict the trespassers, remove their temporary structures, and restore physical occupancy to the rightful party who was dispossessed within the two-month window.
  • Strict Burden of Proof: The dispossessed owner must produce evidence (such as recent utility bills, photograph records, police GD receipts, and witness affidavits) demonstrating that their physical occupancy existed within the preceding 60 days.

5. Legal Matrix: Section 144 vs. Section 145 vs. Civil Injunction

6. The Role of Police Spot Inquiry & AC Land Revenue Reports

When a petition is admitted under Section 144 or Section 145, the Executive Magistrate does not rely solely on affidavits. The court calls for formal institutional reports that form the backbone of the judicial record:

  1. Police Spot Inquiry Report (Todontoprotibedon): The Magistrate directs the local Police Station to conduct a physical visit to the disputed land. An officer of the rank of Sub-Inspector visits the plot, interrogates neighboring landowners, inspects physical boundary pillars, verifies who possesses the keys, and prepares a written report stating whether tension exists and who is in physical control.
  2. AC Land Revenue Verification Report: In complex cases, the Magistrate directs the Assistant Commissioner (Land) to examine the official revenue record. The Union Land Assistant Officer (Tehsildar) inspects the CS, SA, RS, and City Jarip (BS) Khatians, verifies e-Namjari mutation records, and reports whether the government retains any Khas land interest.

Landowners must actively monitor these inquiries through their advocate. Submitting certified copies of mutation Khatians, tax dakhilas, and approved building plans directly to the investigating police officer ensures that the formal report reflects authentic factual ownership.

7. Section 146 CrPC: Attachment of Disputed Property & Receivership

In situations where both parties claim physical possession and produce contradictory evidence such that the Magistrate is unable to satisfy themselves as to who was in actual possession, the law provides an emergency safeguard: Section 146 of the CrPC.

Under Section 146(1), if the Magistrate decides that none of the parties was in possession, or is unable to determine who was in possession, the Magistrate may attach the subject of dispute until a competent civil court has determined the rights of the parties or the claim to possession.

Key implications of an attachment order under Section 146 include:

  • Appointment of a Receiver: Under Section 146(2), the Magistrate may appoint a Receiver (often the local Union Land Assistant Officer or a government official) to take custody of the land, harvest crops, collect commercial rents, and deposit proceeds into the government treasury.
  • Exclusion of Both Parties: Both rival claimants are physically barred from entering the property. No construction, cultivation, or leasing can occur while the attachment persists.
  • Withdrawal of Attachment: The attachment continues until a civil court passes an injunction decree or final judgment settling title, at which point the civil court directs the Receiver to hand over possession to the decree holder.

8. Transitioning from Magistrate Orders to Civil Court Title Suits

A critical strategic reality in Bangladeshi land litigation is that an order under Section 145 CrPC is never a final determination of ownership. It is a police power order designed to maintain order pending civil adjudication. A clever trespasser who manipulates a local police report may temporarily win a Section 145 declaration, but that order is completely subservient to a decree from a competent civil court.

To convert temporary magistrate protection into permanent legal security, landowners must coordinate two judicial tracks:

  • Institution of a Civil Title Suit: File a formal Title Suit for Declaration of Title and Recovery/Confirmation of Possession before the Assistant Judge or Joint District Judge under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act 1877.
  • Application for Temporary Injunction (Order 39 Rules 1 & 2 CPC): Move an application in the civil suit for a Temporary Injunction restraining the defendant from entering the land or altering its nature. Once the civil court issues an injunction order, that civil order legally supersedes any conflicting magistrate order under Section 145.
  • Criminal Revision Before Sessions Judge: If an Executive Magistrate passes an illegal order under Section 144 or 145, the aggrieved party can challenge it by filing a Criminal Revision under Section 435/439A of the CrPC before the Sessions Judge Court. Read our guide on property partition lawsuits in Bangladesh.

9. Illustrative Scenario: Thwarting Commercial Land Grabbing in Dhaka

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): An overseas Bangladeshi engineer residing in Melbourne owned a 5-katha commercial plot in Uttara Sector 18, Dhaka, purchased through a registered Saf-Kabala deed with updated AC Land e-Namjari mutation. While the owner was abroad, a politically connected real estate broker entered the vacant plot with armed thugs, broke the boundary gate, dumped construction gravel, and claimed to hold an unverified unregistered bayna agreement.

Informed by local security, the expatriate engaged Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber. Our litigation team moved swiftly:

  1. Filed an emergency petition under Section 144/145 CrPC before the Court of the Additional District Magistrate (ADM), Dhaka, attaching certified copies of the registered title deed, mutation Khatian, and current year land tax dakhila.
  2. Obtained an immediate ex-parte restraining order from the ADM directing both parties to maintain strict status quo and ordering the Officer-in-Charge of the local police station to submit an emergency Spot Inquiry Report.
  3. Accompanied the police Sub-Inspector during the on-site investigation, presenting original revenue records and securing neighbor statements verifying that the client had maintained unbroken possession for over eight years.
  4. When the grabbers attempted to construct a temporary boundary wall in violation of the order, moved an emergency application before the ADM, who directed police to halt construction immediately and seize the building materials.
  5. Converted the interim protection into a final Section 145 declaration of possession, while simultaneously instituting a Title Suit in the civil court to obtain a permanent injunction, permanently shielding the property from further encroachment.

10. Talk to an Advocate: Emergency Land Protection & CrPC Petitions

If your ancestral land, commercial property, or boundary premises in Bangladesh is threatened by illegal grabbing, trespass, or construction encroachment, swift intervention before the Executive Magistracy and civil courts is essential. Advocate Md. Shah Alam and his experienced land litigation team provide rapid representation across Uttara, Dhaka Metropolitan Courts, and the High Court Division.

Need an advocate for this matter in Bangladesh? Send your documents on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: a first document review can be done remotely.

Our principal chamber is located in Uttara, Dhaka, minutes from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, alongside our daily litigation chamber at the Dhaka Judge Court.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can an Executive Magistrate decide who owns land in a Section 144 or 145 case?

No. The Executive Magistrate has zero legal jurisdiction to decide proprietary title or ownership. The magistrate's authority under Section 144 and 145 CrPC is strictly confined to maintaining public peace and inquiring into actual physical possession.

How long does a Section 144 restraining order remain valid?

Under Section 144(6) of the CrPC, an order issued by an Executive Magistrate is valid for a maximum duration of sixty (60) days, unless formally extended by a government gazette notification.

What is the two-month rule in Section 145 CrPC land cases?

Under the first proviso to Section 145(4), if a party was forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed within two (2) months prior to the date of the magistrate's preliminary order, the court can treat them as if they were in possession and restore their physical occupancy.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi (NRB) file a Section 144 or 145 petition from abroad?

Yes. An expatriate owner can file an emergency petition through an advocate or an authorized local attorney holding a duly executed and authenticated Special Power of Attorney.

What happens if both parties produce confusing claims of possession?

If the magistrate cannot determine which party was in actual possession, the court can attach the property under Section 146 CrPC and appoint a Receiver to manage the land until a civil court determines ownership.

What is the difference between a civil injunction and a Section 144 order?

A civil injunction under Order 39 CPC protects legal title and can remain in force for years throughout a civil lawsuit. A Section 144 CrPC order is a 60-day police-enforced emergency measure designed to prevent immediate bloodshed and violence.

What happens if someone violates a Section 144 order issued by a Magistrate?

Violating an order under Section 144 CrPC constitutes a criminal offence punishable under Section 188 of the Penal Code 1860 (disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant), leading to criminal prosecution and police arrest.

How do I challenge an illegal order passed by an Executive Magistrate?

An illegal or arbitrary order passed by an Executive Magistrate under Section 144 or 145 CrPC can be challenged by filing a Criminal Revision under Section 435/439A of the CrPC before the Sessions Judge Court.

entries.body:
Second Marriage Without Divorce: Section 494 Penal Code Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-09 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Marrying a second partner while a previous legal marriage remains legally subsisting is one of the most contentious issues in Bangladeshi family and criminal jurisprudence. Spouses frequently believe that an informal separation, a verbal pronouncement of talaq, or an affidavit of marriage entered into abroad terminates their marital ties. Under the Penal Code 1860, marrying again during the lifetime of a husband or wife without a prior, legally completed divorce constitutes the criminal offence of bigamy under Section 494, punishable with rigorous imprisonment up to seven years. Furthermore, for Muslim citizens, contracted polygamous unions without prior statutory permission violate Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, triggering separate criminal penalties and immediate dower liabilities.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

📋 In This Article
