  2. 2. Muslim Husbands: Polygamy Restrictions under Section 6 of MFLO 1961
  3. 3. When a Wife Marries Without Divorce: Absolute Criminal Bigamy
  4. 4. The 90-Day Legal Rule: Why Verbal Talaq or Unregistered Divorce Fails
  5. 5. Procedure to File a CR Case Before the Judicial Magistrate Court
  6. 6. Summary Matrix: Section 494 Penal Code vs. Section 6 MFLO 1961
  7. 7. Financial Penalties: Immediate Dower Acceleration and Family Court Maintenance
  8. 8. Illustrative Scenario: Litigating an Unauthorized Second Marriage
  9. 9. Cross-Border & NRB Considerations: Foreign Marriages and Evidentiary Proof
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate

1. Core Elements of Bigamy under Section 494 of the Penal Code 1860

Section 494 of the Penal Code 1860 establishes that whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

To sustain a criminal conviction under Section 494, the prosecution or complainant must prove three essential factual ingredients beyond reasonable doubt:

  • First Marriage Subsisting: The accused had entered into a legally valid first marriage that was recognized under their personal law, and that first marriage had not been dissolved by a final, lawful decree of divorce or death.
  • Spouse Living: The first spouse was alive at the time the second marriage ceremony was performed.
  • Second Marriage Contracted: The accused entered into a second ceremony of marriage which would have been valid but for the subsistence of the prior marriage.

Under Schedule II of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, an offence under Section 494 is classified as non-cognizable (meaning the police cannot register an FIR directly without a Magistrate's order), bailable, and compoundable by the aggrieved husband or wife with the permission of the court.

2. Muslim Husbands: Polygamy Restrictions under Section 6 of MFLO 1961

Under classical Islamic jurisprudence, a Muslim male is permitted up to four simultaneous wives under strict conditions of equal treatment. However, in Bangladesh, this religious permission is heavily regulated and restricted by Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (MFLO).

Under Section 6(1) of the MFLO, no man, during the subsistence of an existing marriage, shall, except with the previous permission in writing of the Arbitration Council, contract another marriage, nor shall any such marriage contracted without such permission be registered under the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974. The Arbitration Council consists of the Chairman of the local Union Parishad, Ward Councillor, or Cantonment Executive Officer, alongside a representative of the husband and each existing wife.

Permission is only granted under statutory rules upon proof that the existing wife is sterile, physically unfit for conjugal relations, or mentally incapacitated. If a husband marries without such written permission, he commits a direct statutory offence under Section 6(5) of the MFLO, rendering him liable to imprisonment up to one year or a fine up to 10,000 BDT, or both. For more details on husband and wife rights in polygamous marriages, review our analysis on polygamy law and second marriage in Bangladesh.

3. When a Wife Marries Without Divorce: Absolute Criminal Bigamy

While Muslim men have a conditional, heavily regulated statutory procedure under the MFLO to take a second wife, no personal law in Bangladesh—whether Muslim, Hindu, Christian, or Buddhist—permits a married woman to contract a second marriage while her first marriage subsists.

Polyandry is strictly void under all legal systems in Bangladesh. Consequently, if a married woman contracts a second marriage with another man without obtaining a final legal divorce from her first husband, that second marriage is completely void ab initio. The woman is directly punishable under Section 494 of the Penal Code with up to seven years of imprisonment.

Dealing with bigamy, unlawful second marriage, or matrimonial fraud in Bangladesh? Consult an experienced family and criminal defense advocate. Reach out on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for confidential legal assessment.

Furthermore, the second husband, if he entered into the marriage knowing or having reason to believe that the woman was already the lawful wife of another living man, can be prosecuted as an abettor under Section 109 of the Penal Code or charged with adultery or fraudulent marriage under related provisions. For an in-depth examination of second marriage consequences, see our guide on second marriage rights and legal consequences in Bangladesh.

4. The 90-Day Legal Rule: Why Verbal Talaq or Unregistered Divorce Fails

A widespread defense asserted by defendants facing Section 494 or Section 6 MFLO charges is that they had verbally pronounced talaq to their spouse, signed an informal separation paper on non-judicial stamp paper, or left the marital home months before the second marriage occurred. In Bangladeshi courts, this defense routinely collapses.

Under Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, any husband who pronounces talaq in any form whatsoever must immediately give written notice of having done so to the Chairman of the Union Parishad or City Corporation, and must supply a copy thereof to the wife. Talaq does not take legal effect until the expiration of ninety (90) days from the day on which notice is delivered to the Chairman.

During these ninety days, the marriage remains fully legally intact. If a spouse marries before the formal 90-day period expires and before the Chairman issues the final Failure of Reconciliation Certificate, the prior marriage is still in force at law, rendering the second marriage strictly bigamous and illegal. For comprehensive procedural rules on divorce completion, review our step-by-step guide on divorce procedure in Bangladesh.

5. Procedure to File a CR Case Before the Judicial Magistrate Court

Because Section 494 of the Penal Code is non-cognizable, police officers will not register an FIR on a walk-in basis at a police station. Instead, the legal remedy requires the aggrieved spouse to file a Complaint Register (CR) case directly in the court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) pursuant to Section 190 and Section 198 of the CrPC.

Under Section 198 of the CrPC, no court shall take cognizance of an offence under Chapter XX of the Penal Code (which includes Section 494) except upon a complaint made by some person aggrieved by the offence—specifically the first husband or first wife. The complainant, accompanied by an advocate, appears before the Magistrate to give sworn testimony under Section 200 CrPC.

The complainant must submit documentary evidence demonstrating the first marriage (the certified Nikahnama and marriage certificate) alongside proof of the second marriage (such as the second Nikahnama, wedding invitation cards, photographs, or witness affidavits). Upon examining the complainant, the Magistrate either issues a summons or warrant of arrest directly under Section 204 CrPC, or directs a local judicial inquiry under Section 202 CrPC. If you need assistance with Magistrate complaints, review our guide on criminal complaint procedures in Bangladesh.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

6. Summary Matrix: Section 494 Penal Code vs. Section 6 MFLO 1961

Complainants and legal practitioners frequently evaluate whether to invoke the general Penal Code, the specific 1961 Family Ordinance, or both. The following comparative matrix outlines the operational differences:

Legal Dimension Section 494 Penal Code 1860 Section 6 Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961
Target Offence Bigamy (second marriage void due to subsisting first marriage) Contracting second marriage without Arbitration Council permission
Applicability All citizens (Muslim, Hindu, Christian, Buddhist) Muslim male citizens residing in Bangladesh or abroad
Maximum Imprisonment Imprisonment up to 7 years Imprisonment up to 1 year
Financial Fine Discretionary judicial fine Fine up to 10,000 BDT + immediate payment of entire dower
Cognizance Route CR Case filed by aggrieved spouse under Section 198 CrPC Complaint filed by existing wife or Arbitration Council Chairman
Validity of Second Union Completely void ab initio Marriage remains legally valid under personal law despite penalty

7. Financial Penalties: Immediate Dower Acceleration and Family Court Maintenance

Beyond criminal prosecution and jail terms, contracting an unauthorized second marriage triggers immediate, severe civil financial liabilities under Bangladeshi family law. The most significant of these is the automatic acceleration of the wife's dower (Denmohar).

Under Section 6(5)(a) of the MFLO 1961, any husband who enters into a second marriage without statutory permission must immediately pay the entire amount of the dower, whether prompt (Mu'ajjal) or deferred (Muwajjal), due to the existing wife or wives. Any deferred dower that was previously payable only upon divorce or the husband's death becomes immediately due and payable in full on the day of the second marriage ceremony.

If the husband fails to pay the dower immediately, the existing wife can file a suit in the Family Court under the Family Courts Act 2023 for recovery of the full dower amount along with past and ongoing monthly maintenance (Nafaqah). The Family Court possesses the power to attach the husband's bank accounts, garnish salary, seize immovable properties, and commit the husband to civil jail for non-payment. For a detailed guide on dower recovery, consult our resource on dower and maintenance recovery in Bangladesh.

8. Illustrative Scenario: Litigating an Unauthorized Second Marriage

To illustrate how bigamy litigation unfolds in the courts of Dhaka, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A software architect living in the United Kingdom married a Bangladeshi woman in Dhaka in 2018, properly registering the Nikahnama. In 2023, while residing in London, the husband sent a brief WhatsApp message stating he was divorcing her, but never served written notice on the City Corporation Mayor or sent formal notices pursuant to Section 7 of the MFLO. Six months later, he returned to Dhaka and secretly married a second woman, registering a new marriage through a local Kazi.

Upon discovering the second marriage, the first wife engaged a Supreme Court advocate in Dhaka. The advocate verified that no divorce proceedings had ever been filed with the City Corporation Arbitration Council, rendering the first marriage fully subsisting under law. The advocate filed a Complaint Register (CR) case before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court under Section 494 of the Penal Code and Section 6(5) of the MFLO.

The CMM Court issued an arrest warrant against the husband. Simultaneously, the wife filed a Family Court suit for recovery of her 25 Lakh BDT dower and maintenance. Confronted with criminal detention and asset attachment, the husband was compelled to appear, deposit substantial financial security, and ultimately negotiate a comprehensive legal settlement granting the first wife full financial recovery.

9. Cross-Border & NRB Considerations: Foreign Marriages and Evidentiary Proof

Cross-border bigamy cases involving non-resident Bangladeshis in North America, Europe, and Australia are increasingly common. In many instances, a spouse who is legally married in Bangladesh travels abroad and enters into a civil marriage with a foreign national to obtain immigration residency or citizenship, falsely declaring themselves 'single' on visa applications.

If you are an aggrieved spouse residing in Bangladesh or abroad, securing admissible evidentiary proof is the cornerstone of criminal prosecution:

  • Procure the Original Certified Nikahnama: Obtain a certified copy (Nokol) of the first marriage record from the Kazi office or District Registrar, attested by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA).
  • Gather Proof of the Second Marriage: Obtain certified copies of the second marriage certificate, whether registered in Bangladesh or abroad (e.g., UK General Register Office or US County marriage records). Foreign documents must be authenticated and apostilled.
  • Verify Municipal Divorce Status: Request an official certificate from the relevant City Corporation Mayor or Union Parishad Chairman confirming that no Section 7 MFLO divorce notice was received or that reconciliation proceedings were never concluded.
  • Execute Power of Attorney for Court Filing: An overseas spouse does not need to travel to Bangladesh to initiate litigation; they can execute an embassy-attested Special Power of Attorney authorizing a lawyer or relative to file the CR complaint and Family Court suit.

For dedicated assistance with cross-border matrimonial litigation, consult our specialized divorce and family lawyer services in Bangladesh and criminal defense counsel.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a Family & Criminal Law Advocate: To file a CR bigamy case under Section 494 Penal Code, recover unpaid dower and maintenance, or defend against false allegations, message our chamber on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call our direct line at +880 1712-655546. Overseas spouses can instruct counsel via power of attorney.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is second marriage without divorce a crime in Bangladesh?

Yes. Under Section 494 of the Penal Code 1860, marrying again while a first marriage subsists is the criminal offence of bigamy, punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. For Muslim men, contracting a second marriage without Arbitration Council permission also violates Section 6 of the MFLO 1961.

Can a Muslim husband marry a second wife legally in Bangladesh?

A Muslim husband may only marry a second wife if he submits a formal application and obtains prior written permission from the statutory Arbitration Council under Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961. Without this permission, the second marriage is a criminal offence.

What is the punishment under Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961?

Under Section 6(5) of the MFLO, contracting a second marriage without written permission is punishable with simple imprisonment up to one year, or a fine up to 10,000 BDT, or both, alongside the immediate mandatory payment of the entire dower to the existing wife.

Does an informal separation or verbal talaq protect against bigamy charges?

No. A verbal talaq has no legal effect under Section 7 of the MFLO 1961. A divorce only becomes legally final after written notice is served on the City Corporation or Union Parishad Chairman and ninety days elapse. Marrying before this period is bigamy.

Can a wife file a police FIR directly for bigamy in Bangladesh?

No. Section 494 of the Penal Code is non-cognizable under Schedule II of the CrPC. Police cannot register an FIR directly. The aggrieved spouse must file a Complaint Register (CR) case directly before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or Chief Judicial Magistrate Court.

What happens to the wife's dower (Denmohar) if the husband marries a second wife?

Under Section 6(5)(a) of the MFLO, the entire dower—both prompt and deferred—becomes immediately payable in full on the date of the second marriage. The existing wife can immediately file a Family Court suit to recover the full amount.

Is Section 494 Penal Code bailable in Bangladesh?

Yes. Section 494 is classified as bailable and compoundable with the permission of the court under Schedule II of the CrPC. However, if warrants are issued and the accused absconds, the court may refuse bail until appearance or surrender.

Can an overseas wife sue her Bangladeshi husband for bigamy from abroad?

Yes. An overseas wife can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission in her country of residence, empowering an advocate in Dhaka to file both the CR criminal case and Family Court financial claims.

Section 54 CrPC Arrest Without Warrant Bangladesh – Rights, Remedies & Challenges

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-06 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) gives police in Bangladesh the authority to arrest a person without a warrant under nine specific grounds. While this power exists to protect public order and enable rapid law enforcement, it has historically been misused for arbitrary detention. The landmark BLAST v Bangladesh Supreme Court case established 15 binding safeguards that police must follow — and knowing these safeguards is your most powerful defence against an unlawful arrest.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order

📋 In This Article

  5. What Police Must Do After a Section 54 Arrest
  6. Habeas Corpus Petition at the High Court

What Is Section 54 CrPC and Why Does It Matter?

Section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC) — as applied in Bangladesh — is the primary statutory provision that empowers police officers to arrest a person without an arrest warrant issued by a magistrate. Unlike a regular arrest based on a court-issued warrant, a Section 54 arrest is a unilateral police action requiring no prior judicial authorisation.

This power is extraordinary because it overrides the ordinary rule that deprivation of liberty requires judicial approval. Bangladesh courts have consistently recognised that arrest without warrant represents one of the most acute interferences with individual freedom guaranteed under Article 32 of the Constitution (protection of right to life and personal liberty) and Article 33 (safeguards as to arrest and detention).

Section 54 has been chronically misused in Bangladesh for:

  • Detaining political opponents or activists
  • Arresting persons to extort money or extract confessions
  • Harassing individuals without any genuine suspicion of an offence
  • Circumventing the warrant requirement by fabricating grounds for suspicion

Understanding your rights under Section 54, and the protections the Supreme Court has built around it, is therefore not merely academic — it is potentially life-saving.

The Nine Grounds for Arrest Without Warrant Under Section 54

Section 54 of the CrPC lists nine specific situations in which a police officer may arrest a person without a warrant. These are the only legally valid grounds — any arrest purportedly under Section 54 that does not fit one of these grounds is unlawful:

  1. Cognizable offence involvement: The person has been involved in or reasonably suspected to have been involved in any cognizable offence (an offence for which police can arrest without warrant under the First Schedule to the CrPC).
  2. Proclaimed offender: The person is a proclaimed offender (publicly declared as wanted by a court).
  3. Possession of stolen property: The person is found in possession of any implement of housebreaking, or property reasonably suspected to be stolen.
  4. Housebreaker or suspected housebreaker: The person is a reputed thief, housebreaker, or someone known to associate with such criminals.
  5. Obstruction of justice: The person has been concerned in or is reasonably suspected to have been concerned in a cognizable offence committed outside Bangladesh.
  6. Deserter from armed forces: The person is reasonably suspected to be a deserter from the Bangladesh Army, Navy, or Air Force.
  7. Released convict under restriction: The person, being a released convict, commits a breach of any rule relating to notification of address.
  8. Warrant from another district: A requisition has been received from another police station requiring the arrest of the person.
  9. Persons in suspicious circumstances at night: A person who is found at night with no satisfactory explanation of their presence near any place where a recent cognizable offence was committed.

In practice, ground (1) — cognizable offence suspicion — is by far the most commonly invoked. The critical word is reasonably suspected: mere suspicion without reasonable basis is insufficient to justify a Section 54 arrest.

The Landmark BLAST v Bangladesh Case (55 DLR 2003)

The most important judicial decision on Section 54 arrests in Bangladesh is Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST) v Bangladesh, reported at 55 DLR 363 (2003) — commonly known as the BLAST case. This was a public interest litigation filed before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court challenging the systematic misuse of Section 54 and Section 167 (remand) powers by police.

The High Court Division conducted extensive hearings, examined evidence of police abuse, and ultimately issued a landmark judgment that:

  1. Declared that Section 54 arrests as commonly practised were frequently unconstitutional, violating Articles 27, 31, 32, 33, and 35 of the Constitution.
  2. Issued 15 specific directions (safeguards) that police must follow in every Section 54 arrest — which function as binding rules of conduct enforceable through contempt of court proceedings.
  3. Called upon the Legislature to amend Section 54 and Section 167 CrPC to bring them into conformity with constitutional requirements.
  4. Held that Bangladesh must pay compensation to victims of unlawful Section 54 arrests.

The BLAST case was appealed to the Appellate Division, which substantially upheld the High Court directions while modifying some procedural aspects. As a result, the 15 safeguards from the BLAST case currently constitute the binding legal framework for all Section 54 arrests in Bangladesh.

The 15 Safeguards for Section 54 Arrests – Full Table

Following the BLAST v Bangladesh decision, the following 15 safeguards are currently mandatory for every Section 54 arrest in Bangladesh. Violation of any of these safeguards by police renders the arrest unlawful and opens the arresting officer to civil and criminal liability:

#SafeguardDetails
1Grounds to be disclosedPolice must immediately inform the arrested person of the grounds of arrest in a language they understand.
2No torture or coercionNo physical or mental torture or coercion of any kind during arrest or detention.
3Inform nearest relativePolice must immediately inform the nearest relative or friend of the arrested person about the arrest and place of detention.
424-hour production ruleThe arrested person must be produced before the nearest Judicial Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding transit time.
5Right to engage a lawyerPolice must allow the arrested person to consult a lawyer of their choice before the first production before the magistrate.
6Medical examination on arrestA medical examination must be conducted by a government medical officer at the time of arrest to document the arrested person physical condition.
7Medical examination after interrogationA further medical examination must be conducted after each interrogation session to detect any injury inflicted during questioning.
8No interrogation without lawyerInterrogation cannot commence until the arrested person has been given a reasonable opportunity to engage a lawyer.
9Register of arrested personsEvery police station must maintain an accurate register of all persons arrested under Section 54, open to inspection by the magistrate and relatives.
10Reasons to be recordedThe arresting officer must record the specific reasons for the arrest in the General Diary at the time of arrest.
11Magistrate inquiry before remandBefore granting remand (police custody), the magistrate must ask the arrested person if they have been tortured and must examine their physical condition.
12Remand in exceptional cases onlyPolice remand should be granted sparingly and only for cogent reasons. Routine remand requests must be refused.
13Lawyer present during remand interrogationThe arrested person lawyer must be allowed to be present outside the interrogation room during police remand (in view but not in hearing).
14Compensation for unlawful arrestWhere a Section 54 arrest is found to be unlawful, the State must pay compensation to the victim.
15Right to free legal aidPersons who cannot afford a lawyer must be informed of their right to free legal aid and assisted in accessing it.

What Police Must Do After a Section 54 Arrest

Following the BLAST case directions and existing provisions of the CrPC, police have specific mandatory obligations after making a Section 54 arrest:

  • Immediate disclosure of grounds: The arrested person must be told why they are being arrested in language they understand, at the time of arrest.
  • Entry in General Diary: The arrest must be recorded in the police station General Diary with the time, date, place, and specific grounds within minutes of arrest.
  • Inform family: The nearest relative must be notified as soon as possible — delay in notifying family is itself a violation of the BLAST directions.
  • Medical examination: A government doctor must examine the arrested person before any interrogation begins.
  • Production before magistrate within 24 hours: This is a constitutional mandate under Article 33(2). Failure to produce the arrested person within 24 hours (excluding travel time) is unlawful detention and constitutes an independent violation of constitutional rights.
  • Bail consideration: If the police cannot file a charge sheet within 24 hours, the arrested person may apply for bail before the magistrate, who must consider the application on its merits.

Violations of these obligations — especially failure to produce within 24 hours and failure to notify family — are unfortunately still common in Bangladesh. Knowing and asserting these rights firmly (or having a lawyer do so) is critical to preventing prolonged unlawful detention.

Habeas Corpus Petition at the High Court

If a person is unlawfully detained — whether under Section 54 or any other provision — the most powerful legal remedy available in Bangladesh is a habeas corpus petition filed at the High Court Division of the Supreme Court under Article 102(2)(b) of the Constitution.

A habeas corpus petition literally means produce the body — it commands the detaining authority to bring the detained person before the court and justify the legality of the detention. If the court finds the detention unlawful, it orders immediate release.

Key features of the habeas corpus remedy in Bangladesh:

  • Who can file: Any person — including family members, lawyers, or human rights organisations — can file on behalf of the detained person. The detained person themselves need not be physically present to file the petition.
  • Urgency: The High Court treats habeas corpus petitions with priority. Urgent cases can be listed for hearing within hours of filing.
  • Effect of rule: When the High Court issues a Rule calling upon the government to show cause, it typically also directs that the detained person be produced before the court and may grant interim bail pending the hearing.
  • Burden of proof: The burden is on the detaining authority (police/government) to justify the legality of the detention. If they cannot, the court orders release.
  • Compensation: Consistent with the BLAST directions, the High Court has the power to award monetary compensation against the State for unlawful detention.

Compensation for Wrongful Arrest in Bangladesh

Bangladesh law recognises the right to compensation for victims of wrongful arrest and unlawful detention, though the remedies are not as systematically developed as in some jurisdictions. Currently available compensation mechanisms include:

Constitutional Compensation Under Article 102

Following the BLAST case, the High Court has awarded compensation in cases of proven unlawful Section 54 arrests under its Article 102 jurisdiction. Compensation amounts have varied but tend to be modest, reflecting the underdeveloped nature of this remedy. Establishing the quantum of compensation requires demonstrating loss of income, physical harm, and psychological suffering.

Civil Suit for Damages

A person wrongfully arrested may file a civil suit for damages against the State (under the Government Pleaders Act) and the individual police officer responsible for the unlawful arrest. Claims can include general damages for loss of liberty, special damages for lost income and medical expenses, and in egregious cases, exemplary damages.

Complaint to the National Human Rights Commission

The National Human Rights Commission of Bangladesh (established under the National Human Rights Commission Act 2009) can investigate complaints of unlawful arrest and recommend compensation. While the Commission lacks enforcement powers, its recommendations carry significant moral authority and can be used in subsequent court proceedings.

The Torture and Custodial Death Prevention Act 2013

Bangladesh enacted the Torture and Custodial Death (Prevention) Act 2013 — a landmark piece of legislation — to criminalise torture in custody and provide legal accountability for custodial deaths. This Act is directly relevant to Section 54 arrests because most custodial abuse occurs in the hours and days following an arrest without warrant.

Key provisions of the 2013 Act include:

  • Section 4: Torture by a public official (including police) is a criminal offence punishable by rigorous imprisonment of 5 years and a fine. Torture is defined broadly to include physical and mental suffering inflicted for purposes of extracting confession, punishment, intimidation, or discrimination.
  • Section 5: Custodial death (death of a person in police or prison custody) is punishable by life imprisonment and a fine.
  • Section 6: A public official who fails to prevent torture or custodial death when they had the power and knowledge to do so is also criminally liable.
  • Section 7: The Act establishes a right to compensation for torture victims and families of custodial death victims.
  • Section 9: Confessions obtained by torture are inadmissible in evidence.

Despite the existence of the 2013 Act, enforcement has been limited. Filing a complaint of custodial torture requires courage and legal support, as police tend to deny such allegations. Documentary evidence — medical examination reports, witness statements, and photographs — is essential to any such complaint.

Section 54 vs Warrant Arrest – Key Differences

Understanding the difference between an arrest made under a court-issued warrant and a Section 54 arrest without warrant helps you understand the different legal protections available to you:

FeatureWarrant ArrestSection 54 Arrest Without Warrant
Prior judicial authorisation?Yes — issued by a Judicial MagistrateNo — police decision only
Grounds required?Specified in the warrant by the courtOne of 9 grounds under Section 54
Risk of abuse?Lower — judicially supervisedHigher — unilateral police discretion
Challenge mechanism?Challenge the warrant at issuing courtHabeas corpus at High Court or bail application before magistrate
Applicable safeguards?CrPC proceduresCrPC + 15 BLAST safeguards
Production before magistrate?Within 24 hoursWithin 24 hours (constitutional requirement)

How to Protect Yourself If Arrested Under Section 54

If you or a family member is arrested under Section 54, take these practical steps immediately:

  1. Stay calm and assert your rights: Politely but firmly ask the arresting officer to identify themselves and state the specific grounds for the arrest. Note their name and badge number if possible.
  2. Do not resist physically: Physical resistance to an arrest — even an unlawful one — can result in additional charges. Assert your rights verbally and legally, not physically.
  3. Request to call a lawyer or family member: Invoke your right under BLAST safeguard 3 and 5 to contact a lawyer and notify your family. If denied, note this violation carefully.
  4. Do not sign any document under pressure: Do not sign any statement, confession, or acknowledgment without your lawyer being present and advising you.
  5. Request medical examination: Invoke your right to a medical examination before any interrogation begins (BLAST safeguard 6).
  6. Contact a lawyer urgently: Your lawyer can file a habeas corpus petition at the High Court, apply for bail before the magistrate, and document any violations of the BLAST safeguards.
  7. Document everything: As soon as you are released, write down every detail of the arrest — time, place, officers involved, what was said and done. This documentation is valuable for any subsequent legal action.

Get Legal Help Today

An arrest under Section 54 CrPC without warrant is one of the most stressful legal emergencies a person can face. Time is critical — the 24-hour production window, bail applications, and habeas corpus petitions must all be acted upon rapidly to be effective.

Shah Alam, practising from his Uttara, Dhaka chamber, has extensive experience in criminal law including Section 54 arrests, police remand proceedings, habeas corpus petitions at the High Court, and bail applications before both magistrate courts and the Sessions Court. His team can be reached urgently for situations involving unlawful arrest or detention.

If you or someone you know has been wrongfully arrested or is being held in unlawful custody, contact us immediately. Speak with our criminal lawyer or consult our bail lawyer for emergency legal assistance.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Section 54 CrPC in Bangladesh?

Section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (as applied in Bangladesh) authorises police officers to arrest a person without a court-issued warrant under nine specific grounds, including reasonable suspicion of involvement in a cognizable offence. The BLAST v Bangladesh Supreme Court case (55 DLR 2003) established 15 binding safeguards that police must follow in every Section 54 arrest.

How long can police hold someone under Section 54 without producing them before a magistrate?

Under Article 33(2) of the Constitution of Bangladesh, a person arrested without a warrant must be produced before the nearest Judicial Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey. Detention beyond 24 hours without magistrate production is unlawful and grounds for immediate habeas corpus petition at the High Court.

What is the BLAST case and why does it matter for Section 54 arrests?

BLAST v Bangladesh (55 DLR 363, 2003) is a landmark Supreme Court case in which the High Court Division declared systematic misuse of Section 54 unconstitutional and issued 15 mandatory safeguards for all Section 54 arrests. These safeguards — including the right to inform family, access a lawyer, and receive a medical examination — are currently binding on all police officers in Bangladesh.

Can I get compensation if I was wrongfully arrested under Section 54 in Bangladesh?

Yes. Following the BLAST case, the High Court can award compensation against the State for proven unlawful Section 54 arrests under Article 102 of the Constitution. You can also file a civil damages suit against the State and the arresting officer, or lodge a complaint with the National Human Rights Commission.

What should I do if police torture me in custody after a Section 54 arrest?

Under the Torture and Custodial Death (Prevention) Act 2013, torture by a public official is a criminal offence punishable by up to 5 years imprisonment. You should immediately seek a medical examination upon release to document injuries, consult a criminal lawyer, and file a complaint. The lawyer can also file a writ petition at the High Court for compensation and investigation of the responsible officers.

Can a lawyer be present during police interrogation after a Section 54 arrest?

Under the BLAST case safeguards, a police officer cannot begin interrogating an arrested person until they have been given a reasonable opportunity to engage a lawyer. Furthermore, during police remand interrogation, the arrested person lawyer must be allowed to remain outside the interrogation room in view (though not in hearing). Denial of this right is a violation of the BLAST directions.

Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, 471 Penal Code: Bail & Defense in Bangladesh

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-09 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In Bangladesh, financial disagreements, failed commercial partnerships, and disputed land transactions are frequently converted into aggressive criminal cases by invoking Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, and 471 of the Penal Code 1860. Complainants bundle allegations of criminal breach of trust, cheating, and document forgery to secure police arrest or exert overwhelming settlement leverage. For business owners, property holders, and non-resident Bangladeshis implicated in such cases, understanding which sections are bailable, how bail is secured under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), and how the High Court Division quashes frivolous proceedings under Section 561A CrPC is critical to safeguarding personal liberty.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

📋 In This Article

  2. 2. Bailable vs. Non-Bailable Classifications under Schedule II CrPC
  3. 3. Strategic Bundling: Why Complainants Combine Sections 406, 420 & 467
  4. 4. Regular Bail Procedure in the Magistrate and Sessions Courts
  5. 5. Anticipatory Bail Before the High Court Division (Section 498 CrPC)
  6. 6. Summary Matrix: Offence Elements, Bail Status & Statutory Penalties
  7. 7. Quashing Malicious Criminal Proceedings under Section 561A CrPC
  8. 8. Illustrative Scenario: Managing a Weaponized Land Forgery Case
  9. 9. Essential Defense Checklist for Business Executives and Landowners
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate

1. Statutory Breakdown: What Each Section Penalizes

The Penal Code 1860 contains an extensive framework criminalizing financial deception, breach of fiduciary obligations, and documentary falsification. To evaluate legal exposure, an accused individual must understand the distinct statutory ingredients of each frequently cited section:

  • Section 406 (Criminal Breach of Trust): Punishes anyone who dishonestly misappropriates, converts to their own use, or disposes of property entrusted to them in violation of any legal direction or contractual duty. Penalty: imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both.
  • Section 420 (Cheating and Dishonestly Inducing Delivery of Property): Requires proof that the accused cheated the victim and dishonestly induced them to deliver any property, or make, alter, or destroy the whole or part of a valuable security. Penalty: imprisonment up to 7 years and mandatory fine.
  • Section 467 (Forgery of Valuable Security, Will, etc.): Criminalizes the forgery of documents purporting to be a valuable security, a will, or an authority to adopt or receive money. Penalty: imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine.
  • Section 468 (Forgery for Purpose of Cheating): Punishes the act of committing forgery intending that the document shall be used for cheating. Penalty: imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
  • Section 471 (Using as Genuine a Forged Document): Imposes criminal liability on anyone who fraudulently or dishonestly uses as genuine any document which they know or have reason to believe to be a forged document. The punishment mirrors the penalty for the actual forgery.

2. Bailable vs. Non-Bailable Classifications under Schedule II CrPC

A widespread misconception among defendants in Bangladesh is that because Section 420 is the primary charge, bail can be claimed as a matter of right at the police station or before the Magistrate. The legal reality is determined strictly by the classification table in Schedule II of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898.

Under Schedule II, Section 420 is categorized as a cognizable and bailable offence. In contrast, Section 406 is cognizable and non-bailable. Furthermore, Section 467 and Section 468 are both classified as cognizable, non-bailable, and non-compoundable offences. For Section 471, the bail status corresponds directly to whether the underlying document forged was bailable or non-bailable.

When an FIR (First Information Report) or a Complaint Register (CR) case includes both bailable and non-bailable sections, the entire case is governed by non-bailable procedural rules. Police officers cannot release the suspect on personal bond, and the court must evaluate any release application under the judicial discretion governed by Section 497 of the CrPC.

3. Strategic Bundling: Why Complainants Combine Sections 406, 420 & 467

In day-to-day legal practice across Dhaka and the district courts, complainants routinely combine Sections 406 and 420 alongside forgery sections. In strict legal theory, Section 406 and Section 420 are antithetical: Section 406 presupposes lawful entrustment of property followed by dishonest conversion, whereas Section 420 requires dishonest intention from the very inception of the transaction that induced the victim to part with property.

Despite this mutual exclusivity, complainants routinely draft omnibus complaints alleging both entrustment and initial fraudulent deception, then add Section 467 by claiming that a receipt, deed, cheque, or power of attorney was fabricated. The strategic objective is twofold: first, to ensure the offences are non-bailable so that the accused faces immediate arrest; second, to elevate the potential sentence to life imprisonment under Section 467, thereby preventing summary disposal and increasing settlement pressure.

Facing cheating, forgery, or criminal breach of trust charges in Bangladesh? Immediate intervention is vital to secure bail and protect against wrongful detention. Message our criminal defense advocates on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for swift legal assistance.

Courts are well aware of this tendency. When assessing bail, experienced judges scrutinize the complaint to determine whether the inclusion of Section 467 is supported by concrete documentary evidence or is merely a colorable device engineered to prevent bail on a commercial transaction.

4. Regular Bail Procedure in the Magistrate and Sessions Courts

If an accused person is arrested by law enforcement or voluntarily surrenders before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM), the defense must file an application for regular bail under Section 497 of the CrPC.

Under Section 497(1), bail shall not be granted if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life. Because Section 467 carries potential life imprisonment, Magistrate Courts frequently decline bail on jurisdictional caution, particularly during the early stages of police investigation before the filing of a formal Police Report (Charge Sheet) under Section 173 CrPC.

However, the proviso to Section 497(1) grants the court discretion to release any person who is under sixteen years of age, a woman, or sick or infirm. Furthermore, under Section 497(2), if the court satisfies itself that there are no reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed a non-bailable offence, but that there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry, the accused shall be released on bail pending such inquiry. If the Magistrate rejects bail, the defense immediately moves a bail petition before the Sessions Judge or Metropolitan Sessions Judge under Section 498 CrPC. For a broader overview of regular surrender, review our guide on regular bail under Section 497 CrPC.

5. Anticipatory Bail Before the High Court Division (Section 498 CrPC)

When an individual discovers that an FIR has been lodged at a police station or a warrant of arrest has been issued in a CR case under Sections 406, 420, and 467, remaining at liberty is critical to mounting an effective defense. Under Section 498 of the CrPC, the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh possesses concurrent jurisdiction to grant anticipatory bail (pre-arrest bail).

Anticipatory bail is an extraordinary equitable remedy. The Supreme Court Appellate Division in landmark rulings has established that to obtain anticipatory bail, the applicant must demonstrate an apprehension of arrest based on specific allegations, establish that the prosecution is motivated by political, personal, or commercial malice, and physically present themselves before the High Court Division bench on the date of the hearing.

If the High Court Division finds prima facie evidence that a civil breach of contract has been deliberately criminalized to harass the petitioner, it typically grants anticipatory bail for a limited window (ranging from four to eight weeks) with a direction to surrender before the relevant Sessions Court. During this protected window, law enforcement agencies are prohibited from arresting the petitioner. For complete procedural protocols, consult our detailed resource on anticipatory bail under Section 498 CrPC.

6. Summary Matrix: Offence Elements, Bail Status & Statutory Penalties

The procedural distinctions between these interrelated sections dictate the defense strategy. The following table synthesizes the legal status of each provision under the Penal Code 1860 and CrPC 1898:

Penal Code Section Core Offence Allegation Police Power & Bail Status Maximum Statutory Penalty Trial Court Jurisdiction
Section 406 Criminal breach of trust Cognizable; Non-Bailable; Compoundable with court consent Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both Magistrate of the First Class
Section 420 Cheating & dishonest inducement to deliver property Cognizable; Bailable; Compoundable with court consent Imprisonment up to 7 years, and fine Magistrate of the First Class
Section 467 Forgery of valuable security, will, or trust document Cognizable; Non-Bailable; Non-Compoundable Imprisonment for life, or up to 10 years, and fine Court of Session / Special Magistrate
Section 468 Forgery committed for the purpose of cheating Cognizable; Non-Bailable; Non-Compoundable Imprisonment up to 7 years, and fine Magistrate of the First Class / Sessions
Section 471 Fraudulently using as genuine a forged document Cognizable; Bailable if forged doc bailable; Non-Compoundable Same punishment as for forging the document Court having jurisdiction over forged document

7. Quashing Malicious Criminal Proceedings under Section 561A CrPC

Securing bail provides temporary liberty, but the underlying criminal case remains pending for years unless dismissed or resolved. In situations where the dispute is overwhelmingly civil in nature—such as an alleged non-payment under a supply agreement, delay in land handover, or partnership accounting disagreement—the High Court Division possesses inherent jurisdiction under Section 561A of the CrPC to quash the proceedings.

To succeed in a quashing petition under Section 561A CrPC, the petitioner must demonstrate that the FIR or complaint, even if accepted on its face as true, does not disclose the essential legal elements of a criminal offence, or that the continuation of the trial constitutes a flagrant abuse of the process of the court. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has consistently established that a mere breach of contract does not give rise to criminal liability under Section 420 unless dishonest intent existed at the inception of the agreement.

Similarly, where Section 467 is alleged without producing the allegedly forged instrument or obtaining a handwriting examiner's forensic report, the High Court Division regularly issues a Rule Nisi accompanied by an order staying all further criminal proceedings in the subordinate court. To examine the grounds for terminating false criminal litigation, review our analysis on quashing criminal cases under Section 561A CrPC.

8. Illustrative Scenario: Managing a Weaponized Land Forgery Case

To illustrate how these interrelated provisions interact in practical litigation, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A real estate developer in Gulshan entered into an agreement with a landowner to construct a multi-story residential complex. Due to delays in obtaining municipal building plan approvals from the development authority, project construction fell twelve months behind the original contractual schedule. Instead of filing a civil suit for breach of contract or seeking arbitration, the landowner lodged an FIR with the police station invoking Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, and 471 of the Penal Code.

The landowner alleged that the developer had dishonestly misappropriated advance funds (Section 406), fraudulently induced the contract (Section 420), and forged an addendum letter extending the construction timeline (Sections 467/468). Armed with the non-bailable Section 467 charge, police officers raided the developer's corporate offices. The developer immediately moved an anticipatory bail application before the High Court Division under Section 498 CrPC.

The High Court Division evaluated the primary contractual documents, observed that the dispute centered entirely on commercial performance and force majeure delays, and granted anticipatory bail for six weeks. Concurrently, the defense filed a Criminal Miscellaneous petition under Section 561A CrPC. The High Court issued a Rule Nisi and stayed all criminal proceedings, observing that converting a pure civil breach into a criminal forgery prosecution was an abuse of judicial process.

9. Essential Defense Checklist for Business Executives and Landowners

If you or your company are implicated in a criminal case involving Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, or 471, taking deliberate, structured steps will protect your liberty and preserve your legal defense:

  • Procure Certified Copies of the FIR / Complaint: Immediately obtain the formal ejahar or complaint copy from the court to identify the exact sections invoked and the specific factual assertions.
  • Secure Document Chains and Communications: Collect all written agreements, emails, bank transfer vouchers, and receipts demonstrating that money or property was transferred pursuant to a legitimate commercial transaction.
  • Do Not Evade Process Unrepresented: Evading police without an anticipatory bail petition risks proclamation and attachment under Sections 87 and 88 of the CrPC.
  • File for High Court Anticipatory Bail Immediately: If non-bailable sections (406, 467, 468) are present, approach the High Court Division under Section 498 CrPC before subordinate police arrest occurs.
  • Challenge Handwriting and Signatures Forensically: In forgery allegations, demand that questioned documents be forwarded to the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) forensic handwriting experts for scientific comparison.
  • Initiate Section 561A Quashing Proceedings: If the transaction is fundamentally contractual or governed by an arbitration clause, move the High Court Division to stay proceedings and terminate the frivolous prosecution.

For dedicated representation across the Magistrate, Sessions, and Supreme Court benches, examine our specialized criminal defense legal services and bail advocacy services in Bangladesh.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a Criminal Defense Advocate in Dhaka: To apply for anticipatory bail before the High Court Division, represent you before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court, or file a quashing application under Section 561A CrPC, reach out on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call our chamber at +880 1712-655546. Confidential consultations are available for domestic and international clients.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Section 420 Penal Code bailable in Bangladesh?

Yes. Standalone Section 420 (cheating) is classified as a bailable offence under Schedule II of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898. However, complainants rarely file Section 420 alone; they typically add non-bailable sections like 406 or 467.

Is Section 406 Penal Code bailable in Bangladesh?

No. Section 406 (criminal breach of trust) is classified as a non-bailable offence under Schedule II of the CrPC. Bail cannot be claimed as a matter of right and is subject to the judicial discretion of the court under Section 497 CrPC.

What is the punishment for forgery under Section 467 Penal Code?

Section 467 carries severe penalties, including imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, alongside a mandatory fine. Because of the potential life sentence, Magistrate Courts rarely grant bail.

Can Sections 406 and 420 be charged together in the same case?

While complainants frequently bundle them, the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly held that Sections 406 and 420 are conceptually inconsistent. Section 406 requires lawful entrustment followed by breach, whereas Section 420 requires fraudulent intention at the inception.

How can I obtain anticipatory bail if accused under Section 467?

You must file an anticipatory bail application before the High Court Division under Section 498 of the CrPC. The applicant must appear in person before the bench and show that the charges are motivated by malice or arise from a civil commercial dispute.

What should I do if a business partner files a false 420 case against me?

Secure all contracts, bank records, and correspondence proving that the matter is a civil breach of contract. Apply for bail, and subsequently petition the High Court Division under Section 561A CrPC to quash the criminal proceedings as an abuse of process.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi be arrested at Dhaka airport for a pending 420/406 warrant?

Yes. If a Magistrate Court issues an arrest warrant and police notify immigration authorities, an overseas traveler can be offloaded and arrested upon arrival at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport unless anticipatory bail or a stay order has been secured.

What is the difference between Section 468 and Section 471 Penal Code?

Section 468 punishes the actual act of forging a document with the intent to cheat. Section 471 punishes anyone who fraudulently uses an already forged document as genuine, knowing or having reason to believe it to be forged.

How to Sell Property in Bangladesh While Living Overseas: Legal Steps, Taxes and Proceeds

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-04 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Selling property from abroad can be as risky as buying it: fake buyers, brokers who demand advance money, delayed payments and tax surprises. A well-planned sale protects both your price and your title. This guide is written by <a href="/advocate-md-shah-alam" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">Advocate Md. Shah Alam</a>, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, for Bangladeshis living in the UK, USA, UAE, Canada and elsewhere. For case-specific help call or WhatsApp the chamber on <a href="tel:01712655546" style="color:var(--gold);font-weight:bold">01712655546</a>.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

  2. Step 2: Find and Screen the Buyer
  3. Step 3: Agreement for Sale
  4. Step 4: Executing the Deed, Personally or by Attorney
  5. Step 5: Taxes and Registration Costs
  6. Step 6: Receiving and Sending Money Abroad
  7. Common Pitfalls

Step 1: Make Your Title Sale-Ready

Buyers and banks check the same documents you would check when buying (see our buyer checklist). Fix gaps before listing:

  • Mutation in your name and recent land tax receipts.
  • Certified copies of all earlier deeds.
  • Heirship certificate if the land was inherited, with all heirs ready to sign.
  • A clear map and area measurement.
  • No mortgage, court order or acquisition notice.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Step 2: Find and Screen the Buyer

Use reputable agents but never pay a broker upfront. Check the buyer's identity (NID), source of funds and, if a company, its RJSC registration. Avoid buyers who push for fast cash or ask you to register before payment. A bank-financed buyer is usually safer.

Step 3: Agreement for Sale

Sign a written agreement for sale with a part payment (earnest money), the balance schedule, a deadline and consequences of default. Describe the plot exactly (dag number, khatian number, mouza, area). Ask your advocate to draft it, and give the buyer a copy signed by both sides.

Step 4: Executing the Deed, Personally or by Attorney

If you can travel, signing in person is simplest. If not, give a special Power of Attorney that names this buyer, a minimum price and a time limit (see our Power of Attorney guide). The attorney then signs and registers the deed at the Sub-Registrar office. Never give a general irrevocable PoA to sell, and require the attorney to hand over the money only through your bank account.

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Step 5: Taxes and Registration Costs

On a sale, expect to deal with:

  • Registration fee and stamp duty: usually borne by the buyer by agreement.
  • Source tax / advance tax: collected by the registering office on the transfer.
  • Capital gains tax: may apply depending on the holding period and rules under the Income Tax Act 2023; the rate and exemption change often, so check the current law.
  • Land development tax clearance: up to date at the time of sale.

Ask your advocate or a tax professional for a written breakdown and keep copies of all receipts.

Step 6: Receiving and Sending Money Abroad

Take payment into your Bangladeshi bank account. Moving sale proceeds abroad is regulated by the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 and Bangladesh Bank rules; generally, repatriation requires proof of source, tax clearance and permission through an authorised dealer bank. If you plan to move money out, speak to the bank before you sell, so the documents are ready. Alternatively, invest or hold the money in an NRB (foreign currency) account if eligible.

Common Pitfalls

  • Registering the deed before receiving the main payment.
  • Accepting cash payments with no receipt.
  • Letting the buyer fill in the deed price below the market price (under-valuation risks tax and legal problems).
  • Forgetting to cancel an old Power of Attorney after the sale.
  • Leaving the mutation to the buyer without a written commitment.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I sell my property in Bangladesh without going there?

Yes, with a properly attested Power of Attorney and your advocate's help. Signing in person is safer if you can travel.

Is capital gains tax payable on property sale?

It can be, depending on the current Income Tax Act rules and exemptions. Get tax advice before you fix the price.

Can I send sale money abroad?

It is possible but regulated. You need proof of source, tax clearance and approval through an authorised bank under Bangladesh Bank rules.

Who pays registration cost, buyer or seller?

By custom the buyer pays registration fee and stamp duty, but this can be agreed in writing.

What if the buyer does not pay the balance?

Do not register the deed. You can cancel the agreement per its terms and keep earnest money, or file a suit for breach of contract.

Seller Refusing Land Registration After Bayna? Legal Remedies

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-10 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Entering into a contract for sale of immovable property (Bainapatra or Bayna Deed) is the standard preliminary step for buying land, commercial plots, or residential apartments in Bangladesh. Buyers frequently pay substantial advance earnest money—ranging from tens of lakhs to crores of BDT—trusting the seller to complete mutation, clear utility liens, and execute the final Saf Kabala transfer deed. However, due to rapid property appreciation, third-party broker meddling, or sheer bad faith, sellers often renege on the deal, refuse to accept the remaining balance, or secretly attempt to sell the property to a higher bidder. Under Section 12 and Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act 1877, a buyer is not helpless; the law empowers you to freeze the property and compel the civil court to execute the transfer on the defaulting seller's behalf.

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Registration Fee & Stamp Duty1% Registration Fee + 1.5% Stamp Duty on deed value
Local Government Tax & VAT2%–3% Local Govt Tax + 1.5%–4.5% VAT (varies by City/Pourosova/Union)
Source Tax (Gain Tax / TDS)1% to 8% depending on mouza classification under Income Tax Act 2023
Official Land & Mouza Portalsland.gov.bd, dlrms.land.gov.bd, and eporcha.gov.bd
📋 In This Article
  1. 1. The Legal Framework: Mandatory Registration of Bayna Deeds (Section 17A)
  2. 2. Section 21A Prerequisites: Written Contract and Balance Court Deposit
  3. 3. Limitation Deadlines: The Strict One-Year Rule under Article 113
  4. 4. Immediate Tactical Steps: Advocate Notice and Order 39 Injunction
  5. 5. Filing the Suit for Specific Performance in the Joint District Judge Court
  6. 6. Summary Matrix: Specific Performance vs. Refund of Advance with Penalty
  7. 7. Execution of Decree: How the Civil Court Registers the Deed for You
  8. 8. Illustrative Scenario: Buyer Compelling Registration Against an Unruly Seller
  9. 9. Essential Due Diligence Checklist for Buyers Before Signing Bayna Deeds
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate

1. The Legal Framework: Mandatory Registration of Bayna Deeds (Section 17A)

Prior to 2004, contracts for the sale of land in Bangladesh were frequently executed on informal non-judicial stamp papers without official registration. Sellers exploited this informality by signing multiple unregistered Bayna deeds with different buyers, pocketing advances from all, and tying victims up in endless criminal or civil disputes.

To eliminate this predatory practice, parliament enacted sweeping amendments through the Registration (Amendment) Act 2004 and the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act 2004. Under Section 17A of the Registration Act 1908, a contract for the sale of any immovable property must be in writing, executed on prescribed non-judicial stamp paper, and presented for registration before the relevant Sub-Registry Office within thirty (30) days from execution.

Under Section 17A(2), an unregistered contract for sale has zero legal validity in respect of immovable property and cannot be received as evidence of any transaction affecting the land. Consequently, buyers must ensure that their Bayna deed is formally registered at the Sub-Registry Office; an informal notarized agreement cannot sustain a specific performance lawsuit.

2. Section 21A Prerequisites: Written Contract and Balance Court Deposit

The legal enforceability of a registered contract for sale is strictly governed by Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act 1877. This statutory provision establishes an affirmative right for the buyer while creating mandatory procedural prerequisites.

Under Section 21A, no suit for the specific performance of a contract for the sale of immovable property shall lie unless:

  • Registered Instrument: The contract is in writing and duly registered under the Registration Act 1908.
  • Mandatory Balance Deposit: The plaintiff deposits the remaining balance of the contract price in the civil court at the time of filing the plaint, or furnishes sufficient bank guarantee security if permitted by the court.

This statutory balance deposit requirement separates genuine purchasers from speculative litigants. By depositing the remaining consideration into the government treasury chalan, the buyer demonstrates absolute readiness and willingness to perform their contractual obligations, stripping the defaulting seller of any equitable defense.

3. Limitation Deadlines: The Strict One-Year Rule under Article 113

Time is of the essence when a land seller shows signs of default. Under Article 113 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act 1908, the statutory limitation period for filing a suit for specific performance of a contract is strictly one (1) year.

The limitation clock begins running from one of two dates:

  1. Date Fixed for Performance: If the registered Bayna deed specifies a fixed date or timeframe for final deed registration (e.g., 'within six months from the date of execution'), the one-year limitation period begins running immediately upon the expiry of that specified date.
  2. Date of Refusal: If no fixed date was stipulated in the agreement, the limitation period begins running from the date when the plaintiff has formal notice that performance is refused by the seller.

Did a seller take your Bayna advance money and refuse to register the land deed in Bangladesh? Immediate legal action before the statutory limitation expires is essential to freeze the land and compel transfer. Message our property litigation team on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for strategic advice.

Missing this one-year statutory deadline is fatal to the lawsuit. If you wait beyond the limitation window, your legal right to compel property registration is permanently extinguished, leaving you with only a subordinate money suit for refund of the advance. For title vetting insights, review our guide on remote land title search in Bangladesh.

4. Immediate Tactical Steps: Advocate Notice and Order 39 Injunction

The moment a seller begins making excuses—refusing to deliver mutation papers, demanding unauthorized extra money, or evading telephone calls—the buyer must establish a formal evidentiary paper trail.

The first mandatory procedural step is issuing a formal Legal Notice through an advocate via registered post with acknowledgment due (A/D). The notice must recite the registered Bayna deed particulars, specify that the buyer is ready with the remaining balance, propose a specific date, time, and Sub-Registry Office for final Saf Kabala execution, and warn that failure to attend will trigger immediate civil litigation.

Concurrently with filing the plaint in court, the buyer must file an emergency application for temporary injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The application requests the court to restrain the seller from transferring, mortgaging, selling, leasing, or altering the physical character of the property pending final disposal of the suit. Obtaining an interim injunction prevents the seller from creating third-party purchaser complications.

5. Filing the Suit for Specific Performance in the Joint District Judge Court

Because suits for specific performance of immovable property typically involve substantial pecuniary valuations, they fall under the original jurisdiction of the Joint District Judge Court having territorial authority over where the land is located.

The procedural journey encompasses:

  • Plaint Drafting & Court Fees: The plaint must set forth the complete transaction history, assert the plaintiff's continuous readiness and willingness, and attach the registered Bayna deed. The plaintiff pays the statutory ad valorem court fee under the Court Fees Act 1870 (capped at the statutory maximum).
  • Depositing the Treasury Chalan: The plaintiff deposits the remaining balance via treasury chalan, submitting the original receipt with the plaint.
  • Service of Summons: Summons are served on the defaulting seller under Order 5 CPC. If the seller evades service, summons are published in national daily newspapers.
  • Written Statement & Trial: The seller files a written statement (Jabab). The court frames issues, takes documentary and oral evidence, and hears final legal arguments.

6. Summary Matrix: Specific Performance vs. Refund of Advance with Penalty

A purchaser facing seller breach must evaluate whether to pursue compulsory land registration or demand a financial refund with contractual penalties. The following matrix outlines the strategic distinctions:

Remedy Pathway Governing Statute Prerequisites & Deposits Ultimate Relief Obtained
Specific Performance of Contract Specific Relief Act 1877 (Sec 12, 21A) Registered Bayna deed; mandatory deposit of balance consideration Court executes and registers final Saf Kabala deed to buyer
Refund of Advance with Penalty / Compensation Specific Relief Act 1877 (Sec 19) / Contract Act (Sec 73) No balance deposit required; proof of advance payment vouchers Money decree for double the advance or damages plus interest
Criminal Cheating Prosecution The Penal Code 1860 (Sec 406, 420) Proof of fraudulent dishonest inducement at inception Criminal conviction/fine; does not transfer land title directly
Temporary Injunction / Status Quo Code of Civil Procedure (Order 39) Prima facie case, irreparable loss, balance of convenience Freezes property, preventing third-party sale or construction

7. Execution of Decree: How the Civil Court Registers the Deed for You

A common concern among buyers is: 'What if the court passes a decree, but the stubborn seller still refuses to go to the Sub-Registry Office?' The civil procedure code provides a foolproof enforcement mechanism.

When the Joint District Judge decrees the suit for specific performance, the judgment grants the seller a fixed period (typically 30 to 60 days) to appear at the Sub-Registry Office, accept the deposited balance from the court, and execute the Saf Kabala deed. If the seller willfully fails or refuses to appear within the stipulated period, the decree-holder files a Title Execution Case (Jari Mamla) under Order 21, Rule 34 of the CPC.

Under Order 21, Rule 34, the civil court itself steps into the shoes of the defaulting seller. The presiding judge drafts the deed, delivers notice to the Sub-Registrar, and authorizes the Court Nazir or Sheristadar to attend the Sub-Registry Office. The court officer signs and presents the deed for registration on behalf of the judgment-debtor. The resulting registered deed carries absolute, incontestable statutory validity under Bangladeshi property law.

8. Illustrative Scenario: Buyer Compelling Registration Against an Unruly Seller

To illustrate how specific performance litigation operates in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A software executive in Uttara, Dhaka, agreed to purchase a 5-katha residential plot in Bashundhara for 1.2 Crore BDT. The parties executed a registered Bayna Deed under Section 17A of the Registration Act, with the buyer paying 40 Lakh BDT as advance earnest money, and stipulating a four-month timeframe to complete the remaining 80 Lakh BDT upon delivery of municipal mutation papers. Within three months, land values in the sector surged by 25%.

The seller abruptly stopped answering phone calls, refused to provide the mutation porcha, and engaged local brokers to sell the plot to a third party for 1.5 Crore BDT. The buyer retained a Supreme Court land advocate. The advocate immediately issued a formal statutory legal notice demanding registration, followed by filing a Suit for Specific Performance before the Joint District Judge Court, Dhaka, under Section 21A.

The buyer deposited the remaining 80 Lakh BDT into the government treasury chalan on the day of filing. Concurrently, the advocate moved an Order 39 injunction petition, and the court issued an immediate order restraining the seller from transferring or encumbering the land. Confronted with the frozen land title and the deposited court balance, the seller realized evading the transaction was legally impossible and appeared before the court to execute the final Saf Kabala deed.

9. Essential Due Diligence Checklist for Buyers Before Signing Bayna Deeds

Protecting your financial investment begins before a single BDT changes hands. Follow this mandatory due diligence protocol prior to executing any land agreement in Bangladesh:

  • Demand Registered Bayna Only: Never settle for an unregistered agreement or notary public stamp. Insist that the Bayna deed is formally registered at the local Sub-Registry Office.
  • Verify CS, SA, RS, and BS Khatians: Confirm that the seller's name or immediate predecessor's name is recorded in the latest BS/City Jarip Khatian and that the chain of title is unbroken.
  • Check Mutation & Up-to-Date Khajna: Verify that the land has been mutated (Namjari) in the seller's name by the relevant AC Land and that Land Development Tax receipts (Dakhila) are cleared for the current fiscal year.
  • Stipulate Clear Handover Deadlines: Explicitly state the final date for deed execution, consequences of seller default, and a clause specifying that the buyer reserves the right to seek specific performance under Section 21A.
  • Pay Advances Through Banking Channels: Never pay Bayna advances in unrecorded cash. Utilize account-payee cheques, pay orders, or RTGS bank transfers with clear payment reference memos.

For dedicated assistance with property transactions and civil litigation, explore our specialized land dispute lawyer services and Supreme Court civil practice.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a Land Advocate in Dhaka: To draft statutory advocate notices, obtain temporary injunctions under Order 39 CPC, or file a Suit for Specific Performance under Section 21A in Dhaka and district courts, reach out on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call our chamber at +880 1712-655546. Overseas buyers and NRBs can instruct counsel remotely via power of attorney.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I force a seller to register land if they refuse after taking Bayna in Bangladesh?

Yes. If you have a registered Bayna Deed, you can file a Suit for Specific Performance of Contract under Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act 1877 to compel the seller to execute the deed, or have the court register it on their behalf.

Is an unregistered Bayna deed legally enforceable in court?

No. Under Section 17A of the Registration Act 1908 and Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act 1877, an unregistered contract for sale of immovable property cannot sustain a suit for specific performance.

Do I have to deposit the remaining land price in court when filing the suit?

Yes. Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act makes it mandatory for the purchaser to deposit the remaining balance of consideration in court at the time of filing the plaint, demonstrating absolute readiness and willingness.

What is the limitation period to file a suit for specific performance in Bangladesh?

Under Article 113 of the Limitation Act 1908, the lawsuit must be filed within one (1) year from the date fixed for performance, or from the date when the seller formally refused performance.

How can I stop the seller from selling the land to someone else during the lawsuit?

You must file an application for temporary injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) to restrain the seller from transferring, mortgaging, or altering the land pending final decree.

What happens if the court decrees specific performance but the seller refuses to sign?

Under Order 21, Rule 34 of the CPC, the civil court itself executes and registers the Saf Kabala deed on behalf of the defaulting seller through a court-appointed officer, granting the buyer full legal ownership.

Can I claim double the advance money back instead of the land?

Yes. Under Section 19 of the Specific Relief Act and contractual terms, a buyer can plead in the alternative for compensation, demanding a refund of the earnest money alongside agreed penalty damages.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi buyer file a specific performance suit from abroad?

Yes. An overseas Bangladeshi can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission, authorizing a lawyer or relative to deposit the balance and conduct the lawsuit in Bangladesh.

Seller Sells Land to Someone Else: Legal Remedies for Double Sale in Bangladesh

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-10 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Picture a nightmare scenario: you negotiate the purchase of a valuable plot of land in Dhaka, pay the agreed consideration, execute and register a formal Saf Kabala deed at the Sub-Registry Office, and begin preparing for mutation. Months later, you arrive at the property only to find construction materials piled high and an aggressive stranger waving a deed, claiming they purchased the exact same plot from your seller. In Bangladesh's heated real estate market, 'double sale' (selling the same land to multiple buyers) is one of the most destructive forms of property swindling. Fortunately, under the Registration Act 1908, the Specific Relief Act 1877, and the Land Crime Prevention and Redress Act 2023, the law strictly protects the prior registered purchaser and prescribes severe criminal punishment—including up to 7 years non-bailable imprisonment—for fraudulent sellers.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka
