The Anatomy of Double Sale Land Fraud in Bangladesh

Land in Bangladesh is exceptionally scarce and commands astronomical market valuations, particularly across Dhaka, Chattogram, and rapidly urbanizing district headquarters. This scarcity has fueled predatory land syndicates and unscrupulous sellers who exploit administrative backlogs between the Sub-Registry Office and the Assistant Commissioner (Land) office. In a typical double sale scheme, a landowner sells a plot to Buyer A, receives the full purchase price, and executes a registered Saf Kabala deed. However, before Buyer A completes their field mutation (Namjari) and updates the revenue records, the dishonest seller takes advantage of the fact that the old RS or BS Khatian still displays their name, and executes a second registered deed for the same plot to Buyer B, pocketing money twice.

In other scenarios, sellers execute an unregistered Bayna deed (agreement for sale) with Buyer A, take a heavy advance, and then secretly sell the property outright to Buyer B. Regardless of the exact variation, discovering that your purchased land has been transferred to another person causes overwhelming panic. Understanding how property registration statutes and landmark 2023 criminal enactments operate is crucial to reclaiming your rightful property.

Priority of Deeds Under the Registration Act 1908

The foundational bedrock of Bangladesh property law is the doctrine of priority. Under Section 47 of the Registration Act 1908, a registered document operates not from the date of its ultimate delivery from the registry office, but from the time from which it would have commenced to operate whether no registration thereof had been required—meaning from the date of its original execution.

Furthermore, under Section 48 and Section 49 of the Registration Act 1908, a registered document relating to land takes absolute effect against any subsequent or unrecorded claim. Under the Latin maxim Nemo dat quod non habet (no one can give what they do not have), once the seller executed and registered the first Saf Kabala deed in favor of Buyer A, the seller's entire right, title, and interest were completely extinguished. The seller possessed zero title to transfer to Buyer B. Consequently, the second deed is a legal nullity (void ab initio), conveying nothing to the second buyer regardless of how much money they paid.

Land Crime Prevention and Redress Act 2023: Heavy Penalties

Historically, victims of double sale fraud were forced to endure decades of sluggish civil litigation while fraudulent sellers enjoyed their illicit millions. To terminate this culture of impunity, the Parliament of Bangladesh enacted the historic Land Crime Prevention and Redress Act 2023 (Bhumi Oporadh Protirodh O Protikar Ain 2023).

This landmark statute specifically criminalizes fraudulent double transactions:

  • Section 4 (Fraudulent Document Execution): Creating, signing, or registering any deed or document knowing that the seller does not possess lawful ownership or has already alienated the property is a cognizable and non-bailable offense.
  • Section 5 (Selling Land Multiple Times): Executing a deed of sale or transfer for land that has already been sold or committed to another person carries rigorous imprisonment for up to seven (7) years and heavy monetary fines.
  • Summary Restitution Powers: The Act empowers Executive Magistrates and specialized courts to take immediate cognizance, issue non-bailable arrest warrants against fraudulent sellers, and issue summary possession protection orders.

Coupled with traditional charges under Section 420 (cheating) and Section 406 (criminal breach of trust) of the Penal Code 1860, this modern enactment gives defrauded buyers immediate, aggressive leverage against dishonest sellers.

Civil Court Remedies: Deed Cancellation and Declaration

While criminal proceedings penalize the perpetrator, they do not automatically cancel the fraudulent second deed recorded in the Sub-Registry Office's volume books. To eliminate any cloud on your title, you must file a formal Title Suit in the Court of the Joint District Judge having territorial jurisdiction:

  1. Cancellation of Subsequent Deed (Section 39 Specific Relief Act 1877): Under Section 39, any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, and who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding, may cause serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or cancelled. The court passes a decree directing the Sub-Registrar to record a note of cancellation against the fraudulent deed in the register.
  2. Declaration of Title (Section 42 Specific Relief Act 1877): The suit simultaneously seeks a judicial declaration that the plaintiff is the sole, exclusive, and rightful owner of the suit land by virtue of their prior registered deed.
  3. Permanent Injunction (Section 54 Specific Relief Act 1877): A perpetual injunction permanently restraining the defendant seller and the second purchaser from entering upon, disturbing possession of, or alienating the suit property.

Faced with a fraudulent land sale, double deed, or boundary grab in Bangladesh? Send your deeds and Khatian records on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007. Overseas clients and local landowners can arrange an immediate title audit.

Securing an Immediate Temporary Injunction (Order 39 CPC)

The single most urgent procedural step upon filing your Title Suit is moving an interlocutory application for a Temporary Injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). If the second buyer begins pouring concrete, constructing boundary walls, or selling sub-plots to third parties, reversing that physical reality during a multi-year trial becomes an uphill battle.

To secure an injunction, your advocate must establish the three classic legal tests:

  • Prima Facie Case: Proved conclusively by presenting your certified earlier registered deed and payment receipts.
  • Balance of Convenience: Demonstrating that preserving the property in status quo favors the lawful prior purchaser rather than a fraudulent subsequent interloper.
  • Irreparable Injury: Proving that if the second buyer alters the topography or builds structures, monetary compensation will not adequately remedy the injury.

Upon satisfaction, the civil court grants an ad-interim injunction restraining both defendants from altering the physical character of the land, felling trees, raising structures, or executing further transfers until the disposal of the suit.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Sub-Registry Office Balam Book Searches and Document Audits

To build an ironclad case, your advocate must conduct a forensic document audit at the relevant Sub-Registry Office. Many victims make the mistake of relying only on the paper deed handed to them. A comprehensive legal audit requires:

  1. Balam Book Search (Form 36): Conducting an official search in the Balam (volume) books and Index I/II for the past 12 to 25 years to trace every transaction executed under the relevant CS, SA, RS, and City/BS Khatian and Dag (plot) numbers.
  2. Non-Encumbrance Certificate (NEC): Applying for an official Non-Encumbrance Certificate from the Sub-Registrar confirming whether any mortgages, attachments, or secondary deeds have been recorded against the plot.
  3. Certified Copies of the Subsequent Deed: Procuring the certified copy of the second deed to inspect how the seller described their title, whether they forged an NID, or whether the second buyer acted in collusion with full knowledge of your prior purchase.

These certified extracts constitute primary documentary evidence that refutes any claim by the second buyer that they were an 'innocent purchaser without notice.'

Role of AC Land Mutation and Kharij Contests

Parallel to the civil court battle, the administrative dispute plays out before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) office. If the second buyer has submitted an online mutation application (E-Namjari) to open a new Khatian in their name, you must immediately file a formal written objection.

Under the Land Management Manual and Ministry of Land circulars, an AC Land is strictly prohibited from mutating land in favor of a subsequent buyer when a prior registered deed exists for the exact same Dag and parcel. You must submit your certified prior deed, tax receipts (Dakhila), and a certified copy of the civil court's injunction order. The AC Land will reject the second buyer's mutation application (Namonjur), preventing them from acquiring revenue legitimacy. If the AC Land has already erroneously opened a Khatian for the second buyer, your advocate can file an E-Namjari Miss Case or an appeal before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) under Section 147 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 to cancel the fraudulent Khatian.

Comparison Table: First Buyer Rights vs. Second Buyer

The table below outlines the legal status and rights of the competing purchasers in a double sale fraud scenario:

ParameterFirst Purchaser (Your Position)Second Purchaser (Subsequent Deed)
Legal Ownership & TitleAbsolute title under Registration Act §48Zero title; deed is void ab initio
Remedy Against DeedEntitled to decree of cancellation under §39Deed subject to mandatory court cancellation
Protection of PossessionProtected via Order 39 Injunction & §145Can be summarily evicted as illegal trespasser
Mutation (Namjari) RightLawfully entitled to Namjari KhatianMutation must be rejected / cancelled
Recourse for Stolen MoneyKeeps the land; can claim damagesMust sue seller for money refund under §420

As the first purchaser, the law stands entirely on your side. The second buyer's only lawful recourse is suing the fraudulent seller to recover their money.

Illustrative Scenario: Defeating a Double Sale Syndicate

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how aggressive civil and criminal actions dismantled a double sale fraud in Savar:

An expatriate living in Birmingham, UK, purchased a 5-katha residential plot in Savar in January 2024 for BDT 45,00,000. The seller executed and registered a valid Saf Kabala deed before the Savar Sub-Registrar. Because the buyer returned to the UK shortly after, he delayed physical possession and mutation. Eight months later, the seller, realizing the owner was abroad, executed a second registered deed for the exact same plot to a local housing company for BDT 55,00,000. When the expatriate's brother visited the plot in October 2024, the housing company had erected signboards and stationed private security guards.

Acting through a Special Power of Attorney, the expatriate engaged a Supreme Court advocate. The legal team immediately executed a three-pronged counter-attack: first, they filed a Title Suit in the Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka, for cancellation of the housing company's deed and declaration of title, successfully securing an ad-interim Temporary Injunction under Order 39 CPC halting all construction. Second, they filed a formal objection before the Savar AC Land, blocking the housing company's mutation application.

Third, the advocate lodged a criminal prosecution under Section 5 of the Land Crime Prevention and Redress Act 2023 and Section 420 of the Penal Code. The Magistrate Court issued non-bailable arrest warrants against the seller. Within forty-eight hours of the seller's arrest by police, the housing company, realizing their deed was legally worthless and facing injunction contempt proceedings, withdrew their guards. The seller's family was forced to refund the housing company's money to secure bail, and the expatriate's lawful ownership and mutation were fully restored.

Talk to an Advocate

If you have discovered that a seller has fraudulently transferred your land to another buyer, time is your greatest adversary. Every day of delay allows the fraudulent party to erect structures, alter boundary demarcations, or sell to innocent third parties. A skilled land lawyer will immediately initiate Title Suit proceedings for deed cancellation, secure emergency injunctions from the civil court, block fraudulent mutations at the AC Land office, and invoke the stringent penal provisions of the Land Crime Prevention and Redress Act 2023.

Need an advocate for a land dispute, double deed, or property fraud case in Bangladesh? Send your deeds and Khatian records on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: remote title verification and court representation available.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which buyer owns the land if a seller sells it twice in Bangladesh?

The first buyer who executed and registered the valid Saf Kabala deed owns the land. Under Section 48 of the Registration Act 1908, prior registration takes absolute priority. Once the first deed is registered, the seller has no remaining title to pass to a second buyer.

What is the punishment for a seller who executes a double sale in Bangladesh?

Under Section 5 of the Land Crime Prevention and Redress Act 2023, selling land to multiple parties carries rigorous imprisonment for up to 7 years and heavy fines. The offense is cognizable and non-bailable.

How do I cancel the second buyer's fraudulent deed?

You must file a Title Suit in the Court of the Joint District Judge under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act 1877 for Cancellation of Deed. The court passes a decree adjudging the second deed void and directs the Sub-Registrar to record its cancellation.

Can the second buyer claim they are an innocent purchaser without notice?

In real property law, registration in the official Sub-Registry Office Balam books operates as constructive notice to the entire world. A second buyer cannot claim innocence to defeat a valid, prior registered deed.

How can I prevent the second buyer from building on the land while the case is ongoing?

Your advocate will file an application for a Temporary Injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The court can issue an immediate order restraining the second buyer from altering the land, felling trees, or building structures.

What if the second buyer already managed to get Namjari (mutation) in their name?

You can file an E-Namjari Miss Case or an appeal before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) under Section 147 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. Since mutation does not create title, the revenue authority will cancel the Khatian upon presentation of the prior registered deed.

What happens if I only had an unregistered Bayna deed and the seller sold to someone else?

Under Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act 1877, a contract for sale (Bayna) must be registered. If your Bayna deed was registered, you can sue for Specific Performance. If it was unregistered, you cannot compel transfer of the land and can only sue to recover your advance money with damages under the Penal Code.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi (NRB) pursue this litigation without coming to Bangladesh?

Yes. An NRB landowner can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh High Commission or Embassy abroad, appointing a trusted local representative and retaining an advocate to handle the civil litigation and police complaints.

Selling Ancestral Property Without All Heirs' Consent in Bangladesh: Legal Rules

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-12 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

A perennial source of bitter family conflict across Bangladesh occurs when joint ancestral property (Paitrik Sompotti) is left undivided following the demise of parents. Suddenly, one aggressive brother, uncle, or co-heir secretly negotiates with an outside developer or stranger, executes a registered sale deed for a specific prime portion of the family land or homestead, and pockets the cash without obtaining the consent of other siblings. The unsuspecting sisters, living elsewhere or abroad, return to find strangers erecting boundary walls across their childhood homestead. In Bangladesh, joint property rights are governed by clear statutory checks under the Transfer of Property Act 1882, the Partition Act 1893, and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. Understanding how to block unauthorized sales, enforce pre-emption rights, and institute Partition Suits is vital to protecting your rightful inheritance.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

  7. Special Protection for Sisters and Overseas NRB Heirs

  10. Talk to an Advocate

The Ancestral Property Conflict in Bangladesh

In Bangladesh, land succession is governed by religious personal laws (Muslim Faraiz or Hindu Succession). Upon the demise of a parent, all surviving legal heirs automatically become joint tenants-in-common, owning undivided shares in every square inch of the estate. While this communal ownership reflects family solidarity, it frequently degenerates into predatory land grabs.

A pervasive problem occurs when one brother or male heir, residing on the physical property while sisters or other siblings live in different cities or abroad, treats the entire ancestral estate as his personal fiefdom. Needing money, he enters into private negotiations with aggressive developers or local influential buyers. Without consulting other co-sharers or initiating a formal partition, he executes a registered deed purporting to sell a specific prime roadside corner or residential portion of the homestead. The co-sharers are suddenly confronted with armed laborers fencing off their land. Understanding the legal limitations of joint ownership and the precise statutory remedies available is essential to halting this expropriation.

Undivided Share vs. Specific Demarcation: The Legal Rule

The core legal principle governing joint property in Bangladesh is that prior to a formal, registered Deed of Partition (Aposh Batwara) or a civil court partition decree, no co-sharer owns any specific physical spot or boundary. Every co-heir holds an undivided fractional interest across the entire undivided parcel.

Consequently, under the Transfer of Property Act 1882, while a co-heir is legally entitled to alienate their undivided fractional share (e.g., their 4-anna or 25% mathematical entitlement), they have zero legal authority to sell a specific demarcated plot (such as 'the front 2 decimals facing the main road'). If an aggressive co-heir executes a deed specifically defining and transferring a particular physical parcel without the concurrence of other co-sharers, that specific demarcation is legally void against the non-consenting heirs. The purchaser merely steps into the shoes of the seller as an undivided co-sharer and cannot claim exclusive possession of any specific corner.

Section 44 Transfer of Property Act: Dwelling House Shield

The legislature recognized that allowing third-party strangers into an undivided family homestead destroys family privacy and social peace. To prevent this, the second paragraph of Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 provides an extraordinary statutory shield:

'Where the transferee of a share of a dwelling-house belonging to an undivided family is not a member of the family, nothing in this section shall be deemed to entitle him to joint possession or other common or part enjoyment of the house.'

This statutory provision is of monumental importance. It establishes that even if a stranger holds a valid registered deed purchased from an unscrupulous co-heir, that stranger has absolutely no legal right to enter the family homestead, break locks, construct rooms, or reside on the premises. If the stranger attempts to force entry, they commit criminal trespass under Section 441 of the Penal Code 1860, and the civil court will grant an immediate injunction restraining them from entering the dwelling house.

Need legal guidance or representation for your case in Bangladesh? Send your documents and dispute details on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007. Overseas clients and local litigants can arrange an immediate confidential document review.

Statutory Pre-emption Rights Under SAT Act Section 96

When an ancestral co-heir sells their share to an outside stranger without offering it first to family members, the remaining co-heirs possess an aggressive statutory weapon: the right of Pre-emption (Ogrokroy). In Bangladesh, pre-emption is governed by Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (SAT Act) and Section 4 of the Partition Act 1893.

Under Section 96 SAT Act, if a portion or share of a holding of land is transferred to any person who is not a co-sharer in the holding, any co-sharer tenant has the legal right to apply to the civil court within two (2) months of the service of notice of transfer, or within two months of learning of the transfer, to have the transferred property forcibly re-transferred to themselves upon depositing the consideration money plus statutory compensation into court. Furthermore, under Section 4 of the Partition Act 1893, if the buyer of a dwelling house share sues for partition, the family members have the absolute statutory right to compel the court to value the share and allow the family to buy out the stranger, expelling them permanently from the ancestral home.

Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) and Advocate Commissioners

The definitive, permanent legal remedy to resolve undivided ancestral land disputes is instituting a formal Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) in the Civil Court having territorial jurisdiction. The suit proceeds in two distinct judicial phases:

  1. Preliminary Decree: The civil court examines the genealogy (Warishan tree), examines CS, SA, RS, and City/BS Khatians, and delivers a preliminary decree declaring the precise fractional share (Saham) belonging to each co-heir and setting aside any unauthorized demarcation.
  2. Appointment of Advocate Commissioner: Following the preliminary decree, the court appoints a neutral Advocate Commissioner accompanied by a government surveyor (Amin) to visit the physical land. The commissioner surveys the entire plot, evaluates road frontage, valuation, and existing possession, and drafts a scientific field demarcation (Batwara map) allocating separate physical plots to each co-heir.
  3. Final Decree: The court hears objections, approves the commissioner's report, and passes a Final Decree, permanently carving out separate, independent titles and boundaries for each heir, ending joint friction forever.

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Securing Emergency Injunctions Under Order 39 CPC

Because a Partition Suit takes time to conclude through trial and commission, the urgent battle is preserving the property in status quo. If the rogue buyer or aggressive co-heir rapidly cuts down ancestral fruit orchards, demolishes family structures, or erects commercial buildings, the character of the land is permanently altered.

Upon filing the Partition Suit, your advocate immediately submits an interlocutory petition for a Temporary Injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The court evaluates whether the petitioner is an undisputed co-sharer and whether construction without formal partition causes irreparable harm. Upon satisfaction, the civil court grants an ad-interim injunction restraining all parties, including the outside buyer, from altering the physical character of the land, cutting trees, raising any construction, or executing further sale deeds until the disposal of the partition suit.

Special Protection for Sisters and Overseas NRB Heirs

A notorious social injustice in Bangladesh involves male siblings disenfranchising their married sisters or overseas expatriate (NRB) brothers. Brothers frequently tell their sisters, 'Our father gave you gold at your wedding, so you have no claim on the land,' or they forge heirship certificates excluding sisters' names entirely to obtain fraudulent mutations (E-Namjari).

Under Islamic law and the statutory laws of Bangladesh, a daughter's right to inherit ancestral land from her parents is absolute, divine, and unalienable. Dowry or marriage gifts do not extinguish a daughter's statutory inheritance. If brothers forge a Warishan certificate or execute sale deeds concealing sisters, the sisters can institute criminal prosecution for forgery under Sections 467 and 468 of the Penal Code, cancel the fraudulent mutation via an E-Namjari Miss Case before the AC Land, and file a Partition Suit claiming their full Faraiz shares. For overseas Bangladeshis residing in the UK, USA, or Canada, these proceedings can be fully executed through a registered Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy.

Comparison Table: Lawful Co-Heir Rights vs. Third-Party Buyer

The table below summarizes the legal rights of existing co-heirs versus an outside buyer who purchased an undivided share without unanimous consent:

Legal IssueLawful Non-Consenting Co-HeirsOutside Third-Party Buyer
Right to Specific Demarcated PlotRetains joint undivided ownershipZero right to specific plot before court partition
Joint Possession of Dwelling HouseAbsolute statutory right to resideExplicitly barred under Transfer of Property Act §44
Pre-emption VulnerabilityCan forcibly repurchase under §96 SAT ActSubject to statutory buyout by family members
Right to Construct BuildingsCannot build without unanimous consentRestrained immediately via Order 39 Injunction
Ultimate Legal RemedyEntitled to separate Saham via Batwara decreeMust wait for Advocate Commissioner allocation

The law firmly shields ancestral families against outside intrusion, subordinating the third-party buyer's interests to the comprehensive partition decree of the civil court.

Illustrative Scenario: Blocking an Illegal Ancestral Sale in Sylhet

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how joint heirs protected their ancestral homestead in Sylhet:

A deceased expatriate businessman left behind an undivided 24-decimal homestead in Beanibazar, Sylhet, inherited by three sons and two daughters. Two sons and both daughters lived abroad in London, while the eldest son remained in Sylhet managing the family home. In mid-2024, the eldest son incurred massive personal debts. Without informing his four expatriate siblings, he negotiated with a local commercial developer, executed a registered Saf Kabala deed purporting to sell the entire front 10 decimals facing the highway, and received BDT 60,00,000.

Two months later, the London-based siblings were alerted by relatives that the developer had brought bulldozers to level the front garden and construct a commercial shopping complex. Acting swiftly through a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh High Commission in London, the siblings engaged a Supreme Court advocate. The legal team immediately obtained certified copies of the sale deed, which revealed that the brother had purported to sell a demarcated roadside parcel exceeding his mathematical Faraiz share.

The advocate filed an urgent Partition Suit in the Court of the Joint District Judge, Sylhet, coupled with an interlocutory petition under Order 39 Rules 1-2 CPC and Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act. The judge issued an immediate status quo injunction restraining all construction and prohibiting the developer from entering the homestead. Concurrently, the advocate filed a Pre-emption case under Section 96 SAT Act depositing the statutory funds into the treasury. Faced with an unyielding judicial injunction and the certainty of pre-emption buyout, the developer terminated the transaction, the brother was compelled to refund the funds, and the court proceeded with a formal preliminary partition decree securing all five siblings' equal rights.

Talk to an Advocate

Navigating complex litigation in Bangladesh requires meticulous evidentiary preparation, prompt statutory filings, and strategic courtroom advocacy. Whether you are dealing with business debts, family property partitions, corporate oppression, employee theft, or administrative overreach, attempting to resolve disputes without seasoned legal counsel frequently causes irreversible procedural defaults. A qualified advocate protects your rights, secures urgent injunctions or stay orders, and ensures complete statutory compliance across civil, criminal, and constitutional forums.

Need an advocate for this legal matter in Bangladesh? Send your case documents on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: remote consultation and court representation available.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a brother sell ancestral property without his sisters' permission in Bangladesh?

A brother can sell only his own undivided share (Saham) calculated under Islamic Faraiz rules. He cannot sell his sisters' shares, nor can he sell any specific demarcated portion of the property without their formal written consent or a registered partition deed.

What is Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882?

Section 44 protects undivided family dwelling houses. It explicitly dictates that if an outsider buys an undivided share of an ancestral family home, the buyer does NOT acquire the right to joint possession or enjoyment of the house, preventing strangers from entering family residences.

How do I stop someone from building on undivided ancestral land?

You must immediately file a Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) in the Civil Court along with an application for a Temporary Injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The court will issue an injunction restraining all construction.

What is the Pre-emption (Ogrokroy) right in ancestral land?

Under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, when a co-sharer sells their agricultural land share to a stranger, the other co-heirs have the legal right to apply to court to buy back that share at the registered price plus statutory compensation.

Can a co-heir sell a specific portion (e.g., roadside land) before partition?

No. Before a formal partition deed or civil court decree, all co-heirs own undivided interests across the entire land. A sale of a specific demarcated plot without consent is legally void regarding that demarcation, and the buyer only gets an undivided fractional share.

How long does a Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) take in Bangladesh?

A contested Partition Suit generally takes between 1 to 3 years, proceeding through a preliminary decree of shares, appointment of an Advocate Commissioner for physical surveying, and issuance of a final partition decree.

Do married daughters have the same land rights as sons in ancestral property?

Yes. Under Islamic inheritance law, daughters have statutory fixed shares in both their father's and mother's estates. Their inheritance rights are permanent and cannot be denied or bypassed on grounds of receiving wedding gifts or dowry.

Can an overseas Bangladeshi (NRB) stop an illegal ancestral sale from abroad?

Yes. An NRB heir can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, empowering a trusted relative or lawyer in Bangladesh to file civil injunctions and partition suits on their behalf.

How NRBs Can Sell Property in Bangladesh and Legally Repatriate Money to USA, UK & Canada (2026 Guide)

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-26 · 19 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Liquidating inherited real estate, commercial assets, or residential apartments in Bangladesh and transferring the sale proceeds to the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, or Australia represents one of the most complex financial and legal operations for Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs). Because Bangladesh maintains capital account exchange restrictions under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947, foreign currency cannot be freely wired abroad without adhering to rigorous regulatory guidelines issued by Bangladesh Bank and tax clearances from the National Board of Revenue (NBR). Many expatriates, frustrated by paperwork, fall prey to illegal underground remittance networks (Hundi), exposing themselves to asset freezing under the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012 and punitive tax audits from the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS FATCA) or UK HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC). This master guide sets out the definitive, 100% legal roadmap to selling real estate, securing NBR tax clearance, navigating Bangladesh Bank outward remittance approvals, and safely wiring millions of Taka into overseas bank accounts.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

  10. 10. Real-Life Case Study: London NRB Repatriating £180,000 from Sylhet
  11. 11. Pitfalls That Freeze Expatriate Funds in Bangladesh

1. The Regulatory Landscape: Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947

Cross-border financial flows in Bangladesh are governed by the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 (FERA), administered by the Foreign Exchange Policy Department (FEPD) of Bangladesh Bank through the Guidelines for Foreign Exchange Transactions (GFET, Vol-1 & Vol-2).

Crucially, Bangladesh operates with full current account convertibility (for imports, services, and travel) but maintains partial capital account convertibility. Under Section 4 and 5 of FERA 1947, no person resident in Bangladesh or holding assets in Bangladesh may transfer capital outside the country without general or special permission from Bangladesh Bank.

However, Bangladesh Bank has enacted targeted circulars recognizing the legitimate property rights of Non-Resident Bangladeshis. Expatriates who acquired property through lawful inheritance or who purchased property using documented inward foreign currency remittances are entitled to repatriate liquidation proceeds, provided all domestic tax liabilities have been extinguished and full source verification is provided.

2. Pre-Sale Prerequisite: Clean Title, Inheritance Proof & e-Mutation

A buyer may be willing to buy your land on an old manual deed, but Bangladesh Bank will reject outward remittance if the title chain has even a minor administrative defect. Before marketing the asset, the overseas heir must compile an unimpeachable legal dossier:

  1. Warishan / Succession Certificate: Issued by the relevant City Corporation Mayor/Councilor or Union Parishad Chairman, certifying all surviving legal heirs of the deceased parent with national ID numbers.
  2. e-Namjari (ই-নামজারি ও জমাখারিজ): The ancestral Khatian must be separated, and a distinct digital Mutation Khatian must be generated in the names of the living heirs. Attempting to sell land while it remains registered in the deceased ancestor's name makes it impossible to open the required seller bank account.
  3. Digital Land Tax Dakhila (ভূমি উন্নয়ন কর দাখিলা): Up-to-date land tax receipts downloaded from ldtax.gov.bd for the current fiscal year.
  4. Non-Encumbrance Certificate (NEC - দায়মুক্ত সনদ): Form 41 certificate issued by the Sub-Registrar certifying that the land is free from prior mortgages, attachments, or lis pendens lawsuits.

3. Safe Consideration Structures: Eliminating Cash & Hundi Risks

The biggest obstacle to legal repatriation is the traditional Bangladeshi market practice of under-declaring deed values and accepting substantial payments in cash (কালো টাকা). Expatriates must strictly reject this practice:

The Golden Rule of Repatriation: Bangladesh Bank will ONLY permit foreign currency remittance equal to the net declared sale value on the registered deed, deposited via official banking instruments, minus verified tax deductions. If you sell a flat for BDT 3 Crore but declare BDT 1.5 Crore on the registered deed, you can NEVER legally transfer the remaining BDT 1.5 Crore out of Bangladesh.

Mandatory Payment Protocols:

  • Bank Draft / Account-Payee Pay Order: Issued directly by the buyer's commercial bank payable to the seller's verified bank account in Bangladesh.
  • Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS): Direct electronic bank-to-bank transfer for instantaneous audit trails.
  • Escrow Agreement: For high-value transactions, retaining an advocate to hold the registered deed in escrow until the bank draft clears provides total security for both overseas seller and domestic buyer.

4. Taxation on Real Estate Disposals Under Income Tax Act 2023

The Income Tax Act, 2023 (আয়কর আইন, ২০২৩) introduced modernized provisions regarding real estate asset disposals and source tax withholding:

A. Advance Source Tax (উৎস কর - Section 125)

Under Section 125 of the 2023 Act, the Sub-Registrar cannot register a sale deed unless advance tax is deducted at source. Rates depend on the geographical location and classification of the property:

  • Dhaka, Chattogram & Commercial Hubs: 8% of deed value or statutory square-feet/katha rate (whichever is higher) in prime areas like Gulshan, Banani, Motijheel, Dhanmondi, Uttara.
  • Other City Corporations & Municipalities: 4% to 6% of deed value.
  • Rural / Upazila Areas: 2% to 3% of deed value.

B. Capital Gains Tax (মূলধনী লাভ কর - Section 89)

Capital gains tax is assessed on the net profit: Sale Consideration minus (Original Acquisition Cost + Documented Improvement Costs + Registration Expenses). For inherited property where acquisition cost was zero or nominal, the fair market value at the time of inheritance is considered. Expatriates must file an annual tax return with their designated NBR Taxes Circle to finalize assessment.

C. Obtaining the NBR Tax Clearance Certificate (কর প্রত্যয়নপত্র)

Once taxes are deposited via Treasury Chalan, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes (DCT) conducts scrutiny and issues a formal Tax Clearance Certificate under the seal of the National Board of Revenue. This certificate is the single most important document required by Bangladesh Bank to authorize foreign exchange release.

5. Complete Tax & Registration Fee Breakdown Table (2026)

The following table provides a comprehensive overview of statutory taxes and fees applicable to property disposals in Bangladesh:

Fee / Tax ComponentStatutory BasisApplicable Rate (Dhaka / Urban)Bearing Party
Advance Source Tax (AIT)Sec 125, Income Tax Act 20234% to 8% (depending on zone)Seller (deducted at registry)
Capital Gains TaxSec 89, Income Tax Act 202315% on net capital gainSeller (adjusted against source tax)

Registration FeeRegistration Act 19081.0% of deed valueBuyer

Outward Remittance Banking FeeBangladesh Bank / AD Tariff0.25% to 0.50% + SWIFT chargeRemitter (Expat)

6. Step-by-Step Bangladesh Bank Outward Remittance Approval (Form TM)

Repatriating funds is executed through an Authorized Dealer (AD) Commercial Bank (e.g. Standard Chartered Bank, HSBC, BRAC Bank, The City Bank, Eastern Bank):

  1. Account Opening & Deposit: Open a Non-Resident Taka Account (NRTA) or specialized resident account. The buyer deposits consideration via account-payee pay order.
  2. Filing Form TM (Transfer of Money): The expatriate or their legal attorney submits Form TM to the Foreign Exchange Operations Department of the AD bank, requesting conversion and outward wire transfer.
  3. Bank Scrutiny & Dossier Preparation: The AD Bank's compliance department audits the registered deed, title chain, tax clearance certificate, proof of inheritance, and foreign residency documents.
  4. Submission to Bangladesh Bank: The AD bank submits the comprehensive dossier to the Foreign Exchange Policy Department (FEPD), Bangladesh Bank Headquarters, Motijheel, Dhaka.
  5. Central Bank Scrutiny & Approval: Bangladesh Bank verifies that no money laundering red flags exist and issues a formal Approval Letter.
  6. SWIFT Outward Remittance: The AD bank purchases foreign currency (USD, GBP, CAD) at the prevailing interbank exchange rate and transmits the funds via SWIFT to the seller's overseas account in New York, London, Toronto, etc.

7. Authorized Banking Channels: NITA, NRTA, and Resident Accounts

Expatriates should choose the correct banking vehicle:

  • Non-Resident Investor's Taka Account (NITA): If an expatriate originally bought property in Bangladesh using inward foreign remittance routed through a NITA account, liquidation proceeds can be credited directly back to the NITA account and repatriated outward without prior approval from Bangladesh Bank under standard GFET standing orders.
  • Non-Resident Taka Account (NRTA): Used for general income generated in Bangladesh (rents, business proceeds). Remittance requires Bangladesh Bank permission.
  • Special Remittance Quota: Under recent Bangladesh Bank policy relaxations, genuine expatriate inheritances can be remitted up to authorized thresholds per fiscal year under controlled commercial bank review without lengthy central bank delays.

8. Double Taxation Relief: US (IRS), UK (HMRC), and Canada (CRA)

A paramount concern for expatriates is whether receiving large property sale proceeds will subject them to crippling double taxation in their resident country:

United States (IRS Compliance):

US citizens and Green Card holders are taxed on worldwide income. You must report the capital gain on IRS Form 1040 (Schedule D). However, under the US-Bangladesh Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA), you can claim the Foreign Tax Credit (IRS Form 1116) for source tax and capital gains tax already paid to the Bangladesh NBR, offsetting dollar-for-dollar against your US tax liability.

United Kingdom (HMRC Compliance):

UK residents must declare foreign capital gains on their Self Assessment return. Under the UK-Bangladesh Bilateral Tax Convention, Double Taxation Relief (DTR) ensures credit is given for Bangladeshi taxes paid. Keep all NBR Treasury Chalan receipts and registered sale deeds safely.

Canada (CRA Compliance):

Canadian permanent residents and citizens must declare foreign capital property dispositions on Schedule 3 and file Form T1135 (Foreign Income Verification Statement) if foreign assets exceed $100,000 CAD. Canadian Foreign Tax Credits prevent duplicate taxation on verified remittances.

9. Document Checklist for Bangladesh Bank & Commercial AD Banks

Prepare this documentation package in triplicate with your legal counsel:

  • Original certified copy of the Registered Sale Deed (সাফ কবলা দলিল).
  • Chain of title deeds (বায়া দলিল) spanning at least 25 years.
  • Original Succession / Warishan Certificate with English translation.
  • e-Namjari Khatian, DCR receipt, and current fiscal year Land Tax Dakhila.
  • NBR Advance Source Tax Chalan (Section 125) and NBR Tax Clearance Certificate.
  • Completed Form TM signed by the applicant or authorized Power of Attorney.
  • Proof of overseas residence (US Passport/Green Card, UK Passport/BRP, Canadian Passport/PR).
  • Official bank statement showing deposit of buyer's pay order into seller's account.
  • Letter of Undertaking from the seller declaring no other remittances were made against the same asset.

10. Real-Life Case Study: London NRB Repatriating £180,000 from Sylhet

Background: Mr. Fakhrul Islam, a British Bangladeshi restaurateur residing in Tower Hamlets, London, decided to sell a 12-decimal ancestral commercial plot in Amberkhana, Sylhet. The agreed sale consideration was BDT 2.8 Crore (approx. £180,000 GBP).

Execution Strategy:

  1. Our chamber conducted full due diligence, updated the e-Namjari in Mr. Fakhrul's name, and vetted the buyer's financial credentials.
  2. The entire consideration was paid via two Account-Payee Pay Orders from Dutch-Bangla Bank directly into Mr. Fakhrul's Non-Resident Taka Account at Standard Chartered Bank, Dhaka.
  3. The sale deed was registered at the Sylhet Sadar Sub-Registry, and 6% advance source tax (BDT 16.8 Lakh) was deposited to the NBR treasury.
  4. We filed the capital gains assessment before Taxes Circle-14, Sylhet, and obtained an unreserved NBR Tax Clearance Certificate within 14 working days.
  5. We compiled the Form TM file and submitted it through Standard Chartered Bank's Foreign Exchange Operations to Bangladesh Bank.
  6. Bangladesh Bank granted outward remittance approval within 5 weeks. Standard Chartered converted BDT 2.63 Crore (net of taxes) into GBP and wired £172,400 directly to Mr. Fakhrul's Barclays Bank account in London via SWIFT.

11. Pitfalls That Freeze Expatriate Funds in Bangladesh

Avoid these catastrophic mistakes that frequently lead to permanent capital lock-in:

  • Accepting Undeclared Cash: Accepting cash under the table leaves you with piles of local currency that cannot be deposited without triggering Anti-Money Laundering (BFIU) freezing orders.
  • Attempting Informal Remittance (Hundi): Using Hundi brokers exposes you to criminal prosecution under Section 4 of the Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012 (up to 12 years imprisonment) and forfeiture of all assets.
  • Selling on Power of Attorney Without Banking Authority: If an expat executes a Power of Attorney to a relative but forgets to grant specific banking and remittance authority, the agent cannot operate bank accounts or sign Form TM.
  • Missing NBR Tax Files: Attempting to remit funds without an active e-TIN and official tax clearance certificate will result in immediate rejection by the commercial bank.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I legally wire money from selling my house in Bangladesh to my US or UK bank?

Yes. Outward remittance of property sale proceeds is fully legal under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947, provided you secure prior approval from Bangladesh Bank through an Authorized Dealer commercial bank supported by an NBR Tax Clearance Certificate.

How long does Bangladesh Bank take to approve an outward property remittance?

Once a complete, audited file with all tax receipts, title deeds, and Form TM is submitted by the Authorized Dealer bank, Bangladesh Bank typically issues approval within 4 to 8 weeks.

What is the tax rate on property sales in Bangladesh for overseas citizens?

Advance source tax of 2% to 8% (depending on property location) is collected at the Sub-Registry at registration, which is adjusted against capital gains tax (typically 15% on net capital gains) under the Income Tax Act 2023.

Will the US IRS or UK HMRC tax my remittance from Bangladesh?

You must report the capital gain on your foreign tax return, but Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAA) allow you to claim Foreign Tax Credits for all taxes paid to the Bangladesh NBR, generally eliminating duplicate tax.

Can I sell property in Bangladesh if I do not have a Bangladeshi National ID (NID)?

Yes. Non-Resident Bangladeshis without an NID can use their valid Bangladeshi Passport or foreign passport with a 'No Visa Required' (NVR) seal and Dual Nationality Certificate.

Can my appointed attorney receive the sale proceeds into their personal bank account?

It is strongly advised against. Consideration should be deposited directly into a bank account opened in the name of the legal owner (the expat) to maintain complete audit traceability for Bangladesh Bank and foreign tax authorities.

What is Form TM in Bangladesh banking?

Form TM (Transfer of Money) is the statutory foreign exchange application form prescribed by Bangladesh Bank for any cross-border outward remittance of funds through Authorized Dealer banks.

Can I transfer the sale money in multiple installments instead of one lump sum?

Yes. Bangladesh Bank allows phased remittances across different fiscal tranches, or you can wire the entire approved amount in a single lump sum via SWIFT.

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-04 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Sending money home is the backbone of millions of Bangladeshi families, and the government rewards legal remittance. But using hundi or informal channels can freeze your accounts, trigger money laundering cases and cost you valuable benefits. Legal Channels for Remittance

  • Banks and exchange houses: direct account credit or cash pickup.
  • Mobile financial services: bKash, Nagad and others through authorised international partners.
  • Digital remittance apps: regulated services that deliver to bank or mobile accounts.
  • Bank drafts and cheques: for large amounts, deposited into your account.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Why Hundi Is Dangerous

Hundi (hawala) payments avoid the banking system and are illegal. Consequences include seizure of money, criminal charges, the receiver's account being frozen and no legal protection if the agent disappears. Using hundi also means you lose the remittance incentive and may have problems proving the source of funds for investment later.

Remittance Incentive

The government has offered an incentive on legal inward remittances, which has been a few percent of the amount sent, paid through the receiving bank. The rate, the cap and the eligible channels change from time to time. Check the latest circular from Bangladesh Bank or ask your bank.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Tax and Source of Funds

Remittance sent by a Bangladeshi worker or resident abroad through legal channels is generally not taxed as income in Bangladesh, and the authorities usually do not ask for the source. However, tax and reporting rules change, and if you hold assets in Bangladesh you may have to report them in a return. Keep payslips, tax returns and bank statements from abroad. See a tax lawyer if your situation is complex.

Investing Remittance: Land, Bonds, Business

  • Property: buy through bank transfer to the seller, and keep the remittance record as proof of source (see land buying checklist).
  • Wage earner bonds and NRB accounts: available through banks; check interest and eligibility.
  • Business: bring in capital by inward remittance to qualify for registration and later repatriation of profit.
  • Shares: NRBs can invest through a dedicated account with a broker, subject to rules.

Practical Tips

  1. Always send to the account of the intended person, in their own name.
  2. Keep the remittance slip or transaction ID.
  3. Avoid structured small transfers just to hide amounts.
  4. Use the same remitter name for consistent record.
  5. For very large transfers, inform the bank in advance and keep documentation.

This article is general legal information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change; confirm current requirements with the relevant office or a qualified advocate before acting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is sending money by hundi illegal in Bangladesh?

Yes. It is prohibited under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 and linked laws and can lead to criminal action.

Do I pay tax on remittance sent to Bangladesh?

Generally remittance through legal channels is not taxed as income, but check current rules and reporting duties.

What is the remittance incentive?

A government cash incentive on remittance sent through legal channels; the rate changes so check the current circular.

Can I use remittance to buy land?

Yes. Pay through bank channels and keep the remittance proof as the source of funds.

Can I send money back out of Bangladesh?

It is restricted and needs bank approval and documentation. Plan before you invest.

Sexual Harassment Law Bangladesh – Workplace & Public Harassment Laws & Remedies

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-06 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Sexual harassment remains a serious problem in Bangladesh — in workplaces, educational institutions, public spaces, and increasingly in digital environments. Bangladeshi law provides several overlapping legal frameworks for victims to seek justice, from the landmark 2009 Supreme Court guidelines to the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000 and the Cyber Security Act 2023. This comprehensive guide explains every available legal remedy, how to file a complaint, and what penalties perpetrators face.

The 2009 Supreme Court Guidelines — Bangladesh's Foundational Framework

The most significant legal development in sexual harassment law in Bangladesh came through a landmark Supreme Court ruling in Bangladesh National Women Lawyers Association (BNWLA) v Government of Bangladesh and Others (2009). The High Court Division of the Supreme Court issued comprehensive guidelines addressing sexual harassment in workplaces and educational institutions, broadly similar in scope to India's Vishaka Guidelines.

These guidelines were issued under the Court's constitutional authority (Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh) in the absence of comprehensive dedicated legislation at the time. The key provisions of the 2009 BNWLA guidelines include:

  • Mandatory Complaint Committee: All employers and heads of educational institutions are required to establish a sexual harassment complaint committee with a female majority.
  • Definition: The guidelines provide a broad definition of sexual harassment covering physical, verbal, non-verbal, and visual conduct of a sexual nature.
  • Duty to Prevent: Employers have an affirmative duty to prevent harassment and create a safe working environment.
  • Awareness: Employers must display and circulate the guidelines in the workplace and inform employees of their rights.
  • Interim Relief: Victims may seek interim relief, including transfer of the accused or the complainant (at the complainant's option) during the inquiry.

Although these are court-issued guidelines rather than parliamentary legislation, they have the force of law and non-compliance can expose employers to contempt of court proceedings and civil liability.

Definition of Sexual Harassment Under Bangladesh Law

The 2009 BNWLA guidelines provide the most comprehensive definition of sexual harassment currently operative in Bangladesh. Sexual harassment is defined to include:

  • Physical harassment: Unwanted touching, grabbing, pinching, brushing against a person's body, assault, or molestation of a sexual nature.
  • Verbal harassment: Unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favours, sexually coloured comments or jokes, lewd remarks, or use of obscene language.
  • Non-verbal / gestural harassment: Staring, leering, winking, making obscene gestures, displaying pornographic material, or sending sexually explicit communications.
  • Visual harassment: Showing pornographic or sexually explicit material to a person without consent.
  • Digital / cyber harassment: Sending unwanted sexually explicit messages, images, or videos via phone, email, social media, or other digital platforms. This is now further covered under the Cyber Security Act 2023.
  • Eve teasing (উত্ত্যক্তকরণ): Public harassment of women through verbal abuse, catcalling, blocking path, or persistent following in streets, markets, public transport, or other public places. Eve teasing has been specifically addressed through dedicated government campaigns and enforcement drives under Section 10A of the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000.

It is important to note that sexual harassment is defined by the unwelcome nature of the conduct from the victim's perspective — it does not require physical contact, and a single severe incident can be sufficient to constitute harassment.

Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000 — Key Provisions

The Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000 (নারী ও শিশু নির্যাতন দমন আইন, ২০০০), as amended in 2003, is Bangladesh's primary criminal statute addressing violence and harassment against women and children. The relevant sections for sexual harassment are:

  • Section 9 — Rape: Defines and penalises rape, including gang rape, with penalties ranging from life imprisonment to death in aggravated cases. Section 9(4A) addresses rape resulting in death of the victim.
  • Section 10 — Sexual Assault: Covers sexual assault short of rape — defined as any act by a man of touching a woman's sexual organs or committing any indecent act with sexual intent without her consent. Penalty: up to 10 years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine.
  • Section 10A — Eve Teasing: Specifically criminalises public harassment of women and children, including verbal, gestural, and physical harassment in public places. Penalty: up to 2 years' imprisonment, or a fine up to Tk 10,000, or both.
  • Section 11 — Dowry-related Violence: Covers harassment and violence related to dowry demands, which overlaps with domestic harassment situations.
  • Section 12 — Kidnapping: Covers kidnapping and abduction of women and children for sexual exploitation.
  • Section 14 — Acid Attack: Specifically penalises acid throwing or use of corrosive substances, which is often harassment-related. Penalty: death or life imprisonment.

Cases under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000 are tried before special Nari O Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal (Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunals) established in each district. These tribunals have exclusive jurisdiction over these offences and are required to complete trials within 180 days under Section 20 of the Act.

Penal Code Provisions on Harassment and Assault

The Penal Code 1860 also contains several provisions relevant to sexual harassment, which apply where the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000 does not specifically cover the conduct:

  • Section 294 — Obscene Acts and Songs: Penalises committing an obscene act in a public place or uttering obscene words to the annoyance of others. Penalty: up to 3 months' imprisonment, or fine, or both.
  • Section 354 — Assault or Criminal Force with Intent to Outrage Modesty: Penalises assault or use of criminal force against a woman intending to outrage her modesty, or with the knowledge that it will likely outrage her modesty. Penalty: up to 2 years' imprisonment, or fine, or both. This section is commonly used in cases of groping, inappropriate touching, and physical molestation that fall short of the threshold under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000.
  • Section 509 — Word, Gesture or Act Intended to Insult the Modesty of a Woman: Penalises any word, gesture, or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman, or intrudes upon her privacy. Penalty: up to 1 year's imprisonment, or fine, or both. This section is often used for verbal harassment, catcalling, and inappropriate gestures.
  • Section 503 — Criminal Intimidation: Applicable where a harasser threatens the victim with injury to her reputation, person, or property to compel her to do something she is not legally obliged to do.

Under Section 198 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, an offence under Section 509 of the Penal Code is a cognizable offence, meaning police can arrest without a warrant upon receiving a complaint.

Workplace Harassment — Mandatory Complaint Committee

One of the most significant aspects of the 2009 BNWLA Supreme Court guidelines is the mandatory requirement for employers to establish a Sexual Harassment Complaint Committee at every workplace with 10 or more employees. The structure and procedure of this committee is as follows:

Committee Composition

  • The committee must have a female majority — at least half of the members must be women.
  • The chairperson must be a senior female employee.
  • At least one member should be from an NGO or legal background with expertise in gender issues.
  • A member of the workers' union (if any) should be included.

Complaint Procedure Before the Committee

  1. The complainant submits a written complaint to the committee within 3 months of the last incident of harassment (time can be extended in justified cases).
  2. The committee must acknowledge receipt of the complaint within 7 days.
  3. The inquiry must be completed within 60 days of receipt.
  4. Both complainant and accused have the right to be heard; the accused has the right to respond to the allegations.
  5. The committee may recommend interim relief to the employer (e.g., transfer of the accused, leave for the complainant).
  6. Upon completion of inquiry, the committee submits a report to the employer with findings and recommendations.
  7. The employer must act upon the recommendations within 60 days of receiving the report.

Consequences for Non-Compliance

Employers who fail to establish a complaint committee, or who fail to act on committee recommendations, can face contempt proceedings before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court, as the 2009 guidelines carry the force of a court order. Additionally, victims can file a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution seeking enforcement.

Cyber Sexual Harassment Under the Cyber Security Act 2023

With the explosive growth of social media and digital communications in Bangladesh, cyber sexual harassment has become a major concern. The Cyber Security Act 2023 (সাইবার নিরাপত্তা আইন, ২০২৩), which replaced the widely criticised Digital Security Act 2018, contains specific provisions addressing online harassment:

  • Section 21 — Publication of Obscene/Defamatory Content: Publishing, distributing, or transmitting any obscene, degrading, or harassing content about a person — including morphed or fabricated images — without consent. This is now a non-bailable offence. Penalty: up to 10 years' imprisonment, or up to Tk 25 lakh fine, or both for repeat offences.
  • Section 24 — Hacking and Unauthorised Access: Gaining unauthorised access to someone's accounts or devices to obtain private images or personal information for the purpose of harassment.
  • Revenge Pornography: Sharing intimate images of a person without consent (commonly called revenge porn) falls under Section 21 and related provisions. This is treated as a serious offence with significant penalties.
  • Online Stalking and Threatening: Persistent online contact, threatening messages, or impersonation for the purpose of harassment or intimidation can attract multiple charges under the Cyber Security Act 2023 and the Penal Code.

Complaints for cyber sexual harassment should be filed with the Cyber Crime Investigation Division (CCID) of the Bangladesh Police, available at cybercrime.gov.bd. Evidence (screenshots, message logs, URLs, email headers) must be preserved immediately and submitted with the complaint.

How to File a Sexual Harassment Case in Bangladesh

Victims of sexual harassment in Bangladesh have multiple avenues to seek redress. The appropriate avenue depends on the nature of the harassment, the relationship between parties, and the urgency of the situation.

Option 1 — Internal Complaint Committee (Workplace / Educational Institution)

Submit a written complaint to the employer's or institution's Sexual Harassment Complaint Committee. This is the first recommended step for workplace harassment. The committee process is confidential and faster than court proceedings.

Option 2 — Police Complaint / First Information Report (FIR)

For physical assault, eve teasing, or cyber harassment, file a complaint directly with the nearest police station. Sexual assault cases under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000 are cognizable — police can and must register an FIR. For eve teasing under Section 10A, a complaint can also be filed before the nearest Magistrate (Section 200, CrPC 1898) if police are unresponsive.

Option 3 — Case Before Nari O Shishu Nirjatan Daman Tribunal

Serious offences under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000 (Sections 9, 10) are tried exclusively by these special tribunals. After police investigation and charge sheet, the case proceeds before the tribunal.

Option 4 — Writ Petition Before the High Court Division

Where an employer fails to act on a complaint committee recommendation, or where constitutional rights are violated, a writ petition can be filed before the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh seeking enforcement of the 2009 BNWLA guidelines.

Option 5 — Civil Suit for Damages

A victim may also file a civil suit claiming damages for mental distress, reputational harm, and loss of income caused by harassment. This can run concurrently with criminal proceedings.

Evidence in Sexual Harassment Cases

Gathering and preserving evidence is critical in sexual harassment cases, particularly because such incidents often occur in private settings without independent witnesses. The following types of evidence are recognised and admissible in Bangladesh courts:

  • Direct witness testimony: Statements from the victim, eyewitnesses, or persons who observed the aftermath (e.g., seeing the victim immediately after the incident in a distressed state).
  • Medical evidence: For physical assault, a medical examination report (prepared by a registered medical officer) is important. Under Section 9 of the WCRPA 2000, the investigating officer is required to arrange for a medical examination of the victim within 24 hours of receiving the complaint.
  • Documentary evidence: Text messages, WhatsApp messages, emails, social media posts, and screenshots are admissible as electronic records under the Evidence Act 1872 (as amended) and the Cyber Security Act 2023. Preserve all digital communications without alteration — do not delete any messages even if offensive.
  • CCTV footage: If the harassment occurred in a workplace, educational institution, or public place with CCTV coverage, immediately request the employer or relevant authority to preserve and provide the footage before it is overwritten.
  • Prior complaint records: Evidence that the accused has a history of similar complaints is relevant to establish a pattern of conduct.
  • Character evidence limitations: Under the Evidence Act 1872, the victim's past sexual history or character is generally not admissible to undermine the credibility of the complaint in rape and sexual assault cases.

Victim Support, Confidentiality and Protection from Retaliation

Victims of sexual harassment in Bangladesh are entitled to several protective measures designed to encourage reporting and prevent secondary victimisation:

  • Confidentiality: The 2009 BNWLA guidelines require strict confidentiality throughout the complaint committee process. The names and personal details of the complainant must not be disclosed without consent. Similarly, criminal courts have the power to hold proceedings in camera (in private) in sensitive cases.
  • Protection from Retaliation: Taking adverse action against a complainant (such as demotion, dismissal, or hostile treatment) constitutes workplace victimisation and can itself form the basis of a legal complaint and civil action.
  • One-Stop Crisis Centres (OCC): The Government of Bangladesh has established One-Stop Crisis Centres at major public hospitals (including Dhaka Medical College Hospital and other district hospitals) that provide integrated support to women victims of violence — including medical care, psychological counselling, police assistance, and legal aid — in a single location.
  • National Legal Aid Services: Under the Legal Aid Services Act 2000, victims with insufficient means can apply for free legal representation through the National Legal Aid Services Organisation (NLASO) for criminal cases.
  • Bangladesh National Women Lawyers Association (BNWLA): Provides free legal counselling, court assistance, and shelter for women victims of harassment and violence. Reachable via their national helpline.
  • National Emergency Helpline: The Government of Bangladesh operates a dedicated helpline (999 for police, 10921 for women's affairs) for victims of violence and harassment.

Common Challenges Victims Face and How to Overcome Them

Despite the legal framework, sexual harassment victims in Bangladesh continue to face significant practical challenges. Understanding these challenges — and their solutions — is essential for effective legal advocacy:

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the time limit for filing a sexual harassment complaint in Bangladesh?

For internal workplace complaints before the employer's complaint committee, the current guideline suggests filing within 3 months of the last incident, though extensions are possible for justified reasons. For criminal complaints under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000, there is generally no strict limitation period, though prompt reporting is strongly recommended as delay can affect evidence availability and court credibility. For cases under the Penal Code, standard limitation periods under the Code of Criminal Procedure apply.

Can a man file a sexual harassment complaint in Bangladesh?

Yes, men can be victims of sexual harassment in Bangladesh. While most provisions of the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000 are gender-specific (protecting women and children), the general Penal Code provisions (Sections 294, 354, 509) and the Cyber Security Act 2023 apply to victims of any gender. Men can file complaints under these provisions. The 2009 BNWLA guidelines focus on women in workplaces but do not prohibit male complainants from seeking relief through other channels.

Is eve teasing a bailable or non-bailable offence in Bangladesh?

Eve teasing under Section 10A of the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act 2000 is currently a bailable offence, with a maximum sentence of 2 years' imprisonment or a fine up to Tk 10,000. However, if the harassment involves physical contact (touching, groping), it may be prosecuted under Section 10 (Sexual Assault), which is a non-bailable offence with significantly higher penalties. The exact charge depends on the specific conduct involved.

What should I do if my employer does not have a sexual harassment complaint committee?

Under the 2009 BNWLA Supreme Court guidelines, every employer with 10 or more employees is legally required to establish a complaint committee. If your employer does not have one, you can: (1) report the harassment directly to the police; (2) file a complaint before the nearest Magistrate; (3) file a writ petition before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court directing the employer to comply with the BNWLA Guidelines and provide you with a mechanism for redress; and (4) approach a legal aid organisation or NGO for assistance.

Can I sue my harasser for compensation in civil court in Bangladesh?

Yes. In addition to criminal proceedings, a victim of sexual harassment can file a civil suit for damages in the Civil Court claiming monetary compensation for mental distress, reputational harm, loss of employment opportunities, and other losses suffered as a result of the harassment. Civil and criminal proceedings can run simultaneously. Obtaining a conviction in the criminal case significantly strengthens the civil claim, though it is not a prerequisite.

What evidence should I preserve for a cyber harassment case?

For a cyber harassment case, preserve the following immediately: (1) screenshots of all offending messages, posts, or images (with timestamps visible); (2) the URL/link to the offending content; (3) full email headers if harassment occurred via email; (4) any witness who has seen the content; (5) your call logs or message logs showing persistent contact. Do not block the harasser before taking screenshots, as this may delete conversation history. Report to the Cyber Crime Investigation Division (CCID) at cybercrime.gov.bd as soon as possible, as online content can be deleted quickly.

Marriage with Foreign Nationals & Interfaith Civil Marriage in Bangladesh: Special Marriage Act 1872 Guide (2026)

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-02 · 19 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

In an increasingly interconnected globalized world, unions between Bangladeshi citizens and foreign nationals (American, British, Canadian, European, Australian citizens) as well as interfaith couples (Muslim-Hindu, Christian-Muslim, Hindu-Buddhist) are increasingly common. However, solemnizing a marriage involving differing religious faiths or foreign citizens in Bangladesh frequently encounters severe societal and legal confusion. Under standard Bangladeshi personal laws (Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, Hindu Marriage Registration Act 2012, Christian Marriage Act 1872), marriages are strictly confessional, often requiring one partner to convert. For couples who desire to marry **without religious conversion**, the sole statutory civil mechanism in Bangladesh is the historic **Special Marriage Act, 1872 (Act No. III of 1872)**. Navigating the mandatory 14-day public notice requirement, single-status affidavits, embassy No Objection Certificates (NOC), and registrar declarations is vital to guarantee that the marriage is 100% legally binding in Bangladesh and fully admissible for foreign spousal visas (such as the US CR-1/IR-1, UK Spousal Visa, or Canadian Family Class Sponsorship). This master guide details the complete civil marriage legal roadmap.
