Trademark vs Copyright vs Patent: Key Differences

Many business owners confuse these three types of intellectual property. Here is a clear comparison:

AspectTrademarkCopyrightPatent
What it protectsBrand identity (names, logos, slogans)Original creative expression (books, art, software)Inventions and industrial processes
Governing LawTrademarks Act 2009Copyright Act 2000Patents and Designs Act 1911
Registration required?Yes — at DPDTNo (automatic), but optional registration availableYes — at DPDT
Duration7 years, renewable forever in 10-year periodsLife of author + 60 years16 years from filing (non-renewable)
Registering AuthorityDPDT (Dept. of Patents, Designs and Trademarks)Copyright Office, Ministry of Cultural AffairsDPDT
Criminal Penalty for InfringementUp to 2 years imprisonment; fine up to BDT 3 lakhUp to 4 years imprisonment; fine up to BDT 2 lakhFine and civil damages
Filing Cost (approx)BDT 3,000-6,000 per classBDT 300-1,000BDT 5,000-15,000 depending on type

How to Stop Trademark Infringement in Bangladesh

If someone is using a mark identical or deceptively similar to your registered trademark — on products, packaging, websites, or advertising — you have several legal options, which are typically pursued in escalating order:

  1. Cease and Desist Letter: The first step is usually a formal legal letter from your advocate demanding that the infringer immediately stop using the mark, destroy infringing stock, and pay compensation. Many infringers comply at this stage to avoid litigation costs. The letter should cite your registration number, describe the infringing acts, and set a response deadline (typically 14-21 days).
  2. Civil Suit for Trademark Infringement: Under Section 77 of the Trademarks Act 2009, a registered trademark owner can file a civil suit in the District Court seeking: (a) temporary and permanent injunction restraining further use; (b) damages (actual loss suffered); (c) account of profits (the infringer's gains); (d) delivery up and destruction of infringing goods.
  3. Criminal Complaint: Under Section 73 of the Trademarks Act 2009, trademark infringement is a criminal offence. A criminal complaint can be filed with the police or directly in a Magistrate's Court. Police can raid the infringer's premises, seize infringing goods, and arrest the accused. Criminal proceedings run parallel to civil proceedings.
  4. Customs Recordal (Border Measures): Under the Customs Act 1969, you can record your trademark with the Bangladesh Customs authority to prevent import of counterfeit goods bearing your mark. Customs officers can detain and seize suspected infringing shipments.
  5. Domain Name Disputes: If someone is using your brand name as a .bd domain, you can file a complaint with the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) or pursue a Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy (UDRP) proceeding for international domains (.com, .net, etc.).

Common Infringement Scenarios in Bangladesh:

  • Copying product packaging (trade dress infringement) in fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector
  • Using similar brand names for pharmaceuticals or food products
  • Selling counterfeit garments with copied brand labels
  • Using a client's old trademark after a business relationship ends

Penalties for Trademark Infringement

The Trademarks Act 2009 provides both civil and criminal remedies for trademark infringement. The criminal penalties under the Act are significant:

  • Section 73(1): Any person who counterfeits a registered trademark is punishable by imprisonment for a term not less than 6 months and not more than 2 years, with a fine of not less than BDT 50,000 and not more than BDT 3,00,000 (three lakh).
  • Section 73(2): A second or subsequent offence attracts a minimum sentence of 1 year imprisonment and a minimum fine of BDT 1,00,000.
  • Section 76: Possession of instruments for counterfeiting a trademark is also an offence.
  • Section 77: Falsely applying a registered trademark to goods is separately punishable.

Civil Remedies: In addition to criminal penalties, the trademark owner can recover:

  • Actual damages suffered as a result of infringement
  • Account of profits earned by the infringer
  • Conversion damages (treating infringing goods as the trademark owner's property)
  • Delivery up and destruction of infringing goods and packaging
  • Costs of litigation

Practical Reality: Criminal enforcement in Bangladesh's trademark cases can be slow and requires an active complainant. The most effective strategy currently is to combine a swift civil injunction (which can be obtained on an ex-parte basis, without hearing the other side, in urgent cases) with a criminal complaint. A court injunction stops the infringement immediately while the full case is litigated.

Geographical Indications and Emerging IP Issues

Bangladesh has taken significant steps to protect its traditional and geographically distinctive products. The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 2013 provides protection for products whose quality, reputation, or other characteristics are essentially attributable to their geographic origin.

Notable GI Registrations in Bangladesh:

  • Jamdani saree — registered as a Geographical Indication, recognized by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage
  • Hilsa fish of Bangladesh — registered to protect the distinctive branding of Bangladeshi Hilsa
  • Muslin of Dhaka — efforts underway for full GI protection
  • Rajshahi silk — under GI application process

Emerging IP Issues for Bangladeshi Businesses:

  • Software and App IP: As Bangladesh's IT sector grows, disputes over code ownership, app cloning, and API piracy are increasing. These are addressed under the Copyright Act 2000 and potentially the Digital Security Act 2018 (now the Cyber Security Act 2023).
  • Social Media Brand Infringement: Fake Facebook pages, Instagram accounts, and YouTube channels impersonating brands are a growing problem. These require both IP law action and complaints to the platforms' IP enforcement teams.
  • Traditional Knowledge: Bangladesh has indigenous traditional knowledge (medicinal plants, textile patterns) that may be exploitable by foreign corporations without IP protection — a subject of ongoing legislative debate.

Businesses operating in Bangladesh should conduct periodic IP audits to ensure their brand assets are fully protected. Our corporate law team at the Uttara, Dhaka chamber of Advocate Md. Shah Alam assists clients with trademark searches, DPDT filings, opposition proceedings, and infringement enforcement actions. Whether you are a startup protecting your first logo or an established company fighting counterfeiters, we provide comprehensive IP legal support.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does trademark registration take in Bangladesh?

Currently the full trademark registration process at the DPDT takes approximately 18-24 months from the filing date. This includes formal examination, substantive examination, publication in the Trademarks Journal (2-month opposition window), and issuance of the registration certificate. If an opposition is filed, the process can take longer.

Do I need to register my copyright in Bangladesh?

No. Copyright protection is automatic upon creation of an original work under the Copyright Act 2000. Registration at the Copyright Office is optional but highly recommended because it creates a public record of ownership, establishes a legal presumption of ownership in court, and is often required for commercial licensing agreements.

What is the penalty for trademark infringement in Bangladesh?

Under the Trademarks Act 2009, Section 73, criminal penalties for trademark counterfeiting include 6 months to 2 years imprisonment and a fine of BDT 50,000 to BDT 3,00,000 (three lakh). For repeat offenders, minimum imprisonment is 1 year and minimum fine is BDT 1,00,000. Civil remedies include injunction, damages, and destruction of infringing goods.

Can I register a trademark in Bangladesh if I am a foreign company?

Yes. Foreign companies can register trademarks in Bangladesh directly or through a local trademark agent. Bangladesh is a member of the Paris Convention, so foreign trademark holders can claim priority from their home country filing date if they file in Bangladesh within 6 months. Registration must be applied for at the DPDT in Dhaka.

What is the difference between a trademark and a trade name in Bangladesh?

A trademark identifies the goods or services of a particular business (registered at DPDT under the Trademarks Act 2009). A trade name or company name is the name under which a business operates (registered at the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies under the Companies Act 1994). Both can overlap — a company name can also be a trademark — but they require separate registrations with different authorities.

How do I stop someone from copying my logo or brand in Bangladesh?

If your trademark is registered, you can: (1) send a cease and desist letter through your advocate; (2) file a civil suit seeking injunction and damages under Section 77 of the Trademarks Act 2009; (3) file a criminal complaint under Section 73 of the Act. An ex-parte injunction from a district court can stop the infringement immediately while the case is heard. Contact a corporate IP lawyer immediately if you discover infringement.

What Is a Trademark Under Bangladesh Law?

A trademark is any sign, symbol, word, name, logo, device, or combination thereof that distinguishes the goods or services of one business from those of another. In Bangladesh, trademarks are governed by the Trademarks Act 2009 and the Trademarks Rules 2015. The registration authority is the Department of Patents, Designs and Trademarks (DPDT), operating under the Ministry of Industries.

A registered trademark gives the owner:

  • The exclusive right to use the mark in Bangladesh for the registered goods/services
  • The right to take civil and criminal legal action against infringers
  • Presumption of ownership and validity in any dispute
  • A valuable business asset that can be licensed or transferred
  • Protection against customs import of counterfeit goods bearing the mark

Without registration, your rights depend on building a reputation through use (passing-off law) — a slower, more expensive, and less certain protection than statutory registration.

Why Trademark Registration Is Essential for Your Business

Many Bangladesh businesses delay trademark registration until a problem arises — by which point a competitor may have already registered the same mark, or a counterfeit operation has seriously damaged the brand. Common real-world problems that trademark registration prevents:

  • Competitors registering your name first: Without registration, a rival can apply for and register your brand name, forcing you to rebrand or pay to buy back your own name.
  • Counterfeit goods: Registered trademark owners can ask Customs to seize imported fake goods at the border — unregistered owners cannot.
  • Disputes with franchisees or distributors: A clear registered mark makes licensing and enforcement much simpler.
  • E-commerce platform brand protection: Platforms like Daraz Bangladesh require trademark registration evidence to remove copycat sellers.
  • Export markets: Many international buyers and distributors require registered trademarks before they will stock or distribute your products.

A corporate lawyer in Dhaka will advise on a comprehensive trademark strategy — not just a single registration, but protection across all relevant classes and countries.

Who Can Apply for a Trademark in Bangladesh?

The following persons and entities can apply for trademark registration in Bangladesh:

  • Bangladeshi individuals (citizens)
  • Bangladeshi companies (private limited, public limited, partnership firms)
  • Foreign nationals and foreign companies (through a registered agent in Bangladesh)
  • Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) through a local representative

There is no requirement to be currently using the trademark to apply — Bangladesh allows applications based on proposed use. However, you must intend to use the mark in commerce in Bangladesh. Trademark agents (lawyers or IP firms) typically handle DPDT filings on behalf of clients.

What Can Be Registered as a Trademark?

Under the Trademarks Act 2009, the following types of marks may be registered:

  • Word marks: Company names, product names, slogans
  • Device/logo marks: Logos, symbols, graphic designs
  • Combination marks: Word + logo together
  • Colours: Specific colour combinations that identify a brand
  • Shape marks: Distinctive product shapes (less common in Bangladesh)
  • Sound marks: Audio jingles or sounds (rarely registered in Bangladesh currently)

What cannot be registered:

  • Generic or descriptive terms (e.g., "Best Rice" for a rice brand)
  • Deceptive or misleading marks
  • Marks identical or confusingly similar to already-registered marks
  • National emblems, flags, or official symbols
  • Scandalous or offensive marks
  • Marks that are purely geographic names

The Trademark Registration Process: Step-by-Step

The trademark registration process in Bangladesh involves the following steps:

  1. Trademark search: Before filing, conduct a search in the DPDT database to check if an identical or confusingly similar mark already exists. A trademark lawyer in Dhaka can perform a comprehensive search including pending applications that may not yet appear online.
  2. Choose trademark class(es): Bangladesh uses the International Classification of Goods and Services (Nice Classification). You must select the correct class(es) for your goods/services. Each class requires a separate application and fee.
  3. Prepare the application: The TM-1 form is completed with your details, a representation of the mark, the list of goods/services, and the date of first use (if the mark is already in use).
  4. File with DPDT: The application, power of attorney, and government fee payment are submitted to the Department of Patents, Designs and Trademarks in Dhaka.
  5. Examination: DPDT examines the application for compliance with the Trademarks Act. If there are objections, they are communicated and you have an opportunity to respond.
  6. Publication in the Bangladesh Gazette: If accepted, the mark is published in the Official Gazette for opposition. Any party who believes the registration should not be granted has 2 months from the date of advertisement to file an opposition.
  7. Registration: If no opposition is filed, or opposition is resolved in your favour, the trademark is registered and a Certificate of Registration is issued.

Government Fees for Trademark Registration

Current DPDT government fees for trademark registration (per class) in Bangladesh:

  • Application fee: BDT 4,000 per class (for individuals); BDT 8,000 per class (for companies/entities)
  • Registration fee: BDT 6,000 per class (upon acceptance, before certificate issuance)
  • Renewal fee (every 10 years): BDT 6,000–8,000 per class depending on entity type

These are government fees only. Professional fees of a trademark agent or lawyer are additional. Fees are subject to revision — confirm current rates at the DPDT website or through your lawyer before filing.

Note: If you need to register your trademark in multiple classes (e.g., both clothing and retail services), each class requires a separate application and fee.

Documents Required for Trademark Application

To file a trademark application in Bangladesh, you will need:

  • TM-1 Form (available from DPDT or prepared by your lawyer)
  • Clear representation of the trademark (logo/word — in specified format)
  • List of goods/services and their Nice Classification class numbers
  • Power of Attorney authorising your trademark agent/lawyer to file on your behalf
  • NID (for individuals) or Certificate of Incorporation (for companies)
  • Trade licence copy (recommended)
  • Proof of use (if claiming prior use — invoices, advertisements, photos)
  • Government fee payment receipt (treasury challan or online payment confirmation)

How Long Does Trademark Registration Take?

The trademark registration timeline in Bangladesh:

  • Filing to examination: 3–6 months
  • Examination to Gazette publication (if accepted): 3–6 months
  • Opposition period: 2 months from Gazette publication
  • Registration certificate: 1–2 months after opposition period closes
  • Total typical timeline: 18–36 months end-to-end

While registration takes time, the date of application filing becomes your priority date — you are legally protected as if the trademark was registered from the filing date, once registration is eventually granted. This is why it is important to file as early as possible, especially for a new business.

Trademark Classes: Choosing the Right Class

The Nice Classification divides all goods and services into 45 classes (1–34 for goods; 35–45 for services). Choosing the wrong class is a costly mistake — you will not be protected for goods/services outside your registered class(es). Common classes for Bangladesh businesses include:

  • Class 25: Clothing and apparel (ready-made garments, RMG)
  • Class 30: Food products (biscuits, rice, tea, spices)
  • Class 35: Retail and advertising services
  • Class 38: Telecommunications services
  • Class 42: IT and software services
  • Class 44: Medical and healthcare services

Your corporate lawyer in Dhaka will analyse your business model and recommend the correct class or combination of classes to ensure comprehensive protection.

Trademark Infringement and Legal Remedies in Bangladesh

Once your trademark is registered, you have powerful legal remedies against infringers:

  • Civil suit for infringement: You can file a civil suit in the District Court (or High Court Division if the case warrants) seeking an injunction to stop the infringement, damages or account of profits, and delivery up or destruction of infringing goods.
  • Criminal complaint: The Trademarks Act 2009 provides criminal penalties for trademark infringement — imprisonment of up to 2 years and/or fines. Criminal complaints can be filed before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM).
  • Customs seizure: Registered trademark owners can record their mark with Customs, enabling authorities to seize imported counterfeit goods at the border.
  • Interim injunction: Courts can grant urgent ex parte interim injunctions — stopping infringement immediately without waiting for the defendant's reply — in cases of clear trademark violation.

Contact Adv. Shah Alam if you need to take enforcement action against a trademark infringer or if you have received a cease-and-desist letter from a trademark owner.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a trademark registration to operate a business in Bangladesh?

No, registration is not legally mandatory to run a business. However, without registration, you have very limited protection against competitors who copy your brand name or logo. Registration is strongly recommended as soon as you launch any brand, product, or service.

Can I register a trademark that is already in use but not registered?

Yes. If you have been using a mark for years without registering, you can still apply to register it. Proof of prior use actually strengthens your application. However, if a third party has already registered the same or similar mark, you may face complications.

How long does a trademark registration last in Bangladesh?

A registered trademark in Bangladesh is valid for 10 years from the date of application. It can be renewed indefinitely for further 10-year periods upon payment of the renewal fee. Failure to renew results in the mark being removed from the register.

Can a foreigner register a trademark in Bangladesh?

Yes. Foreign individuals and companies can register trademarks in Bangladesh through a local trademark agent or lawyer. Bangladesh is also a signatory to the Paris Convention, allowing foreign trademark holders to claim priority from their home country application.

What is the difference between the ™ and ® symbols?

™ (TM) indicates that you claim rights in the mark — it can be used even without registration. ® (R in a circle) may only be used legally after the trademark is officially registered with the DPDT. Using ® before registration is an offence under the Trademarks Act 2009.

Can I oppose someone else's trademark application in Bangladesh?

Yes. Once a trademark is published in the Bangladesh Gazette, you have 2 months to file a Notice of Opposition if you believe the registration should not be granted — for example, because it conflicts with your already-registered mark or one that you have used extensively.

Travel Ban & Airport Offload in Bangladesh: Legal Rights, 74 DLR Rules & High Court Writ Remedies

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-08 · 19 minutes

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

For overseas Bangladeshi expatriates, foreign investors, dual citizens, and business professionals, being abruptly offloaded or turned away at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (HSIA) in Dhaka is a distressing experience. Often, travelers only discover they are blacklisted or subject to an administrative travel embargo after checking their baggage and presenting their passport at immigration control. In Bangladesh, arbitrary travel bans imposed solely by executive agencies, intelligence memos, or police watchlists violate the fundamental right to freedom of movement. Under Article 36 of the Constitution of Bangladesh and the landmark Appellate Division judgment in 74 DLR (AD) 1, no authority can lawfully restrict a citizen from travelling abroad without prior sanction from a competent judicial court. This definitive legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate based in Uttara, Dhaka, explains your constitutional protections, judicial precedents, and the precise legal steps to obtain High Court writ clearance.

1. Constitutional Protection: Freedom of Movement Under Article 36

In the jurisprudence of Bangladesh, the right of a citizen to travel abroad, leave the country, and return unhindered is an integral dimension of personal liberty. Article 36 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh explicitly guarantees that subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the public interest, every citizen shall have the right to move freely throughout Bangladesh, to reside and settle in any place therein, and to leave and re-enter Bangladesh.

This fundamental right operates alongside Article 31 (the right to the protection of law and to be treated only in accordance with law) and Article 32 (protection of life and personal liberty). Decades of Supreme Court precedent, beginning with the historic judgment in Hussain Muhammad Ershad v. Bangladesh (2001) 21 BLD (AD) 69, have confirmed that travelling abroad for employment, education, medical treatment, family reunion, or commerce is a constitutional entitlement rather than an executive concession.

Because fundamental rights are directly enforceable, Article 44 empowers any citizen whose freedom of movement is arbitrarily curtailed by the state or its law enforcement apparatus to invoke the extraordinary writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102. When state actors bypass statutory due process, the judiciary acts as a constitutional shield.

2. Landmark Ruling: 74 DLR (AD) 1 and the 3-Day Judicial Rule

For years, investigatory bodies and law enforcement agencies frequently issued unilateral letters to the Special Branch (SB) of Police requesting that specific individuals be barred from boarding flights. This administrative practice was decisively struck down by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the landmark judgment of Durnity Daman Commission (ACC) v. G.B. Hossain & Others, reported in 74 DLR (AD) 1 (2022) (disposing of Civil Appeal No. 27 of 2021 and related civil petitions on 27 September 2021).

The highest court laid down definitive constitutional principles that govern all travel restrictions across Bangladesh:

  • Executive Orders Are Not Law: The apex court held unequivocally that executive instructions or internal departmental memos lacking specific statutory authorization cannot be construed as law under Article 36. An administrative letter from an agency director or police officer cannot strip a citizen of their constitutional right to travel.
  • The Three-Day Confirmation Requirement: If an agency believes an individual under active inquiry or investigation might flee the country to evade justice, it may provisionally stop them only in genuine emergency circumstances. However, that restriction must be submitted to and formally confirmed by the competent trial court or Special Judge within three (3) working days. If no judicial confirmation is obtained within three working days, the travel embargo automatically lapses and becomes unlawful.
  • Judicial Review of Proportionality: The judiciary, not the executive, retains the final authority to evaluate whether an embargo is reasonable, proportionate, and strictly necessary in the public interest. The mere existence of an unproven allegation or preliminary inquiry does not warrant the deprivation of liberty.

3. How Travel Bans and Airport Embargoes Are Imposed in Bangladesh

Travel restrictions in Bangladesh generally arise through three distinct channels, ranging from legitimate judicial directives to unauthorized executive blacklists:

  1. Formal Court Orders: A Senior Special Judge, Metropolitan Sessions Judge, or Judicial Magistrate presiding over an active criminal trial or loan default suit (such as Artha Rin Adalat proceedings) issues a formal judicial order directing the Immigration Department to restrict the travel of an accused who has jumped bail or failed to appear after summons.
  2. Lookout Circulars & Intelligence Lists: The Special Branch (SB) of Police, Criminal Investigation Department (CID), or national intelligence agencies maintain digital watchlists at land, sea, and international air ports of entry. Problems arise when names remain on digital databases long after cases have been stayed, resolved, or acquitted.
  3. Departmental Inquiry Letters: Statutory bodies such as the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC), Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU), or National Board of Revenue (NBR) occasionally issue letters directly to airport immigration requesting offloading before formal charges are filed in court. Under 74 DLR (AD) 1, this mechanism is legally unenforceable unless ratified by a judge within three working days.

4. Common Reasons for Unlawful Offloading at Dhaka Airport (HSIA)

Facing a travel embargo or airport offloading in Bangladesh? Contact our Supreme Court chamber immediately on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007. Overseas clients and family members can arrange rapid emergency document review.

At Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (HSIA) in Uttara, Dhaka, passengers are frequently offloaded under circumstances that lack valid judicial sanction. Understanding the underlying pretext enables an advocate to formulate swift countermeasures:

  • Preliminary Inquiries Without Charge Sheets: Travelers are stopped simply because an agency has received an anonymous petition or commenced an initial fact-finding inquiry, even though no First Information Report (FIR) has been lodged.
  • False or Harassing FIRs: Opponents in land disputes, commercial conflicts, or marital breakdowns maliciously name expatriates in frivolous criminal FIRs. When the immigration terminal flags an active case number, officers offload the passenger even if no arrest warrant was issued by a magistrate. Review our guide on quashing false FIR criminal cases under Section 561A CrPC.
  • Name Similarity and Identity Confusion: Expatriates with common names (such as Md. Alam, Md. Hossain, or Md. Islam) are stopped because their name resembles that of an accused person on a police lookout list, despite possessing distinct parentage, NID, and passport credentials.
  • Uncancelled Historical Notices: Individuals who previously obtained regular bail or case acquittal remain flagged in immigration computer systems because the local police station failed to transmit the final disposal report to the Special Branch central database.

5. Pre-Emptive Relief: Seeking Clearance from Special Judge or Magistrate Courts

When an individual anticipates an airport embargo due to pending litigation, the most direct judicial remedy is to file an interlocutory petition before the trial court handling the proceedings.

If a criminal proceeding is pending before a Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM), Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM), or Metropolitan Sessions Judge, the accused can submit a formal application for Permission to Travel Abroad. The petition must articulate the compelling necessity of travel (such as overseas employment contracts, university enrolment, medical treatment abroad, or family residence), specify travel dates, and furnish reliable local sureties guaranteeing return. Courts routinely grant temporary travel permission with conditions requiring the petitioner to surrender their passport upon re-entry.

If the traveler faces an imminent risk of arrest at the airport due to a freshly lodged false FIR, applying for Anticipatory Bail under Section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 before the High Court Division is vital before approaching the departure terminal. Read our detailed guide on anticipatory bail under Section 498 CrPC and airport arrest protection.

6. High Court Writ Petition Under Article 102: Emergency Travel Orders

Where an individual is offloaded without a lawful court order, or where an agency places an unlawful embargo on their passport without formal criminal charges, the primary constitutional remedy is filing a Writ Petition under Article 102(1) and (2) of the Constitution before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

The legal mechanism involves several coordinated steps:

  1. Drafting the Writ Petition: The petition asserts that the impugned travel restriction or airport offloading infringes fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 31, 32, and 36, citing the binding precedent of 74 DLR (AD) 1. The Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Inspector General of Police (IGP), the Special Branch (Immigration), and the inquiring agency are cited as respondents.
  2. Motion Hearing Before the Writ Bench: A Supreme Court advocate moves the petition before a designated Division Bench of the High Court Division, arguing the illegality of the embargo.
  3. Issuance of Rule Nisi and Ad-Interim Direction: The High Court routinely issues a Rule Nisi calling upon the state respondents to show cause why the unlawful restriction should not be declared without lawful authority. Concurrently, the bench grants an Ad-Interim Direction restraining immigration authorities from obstructing or offloading the petitioner from boarding any international flight for a specified duration (typically 3 to 6 months).
  4. Service of Certified Order on Airport Immigration: The certified operative part of the High Court order is officially served on the Special Superintendent of Police (Immigration) and the airport duty officer at HSIA, ensuring smooth airport clearance.

7. Statutory Comparison: Lawful Judicial Orders vs. Arbitrary Executive Bans

Understanding the strict legal distinctions between authorized judicial travel restrictions and unlawful administrative embargoes helps citizens evaluate their legal options:

ParameterLawful Judicial Travel BanArbitrary Executive Embargo
Issuing AuthorityCompetent Trial Court, Special Judge, or MagistrateInvestigating Agency, Police SB, or Departmental Officer
Legal FoundationStatutory powers under CrPC, Special Powers Act, or Money Loan Court ActInternal departmental letter, circular, or verbal watchlist entry
Constitutional ValidityValid under reasonable statutory restriction clause of Article 36Unconstitutional; violates Articles 31, 32, and 36 (74 DLR (AD) 1)
Judicial Confirmation WindowAlready issued through formal judicial processMust be judicially confirmed within 3 working days, otherwise void
Primary RemedyApplication for travel permission or revision before Appellate CourtWrit Petition under Article 102 before the High Court Division
Resolution Timeline3 to 14 days depending on court calendar and state reply24 to 72 hours for emergency ad-interim High Court writ order

8. Step-by-Step Protocol if Stopped by Immigration Police

If you or a family member are unexpectedly stopped or offloaded by Special Branch immigration personnel at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, executing the following immediate protocol protects your legal remedies:

  1. Remain Calm and Request Written Reasons: Do not engage in heated arguments. Courteously ask the immigration officer to state the legal ground for offloading and request a copy of the written order, reference letter, or memo number under which you are being detained.
  2. Collect Airline Documentation: Request your airline to furnish an official offload certificate or stamp on your boarding pass confirming that you were prevented from boarding due to an immigration hold. This proves administrative obstruction.
  3. Document Officer Names and Times: Record the names of duty immigration personnel, desk numbers, flight details, and exact times. Retain all boarding passes, ticket receipts, and baggage reclaim tags.
  4. Contact a Supreme Court Advocate Promptly: Transmit copies of your passport, boarding passes, offload memo, and any known case details to your legal counsel. Our Uttara chamber is situated minutes away from HSIA, enabling immediate coordination.
  5. Issue Pre-Writ Demand Notice or Move Emergency Bench: If the offload occurred without a court warrant, your advocate can immediately file a Writ Petition before the vacation or regular Division Bench of the High Court Division to secure emergency travel relief.

9. Travel Clearance Safeguards for NRBs, Dual Citizens and Investors

Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) visiting home from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and European Union countries face heightened vulnerability when entangled in domestic property or corporate disputes. Estranged business partners or relatives often lodge malicious complaints specifically timed to trigger airport holds when the expatriate attempts to fly back to their overseas employment.

To safeguard cross-border travel:

  • Verify Police Clearance Status: Before visiting Bangladesh, obtain an updated online police clearance certificate to identify any pending FIRs registered against your national identity or passport number. See our comprehensive guide on police clearance certificate from abroad.
  • Maintain Dual Citizenship & NVR Documentation: Dual citizens should carry both their foreign passport with a valid No Visa Required (NVR) seal and their Bangladeshi NID or dual nationality certificate. Learn more about dual citizenship and NVR rights for Bangladeshi Americans and expatriates.
  • Appoint an Authorized Advocate via Power of Attorney: If you must return abroad while legal proceedings are ongoing, execute a formal Power of Attorney or Vakalatnama empowering a Supreme Court advocate to represent you in court without requiring your physical attendance at routine call dates.
  • Check Litigation Portals in Advance: Have your legal counsel search district court registers and the Supreme Court cause list prior to your scheduled departure date.

10. Illustrative Scenario: Emergency High Court Stay for an Overseas Executive

Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): A dual Bangladeshi-British IT consultant residing in London arrived in Dhaka to resolve a property partition matter in Sylhet. Two weeks later, while attempting to board a return flight to Heathrow at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, immigration officers stopped him at the passport control counter. The duty officer informed him that an administrative 'lookout letter' had been submitted by an investigatory desk regarding an alleged financial discrepancy in a private software company where he had briefly served as an unpaid technical advisor five years earlier. No formal FIR, court warrant, or summons had ever been served upon him.

Offloaded from his flight and facing immediate dismissal from his primary employment in the United Kingdom, the expatriate consulted Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber. Our legal team took swift action:

  1. Secured airline offloading documentation and drafted an emergency Writ Petition under Article 102 of the Constitution within 24 hours, highlighting the violation of Article 36 and invoking the 3-day judicial confirmation mandate under 74 DLR (AD) 1.
  2. Appeared before a Division Bench of the High Court Division, demonstrating that the petitioner had never been formally charged in any court and that the agency had failed to seek judicial ratification within three working days.
  3. The High Court Division issued a Rule Nisi and granted an Ad-Interim Order directing immigration authorities at all international airports in Bangladesh not to obstruct the petitioner from travelling abroad for a period of six months.
  4. Obtained a certified court order copy, officially transmitted it to the Special Superintendent of Police (Immigration) at the Special Branch headquarters and HSIA airport desk, and successfully escorted the client through immigration control onto a rescheduled flight without further impediment.

11. Talk to an Advocate: Legal Defense & Travel Clearance

If you, your business colleague, or an overseas relative is facing an unexpected travel ban, airport offloading, or unlawful immigration blacklisting in Bangladesh, swift constitutional and criminal defense is essential. Advocate Md. Shah Alam and his dedicated team of Supreme Court advocates provide prompt representation before trial courts and the High Court Division.

Need an advocate for this matter in Bangladesh? Send your documents on WhatsApp to +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. Overseas clients: a first document review can be done remotely.

Our principal chamber is conveniently located in Uttara, Dhaka, minutes from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, ensuring immediate emergency support for travelers, alongside our daily litigation chamber at the Supreme Court Bar Association and Dhaka Judge Court.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can immigration police stop me from travelling abroad without a court order?

Under Article 36 of the Constitution and the Appellate Division judgment in 74 DLR (AD) 1, immigration authorities cannot permanently ban or offload a citizen based solely on executive letters or internal memos without an order from a competent judicial court. Any emergency provisional embargo must be confirmed by a court within 3 working days.

What should I do immediately if offloaded at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport?

Immediately request the immigration officer to state the written reason or memo number for the hold. Collect an offloading slip or stamp from your airline, record the duty officer's details, and contact a Supreme Court advocate to file an emergency Writ Petition or seek court permission.

How quickly can the High Court Division issue a travel clearance order?

In urgent matters where an offloaded passenger has valid overseas employment, university deadlines, or medical emergencies, an experienced Supreme Court advocate can draft, file, and move a Writ Petition under Article 102 within 24 to 48 hours to secure an ad-interim travel clearance direction.

Can the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) impose a travel ban during inquiry?

The ACC cannot independently stop anyone from leaving the country based merely on an internal letter. Under the Supreme Court guidelines in 74 DLR (AD) 1, the ACC must apply for and obtain an order from the Senior Special Judge within 3 working days to validate any travel restriction.

How can a dual citizen or foreign passport holder challenge an airport blacklist?

Foreign passport holders and dual citizens possess constitutional protections under Articles 31 and 32 while residing within Bangladesh. They can challenge unlawful offloading through a High Court Writ Petition and notify their respective embassy or high commission for consular assistance.

Does having a police General Diary (GD) or civil family dispute warrant a travel ban?

No. A General Diary (GD) entry is merely an informational record and confers zero legal authority to restrict travel. Similarly, private civil disputes or family lawsuits do not prohibit foreign travel unless a competent civil or family court explicitly issues a restraining injunction.

What documents are required to file a Writ Petition against an airport travel embargo?

Key documents include: (1) Passport biodata page and flight tickets; (2) Airline offload certificate or stamped boarding pass; (3) Copies of any police notice or letter if provided; (4) Evidence demonstrating urgent overseas necessity (job contract, visa, medical records); and (5) A sworn affidavit of facts.

Can an overseas client retain a Supreme Court advocate remotely to lift a travel ban?

Yes. An individual who has already left Bangladesh or is represented through family members can retain a Supreme Court advocate remotely. The advocate can examine court dockets, file petitions, or appear before the High Court Division through a formal Vakalatnama or Power of Attorney.

VAT Audit & Demand Notice Defense in Bangladesh: 2012 Act

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-10 · 13 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Operating a commercial enterprise, manufacturing facility, or service company in Bangladesh requires navigating the rigorous compliance regime of the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act 2012 (VAT Act 2012). During routine audits, intelligence investigations, or desk reviews, VAT Commissionerates frequently serve registered taxpayers with aggressive audit observations and show-cause notices under Section 73, alleging input tax credit disallowances, unrecorded turnover, or shortfall in withholding VAT (VDS). Unchallenged show-cause notices culminate in unilateral final demand orders, accompanied by coercive bank account attachments under Section 83. Understanding the statutory hierarchy of appeals—from the Commissioner (Appeals) under Section 121 to the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal under Section 122 and the High Court Division under Article 102—is essential to shield corporate balance sheets.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

  2. 2. Technical Defenses: Input Tax Credits, VDS Compliance & Mushak 6.3
  3. 3. The Adjudication Hearing: Presenting Books Before the Joint/Deputy Commissioner
  4. 4. The First Appeal under Section 121: Timelines & The 10% Pre-Deposit Rule
  5. 5. Second Appeal Before the VAT Appellate Tribunal (Section 122)
  6. 6. Summary Matrix: VAT Dispute Stages, Pre-Deposits & Fora
  7. 7. Resisting Coercive Recovery: Defending Against Section 83 Bank Freezes
  8. 8. High Court Division Reference Applications & Constitutional Writs (Article 102)
  9. 9. Illustrative Scenario: Overturning an Arbitrary 5 Crore BDT VAT Demand
  10. 10. Talk to an Advocate

1. VAT Audit Triggers: How Section 73 Show-Cause Notices Arise

Under the automated VAT online system (IVAS) established pursuant to the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act 2012, registered corporate entities submit monthly returns (Mushak 9.1). Discrepancies between annual audited financial statements, corporate income tax returns submitted to the National Board of Revenue (NBR), and monthly VAT declarations frequently trigger comprehensive audits.

Audits are conducted by the operational Commissionerate audit wings or the central Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (CIID). Common allegations include unrecorded sales turnover, claiming input tax rebates without matching tax invoices (Mushak 6.3), or failing to deduct and deposit Withholding VAT (VDS) under the VAT Deduction at Source Rules 2020.

When discrepancies are flagged, the revenue officer serves a formal show-cause notice under Section 73 of the VAT Act 2012. The notice quantifies an alleged evaded tax amount and summons the taxpayer to explain why the demand, alongside statutory monthly interest of 1% under Section 127 and heavy administrative penalties, should not be confirmed.

2. Technical Defenses: Input Tax Credits, VDS Compliance & Mushak 6.3

A successful defense against a Section 73 notice depends upon structured accounting and statutory reconciliation. Under Section 46 of the VAT Act 2012, a registered supplier is statutorily entitled to claim input tax rebate on goods and services acquired for commercial output, provided tax is documented on a genuine Mushak 6.3 invoice and paid through banking channels.

Audit officers frequently disallow input rebates on technical grounds—such as minor spelling mismatches in the company name, missing treasury chalan numbers, or suppliers failing to upload invoices in the central system. Defense counsel must demonstrate that the taxpayer exercised reasonable commercial diligence and that technical paperwork defects cannot nullify substantive statutory rebate rights.

Similarly, for Withholding VAT (VDS) allegations under Section 49, the defense must compile certified bank transfer slips and VDS certificates (Mushak 6.6) demonstrating that tax was withheld and deposited into the government treasury within the prescribed statutory period, eliminating alleged liability.

3. The Adjudication Hearing: Presenting Books Before the Joint/Deputy Commissioner

Once the written reply is filed, the matter proceeds to an adjudication hearing under Section 73(3) of the Act before the competent revenue authority—typically an Assistant Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner, Joint Commissioner, or Commissioner of VAT, depending on the pecuniary threshold of the demand.

The hearing represents the taxpayer's primary opportunity to present original purchase registers (Mushak 6.1), sales registers (Mushak 6.2), commercial bank statements, and audited balances. Specialized tax advocates present oral arguments highlighting that audit teams applied arbitrary gross-profit estimates or incorrectly reclassified exempt items under the First Schedule of the Act.

Served with a VAT audit notice, show-cause letter, or bank freeze order in Bangladesh? Fast legal intervention by specialized tax litigators prevents arbitrary account seizure and penalty accruals. Message our corporate tax team on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 for strategic advice.

Following the hearing, the adjudicating officer issues a formal Adjudication Order (Churanto Adesh). If the officer accepts the reconciliation, the proceedings are dropped. However, if the officer confirms the demand, the enterprise has ninety days to seek appellate relief. For broader tax compliance principles, review our guide on tax and VAT legal counsel in Bangladesh.

4. The First Appeal under Section 121: Timelines & The 10% Pre-Deposit Rule

When an unfavorable adjudication order is passed, the taxpayer must not ignore the document. Allowing an adjudication order to become final converts the demand into an undisputed government debt enforceable by coercive distress.

Under Section 121 of the VAT Act 2012, any person aggrieved by an order passed by a revenue officer below the rank of Commissioner may file an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals). The statutory limitation period is ninety (90) days from the date of receipt of the adjudication order. The Commissioner (Appeals) may condone a delay of an additional thirty (30) days upon proof of sufficient cause.

Crucially, Section 121(4) imposes a mandatory financial prerequisite: the appellant must deposit ten percent (10%) of the disputed tax amount (excluding penalties and interest) at the time of filing the appeal through government treasury chalan. Without proof of this 10% deposit, the memorandum of appeal cannot be admitted for hearing. The Commissioner (Appeals) examines the merits, may stay coercive recovery, and passes an appellate order confirming, altering, or annulling the demand.

5. Second Appeal Before the VAT Appellate Tribunal (Section 122)

If the Commissioner (Appeals) rejects the appeal or confirms an unreasonable demand, the taxpayer's next statutory recourse is the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal (CEVAT) established under Section 122 of the VAT Act 2012. The Appellate Tribunal is a high-level, independent judicial body comprising judicial members (District Judges) and technical members (Customs/VAT Commissioners).

The appeal before the Tribunal must be filed within ninety (90) days of receiving the order from the Commissioner (Appeals) or an order passed directly by a Commissioner. Under Section 122(4), the appellant must deposit an additional ten percent (10%) of the disputed tax amount, bringing the total pre-deposit to twenty percent (20%).

The Appellate Tribunal operates as the final court of fact. It has statutory authority to examine witness evidence, review complex accounting methodologies, summon books of accounts, and evaluate whether the revenue department acted within the four corners of the statute. Judgments delivered by the Appellate Tribunal establish authoritative precedents for the entire VAT administration.

6. Summary Matrix: VAT Dispute Stages, Pre-Deposits & Fora

The statutory appeal stages, financial deposit mandates, and appellate venues are synthesized in the following comparative matrix:

Dispute Level Adjudicating / Appellate Authority Pre-Deposit Requirement Filing Limitation Period
Primary Adjudication Assistant / Deputy / Joint Commissioner (Sec 73) Nil (Written reply to show-cause) 15 to 30 days from notice service
First Statutory Appeal Commissioner of VAT (Appeals) (Sec 121) 10% of disputed tax amount 90 days (+30 days condonation)
Second Statutory Appeal Customs, Excise & VAT Appellate Tribunal (Sec 122) Additional 10% (cumulative 20%) 90 days from appellate order
High Court Reference / Writ High Court Division (Sec 125 / Art 102) Nil (Discretionary court security) 90 days for Ref; prompt for Writ

7. Resisting Coercive Recovery: Defending Against Section 83 Bank Freezes

One of the most drastic enforcement mechanisms under the VAT Act 2012 is Section 83 ('Recovery of Government Dues'). If a taxpayer fails to pay a confirmed demand or misses the appeal deadline, the VAT Commissionerate issues direct attachment notices to commercial banks under Section 83(1)(c).

The bank is commanded to immediately freeze all operating accounts, fixed deposits, and credit lines of the company, and transmit the funds directly to the NBR treasury. A bank freeze completely paralyzes payroll, vendor payments, and export-import operations. Furthermore, under Section 83(1)(d), officers may padlock commercial premises or seize factory stock.

However, coercive recovery under Section 83 cannot be initiated while an appeal is actively pending before the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Appellate Tribunal, provided the mandatory pre-deposit was made. If revenue officers issue premature attachment notices in violation of statutory stay principles, emergency legal remedies must be activated immediately.

8. High Court Division Reference Applications & Constitutional Writs (Article 102)

When the statutory tribunal process is exhausted or bypassed due to administrative illegality, the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh provides decisive judicial protection.

Under Section 125 of the VAT Act 2012, an aggrieved taxpayer or the Commissioner may file a Reference Application before the High Court Division within ninety days on any question of law arising out of the order of the Appellate Tribunal. The High Court evaluates whether the Tribunal misinterpreted statutory definitions or misapplied tax rates.

Concurrently, where revenue officers freeze bank accounts without serving the underlying adjudication order, demand extortionate pre-deposits, or act with mala fides, the company can petition the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution for a Writ of Mandamus or Certiorari. The High Court routinely stays illegal bank freezes, directs unfreezing of commercial accounts, and commands the department to hear appeals on their legal merits. For broader corporate litigation strategies, explore our guide on company and corporate legal services.

9. Illustrative Scenario: Overturning an Arbitrary 5 Crore BDT VAT Demand

To illustrate how technical VAT defense operates in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A consumer goods manufacturing company in Gazipur received a show-cause notice under Section 73 from the Dhaka North VAT Commissionerate claiming a tax shortfall of 5 Crore BDT plus 2.5 Crore BDT in penalties. The audit team alleged that the enterprise claimed unverified input tax rebates over a 24-month period and failed to deposit VDS on advertising expenditures.

The company engaged a Supreme Court tax advocate. The legal team audited the transaction history, compiled every original Mushak 6.3 invoice, cross-referenced bank clearing slips, and demonstrated that 98% of suppliers had properly recorded transactions in the central IVAS system. Despite this reconciliation, the Deputy Commissioner confirmed the demand ex-parte.

The advocate immediately filed an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) under Section 121, depositing the statutory 10% chalan. When the Commissionerate attempted to freeze the company's operating bank accounts under Section 83 during the appeal pendency, the advocate filed an emergency Writ Petition before the High Court Division. The High Court stayed the bank attachment, reprimanded the department for coercive measures during active appeal, and directed the Commissioner (Appeals) to conduct a full evidentiary review. The appellate authority subsequently vacated 92% of the disputed demand, saving the enterprise from insolvency.

10. Talk to an Advocate

Talk to a VAT & Tax Advocate in Dhaka: To draft responses to Section 73 show-cause notices, file appeals before the Commissioner (Appeals), represent your enterprise before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, or move High Court Division writs against unlawful account attachments, reach out via WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007 or call +880 1712-655546. Retainers and case vetting available for domestic and multinational corporations.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a Section 73 show-cause notice under the VAT Act 2012?

A Section 73 notice is an official legal demand issued by a VAT revenue officer alleging non-payment, short-payment, or irregular rebate of VAT, requiring the taxpayer to show cause why the demanded tax and penalties should not be confirmed.

How long do I have to reply to a VAT show-cause notice in Bangladesh?

The show-cause notice typically stipulates a deadline of 15 to 30 days. It is critical to request an extension if additional time is needed to reconcile accounting ledgers and retrieve Mushak 6.3 invoices.

What is the pre-deposit requirement to file a first VAT appeal?

Under Section 121(4) of the VAT Act 2012, the appellant must deposit ten percent (10%) of the disputed tax amount (excluding penalties and interest) through government treasury chalan to have the appeal admitted.

What is the role of the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal?

The Appellate Tribunal established under Section 122 serves as the final independent statutory court of fact, reviewing complex accounting, legal interpretations, and procedural errors committed by subordinate revenue officers.

Can VAT officers freeze my company's bank accounts under Section 83?

Yes. Section 83 empowers authorities to attach commercial bank accounts for unpaid government dues. However, freezing accounts while an appeal is actively pending with statutory pre-deposit is illegal and can be stayed by the High Court.

How can the High Court Division intervene in a VAT dispute in Bangladesh?

The High Court Division hears Reference Applications on questions of law under Section 125, and issues Writ Petitions under Article 102 of the Constitution to stay unlawful bank account attachments, arbitrary seizures, or violations of natural justice.

What evidence is required to prove a valid input tax rebate in a VAT audit?

You must produce valid tax invoices (Mushak 6.3), entries in the purchase register (Mushak 6.1), proof of payment via recognized banking channels, and matching records in the monthly Mushak 9.1 return.

Can a foreign company operating in Bangladesh challenge VAT audit assessments?

Yes. Foreign branches, liaison offices, and joint-venture companies enjoy identical statutory rights to challenge audit observations, file appeals before the Tribunal, and seek constitutional writ protection before the Supreme Court.

VAT Law and Compliance Bangladesh – Complete Guide

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-05-21 · 12 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Value Added Tax (VAT) is the single largest source of government revenue in Bangladesh, yet many businesses remain non-compliant due to complex registration and filing requirements. Whether you are a new entrepreneur or an established company, understanding the VAT Act 2012 and its regulations is essential to avoiding heavy penalties and legal action. This guide provides a thorough breakdown of VAT law, compliance obligations, and what to do when the National Board of Revenue (NBR) challenges your filings.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order
Official Portalssupremecourt.gov.bd, judiciary.gov.bd, pcc.police.gov.bd & land.gov.bd
Supreme Court ChamberAdvocate Md. Shah Alam — Uttara & Dhaka Judge Court (+880 1712-655546)
📋 In This Article
  1. Overview of the VAT Act 2012 in Bangladesh
  2. VAT Registration: Who Must Register and How
  3. VAT Rates and Applicable Schedules
  4. Filing VAT Returns: Procedure and Deadlines
  5. Input Tax Credit and Deduction Rules
  6. Penalties for VAT Non-Compliance in Bangladesh
  7. VAT Appeal and Dispute Resolution Process

Overview of the VAT Act 2012 in Bangladesh

Bangladesh's primary VAT legislation is the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act, 2012 (commonly called the VAT Act 2012), which came into full force on 1 July 2019 after several years of phased implementation. It replaced the older VAT Act 1991 and brought sweeping changes to the tax structure, compliance mechanism, and administrative framework of indirect taxation in the country. The Act is administered by the National Board of Revenue (NBR) under the Ministry of Finance.

The core philosophy of the VAT Act 2012 is a multi-stage, invoice-based VAT system where tax is collected at each stage of the supply chain — from manufacturing to wholesale to retail — with businesses entitled to offset the VAT they paid on inputs (input tax credit) against the VAT they collect on outputs. This prevents the cascading tax effect that plagued the earlier system.

In addition to VAT, the Act also governs Supplementary Duty (SD), which applies to luxury goods, tobacco, and certain services. Together, VAT and SD form the backbone of Bangladesh's indirect tax regime. Key subordinate legislation includes the VAT and SD Rules 2016 and various NBR general orders (SROs) that modify rates and exemptions periodically.

For businesses operating in Bangladesh, compliance with the VAT Act 2012 is not optional. NBR conducts regular audits, and failure to maintain proper VAT accounts, issue VAT invoices, or file timely returns can result in substantial fines, interest charges, and even criminal prosecution. Consulting a qualified company and corporate lawyer in Dhaka is strongly advised before commencing any business activity that may attract VAT liability.

VAT Registration: Who Must Register and How

Under the VAT Act 2012, any person engaged in an economic activity whose annual turnover exceeds the prescribed threshold must obtain VAT registration from the NBR. As of the current SRO provisions:

  • Mandatory VAT registration applies to businesses with annual turnover above BDT 3 crore (30 lakh) — these entities must charge VAT at the standard rate.
  • Businesses with turnover between BDT 50 lakh and BDT 3 crore fall under the Turnover Tax (TT) regime, paying a flat 4% turnover tax instead of full VAT.
  • Businesses below BDT 50 lakh are generally exempt, though voluntary registration is permitted.

The registration process is conducted through the NBR's online VAT registration portal (mushak.gov.bd). Applicants must submit:

  1. Application through BIN (Business Identification Number) system
  2. Trade license from the relevant city corporation or municipality
  3. TIN (Tax Identification Number) certificate
  4. National ID card of the proprietor/directors
  5. Bank account details
  6. Premises ownership or rental documents
  7. Description of goods/services supplied

Upon successful verification, the NBR issues a Business Identification Number (BIN), which is the VAT registration certificate. The BIN must be displayed at the business premises and quoted on all VAT invoices. Certain sectors — such as importers, manufacturers of excisable goods, and service providers in specified categories — must register regardless of turnover threshold.

Failure to register when required is a serious offence under Section 85 of the Act and can attract penalties equal to the VAT evaded plus additional fines. If you are unsure whether your business is required to register, consult an experienced tax lawyer in Bangladesh for a comprehensive assessment of your obligations.

VAT Rates and Applicable Schedules

Bangladesh applies VAT at multiple rates depending on the nature of the goods or services. The primary rates under the VAT Act 2012 are as follows:

  • Standard Rate: 15% — Applies to most taxable goods and services not specifically listed in the schedules.
  • Reduced Rates: Certain goods and services enjoy reduced VAT rates through scheduled exceptions — e.g., 5%, 7.5%, or 10% — which are updated annually through Finance Acts or SROs.
  • Zero Rate (0%): Exports of goods and certain specified services are zero-rated, meaning the business charges no VAT but can still claim input tax credits on purchases used to produce those exports.
  • Exempt Supplies: Listed in the First Schedule of the Act — these include essential food items, agricultural inputs, health services, educational services, and more. Suppliers of exempt goods cannot charge VAT but also cannot claim input tax credit.

Supplementary Duty (SD) is levied in addition to VAT on specified goods and services considered luxury or harmful — such as cigarettes, alcohol, certain vehicles, mobile phone services, and air-conditioned restaurants. SD rates range from 10% to 350% depending on the product category.

The Finance Act issued every year (typically in June, coinciding with the national budget) amends VAT rates and the schedules. Businesses must stay updated on these annual changes to ensure correct charging and claiming of VAT. Failure to apply the correct rate — whether charging too little or claiming unentitled credits — can trigger an NBR audit. A corporate lawyer familiar with tax law can help businesses conduct annual compliance reviews after each Finance Act is enacted.

Filing VAT Returns: Procedure and Deadlines

Registered VAT payers in Bangladesh are required to file monthly VAT returns using the prescribed Mushak-9.1 form (for standard VAT registrants) or Mushak-9.2 (for turnover tax payers). The return covers all transactions — both purchases and sales — during the calendar month.

Key Deadlines

The VAT return must be submitted to the relevant VAT Circle Commissionerate by the 15th day of the following month. For example, VAT return for January must be filed by 15 February. Payment of the net VAT liability must also be made by this deadline through treasury challans or electronic banking channels approved by NBR.

Documents and Records Required

  • All VAT invoices (Mushak-6.3) issued to customers during the month
  • Purchase invoices received from suppliers showing input VAT paid
  • Import entries (for importers) — Bill of Entry with VAT payment proof
  • Export documentation (for zero-rated supplies)
  • VAT account book (Mushak-13) maintained on a monthly basis

Filing Process

Returns are now filed electronically through the iBAS++ system or through the VAT online portal. Large taxpayers under the Large Taxpayers Unit (LTU) must file electronically without exception. Medium and small taxpayers may still file manually at the VAT Circle office in some jurisdictions, though NBR is progressively mandating online filing for all.

Late filing attracts automatic interest at 2% per month on unpaid VAT and a fixed penalty under Section 85. Businesses with complex supply chains or those dealing in both taxable and exempt supplies should prepare their returns carefully, as apportionment of input tax credit can be technically challenging. Seeking advice from a qualified tax lawyer in Dhaka before filing disputed or complex returns can prevent costly errors.

⚖️ Legal Case Evaluation & Chamber Appointment

Have your property disputes, bail matters, family issues, or litigation documents reviewed in person by Advocate Md. Shah Alam at Uttara or Dhaka Judge Court.

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Input Tax Credit and Deduction Rules

Input Tax Credit (ITC) is the cornerstone of the VAT system — it prevents double taxation by allowing a registered business to offset the VAT it paid on its purchases (inputs) against the VAT it collects on its sales (outputs). Only the net difference is payable to the government. However, the rules governing ITC eligibility are strict and must be carefully observed.

Conditions for Claiming ITC

  • The business must be VAT registered with a valid BIN.
  • The purchase must be used in making taxable supplies — ITC cannot be claimed on purchases used for exempt supplies or personal consumption.
  • The supplier must have issued a proper VAT invoice (Mushak-6.3) containing their BIN, the VAT amount charged, description of goods/services, and the buyer's BIN.
  • The ITC must be claimed within 4 months of the relevant tax period (though this can be extended in certain circumstances).
  • The VAT paid must be verifiable through the NBR's online database if requested during audit.

Blocked ITC

Not all input VAT is creditable. The VAT Act 2012 and Rules specifically block ITC on certain categories of purchases including: entertainment expenses, motor vehicles used for non-business purposes, goods purchased for personal use of employees, and purchases from non-registered suppliers. Claiming ITC on blocked items is treated as tax evasion.

Mixed Supplies and Apportionment

Businesses making both taxable and exempt supplies must apportion their input tax on a fair and reasonable basis — typically based on the ratio of taxable turnover to total turnover. The methodology must be disclosed in the VAT return and agreed with the Commissionerate if the amounts are significant. Disputes over ITC apportionment are among the most common VAT litigation matters in Bangladesh, and having a competent corporate lawyer review your ITC position before audit can save substantial sums.

Penalties for VAT Non-Compliance in Bangladesh

The VAT Act 2012 contains a comprehensive penalty regime under Chapter Fourteen (Sections 85–97). Non-compliance can result in civil penalties, interest charges, and in serious cases, criminal prosecution. Below is a summary of the key penalties:

  • Failure to Register: Penalty up to the amount of VAT evaded during the unregistered period, plus interest at 2% per month.
  • Late Filing of Return: Fixed penalty of BDT 10,000 per return, plus 2% per month interest on unpaid VAT.
  • Failure to Issue VAT Invoice: Penalty of BDT 20,000 per instance or the amount of VAT involved, whichever is higher.
  • Incorrect Return: Where a return understates output VAT or overclaims ITC, the shortfall is recoverable with 2% per month interest plus a penalty of up to 50% of the understated amount.
  • Fraud and Tax Evasion: Under Section 92, wilful evasion of VAT is punishable by imprisonment up to 5 years and/or fine up to 3 times the evaded amount.
  • Obstruction of VAT Officers: Refusing access to records or obstructing a VAT audit can result in immediate penalties and referral to law enforcement.

NBR also has powers to seize goods and premises, issue demand notices, and pursue recovery through certificate proceedings. In cases of large-scale fraud, NBR can file criminal complaints at the Customs, Excise, and VAT Commissionerate Courts.

If you have received an NBR demand notice, show-cause notice, or are under audit, it is critical to engage a tax lawyer in Bangladesh immediately. Responding incorrectly to an NBR notice can waive important legal rights and defences. Advocate Md. Shah Alam has experience representing clients before VAT authorities and appellate tribunals.

VAT Appeal and Dispute Resolution Process

When a business disputes an NBR assessment, demand, or penalty, the VAT Act 2012 provides a structured multi-tier appeal mechanism. Acting quickly is essential, as strict time limits apply at each level.

Step 1: Objection to the Commissionerate

The first step is filing a written objection (representation) to the Commissioner of VAT in the relevant Commissionerate within 90 days of the disputed assessment. A deposit of the undisputed portion of tax may be required. The Commissioner or an authorised officer will hear the case and issue a decision.

Step 2: Appeal to the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal

If the business is dissatisfied with the Commissionerate decision, it can appeal to the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal within 90 days of the order. The Tribunal, comprising senior judicial and technical members, hears evidence and legal arguments from both sides. Filing an appeal typically requires a pre-deposit of a percentage of the disputed amount (as specified by the court or as per NBR policy at the time of filing).

Step 3: Appeal to the High Court Division

Questions of law arising from Tribunal decisions can be appealed to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh by way of a VAT Reference Case. This is strictly limited to legal questions — not fresh factual disputes. The High Court can affirm, modify, or reverse the Tribunal's order. In rare cases of urgency or fundamental rights violations, a Supreme Court lawyer may also file a writ petition challenging the legality of an assessment.

Alternative Resolution: Reconciliation and Settlement

NBR has introduced Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) for VAT disputes under Section 108A of the Act, allowing taxpayers to resolve disputes through a neutral facilitator without formal litigation. ADR is faster, confidential, and often results in mutually agreeable settlements. However, ADR is not available in cases involving fraud or criminal allegations.

Given the complexity of VAT law and the technical nature of tribunal proceedings, engaging an experienced tax lawyer in Dhaka from the outset of any dispute is strongly recommended to protect your legal and commercial interests.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the VAT rate in Bangladesh in 2026?

The standard VAT rate in Bangladesh is 15% under the VAT Act 2012. Reduced rates of 5%, 7.5%, and 10% apply to specific goods and services. Exports are zero-rated, and certain essential goods and services are fully exempt. Supplementary Duty (SD) is levied on top of VAT for luxury and specified goods.

Who needs to register for VAT in Bangladesh?

Any business with annual turnover exceeding BDT 3 crore must register for standard VAT. Businesses with turnover between BDT 50 lakh and BDT 3 crore pay Turnover Tax at 4%. Importers and manufacturers of excisable goods must register regardless of turnover. Registration is done online through the NBR portal and results in issuance of a BIN number.

What happens if I file my VAT return late in Bangladesh?

Late filing of a VAT return attracts a fixed penalty of BDT 10,000 per return plus 2% per month interest on any unpaid VAT. Repeated non-filing can trigger an NBR audit, demand notice, and in serious cases, criminal proceedings for VAT evasion under Section 92 of the VAT Act 2012.

Can I appeal an NBR VAT demand notice?

Yes. You can first file a representation (objection) to the Commissioner of VAT within 90 days. If unsuccessful, appeal to the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal within another 90 days. Legal questions can be taken to the High Court Division by way of a VAT Reference. Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) is also available for eligible cases.

What is input tax credit and how does it work in Bangladesh?

Input Tax Credit (ITC) allows VAT-registered businesses to deduct the VAT they paid on purchases (inputs) from the VAT they collect on sales (outputs). Only the net amount is paid to NBR. ITC is only claimable on purchases supported by valid VAT invoices (Mushak-6.3), used in taxable supplies, and claimed within 4 months of the relevant tax period. Purchases used for exempt supplies or personal use are blocked from ITC.

Is VAT applicable to online businesses and e-commerce in Bangladesh?

Yes. Online businesses and e-commerce platforms in Bangladesh are subject to the same VAT rules as physical businesses. If annual turnover exceeds the applicable threshold, VAT registration is mandatory. NBR has also issued specific guidance on VAT collection by digital platforms and non-resident digital service providers supplying to Bangladeshi consumers.
