VAT Registration & Return Filing Bangladesh – Business Guide to NBR Compliance

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-07-06 · 14 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Value Added Tax (VAT) is the backbone of Bangladesh's indirect tax system, contributing over 35% of total national revenue. For businesses operating in Bangladesh, understanding and complying with the VAT and Supplementary Duty Act 2012 is not optional — non-compliance can result in heavy penalties, forced closure, and criminal prosecution. This comprehensive 2026 guide covers everything a business owner needs to know about VAT registration, monthly return filing, input tax credits, and how to handle VAT audits and demand notices from the National Board of Revenue (NBR).

: · Land & Property Registration Lawyer Bangladesh

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Registration Fee & Stamp Duty1% Registration Fee + 1.5% Stamp Duty on deed value
Local Government Tax & VAT2%–3% Local Govt Tax + 1.5%–4.5% VAT (varies by City/Pourosova/Union)
Source Tax (Gain Tax / TDS)1% to 8% depending on mouza classification under Income Tax Act 2023
Official Land & Mouza Portalsland.gov.bd, dlrms.land.gov.bd, and eporcha.gov.bd
📋 In This Article
  1. Overview: The VAT and Supplementary Duty Act 2012
  2. Who Must Register for VAT in Bangladesh?
  3. How to Register for VAT Online at the NBR Portal
  4. Mushak Forms: The Complete Filing System
  5. Monthly VAT Return Filing (Mushak-9.1)
  6. Input Tax Credit: How to Recover VAT You Pay on Purchases
  7. VAT Rates by Sector in Bangladesh
  8. Penalties for VAT Non-Compliance
  9. VAT Audit Process: What to Expect
  10. How to Respond to a VAT Demand Notice
  11. VAT Appellate Tribunal: Challenging NBR Decisions
  12. Get Expert VAT Legal Advice

Overview: The VAT and Supplementary Duty Act 2012

Bangladesh's VAT system is governed by the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act 2012 (VAT Act 2012), which came into full effect on 1 July 2019 after several years of delayed implementation. The Act replaced the outdated VAT Act 1991 and introduced a modern, invoice-based VAT system aligned with international best practices.

Key Concepts Under the VAT Act 2012:

  • Standard VAT Rate: 15% on most goods and services (Section 15)
  • Supplementary Duty (SD): An additional consumption tax on luxury goods, tobacco, alcohol, and petroleum products — rates range from 1% to 500%
  • Truncated Rate: Certain service sectors pay a fixed percentage of supply value as VAT (not the full 15%) — e.g., retail traders may pay at a truncated rate
  • Zero Rate (Export): Exported goods and services are zero-rated (0% VAT) under Section 25, allowing exporters to claim refunds of input VAT paid
  • VAT Exemptions: Certain goods and services are exempt from VAT (listed in the First Schedule of the Act) — primarily agricultural produce, essential medicines, and educational materials

Administering Authority: VAT is administered by the National Board of Revenue (NBR) through its VAT department — specifically the Large Taxpayer Unit (LTU) for large businesses and VAT Commissionerates for others. The NBR's online portal for VAT is vat.gov.bd (also accessible through the integrated government portal).

As of 2026, the NBR has significantly strengthened VAT enforcement through digital means — Electronic Fiscal Devices (EFDs) are now mandatory for most retail and service businesses, automatically recording each transaction and transmitting data to the NBR.

Who Must Register for VAT in Bangladesh?

Whether and how you register for VAT in Bangladesh depends on your annual turnover:

  • Above BDT 3 Crore (30 million) annual turnover: Mandatory full VAT registration. You must collect 15% VAT from customers, file monthly returns (Mushak-9.1), and claim input tax credits.
  • BDT 50 Lakh to BDT 3 Crore annual turnover: Eligible for the Turnover Tax (Package VAT) scheme under Section 64. You pay a simplified flat tax of 4% on turnover (not on VAT base) and file a simplified annual return. This was previously the Mushak-6.3 threshold at BDT 30 lakh, revised upward.
  • Below BDT 50 Lakh annual turnover: Exempt from VAT registration (micro-business exemption). However, if you are in the supply chain of a VAT-registered business, you may still need to register at the buyer's request for input tax credit purposes.

Mandatory Registration Regardless of Turnover: Certain businesses must register for VAT regardless of turnover, including:

  • Importers and exporters
  • Manufacturers in specified sectors (garments, pharmaceuticals, food processing)
  • Businesses supplying to VAT-registered large buyers who need input tax credit
  • Service providers in specified sectors (consulting, legal, accounting, advertising, telecom)
  • Businesses operating in export processing zones (EPZs)

Voluntary Registration: A business below the threshold can voluntarily register for VAT if it benefits from input tax credit claims — for example, a supplier to export-oriented factories.

How to Register for VAT Online at the NBR Portal

VAT registration in Bangladesh is done online through the NBR VAT portal. Here is the step-by-step process:

  1. Access the NBR VAT Portal: Go to vat.gov.bd and click on New Registration. You can also access this through the integrated government services portal.
  2. Business Information Entry: Enter your business details: business name, address, trade license number, TIN (Tax Identification Number), nature of business activities, and HS code (Harmonized System code) for goods or service category code.
  3. Owner/Director Information: Enter the NID and personal details of all proprietors, partners, or directors.
  4. Bank Account Details: Provide the business bank account number and branch for VAT payment verification.
  5. Document Upload: Upload scanned copies of: (a) Trade License, (b) TIN Certificate, (c) NID of proprietor/directors, (d) Bank account details/cancelled cheque, (e) Tenancy agreement or ownership document for business premises, (f) Company incorporation documents (for companies).
  6. Application Submission: Submit the completed application. You will receive an acknowledgment with a reference number.
  7. Field Verification: A VAT Inspector may visit your business premises to verify the information. Currently this process takes approximately 7-15 working days for straightforward applications.
  8. BIN Issuance: Upon approval, you receive a Business Identification Number (BIN) — a unique 9-digit VAT registration number. The BIN Certificate is downloadable from the portal.

Important: Your BIN must be displayed at your business premises and printed on all VAT invoices (Mushak-6.3 challan or Mushak-6.2 tax invoice).

Mushak Forms: The Complete Filing System

The VAT filing system in Bangladesh uses a series of standardized forms called Mushak forms. Understanding which form to use and when is essential for compliance. The key forms currently in use under the VAT Act 2012 are:

FormPurposeWhen Used
Mushak-6.1Tax Invoice for full VAT registrantsEvery sale of goods or services by a full VAT registrant
Mushak-6.2Simplified Tax InvoiceRetail sales where buyer does not need input credit
Mushak-6.3Turnover Tax ChallanBusinesses under the turnover tax scheme
Mushak-6.6Credit Note (debit/credit adjustment)When goods are returned or price adjustments made
Mushak-6.7Debit NoteWhen additional charges are applied after original invoice
Mushak-9.1Monthly VAT ReturnFiled by all full VAT registrants by the 15th of each month
Mushak-4.3VAT Payment ChallanWhen paying VAT to government account at Sonali Bank
Mushak-19Refund ApplicationWhen claiming a VAT refund (e.g., exporters)

Monthly VAT Return Filing (Mushak-9.1)

Full VAT registrants (BIN holders with turnover above BDT 3 crore) must file a monthly VAT return using Form Mushak-9.1. The return is due by the 15th day of the following month (i.e., the return for June is due by 15 July). This is a strict deadline — filing even one day late attracts penalties.

What the Mushak-9.1 Return Contains:

  • Total output VAT collected from customers during the month
  • Total input VAT paid on purchases (purchases and import duty)
  • Net VAT payable (output VAT minus input VAT credit)
  • Details of all purchase and sale transactions
  • Adjustments for credit notes and debit notes
  • Details of any exempt or zero-rated supplies

How to File: As of 2026, the Mushak-9.1 return must be filed online through the NBR VAT portal (vat.gov.bd). Paper filing is no longer accepted by most commissionerates. After filing, VAT payable must be deposited to the government account through a Treasury Challan (Mushak-4.3) at Sonali Bank or via online banking (IBAS++ system).

Nil Return: If there were no sales during a month, a nil return must still be filed. Failure to file even a nil return is a compliance violation.

Record Keeping: Under Section 66 of the VAT Act 2012, every registered person must maintain VAT account books (purchase register, sales register, input VAT credit register) for a minimum of 5 years from the date of the relevant transaction. These records must be produced on demand during a VAT audit.

Input Tax Credit: How to Recover VAT You Pay on Purchases

The input tax credit (ITC) system is one of the most valuable features of the VAT Act 2012. It allows VAT-registered businesses to recover the VAT they paid on their business purchases, reducing their net VAT liability to the government.

How ITC Works (Example):

  • You purchase raw materials worth BDT 1,00,000 and pay 15% VAT = BDT 15,000 input VAT
  • You manufacture a product and sell it for BDT 2,00,000 and collect 15% VAT = BDT 30,000 output VAT
  • Net VAT payable = BDT 30,000 (output) - BDT 15,000 (input) = BDT 15,000
  • You only pay BDT 15,000 to the government, not the full BDT 30,000

Conditions for Claiming ITC:

  • The purchase must be for business purposes (not for personal use)
  • You must hold a valid tax invoice (Mushak-6.1) from the supplier showing their BIN
  • The supplier must also be VAT-registered and must have reported the sale in their return
  • The goods or services must not be used for an exempt supply
  • ITC must be claimed in the same month or within 4 months of the purchase

ITC on Capital Machinery: VAT paid on capital machinery and equipment used in production is creditable, subject to conditions. For machinery worth over BDT 10 lakh, the ITC is typically taken over 12 months in equal installments.

ITC for Exporters: Exporters make zero-rated supplies — they charge no VAT to foreign buyers. But they pay input VAT on their local purchases. They are entitled to a VAT refund for this input VAT. Refund claims are filed using Form Mushak-19 and are subject to verification by the VAT Commissionerate. Refund processing currently takes 3-12 months.

VAT Rates by Sector in Bangladesh

Bangladesh applies different VAT rates depending on the sector. Here is a summary of key sectors and their applicable VAT rates as of 2026:

Sector / ActivityVAT RateNotes
Manufacturing (most goods)15%Standard rate
Export of goods and services0% (zero-rated)Full input credit refundable
Restaurant and food service5% (truncated)Applied on supply value; no input credit
Construction (contractors)7.5% (truncated)Applied on contract value
IT services (software, IT enabled)0% (exempt for IT-ITES)Incentive for digital economy
Telecommunication services15% + supplementary dutyMobile talk time: 15% VAT + SD
Real estate (developer sales)2% on flat/apartment saleOn deed value above threshold
Legal and accounting services15%Professional services — standard rate
Essential medicines (listed)0% (exempt)First Schedule — healthcare policy
Tobacco products15% VAT + high supplementary dutySD ranges from 45% to 65%

Note: VAT rates are subject to change in each year's Finance Act/Budget. Always verify current rates with an accountant or tax lawyer before filing.

Penalties for VAT Non-Compliance

The VAT and Supplementary Duty Act 2012 imposes significant penalties for non-compliance. NBR VAT enforcement has become increasingly aggressive as of 2026, with digital EFD data allowing the department to identify discrepancies more easily. Key penalties include:

  • Failure to Register (Section 85): Operating without VAT registration when required — penalty of BDT 10,000-50,000 and collection of all VAT due from the date business commenced.
  • Late Filing of Return (Section 86): Penalty of BDT 10,000 for the first month's late filing, plus BDT 1,000 per day for each subsequent day of delay. Interest at 2% per month is also charged on the outstanding VAT amount.
  • False Return or Under-Declaration (Section 90): Penalty of 2-3 times the amount of tax evaded. This is in addition to the principal tax plus interest.
  • Tax Evasion (Section 91): Criminal penalty of 3-5 years imprisonment plus fine equal to the evaded amount. Criminal cases are filed by the VAT Commissionerate in Magistrate Courts.
  • Failure to Issue Tax Invoice (Section 87): Penalty of BDT 5,000-20,000 per violation plus potential business licence suspension.
  • Failure to Maintain Records (Section 88): Penalty of BDT 10,000 for failure to maintain required books, with additional penalties per inspection if non-compliance continues.
  • Failure to Install EFD (Electronic Fiscal Device): Businesses required to use EFDs face penalties of BDT 50,000 per device not installed, plus potential sealing of business premises.

VAT Audit Process: What to Expect

The NBR VAT department conducts periodic audits of registered businesses to verify the accuracy of VAT returns and the completeness of records. Understanding the audit process helps you prepare adequately and respond appropriately.

Types of VAT Audits:

  • Routine Audit: Periodic examination of VAT records — typically targeting businesses in high-revenue sectors or those flagged by risk analysis software
  • Intelligence-Based Audit: Triggered by specific information about tax evasion — informant complaints, EFD data anomalies, or cross-matching with customs and income tax data
  • Refund Verification Audit: Conducted before approving large VAT refund claims (especially for exporters)

The Audit Process:

  1. The VAT Commissionerate issues an audit notice specifying the period to be audited and the documents required (typically 15-30 days advance notice)
  2. You must produce all VAT books, invoices, purchase records, bank statements, and contract documents for the specified period
  3. The VAT auditor examines the records and may interview your accounts staff
  4. The auditor issues a Draft Audit Report identifying discrepancies or proposed additional tax demands
  5. You have the right to respond to the draft report and provide explanations within the specified period (usually 15-30 days)
  6. The VAT Commissionerate issues a Final Audit Report and a Demand Notice if tax is found due

Preparation for VAT Audit: Maintain meticulous records, reconcile your VAT returns with your accounting books monthly, and retain all original tax invoices for 5 years. If you are aware of discrepancies before an audit notice arrives, consider a voluntary disclosure to the VAT Commissionerate — this typically results in lower penalties than being caught in an audit.

How to Respond to a VAT Demand Notice

If the NBR issues a VAT demand notice (also called a Tax Recovery Notice), you must take immediate action within the specified timeframe — typically 30 days from the date of notice. Ignoring a VAT demand notice escalates to coercive recovery measures including bank account freezing and asset attachment.

Steps to Take Upon Receiving a VAT Demand Notice:

  1. Read and Understand the Demand: Identify the period, the amount demanded, and the grounds for the demand (late filing, under-declaration, disallowed input credit, etc.).
  2. Consult a VAT Advocate Immediately: This is not the time for DIY — a VAT lawyer or tax consultant can assess whether the demand is legally valid and the best response strategy.
  3. Gather Evidence: Collect all invoices, returns, and records relating to the disputed period. Identify any calculation errors in the NBR's demand.
  4. File a Reply (Objection): Submit a written reply to the VAT Commissionerate explaining why the demand is incorrect and attaching supporting documents. A well-reasoned reply with strong documentary evidence can result in full or partial withdrawal of the demand.
  5. Pay What Is Undisputed: If you agree with part of the demand (e.g., a small late filing penalty), pay that amount to demonstrate good faith and prevent coercive recovery.
  6. File an Appeal if the Reply Is Rejected: If the Commissionerate rejects your reply and upholds the demand, you have the right to appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) within 30 days of the rejection order.

VAT Appellate Tribunal: Challenging NBR Decisions

When internal NBR appeals (to the Commissioner Appeals) fail, taxpayers can challenge VAT decisions before the independent VAT Appellate Tribunal established under Section 118 of the VAT Act 2012. The Tribunal is presided over by a judicial officer (usually a retired District Judge or senior tax official) and has the power to uphold, modify, or reverse VAT demand decisions.

Appeal Process:

  1. File appeal within 90 days of receiving the Commissioner Appeals' rejection order
  2. Deposit either the full demanded amount or a portion (typically 10%) as security before the appeal is admitted (pre-deposit requirement under Section 116)
  3. Submit grounds of appeal in writing, supported by documentary evidence
  4. The Tribunal hears both parties (taxpayer and NBR) and may call for additional evidence
  5. The Tribunal issues a written order — which is binding on both parties

Further Appeal to the High Court: If the Tribunal's decision is adverse, you can appeal further to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court on questions of law (not facts) within 60 days of the Tribunal's order.

Practical Note: VAT litigation can be expensive and time-consuming. Many businesses prefer to negotiate a settlement with the VAT Commissionerate before the formal appeal process escalates. However, when the NBR's demand is legally unjustified — for example, based on an incorrect interpretation of the law or refusal to allow legitimate input tax credits — pursuing the appeal to the Tribunal and beyond is both justified and often successful.

Our corporate law team at the Uttara, Dhaka chamber of Advocate Md. Shah Alam provides comprehensive VAT advisory and litigation services — from initial registration assistance to defending complex VAT audit cases and representing clients before the VAT Appellate Tribunal. Contact us for expert guidance on all VAT compliance and dispute matters.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the current VAT turnover threshold for mandatory registration in Bangladesh?

As of 2026, businesses with annual turnover above BDT 3 crore (30 million) must register for full VAT and file monthly Mushak-9.1 returns. Businesses with turnover between BDT 50 lakh and BDT 3 crore can opt for the simplified Turnover Tax scheme. Businesses below BDT 50 lakh are generally exempt from VAT registration, though mandatory registration may still be required in specific sectors.

What is a BIN number and why is it important?

A BIN (Business Identification Number) is a unique 9-digit number issued by the NBR upon VAT registration. It is the equivalent of a VAT registration number. Your BIN must be displayed at your business premises, printed on all tax invoices (Mushak-6.1 forms), and used in all VAT correspondence with the NBR. Without a BIN, your customers cannot claim input tax credit on purchases from you.

What is the deadline for filing the monthly VAT return (Mushak-9.1) in Bangladesh?

The Mushak-9.1 monthly VAT return must be filed by the 15th day of the month following the return period. For example, the return for June must be filed by 15 July. Filing after this deadline attracts a penalty of BDT 10,000 for the first month, plus BDT 1,000 per day thereafter, plus 2% monthly interest on the outstanding VAT amount.

Can I claim input tax credit on all my business purchases?

Not on all purchases. Input tax credit is available only for purchases used in taxable supplies (not for exempt supplies or personal use), supported by a valid tax invoice (Mushak-6.1) from a VAT-registered supplier, and claimed within 4 months of the purchase. You cannot claim input credit on purchases from unregistered suppliers or on goods/services used to make VAT-exempt supplies.

What happens if I receive a VAT demand notice from the NBR?

You have 30 days from the date of the demand notice to file a reply (objection) to the VAT Commissionerate. Your reply should explain why the demand is incorrect and attach supporting documents. If the Commissionerate rejects your reply, you can appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) within 30 days and then to the VAT Appellate Tribunal. Do not ignore a VAT demand notice — failure to respond leads to coercive recovery including bank account freezing.

Is VAT applicable on exported goods and services from Bangladesh?

Exported goods and qualifying exported services are zero-rated under the VAT Act 2012, meaning 0% VAT is charged to the foreign buyer. However, the exporter continues to pay input VAT on their local purchases (raw materials, services). The exporter is entitled to claim a refund of this input VAT by filing Form Mushak-19 with the VAT Commissionerate. Refund processing currently takes 3-12 months depending on the commissionerate.

entries.body:
Vested Property (Arpita Sampatti) Release in Bangladesh: Legal Procedure for Overseas Heirs & NRBs (2026)

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-10-26 · 18 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

For hundreds of thousands of expatriates belonging to religious minority communities residing in India, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada, ancestral real estate in Bangladesh has remained locked in a painful historical injustice known as the **Vested Property Act (formerly Enemy Property Act 1965)**. Millions of acres of legitimate ancestral homesteads, agricultural acreage, and commercial plots were wrongfully classified as 'Vested Property' (অর্পিত সম্পত্তি) due to bureaucratic manipulation, fraudulent settlement surveys, or malicious land grabbing during family migration. With the landmark enactment of the **Vested Property Return (Amendment) Act 2011 & 2013**, the legal architecture underwent a historic transformation, establishing specialized **Vested Property Return Tribunals** where legitimate heirs can demand the complete de-listing, release, and physical restoration of their ancestral estate. This definitive legal guide walks overseas heirs through the critical difference between 'Ka' and 'Kha' schedules, evidentiary requirements to prove unbroken lineage, tribunal litigation workflows, appellate remedies, and Supreme Court writ petitions.

: · Land & Property Dispute Lawyer in Dhaka

  4. 4. Who Has Standing to Claim as an Overseas Heir? (Succession Rights)
  5. 5. Complete Documentary Checklist Required to Prove Title
  6. 6. Procedural Workflow: Filing a Case in the Vested Property Return Tribunal
  7. 7. Summary Matrix: Tribunal Case Steps, Timelines & Authorities
  8. 8. Appellate Remedies: Vested Property Appellate Tribunal & High Court Writs
  9. 9. Enforcing Release Decrees: DC Office Clearance, AC Land Mutation & Possession
  10. 10. Real-Life Case Study: Reclaiming 8 Acres of Ancestral Land in Sylhet from Canada
  11. 11. Key Defenses Used by Government & Land Grabbers (And How to Defeat Them)
  12. 12. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1. Historical Evolution: From Enemy Property 1965 to Vested Property Return Act

The origin of Vested Property represents one of the most litigated property controversies in South Asian legal history:

  • Defence of Pakistan Rules 1965: Following the September 1965 Indo-Pakistan war, the Pakistani military regime promulgated the Enemy Property (Custody and Registration) Order 1965. Lands belonging to individuals who migrated to India were declared 'Enemy Property' and placed under government custody.
  • Post-Independence Legislation (1974): After the liberation of Bangladesh in 1971, parliament enacted the Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) Act, 1974 (Act XLVI of 1974), renaming enemy property as 'Vested Property'.
  • Widespread Bureaucratic Abuse: In practice, corrupt settlement officers and local land cartels routinely listed properties belonging to Hindu families who never left Bangladesh as vested property, using fake survey entries to seize valuable lands.
  • The Legislative Remedy (2001, 2011 & 2013): After decades of civil rights advocacy, parliament passed the Vested Property Return Act, 2001 (অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১). Comprehensive amendments in 2011 and 2013 created judicial tribunals to adjudicate genuine claims and permanently repealed the abusive Kha Schedule.

2. The Crucial Difference: 'Ka' Schedule vs 'Kha' Schedule Explained

Understanding which government gazette list encumbers your ancestral property is the single most critical diagnostic step:

A. 'Ka' Schedule (ক-তফসিল — Returnable via Tribunal)

'Ka' Schedule properties comprise lands that were in actual physical possession, custody, or temporary commercial leasehold of the government. Under Section 9 and 10 of the Act, to recover a 'Ka' Schedule property, legal heirs must file an original application before the Vested Property Return Tribunal of the respective district.

B. 'Kha' Schedule (খ-তফসিল — Permanently Repealed & Free)

'Kha' Schedule properties were lands that were NEVER in government custody but were maliciously listed in gazettes while genuine owners or co-sharers resided on the land. Following nationwide public outrage, parliament passed the Vested Property Return (Amendment) Act, 2013 (Act No. 34 of 2013), which completely repealed, dropped, and annulled the Kha Schedule across Bangladesh:

Ministry of Land SRO & Standing Circular: If your ancestral land was listed under the 'Kha' Schedule, you do NOT need to file any court case or tribunal petition. The listing is legally non-existent. You have the right to apply directly for digital e-Namjari mutation, pay Land Development Tax, and sell or transfer the property without any government NOC.

3. Statutory Framework: Vested Property Return Act 2001 (as amended 2011 & 2013)

The return of vested property is governed by the following core statutory mechanisms:

  • Section 2(f): Defines a 'permanent owner' (মূল মালিক) as a person who was a citizen and continuous resident of East Pakistan / Bangladesh and whose property was erroneously treated as enemy property.
  • Section 9: Establishes the right of original owners or their lawful successors to apply for the return of property.
  • Section 10: Governs the jurisdiction and powers of the Vested Property Return Tribunal (অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ ট্রাইব্যুনাল), which has the full powers of a Civil Court under the CPC 1908.
  • Section 16: Establishes the Vested Property Return Appellate Tribunal (অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আপিল ট্রাইব্যুনাল) headed by a District Judge.
  • Section 28: Gives the provisions of the Act overriding effect over any other conflicting law or decree.

4. Who Has Standing to Claim as an Overseas Heir? (Succession Rights)

A common misconception among expatriates is that holding citizenship of the USA, UK, Canada, or India bars them from reclaiming vested property in Bangladesh. This is legally incorrect:

  1. Statutory Standing of Heirs: Under Section 2(f) and Section 9 of the 2001 Act, an application can be instituted by the original owner or their lawful successors (উত্তরাধিকারী) according to personal succession law (Hindu Dayabhaga School, Christian Succession Act, or Islamic law).
  2. Lineage Tracing: As long as the claimant can establish through authenticated Warishan Certificates that they are the direct biological or legal heir of the recorded ancestor on the CS or SA Khatian, they possess full legal standing.
  3. Representation via Power of Attorney: Overseas heirs living in Toronto, London, New York, or Kolkata can execute a Special Power of Attorney before the Bangladesh diplomatic mission to conduct the case entirely through their advocate in Bangladesh.

5. Complete Documentary Checklist Required to Prove Title

The Vested Property Return Tribunal operates under strict rules of civil evidence. Your advocate must assemble an airtight documentary dossier:

  • Certified copy of the CS (Cadastral Survey) Khatian showing original family title.
  • Certified copy of the SA (State Acquisition Survey 1956) Khatian confirming lawful possession prior to the 1965 war.
  • Original or certified copies of registered title deeds (বায়া দলিল / পিট দলিল) demonstrating lawful acquisition.
  • Official Warishan / Heirship Certificate (ওয়ারিশান সনদ) issued by the Union Parishad Chairman or City Corporation Mayor tracing the genealogical tree (বংশলতিকা).
  • Certified extract of the Vested Property Gazette (গেজেট) showing the exact plot number and schedule.
  • Historical Land Development Tax Dakhilas (খাজনা দাখিলা) and municipal holding tax receipts.
  • Proof that the original owner did not migrate as an enemy national during the September 1965 conflict.

6. Procedural Workflow: Filing a Case in the Vested Property Return Tribunal

Litigating a vested property release proceeds through structured judicial stages:

  1. Filing the Application (দরখাস্ত দাখিল): The petition is filed before the District Vested Property Return Tribunal. The government, represented by the Deputy Commissioner (DC) and Assistant Commissioner (Land), is arrayed as the principal opposite party.
  2. Summons & Written Objection: The government files a Written Objection (লিখিত আপত্তি) through the Government Pleader (GP).
  3. Adducing Evidence (সাক্ষ্য গ্রহণ): The claimant's attorney produces certified historical Khatians, title deeds, and presents witness testimonies proving continuous residence and succession.
  4. Tribunal Judgment & Release Decree: If satisfied that the listing was erroneous and succession is authentic, the Tribunal passes a formal Judgment and Decree ordering the release of the property from the Vested Property Register.

7. Summary Matrix: Tribunal Case Steps, Timelines & Authorities

The following table illustrates the complete lifecycle of a Vested Property recovery case:

StageAdjudicating AuthorityEstimated TimelineRequired Key Action
Schedule VerificationDC Office Gazette Records1 to 2 WeeksDetermine if land is Ka or Kha schedule
Tribunal LitigationDistrict Vested Property Return Tribunal12 to 24 MonthsSubmit CS/SA Khatians; prove unbroken lineage
Appellate Tribunal AppealVested Property Appellate Tribunal6 to 12 MonthsMandatory appeal within 45 days if aggrieved
High Court Revision / WritSupreme Court High Court Division6 to 18 MonthsChallenge Appellate Tribunal errors; seek Mandamus
Executive De-listing & MutationDC Office & AC (Land) Office1 to 3 MonthsDe-list from VP Register; execute e-Namjari

8. Appellate Remedies: Vested Property Appellate Tribunal & High Court Writs

If the District Tribunal rejects your claim or if the Deputy Commissioner files a routine appeal against a favorable decree:

  • Appellate Tribunal Appeal (Section 16): Under Section 16 of the Act, an appeal must be preferred before the Vested Property Return Appellate Tribunal within 45 days of the original decree. The Appellate Tribunal, presided over by a senior District Judge, re-evaluates evidence and passes final judgment.
  • Supreme Court High Court Division Remedies: If the Appellate Tribunal commits an error of law, the claimant can move the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh via a Civil Revision petition under Section 115 of the CPC or a Constitutional Writ Petition under Article 102 to quash illegal government claims.

9. Enforcing Release Decrees: DC Office Clearance, AC Land Mutation & Possession

Securing a court judgment is only half the victory; practical administrative execution must follow:

  1. DC Office De-listing Order: The Tribunal transmits an official decree to the District Collector. The DC issues an administrative memo directing the AC (Land) to strike the property off the government's Vested Property Register (ভি-পি ভলিউম).
  2. e-Namjari Mutation: The claimant submits the release decree and DC memo online at mutation.land.gov.bd. The AC (Land) opens a dedicated Mutation Khatian in the claimant's name.
  3. Termination of Government Leases: Under Section 19 of the Act, any temporary agricultural or commercial lease granted by the government to third parties automatically terminates upon issuance of the release decree.
  4. Delivery of Physical Possession: The AC (Land), accompanied by local revenue staff and police, visits the land, conducts demarcation, and formally hands over physical possession to your attorney.

10. Real-Life Case Study: Reclaiming 8 Acres of Ancestral Land in Sylhet from Canada

Background: The Roy family, residing in Toronto, Canada, owned 8.5 acres of ancestral tea garden and farmland in Beanibazar, Sylhet. Following the 1965 war, local revenue staff wrongfully recorded the land as Ka-Schedule Vested Property, leasing parcels to local political syndicates.

Legal Rescue Implemented:

  1. The Roy brothers executed a Special Power of Attorney at the Bangladesh Consulate General in Toronto, which our team authenticated at MOFA and stamped at Sylhet DC office in 20 days.
  2. We instituted Vested Property Case No. 112/2023 before the Vested Property Return Tribunal, Sylhet.
  3. We produced certified 1938 CS Khatians and 1956 SA Khatians proving continuous family title, alongside birth records establishing that their late father remained in East Pakistan until 1978.
  4. The Tribunal ruled in our favor, passing a decree of release. When the DC filed a routine appeal, we successfully defended the decree before the Appellate Tribunal.
  5. The Sylhet DC office issued an executive order de-listing all 8.5 acres. We completed digital e-Namjari in the Canadian heirs' names, terminating all unauthorized leases. Today, the Roy family holds unencumbered freehold title.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can an expat living in Canada, USA, or India claim vested property without coming to Bangladesh?

Yes. An overseas heir can execute a Special Power of Attorney before the Bangladesh Embassy or Consulate General abroad, empowering an enrolled Supreme Court advocate to file and conduct the tribunal case in Bangladesh.

What is the legal status of the 'Kha' Schedule of Vested Property?

The Kha Schedule was completely abolished and repealed by the Vested Property Return (Amendment) Act 2013. Properties in Kha schedule are free from government claim and can be mutated directly at the AC Land office.

Can Hindu NRBs inherit and recover ancestral property in Bangladesh?

Yes. Succession is governed by Hindu Dayabhaga personal law, and legitimate heirs have equal statutory standing under the 2001 Act to reclaim ancestral property regardless of their current nationality.

What happens if a third party is currently leasing the vested land from the government?

Under Section 19 of the Vested Property Return Act, any temporary government lease automatically terminates upon the passing of a final release decree by the Tribunal.

What should I do if the deadline for filing in the Vested Property Tribunal has passed?

If initial gazette deadlines were missed due to absence abroad or lack of notice, your advocate can file a Constitutional Writ Petition under Article 102 in the Supreme Court High Court Division to secure delayed consideration.

How long does a Vested Property Tribunal case take?

A contested case typically takes 12 to 24 months in the District Tribunal, and an additional 6 to 12 months if an appeal is preferred before the Appellate Tribunal.

Can I sell the land immediately after obtaining a Vested Property release decree?

Yes, once the release decree is enforced, the property is struck off the VP register, and e-Namjari mutation is completed in your name, you hold full freehold title and can sell or transfer the land freely.

Does having an Indian passport prevent me from reclaiming vested property in Bangladesh?

No. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly held that lawful succession rights cannot be extinguished merely because heirs reside abroad or hold foreign nationality.

Warrant vs. Summons Bangladesh: What Is the Difference?

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-03-26 · 6 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Receiving a legal notice from a Bangladesh court can be alarming — especially when you are not sure whether it is a summons requiring your appearance or a warrant authorizing your arrest. These are fundamentally different legal instruments with very different consequences. Confusing them can lead to serious mistakes.

: · Urgent Bail & Supreme Court Lawyer Dhaka

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order
Official Portalssupremecourt.gov.bd, judiciary.gov.bd, pcc.police.gov.bd & land.gov.bd

📋 In This Article

  2. What is an Arrest Warrant in Bangladesh?

  4. When Does a Court Issue a Summons vs. a Warrant?

  7. Non-Bailable vs. Bailable Warrants
  8. Getting an Arrest Warrant Cancelled (Recall)

What is a Court Summons in Bangladesh?

A summons is a formal court document issued under the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC) that directs a person to appear before the court on a specific date. A summons:

  • Does not authorize the police to arrest the person.
  • Is served through the court bailiff or police, but the person retains their freedom.
  • Requires compliance — failing to appear without a valid reason is a contempt of court and may lead to a warrant being issued.
  • Is typically used in summons-triable cases (less serious offences) or to call witnesses.

If you receive a summons, respond through a criminal lawyer in Dhaka — do not simply ignore it.

What is an Arrest Warrant in Bangladesh?

An arrest warrant is a written court order authorizing the police to arrest and bring a specific person before the court. A warrant:

  • Gives police the legal authority to apprehend the named person wherever found.
  • Must specify the name/description of the person, the offence, and be signed by the issuing Magistrate.
  • Remains in force until executed (the person is arrested) or the court recalls it.
  • Can be made bailable or non-bailable by the issuing Magistrate.

Key Differences: Summons vs. Warrant

FeatureSummonsArrest Warrant
Police authority to arrest?❌ No✅ Yes
Person remains free?✅ Yes⚠️ Can be arrested
Signed by?Court officialMagistrate only
Issued in what cases?Summons-triable or witness appearanceWarrant cases or failure to comply with summons
Consequence of ignoring?Warrant may be issuedForcible arrest

WhatsApp Consultation Direct Call: +880 1712-655546

Non-Bailable vs. Bailable Warrants

Warrants may be classified as:

  • Bailable Warrant: The officer executing the warrant must release the arrested person on bail upon their furnishing security. This is the less severe type.
  • Non-Bailable Warrant: The arrested person must be produced before the court — no bail can be granted at the point of arrest by the police. Only the court can grant bail. This is the most serious type and requires immediate legal action.

If you learn that a non-bailable warrant has been issued against you, contact a criminal lawyer immediately to apply to the court to recall the warrant before it is executed.

Getting an Arrest Warrant Cancelled (Recall)

A person against whom a warrant has been issued can apply to the court to recall (cancel) the warrant before it is executed. The process:

  1. File a petition to the issuing court explaining why the warrant was issued (typically: failure to attend a previous hearing).
  2. Provide a valid explanation for the non-appearance (illness, unawareness of the case, etc.).
  3. Offer an undertaking to appear on all future dates.
  4. The court may recall the warrant and instead direct the person to appear on a fixed date.

Acting quickly through a lawyer before the warrant is executed is critical — once arrested under a non-bailable warrant, obtaining bail becomes significantly more complicated.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can police arrest me based on a summons?

No. A summons alone does not authorize arrest. However, if you fail to comply with a summons, the court may issue an arrest warrant. At that point, police can arrest you.

How do I know if a warrant has been issued against me?

Warrants are not always publicly advertised. You should check court records if you suspect a case has been filed against you. Many people discover warrants only when police arrive. Regular check-ins with a criminal lawyer if you have any ongoing legal matter is advisable.

What should I do if I receive a summons?

Do not ignore it. Engage a criminal lawyer who will appear on your behalf for the specified date or apply for an exemption from personal attendance if appropriate.

Can I apply for anticipatory bail if I know a warrant may be issued?

Yes. If you have reason to believe a warrant is imminent, you can apply for anticipatory bail (bail before arrest) under Section 498 CrPC. This is the best protective step to take.

Can summons be issued for civil cases too?

Yes. In civil proceedings, summons are issued to defendants and witnesses under the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. Failure to comply with a civil court summons also has serious consequences.

Divorce Cost Bangladesh – Court Fees, Lawyer Fees & Total Expenses

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-09-22 · 11 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Divorce in Bangladesh is a difficult and often expensive process. Whether you are considering talaq (husband-initiated divorce), khul (wife-initiated divorce), or a court-ordered dissolution of marriage, understanding the full cost involved is essential for financial planning and realistic expectations. In 2026, the total cost of divorce in Bangladesh — including court fees, lawyer fees, nikah registrar fees, and other expenses — can range from as little as ৳5,000 for a simple mutual consent divorce to over ৳2,00,000 for a contested court battle. This comprehensive guide breaks down every cost you should expect.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

Types of Divorce in Bangladesh Under Muslim Law

For Muslim couples (the vast majority of Bangladesh's population), the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 governs the divorce process. There are three main types of divorce available:

TypeWho InitiatesLegal BasisTypical Duration
TalaqHusbandMuslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, Section 790 days (mandatory arbitration period)
KhulWife (by returning dower)Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, Section 890 days if husband agrees; otherwise requires court
Court Divorce / Judicial DissolutionWife (via court)Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 19396 months to 3+ years
Mutual ConsentBoth partiesCombination of Talaq + Khul or court90 days (fastest route)

For Hindu, Christian, and other religious minorities in Bangladesh, different laws apply:

  • Hindu couples: The Hindu Marriage Registration Act 2012 governs registration, but divorce is governed by customary law and the Specific Relief Act. Court proceedings are typically required.
  • Christian couples: The Divorce Act, 1869 governs dissolution of marriage for Christians in Bangladesh.

This guide primarily focuses on the most common scenario: Muslim divorce under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961. The procedure and costs for Hindu and Christian divorce differ and should be discussed with a lawyer.

Type 1: Talaq (Husband-Initiated Divorce) – Cost Breakdown

Talaq is the most common form of divorce in Bangladesh and is the husband's right to pronounce divorce under Islamic law. Under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, Section 7, the procedure is strictly regulated:

The Talaq Process

  1. The husband pronounces talaq and gives written notice to the Chairman of the Union Parishad/Pourashava/City Corporation ward within 30 days of pronouncing talaq
  2. The Chairman sends a copy of the notice to the wife
  3. An Arbitration Council is constituted within 30 days of receipt of notice — consisting of a representative of each party and the Chairman
  4. The Arbitration Council has 90 days to attempt reconciliation
  5. If reconciliation fails within the 90-day period, the talaq takes effect at the end of 90 days
  6. During the 90-day iddat period, the wife is entitled to maintenance

Costs for Talaq (2026)

Cost ItemAmount (2026)
Union Parishad/City Corporation Notice Fee৳50–৳200 (fixed government fee)
Arbitration Council proceedings (if any hearing)৳500–৳2,000
Lawyer fee for drafting notice and advising৳3,000–৳20,000
Wife's unpaid Dower (Mahr) — legally dueAs per nikah contract (can be ৳10,000 to several lakhs)
Maintenance during iddat (90 days)Variable based on husband's income
Total (without dower/maintenance)৳3,550–৳22,200

The most significant cost in a talaq is not the procedure itself, but the outstanding Mahr (dower) that the husband must pay to the wife. The Mahr amount is set in the marriage contract (Nikah Nama) and can range from a nominal amount to several lakhs of taka. The wife has an absolute legal right to claim her Mahr before or at the time of divorce.

Type 2: Khul (Wife-Initiated Divorce) – Cost Breakdown

Khul is the wife's right to initiate divorce by returning (or forgoing) her Mahr (dower) to the husband in exchange for the release from the marriage. Under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, Section 8, khul can be done with or without court involvement.

Khul Without Court (If Husband Agrees)

If both parties agree, khul can be completed through the Arbitration Council under the local Union Parishad/City Corporation without going to court:

  1. Wife applies to the Chairman of the local Union Parishad/Pourashava with a written request for khul
  2. Chairman constitutes an Arbitration Council
  3. Parties negotiate the terms of khul (typically, wife returns all or part of her Mahr)
  4. If agreement is reached, Chairman records the divorce and issues a certificate
  5. The 90-day arbitration period applies

Costs for Khul (Without Court) 2026

Cost ItemAmount (2026)
Union Parishad/City Corporation Application Fee৳50–৳200
Arbitration Council proceedings৳500–৳3,000
Lawyer fee (if engaged)৳5,000–৳30,000
Mahr to be returned/waivedAs per nikah contract
Total (without Mahr amount)৳5,550–৳33,200

Khul Via Family Court (If Husband Refuses)

If the husband refuses to accept the khul, the wife must file for Judicial Dissolution of Marriage under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939 in the Family Court. This is significantly more expensive and time-consuming. See the next section for the full cost breakdown of court divorce.

Type 3: Court Divorce / Dissolution of Marriage – Cost Breakdown

A court divorce (also called Judicial Dissolution of Marriage) is required when the wife wants a divorce but the husband refuses to give talaq or accept khul, or when the husband's whereabouts are unknown, or when the marriage was void/invalid. This is governed by the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939 and heard in the Family Court under the Family Courts Ordinance 1985.

Grounds for Judicial Dissolution

Under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939, a wife can seek dissolution of marriage on the following grounds:

  • Husband's whereabouts have been unknown for 4+ years
  • Husband has failed to provide maintenance for 2+ years
  • Husband has been sentenced to 7+ years' imprisonment
  • Husband has failed to perform marital obligations for 3+ years without reasonable cause
  • Husband was impotent at time of marriage and remains so
  • Husband has been insane for 2+ years or suffers from leprosy or virulent venereal disease
  • Wife was given in marriage before age 15 and repudiates the marriage before age 18 (option of puberty)
  • Husband treats wife with cruelty (physical, emotional, financial)

Costs for Court Divorce 2026

Cost ItemAmount (2026)
Court Filing Fee৳200–৳1,000 (based on claim value)
Process fee (summons service)৳100–৳500
Advocate fee (Dhaka)৳20,000–৳1,50,000+
Advocate fee (District towns)৳10,000–৳60,000
Miscellaneous court costs (witnesses, etc.)৳2,000–৳20,000
Maintenance pendente lite (during trial)Court may order monthly maintenance from husband
Total (Dhaka, contested)৳25,000–৳2,00,000+
Total (District, uncontested)৳12,000–৳70,000

Lawyer Fees for Divorce in Bangladesh 2026

Lawyer fees are typically the largest variable cost in any divorce proceeding. Fees vary significantly based on the lawyer's experience and reputation, the location (Dhaka vs. other cities), the complexity of the case, and whether the case is contested or uncontested.

Lawyer Fee Ranges by City (2026)

LocationSimple/Uncontested DivorceContested Divorce (Family Court)Complex Contested + Appeals
Dhaka (Experienced Lawyer)৳15,000–৳40,000৳50,000–৳1,50,000৳1,50,000–৳5,00,000+
Dhaka (Mid-level Lawyer)৳8,000–৳20,000৳25,000–৳70,000৳80,000–৳2,00,000
Chattogram / Sylhet৳5,000–৳15,000৳20,000–৳60,000৳60,000–৳1,50,000
Rajshahi / Khulna / Barishal৳3,000–৳10,000৳15,000–৳40,000৳40,000–৳1,00,000
Upazila/Rural Areas৳2,000–৳8,000৳10,000–৳30,000৳30,000–৳75,000

What Lawyer Fees Typically Include

  • Initial consultation and case assessment
  • Drafting of petitions, replies, and legal documents
  • Attending all court hearings
  • Client counseling and advice throughout the process
  • Negotiating settlements where possible
  • Filing for maintenance, child custody if needed

What May Be Charged Separately

  • Filing fees and court fees (paid to court directly)
  • Witness examination fees
  • Expert witness fees (if needed)
  • Traveling to multiple court dates (for lawyers from outside the district)
  • Appeal fees if the case goes to the High Court

Court Fees for Family Cases in Bangladesh 2026

Under the Court Fees Act, 1870 and the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985, the court fees for family cases in Bangladesh are generally modest. Here is a breakdown of official court fees:

Case TypeCourt Fee (2026)
Dissolution of marriage petitionFixed fee: ৳200
Dower (Mahr) recovery suit — up to ৳1 lakh৳100–৳500 (percentage of claim)
Dower recovery suit — above ৳1 lakhAd valorem (percentage) rate on claim amount
Maintenance suitFixed fee: ৳50–৳200
Child custody petitionFixed fee: ৳200
Guardianship applicationFixed fee: ৳200
Restitution of conjugal rightsFixed fee: ৳200
Process/summons fee৳100–৳500 per respondent

Miscellaneous Court Costs

  • Certified copies of court orders: ৳10–৳50 per page
  • Vakalatnama (power of attorney to lawyer) stamp: ৳20–৳100
  • Affidavit notarization: ৳50–৳200
  • Translation fees (if any document is not in Bengali): ৳200–৳1,000+

The low official court fees in family cases mean that the dominant cost in divorce is almost always the lawyer's fee, not the government fees. This is why selecting the right lawyer with appropriate fees for your circumstances is the most important financial decision in a divorce proceeding.

Maintenance (Nafaqah) and Dower (Mahr) Costs

Two additional significant financial obligations arise from divorce under Muslim law in Bangladesh that are separate from the divorce process costs themselves:

Mahr (Dower)

Mahr is the amount agreed upon in the Nikah Nama (marriage contract) that the husband must pay to the wife. In Bangladesh, Mahr is often a symbolic amount on the Nikah Nama (sometimes as little as ৳5,000 or even less) to avoid large payments. However, the wife has an absolute legal right to her Mahr at any time, including at divorce.

  • Prompt Mahr: Due immediately upon marriage (or whenever the wife demands it)
  • Deferred Mahr: Due at divorce or the husband's death, whichever comes first

If the Mahr is not paid voluntarily, the wife can file a suit in the Family Court for recovery of Mahr. The court will enforce payment, and if the husband cannot pay, the court can order attachment of his property.

Iddat Maintenance

During the iddat period (90 days after talaq or court dissolution), the husband is legally required to provide maintenance to the wife. The amount is based on the husband's income and the wife's needs, and can be determined by court if parties disagree.

Maintenance (Nafaqah) During Marriage and Post-Divorce

Under Muslim law, a husband is required to provide reasonable maintenance to his wife during marriage. At divorce, the wife is entitled to maintenance only during the iddat period. After iddat, the husband's maintenance obligation ends (unlike Western divorce which may involve ongoing alimony). However, if there are minor children, the father must provide maintenance for the children until they reach majority age.

Child Maintenance

Courts in Bangladesh typically award child maintenance based on:

  • The father's income (typically 20%–40% of monthly income for one child)
  • The child's needs and standard of living
  • Number of children

Child maintenance is separate from the cost of the divorce itself but is often litigated simultaneously in the Family Court.

Child Custody and Guardian Cases: Additional Costs

When couples with minor children divorce, child custody and guardianship disputes are common and add significantly to the overall cost and duration of the process.

Child Custody Under Bangladesh Law

Under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 and Muslim personal law as applied in Bangladesh:

  • Physical custody (hizanat): The mother has the right to physical custody of young children — boys until age 7 and girls until puberty under classical Hanafi law. Courts may extend this if in the child's best interest.
  • Legal guardianship: The father is considered the natural legal guardian and has authority over the child's major life decisions (education, marriage, etc.)
  • Best interests of the child: Courts in Bangladesh increasingly apply the 'best interests of the child' standard, which may override traditional Hanafi custody rules in appropriate cases

Additional Costs for Custody Cases

Cost ItemEstimated Amount
Guardianship petition filing fee৳200
Welfare report (if court orders social investigation)Government cost — usually nil
Additional lawyer's fee for custody litigation৳10,000–৳60,000 additional
Appeal to High Court (if needed)৳30,000–৳1,50,000+ additional

Child custody disputes can significantly extend the duration and cost of divorce proceedings. Uncontested custody agreements between the parties (formalized in a consent order) are the most cost-effective approach and are increasingly encouraged by Family Courts.

Total Cost Comparison: Talaq vs Khul vs Court Divorce

Here is a comprehensive comparison of the total expected costs for each type of divorce in Bangladesh in 2026, across different scenarios:

Divorce TypeSimple / UncontestedModerate ComplexityHighly Contested
Talaq (Husband-initiated, wife agrees)৳5,000–৳15,000৳15,000–৳40,000৳40,000–৳1,50,000
Khul (Wife-initiated, husband agrees)৳8,000–৳20,000৳20,000–৳60,000৳60,000–৳1,50,000
Mutual Consent (both agree on all terms)৳5,000–৳12,000৳12,000–৳30,000N/A
Court Dissolution (wife petitions, uncontested)৳15,000–৳40,000৳40,000–৳80,000N/A
Court Dissolution (wife petitions, contested)N/A৳50,000–৳1,20,000৳1,20,000–৳5,00,000+

Note: These costs are for lawyer and court fees only. Additional costs for Mahr payment, maintenance, and child custody (if applicable) are not included and can add substantially to the total.

Estimated Timeline by Divorce Type

Divorce TypeMinimum TimelineTypical Timeline
Talaq (uncontested)90 days (mandatory)3–6 months
Khul (uncontested)90 days3–6 months
Court Dissolution (uncontested)6 months6–18 months
Court Dissolution (contested)1 year2–5 years

Ways to Reduce Divorce Costs in Bangladesh

Divorce can be expensive, but there are practical ways to manage and reduce costs without compromising your legal rights:

1. Negotiate and Agree Before Filing

The single most effective way to reduce divorce costs is for both parties to reach agreement on all major issues (property division, Mahr, maintenance, child custody) before filing any court case. Uncontested divorces cost a fraction of contested ones. A neutral mediator or mutual family members can help facilitate agreement.

2. Use the Arbitration Council Properly

The mandatory Arbitration Council under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 is a free (or nearly free) government service designed specifically to resolve divorce disputes. Take the arbitration process seriously — a resolution here costs almost nothing compared to years in court.

3. Mutual Consent Divorce

If both parties agree to divorce and agree on terms (Mahr, maintenance, custody), a mutual consent divorce through the Union Parishad Arbitration Council is the fastest and cheapest route, typically costing less than ৳15,000 total including lawyer fees.

4. Choose an Appropriate Lawyer

A very expensive senior lawyer is not always necessary. For straightforward uncontested divorces, a competent mid-level lawyer can handle the case efficiently at significantly lower cost. Get consultations from 2–3 lawyers and compare fees before committing.

5. Avoid Unnecessary Litigation

Additional case filings (multiple maintenance applications, custody applications, interim orders) each add cost and time. Focus on the essential case first and add ancillary cases only when absolutely necessary.

6. Consider Legal Aid

If you genuinely cannot afford a private lawyer, you may be eligible for legal aid from the National Legal Aid Services Organization (NLASO). Contact the District Legal Aid Office at your local court to check eligibility. NLASO provides free legal representation for eligible low-income individuals.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does a divorce take in Bangladesh?
A: The minimum time for any divorce is 90 days (the mandatory arbitration/iddat period). An uncontested divorce takes 3–6 months. A contested court divorce takes 1–5 years depending on complexity and court backlog.

Q: Can a wife get divorce without going to court?
A: Yes, if the husband agrees. The wife can initiate khul through the Union Parishad Arbitration Council without going to court if the husband accepts the khul. If the husband refuses, the wife must file a dissolution of marriage suit in the Family Court.

Q: Does the wife have to return the Mahr to get a divorce?
A: In a khul divorce, the wife traditionally returns the Mahr or agrees to waive it in exchange for the divorce. However, in a court dissolution of marriage (where cruelty or other grounds exist), the wife may not have to return the Mahr. The court has discretion to determine Mahr obligations based on the grounds of divorce.

Q: Can the husband prevent the wife from getting a court divorce?
A: The husband cannot legally prevent a court divorce if valid grounds exist under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939. However, a contested husband can delay the process for years through legal challenges, which is one reason contested divorces are expensive.

Q: What happens to jointly owned property in divorce?
A: Unlike Western divorce systems, Bangladesh Muslim law does not automatically divide marital property equally. Property owned by each spouse before and during the marriage generally remains their separate property. The wife's main financial claims are for her Mahr, iddat maintenance, and child maintenance. For jointly invested or purchased property, a separate civil suit for partition or recovery may be required.

Q: Is divorce legal in Bangladesh for Hindus?
A: Bangladesh does not have a statutory Hindu divorce law. Hindu couples generally cannot divorce through a court procedure in the Western sense. However, in practice, desertion and separation are common, and legal separation agreements can be drafted. This is a complex area of law where consultation with a lawyer is essential.

How Adv. Shah Alam Can Help

Divorce is one of the most emotionally and financially challenging experiences of a person's life. At the Law Chamber of Adv. Md. Shah Alam in Uttara, Dhaka, we provide compassionate, professional, and cost-effective legal assistance for all aspects of divorce and family law in Bangladesh:

  • Talaq advisory: We advise husbands on the proper procedure for talaq under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, ensure all notices are correctly filed, and minimize the risk of legal complications
  • Khul negotiation: We represent wives seeking khul, negotiate the terms of the khul agreement with the husband or his representatives, and ensure the process is completed correctly and quickly through the Arbitration Council
  • Family Court litigation: We represent wives seeking dissolution of marriage under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939, including filing the petition, presenting evidence of the grounds, and arguing for the decree
  • Mahr recovery: We file and argue suits for recovery of outstanding Mahr (dower) — your most significant financial right in a divorce
  • Maintenance applications: We apply for interim and permanent maintenance (nafaqah) from the Family Court, ensuring you and your children receive adequate financial support during and after the divorce process
  • Child custody: We represent your interests in child custody and guardianship proceedings, focusing on the best interests of the child while protecting your parental rights
  • Mediation: Where appropriate, we facilitate mediated settlements between parties to resolve all issues quickly and cost-effectively, avoiding years of court battles

Our chamber is located in Uttara, Dhaka, and we handle family law cases across all districts of Bangladesh. We offer a free initial consultation — completely confidential — to assess your situation.

Wife Leaves or Forced Out of In-Law's House: Husband Legal Remedies in Bangladesh

By Advocate Md. Shah Alam · 2026-11-10 · 10 min read

⚠️ Legal Disclaimer: This article provides general legal information only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice specific to your situation, consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam directly at +880 1712-655546.

Imagine coming home from work to discover that after an intense argument with your parents, your wife has packed her belongings and returned to her father's home, cutting off communication. Or imagine your own family members forcing your wife out of the house against your wishes during an escalating domestic dispute. In Bangladesh, matrimonial friction involving in-laws frequently triggers panic, threats of criminal litigation, and legal confusion. Understanding your exact statutory rights under the Family Courts Act 2023, the Domestic Violence Act 2010, and Muslim family law is essential to preserve your marriage, protect your family from false criminal cases, and establish a legally sound path forward.

: · Divorce & Family Court Lawyer in Bangladesh

Quick Answer Table — Key Legal Facts at a Glance (2026)

Key Legal AspectOfficial Rule, Fee & Law (2026)
Governing StatuteCode of Criminal Procedure 1898 (Sections 496, 497, 498, 499) & Penal Code 1860
Bail & Surety RequirementExecution of Form-42 Bail Bond (PR Bond / Jamindar Surety) upon court bail order

  2. Immediate Protective Step: Filing a General Diary (GD)
  3. Formal Legal Notice for Reconciliation and Co-habitation

  5. Domestic Violence Act 2010: Residence Orders and In-Laws
  6. Shielding Against Preemptive False Dowry Allegations

The Real-Life Dilemma: In-Law Friction and Separation

In Bangladesh's socio-cultural context, joint and extended family households remain common. While this living arrangement provides community support, it can also create intense psychological friction between a newly married wife and her in-laws. Misunderstandings regarding household chores, privacy, finances, or personal boundaries frequently boil over into severe confrontations. In many instances, the wife packs her bags and returns to her paternal home, refusing all contact. In other tragic scenarios, overbearing in-laws expel the wife from the marital home while the husband is away at work or trapped in the middle, torn between parental obligations and marital devotion.

When this rupture occurs, the immediate reaction of both families often escalates the crisis. The wife's family may accuse the husband and his relatives of mental torture and unlawful dowry demands under the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 or Section 11(ga) of the Nari O Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 2000. Conversely, the husband may feel paralyzed, fearing that contacting her will trigger aggressive police complaints. The law in Bangladesh does not leave husbands helpless, but it requires calm, strategic, and legally documented steps rather than emotional outbursts.

Immediate Protective Step: Filing a General Diary (GD)

The very first legal safeguard a husband must execute when his wife leaves the matrimonial home or is forced out by domestic disputes is lodging a General Diary (GD) at the local police station (Thana) having territorial jurisdiction over the residence. Alternatively, this can be submitted through the Bangladesh Police online GD portal (gd.police.gov.bd).

The purpose of this GD is not to criminalize the wife or file a hostile complaint against her. Rather, it serves as a crucial contemporaneous protective record. When marital discord erupts, a common litigation tactic is for the estranged wife's family to lodge an FIR alleging that she was physically assaulted for unpaid dowry on the very day she left, or that she was unlawfully confined. A properly drafted GD establishes the objective timeline:

  • It states the exact date and time the wife departed the residence, noting that she left of her own accord or following a family disagreement.
  • It explicitly notes that she took her personal ornaments, clothing, and identification papers safely without any physical obstruction.
  • It affirms that the husband made no demands for dowry and remains committed to maintaining her and preserving the marriage.
  • It records the husband's sincere apprehension that third-party agitators may file fabricated criminal petitions against him and his elderly parents.

Having a certified, police-stamped GD on record creates an invaluable evidentiary defense if retaliatory criminal cases are subsequently filed in the Magistrate Court or Nari O Shishu Tribunal.

Formal Legal Notice for Reconciliation and Co-habitation

Once the protective GD is recorded, the husband should not resort to informal verbal arguments or harassing text messages, which can easily be twisted into evidence of stalking or cyber harassment. Instead, he should instruct an experienced family law advocate to draft and dispatch a formal Legal Notice through registered post with acknowledgement due (AD) to her paternal address.

A well-crafted legal notice strikes a balanced, respectful, yet firm tone:

  1. Reaffirmation of Marital Commitment: The notice cites the registered Kabinnama, affirms the solemnity of the marriage, and declares that the husband holds deep affection for his wife and desires to resume peaceful cohabitation.
  2. Address the Root Conflict: If the separation was caused by conflict with the husband's parents or siblings, the notice should clearly offer a viable solution, such as arranging a separate, self-contained rental flat away from the in-laws to safeguard her mental peace and dignity.
  3. Formal Invitation to Return: It provides a reasonable window (typically 15 to 30 days) inviting her to return to the matrimonial home or meet with respected community mediators for amicable reconciliation.
  4. Warning Against Unlawful Dissolution: It reminds the recipient that unilateral abandonment without lawful cause infringes upon reciprocal marital obligations under Muslim personal law.

This document proves beyond doubt in any future judicial proceeding that the husband did not abandon his wife and made earnest, formal efforts to restore the conjugal relationship.

Family Courts Act 2023: Restitution of Conjugal Rights

If the legal notice goes unanswered or the wife's family flatly refuses to allow communication, the husband's definitive civil remedy lies in the Family Court. Under Section 5(a) of the Family Courts Act 2023 (which updated and replaced the Family Courts Ordinance 1985), the Family Court exercises exclusive civil jurisdiction over suits relating to the Restitution of Conjugal Rights (Dampattya Punoruddhar).

Filing a suit for Restitution of Conjugal Rights achieves several profound legal objectives:

  • Mandatory Pre-Trial Conciliation: Under Section 11 of the Family Courts Act 2023, the Family Court judge is statutorily mandated to conduct in-camera pre-trial conciliation. Both husband and wife are summoned into the judge's private chambers without aggressive relatives, allowing the court to explore whether the marriage can be salvaged through separate living arrangements or mutual commitments.
  • Neutral Ground for Dialogue: Many estranged wives want to return but are restrained by dominating parents or siblings. The Family Court provides an authoritative, neutral environment where she can voice her true desires freely before a judicial officer.
  • Judicial Decree: If conciliation fails and the trial proceeds, the court evaluates whether the wife had a lawful excuse (such as proven physical cruelty or unpaid prompt dower) to refuse cohabitation. If no lawful excuse exists, the court passes a decree for Restitution of Conjugal Rights declaring that she is legally obligated to reside with her husband.

It is important to understand that in modern jurisprudence, a decree for Restitution of Conjugal Rights cannot be executed by physical force or police arrest. However, the decree permanently documents that the husband is not at fault, serving as a complete defense against claims that he deserted his spouse.

Domestic Violence Act 2010: Residence Orders and In-Laws

Where the wife was physically forced out of the home by the husband's parents or siblings, the statutory framework of the Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act 2010 comes directly into play. Under Section 3 of this Act, domestic violence encompasses not only physical and sexual violence, but also emotional, verbal, and economic abuse—including unlawfully expelling a woman from the shared household.

Under Section 10 and Section 11 of the Domestic Violence Act 2010, an aggrieved wife has the statutory right to apply to the Judicial Magistrate Court for a Residence Order. The court can order that the wife not be evicted from the shared household, or mandate that the family provide her with suitable alternative accommodation commensurate with their financial standing. If the husband wishes to protect his wife from hostile in-laws, he can proactively secure an independent rental apartment and present the tenancy agreement to the court, demonstrating full compliance with spousal accommodation obligations and neutralizing any domestic violence petitions aimed at his extended family.

Shielding Against Preemptive False Dowry Allegations

The single greatest hazard a husband faces following marital separation is retaliatory criminal litigation. Spouses and their advisers frequently weaponize Section 11(ga) of the Nari O Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 2000 (simple hurt for dowry) or Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018. Because offenses under Nari O Shishu are non-bailable, police or court warrants can result in immediate custody, devastating professional careers and government employment.

To establish an impenetrable defense, the husband must compile a comprehensive paper trail:

  1. Contemporaneous Records: Produce the certified Thana GD and Advocate Legal Notice dispatched prior to the filing of the criminal case, proving that the dispute originated from domestic estrangement rather than unlawful dowry demands.
  2. Section 5 Dowry Prohibition Act Counter-Prosecution: Section 5 of the Dowry Prohibition Act 2018 makes it a specific criminal offense—punishable by up to 5 years imprisonment and severe fines—to institute a false or malicious dowry complaint against a spouse or in-laws.
  3. Anticipatory Bail Petitions: If an FIR or CR case is lodged, the husband and his implicated family members can approach the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh under Section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) for Anticipatory Bail, shielding them from arrest while the case is investigated.

Documenting your legal posture before the opponent strikes is the definitive difference between spending weeks in custody and securing complete exoneration.

Maintenance and Dower Liabilities During Separation

A critical question during separation is whether the husband must continue paying spousal maintenance (Khorposh) while his wife resides at her father's home. Under Islamic jurisprudence and Section 9 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, a husband is legally bound to provide adequate maintenance to his wife, encompassing food, clothing, shelter, and medical care.

However, an important legal nuance applies: if a wife leaves the matrimonial home voluntarily without any lawful justification (such as extreme cruelty, torture, or non-payment of prompt dower), and refuses to return despite the husband's reasonable offers of a safe home, she may be classified as Nashizah (rebellious or disobedient) under personal law. During the period of unjustified refusal, her entitlement to ongoing maintenance can be contested in the Family Court.

Nevertheless, legal prudence dictates that the husband should not abruptly stop financial support while the dispute is pending. If children are involved, child maintenance is absolute and non-negotiable under all circumstances. Sending a reasonable monthly allowance via verifiable banking channels or mobile financial services (with clear transaction descriptions: 'Spousal and Child Maintenance') completely disarms claims that the husband subjected her to economic starvation.

The table below provides a comparative overview of the legal steps a husband can pursue when his wife is separated due to in-law friction:

Separate Residence OfferDomestic Violence Act 2010 §11Eliminate friction between wife and in-lawsNeutralizes domestic violence claims against parents
Voluntary Maintenance TransferMFLO 1961 Section 9Provide verifiable living support during separationDefeats claims of economic abuse and abandonment

Executing these steps sequentially establishes an unassailable legal position, whether the ultimate outcome is reconciliation or an orderly, lawful dissolution.

Illustrative Scenario: Resolving In-Law Estrangement

The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) demonstrates how a structured legal defense protected a family in Dhaka:

A software engineer living in a joint family residence in Mirpur married in late 2024. Within six months, severe domestic friction arose between his mother and his wife over household management. Following a bitter argument, the wife's brothers arrived with vehicles, took all her personal belongings, and brought her to her parental home in Cumilla. The husband attempted to call her, but her brothers threatened him with a dowry torture lawsuit under the Nari O Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain unless he paid BDT 10,00,000 immediately as 'settlement compensation.'

Rather than submitting to blackmail or reacting impulsively, the husband consulted an advocate. Within 24 hours, they lodged a comprehensive General Diary at Mirpur Model Thana, documenting the exact date, the departure in her brothers' vehicles, and the extortionate phone calls. Two weeks later, the advocate dispatched a formal Legal Notice offering to lease a separate two-bedroom apartment in Dhanmondi exclusively for the couple, away from both sets of in-laws.

When the wife's family ignored the notice, the husband instituted a suit for Restitution of Conjugal Rights in the Family Court. During mandatory pre-trial conciliation under Section 11 of the Family Courts Act 2023, the judge reviewed the GD, the legal notice, and the tenancy agreement for the separate flat. Confronted with this unassailable documentation, the wife admitted in the judge's private chambers that she wished to live with her husband, but her family had coerced her into demanding cash. The court mediated a signed reconciliation agreement: the couple moved into their independent residence, and the threatened false criminal litigation evaporated entirely.

Talk to an Advocate

Matrimonial crises involving in-law conflict require delicate handling, seasoned emotional judgment, and uncompromising legal precision. One misstep—such as sending an angry voice message or ignoring a police summons—can transform a simple domestic disagreement into years of harrowing criminal litigation in the Magistrate Courts. A skilled family law advocate helps you de-escalate tensions, safeguard your elderly parents from malicious prosecution, and navigate the Family Court conciliation process with dignity and strength.
